PWM’s Strategic Direction 2013 - 2017 
 
PWM is guided by its Goal, Vision, Mission and Values to take on the challenge in implementing this 
Strategic Plan for 2013 – 2017. 
 
Goal 
“To mobilise, educate and equip the communities with relevant skills and resources to make 
informed decisions to protect and utilise their natural resources sustainably.” 
 
Vision 
“Well informed, organized, motivated and self-reliant societies living in peace and harmony with 
their environment.” 
 
Mission  
“PWM is committed to facilitate, formalize and strengthen conservation & sustainable community 
development efforts through education and consensus building processes with effective networking 
and partnerships.” 
 
New Core Values 
1. Environmental Stewardship: PWM believes in the protection of the environment and its 
biodiversity. 
2. Indigenous Peoples: PWM promotes and values the cultures of Melanesian societies. 
3. Community Empowerment: PWM believes in facilitating and empowering members of the 
community in taking the lead in their own development. 
4. Partnerships and Networking: PWM promotes strong and effective partnerships and 
networking with relevant stakeholders. 
5. Transparency and Accountability: PWM promotes good governance through transparency 
and accountability. 
 
Supporting Values 
I. 
Trust and Reliability: 
PWM staff must be trusted and relied to accomplish their respective duties with 
minimum supervision. 
II. 
Respect and Equality: 

PWM Strategic Plan 
 
2013 - 2017
 
8 
 
PWM is an equal opportunity organization that provides opportunity for both men and 
women to work side by side to maximise the expected outputs. 
III. 
Participation and Consultation: 
PWM resolved to engage the management and project levels through participation and 
consultation. 
IV. 
Honesty and Integrity: 
PWM staff are expected to maintain an honest profile and good reputation while 
working for the organization. 
V. 
Transparent and Accountable: 
PWM will seek to develop and apply all processes that allow it to be transparent and 
accountable in all its transaction between donors, partners and communities. 
VI. 
Confidentiality: 
PWM staff are required to keep all confidentially all times regarding operations of the 
organization where harm is likely to be attracted to the organization. 
VII. 
Commitment and Dedication: 
PWM staff are required to commit him/herself thoroughly to the goals and objectives of 
the organization at all times. 
VIII. 
Time Management: 
PWM has resolved to apply methods and approaches that promote time management 
for all staff in such ways to improve productivity and output. 
IX. 
Effective and Efficient: 
PWM has recognised that efficiency and effectiveness are required from all staff in every 
endeavour so that sloppiness and time wasters are minimised. 
X. 
Attitude and Conduct: 
PWM staff are required to maintain a cordial attitude and respectable behaviour at the 
office environment and most importantly at the community level. 
XI. 
Stewardship: 
PWM requires all staff to be good stewards of all assets and resources such that 
maximum benefit is accrued to the organization. 
XII. 
Love and Self-esteem: 
PWM staff are expected to maintain a high self-esteem profile that will motivate their 
actions and attitudes to all persons within and outside the organization.

Executive Summary 
 
Its no mistake that the title of this report borrows from the report conducted ten years ago by 
Greg Abare, Paul Chatterton and Tialepa Samuel (Abare et al 2001). Following our terms of 
reference, we have tried to assess the changes between the Managalas Sustainable 
Development Project in 2000 and today, 2010, and especially to examine how well the first 
reports recommendations may have been heeded. Rather than call our follow‐up Lek istrong 
nau or Yumi sanap pinis, suggesting all such work had been completed, and that all the old 
issues solved, we chose to call this Strongim leg gen‐‐‐to imply that much still has to be done. It 
is our assessment that much has to be rebuilt for the project before Partners with Melanesians 
(PwM) can safely handover to Managalas Development Foundation [MDF], as planned.  
 
Still, one of the important points to be made about this‐‐‐as any other conservation project in 
Papua New Guinea (PNG)is that there is never an end, never a mission accomplished 
moment when people can walk away satisfied. In the Introduction and the Conclusion here we 
cite studies of similar projects that explain the particular politics involved in this kind of work: 
what scholars have come to call the political ecology of Papua New Guinea (Van Helden 1998, 
West 2006). Much of what has transpired on the Managalas Plateau is much like issues in 
Crater Mountain, Bismark‐Ramu, Lak, Collingwood Bay and other PNG high profile conservation 
projects. The chore now is to figure out how to move forward from this: how to set a precedent 
for successful conservation efforts in the future. We are therefore concerned that our 
evaluation become more than a report card, and that it is circulated as widely as possible to all 
stakeholders, including those on the Plateau. If it happens to misrepresent the events of the 
recent past, we apologize: but we also hope the discussion generates more positive changes 
than did the last report. It would be yet another terrible waste of precious donor funding if the 
recommendations and anecdotal opinions contained in this document were placed on a shelf 
and forgotten, or written off as too extreme. 
  
It is our firm belief that conservation is always worth it, and that however rocky the effort, it is 
never wasted. Even the most difficult projects in PNG have succeeded in transforming peoples 
awareness of their rainforest from being the home of spirits, and a source of limitless protein, 
to the most precious heirloom one generation can bequeath to the next. The simple fact is that 
the more time a conservation NGO spends in a target community, the more people come to 
value their forest. Thus, everything we say here is predicated on the assumption that the 
Managalas Sustainable Development Project can and will continue through a transition from 
Partners with Melanesians to the Managalas Development Foundation. 
 
Summary of findings 

Strongim Lek Gen   Nancy Sullivan and Assoc 2010 
 
6 
 
 
Managalas Sustainable Development Project (MSDP) has been a success on many levels. Its 
main conservation objectives have been advanced, which is a considerable accomplishment. 
The consensus built to get to this point, twenty years on, is unparalleled elsewhere in PNG.  
Rainforest on the Managalas Plateau has been spared from predatory logging and other 
environmental threats. 
But the threats still exist, and the pressure to capitulate to them appears to have escalated in 
the last few years. People told us in a couple of zones that they are now ready for logging and 
mining, they have had enough of conservation with no visible benefits to their lifestyle.  
Sentiments like these are ever‐present in conservation projects, and constitute the most 
serious threats to their sustainability. The implication is that once the NGO(s) and their 
programs disappear, so too will the rainforest. But as part of the predictability of these projects, 
some policy needs to exist that will constantly address such threats. The best buffer is always 
rainforest literacy, which, over time, can convince the disgruntled that their best interests lie in 
conservation after all. But more fundamentally, the consensus building process needs to 
include awareness of the NGOs limitations and the fact that they are facilitators, not 
benefactors. Where we heard these comments we also learned that the PwM team had rarely 
come around to visit, and certainly had made little effort to explain their efforts on that zones 
behalf. Negligence has an enormous price in conservation. 
The levels on which PwM has not been successful are predictable, but not insoluble. There are 
political problems, organizational problems, and gender equity problems. These are all related. 
It appears that the nepotism and wantokism that clogs the wheels on the community level has 
also come to plague the office in Port Moresby. Understandably, the MOCP project officer who 
brought down that project and almost the entire NGO, Paul Konia, has now been fired and the 
staff rebuilt. But part of the collateral damage of that issue was the retirement of Pauls wife, 
Ruth, who played an important role both in the office and as a role model for women in the 
field. In addition, the project itself has not been recorded thoroughly, so has yet to be resolved 
in the minds of Plateau villagers. As a result, a real spike in the anti‐Highlands sentiment can be 
heard everywhere we traveled, with people attributing the misdemeanors of Paul to all 
Highlanders, and therefore expressing their bigoted distrust of the current Executive Director, 
Kenn Mondiai. The fear on the ground is that monies intended for the Plateau project are being 
misdirected to the new highlands projects, and that PwM is no longer dedicated to Oro. The 
prevalence of misinformation on the ground reflects very poor communication and 
transparency on the part of PwM. However many toksaves have been conducted, they have 
clearly not be enough. 
On the other hand, the success of the Tok Pisin literacy program is remarkable. Such is the Tok 
Pisin fluency on the Plateau that it now seems even more important to introduce English 
language training. Now that SIL has left the Plateau, however, there is a dramatic drop off in 
interest and application.  
Communication has been important to the project for its absence. Charters and vehicles are 
expensive, which has kept the travel from Port Moresby to the Plateau down recently. But the 

Strongim Lek Gen   Nancy Sullivan and Assoc 2010 
 
7 
 
lack of telephone or radio communication has been even more subversive. Telephone access 
can hardly be attributed to the Partners negligence (although it can be argued that a campaign 
to bring Digicel or Bemobile towers would have been very important to the project), but radio 
communication seems to be a service PwM promised, then provided, and ultimately 
abandoned for various technical and perhaps financial reasons. As a result, the lack of 
communication has exacerbated the frustrations of people in virtually all zones. Many of the 
sociopolitical problems that have emerged in the last couple of years could have been 
dissipated by regular radio communication between the office and the field. This is a vital link 
that needs to be established now. 
The roll of programs and legal battles has been poorly scheduled. It is our assessment that the 
legal status of the zone should have been established before some of the projects began. 
Conservation status has not been established, and twenty years later certain zones are ready to 
invite resource developers instead. We believe that the legal status of the plateau should have 
come well before most of the entrepreneurial programs. 
At 
the 
village 
level 
only 
selected 
participants take part in programs and this 
approach can encourage biased selection, 
undermining 
the 
objectives 
of 
full 
participation. The level of involvement and 
interest has been reduced in the recent 
years and one of the contributing factors is 
the repetition of program activities. One 
interviewee 
commented 
called 
it: 
awareness, awareness and no action. 
Awareness 
and 
training 
without 
appropriate 
technologies/materials 
has 
come to look like a con game for the villagers. Most of zones are not currently benefiting from 
the programs. This has led people to call PwM lazy or disinterestedeven incapable or 
unwilling to walk to distant zones like 4, 9 and 10.  
There are a lot of conflicts, misunderstandings, and rumours circulating across the Plateau. Our 
impression is that these have increased in the past two or three years. People tell us that staff 
are being paid for not performing, both at the CBO and the NGO level. This perception will 
affect the sustainability of the conservation effort because it will erode consensus over time. To 
keep the project viable, PwM and MDF must urgently resolve their difference and allow 
cooperation to prevail. Only then can the two skill sets combine to preserve the project. 
 
Women are pleased to take part in program activities and have not been as systematically 
denied power as was the case leading up to the 2001 evaluation. A number of women have 
joined CBOs and there are more women on the Boards than before. But it is a long road to 
gender parity in the western sense, and cannot be forced upon PNG communities of the 
women themselves. A better approach to gender parity would be to focus on their economic 
needs as separate from those of the menfolk, and to establish microfinance and training 

Strongim Lek Gen   Nancy Sullivan and Assoc 2010 
 
8 
 
programs restricted to women alone. The new Gender Officer for MDF must also make rounds 
to all the zonesthis is crucial, as women everywhere feel neglected. 
 
The following are our major recommendations. The data upon which they are based is spelled 
out and discussed in the body of the report. 
 
a. Recommendations 
There are several major recommendations that would apply to all zones on the Plateau, and all 
participants in the MSDP. Following these here, we add particular recommendations that 
emerged from findings in each zone. 
Education: 
Recommendation: Restart the education and enterprise programs immediately. Conservation, 
Forest Literacy, eco‐enterprise and sustainable livelihood programs are very effective and 
consistent, but it appears programs were only implemented according to Activity Funding. Most 
communities claim that the programs have not been implemented for the past 3‐5 years.  
Elsewhere, people say trainings and or workshops have been conducted just once a year. 
They must be conducted on time, and as equably as possible. Programs and activities do not fall 
on schedule time but are delayed. They are also concentrated in the West subdivision of the 
project area, which has led to unequal distribution of goods and services, as well as loss of 
interest from the eastern communities.  
Consensus: 
Recommendation: The consensus building process should be revisited and redesigned and use 
that process to sorted issues, misunderstanding, and frustrations in relation to the 28 priority 
projects. PwM to seek external support to facilitate this confidence and trust building process. 
MDF does not have the financial capacity, nor the knowledge and skills on how to manage and 
administrate resources. There appears to have been, and in some case still be, misuse of 
resources in both the management and board levels of MDF and PwM.  
Those who argue in favor of MDF reason that the staff has the capability in terms of 
management and administration but that they are hindered by funding given by PwM under the 
program budget. It seems that the incentives as well as other aspects of the project are not fully 
catered for. This has led to staff losing interest and commitment in doing their job. However, 
most have sacrificed time, effort and resources to carryout activities and other management 
and administrative functions. 
Recommendation: Identify relevant or appropriate stakeholders and establish dialogue with 
them and have them feel that they part of the programs. Development and documentation of 
concept papers of each program, to be given to relevant stakeholders specifying their roles and 
how they will benefit from the programs. Have specific activities like stakeholder workshops, 
meetings for this purpose. 

Strongim Lek Gen   Nancy Sullivan and Assoc 2010 
 
9 
 
 
Recommendation: PwM staff must walk the Plateau. They must meet MDF in the zones, walk 
through the villages and focus on the most remote and neglected zones together with the MDF 
personnel. 
 
Recommendation: Focus on communication from the zones to the field and Port Moresby 
offices. This means providing CB/VHF radios and also lobbying Digicel and Telikom for towers. 
The single most important tool for the transition‐‐‐including sustaining consensus and building 
networksis regular and open communication.  
 
Recommendation: Bring in volunteers. Because individuals have been so influential on the 
Plateau, we recommend new volunteers be recruited from National Volunteer Service, VSO, or 
Australian Volunteer Services, to reanimate some of the excitement in the Project that could be 
felt fifteen years ago when Nancy Sullivan first walked across the Plateau. These people come 
for two or three years (hopefully longer), and while they dont always succeed in building the 
capacity they might hope, they almost always leave a positive impact upon their host 
communities.  As literacy or adult education volunteers, agricultural consultants, health 
workers, even volunteer clerical workers for the MDF office, their skill sets are always needed.   
Conservation: 
Recommendation: Fast track conservation status efforts. 
 
Recommendation: Draft land use plans for each zone, and institute both rewards and penalties 
for adhering to them.  In some cases, families that follow plans closely should be given priority 
treatment to other programs (like training, enterprise, etc). 
 
Recommendation: Address the existing mining and logging threats in key zones. Investigate the 
levels of outreach each developer has made to the community and remind CBOs of the 
conservation objectives of MSDP. 
 
Recommendation: Establish a butterfly project in zone 4 where there are serious threats at the 
border from mining. Need a flagship species of flora or fauna for local conservation 
understanding (not so much to sell to donors).

INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND 
 
This is the fourth Strategic Planning Document for Partners With Melanesians Inc. since its 
establishment in 1984. 
Partners With Melanesians Inc. is the longest serving Conservation NGO’s still functional amidst the 
changing and challenging political and socio-economic conditions which caused similar organizations 
to change their visions, missions, objectives and aspirations or to cease operations. 
 
The first strategic plan for PWM from 2002 – 2006 was developed in 2001, following the first 
external evaluation of PWM’s work on the proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project. The 
strategic document pointed PWM in the direction of concrete and distinct ground work in preparing 
the application for acquiring the conservation area status for the Managalas Conservation Area 
Project, while paving the way for PWM to extend its work to new sites. In 2006, PWM did scoping 
visits to new areas, broadening her horizon beyond the terrain of the Managalas plateau to 
neighbouring areas of Wowonga and Musa. Scoping was also conducted in the Lembena area 
bothering the East Sepik, Enga and Western Highlands Provinces. Wowonga and Musa did not pass 
the criteria due to various reasons, while PWM began community mobilizing in Lembena at the 
invitation of the locals. However, local political differences interfered with work which resulted in 
the early exit. Subsequently, PWM in consultation with the donor and partners shifted its efforts and 
concentrated its efforts in working with the Karimui Conservation Area Project, since the local CBO 
there for 4 years consistently requested and followed PWM to work with them as its partner.  
 
 
The Second Strategic Planning Document from 2007 – 2011 ensured high concentration of 
sustainable livelihood activities to support the conservation efforts on the Managalas Plateau. For 
instance, the Managalas Organic Coffee Project, which has the potential to be highly profitable, yet, 
high establishment, operational and logistics costs from the farmers to the markets, coupled by 
natural disaster and miss-management led to an early closure without realizing its full potential. The 
document also highlighted systems and procedures to be put in place along the systematic and 
strategic lines of the various programs that should be accomplished with a thorough Organizational 
Development. Towards the end of that phase, a second evaluation was conducted with specific 
recommendations for way forward. In 2011, Inaina Wildlife Management Area and the proposed 
Karimui Conservation Area Project became PWM’s project sites.  
 
The following year, PWM ensured a desk-top organizational development review in March 2012, of 
which recommendations from the review set the basis for the organizational development workshop 
that took place between end of June – to early July 2013. The organizational development workshop 
ensured PWM was characterized through the different stages of an organizational development 
cycle, where PWM’s life stage was clearly visible as one reaching its final stage. 
 
The Third Strategic Planning Document from 2013 – 2017 made certain the recommendations from 
the second evaluation were considered for implementation. While PWM is working on ensuring 
recommendations are being implemented to ensure effective and efficient systems and procedures 
to ensure its success and growth, there is need for the organization to review and renew its 

 
 pg. 3 
 
Ruth Konia – May 2017 
strategies as was evident from the outcome of the Organizational Development Report. 
Consequently, PWM conducted an organizational retreat in February 2016.  
 
During the retreat, PWM revisited its Vision, Mission, Goal, Objectives and Values, making slight 
alterations to fit into the changing economic and social conditions. PWM re-defined its Vision from: 
“Well informed, organized, motivated and self-reliant societies living in peace and harmony with 
their environment” to “Melanesian societies living in peace and harmony with nature and the 
environment”. The Mission was also redefined to link the objectives. It was highlighted during the 
retreat that communities perceived PWM as the one responsible for ensuring community 
development, thus the word development was changed to correct this miss-conception. From: 
“PWM is committed to facilitate, formulate and strengthen conservation and sustainable community 
development efforts through education and consensus building process with effective networking 
and partnerships” to “PWM is committed to facilitate, formulate and strengthen conservation and 
sustainable community initiatives through education and consensus building process with effective 
networking and partnerships”. 
 
For over three (3) decades, PWM’s first project site, the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area was 
at the final stages of being declared the county’s biggest conservation area under the old 
Conservation Areas Act (1978). 
 The Conservation Area application was approved by the National Executive Council on 15th of 
December 2016 and gazetted by the Governor General on the 22nd of March 2017. 
 
Towards the end of 2016, PWM conducted scoping and stakeholder community consultations in the 
Collinwood Bay area of the Oro Province. A series of community consultations and meetings with the 
communities continued to 2017 to iron out issues amongst the tribal groups and existing CBOs 
before PWM rolls out its programs. Concrete work is expected to commence in 2018, as activity 
plans have been incorporated into the next four years (2018-2021) funding application to RFN.  
This has now become another one of PWM’s projects. 
 
The hard work of community mobilization, education awareness and consensus building has been 
rewarded with the granting of the conservation area status for the Managalas Conservation Area, 
however, the real challenge beyond 2018 is the strengthening of the local umbrella organization 
with the necessary capacity in terms of skills, knowledge and resources to be equipped in managing 
the conservation area while ensuring the environment is sustainably managed and local 
communities continue to utilise their resources in the conservation area. The challenge also remains 
true for the Inaina Wildlife Management Area in the Central Province. The Inaina WMA was granted 
the WMA status on 18th July, 2016 and the official launching of the WMA status at Inaina was on 23rd 
March, 2017. 
 
Time is rife for another evaluation of PWM projects amidst these achievements and challenges. It is 
time to re-organise, restructure and develop new partnerships with external players. 
 
In this fourth strategic document, PWM is aligning its work with the Government’s Vision 2050, 
especially Pillar 5 on “Environmental Sustainability and Climate Change,” and as embedded in the 4th 

 
 pg. 4 
 
Ruth Konia – May 2017 
Goal of the Country’s Constitution “Papua New Guinea’s natural environment to be conserved and 
used for the collective benefit of us all and are replenished for the benefit of future generations”. 
 
PWM is also guarded by the overarching policies including the ‘Environment Act 2000’ and the 
‘Protected Areas Policy’ in achieving conservation outcomes in its efforts, all the while, taking into 
consideration the ‘Conservation Areas Management Act’ and the ‘Flora and Fauna Wildlife 
Management Act’ (outdated but now incorporated or amalgamated into the Conservation Act 2000) 
which will still be used as guiding posts for her efforts. 
 
PWM is committed in working with local communities and resource owners through networking and 
partnerships with other national and international NGOs and donor organizations, private and public 
sectors including the respective local, provincial and national government agencies in building the 
capacities of the resource owners in conserving, managing and utilising their resources for their 
livelihoods for now and future generations.  
 
This document contained the nine (9) key strategies and expected results which will be deliberated 
in a detailed work plan over the five years of this document. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 pg. 5 
 
Ruth Konia – May 2017 
PWM is guided by its Vision, Mission, Goal and Values in realising its

“Melanesian societies living in peace and harmony with nature and the environment”

“PWM is committed to facilitate, formulate and strengthen conservation and sustainable community 
initiatives through education and consensus building process with effective networking and 
partnerships” 
 
Goal  
“To mobilise, educate and equip the communities with relevant skills and resources to make 
informed decisions to protect and utilise their natural resources sustainably” 
 
 
 Core Values 
1. Environmental Stewardship: PWM believes in the protection of the environment and its 
biodiversity. 
2. Indigenous Peoples: PWM promotes and values the cultures of Melanesian societies. 
3. Community Empowerment: PWM believes in facilitating and empowering members of the 
community in taking the lead in their own development. 
4. Partnerships and Networking: PWM promotes strong and effective partnerships and 
networking with relevant stakeholders. 
5. Transparency and Accountability: PWM promotes good governance through transparency 
and accountability. 
 
Supporting Values 
I. 
Trust and Reliability: 
PWM staff must be trusted and relied to accomplish their respective duties with 
minimum supervision. 
II. 
Respect and Equality: 
PWM is an equal opportunity organization that provides opportunity for both men and 
women to work side by side to maximise the expected outputs. 
III. 
Participation and Consultation: 
PWM resolved to engage the management and project levels through participation and 
consultation.

Honesty and Integrity: 
PWM staffs are expected to maintain an honest profile and good reputation while 
working for the organization. 
V. 
Transparent and Accountable: 
PWM will seek to develop and apply all processes that allow it to be transparent and 
accountable in all its transaction between donors, partners and communities. 
VI. 
Confidentiality: 
PWM staff are required to keep all confidentially all times regarding operations of the 
organization where harm is likely to be attracted to the organization. 
VII. 
Commitment and Dedication: 
PWM staff are required to commit him/herself thoroughly to the goals and objectives of 
the organization at all times. 
VIII. 
Time Management: 
PWM has resolved to apply methods and approaches that promote time management 
for all staff in such ways to improve productivity and output. 
IX. 
Effective and Efficient: 
PWM has recognised that efficiency and effectiveness are required from all staff in every 
endeavour so that sloppiness and time wasters are minimised. 
X. 
Attitude and Conduct: 
PWM staff are required to maintain a cordial attitude and respectable behaviour at the 
office environment and most importantly at the community level. 
XI. 
Stewardship: 
PWM requires all staff to be good stewards of all assets and resources such that 
maximum benefit is accrued to the organization. 
XII. 
Love and Self-esteem: 
PWM staff are expected to maintain a high self-esteem profile that will motivate their 
actions and attitudes to all persons within and outside the organization.

Partners with Melanesians Strategic Journey 
“Documenting Partners With Melanesians history of project design and 
outcomes to determine its capacity to deliver conservation and 
sustainable livelihood programs effectively in rural PNG. “   
 
Evengelyn Kove and Melissa Brosnan,  
Ruth Konia and Kelly Kalit, Reviewers  
Partners with Melanesians 
 
 
 
 

ACKNOWLEDGEMENT 
The earlier documentations provided basis to this paper however, it is one of the biggest documentation 
undertaken so far by Partners With Melanesians. The main objective is to set the precedence for proper 
documentation to follow after understanding the strategic journey PWM took to be where it is now and 
where it wants to go. This document is a living document that can be used as a guide for other 
documentation.  
The task of documentation was limited to the availability of reports, interviews from PWM management 
and staff including project local partners and other national stakeholders. This also means that this 
documentation is subject to change overtime.   
The Documentation team comprised of myself and Melissa Brosnan want express our gratitude to PWM 
management; Mr. Kenn Mondiai (the Executive Director), Mr. Rufus Mahuru (Program Manager) and 
Mrs. Jacinta Gure (Finance and Admin Manager) for entrusting the both of us to undertake this very 
important initiative as part of its 2017 work plan. We would like to extend our gratitude to the PWM 
Board of Directors for your interest and support to this very important document.  
Our sincere thanks to PWM staff for your insights and also our Local partners namely Managalas 
Conservation Foundation, Inaina Fagagara Development Foundation and Karimui Conservation Resource 
Management Program for your contribution which have truly added value to this work.   
Our appreciation goes out also to our national stakeholders not forgetting former staff and individuals 
who participated one way or the other in helping this come to fruition.  
We also want to appreciative the efforts of one of PWM’s Board of Directors, Mr. Kelly Kalit (2014-
2018), a former staff & PWM Program Manager Ms. Ruth Lagdom Konia (2001-2009) for taking the time 
to review the document.  
Most importantly, we would like to acknowledge the financial and technical support of the Government 
of Norway through the Rainforest Foundation. Without their support our achievements over the years 
to present would not have been possible.  
It is our hope that this document will add value to PWM’s strategic planning in 2018 and beyond. It is 
also our vision that this document will be of use to other Environmental NGOs and the likes in the area 
of Protected Areas and Community Based Natural Resource Management in PNG.

Introduction 
For over twenty (20) years of facilitating community mobilization for sustainable community livelihood 
and conservation, Partners With Melanesians (PWM) have come a long way.  
With a new direction of its fourth Strategic development plan from 2018 – 2022, it is very important that 
PWM evaluates its key project outcomes in order to re-organize, restructure and develop new 
partnerships with external players.  This time is also significant for PWM as it looks forward to winding 
down its main multi five year project funded by Rainforest Foundation of Norway (RFN) from 2013-2017. 
Understanding the plight of major commercial development bypassing socio-economic and 
environmental laws and regulations in marginalized societies in PNG, RFN provided technical and 
financial support since 1997 to advocate and promote indigenous rights to natural resources through 
conservation and sustainable resource development. This dream has been finally realized in one its 
longest and biggest project undertaken by PWM and that is the Managalas conservation Area project 
gazette and declared in November 2017.   Another major achievement for PWM is the gazettal and 
declaration of Inaina Wildlife Management Area in March 2017.  
However, the real challenge lies ahead which is the management of its Protected Areas and sustainable 
livelihood projects. For PWM, it is a huge step forward as it has passed the first stage of obtaining legal 
status after almost two decades for Managalas Conservation Area and 7 years for Inaina Wildlife 
Management Area. In addition, it seeks to extend its work into other project areas such as Collingwood 
Bay in Oro Province and Karimui in Chimbu Province in the not too distant future.  
For this reason, it is crucial for the organisation to reflect and recollect its success and failures since its 
inception to move forward with a clear sense of direction. The need for documenting PWM’s 
development and conservation achievements was frequently highlighted by the External Evaluation 
‘Stronim lek gen in 2007’ by Nancy Sullivan & Association and as a result, a desktop review of PWM’s 
organizational development was carried out in 2012 by Ruth Konia. The review identified PWM as an 
organization reaching its final stage of growth of one fully becoming specialized in mobilizing 
communities for conservation and Development initiatives. PWM went onto to carry out a staff retreat 
in 2015 to build the team spirit for a united vision, mission and goals to effectively implement in the 
coming years. It was there that Documenting PWM history became a recommendation for two main 
reasons; (1) For the purpose of Organizational Memory; (2) To find out PWM’s capacity to implement 
Conservation and Sustainable Livelihood projects strategically in PNG.  
For this paper, PWM team agrees to find out its capacity to implement Conservation and sustainable 
livelihood projects effectively because of the recurring challenges and risks associated with its programs. 
It hopes to use the findings to better understand these challenges and risks and develop innovative 
strategies to the bridge the gap of its implementation process.  
The documentation involved a number of qualitative methods to gain insight of PWM’s work over a 
number of years which actually draws its data from its library and complemented with surveys and 
interviews conducted respectively. It took almost 7 months to implement as the data collection process, 
analyzing, and the write up were divided within the 7 months’ period. The findings showed strategies 
evolved overtime and settled with community mobilization through Community empowerment and 
capacity building programs to (1) Meet the legal requirements of a Terrestrial Protected Area (2) Enable 
community land use plan for sustainable resource use (3) to Facilitate partnerships with relevant 

agencies for sustainable livelihood projects and appropriate Technology projects. This paper will go into 
the detail of the data collected and the analysis with key recommendations to provide a basis for way 
forward for PWM to consider in its future strategic direction.   
 
Background 
Partners with Melanesian is a National Not for Profit organization which currently focus on community forest 
conservation, promote and encourage indigenous decision making process in terms of sustainable 
resource use at a community level. PWM was registered in 1998 after much interest from donors in the 
work on the Managalas Plateau. Its initial program was more focused on literacy and was known as PNG 
trust formed by the University of Papua New Guinea Language and Literature Department in 1984, 
however, due to the issues that occurred in time and demand for development, the Organization refocused 
its attention to conservation and promoting indigenous rights in decision making process for sustainable 
resource use.   
Its community mobilization and consensus building program basically centered on family units and clan 
groups who are traditionally structured, discussing issues affecting them and using their traditional decision 
making process to enhance their wellbeing.  
After an external evaluation in 2001 carried out on the Managalas Plateau, its key recommendations were 
used to formulate the first strategic plan (2001- 2006 strategic plan)1 for PWM.  This was a way forward for 
PWM as a registered NGO which guided its preparation to put together the application for Managalas to be 
declared as a conservation area. It was then that the complementary program of Rainforest Literacy was 
introduced with Consensus building process.  
Then in 2006, the second strategic plan was developed for 2007 – 20112 with more focus in achieving the 
conservation status. Also PWM saw the need and demand for conservation nationwide, it was looking at 
scaling down its work on the Plateau and venturing into new possible sites at other provinces. After the 2nd 
independent evaluation conducted by consultant Nancy Sullivan & Associates in 2010 made specific 
recommendations as Way Forward for PWM3. Thus these recommendations formed the basis that 
identified the need for an organizational development to determine a structure along the strategic lines of 
the programs.  
According to the two external evaluations conducted (Stronim lek 1 in 2001 and Stronim lek 2 in 2010)4 
done for Managalas Project. The report has recommended that PWM needs to review its Organizational 
Development which resulted in a desktop Review in 20125. The desktop review went further into identifying 
the need and importance for PWM to have in place a Standard Operation Procedures to guide the

The 3rd strategic plan 2013 – 20176 in April 2012 saw a beginning of a new era for PWM in its effort to 
continue in strengthening the management of the Managalas Conservation Project Area. PWM has over 20 
years of experience of facilitating community mobilization with the focus on conservation and community 
sustainable livelihood projects. Since its inception, PWM has encountered challenges with its 
managements and administration, funds and budget including community related issues in its projects, 
however, despite all these challenges PWM persevered by continuously learning from its experience, re-
designing and adjusting its policies, structure and strategies to meet the demands of development and 
expectations of people with the focus on conservation.  PWM has also improved its capacity building by 
employing experts in certain programs to help the organization meet its mission, vision and goal. Looking 
beyond 2017 under the current circumstances of PWM winding down its RFN five-year contract from 2013-
2017, it anticipates the possibility of renewing another 5 years as well as fostering new partners to sustain 
its work of conservation and livelihood projects in PNG communities. With that hope of direction, it is only 
strategic for PWM to acknowledge its niche within the conservation and livelihood space for a greater 
impact.  
TARGET AUDIENCE 
This paper is purposely for Partners With Melanesians as part of its organizational memory and most 
importantly to inform its strategic development plan for the next 5 years. It is PWM’s Discretion to share 
this information with whomever it agrees to. However, parts of this information under certain 
circumstance can be shared to its project partners such as its beneficiaries, its donor and other relevant 
partners deemed appropriate.

OBJECTIVES   
This paper documents the history of PWM from which the lessons learnt and challenges are also 
captured provided with solutions for the way forward in promoting forest protection and sustainable 
livelihood through consensus and community mobilization. 
As per the terms of reference, the documenting of PWM history are in terms of;  
1.  Evaluate and review the goals, strategies and procedures of each project programs and how this 
programs and projects have been implemented to see the trend of its successes and challenges 
(strategic development) 
2. Identify the current status of Partners with Melanesian Inc. in relation to conservation and livelihood 
program in PNG (Situation Analysis) 
3.  Identify the lessons learnt and recommendations made from previous reports and has this taken into 
consideration and action and how can PWM take these recommendations to achieve its mission and 
goals with a new direction for its next 5-year strategic plan 2018- 2022.  (Strategic Future)  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

METHODOLOGY 
This method used for the compilation of this paper was by literature review, review of project activities 
and interviews conducted internally (Management and staff of PWM) and External (Key stakeholders). It 
included review of all documents of PWM and the project sites mostly evaluations on MCA and desktop 
reviews. Qualitative method was used to collect data and information and analyze accordingly.

1. Introduction 
 
1.1 Background and objectives 
 
Partners with Melanesians (Partners) is a Papua New Guinean organisation committed to 
establishing the conditions for sustainable development in areas of Papua New Guinea where 
poverty and high conservation value intersect.  For the past decade, Partners has worked with the 
people of the Managalas Plateau in the Owen Stanley Ranges of Oro Province to develop 
community institutions, initiate eco-enterprises, establish conservation areas and set up a 
framework for local on-making on sustainable development.  The Norwegian Rainforest 
Foundation has been a major sponsor of this endeavour since 1996 through the “Managalas 
Sustainable Development Project”.  NRF provided considerable support, training, exposure as 
well as order of PGK 1.516 million (USD 546,000).   
 
The current program of assistance is now reaching completion and NRF is seeking to evaluate its 
success prior to further investments.  This evaluation will also address formal requirements of the 
Norwegian government aid agency, NORAD, who are major contributors to NRF.  
 
The evaluation was conducted between September and November 2000 by a team of three 
including Greg Abare, Paul Chatterton and Tialepa Samuel.   
 
The objectives of the evaluation are to: 
 
document and learn from past and current activities, processes and achievements of Partners in the 
Managalas Plateau 
 
assist Partners to check the effectiveness, efficiency, impact, relevance and sustainability 
of their current programs with the peoples of the Managalas Plateau including project management systems 
and relationships with donors, partners and stakeholders 
 
identify issues and suggest steps for future improvement and specifically to identify areas  for 
strengthening and improvement as the project moves into the next phase 
 
The evaluation examines program management, project design and implementation, stakeholder 
relationships and learning systems.  It explores those aspects of Partners activities supported by 
NRF.  The evaluation particularly probes the relationship between Partners and the communities 
of the Managalas Plateau and the extent to which this promotes a sustainable improvement in life 
quality.  It also examines the ability of Partners to maintain this relationship with the effective 
support of donors and other stakeholders. 
 
Questions at the heart of this work include the extent to which the project … 
 
1. identifies and engages all the traditional clan groups as well as currently functioning 
women, church and youth groups across the Plateau 
2. identifies and engages all other government, non-government and private sector 
stakeholders 
3. ensures that participating clan groups receive relevant information on development 
opportunities feasible in the area as well as development issues affecting them 
4. reaches broad agreement on a set of sustainable development guidelines for the Plateau  
5. maps external boundaries that mark the area for this agreement  

Strongim Lek  Evaluation of the Managalas Sustainable Development Project - October 2000 
5 
6. has obtained official recognition of sustainable development guidelines and boundary 
map 
7. establishes ways to monitor the use of natural resources for sustainability 
8. institutionalised the production of annual action plans by zone and combined fora 
9. increased the spread of benefits from project activities 
10. expanded government, nongovernment and private sector involvement (including local 
government) in implementing individual zone and combined zone action plans 
11. institutionalised the cycle of information, consensus-building, clarification of goals and 
objectives and revised action plans 
12. professionalised the project support provided by the Port Moresby office 
 
1.2 Methodology and approach 
 
This is a participatory evaluation.  As far as possible, analysis and solutions have been conducted 
by and with those groups who are responsible for implementing the change.  It aims to ensure 
that the process of learning is one that is shared as broadly as possible among project 
beneficiaries, implementors and other stakeholders.  Methodological concepts applied during this 
evaluation include: 
 
 stakeholders - The evaluation sought contributions from all stakeholders in the project 
including local communities, CBO managers, government officers, partner groups, 
Partners staff and Board members and donors.  Equally, attention was given to the 
elements within the community (gender, age, ethnic origin, residential status, location and 
religion) as well as in the broad network of Partners relations outside of Managalas.   
 
 dimensions – The evaluation sought to review the project across a number of 
dimensions including socio-cultural, economic, ecological and institutional and to explore 
the relation between these.  A set of indicators was developed to guide this analysis and to 
ensure a holistic approach (see Annex 2). 
 
 self-evaluation – The recommendations of the evaluation team are based solidly on the 
results of a sequence of discussions and feedback within stakeholder groups.  Analysis 
and recommendations were developed individually and in groups by (1) staff and board 
members, (2) steering committee members, (3) villagers and (4) other stakeholders.  The 
role of the evaluation team was to facilitate discussion, problem solving and 
documentation as well as to highlight issues or contradictions between groups.  This 
process of self-evaluation helps to ensure that participants are fully involved in 
discussions, have a commitment to the results and therefore and more likely to carry 
through proposed changes.  
 
 feedback - The results of this self-examination were summarised and reported back to 
each of the groups for comment and further refinement. This ensured that conclusions 
and recommendations of the evaluation are well understood and broadly supported.

 participant solutions – The evaluation team recognises the ability of most groups to 
address their own problems.  By and large the conclusions and recommendations of this 
reported have been developed by stakeholders of the project.  The evaluation team has 
only sought to add to these major issues require external intervention. 
 
 appropriate reporting – Where possible, conclusions are recorded by group members in 
their own words.  Two reports have been produced.  A detailed technical report written 
in technical English provides the full range of observations, issues and conclusions made 
by the team.  To ensure the results are accessible to all, a summary of the evaluation is 
also provided in Tok Pisin and two Managalas vernacular languages in the form of an 
illustrated poster.  These will be distributed through the Plateau.  
 
The evaluation examines success from five viewpoints … 
 
1 Relevance - the degree to which the project can be justified in relation to local and national 
development priorities. 
 
2 Effectiveness - the extent to which the purpose has been achieved. Whether this can be 
expected to happen on the basis of the outputs of the project.  
 
3 Efficiency - how the results stand in relation to the effort expended. How economically 
inputs are converted to outputs. Whether the same results could have been achieved in 
another way.  This is important in order for us to find out to what degree the outputs 
achieved derive from efficient use of financial, human and material resources. It means 
comparing inputs with outputs. 
 
4 Impact - the changes and effects positive and negative, planned and unforeseen of the 
project, seen in relation to target groups and others who are affected. 
 
5 Sustainability - an assessment of the extent to which the positive effects of the project will 
still continue after external assistance has been concluded. 
 
 
The evaluation team sought to use a range of approaches to gather information.  Advice was 
obtained on evaluation methodology.  The team shared information with other evaluators of 
similar organisations and projects, including with teams evaluating the Bismarck-Ramu Group 
and the Individual and Community Rights Advocacy Forum as well as using web and library 
resources.  The team examined Partners documentation and other written sources of 
information. Questionnaires were provided to staff primarily to obtain necessary background 
information on projects, staff roles and responsibilities, activities, and achievements. 
 

Strongim Lek  Evaluation of the Managalas Sustainable Development Project - October 2000 
7 
Much effort was devoted to discussions with individuals and groups through face-to-face, 
phone and email interviews with relevant stakeholders.  Workshops were conducted with key 
groups including: Partners staff, consultants and Board (in wk 1 and 4); the Managalas Steering 
committee (at the start and end of the two week field visit); and with individual villages and 
zones.  In each village/zone workshop, discussions were conducted separately in three groups 
with elders, other men and women as well as in plenary.  The workshops provided further 
information as well as insights into group dynamics and group responses to issues that 
augmented individual interviews.  In some cases, participatory rural appraisal tools such as 
mapping and timeline were used to identify achievements and to explore social relations. 
 
Finally, but perhaps most importantly, the team spent two weeks walking across the Plateau.  The 
route was chosen to allow exposure to contrasting areas of high and low attention and access to 
services.  In all but one case, team members stayed at least two nights in each location allowing 
more thorough discussions. The full itinerary of the team and a list of persons consulted can be 
found in Annex 1. 
 
Support provided by Partners staff was quite adequate although there considerable difficulty was 
experienced in discussing evaluation matters with the Executive Director due to his regular 
absence on study leave.

1.3 Structure of the Report 
 
This report is structured as follows: 
 
 Chapter 2: provides a broad overview of Partners with Melanesians and the 
Managalas Sustainable Development Project.  It examines the hierarchy of objectives 
being applied in the project, staffing and other resources and results achieved in the 
past four years.  The organisational structure of Partners is discussed. 
 
 Chapter 3: examines the Managalas Sustainable Development Project through the 
dimensions of community engagement, community development, sustainable 
business, environment, community institutions and management.  In each case, key 
issues that emerged from stakeholder discussions are explored and options examined.  
Each topic is examined through as series of agreed indicators of effective operation. 
 
 Chapter 4: presents the conclusions and recommendations of the evaluation while …

implementation of the project.

2. Project description 
 
2.1 The Managalas Plateau 
 
The Managalas Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 to 1000 metres altitude above the 
coastal plain of Oro Province, Papua New Guinea.  It sits between the Owen Stanley Ranges to 
the south and west, the Sibium Ranges to the south-east and Mount Lamington and the 
Hydrographers to the north and east.  The 300,000 hectares of the Plateau encompass an 
extraordinary diversity of environments including alpine heath at 3,800 metres, montane and hill 
forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens. 
 
Like many of the mountainous mid-altitude valleys of PNG, the Plateau is an area of high quality 
agricultural land and relatively dense populations.  The surrounding mountains, by contrast, are 
generally infertile and little populated. 15,000 people from around 150 clan groups live in 40 
village communities on the Managalas Plateau.  These are largely subsistence farmers and depend 
almost exclusively on the environment for their livelihood.  Ten dialects are found on the plateau 
that together make up three broad languages (Barai, Managalas and Aomie). 
 
The Managalas Plateau is relatively isolated and remote from urban Papua New Guinea.  It is 
linked to the Oro Provincial Capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality four-wheel drive road and by 
two airstrips as well as by foot-tracks.  This allows a limited sale of coffee and other produce 
during dry conditions but high freight costs and poor maintenance prevent regular trade.   
 
Government services are restricted to a number of community schools, a top up school, two aid 
posts and a station and Health Centre at Afore.  The Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL) 
introduced an adult literacy program to the Plateau in the 1960’s and this has provided an 
important foundation for many of the development processes now taking place on the Plateau. 
 
Over the past decade a number of proposals for timber extraction, oil palm and mining 
development have been presented to the Managalas Plateau.  While welcoming the opportunity 
for development, Managalas communities are actively opposing many of these projects due to the 
poor consultation with resource owners and the failure to guarantee benefits or environmental 
protection. 
 
2.2 Partners with Melanesians 
 
Partners with Melanesians Inc is a Papua New Guinean organisation established in 1984 at the 
University of Papua New Guinea and registered as a non-profit association (Reg No. 5-896).

Partners with Melanesians                Biodiversity Summary Report: Managalas Plateau                    Page 1  

MPCA Biodiversity Summary Report- By Jacinta. Mimigari
Acknowledgement
I would sincerely like to thank everyone who has helped me in compiling this Summary 
Report of the Biodiversity Surveys that were carried out in the Proposed Managalas 
Conservation Area from November 2004, 2005 and May 2006.
My sincere thank you to Mr. Jones Hiaso in editing my work and making sure that what I did 
is in accordance to the findings that was carried out by the experienced Scientist of the 
University of Papua New Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. I 
would also like to thank the Management and Staff of Partners with Melanesians in having 
faith in me in compiling this Biodiversity Summary Report. 
Summary
The following Report provides a Summary of the outcome of a three phase preliminary 
Biodiversity survey done in the Managalas Plateau, in November 2004, 2005 and May 2006 
basically to identify the Biodiversity significance of the Managalas Proposed Conservation 
Area. 
Very high diversity of species inhabits the mountains of the conservation area that may play 
a big role in diverse species distributions that can be so attractive to tourist, scientist, 
researchers and the public at large. The conservation area is in its proposal stage, required 
biological information's to be recognized diverse and unique in it's natural resources, 
especially the important species, endemic, protected, rare and threatened. The information's 
were much required by Partners with Melanesia, that it funded three biodiversity surveys 
dating back in November, 2004, November 2005 and May 2006. After the three biodiversity 
surveys, Partners with Melanesia is now furnished with the needed information's of the area, 
in both plants and animals. Should that be sufficient biological information's, Department of 
Environment and conservation be convinced that the area be declared a conservation area.
Managalas Plateau, for it's conservation area, stretches from the Foothill Mountains of 
Sibium in the south-east, Owen Stanley Ranges in the south-west, Owalama Ranges at west, 
and Guava Ranges in the north-west with it's high diversity, stretching to the lower altitude 
plains towards Oro Bay. Much of the lower plains of the conservation area is disturbed 
vegetation's, due to high number of villages that much of the area have been 
cultivated for subsistence cash cropping, which includes small plantations of coffee, vanilla, 
and coconut. The Upper Mountain and hills remains very high in its natural 
resources may deplete through careless management's and other major developments. The 
areas have been divided into ten zones for equal dissemination of conservation related 
activities and viable projects that can generate cash income to the local people of the area. 
_____________________________________________________________________
Partners with Melanesians                Biodiversity Summary Report: Managalas Plateau                    Page 2  

MPCA Biodiversity Summary Report- By Jacinta. Mimigari
1. Introduction
The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses about 360 000 hectares of pristine 
rainforest comprising of lowland hill and Montane forests in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari 
District, Oro Province. The Forest are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form the 
main catchments for the Bariji and Musa River. The area is bordered by the Owen Stanley 
Range, to the Southwest and the Sibium Range to the Southeast. Popondetta town and the 
famous Kokoda Trail are situated north of the Proposed Conservation Area. 
Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, 
but at the moment is poorly documented. Hence having the area declared a CA then this can 
allow further research into the rich diverse forest. Biologists from the University of PNG and 
Officers from the Department of Environment and Conservation have so far carried out three 
Biodiversity surveys but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete.  This is 
evident from the diverse frog fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs are a good 
indicator of a rich and a vibrant environment.
This report highlights the summary of all the three Biodiversity Surveys that were carried out 
in and around the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.
2. Objectives of the Biodiversity Surveys
The conservation area remains un-exploited for major developments, except for mini 
sustainable projects enhancing human well-being. The 350,000 hectare area, were 
categorized into 10 zones for proper and equal dissemination of conservation related 
programs for all to be aware and understand. Small projects encouraged by Partners with 
Melanesia were introduced in different zones to help generate small cash income for the local 
landowners. The projects are so small that they have little biological effects, which can 
change the ecosystems of the living organisms and plants, but it may not be that threatened to 
many fauna and flora species of the area. The area is virtually high in biological diversity 
naturally valued in their own ecological characteristics establishing high profiles that makes 
this conservation area a place encourageable for future generations and education.
Both the plants and bird species remain widely distributed and were common for any 
traditional purposes to people. Species depletion occur only when major destruction's takes 
place, reducing population density. After the third biodiversity surveys, bird species were 
more widely distributed than the mammals, reptiles, amphibians, except for the insect 
population that inhabit all vegetation types at all levels of different elevations.
Main objectives Partners With Melanesia would like to have in place for the conservation 
area, were the biological information's which are not readily available at the moment. The 
unique and the important species have to be identified for a better recognition of the area that 
can attract tourist, researchers, scientist and the public at large. For that, such requirements 
were important to identify with the yearly biodiversity surveys to provide:
1. The existing fauna and flora species lists.
2. The protected species of the area.
3. The endemic species of the area.
4. The traditionally important species of the area.
5. Map-out the exact locations of the important species, as a 
guide to promote tourism and other educational purposes.

3.4 Plant Life of the Conservation Area
         The proposed area is very rich in plant biodiversity with little disturbance. The forest is 
intact and has a greater potential to offer to the people of Managalas and PNG many various 
products. However, the forests are also vulnerable to treats from logging, mining, growing 
population etc. Many PNG forests have already been exploited by logging and mining 
companies and have left the forest owners no forest to dwell in freely, or no long term 
benefits to the resource owners.
This may happen to the Managalas forest if it is not protected from exploitation of such 
nature in the future. Therefore, the proposed idea of conserving Managalas for future 
generation is important and is crucial for all stakeholders (landowners, conservation NGO’s, 
Government) to cooperate and work together to protect Managalas proposed area. 
Conservation will bring in various benefits to the local people both directly and indirectly. 
For instance, tourists will be attracted to come into the area to see Bird Wing Butterflies of 
Oro. Bird wing butterflies will disappear if the host plants are destroyed in the forest. There 
is also potential for drug discovery in this forest because drug discovery program has now 
increased in Papua New Guinea and such forest has a potential to offer for drug discovery. 
4. Results 
The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area covers a land area of Over 360, 000 hectares. 
The Managalas plateau itself is situated within and around the Owen stanely Range to the 
South and West, the Sibium range to the South east and mt lamington to the North and East. 
The managals Plateau encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from alpine forest at 
altitudes of 3800 metres to tropical tropical rainforest to the mountains and hills as well as 
Savannah grassland and anthropogenic garden areas. The managlas Plateau is isolated from 
most of the Urban centers within the Oro Province as a result of poor road conditions. 
Through Conservation Programs initiated and conducted by Partners with Melanesians 
(PwM), the people within the Managalas Plateau have decide to conserve their Forest. The 
information collected and compiled on the flora and fauna will be used towards the 
establishment of the Conservation Area status for the Managalas plateau.
The conservation area is an area that is registered by the government as having particular 
biological, topographical, geographical scientific or social importance. Conservation Area is 
established under the conservation Area Act. This law provides for preservation of the 
Environment and the natural cultural Inheritance

5. Discussion
Forest Use: The local people depend heavily on plants and forest resources for their 
livelihood. Plants provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw 
materials for house constructions, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor 
forest products.
6. Conclusion
6.1 Recommendations 
Given the Uniqueness of the forest within the Conservation Area, we highly recommend that 
the forest be conserved. The following are offered for guidance.
-
Proper trapping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or 
resting sites be identified to allow minimal disturbance.
-
The pine is a tree of Scientific and historical significance. Scattered stand of 
these species can be identified and mapped out, both within and outside the 
proposed conservation area s and these areas be protected.
-
The mixed castanopsis forest is very sensitive ton Human disturbance. 
Conversion of these forest type to grassland is already a common feature in 
the highlands of Papua New Guinea. It is strongly recommended that these 
stands be conserved.
-
Proper record of Palnt animal uses be established These requires someone 
with good knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able to readily 
access traditional knowledge.
-
Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally access the 
ecology of the Area. This should also encompasses a full botanical 
reconnaissance survey of the area. Permanent study plots be established and 
consistently monitored.

Dear Mr Alex Uraniun 
Subject: 
Follow up Letter for representation in the Managalas 
Conservation Area    Management Committee
This letter serves as a follow up to the previous letter asking you to be a member 
in the Managalas Conservation Area Management (CAMC). As per advice from 
the Department of Environment and Conservation (DEC), the Assistant District 
Administrator for the sub-district in which a Conservation Area is situated should 
take the position of Chairmanship in the CAMC. Managalas Development 
Foundation (MDF) and Partners with Melanesian Inc (PWM) are in the process of 
establishing this very important committee that will be the overseer of the entire 
project after it is declared and paves the way for PWM to exit. MDF and PWM are 
currently distributing letters to various vital stakeholders that will have 
representatives in this committee to appoint their Reps, (see in attachment the 
CAMC structure and the Reps for the various stakeholders that will be 
represented in the Committee). 
The responsibilities for the CAMC are stipulated in PART V, of the Conservation 
Areas Act 1978 (attached). One of the main and vital responsibilities for the 
CAMC is the development of a Management Plan for the   Conservation Area 
Project after it is declared. Four management plan workshops have been 
conducted with the communities and a draft management plan is in place for the 
CAMC to review, make amendments and finalised for approval by DEC. Both the 
Management Plan and CAMC will be endorsed by the Department of Environment 
and Conservation which will be gazetted by NEC. The management plan will be 
reviewed every five years.   
As you might have seen in the Post Courier dated 18th February 2013, the Public 
advertisement for the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area. This public 
advertisement is the forth step of the eight steps followed in establishing a 
Conservation Area in PNG, and begins the 90 days public viewing which will lapse 
in the second week of May. It is at this stage, open for objections to be submitted 
to the Department of Environment and Conservation via the ofÏces mentioned in 
the advertisement namely (DEC OfÏce Waigani, Oro Provincial Administration 
OfÏce and Afore Sub-District OfÏce). DEC OfÏcers will be doing consultation visits 
to the above ofÏces assessing the progress of the 90 days public viewing and or 
collecting any objections for registration. Thus this letter also serves to establish 
a contact between Afore LLG and the DEC. The contact Person in DEC is Mr 
1

Benside Thomas (+675 71681626 / 76595967) or Ms Madline Lahari (71858522). 
They will notify your ofÏce on their schedule for their consultation visit.
I would appreciate your prompt response to this letter in writing so we can move 
on finalising the committee members and the management plan. 
I appreciate your time and look forward to a timely response. 
Yours faithfully,

Subject:

Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) is a registered local NGO base in the Managalas 
Plateau Afore Sub District Ijivitari Electorate Oro Province. We have been working in collaboration 
with Partners with Melanesian Inc (PWM), a national conservation and community development 
NGO base in Port Moresby to implement conservation and related activities in the Managalas 
Plateau. It is now the 9th year of conservation works in the plateau and we are expecting the 
declaration of the proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project around September 2013.  As 
required under the Conservation Areas Act (CAA) 1978, a Conservation Area Management Plan 
Committee (CAMPC) needs to be established to manage the project after it is gazetted by NEC. In 
preparation towards the declaration, the Managalas local communities with technical assistance 
from PWM have conducted several workshops purposely to develop a draft Management Plan (MP) 
for the project and to identify key stakeholders that will be represented in the CAMPC. One of the

Managalas Conservation Area Management Plan 
Committee Structure
 
3

 Extracted from the Conservation Areas Act 1978 - Part V.
PART V.—CONSERVATION AREA MANAGEMENT COMMITTEES.
25.
Conservation Area Management Committees.
(1)
Where an area is declared to be a conservation area, the Minister shall, as 
soon as is practicable, establish a Conservation Area Management Committee for 
that conservation area.
(2)
A management committee established under Subsection (1) shall consist 
of not less than three members appointed by the Minister by notice in the 
National Gazette.
(3)
Membership of a management committee shall reflect the interests of—
(a)
the owners of the land within the conservation area; and
(b)
the provincial government or provincial government body, Local 
Government Council or Local Government Authority in the province or areas 
within which the conservation area is situated.
(4)
The Constitution of a management committee shall be as determined by 
the management committee and approved by the Council.
(5)
Where the declaration of a conservation area is revoked, the management 
committee for that area shall cease to function.
26.
Procedures of a management committee.
(1)
A management committee shall meet not less than once in every three 
months.
(2)
Subject to this Act and to any direction given by the Minister, a 
management committee shall determine its own procedure.
27.
Functions of a management committee.
(1)
The functions of a management committee in respect of the conservation 
area for which it is established are—
(a)
to manage the conservation area; and
(b)
to make recommendations to the Minister on the making of rules 
applicable within the conservation area; and

(c)
to advise the Minister in respect of co-ordination of development within 
the conservation area; and
(d)
to prepare a management plan for the conservation area outlining the 
manner in which land use will be managed and features of special significance 
conserved; and
(e)
to direct the work of rangers; and
(f)
such other functions as are determined by the Minister.
[Double click Note for Legislative Amendment History. Open Pg_Leg_H.Nfo to see 
earlier provisions.]
(2)
A management plan prepared under Subsection (1)(d) shall be subject to 
approval by the Minister who, in his consideration of such a management plan, 
shall have regard to physical planning considerations.
28.
Rules for conservation areas.
(1)
Subject to Subsection (2), the Minister may, after consultation with—
(a)
the management committee; and
(b)
the Council; and
(c)
as far as practicable the owners of the land within the conservation area; 
and
(d)
the relevant authority,
make rules for the protection, development, land use activities, management 
and control of the conservation area.
(2)
A person who, without reasonable excuse (proof of which is on him) 
contravenes or fails to comply with a provision of a rule made under Subsection 
(1) is guilty of an offence.
Penalty:
A fine not exceeding K500.00.
Default penalty:
A fine not exceeding K200.00.
29.
Powers of a management committee.
Subject to this Part, a management committee has power to do all things that 
are necessary or convenient to be done for or in connexion with the performance 
of its functions.
30.
Annual reports of a management committee.
5

A management committee shall, as soon as practicable after the end of each 
year, furnish to the Minister a report on its operations during that year.
