text:
Partners with Melanesians’ work on Managalas Plateau 
Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PWM) started as an idea by the staff and students of the language 
and literature Department of the University of Papua New Guinea in 1985. Since then, there have 
been numerous developments within the organization as well as events outside of the organization 
that have shaped the history of the organization. 
Initially, it was set up to support groups and communities who were involved in education and 
development initiatives in rural communities of Papua New Guinea. As time progresses PWM started 
work on the Managalas Plateau of the Oro Province in what has come to be one of the best models 
of community mobilizing and community development work around conservation in the country. 
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) is a National Not for Profit, Non-Government Organization (NGO) 
committed to establish, coordinate and promote the work of all members of the community and 
other partner organizations. PWM encourages equal participation and self-reliance, and practices 
sustainable and alternative development processes. Protection of the natural environment, 
biological diversity, sustainable livelihoods and cultural heritage in rural areas of high conservation 
value in Papua New Guinea is the overall goal of this organization. 
Partners with Melanesians through its Exit Strategic program is now venturing into new project site 
and leaving Managalas Plateau. Its focus now on Managalas Proposed conservation Area is to help 
establish the umbrella organization Managalas Development Foundation.  
PWM has been working with the people of managalas since 1985 and through its exit strategy plan 
are ending over the work to the Managalas Development Foundation. 
Conservation Work 
The Publication titled ‘The Biodiversity of Managalas Plateau” is a Summary Report of the four 
phase preliminary Biodiversity Surveys done on the Managalas Plateau, in November 2004, 
November 2005, May 2006 and April 2008.  The main purpose of this investigation (Biodiversity 
Surveys) was basically to identify the Biodiversity Significance of the Proposed Managalas 
Conservation Area and to provide the following information: 
(i) 
Assess the Conservation status of protected, threatened and endemic species 
(ii) 
Identify immediate threats to those animals and other potential threats. 
(iii) 
Provide a checklist of both fauna and flora that to our knowledge protected by CITES and 
our acts of Parliament. 
(iv) 
The existing fauna and flora species lists. 
(v) 
Composition and distribution of flora and fauna species at various altitudes 
(vi) 
Get recommendation for better conservation work in rural areas 
Like most areas of New Guinea, the proposed Managalas Conservation Area (an area of 360 000 
hectares) harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, but at the moment is poorly documented. 
Biodiversity surveys have been carried out but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from 
complete. Ones the area has gained its Conservation Area status then further research can be done. 
The survey methodologies used in the survey were basically; site sampling, ethno-ecological 
interviews with locals, diurnal and nocturnal sampling, cross referencing and observation.  

Recommendations were offered in the report as guidance to better improve conservation work on 
Managalas Plateau and for the sustainability of the project. 
The four biodiversity surveys were conducted in zone 1, zone 2, parts of zone 4, and parts of zone 7. 
There are ten zones within the proposed conservation area, of which, 6 were initially not covered in 
the biodiversity surveys. Reasons for not covering the whole area, is because of the fact that, the 
four surveys have in general covered the lower and the higher altitudes of the plateau. 
The out-come of the biological findings from the four surveys are quite encouraging to have the area 
recognized to be declared a conservation area. Many fauna species of importance were recorded 
with the avid-fauna and the mammalian communities. No new findings were encountered with the 
birds and mammal species of the area, but it is believed that new discoveries were done to the 
hereto-fauna community, especially the frog species of the areas, Murayane mossy mid montane, 
inland of Anatua village and Dakara, Uwate village. 
The insect communities were so large, covering the entire plateau in all habitat types. This ranges 
from butterflies, beetles, bees, ants, spiders, grasshoppers and other insects. The Protected Queen 
Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly was only observed at Tahama Biological survey site. Other parts of the 
plateau have not been observed. The species is more common in the Tufi-Wanigella in the 
Collingwood Bay of Northern Province. 
The plateau has a very rich biodiversity in terms of species distribution and occurrences. Much of the 
natural habitat is undisturbed, except for subsistence cash cropping and mini-agricultural activities 
within the village surroundings. 
Habitat loss, population growth, degradation and fragmentation are the most critical challenges to 
maintaining biodiversity both in Papua New Guinea and globally. 
STATUS OF THE PROPOSED MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA 
 
There are eight steps or procedures that are involved in establishing a Conservation Area in Papua 
New Guinea as per the Conservation Areas Act 1978. In the case of the Managalas Proposed 
Conservation Area, step one (1) and two has been completed.  
Step one (1) include;  
 The consent of the Land owners and signatures of the clan elders. 
 Boundary Mapping 
 CA management committee, land use plans and a High Conservation Value Forest Area 
tool kit are near completion.(this will continue after the declaration)    
Step two (2) includes the endorsement of the submission from the Provincial and Local Level 
Government.  
 The Provincial Government has endorsed the submission when a presentation was made to 
the Oro PEC on the 02nd of December 2008. Afore LLG, signed the endorsement on the 08th 
of June 2011 by the Vice President Lancelot Piritano after two presentations in 
(2010&2011), updating the LLG members on the current status of the CA, advantages and 
disadvantages of a CA, the responsibilities of the LLG in the project, and a clarification on 
the Conservation Areas Act (CAA) by a principle Lawyer from CELCOR Mr Damien Ase who 
is from Managalas.

Two workshops have been conducted in regard to the above heading. The first workshop was held in 
Managalas Plateau (Itokama) in 2004 by Ms Philipa Holden, a South African Conservation Specialist. The 
workshop was an introduction of what a Resource Management is; what important concepts are found in a 
Resource Management Plan document; and to get the Managalas people prepared in creating their own 
Management Plan for their proposed Conservation Area. 
 
The second workshop was a follow up to the first and was facilitated by Jacinta Mimigari at the Afore Council 
Chamber, Afore from 22 September to October 2nd 2008. This workshop was a sort of pre-planning for the 
preparation of the draft Managalas Conservation Area/Resource Management Plan (CAMP). It is a follow up

Conservation Area to the Department of the Environment and Conservation (DEC). Rules were made and 
communities participated in identifying Environmental problems and created rules to minimize these 
problems. The already created Environmental Rules were reviewed and better rules were created to sustain

Background 
People’s livelihood, either directly or indirectly depends on the Natural Resources. Natural Resources 
can be Renewable (Living resources) or non-Renewable (non living Resources). The renewable 
resources such as the air, water, animals, plants and bacteria living on land and water are again rated 
as critical or Non-critical resources. Critical Resources are those Resources that cannot replenish 
themselves when used excessively, e.g. forestry, fishery, etc. The Non-critical resources refer to the 
renewable resources that can replenish themselves even though they have been excessively used, e.g. 
air, water.  
On the other hand, non-renewable resources are resources that are not capable of replenishing 
themselves. They have a fix quantity or volume that once are used, cannot be replenished e.g. ore, 
petroleum, oil, gas etc. The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area is endowed with both renewable 
and non-renewable resources. Partners with Melanesians have been working with the Managalas 
people since 1985, especially carrying out educational and environmental awareness on the 
importance of the natural resources on their livelihoods.      
Conservation Area Management Plan 
Conservation Area Management Plans provide guidance through Policy Statements to assist in the 
preservation and enhancement of the Conservation Area. The plan will eventuate from decisions made on 
the scientific information and local knowledge of resources in the area. The Managalas Proposed 
Conservation Area is not restricted from human activity, thus it requires a management plan. People are 
living within the conservation area and depend on the surrounding to support their living.     
For the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area., the Management plans in this case will be produced or 
compiled by the Land owners themselves because it is their resources and it is them who will manage 
these resources.

significance of individual elements and of the Conservation Area as a whole; 
3.   To provide policy guidance to ensure that the significance of the Conservation Area will be maintained

title: DECLARATION OF MANAGALAS PLATEAU,AFORE LLG DISTRICT
snippet: INDEPENDENT STATE OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA Ministerial Brief To: Hon. John Pundari, MP Minister for Environment and Conservation and Climate Change Date: 3 October 2016 Subject: Declaration of Managalas Plateau of Afore LLG, ljivitari District of Oro Province as a Conservation Area Under the Conservation
text:
INDEPENDENT STATE OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA

Ministerial Brief

To: Hon. John Pundari, MP
Minister for Environment and Conservation and Climate Change

Date: 3 October 2016

Subject: Declaration of Managalas Plateau of Afore LLG, ljivitari District of Oro Province as
a Conservation Area Under the Conservation Areas Act of 1978

A. Purpose

1. To brief you on the contents and implications of this policy submission on the declaration of
Managalas plateau as a conservation area; and

2. To seek your approval and endorsement of this policy submission for presentation to NEC for
its deliberations.

B. Background

3. At two tribal leader's summit in 1997 at Numba (Zone 6) and again in 2005 at Serefuna (Zone
2) at Afore sub district, consensus was reached respectively at both meetings for conservation
and sustainable use of the natural resources of Managalas Plateau for the landowners
numbering some 21,000.

4. Partners with Melanesians (PwM), a national NGO was invited to assist the landowners in
advancing community conservation and development work over the past 32 years through a
program of conservation literacy awareness, biodiversity research and_ institutional
development and capacity building with financial support from development partners, mainly
the Rainforest Foundation of Norway (since 1996 to present) with an expenditure exceeding
PGK10 million.

5. The landowners in consultation with the Afore LLG and Oro Provincial Government submitted
an application for declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area on 8
November 2012 that you received from Oro Governor, Hon. Garry Juffa at the State function
room in Parliament.

6. CEPA appropriately put up a public notice on the daily newspapers starting 18 February 2013
advising the general public of its intension to declare the area and giving a 90 day's timeframe
for any objections.

7. After the expiry of the 90 day’s period, almost all the landowners remain committed/supportive
of proposed declaration of the area except only one individual (Afore LLG President) who has
registered his objection.
 8.

The CEPA officers have had further dialogue with this leader who has maintained his objection.
We have advised him of our intension to declare on the basis of the majority community
support and should he continue with his objection he would have to seek other avenues to
address his grievances including judicial review.

C. Facts and Considerations

9.

10.

11.

12.

13.

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses of about 360 000 hectares of the
pristine rainforest compromising of the lowland hill and Montane forests in the Managalas
Plateau, Afore Local Level Government of |jivitari District, Oro province. The forests are
intersected by many creeks and rivers that form the main catchments for the Bariji and Musa
Rivers. The area is bordered by the Owen Stanley Range to the Southwest and the Sibium
range to the Southwest. Popondetta town and the famous Kokoda Trail are situated north of
the Proposed Conservation Area.

The plateau has a very high biodiversity, with different fauna and flora species, common to rare
and protected. Being a large area, ranges of each fauna species depends entirely on how far
each species can travel. Some are only confined to their required habitats and the food sources
in each vegetation types. This includes the world’s largest butterfly, the Queen Alexander
Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) that is only found in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea and other
endangered and endemic species like Doria’s Tree Kangaroo.

QABB is listed under Appendix A of Convention on Intemational Trade of Endangered Species
(CITES). PNGis a party to CITES (Convention on International Trade of Endangered
Species) Appendix A means that, QABB is on the RED LIST and is endangered if no action is
taken to protect its habitats resulting in extinction.

The major threat on the environment and the forest ecosystems is from agriculture; conversion
of primary forests for both subsistence food production and commercial cash cropping activities
like growing coffee- undertaken by the local communities to enhance human wellbeing.

There are also potential threats from the private sector; especially companies who are
interested in industrial logging and mining in and around the proposed conservation areas.
Initially there was an intrusion and overlap with mining Exploration Lease (EL 1547) but the
boundary map has been adjusted amicably between landowners, the Minerals Resources
Authority, and the Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to allow mining
exploration activities to be undertaken outside the boundary of the proposed conservation area.

Several industrial logging propositions have been made but landowners in the conservation
area have and are still objecting in preference over conservation and small scale ecoforestry to
meet local requirements including housing, construction of schools and health centers.

. There are some level of alternative income earning opportunities that have been supported

over the years for sustainable livelihood purposes especially Arabica coffee at small holder
level; and as it is one of the few areas in the Southern region that huge potential for increased
production. There is also great opportunity for eco-tourism, and there is an initial plan to
develop an eco-tourism industry on the Managalas plateau with linkages with the famous
Kokoda track that create income earning opportunities.

. Several civil society organizations including independent research organizations and NGOs

have been working in the area for the past 34 years under the leadership of Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) with notable achievements that include; conservation education and
awareness, securing 360,000 hectares for conservation; establishment of base line
socioeconomic and biological data; establishment and operationalization of Managalas
Conservation Foundation (MCF) with its Board/management focused on implementation of a
5 -year organizational strategic plan.

i

 17. PwM and MCF are working together under an existing collaborative partnership Memorandum
of Understanding on the mobilization and joint use of both financial and technical resources for
the conservation area program that includes a strategy where all management responsibilities
will be handed over to MCF by PwM to maintain and manage the Conservation Area once
declared.

18. In line with the National Protected Area Policy which the NEC approved in 2014 (NEC
Decision No. 5/2014) that provides for sustainable financing for protected areas, NEC is
asked to approve K8 Million; firstly, K4 million for establishment by CEPA of the Endowment
Fund for Managalas Conservation Area, and secondly, K4 million for Managalas Conservation
Foundation to assist with establishment and operationalization MCF, the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee, staff hire, launching, and development of the
Conservation area management plan.

19. It is proposed that K4 Million will be put into an Endowment Fund to be managed by
representatives from CEPA, Finance Department, National Planning and Monitoring, Oro
Provincial Administration, |jivitari District Development Authority, Afore Level Government,
Partners with Melanesians and Managalas Conservation Foundation under a trust deed.

20. Overseas supporters like the Rainforest Foundation of Norway that have supported the
conservation initiative over the past have expressed their commitment to contribute funds when
the trust fund is established.

21. Managalas conservation area if declared will be the largest terrestrial conservation area in the
country with an increase by 0.9% bringing the total to 4.7% from the current 3.85% and hence
contribute towards achieving the Achi target of protecting 17% of the terrestrial biodiversity by
2020.

Recommendation

Itis recommended that;

22. you note the contents of this policy submission; and

23. approve and sign the attached NEC Policy submission on the Declaration of Managalas
Conservation area for deliberation by NEC

Gunther Joku
Managing Director

HON. JOHN PUNDARI, MP
MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMNT & 
CONSERVATION & CLIMATE CHANGE 
Dated:  7 September 2016
POLICY SUBMISSION NO…………………./2016
FOR MEMBERS OF THE NATIONAL EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
SUBJECT:  DECLARATION OF MANAGALAS PLATEU OF AFORE LLG, 
IJIVITARI, DISTRICT OF ORO PROVINCE AS A CONSERVATION 
AREA UNDER THE 
 
 CONSERVATION AREAS ACT OF 1978
 
 
A.
PURPOSE
1) To brief NEC on the need for declaration and protection of the Managalas 
plateau of Afore Local Level Government, Ijivitari District, Oro Province as a 
conservation Area under the Conservation Areas Act of 1978; 
2) To seek NEC approval for declaration of Managalas plateau as a 
Conservation Area in Papua New Guinea;
3) To seek NEC Direction for the Minister for Environment and Conservation to 
facilitate and complete the Managalas Conservation Area Declaration process 
of by November 2016 including the Gazettal;
4) To seek NEC approval of K8 million for initial start up assistance and one of 
management support for the Managalas Conservation Area and for 
sustainable financing purposes; 
5) To seek NEC direction for Treasury and Finance to make budgetary 
appropriations; PGK4 million for Conservation Environment Protection 
Authority to establish necessary administrative & sustainable financing 
mechanisms for the new Conservation area; and PGK4 million grant for 
Managalas Conservation Foundation for one of mobilization and management 
support including declaration; 
6) To seek NEC approval for the establishment of the Endowment Fund and its 
Trustees; comprising of representatives of Department of Treasury (DoT), 
Department of National Planning and Monitoring (DNPM), Conservation 
Environment and Protection Authority (CEPA), Afore LLG, Managalas 
- 1 -

Conservation Foundation (MCF), Oro Provincial Government (OPG) New 
Britain Palm Oil Limited (NBPOL) and Partners with Melanesians Inc (PwM)
 
7) To seek NEC approval for Conservation Environment Protection Authority 
(CEPA) to take all necessary steps and actions to establish the Managalas 
Conservation Area Endowment Fund (MCAEF) with immediate effect, and
8) To seek NEC approval and granting of tax exemption status to the 
Conservation project area and NGOs on goods and Services Tax, Interest 
Withholding tax and other relevant taxes applicable.
B.
FACTS AND CONSIDERATION
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area & its Biodiversity
9) The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses of about 360 000 
hectares of the pristine rainforest compromising of the lowland hill and 
Montane forests in the Managalas Plateau, Afore Local Level Government of 
Ijivitari District, Oro province. The forests are intersected by many creeks and 
rivers that form the main catchments for the Bariji and Musa Rivers. The area 
is bordered by the Owen Stanley Range to the Southwest and the Sibium 
range to the Southwest. Popondetta town and the famous Kokoda Trail are 
situated north of the Proposed Conservation Area.
10)In terms of boundary, the Proposed Managalas Conservation area extends 
from 14802’ 20” to the West and 1480 34’ 59” to the East, 80 51’ 57” to the 
North and 90 28’ 28” to the South. It covers an area of approximately 360 000 
hectares or 3 600 square kilometers.
11)The Managalas Plateau encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from 
alpine forest at an altitude of 3800 meters to tropical rainforest to the 
mountains and hills as well as savannah grassland and anthropogenic garden 
areas. The Plateau is isolated from most of the urban centers within the Oro 
Province due to deteriorating and underdeveloped transport infrastructure.
12)The plateau has a very high biodiversity, with different fauna and flora 
species, common to rare and protected. Being a large area, ranges of each 
fauna species depends entirely on how far each species can travel. Some are 
only confined to their required habitats and the food sources in each 
vegetation types. This includes the world’s largest butterfly, the Queen 
Alexander Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) that is only found in Oro Province of 
Papua New Guinea and other endangered and endemic species like Doria’s 
Tree Kangaroo.
13)QABB is listed under Appendix A of Convention on International Trade of 
Endangered Species (CITES). PNG is a party to CITES (Convention on International 
Trade of Endangered Species) Appendix A means that, QABB is on the RED LIST 
and is endangered if no action is taken to protect its habitats resulting in extinction.
 14) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978) 
gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to 
CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB.
- 2 -

14)Despite four (4) biological surveys undertaken in the past by friends of the 
Managalas plateau including the Department of Environment and 
Conservation, the Science Faculty of the University of Papua New Guinea, 
and Partners with Melanesia, there is a diverse array of fauna and flora of the 
Managalas plateau that remain to be discovered and documented. Hence 
having the area declared as a Conservation Area can allow further research 
into the rich diverse ecosystems of the area.
Threats to Conservation & Sustainable Natural Resources use 
15) The major threat on the environment and the forest ecosystems is from 
agriculture; conversion of primary forests for both subsistence food production 
and commercial cash cropping activities like growing coffee- undertaken by 
the local communities to enhance human wellbeing. 
16) There are potential threats from the private sector; especially companies who 
are interested in industrial logging and mining in and around the proposed 
conservation areas. Initially there was an intrusion and overlap with mining 
Exploration Lease (EL 1547) but the boundary map has been adjusted 
amicably between landowners, the Minerals Resources Authority, and the 
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to allow mining 
exploration activities to be undertaken outside the boundary of the proposed 
conservation area.
17) Several industrial logging propositions have been made but landowners in 
the conservation area have and are still objecting in preference over 
conservation and small scale ecoforestry to meet local requirements including 
housing, construction of schools and health centers.
Community Support, Capacity and Future Sustainability
 
18) The Managalas communities were educated through a literacy program 
through the University of Papua New Guinea since 1984 on the issues related 
to the destruction of the natural forests and the biodiversity. As a result, all the 
Managalas clan elders and chiefs agreed in at a public forum at zone 6 
(Numba) in 1997 to have the entire Managalas plateau officially declared as a 
conservation area to protect the habitat for the QABB and the forest for the 
future generations. 
19) The respective government agencies at the Provincial and Local level have 
also given their support and endorsement on the declaration of Managalas 
Conservation area; Oro Provincial Executive endorsement on 2nd December 
2008 followed by Afore Local Level Government endorsement on 8th June 
2011.
20) At the invitation of the Managalas communities, the Partners with 
Melanesians (PwM) a national Non- Governmental Organization (NGO) has 
been working in the area since 1997 mainly in raising awareness and building 
capacity with funding assistance from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway up 
to present with a total expenditure of some PGK20 million. PWM Focal 
Programs in the past had been;

Education, training and awareness
- 3 -


Scientific research, data collection and analysis

Support for alternative income earning options

Facilitate conservation area declaration
21) Notable achievements include education and awareness of local 
communities, conservation commitment of 360,000 hectares; establishment of 
base line socioeconomic and biological data; and establishment of a 
community based organization for the area; the Managalas Conservation 
Foundation (MCF) with its Board, management and 5 -year organizational 
strategic plan.
22)There are some level of alternative income earning opportunities that have 
been supported over the years for sustainable livelihood purposes especially 
Arabica coffee at small holder level; and as it is one of the few areas in the 
Southern region, it has huge potential for increased production and marketing 
at premium prices with eco labelling. 
23)There is also opportunity for eco-tourism, there is an initial plan to develop an 
eco-tourism industry on the plateau under the Conservation Area and besides 
that tracking along the famous Black Cat/Ghost Trail from Abau up into the 
Owen Stanley Ranges to upper Musa round Dorobosoro and into Aiari, Suari 
and into the Managalas plateau (the path used by the American soldiers in aid 
of the Australians) at Kokoda is now in the pipe line and it is predicted that it 
will be receiving visitors so employment opportunity and other spin-off benefits 
will be tremendous for the area along the lines of Kokoda Trail.
24) A geographical, socioeconomic and biological profile of the proposed 
Managalas Conservation Area is annexed to this NEC submission and 
“Annex A” that includes information on the people, biodiversity survey results 
and people’s commitment and support for conservation. 
25) PwM and the MCF are working together under an existing collaborative 
partnership Memorandum of Understanding on the mobilization and joint use 
of both financial and technical resources for the conservation area program.
26) Through an exit strategy PwM developed between PwM and MCF, all 
management responsibilities will be handed over to MCF to maintain and 
manage the proposed Conservation Area once declared.
27) In line with the National Protected Area Policy which the NEC approved in 
2014 (NEC Decision No. 5/2014) that provides for sustainable financing for 
protected areas, the NEC consider and approve the amount of K8 Million to 
cover initial costs for the management of the Managalas Conservation Area. 
These includes costs for developing the Management Plan for the 
conservation area including land use plans, establishment of the Managalas 
Conservation Area Management Committee, training of local rangers and 
funding of sustainable income generating projects for the local communities in 
each zones in the project area.
28) To provide for sustainable financing for the management of the conservation 
area, the NEC consider an approve the amount of K4 Million to be set aside 
as an Endowment Fund to be managed by representatives from CEPA, 
Finance Department, National Planning and Monitoring, Oro Provincial 
- 4 -

Administration, Ijivitari District Development Authority, Afore Level 
Government. Partners with Melanesians and Managalas Conservation 
Foundation under a trust deed. 
29) An Endowment Fund is investment fund set up by an institution or 
organisation in which regular withdrawals from the invested capital are used 
for on-going operations or other specified purposes. Sustainable financing is 
required to pay staff, purchase equipment, engage with local communities, 
conduct natural resource monitoring and enforce rules for the protected area. 
The interest generated by the resulting investments provides financial security 
for protected areas. Local communities in the area will benefit in the form of 
jobs, training, sustainable income generation and development projects.  This 
is important due to the fact that the land where the protected area is 
established are owned and controlled by customary clan groups which is 
recognised by the PNG Constitution and relevant laws in the country.
30) In line with the Governments Public Private Partnership and outsourcing 
policy consistent with Pillar 6 objectives of PNG Vision 2050, field 
conservation area management and sustainability issues including education, 
awareness and capacity building functions will be outsourced to Partners With 
Melanesians and Managalas Conservation Foundation by the Government 
(CEPA) given their local knowledge and expertise in the area of conservation 
and development enabled through the sustainable financing mechanism. 
31) An organizational profile of Partners with Melanesians is annexed to this 
submission and marked as “Annex B”. 
32) Employment opportunities will be created through the development and 
implementation of the Managalas Conservation Area Management Plan 
(CAMP) with input and guidance from Afore LLG, CEPA and other interested 
stakeholders.
33)The track is called Ghost Mountain Track and it starts from Gabagaba to Dorobisoro 
in Rigo District and goes over the ranges to Suari, Aijari, Itokama to Gora (covers 
villages in zone 4, zone 1, zone 2, zone 3 and zone 10) in the proposed conservation 
area. The Black Cat Track is another track that goes from Kupiano/Abau over the 
ranges to Safia (Middle-Musa) to Embessa and down to Foru (Lower Musa). So in 
our case we are looking at developing and promoting the Ghost Mountain Track. A 
book was written by James Chalmers about the track called " The Ghost Mountain 
Boys". He walked the track with another Journalist from the USA in 2006.
34) There is considerable ongoing support and commitment by other 
organizations within PNG and abroad who are interested in the biodiversity 
conservation and sustainable use of the natural resources of the Managalas 
plateau. These include Rainforest Foundation of Norway who has consistently 
supported since 1996 and Bishop Museum in the USA, the University of PNG, 
and Department of Community Development, local NGOs and most 
importantly the Oro Provincial Government and its people.
35) Managalas conservation area if declared will be the largest terrestrial 
conservation area in the country with an increase by 0.9% bringing the total to 
4.7% from the current 3.85% and hence contribute towards achieving the Achi 
target of protecting 17% of the terrestrial biodiversity by 2020. 
- 5 -

C.
VIEWS OF THE PRIME MINISTER
36)Prime Minister has been briefed and he supports this submission.
D. 
VIEWS OF OTHER MINISTERS AFFECTED
37)Their views will be sought at NEC.
E.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
38) A one of PGK8 million will be required for initial establishment, 
operationalization and community development support including 
establishment of sustainable financing mechanism by Conservation Protection 
Authority (CEPA) of PGK4 million; and Managalas Conservation Foundation 
(MCF) K4.0 million will be required. 
39) As not for profit organizations (NGOs) are involved in facilitating the 
establishment of the Conservation Area and will take on the responsibility of 
managing it and in recognition of the commitment by the landowners in the 
conservation area to give massive parts of their land for the conservation 
project, the NEC grants tax exemption status including Goods and Services 
Tax, Interest Withholding tax and other relevant taxes application to the 
project.
F.
STAFFING IMPLICATIONS
40) The proposed one of funding assistance will enable both Conservation 
Environment Protection Authority and Managalas Conservation Foundation to 
mobilize manpower required for operationalization of the Managalas 
Conservation Area programs including sustainable financing mechanism.
G.
EMPLOYMENT IMPLICATIONS
41) This project will provide employment opportunities for both local and 
appropriately skilled personnel in the area through Managalas Conservation 
Foundation and other entities associated with the Conservation area and 
other income generation and community development initiatives.
H.
LEGISLATIVE IMPLICATIONS
42) Nil 
I.
CONSTITUTIONAL IMPLICATIONS
43) The Declaration of Managalas Plateau as a conservation area will be in line 
with the 4th Goal of the National Constitution that calls for conservation of 
PNG’s natural resources and the environment for the collective benefit of the 
current and future generations.
J.
DECENTRALISATION IMPLICATIONS
- 6 -

44) Nil
K.
POLITICAL IMPLICATIONS
45) The O’Neill -Dion and PNC lead Government will be seen to be implementing 
its public private partnership and outsourcing policy in contracting the services 
of Partners with Melanesians and Managalas Conservation Foundation in the 
area of conservation and community development.
46)The current Government will also be seen to upholding and supporting the 
decisions of the landowning communities and Government agencies at the 
Provincial and Local level for conservation and sustainable natural resource 
use.
L.
PLANNING IMPLICATION
47) The K8 million one of initial establishment and operationalization support to 
CEPA and MCF needs to be budgeted and released appropriately.
M.
IMPLEMENTATION IMPLICATION
48) CEPA will need to fast track in the establishment and operationalization of 
the sustainable financing mechanism to ensure sustainability and ongoing 
support to the Managalas conservation area.
N.
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPLICATIONS
49) Nil
O.
PREVIOUS POLICY REFERENCE
50). NEC Decision No:12/2008 -  Declaration and Establishment of YUS 
Conservation Area, Kabwum District Morobe Province under the Conservation 
Areas Act (1978).
51) NEC Decision No. 05/2014 – Establishment and Management of Protected 
Area Sustainable Financing Mechanism
P.
RECOMMENDATIONS
52)It is recommended that NEC:
52.1) Notes the contents of this Policy Submission; 
52.2) Approves the declaration and establishment of Managalas plateau     of 
Afore Local Level Government of Ijivitari District of Oro Province as a 
Conservation Area under the Conservation Areas Act 1978; 
52.3) Directs the Minister for Environment and Conservation to take all 
necessary steps in the implementation of this NEC Decision relating to 
declaration of Managalas Conservation Area by October 2016 
including Gazettal;
 
- 7 -

52.4) Approves K8 million for the Managalas Conservation Area; PGK4 for 
establishment of the sustainable financing mechanism by Conservation 
Environment Protection Authority, and PGK4 million for Managalas 
Conservation Foundation for initial establishment, launching and 
community development support;
52.5) Directs the Department of Treasury, Finance, National Planning, 
Monitoring and Implementation to take appropriate actions necessary 
in identifying and provision of the required PGK8 million; 
52.6) Approves the establishments of the Endowment Fund and its Trustees; 
comprising of Representatives of Department of Treasury (DoT), 
Department of National Planning and Monitoring (DNPM), 
Conservation Environment and Protection Authority (CEPA), Afore LLG 
Representative, Managalas Conservation Foundation (MCF), Oro 
Provincial Government (OPG) New Britain Palm Oil Limited (NBPOL) 
and Partners with Melanesians Inc (PwM), 
 
52.7) Directs Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to take all 
necessary steps and actions to establish the Managalas Conservation Area 
Endowment Fund (MCAEF), and
52.8) Approves and grants tax exemption status to the Conservation project 
area and include NGOs (Partner with Melanesians Inc. and Managalas 
Conservation Foundation Inc.,) on Goods and Services Tax, Interest 
Withholding tax and other relevant taxes applicable.
HON. JOHN PUNDARI, MP

title: Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report
snippet: P a g e | 1 Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report Authors: Jacinta Mimigari (PWM) and Bradley Dabadaba (MDF) Managalas Proposed Conservation Area Project Conservation Border Patrol (1) Report February 15- 24th 2010 Report prepared for Partners with Melanesians Inc. Port Moresby, Papua
text:
P a g e | 1  
                                                         Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report                    
 
Authors: Jacinta Mimigari (PWM) and Bradley Dabadaba (MDF) 
              
   
  
 
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area Project 
 
Conservation Border Patrol (1) Report 
 
February 15- 24th 2010 
 
Report prepared for Partners with Melanesians Inc. Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. 
 
 
                 Malchus, Raymond, Alkin and a local preparing to cross the Bareji River: Picture taken by Mr. Bradely DabaDaba. 
 
Report compiled by: Jacinta Mimigari- Conservation Officer (PWM)  
                                  Bradley Dabadaba- Conservation coordinator (MDF) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

P a g e | 2  
                                                         Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report                    
 
Authors: Jacinta Mimigari (PWM) and Bradley Dabadaba (MDF) 
              
   
  
 
Acknowledgement 
 
The team members would like to thank the following zones; Zones 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10 for 
their hospitality and making sure the Patrol was a success. Acknowledgement is also 
extended to the management of both Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and 
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) for the logistical arrangement and approval. Special 
thank you to all the patrol team members especially the Desert Storm and its Commander; 
your jokes, encouragement and support all throughout the patrol was great. 
 
 May the spirit of oneness reign on Managalas Plateau, and let us continue the fight to 
safeguard and protect our home which is also home to the endangered and unique species of 
plants and animals. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Executive Summary 
 
This is the combined report of the Conservation Area border Patrol (1) for targeted zones as 
per the 2010 MDF/PWM Combine Conservation work plan. In light to the Conservation 
area Application procedure, a complete Boundary map of Managalas Conservation Area 
(MCA) is required by the concerned Government Departments.  Therefore the need for a 
patrol to the disputed and threatened areas was planned. The targeted or affected zones are 
zones 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10.   
 
Two Patrols will be done as agreed upon by both PWM and MDF Staff during their 
combine planning workshop that was done in January 2010. As MDF, PWM and the people 
of Managalas are gearing up and preparing to submit their Application to the Government in 
June this year 2010, these patrols are vital to see that all requirements are in place. This first 
patrol is to confirm boundary gaps in the disputed areas and find ways to solve that and also 
to find out about the status of the threatened areas. The second Patrol will be done following 
the recommendations from this report.

Authors: Jacinta Mimigari (PWM) and Bradley Dabadaba (MDF) 
              
   
  
 
Introduction 
 
The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) is found in the Afore Local level 
Government in Oro Province and covers a land area of about 360, 000 hectares. A Boundary 
Map of any proposed Conservation Area is one of the main requirements of the Department 
of Environment and Conservation. There are 18 ward councils found within the MPCA area 
and over 150 clan groups which are then divided into 10 zones. From these 10 zones, there 
are 5 Zones (Zone, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10) with Boundary Dispute/ issues that had prevented the 
mapping team to complete the Boundary of the Managalas Conservation Area, in 2005. To 
tackle this, members of the patrol team were divided into two (Team 1 and team 2) and 
visited the targeted zones. 
 
Team 1 members are: Chrispine Burawa (Team leader), Edwin Noaka, Brian Kasira, and 
Peter Sawari 
 
Team 2 members are: Bradley Dabadaba (Team Leader), Jacinta Mimigari, Douglas Tumai, 
and Malkus Kajia 
 
Team 1 were assigned to Patrol areas on the Western flank of the Plateau, which are zones 
(4, 10) while team 2 were assigned to the Eastern flanks of the plateau (6, 8 and 9) 
excluding Gewoia, due to threats from that area. The teams departed on the 15th of February 
2010 and returned back safely on the 25th of February at MDF base at Afore. 
 
As PWM, MDF and the people of Managlas are in the process of submitting their 
Conservation Area Application, such Boundary Patrols have to be done to see that all 
requirements are met and that the communities are kept informed.  
Found in this report also are recommendations, Action Plans and details of the Patrol.

MCAP Project Site showing the probable gaps  
 
 
Fig 1: Map showing the targeted areas patrolled. 
 
 
 
 
Purposes  
 
The main purpose of the Conservation Area Patrol was to identify disputed Areas/ 
boundaries and investigate and confirm threats in the suspected areas. MDF also see that 
Patrol as an avenue to carry out some of their planned activities such as; 
a) Awareness on reforestation projects 
b) Reorganize clan groups 
c) Explanations on importance of Land use plan 
d) Attend to CBO issues.

Results and Patrol Brief 
 
A briefing was held on the 14th of February 2010, before both teams set off for the Patrol. 
During the briefing, patrol teams were reminded and each encouraged themselves on how to 
constructively attend to possible sensitive issues that could be raised during the Patrol. Each 
teams’ schedules were drawn up, food rations, logistics and patrol equipments were 
distributed during the briefing. (See full briefing minutes in Appendix 3). 
 
At the end of the patrol a combined debrief was organized again by the Conservation Patrol 
Coordinator, Mr. Dabadaba for 1 whole day to allow both teams to highlight issues/ 
challenges identified during the border patrol. The briefing found out that most issues or 
challenges identified by both teams were similar but few new issues were discovered. These 
were the findings; 
 
a) Land disputes and Boundary mapping of the gaps 
Clan leaders and elders explained about the nature of the disputes, and discuss 
amongst themselves how they can tackle this so as to complete the CA Boundary. It 
was also realized that communities themselves have their own internal issues, but the 
Patrol members made it clear to them that this is their own problems/issues to 
handle.  
 
In zone 6, Kingsford. N, who once worked on the mapping project, gave a brief 
background history of the mapping work and the problems faced that hindered the 
completion of the project. From that Recommendations were down. 
 
b) Awareness on Reforestation, Reorganize clan groups, Land use plan and attend to 
CBO’s issues. 
During the meetings communities were informed about the selection criteria for 
potential reforestation project sites. And if communities/clans are interested then 
they should inform their CBO’s about that. The importance of land use plans were 
explained also. MDF also took notes of the CBO’s issues raised by the communities 
and advised the communities to organize and re-elect new board members and CBO 
Staffs to make the CBO function effectively. The power to create an effective CBO 
lies in each community. CBOs were also told to reorganize clan groups and all the 
sub clans must remain under the main clans. Communities were encouraged to work 
closely with their CBOs. It was encouraging to see Ward 5 council member present 
at the meeting in Numba and communities present saw the importance of both 
Government and NGO’s working together. 
The communities were also advised that the above mentioned activities are all in the  
work plan for 2010, and these activities will mostly be carried out by the CBO’s 
therefore the CBO staff, board and community members need to reorganize 
themselves in order to execute these activities.

Comments and Observations (Problems and Threats)

Recommendations 
 
From the patrol these are the following recommendations that have come about. 
These recommendations were done collectively during the Combined Debriefing after the 
Patrol. 
 
A) New Boundary Mapping must curve out Toma area into the CA and leave out Otjer 
villages in Zone 9. 
B) Kingsford Nichoi and Malchus Kajia to be engaged in the second Patrol for final

C) By March 2010 CBO’s to organize concern clan groups to settle Boundary disputes 
and report to MDF/PWM before final mapping takes place. 
D) Celcor to be legal partner to MDF, since celcor has its CBO desk Officer. As 
understood by Partner NGO’s, CELCOR will always be a partner when it comes to 
getting environmental legal advice.

is catching up.

J) Effective Awareness materials must be issued to Zone 4, 9 and 10 
K) PWM to transfer activity funds immediately

Jacinta M and Mr Mambe attended a meeting held with DEC officers (Mr. Benside Thomas 
and Ms Rose Singadan) on the 9th of Mach to give a brief on the Managalas Status in light to

Conclusion 
 
The patrol was done as planned. No one was hurt during the patrol, but only threats were 
given from some locals around zone 9. 
 
It looks likely that the second Patrol will be set on the last week of April and this will 
involve Managalas Conservation Area stakeholders, like Environmental Lawyers and 
Officer from the Department of Environment and Conservation. There is still a number of 
hurdles up ahead that both MDF/ PWM and the Managalas people must face before we put 
down our arrows. 
 
To conclude, it is said that “Conservation is a shared Responsibility” so let’s all stand 
together to safeguard, fight and protect this ever changing Nature. God Bless the Managalas

text:
Partners with Melanesians

“Maintaining the Dance”

Date: Thursday 22" October.

EL NINO ASSESSMENT & BASIC
PREPAREDNESS AWARENESS
SUMMARY REPORT

MANAGALAS CONSERVATION
PRJECT SITE

AFORE, ORO PROVINCE........
 1. Introduction

El Nino effects of drought are being felt everywhere in PNG with evidence all over the media
concerning food &, Water shortages causing health issues for people particularly the local people
who are directly depended on their land to sustain themselves. During this time, Weather Office
has warned the public that it might continue for longer period & the effects are much worse
comparing it to the 1997 Drought impacts. This was a major concern for PwM project sites as it
has affected the ongoing activities of conservation and community development initiatives. For
this reason, PwM has re-strategized and have taken up the task of collecting information on the
status of the communities in its project sites as a lead up activity to present to Department
Responsible to respond accordingly. This is a summary report of the activities implemented in
Managalas whereas for Inaina and Karimui reports have been submitted by Noel Gisawo &
Steven Poya respectively.

2. Purpose/Objectives
The primary purpose of this trip was to send out two patrol teams on the ground to the Eastern
and Western sides of the plateau respectively to inform the community the basic measures to take
during this El Nino drought period & to collect information of its impacts of Drought on the local
communities
Y Objective 1: Communities to take on basic measures while waiting for responsible
agencies to respond
Y Objective 2: Collate report & provide to Mainstream Media
vY Objective 3: to provide this information to PwM to assess & provide reports to
Responsible departments to take further action (Disaster, NARI etc.)

3. Method

3.1 Patrol teams
1. Eastern Team
- MCF staff
- Zone CBOs 5,6,7A,7B, 8 & 9
2. Western team
- MCF staff
- Zone CBOs 1,2,3,4
 3.2 Information Collection
The team was set out to collect general information through observation & interviews with locals
& other stakeholders in each community on the effects of Drought.

Table 1: The 5 Categories defining the Status of Drought impact areas

means that they are dried up. Water is only available at a long distance or some
cannot walk far to_get water and there is a little bit of risk as it involves life

 4, Results

Using table 1, the findings indicated that Managalas community fell under category Three (3)
however, in the event that drought prolongs, quantity of food stored will run out coupled with
poor water quality which will have detrimental effects on Health & Hygiene of the people.

4.1 Direct Impacts

a)

b)

c)

a)

e)

8)

Bush Fires

Bush Fires are a threat since there is lack of rain & almost all the vegetation are dry
enough to start a fire. Fires in this case are commonly started by locals who tend to forget
to put off the fires after clearing bushes for new gardens, cooking in open fire place while
in the garden or hunting.

Food

Lack of rainfall & reduced water table have caused garden food to dry up & even burnt to
the core due to intense heat. Staple foods like banana, native yam & taro have been
reduced & are being substituted with African yam, mammy yam & sago

Water

The water cycle has been affected particularly the lack of rainfall well over 2 months &
still continuing have compromised the supply of fresh water into streams, creeks and
rivers. As a result, many of this streams & creeks have dried up forcing people to walk
long distances to get to mainstream rivers. There are some areas on the plateau that
heavily depend on rainwater harvesting such as Government & mission stations which
most of them have now ran out of water supply and have joined the rest of the villagers to
take refuge near mainstream rivers. With many people including livestock using the
mainstream rivers, it poses the threat of water contamination coupled with poor water
quality causing it not safe for consumption.

Health

The basic human requirements for an individual is to have access to safe drinking water,
sufficient food, secure shelter & good conditions, however in this situation, these
necessities have been compromised & have given way to waterborne diseases &
malnutrition. There have already been reported cases on dysentery, malnutrition &
typhoid in some areas on the plateau.

Schools & Other Service providers
Many of the schools that are being worst hit such as Afore Primary School & those that
are located up in remote areas have closed down including Health Centres & District
office to search for avenues to survive.

Cash Cropping

Market supply in terms of agriculture especially those that are engaged in selling of
garden food have been reduced as well as cash cropping such as Coffee, coconut and
Vanilla as well. There are no surpluses produced to supply the market.

Other Community Projects

There are some community projects such as Conservation Area & Queen Alexandra
Birdwing Butterfly Rehabilitation projects that are being affected & halted at the moment
for this period.
 4.2 Indirect Impacts
Because of these direct impacts, the consequences are that people are doing what they can to
survive such as;
e Families are looking out for each other only and unable to provide for additional people.
¢ People sought other means of survival such as stealing from others garden, livestock & in
some cases using violence to take from the others.
e Public servants have stopped working particularly the health & Education sectors
particularly the areas that are worst hit.
* Much of the economic activities have stopped in terms of agriculture & livestock
© Prices of goods & services have increased
© Community Initiatives have halted as well.

4.3The Vulnerability Status

Using table 2,
a. Natural
Much of Managalas Forests are intact comprising of lowland hill to montane Forests with
presence of grassland in between. Many creeks and rivers form the main catchments of the
Bareji and Musa rivers that intersect the forests. The local people utilize the lower area for
subsistence agriculture, coffee, coconut and vanilla plantations therefore constitutes disturbed
vegetation and secondary re-growths.

Strength

i, Intact Forested Areas with Main river catchment are able to withstand the onslaught of
drought to a certain degree; however, Bush Fires will only be threat. Fact is if it’s
naturally instigated then it will be able to rejuvenate over time.

Challenge

ii. Areas of Disturbed Vegetation are currently victims to the impacts of Drought
particularly with communities living in & around these areas it further puts pressure on
the ecosystem services. As a result, there is occurrence of poor soil quality due to lack of
moisture present causing crops to dry or even die out. Water body of creeks, streams and
rivers are reduced and water quality has dropped as well.

b. Social
Strength

On the plateau, The Zone CBOs have been actively working closely with MCF staff to
coordinate much of the Awareness and the assessment of the situation on the ground using
their Consensus Building Process-a traditional decision making structure to reach out plateau
wide.
 PwM has assisted to mobilize the CBOs to update information. Media was engaged to tell
the plight of the Managalas people in order for relevant agencies to take further action. PWM.
continues to provide that medium for relevant stakeholders to respond accordingly.

Challenges

Communities are spread across the plateau and are far from each other which are quite a
challenge when it comes to effective means of communication particularly getting messages
across to one community to another. There is obviously missing link between stakeholders
onsite to co-share the responsibility of partnership initiatives in terms of resource
mobilization to facilitate the drought situation. For Instance, The CBOs & MCF staff have
worked alone to carry out awareness & collect information on the ground plateau wide for
communities to be on the lookout. The Local level Government was unable to carry out any
emergency exercise as there is lack of plans and enforcements particularly in the areas of
Disaster response, Health & Sanitation & Education causing all to stop function on an
indefinite period leaving many communities to survive off whatever they have or can at the
moment.

ce. Human
Strength

For the locals particularly, traditional knowledge is the only salvage at the moment
particularly in terms of food and water storage such as the yam house or garden house and
the bamboo for water storage.

Challenges

However, it won’t be long until they run out as they are unable to make new gardens. This
will affect the health and hygiene of the people causing many sicknesses and even death at
the extreme. Malnutrition and other water-borne diseases are prevalent during these times

d. Physical

Managalas have been missing out at receiving vital services such as Education & Health in
terms of inadequate facilities to fully function. There is only one effective
Telecommunication the famous Digicel network on the plateau however, its costly to
maintain communication. There is no major water supply but water tanks are supplied to
Education, Health and mission stations only usable when there is rain. Otherwise everyone
else uses the natural fresh water catchments for their consumption.
 e. Financial

Most communities on the plateau are subsistence farmers, a few in each communities are
engaged in other cash crops like Coffee & cocoa and so with this drought situation, the
market supply has decreased due to low crop yield causing farmers with their families to
lose income and are unable to afford goods and services on a daily basis solely depending
on organic enough to keep them going.

Public servants and business persons are able to afford the goods and services however
are spending more to keep up with the demand.

5. Recommendation

Basically the active stakeholders are the CBOs and the MCF on the ground, with the help of
PwM are mobilizing the communities and are currently networking with other stakeholders to
take further action. Emphasis is that only through partnership initiatives can help reduce the
vulnerable sectors particularly the loss of lives & properties.

Immediate action has to be relieving the communities to cope with the impacts however it comes
with a cost which is short term particularly food and clean water supply. Looking long term
would call for actions like Capacity building of locals through Education and Awareness.
Develop long term Disaster risk plans that ties all relevant stakeholders through an MOU ete. It
is important to note that every stakeholder involved have specific roles to play and that needs to
be clarified right from the start which basically means that they all complement each other. For
Instance, PwM plays the role of enabling communities to know the processes/concepts in order
to participate & benefit meaningfully. It also plays the role of networking the communities with
service providers. Thus, immediate action would be;

I. Dialogue with NARI, Disaster and Fire Service on how they can assist by providing
this report.
Il. Engage NARI, Disaster and Fire Service to carry out a plateau wide Awareness &
Workshop on Drought Preparedness for the long run
Ill. Review Climate Change program activities to accommodate the frequent extreme
events phenomenon to offset conservation efforts.

6. Conclusion
The assessment was carried out with the two patrol teams for Eastern & Western side. The
impacts are directly felt by the locals on the plateau which water & food supply are gradually

reduced and will continue to do so if the drought persists. This calls for further assessment and
provide assistance to locals during this harsh times.

 NGO ALARMS DROUGHT WARNING IN MANAGALAS PLATEAU

Words and pictures by JASON GIMA WURI

As the dry season continues to extend due to the El Nino phenomenon, there are rural areas in
Papua New Guinea that are greatly feeling the effects. One such place is the 360 000 hectares
of the Managalas Conservation Area located on the Managalas plateau in Afore Local Level
Government (LLG) west of Popondetta township of Oro Province.

The last time this place experienced rain was over four months ago, and the drought was
making life difficult for the people living on this plateau. According to reports by the cultural
zone Community Based Organizations (CBO) which is managed by the Managalas Conservation
Foundation (MCF), the immediate and major concern for the people has been shortage of fresh
water for cooking, drinking and washing and the shortage of food supply.

This has led to early closure of several schools on a daily basis at the Afore station and along the
plateau with students been sent home. This drought may affect public servants working at
Afore station as well as throughout the Managalas Plateau. With the shortage of water and
food a major concern, there are increasing concerns on health issues as a direct result of the
drought.

A local Non Government Organization (NGO), Partners with Melanesia (PWM) has been doing
alot of conservation work in partnership with the people of Managalas Plateau through the
MCF and CBOs to carry out conservation work throughout the plateau.

PWM Program Manager Rufus Mahuru said that their concern as an NGO was to help carry out
awareness of this plight caused by the El Nino phenomenon.

“Managalas Plateau in particular is our area of concern as they are our partner in the
conservation work that we carry out and are currently seeking refuge in the area proposed for
conservation under the National Protected Area Policy,” Mr Mahuru said.

Project Officer for the Managalas Conservation Foundation (CMF) Dickson Dorebo confirmed
that the most affected areas were along the ranges during this drought mainly because the
ranges were the most rocky and stony areas along the plateau.

“The Managalas plateau is divided into two parts, the west and east and areas like Berefo which
consists of six villages in Ward 15 of Afore Local Level.Government (LLG), Oikol tribe in Ward
One, Aiari, Suari and Jaure villages along the Sibium range and the Owen Stanley range are the
worst hit by this drought,” Mr Dorebo said.

title: “The Consensus”
snippet: “The Consensus” The decision making process at the Managalas Conservation Area Project MANAGALAS PROJECT BACKGROUND The Managalas Proposed Conservation Project is a partnership between Part- ners with Melanesians (PWM), Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and Rainforest Foundation of Norway (RFN)
text:
“The Consensus” 
The decision making process at the Managalas Conservation Area Project  
MANAGALAS PROJECT BACKGROUND 
The Managalas Proposed Conservation Project is a partnership between Part-
ners with      Melanesians (PWM), Managalas Development Foundation 
(MDF) and Rainforest   Foundation of Norway (RFN)  to help the people of 
Managalas living on this plateau to protect their forest and provide       alter-
native options for      sustainable   development to sustain their      livelihood.  
In 1997, with the threat of large scale industrial development approaching 
from all sides of the plateau, the community through their consensus building 
and decision making process agreed          unanimously that, with the help of 
Partners with Melanesians (NGO) and the support of the Rainforest Founda-
tion of Norway (RFN), the project started to provide an         alternative to the 
Government’s plan for destructive resource development. 
The Project is Undertaken through 4 core programmes; 
 Conservation Programme 
 Capacity Building and Training Programme 
 Consensus Building Programme 
 Rainforest Literacy Programme 
Because the people live on a plateau surrounded by high mountains to the 
east and west, in 2001 the community elders through traditional decision 
making   process decided that, a    mapping team is put in place and trained to 
map the outer land    boundaries of the plateau, to secure it and with written 
submission made to the government to have the area  declared a conservation 
area and to stop the industrial developments of logging, mining and palm oil      
plantations. 
The people wanted to secure the natural forest, the fertile land and the moun-
tains that their ancestors once live in harmony with the environment and now 
they are also living there as their fore fathers once did. 
But with the current economic and global interdependency on money, trade 
and other luxury necessities, the Government of Papua New Guinea (PNG), 
wanted to develop their forest resources through logging, dig up their moun-
tains for gold and nickel, clear their forest through  logging and then plough 
up their land for palm oil plantation development.   
CULTURAL AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT ZONES 
The Managalas project is divided up into 10 zones base on the language and 
culture of the local people. There are over 17000 people and over 150 clans 
altogether on the plateau. They have 5 languages and several dialects spoken, 
there is a common dialect that can be spoken and understood by all from the 
eastern and western side of the plateau.  
The cultural zones have their own clan elders and tribal leaders within the        
management structure, with an elected Board in place with staff of three. A 
new structure of decision making and        management was adopted and 
modified to suit the traditional decision making system, whereby an Associa-
tion is formed and they have a Board that  controls and direct the     opera-
tions of the Association. 
Each cultural zone is independent of each other in decision making as they 
have their own land and resources, however, when it comes to an issue that 
affects the whole plateau, the decision is taken at different stage.  
TRADITIONAL DECISION MAKING PROCESS 
The Managalas people are rural base and still maintain their traditional cus-
toms and practices. One that is  very important is the decision making process 
by consensus (similar in all Melanesian  societies). 
A system of community meeting on key issues identified in the villages is       
presented and discussed at these levels: 
♦ Issues discussed at the family level 
♦ Family level decision brought to clan group discussion 
♦ Clan group decision taken to village level with all clans. A decision is 
made for the village. 
♦ Village representatives selected to zone forum where all the villages 
in the same zone attend to discuss, debate and speak about the 
issue. 
♦ Decisions reached at zones forum by   consensus, is taken by a 
group of elders to the bigger combine forum in a central location. 
♦ At combined forums all the elders of the 10 zones  attend.  
♦ As time elapse Government reps on the plateau have also taken part in 
the forum. 
♦ Many other stakeholders also attend from government, NGOs and 
churches as    observers and advisers. At the combine forum all zone 
representatives discuss and debate the issues and through consensus, 
reach decisions and prioritize key issues for the whole plateau. 
 
This normally takes place at the yam harvesting season and where a big feast is 
held to end the decision   making process. All decisions made at the combine 
forum is taken on board by the management of the CBOs and MDF (The um-
brella NGO) to implement the    decisions by developing programme and activi-
ties, which is    improving at a gradual state. 
This is the similar manner in which the community mapping project came about 
in 2001. 
DECISION OVER LAND IS MADE BY CONSENSUS 
The Community Land Boundary        Mapping work, was the initiative of the  
people through consensus from family level to clan, village, zones and district 
level, as it was a major issue especially regarding threat from industrial              
development on their land that will affect their  resources and livelihood. Types 
of industrial     development include; 
 
Palm Oil development, Forestry and Logging plus Gold and Nickel Mining. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
  Fig.1 The Managalas Consensus Building Process for Decision Making  
 
Land in PNG is communally owned, any decision over land 
has to be made by the clan in the village under traditional 
rules and is discussed and decision is made by consensus 
by all members of the clan. 
Important Data About Managalas   Plateau 
• Land Area- +360 000 hectares 
• Population– 15 000 people (2000 census figure) 
• Languages– 5 Main (Omie, Namiai, Barai, Samoi, Ese) several dia-
lects 
• Clans– 150 
• District Administrative HQ– Afore (in plateau) 
• Provincial HQ– Popondetta, 125 km on coast 
• Road distance to coast– 85km 
• No. of  airstrips in plateau– 4 
• Rainfall– 2800 mm/yr 
• Temp– Min-Max 16-32 degrees Celsius 
• Highest point– 2856 m asl 
• Lowest in point– 460 m asl 
• Forest Type– Lowland Rainforest and savannah grassland 
• Soil– Volcanic

INTRODUCTION 
 
The 2018 District Wide Combine Forum which was carried out from the 29th of October to the 01st 
of November in Yombu Village, Zone 8, Afore LLG was a follow up from the two Zone Forums 
held in Dariki (East) and Tahama (West) this year. 
This is the first District Wide Combine Forum after Managalas was officially declared as a 
Conservation Area in Itokama on the 29th of November, 2017. 
This forum is part of the Consensus Building process in which zones or communities come together 
to find ways in addressing issues (Health, Education etc.) that affect them. Hence, the forum looked 
at ways in which the communities came up with action plans through a consensus and how to link 
other stakeholders. 
We encountered minor logistical problems because improper coordinator of MCF, CBO and 
Participants at the forum. The weather also was a contributing factor to the forum starting late, 
however overall, the forum turn was good. Some Zones even brought extra participants to the 
forum and not the anticipated number. 
During the forum we also had the company of a representative from Fisheries, Rodney Isoro and 
John Mongol from the Department of Agriculture and Livestock. 
MCF East Field Coordinator Crispine Burawa facilitated the District Wide Combine Forum with 
the help of his Forum Management Team. 
PWM officers (Hobert Poria, Patrick Vuet, Lillian Bago) also attended the forum in Yombu led by 
Program Manager Rufus Mahuru, to also take note of issues raised during the forum.  
 
PURPOSE 
 
The aim of the District Wide Combine Forum for 2018 was for the people of Managalas to discuss 
major issues that were brought forward from the East and West Zone Forums, together identify a 
way forward and action plans to sustainable manage the CA. Also this forum was basically, to give 
the locals are sense of direction for the life after CA.   
 
DISCUSSION 
 
The forum eventuated from the 29th of October to the 1st of November at Jombu Village, Zone 8, 
Afore LLG.  
Project name

The forum which took approximately three days had a good number of participants (refer to 
participants’ attendance list). MCF Director, Damien Ase was also present at the forum with his 
staff, alongside PWM Staff and Program Manager Rufus Mahuru. 
 
Even though the District Wide Combine Forum ended on a good note, we had notable challenges 
and areas we needed to improve on; 
 Logistical coordination on the ground was a problem, participants were accommodated 
away from the forum venue and water sources which contributed to the forum starting late. 
  The proper forum process wasn’t followed in certain areas of the forum. 
 The Bung Kaikai for MCF, PWM, CBO’s and participants didn’t turn out well. The bung 
kaikai wasn’t enough to feed everyone, the food didn’t correlate to the money given to 
spend. 
 There was no way forward or collective action plan identified during and after the forum. 
 Some of the major issues brought forward from the zone forums were discussed in their 
local language all throughout the forum, which made invited guests and even PWM staff to 
lose concentration. We should have had a Translator for that matter.  
 
From the outcome of the zone forums in Dariki (East) and Tahama (West) participants

3. Establishment of the Afore Council of Women  
4. East CBO Petition 
5. Establishment of Council of Chiefs for Advisory Role in LLG to pass law

Issue #4: Gender Empowerment

forum, with emphasis on further need for awareness/information dissemination throughout the plateau and to 
organize themselves at the CBO level up 
  
Way forward as discussed; 
- 
PWM to employ a Gender Officer to guide/coordinate with MCF Gender Officer to 
mobilize women in the plateau to set up this office come January 2019 
- 
Ensure the steps and process followed to setting up the Afore Council of Women are done in 
line with the Provincial/National Council of Women and the by-laws of PNG. 
 This is what the government should do but NGO is now taking the lead to facilitate 
and therefore, the Oro Provincial Council of Women executives must be notified and 
let them play their part.

to ensure the Afore Council of Women is set up.

understanding of issues between the parties involved. 
 
Issue # 7: Establishment of CA Committee

The forum then revisited the people appointed (x7) during the East/West Zone forums. There was a

The names of the 4 appointed people above will be sent to CEPA for further deliberations on the 
processes and setting up of the full CA Committee. The appointees will then follow necessary 
processes to take office as according to CEPA. 
 
 
 
RESULTS/FINDINGS 
 
There is a lot work to be done when organizing big forums like this, especially; 
 Ground Logistics – Coordination of participants and accommodation was not synchronized 
which added to participants arriving late at the forum venue. 
 Forum Process – It is always important to follow the forum process so that issues are not 
diverted or off track. 
 Networking – During the forum new networks or connections with responsible Government 
Departments were established focusing on SLA activities in the Plateau. Also, there needs to 
be more linking ups and networking with relevant Government bodies so that they too can 
contribute in sustainably managing the plateau. 
 Issues Raised Not Understood – Certain issues raised at Zone Forums and brought forward 
to the District Wide Combine Forum were not clearly understood. From participant’s ill 
response, you could summarize that issues such as ‘Establishment of Afore Council of 
Women’ or ‘Establishment of Council of Chiefs for Advisory Role in LLG to pass Law’ is a 
new concept to them that needs to be clarified precisely.  
 Road Condition – Depending on the weather the road condition can also be a problem if 
you are travelling from Popondetta to Afore. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
The District Wide Combine Forum is a platform where locals come together yearly to discuss, 
identify and create paths for a way forward for everyone.  This process is an effective process, 
whereby it will make way for progress in Managalas by way of consensus. 
 

 
./6 
RECOMMENDATION 
 
From Lillian’s and my observation during the three-day forum at Yombu Village, the following 
areas seriously needs to be looked at; 
 
1. Community Empowerment and Education Awareness Program 
This program is vital and its activities must be revisited/redesigned and aligned with its 
Purpose/objective since it has shifted away from Rainforest Literacy and a part of the 
consensus building process left out. Theatre activities must be included because it is the 
only medium currently being used for awareness and information dissemination purposes 
around the plateau.  
Also, this scriptwriting workshop be changed to content development workshop or 
something along that line (only a suggestion) because as it is, we are no longer developing 
radio scripts for the radio programs and learning objectives for the print materials like it 
used to be. 
The lessons learnt from this Program especially in Managalas must be taken into careful 
consideration and NOT repeated in the new Project areas. 
 
2. Also have a Neutral Forum Facilitator 
It is always essential to have a facilitator who is neutral and will not take sides. Having a 
fair and balanced discussion is fundamental for an effective consensus building process. 
Therefore, facilitation of any forum in the near future must always have a neutral facilitator 
and also a co-facilitator to take on the facilitators responsibility if need be. 
 
3. There is a Need to Identify Proper Program Activities    
In addition to recommendation #1, there is a need to revisit the Consensus Building 
Process/Rainforest Literacy and clarify certain changes. We should be careful NOT to 
repeat the Managalas experience in other project areas because obviously their social 
structure and fabric of society is completely different. Therefore, we must seriously look at 
how best the overall program will suit individual areas.

As you take your place as the Minister of Environment Conservation & Climate Change, we the PWM Board, Management and Staff would like to bring to 
your urgent attention the following as a matter of concern. 
 
The Managalas Conservation Area since, the submission was presented to you on the 8th of November 2012,  and its approval by NEC on the 15th of 
December 2016 with the National Gazettal Notice published by Governor General HE Sir Bob Dadae on the 23rd of March 2017;  
 
The Managalas Community and Oro province have waited patiently for 5 years and are now looking forward to the formal launching and declaration 
which will take place on-site at Itokama, on the western side of the Managalas plateau at a proposed date on 29th November 2017. 
 
It will be a milestone achievement for the Managalas people, Oro Province and PNG as a Country, as Managalas plateau will be the Second Largest 
Conservation Area with a land area of 360, 000 hectares with pristine rainforest, high biodiversity and rich cultural diversity and heritage.  
 
The official launch and declaration will be a great occasion anticipated by many who have longed to see this happen with you as Minister responsible.
