Field trip Report – Conservation Area Workshop with the ALLG Councillors... 
  
Date:  17th May 2011 
 
 
PROGRAM: Conservation Component  
 
ACTIVITY: Afore LLG Resolution: Workshop conducted by PWM & CELCOR to explain to 
the councillors the CA processes and the procedures, Conservation Areas Act and the 
advantages and disadvantages of a Conservation Area.  
 
INTRODUCTION 
During the 2010 Christmas Holiday a team consisting of officers from PWM and CELCOR, went 
up to the Managalas plateau to meet with the Afore LLG President and his 18 ward councillors. The 
purpose of the meeting was to get clarification from them as to why the assembly had adjourned the 
signing of the Conservation Area (CA) resolution to the end of 2011. Unfortunately, only three (3) 
councillors and the President attended. During our meeting with them, the President advice the team 
that they (Afore LLG) have prepared a resolution and issues that they want PWM to address. One 
main issue is for PWM and its Partners to conduct more awareness to the councillors as majority do 
not understand 1) the CA procedures, 2) the advantages and disadvantages of a CA, and explain the 
3) Conservation Area Act. Therefore, this workshop was an action taken to address the main issue 
that the President pointed out above.   
PURPOSE 
The purpose of this trip or workshop was to make awareness to the councillors on the above 
mentioned areas so that they can be in a better position to make decision. In fact a similar workshop 
was also conducted in April 2010.          
METHODS/PROCEDURES 
Officers that went up for the workshop were 
Kenn Mondiai, Damien Ase and Patrick Vuet. 
Damien was late for the flight so he flew over the 
following day. Kenn and I flew on the 11th of 
May 2011 and were supposed to go straight up to 
the project site (Afore), however, a block road 
occurred at Eroro Village where the villagers cut 
down two coconut trees to block the road. We 
couldn’t passed through so we over night at Oro 
Guest House with two councillors (Remingius 
Juharo & Abraham Tarabu)  and Edrick Ninimiro 
(PWM SLA Officer). 

 
 
Field trip Report – Conservation Area Workshop with the ALLG Councillors... 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
We travelled up to Managalas on the 12th of May. 
 
We arrived at around 11 am at Afore. We started the program for that first day after lunch and 
ended at 5pm. As per the two days program, Patrick went through the CA processes and 
procedures, update on the current status of the Conservation Area, and the activities that PWM, 
MDF, the LLG and the communities will do after the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area is 
declared a Conservation Area.    
 
Kenn Mondiai explained the terms used in the legend of the Forestry and mining overlay maps 
that cover the Managalas area. He clarify to them the exploration licences within the proposed CA 
and the logging activities that are slowly moving in passed the CA Boundary line.  
 
After the day’s sessions the floor was open for discussions. They raised some questions where both 
PWM and MDF Staffs made clarification on.  
 
The second day was the session for CELCOR & DEC Officers to go through the legal 
Conservation Areas Act, the advantages and disadvantages of CA and the LLG’s and other 
stakeholder’s roles in the CA Act (CAA) and the MPCA Project. In day one Kenn also went 
through some parts that DEC officers were assigned to stress on, because they were fully 
committed and could not make it to this workshop. 
 
Damien from CELCOR, explain to them the CAA, the roles of the LLG in the project, the threats 
that will occur if not Managalas is declared a conservation Area, and the opportunities 
forthcoming when Managalas is declared a conservation Area.        
RESULTS/FINDINGS 
Nine ward councillors and two women 
representatives, a few village chiefs, 
MDF Board members, a few CA 
committees 
and 
CBO 
managers 
attended the workshop; two other 
councillors who were also in full 
support for the endorsement of the 
LLG resolution could not make it due 
to bad weather condition. George King 
(Ward 5 Councillor), asked Damien if 
the Vice President can sign the LLG 
support 
letter 
on 
behalf 
of 
the 
President. Damien explained to them 
that there are legal processes that they 
need to follow if the President is being 
stubborn to sign. After everything was explained to them, some of them commented that they are 
in support for the signing of the ALLG support letter, but it is the president that is prolonging 
the process for reasons unknown. 
 
Damien asked them to hold a special meeting now that the dead line for DEC is approaching to 
sideline the project. The Vice President has to take the lead to draft a letter to the President 
inviting him for the special meeting. If the President does not attend the special meeting, the Vice 
President can chair the meeting. Minutes must be taken, the time, venue, and location must be 
noted. PWM, CELCOR and MDF assisted the vice president to the draft the letter and signed by 

 
 
Field trip Report – Conservation Area Workshop with the ALLG Councillors... 
 
 
 
 
3 
all the councillors that attended the workshop. Copies of the letter were distributed to the 
councillors absent during the work shop, the Afore District Administrator, and the Afore LLG 
Manager. Copy of the letter to the President is attached to this report.  
 
The councillors set a date for the special meeting to be held on the 26th of May 2011. There will 
only two agendas to be discussed in this meeting they are; 
 
1. The endorsement of the Managalas Conservation Area Submission by Afore LLG. 
2. The MOU between MDF, PwM and Afore LLG with the Oro Provincial Government 
over the Conservation Area and activities thereafter.   
RECOMMENDATIONS 
The Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) Project Director is an obstacle to a smooth 
progress of the project. Some councillors and the communities are not satisfying with the way the 
MDF management is running the organization. There are counts of misappropriation of project 
funds which have fragmented the working relationship between MDF and the community based 
organizations (CBOs). Therefore; he needs to be terminated or suspended. This could be one of 
the issues that are delaying the signing of the LLG Resolution.  
 
Funding allocated for the Afore Local Level Government is not reaching the ward councillors. 
Therefore, they want the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area to be declared and with 
assistance from the NGOs would seek funding from donors to implement projects at their LLG 
wards.  
 
Some participants were commenting that the President be taken to court. Damien advised them to 
take all necessary procedures at the local level to try and get the President sign. After exhausting 
all necessary procedures then the President can be taken to court.     
 
CONCLUSION 
The team successfully carry out the activities as per the program. A few councillors who were 
often against the NGO work were convinced and willing to support the Vice President to sign the 
LLG endorsement letter.

MANAGALAS BOUNDARY MAPPING PROJECT.

Progressive Report

This is the progressive report for the Boundary-Mapping project for the year 2002.. I have prepared this
report due to that since the Mapping Coordinator was created and I occupied the position I have not
submitted any progressive report of the project to the Board because there was no Board meeting
although this year until the last meeting in November and this is going to be the second and the last
meeting for the year 2002 which ! have prepared to write this report to submit to the Board in this
meeting,

Report for the Eastern flank

Kingsford Nichoi a Field Mapping Coordinator for the Easter flank in his progressive report says that
the mapping from Bareji high to Embi Lake has been successfully completed and he now have less
than 14 kilometres from Embi to Mt. Lamington, which he suggested that he would complete that
before the end of the year.

1 talked to him that since Malchus have a big area unmapped so as soon as he complete the 14
kilometres he can go and talk with Malchus and share the western flank and complete the unmapped
area’s quickly skipping the disputed area’s so when we run a next workshop on the westem flank will
ing the disputed parties together and see if we can resolve the dispute together in the workshop and
complete mapping the area.

Waypoints:

‘The waypoints for the Easter flank have all been entered into the computer and only the 14 kilometres
from Embi to Mt. Lamington has yet to be mapped so that waypoints only yet to be entered.

Disputed Arcas

(On the Eastem flank there is no disputes. The Field Mapping Coordinator has resolved some minor
disputes already therefore there is no problem on the side of the project accept the two parties who
failed to sign the MOU he need to do the awareness again with them to come to an agreement to sign
the MOU when we organise the next workshop on the westem flank.

New projects:

During the mapoing workshop at Numba village there was a clan e\der from the Banderi area who was
invited to attend the workshop, in his comments about the workshop was that he is fully supporting the
work of the mapping which he promised to see the Office of the Environment and Conservation for
their support to map his customary land for Conservation and also see the Lands Department also for
their approval and finally see the Orobay Local Level Government Council for their approval to allow
the mapping project to expand to his area which is from Banderi to the Emo river.

The reason why he is supporting the mapping project to expand to his area is that he is very concem
about his future generation due to a palm oil proposal by the Oro provincial government. Due to the
proposal he said to see the above authorities and get their approval before the next workshop so he can
bring all the approved documents and show to us in the workshop for the mapping work to begin.

\
 Western flank report:

Malchus Kajia a Mapping Field Coordinator for the Western flank has not been progressing quickly in

Due to the disputes he had mapped only from Bareji high school towards Gewoia but not reaching
Gewoia due to the dispute.

All this time when he goes down to Gewoia for the mapping he doesn’t do the mapping but to try and
resolve the dispute. Due to that his time and money has been waisted so I instructed him to go ahead
and map from Manana to Aiyari and leave the dispute area out until the mapping is complete and will
‘go back and discuss with them whether they want to be in the project or will map the out.

So the mapping from Manana to Aiyari, Suari and Jaure is not yet done including Jaure to Isio. From
Isio to Nambi is complete and from Nambi to ML Lamington is not yet mapped due to a dispute in the
Gorobuina area,

Waypoints:

‘The waypoints from Nambi to Isio have been entered into the computer as well as the waypoints from
Bareji high to Gewoia. Alll the waypoints are all in the computer and am waiting for the rest of the
areas to be mapped so that I will enter them into the computer, format them by the help of Richard and
finally print the Managalas map out.

Disputed areas:

(On the Western flank there is two disputed areas. They are Babarobo and Gewoia and the Gorobuina
area between Umbuwora and Mt. Lamington. I have already discussed with the two Field Mapping
‘Coordinators that we should not waste our time on the disputed areas. We concentrate on the mapping
and as soon as we complete the whole area then we can go back to the disputed areas and try sit down
with the landowners and resolve the dispute.

New projects:

In my last visit to the zone (4) area-doing awareness for the boundary mapping at Aiyari village and in
the awareness meeting was a councillor from Namudi who was also in the meeting have raised his
cconcem that he does not want to be mapped out from the project. He wanted to be in the project to
conserve his area.

Summary

‘The Managalas Boundary Mapping Project is progressing well however, the delay in completing the
boundary-mapping project is the dispute. The disputes in the areas mentioned above are the ones
delaying the project to complete quickly. Therefore, ! have agreed with the Field Coordinators to skip
the disputed areas, complete the rest and go back to the disputed areas and hear their views if they want
to be in the project then will go ahead and do the mapping or otherwise will map them out.

As the Boundary Mapping Project is the first of it's kind and there are people from outside the
Managalas boundaries are asking the Field Officers if they can expand the project to their areas
because they are starting to know why the boundary mapping is taking place on the plateau. This same
applies to people in other provinces of the country especially people who want to conserve their
environment are coming to us and telling us if we can go ahead and map their area but we told them
that the project is the first of it's kind and it's going to be a model to the other Papua New Guineans so
‘we will not say will come and map your land but just wait till the Managalas Boundary Project will
complete in a way we wanted and when we are satisfied then we can expand to other areas.

‘The mapping project is working in isofation from the MDF so this was discussed in the last Steering
Committee Meeting and all in favour that the Mapping Team on the plateau will now work under MDF
and any requisitions for field activities for funds and progressive reports will have to come through
MDF and back through the same channel. So { as a Mapping Coordinator have raised this agenda in the
steering committee meeting I'd like to see that in order to work asa team under one roof I would like to
see this effective as of 1" of January 2003.

 jickson Darebo
Mapping Coordinator

Field Mapping

between the Embi Lake to the Mt. Lamington. In the Western
Flank from the Bareji High School to Gewoia has been mapped

been mapped. From Manana to Aiari to Suari and to Jaure has
not been mapped. From Jaure to Isio has not been mapped.

been mapped already and from Nambi to Mt. Lamington yet to
be mapped. There is a minor dispute in between Nambi and

Introduction to the progressing of the Boundary Mapping

The main aim of the project is to provide Legal and Technical Support to the communities of the
Managalas Plateau in the preparation and development of a proposal to the National Government to
designate the area as a Conservation Area. The idea came from the clan groups on the plateau during,
the planning process for the Managalas Conservation Project because they want to protect the area
from industrial logging and other large-scale destructive operation. The people of the plateau in their
clan group discussion first agreed the mapping project should be created in the organization so should
had to do the boundary mapping to have the plateau secured or protected from being destroyed by any
giant companies as mining and logging. The group discussion went on from various clan groups in the
plateau for sometimes and there were disagreements from other clan groups, which they don't agree for
the project to be created.

This disagreement has also gone for a while however the people who are working in the programme are
the one's who were doing’most of the awareness and educating the people of the plateau the purpose of
 the boundary mapping project that it will not affect their livelihood. For this reason the mapping project,
truly a focal initiative that the project pariners have supported because itis model that can be replicated
in other communities in Papua New Guinea.

The transferring of mapping technology to the managalas people have enabled them to communicate
their perception to Land Rights and Ownership and resource management system with the
government and outside companies. It has also contributed to the process of resolving land disputes in
the area and in a way it has empowered them to make decisions on how best they can manage their
resources for their use now and for the future generations.

‘The main aim of the mapping project is as follows:

1. To asses the spatial interactions between communities and resources in the proposed Managalas
Conservation Area.

2. To document customary rights of local communities with regard to land and natural resources and to
gather and guard traditional knowledge.

3. To identify key decision makers (clan elders) in relation to land and resource use and management.

4. To identify and resolve boundary disputes between

ferent land owners.

4.0. OBJECTIVES OF POST-HARVEST & QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM (QIP).

1.1. To enable Managalas Coffee Groups to produce quality parchment for premium price under certification markets.
4.2: Better quality attracts good market to sustain good living and healthy environment in the community.

2.0. INTRODUCTION

The Coffee Industry is embarking on the Marketing Demand Drive Extension but have not done it. The shit is in line
with the current emerging market trenches where consumers are becoming more conscious of the coffee they
consumed. Issues such as chemicals residues in the coffee cup, environment, biodiversity, faimess and traceability
are emerging factors which are affecting the coffee farming and business. The consumers want to see that the
farmers are responsible towards the environment in which the coffee is grown. The consumers are also conscious
about the coffee cup and where the coffee originally grown. The challenges to realise the full potential of the coffee,
especially by the smallholder farmers are stil along way to go. The coffee growers in PNG demands CIC to be
innovative, and facilitate the process of maximising the potential in the coffee tree and the business that are
associated,

Apart from traditional coffee marketing (conventional), the emergence of specialty markets for gourmet and organic
certified coffee is causing revolution in the market place. More and more consumers are demanding “traceability” of
coffee from its origin, Global bio terrorism and health conscientiousness of consumers of this century are
demanding sustainable means and under environment friendly conditions including improved living conditions for
farmers. However, entering such markets requires substantial amount of time, effort, capital and of course

risk.

 3.3: PostHarvest & Processing (Day - 02)

quality cannot be developed after harvest therefore good care must be done on what had being developed from the
garden to maintain its quality

4 Picking & Hand Sorting: Pick red ripe cherries only.

pulper must be clean and dry inside the shed,

 + Pulping Cherries

#USE CLEAN DURING PULPING. DO NOT PULP WITHOUT WATER

+ Fermentation
Fermentation is the process of removing mucilage and must be done correctly to get optimum result.

# PARCHMENT FERMENTED MUST BE CHECK AND CLEN WASH WITH CLEAN WATER EVERY AFTERNOON
 4.0: — Construction of Dryer House (Day - 03)

Dry house control parchment from cracking and maintain slow process in drying stages. The cracks in
parchment will contribute to loss in coffee aroma and chemical flavors in the bean. Direct sun drying is not
recommended for drying as it only contributes to low quality and no chemical flavor in cup taste, Farmers do
not have time to turn parchment hourly because they have too many other commitments.

The house can be buit using; clear plastics, kunai leaves (and others) or clear plastic roofing with drying
beds. No standard plans but to production capacity. Do not dry parchment onthe ground but on beds.

441: Parchment Drying

Parchment shell must not be broken or creak during drying stages because the shell prevents nutrients and
aroma taste from evaporating. It is the taste in the cup that consumers enjoy and pay better price. Wet
parchment contains 50% of water level and precaution must be taken during drying.

‘The parchment must be placed on beds off ground to allow air drying as well for even drying of parchment. The
beds can be made of bamboos or shed cloth is highly recommended.

Two recommended drying methods;

(a) Wet drying - Reduce water moister from 50% to 35%. Parchment must be dried under shade for a
week and not directly contacting with the sun light.

(b) Sun drying — Prepared solar dryer because the plastic reflex the heat leaving sun light to penetrate
through and dry the parchment. Two weeks of drying will reduce the moister from 35% shade drying
to fully dry at 10%. Recommended dry moisture content is 10% to 11%.

It will take 3 to 4 weeks to fully dry parchment from 50% MC to 10 - 11% MC for best dried parchment.

The Quality Improvement Program or Post-Harvest is very important to drive the coffee growers to better market for
premium price. This is where the growers will decide whether to continue with coffee management or leave coffee for
other alternative income opportunities.

Coffee pricing is the stimulating factor to coffee sustainability and development of peoples’ livelihood in the

‘Type of organization/Type of involvement.

CELCOR Ine. is a newly established public interest law NGO in Papua New
Guinea and its registered under the Associations Incorporated Act a not-for
profit organization. It is involved in provision of legal advice and assistance
to customary landowners, CBO’s and NGO’s in Papua New Guinea involved
in sustainable’natural resource mangement and conservation activities. It is
also involved in the capacity building of lawyers and Law students in Papua
New Guinea to develop their interest and capacity for careers in public
interest law especially environmental law.

Brief history of the organization.

Center for Environmeatal Law and Community Rights Inc.(CELCOR).
’
 °)

‘The Center for J:uviroumental Law and Community Rights Inc was founded in
Febrvary 2000 to bring the energy and experience of the public interest
environmental law movement to the critical task of strengthening and
developing national and comparative environmental law, policy and
management throughout the country. CELCOR currently has staff of three
lawyers, an Accountant and Admin Assistant. It plans to involve students from
University of Papua New Guinea law Faculty as student interns. CELCOR also
Participates in a joint program for skills share exchange with the Legal Rights
and Natural Resources Center, a Manilla based Public Interest Law NGO and
the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), a International public
Interest Law NGO based in Washington DC, USA.

CELCOR ‘s main goals are:-

. to solve environmental problems and promote sustainable societies through
use of law;

._ to incorporate fundamental principles of ecology and democracy into law;

. to strengthen national environmental law systems and support public interest
‘Lawyers in Papua New Guinea and the region;

. to educate and train public-interest-minded environmental lawyers.

CELCOR aims te provide a full range of environmental and legal services in
both natural and comparative law, including policy research and publishing,
advice and advocacy, education and training and institution building, CELCOR
works in partnership with public interest lawyers, non-government organizations
and international institutions.

CELCOR’s program area includes Policy Research and Development, Direct
Legal Services, Campaign and Networking and Lawyers Capacity Building.
CELCOR aims to contribute to the creation of a “critical mass” of experimental
data and information on options for sustainable community-based forest
management; encourage the strengthening and development of avenues by
which information and experiences are shared by various resource owners and
users and maintain momentum to improve and expand ongoing efforts that
contribute to the knowledge base of institutions concerned with the forestry and
biodiversity sectors.

Capacity of the organisation to carry out the project.

While CELCOR is a new Legal NGO, it’s Lawyers have extensive experience in
the field of environmental policy research and development and environmental
litigation. It stands to play an instrumental role in national policy developments
pertaining to community marine conservation, non-timber forest products, the
integrated protected areas system and the protection of land and resource rights
of customary landowners as guaranteed under the Papua New Guinea
Constitution.

CELCOR is well positioned to stimulate and foster dialogue between national
governments, forest-dependent communities, and NGOs. CELCOK is also well
 positioned to provide insights from lessons and experiences of similar efforts
in other parts of the world by other institutions as itis linked to the Center for
Intemational Environmental Law (CIEL) and the Environmental Lawyers
Worldwide (ELAW) both USA based public interest law NGO’s. CELCOR
also has a skills share exchange program with the Legal Rights and Natural
Resources Center,(LRC) based in Manila, Philippines.

Previous Awards.

‘The organization has not received any awards previously from the GEF/NGO
Small Grants Scheme.

NATURE OF THE PROPOSED ACTIVITY

Primary objectives of the project.

‘The Center for Environmental Law and Community Rights Ine.(CELCOR) is
undertaking activities in collaboration with Partners with Melanesians
(PWM) which will assist local communities on the Managalas Plateau in
Papua New Guinea, a Biodiversity Support Program (BSP) planning-grant
project site, to secure community-based tenurial rights and establish a
national legal precedent that enhance local incentives for promoting
biodiversity conservation, sustainable community-based national resource
management (CBNRM), and eco-enterprise development. Additional funding
is needed to support the perimeter mapping of the Managalas Plateau.

The proposed activities will support arrangement for the participatory
delineation of the perimeter of the land owned by the clans of the Managalas
Plateau and for the preparation of a map that legally identifies the area. This
will complement and comprise an essential component of ongoing activities
already being funded by the Norwegian Rainforest Foundation.

b) (i) Types of activities to be carried out.

© Legal drafting in English and Tokpigin versions of the Managalas Plateau
‘community-based sustainable development guidelines.

© Legal drafting and possible submission of the Government of Papua New
Guinea with clan approval, of a proposed contractual agreement between the
Government and people of the Managalas Plateau for sustainable nutural

resource management on the Plateau.

© Strengthening of CELCOR and PWM expertise on legal strategies for
promoting biodiversity conservation and sustainable (CBNRM) in Papua New
Guinea; and
 © Preparation of a publishable, summary report in English and Tokpigin
describing the rational for the process leading up to the formulation of the
guidelines and proposed agreement.

Specified output from the mapping project will include:-

Skills and information sharing between Indigenous Canadian mapping experts
and Papua New Guineans;

© Training of two Papua New Guineans in the use and application of GPS
(Geoexplorer) units;

© Participation delineation and mapping of the Managalas perimeter boundary
as determined by reference to community based property rights.

Preparation of a cartographic map showing the outer boundaries of the
Managalas Plateau; and

© In-country availability of equipment and expertise for future community
mapping activities in Papua New Guinea.

(ii) Background
The people and the Plateau.

‘The Managalas Plateau is located in the south-eastem tail of Papua New
Guinea, the worlds largest tropical island nation and the demographic giant of
the Pacific that is also known for its extraordinary rich biodiversity. The
10,000 plus people of Plateau live in rural settings and have a long history of
interdependence with and respect for the natural environment. They also have
experience starting up enterprises, including a local coffee co-operative, a
non-formal education association and other community based development
activities, such as making use of a portable sawmill and marketing of okari
nuts, the latter enterprise having previously received support from
Biodiversity Conservation Network (BCN) and now the Norwegian
Rainforest Foundation.

In regards to internal conditions on the plateau, traditional local system of
leadership and dispute resolution is considered to be good, but under
increasing stress. Growing awareness on the plateau of environment problems
and concerns, meanwhile, has been accompanied by increasing evidence of
an enlightened willingness to forgo short-term economic gains that are

environmentally unsustainable.
While no logging companies currently operate in the immediate area,

communities on the plateau nearest the coast are especially vulnerable to

growing
{
 pressures by external forces, particularly logging and mining companies interested in
the commercial exploitation of natural resources. Three clan groups on the plateau,
for example, have already been approached to participate in commercial enterprises to
extract timber and mineral resources. More recently, a large portion of the reportedly
have been designated by the national government without community authorization as
a Forest Management Area (FMA), a legal designation meant to facilitate the
introduction of large-scale commercial logging enterprises. This development is yet
another example of the govemment’s systematic weakening and usurpation of
community-based customary property rights in Papua New Guinea (see below).

Besides the reported FMA designation, the primary current and prospective threats to
biodiversity ad local resources control on the Managalas Plateau include:

efforts to use national laws to convert customary land rights in order to
divest them from the community and register them in the name of wily
individuals;

explorations by externally owned logging and mining companies. As
well as pressures being generated by such companies on the plateau in
areas nearest the coast,

conflict between clans on the plateau, particularly major ones, over
status and positions; and

economic and educational differentiation within clans and
communities.

Although local people are well informed about their customary property rights, itis
important to prepare now to better secure community based tenurial rights so that
biodiversity and other natural resources on the plateau can be managed on a long-term
basis in an environmentally sustainable manner. This needs relates to current
problems as well as other that will likely arise in the future.

During 1996, World Bank funded efforts were undertaken to assist the 100 sub-clans
on the plateau to develop a model of sustainable development and conservation for
themselves and their local ecosystem. These efforts focused on promoting
environmentally aware kinship based planning and decision-making. More specially,
success was achieved among 43 sub-clans in building consensus around a common set
of sustainable development guidelines, promoting collaboration on a set of next steps

and reinforcing core cultural values

‘These efforts, and complementary ones being funded by the Norwegian Rainforest
Foundations are continuing during 2000, Clan elders and other leaders on the plateau
expressed strong support for and authorized the activities envisioned in this proposal,
including the participatory mapping of the perimeter for the Managalas. Plateau using
‘community-based property rights as the primary criteria. Since June 1998, officers
from PWM have been visiting clan groups on the plateau to discuss the perimeter
mapping strategy and to respond to local questions and concerns.

‘The mapping activity will contribute to the on going development of legal strategies
for securing local rights in order to promote conservation sustainable
development on the plateau. These strategies have great potential importance for
establishing a national legal precedent for promoting community based conservation
 and sustainable development in other parts of Papua New Guinea and securing
community based property rights.

Papua New Guinea National Law and Community Based property Rights.

With the exception of a few other island nations of Melanesia, Papua New Guinea
stands alone in recognising that occupation and long-term use of land vests local
people with de facto ownership of these resources, irrespective of documentation or
registration, ‘These rights of ownership cover 90 to 97 percent of the nations
territorial landmass, including the Managalas Plateau. But as already indicated, the
mere constitutional acknowledgement of traditional tenurial rights does not guarantee
the sustainable use of the resource base. Threats to that sustainability come from a
variety of sources, not the least of which is the State’s usurpation of those rights for
public ot private gain.

‘The exercise of community based tenurial rights has not proven to be without mishap.
The customary owners of traditional resources rights in Papua New Guinea are well
aware of their status as owners, but many lack access to the vital information needed
to exercise their rights in ways which contribute to material well being and
sustainable development. One result is that traditional conservation practises in Papua
New Guinea are being undermined buy modernization, especially the growing
influence of the cash economy. Eager to improve their material welfare and provide a
better future for their children some customary owners have sold their rights,
especially to commercial timber enterprises, in return for cash payments and other
inducements that are economically inadequate and environmentally destructive.

Although the Forest Act of 1992 and subsequent amendments have imposed some
festrictions, to ensure that such sales are ostensibly within the legal prerogatives of
local owners. All too frequently, however, the buyers are representatives of
unscrupulous logging companies who prey upon the ignorance and aspirations of
local leaders. By treating local leaders to airplane junkets to Port Moresby and cash
handouts that rarely reflect the value of the rights sold, concessions have been
unethically, if not illegally wrested. As a result, many rural communities have been
deforested or other wise environmentally degraded.

Unfortunately, attempts to circumscribe customary ownership rights in the new Forest
Act may not only be motivated by the need for some degree of national oversight ad
environmental regulation ad planning. Community based customary rights have been
under assault for some time in Papua New Guinea, a fact evident in various laws
enacted both before and since Papua New Guinea secured its political independence
in 1975. Indeed, it is not fare fetched to conclude that nation state of Papua New
Guinea is embarked on a systematic strategy to circumscribe, and in some instances
usurp, customary rights to natural resources date from the pre-independence period
(1975), and they reflect the prevailing Australian attitude that such God given

resources are naturally the property of the State.

Usually invoked on behalf of such lofty purpose as the “public good”, the strategy of
usurping undocumented customary prope:ty rights in the name of the State is well
developed and established in the neighbouring nations of Indonesia and the
Philippines, as well as many other developing countries. This usurpation, which under
 3.

‘mines local systems of natural resource management is perpetuated in ways
that are often confusing to and beyond the range of influence of most

customary owners.

Despite these concems, the national legal landscape in Papua New guinea
remains much more hospitable to local resource users than in any of the
‘Asian or other developing countries. The government and the people of Papua
New Guinea have had considerable experience in devising means for
recognizing customary rights, identifying customary ownership groups and
resolving conflicts that arise where claims and rights overlap,

Difficulties persist however with efforts to formally recognize, i.e, officially
document customary rights. The primary problems arises from the Wester
inspired overemphasis on segregation individual customary rights from the
more broadly defined clan holding, an emphasis, which has already fostered
tensions and other problems on the Plateau and PNG generally.

‘The most promising existing national law for promoting community based
conservation of biodiversity and forests in Papua New guinea is the
Conservation Areas Act of 1978. The Act required customary resources
owners to cede a considerable degree of their existing property rights in
return for unspecified future benefits. But it also enhances local owners
capacities to resist commercial exploitation and encroachment and the people
of the Managalas Plateau may want to have their homelands designated as a
Conservation Area something that has not yet been accomplished anywhere
in Papua New Guinea, or they may opt to develop and propose another legal
arrangement.

ORGANISATION AND INDIVIDUALS THAT WILL BENEFIT
How will the community participate?

‘The project is part of the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project and
as such the community is involved in the project through the clan based
decision making and consensus building. All members of the clan in each of
the zones are given opportunity through the forum process to discuss issue
affecting them and how to address these problems. The mapping of the
boundary of the Managalas Plateau was a decision made by all clan groups
through the clan group discussion and the zone and combine forums.

The final map will have to be approved by all the clan groups using the same
process before it is formally recognized by the government.
 b)

a)

b)

Whether and how women will be involved

‘Women are involved in the planning and decision making as part of the
MCASP although there are cultural beliefs preventing their involvement.
PWM as part of project secured additional funding for Community Aid
‘Abroad to conduct various workshops on women issues and project this year.
There are also plans for women to actively participate in other components of
the MCASP.

HOW THE PROPOSED ACTIVITY WILL BE CARRIED OUT
Role of recipient organization.

CELCOR will provide the legal advice and administrative support assist to
implement the mapping exercise. It will coordinate the work of the Field
Coordinators and their Assistants and ensure the stipulated project activities
are required. CELCOR will prepare the reports on the progress of the project
and the final narrative and Sinancial repost on the project to the GEF Small
Grants Coordinator. It will also use the results to coordinate similar projects in
other parts of the country in collaboration with other NGO"s.

Role of Partner Organisation.

CELCOR is collaborating with Partners with Melanesians Inc which is
implementing the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project on the
plateau. PWM has helped established community based organizations in the
Managalas Plateau with the assistance of CELCOR. Both PWM and the
emerging CBO’s will coordinate the consensus building process to ensure
that the final map gets approved by all clans groups on the Plateau. PWM will
also make available its technical assistant to assist in the project. CELCOR
also works closely with Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL)
and so will seek its assistance with the arrangement for the goverment
recognition of the proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

Are there provisions for scientific 2v:i technical advice/or assistance and
the sources (if any).

‘Yes, CELCOR has recognised the need for technical assistance in the project
to train local counterparts in Mapping using GPS. The training will be done
‘on site and on the job. CELCOR has already contacted a native Canadian
who has wide wealth of experience in the area of boundary mapping along
participatory lines. The technical consultant will be on the project site for up
to a month to train the local Managalas counterparts and assist with the
exercise.
 a)

Are there provisions for dialogue with other NGO’s and Community
groups.

‘As mentioned earlier CELCOR is working closely with Partners with
Melanesians Inc and the emerging Managalas CBO’s on the project. There is

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1. The consultation which ran from 25 March to 29 March 2014, sought to gather views
from key stakeholders regarding the objection raised by the President of Afore Local
Level Government, Douglas Garawa relating to the submission by Partners with
Melanesians Inc. And Managalas Development to the Minister for Environment &
Conservation on 8 November 2012 for the declaration of the Managalas Plateau as
a conservation area under the Conservation Areas Act 1978.

ra Views were sought on the objection submission by the ALLG President, Douglas
Garawa for the declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a CA under the CA Act and
on whether to abandon the proposal or look at other option of creating a PA on the
plateau in line with the wishes of the majority of the clan groups in the area . They
were asked what views they had on the objection submission by the President not to
have the area declared a CA and on a number of potential benefits of the CA and
what importance they attach to them.

3. The Consultation did not invite views on any other measures beyond biodiversity
conservation which should be taken to protect the environment and the sustainable
management of natural resources on the Managalas Plateau.

4, The DEC's view is that this is a remarkable opportunity for PNG to create one of the
country’s largest terrestrial PA’s as well as meeting its obligations under the CBD and
CITES especially for the protection of endangered species especially the QABB. This
will also go towards meeting its protected area target as per the NBSAP of 2007.

5. The responses to the consultation were not as expected especially from key
stakeholders in the proposed CA as the consultation meeting at the Afore station
was marred by threats and intimidation by the ALLG President and his supporters.
‘There was good support from the OPA and OPG through various representatives
who attended the consultation although many were of the view that the total area
for the proposed CA was quite large and should be reduced.

6. Through informal meetings and mobile phone conversations and text messages, the
majority of the clan elders and leaders of CBOs in the proposed CA support the
declaration of the area as a CA under the CA Act. They want the area to be re-
mapped to exclude land belonging to the people who oppose the declaration of the
area as a CA including that of the ALLG President and his clan, the Nituri Clan in Ward
12.
 10.

11.

12.

A quarter of the clan elders from the proposed CA ted by the ALLG President did not
support proceeding with the declaration of the CA. They argued simply abandoning
or postponing the current proposal by PwM and MDF until further consultation and
agreement could take place or “until the timing is right for them to take this option”
reiterating what the ALLG President stated in his objection submission to the
Minister.

Most of the Ward Members in the ALLG on the other hand support the declaration
of the area as a CA but could not speak out in public against the President as he
threatens to withhold funding earmarked for projects in their respective wards if
they support the CA declaration. At the consultation at Afore station, only two Ward
Members spoke in support of the CA declaration at the Consultation. These were the
Ward Members of Wards 13 and Ward 17.

The Consultation at Afore LLG Chambers was chaired by the ADA, Mr. Alex Uranian,
who approached the team in the morning and informed them that he was going to
chair the meeting as he was a neutral person. This was not true as he was aligned
with the ALLG President and supported his objection against the CA submission. This
was evident at the consultation as he picked mostly people who supported the
President in the objection to speak.

A short-coming identified in managing conservation planning in many instances is
that they either fail to be implemented or influence actions on the ground because
they were purely academic exercises or they lacked stakeholder support. For this
reason it is important to respect and promote the rights of local customary
landowners and also allow them full participation in the process for the CA
establishment.

LLGs are key stakeholders in the implementation of PA’s because the
decentralisation system of government has granted them greater autonomy in
designing and spending their own budget and developing local development plans.
To obtain LLG support, it is important that the conservation planning process is not
perceived as a top-down approach. For this reason it is important to promote co-
implementation of the CA with the ALLG.

Benefit sharing from any income earning opportunities from the CA once declared
was a major concern that was raised in the objection submission by the ALLG
President. This issue needs to be properly addressed and mechanisms put in place to.
ensure that any benefits derived from activities in the CA are equitably shared
between the stakeholders.
 13.

14.

15.

A

1.

As it is now with the proposed Managalas CA, there is currently a conflict which
needs to be resolved amicably so that the next steps can be taken to have the area
declared a CA following the process under the CA Act. The conflict is mostly to do
with mis-trust between part of landowning community led by the President of
Afore LLG and the implementing NGO, PwM and its CBO partner, MDF.

Should DEC goes with the wishes of majority of the landowning clans on the plateau
to re-map the proposed CA and have it declared a CA then proper consultations
must be done in the proposed CA to have the consent of the landowners. This
process must be undertaken by independent facilitators and proper documentation
must be developed for this purpose.

‘The issue of incentives for the customary landowners in the proposed CA needs to.
be properly addressed in order to maintain the support for the CA by the
landowners. This has been one of main concerns raised by the ALLG President in his
objection submission. There is already good lesson learnt from the first CA in the
country, the YUS CA which the implementing NGO and its CBO partners can learn
from and adopt as part of the CA project. This has to be done down and not wait
until after the CA declaration as this seems to be the position taken by the
implementing NGO of the CA project.

INTRODUCTION

Scope of the Consultation

The consultation was conducted by DEC from 25-29 March 2014 to gauge the views of key
stakeholders on the issues raised by the President of Afore Local Level Government (ALG)
on the submission for the declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area
under the Conservation Areas Act of 1978. This was done pursuant to Section 14 subsection
(2) (b) of the Act. This subjection of the Act provides as follows:

“(2) On receipt of a representation under Subsection (1), the Minister may invite the person
‘making the representation (b) to enter into consultation with him”.

This subsection of the Act gives the legal mandate to DEC to carry out such consultation
with key stakeholders regarding submission for the declaration of the CA or any objection of
representation by stakeholders.

They key stakeholders for purposes of the consultation were the President of Afore Local
Level Government and the Ward members as well as the local clan elders on the Managalas
Plateau. The Oro Provincial Government (OPG) and the Oro Provincial Administration (OPA)
and the Ijivitari District Office were consulted because of their role in running the affairs of
 the province and its role in dealing with national functions to address issues affecting people
in the province. The other reason was because of the Provincial Governments role in
management of the CA once it is declared as part of the CA Management Committee
pursuant Section 25 of the Act.

Other key government agencies including MRA and PNGFA were consulted separately by
DEC and the implementing NGO of the CA project, PwM. Only MRA has come with written
response and has officially withdrew its exploration activities in the proposed CA. For
PNGFA, there is no official response but according to Senior Officers informally, once the
PEMC through the Provincial Forest Management Plan includes an area in the province as a
protected area then it is a no go zone for PNGFA, i,e logging. The Managalas Plateau is
included as a PA under the Oro Provincial Forest Management Plan. The landowners have
also since 1999 strongly opposed any logging projects in the area because of its adverse
impact on the environment and the local communities.

2. BACKGROUND

‘The Managalas plateau in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea harbours a diverse array of
fauna and flora. And more significantly the plateau is home to the QABB, the world’s largest
birdwing butterfly which is listed on Appendix | of the CITES Convention and which is only
endemic to Oro Province of Papua New Guinea. The proposed Managalas Conservation Area
covers 360,000 hectares of pristine rainforest comprising lowland mountane forests and is
also the water catchment area of the Popondetta plains. The total population of the area is
18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari District. The people live in
75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and speak four (4)
dialects. The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale
environmentally destructive projects like logging, mining and oil palm plantations. Having
being working with international and national NGO partners since the early 1990's the arca is
now in the process of being designated as a conservation area under the Conservation Areas
Act of 1978.

The submission for declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area under the
Conservation Areas Act was submitted by community representatives from the plateau with
the support of MDF and PwM together with the Governor for Oro, Hon. Gary Juffa to the
Minister for Environment & Conservation Hon. John Pundari on 8 November 2012. This was
a result of over 20 years of work on the plateau by the two NGOs and other supporting
groups and institution to not only get the consent of the landowners through the consensus
building process but also getting local groups organised to take on the responsibility of
managing the CA once it is declared and gazetted. The Afore LLG President was supposed to
be part of the team to present the submission but he did not join in the presentation.
Instead, he filed an objection after the submission for the CA declaration was advertised in

 the papers as required under the CA Act. The objection letter was sent to the Minister on 18
March 2013. The 90 day period for the advertisement lapsed on 18 May, 2013.

Thereafter, DEC did not respond to the objection letter by the President of ALLG until
February 2013, which was almost a year after the objection letter was received by the
Department. No satisfactory reasons were given by the Department for the long delay in
responding to the objection letter. Meanwhile, PwM and MDF tried to consult the ALLG
President to discuss the issues and concerns he raised in the objection letter to the Minister
but he turned down the request on numerous occasions. The President instead gave a letter
to the two organisations stopping all activities in the proposed CA until DEC responded to
his objection letter. This affected properly planning and funding arrangement for project
activities especially activities leading up to the official declaration of the Conservation Area
after its approval by the National Executive Council and declaration by the Governor
General and subsequent gazettal as required under the CA Act. The communities in the
proposed CA were geared for the official declaration of the CA by the government so this
was a set- back for them.

In May 2013 PwM carried out its own independent consultation to verify the support by the
clan elders for the objection filed by the President of Afore LLG engaging myself for this
purpose. The consultation was undertaken out and a report was furnished to PwM which
among others recommended for all project activities on the plateau to be put on hold until the
issues raised in the objection letter by the President are addressed and resolved. It was found
that that majority of the clan elders on the plateau did not sign the objection letter by the
President. Because of this in May 2013, PwM engaged this consultant to hold consultative
meetings in selected places with stakeholders to verify the support for the objection to the
declaration of the Managalas Conservation Area by the ALLG President. The consultation
was conducted from 23 May-2™ June 20013 and a report was furnished to PwM with eleven
(11) recommendations to enable the stakeholders especially PwM to address the issues
raised in the objection letter by the Afore Local Level Government President. Attached
herewith and marked with letter “C” is copy of the report on the verification exercise. Since
then numerous correspondences have been exchanged between PwM, MOF and the
President of ALLG with regard to the issues raised in the objection letter with a view to
resolving them so that the declaration of the Conservation Area can proceed after the NEC
approves its declaration as required under the Conservation Areas Act but no agreement
was reached by the parties.

The implementing NGO, PwM and it CBO partner MDF then decided to organise a
plateau/LLG wide Forum to discuss the issues raised by the President in his objection with a
view to resolving them. The forum was held at Ugunomo village from 16-20 December 2013.
The forum was well attended by clan elders from all cultural zones on the plateau and
community leaders where they discussed the five (5) issues selected by the Facilitators in
consultation with PwM and through that addressed the issues raised by the President in his
8
 objection letter to the Minister. The ALLG President was invited to attend and address the
forum on the issues he raised in the objection letter to the Minister but he did not attend.
He also stopped all Ward Members in the LLG not to attend the Forum. The forum went
ahead and all stakeholders present stood by their earlier decision to have the area declared
a CA. Annexed hereto and marked with the letter “D” is a copy of the Forum Report which
was provided to PWM. A video documentary was also produced for the forum which is
attached hereto and Marked with a letter “E”.

The President of Afore Local Level Government, Douglas Garawa filed an objection in a
letter dated 18 March 2013 wherein he raised a lot of issues why the Minister should not
make the NEC submission for it to approve the CA declaration and for the proposal to be
shelved until such time the Managalas people are able to manage the project themselves. The
Department to date has not officially responded to the objection letter by the President of
fore LLG and no reasons were given by the Department for the long delay in responding to
the President's objection letter..

Thereafter, PwM has been communicating with the President to try and hold meetings to
resolve the issues he has raised in his objection letter but the President refused to attend such
meetings saying he will need to get an official response from DEC on his objection letter
first. The President also stopped all project activities saying he still stands by his objection.
This affected the implementation of project activities by PwM and its local partner
Managalas Development Foundation (MDF).

Whlist it has been difficult to pick out the main crux of the ALLG President's objection to the
CA submission because of the manner in which it was set out, some of the main issues
raised by the ALLG President in his objection letter to the Minister dated 25 March 2013
were as follows:

i. Resource Owners/Landowners consent for the proposed Conservation Area
The President stated in his objection that there was no consent from the landowners
in the proposed CA for their land to be included in the CA.

ii, Endorsement and Approval by the Afore Local Level Government and the Oro
Provincial Government.

This is one of the main issues raised by the President in his objection letter. He
stated that the project proponents did not go through the proper processes in
getting the approval or endorsement of the ALLG and OPG through the PEC for
declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a CA under the CA Act.

ii, Complaint Against the Implementing NGO, Partners with Melanesians Inc.
 iv.

vi.

vii.

3

The Afore LLG President raised concerns in his objection letter about the role of the
implementing NGO, PwM in the CA project. He stated that the ALLG made a
resolution to stop the operations of the NGO in the area but it not adhere to the LLG
decision.

Legal mandate of the Afore Local Level Government

The President stated in his objection letter that the LLG has the legal mandate over
any development or issues that concerns the people in the LLG area including
management on the customary land.

‘The CA once declared will benefit individuals and not the Landowners

A

One of the main concerns the ALLG President in his objection submission was that
the project is pushed for by individuals for their own benefit and not for the benefit
of the people in the LLG area. Certain people in the organisation are glued to this
very complicated venture. It is an untapped product and the next thing after total
declaration of the area as a conservation zone, is Carbon Trading.

Role of Community based Organisations, especially Managalas Development
Foundation (MDF)

The Mission

To is to equip and improve the management capacity of the Managalas Development Foundation (MOF)
to manage and operate the Managalas Consevvation Area Support Project.

4, The Background.

The Partners with Melanesia who has been werking for the last 17 years in the Managalas mobilizing and
‘organization 150 villages into living in a way that allows them to live off and protecting their environment
has considered it is time now to move on and allow the loca! people to take control through a local NGO.
The Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) has been established specifically to take over from PwM.
It is a big responsibility for a very new organization and PwM would like some time to phase-out. This
strategy is to outline the obligations ‘of both Pwid and MOF which will be recaptured in a Memorandum of
Understanding (MOU) which a few years latter wil be confirmed into a Memorandum of Agreement
(MOA). At this meeting at Sivarai Namona in June of 2006, the following is the outline of the Exit strategy
which is called elsewhere the Capacity Building Progtam of MDF.

2. The Partnership and the Experience.

Managalas Development Foundation: The Menagales Development Foundation is @ newly established
NGO with an elected board. tt has some staff members who are trying their best to make the organization
work. Partners still working in the Plateau seems to be creating a situation where mother (PwM) and
daughter (MDF) are uncomfortable living togethe’ in the same space. However there is the concern that
MOF is not skilled enough, equipped well and experienced enough to take over the big task of
management and operation of the project. To that end while MOF wants PwM to leave but not before it
trains end equips the organization, Management s not an easy thing and it must develop the capacity to
withstand the pressure from within and pressure from outside like PwM and donors requirement.
However itis better for MOF to learn by experience so it is ready to give ita try with PwM standing over
its shoulders to make sure things are OK over the next few years.

Partners with Managalas: Partners has been in the Plateau for a Jong time and has done quite a lot of
things as the time line shows. It has shown commitment and perseverance and tenacity that have
allowed the Managalas Plateau to evolve into one of the largest community mobilizing projects in the
country. It was initially established to specifically operate the MCASP and it has done that to a certain
level and itis time now for something to happen to take it to another level before things become too
uncomfortable. The Plateau has became a learning experience for PwMs 2s well as MDF and it has
come to a time where organizations to go it on the'r own, the former to transpiant the experience

 INTRODUCTION

Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) was established and registered as a legal entity in
2002. MDF"s growth over the years has seen its strengths and weaknesses reflect the outcomes
and impacts of the activities and the general operations of the organization. MDF through its
mother organization, Partners with Melanesia requested MNCL to facilitate an organization
development intervention to review the current five (5) years strategic plan, review the exit
strategy and strategically re plan for the next 5 years.

“The workshop was conducted from the 2" to 6"" November, 2009, at the St Margaret Nursing
College Conference Centre, Popondetta. There were total of about forty participants who
represented the MDF staff, CBO managers, Partners with Melanesia staff and other partners
and stakeholders.

A variety of tools and approaches were used in a participatory manner to bring out information
needed to develop a clear, workable and achievable plan.

On the outset, it would have been advisable to have a reflection workshop to dissect the
organization and identify the root causes of issues that seem to be ongoing. This was done
whilst doing the planning of the organization but at the surface level. Further organizational
development interventions are planned for the strengthening of MDF.

‘The objectives of the workshop were achieved with the time frame of the plan reduced from
five (5) years to one (1) year. The planning frame work will be used to plan MDF annual plans.
The honours is on the staff and the CBO’s and the larger community to make the plan work.

This report covers the procedures of the workshop and a brief coverage of the essence and
cutcome of discussions. A detailed strategic plan and the reviewed exit strategy are attached as
part of the strategic plan but in separate documents.

BACKGROUND

The socio - economic impact of the Okari Nut Project on the Managalas Plateau became
apparent that the communities became organized around it. The establishment of Partners with
Melanesia was tasked to organize the Managalas communities around their cultural and natural
resources and further carry out research into Okari Nut as a viable Non Forest Product (NFP).
There were already threats of large scale logging moving into the plateau. PWM facilitated
‘communities to be organized into zones and created structures like the Combined Forum
Steering Committee Meeting zone boards, clan committees, zone office and administration
support and support staff. There are ten zones established on the plateau. There were few zones
suspended along the way, while the most organized zones got incorporated as recognized legal
entities with the Investment Promotion Authority (IPA).

‘The Managalas Development Foundation Inc. was formed as the umbrella body for the ten (10)
CBOs. A five (5) Years Strategic Plan was developed in 2004 for 2005 — 2009. There was also
an Exit Strategy that was developed for the purpose of having MDF gradually exit from the
plateau and give MDF its independence. Whilst it has been MDF’s aim to operate
independently soon, it is still obvious that MDF has not reached the level of independently

Managalas Organizational Development Intervention Procedural Report 4
 managing all aspects of the operations of MDF and the plateau at large. This is PWM’s
concem and it is hoped that the capacity building areas identified in both the MDF and CBO
personnel and the organization will be enhanced and built in this planning and implementation
period to enable MDF to work towards getting full independence from PWM.

WELCOME AND OPENING REMARKS

‘The beginning of the workshop had a late start at 10:30 am upon the arrival of the MDF Board
chairman. The chairman, Mr. Malkus Kajia gave an opening speech welcoming all participants
to the workshop. He was especially thankful to ICO, the donor for the financial support to
enable this workshop to eventuate. He was also grateful to the outgoing director Mr. Jacob
Ramoi and director for CELCOR Mr. Damien Ase for securing this fund and CELCOR staff
and Damien for their effort to see work done on the plateatt under the guidance of PWM.

He acknowledged that all participants contribution will help Managalas plan to go forward and
eventually see MDF take on all responsibilities.

The workshop was officially opened at 10:50 am.
