RESULTS
Unfortunately, PwM officers only met up with the Zone CBOs of 5 & 6 while zone 3 & 4 never
showed up due to reasons unknown. With concerns of the time limitation, the team decided to go
ahead with the Zones in the East to implement their Zone Boundary Mapping.

In addition, the 3D Model of the Managalas Plateau display was used to visually point out the zones
concerned whereby the Zone Managers were able to point out their Zone Boundaries. In doing so,
it helped out to identify the areas to collect the coordinate points when using the GPS.

The PwM officers were able to teach the basics on how to collect the Coordinates and note it on
their exercise books for the record. Then we left them to take on the task of getting the GPS
points.

For the CA Border Patrol, it was a team made up of 2 Pw officers (Patrick & 1), Kingsford and 3
local youths that implemented this particular activity. We patrolled over steep snountain ridges,
crossed rivers, waterfalls to get to Sigara & Siana. Even our last leg to Pogani was quite exhausting
because we had to walk on pebbles & unsteady, rough surface rocks just by following the river
channels downstream until we reached Pogani Wara Buum.

There were only 2 meetings held at Siana village and Pogani village. Yhe elders/chiefs from Siana &
Sigara attended the meeting while the same was done in Pogani as well.

In the attachment is the 2 separate meeting minutes fer Siana & Pogani respectively. However,
here are the outcomes of the meetings respectively;

1) The Siana Chief has expressed their concern now that they have reaiised the threats they are
facing in terms of ongoing illegal logging and the proposed Oro Bay township extension to include
their land into the proposed CA. In consensus were the Chief and spokesman for the other 2 clans
of Avaora and Marareja from these 2 villages that border with the Siana chief's Land Boundary as
they are all for Conservation.

2) As for the Pogani Peopie, it is a different story were they are mostly confusing PwM werk with
other NGC who have came before such as Conservation Meianesia that left with a bad record,
Aixer all, it was ali a misunderstanding so it was all discussed and made clear during the meeting.
Hence, ai! their chiefs, elders, community leaders decided to make aware PwM’s work and most
importantly with the information that they have obtained from the discussion would help settle
their land issues. it will be discussed further below.

=== page 5 ===
RECOMMENDATIONS & DISCUSSIONS

For the Zone Boundary mapping, it was implemented as tasked by the zone CBO managers of 5 & 6
of East and the coordinate points were provided to Patrick to produce the internal Boundary
mapping. Gradually overtime, all the zones within the MPCA will be covered.

The meetings that were conducted during the CA border patrol had the common concern for
LAND.

In the case of the Sigara and Siana villages, they share land Boundaries and the fact that all of
Mitataora Clan of Sigara‘s land are within the MPCA while three Clans (Uera, Marareja and Apaora)
of Siana have only part of the land within the MPCA. We did not have to go that far because they
have seen for themselves the damages that are already been done by the ongoing illegal logging
and they face yet another development threat of Oro bay Township and potential prospecting of
mineral resources on their land. With all these that is happening around, the only way is to
safeguard their resources and their environment as a whole.

Action Points

1. It is only considerate that Siana people’ s part of their land on the outer CA boundary be
included as it is a gain to protect as much as possible a bigger landmass of forest area.

2. The Siana and the Sigara people still need Environmental awareness to strengthen &
extend the work of CA. Also to empower the community to mobilise in terms of making
well informed decisions to combat development threats.

3. The Zone CBO responsible (that would be zone 6) must be able to reach out to these
isolated people in terms of information sharing, update on CA work and awareness etc...

For the Pogani people, the misconception of NGO’s work was labelled the same all across whereby
PwM’s work was confused with Conservation Melanesia’s work (CM). CM’s reputation left behind
was not all that good when it ceased work on a particular area on the Plateau. It created an
opportunity for someone smart enough to show invalid documents to the ill informed community
to extend logging into parts of Pogani area. The worst part from information gathered so far is that
PwM proposed CA map was used to falsely claim land rights with support from an expired CM
WMA certificate. Hence, it has created a situation where they see our presence as a threat to them.
Through the meeting, everything was being clarified including our Organisation’s profile and our
work, the initial CA Map and the CA process. The response we got was mixed when we touched the
topic of CA boundary. Hence, now that the pogani chiefs, elders and community leaders are better
informed, they are able to disseminate the correct information to the pogani community. Apart
from this activity, reforestation was monitored as well and it seems that it all comes down to the
issue of land.

INTRODUCTION

The emphasis on Management Plan is very vital for the sustainability of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area. On that note, Workshops were conducted to train & educate the Managatas
community to prepare to take on the responsibility of the core Management team where it is required
of them as stated in the Conservation Areas Act 1978. As principa! stakehoiders in the whole
conservation process, it is compulsory that the targeted groups within the community need to
undergo these workshops to understand what is required of them and in doing so, they are able to
consensually develop the Management Plan & appoint the people that will fully represent the
community based on sound & fair judgment guided by the terms & conditions required under the Act
to implement the Management Pian at the community level. In saying this, apart from other
Workshops, Management Plan Workshop itself was conducted firstly in 2004, followed by 2008 then
in 2011 and now is the 4 time, this workshop has been run.

Now looking at all the 3 past workshops, it has beer noticed that, there were no evaluation done after
each workshop so as to keep track of the information transfer to the participants in terms of
enhancing their knowledge as the workshops progressed on. The fact that the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area is yet to be declared and hence, it gave time to run the Management Pian
workshops ahead. However, the issue identified was not knowing exact'y if they (participants) have
really captured the contents of the workshoos. Thus, monitoring & evaluation on a smalier scale is a
vital component that has been missed out and so it was included in this fourth workshop. It has been
also emphasized strongiy at the Partners With Meianesians (PWM) Midterm planning that in order to
measure the success of your implementation of activities ‘s to moniter & evaluate not only at the end
of the year but at intervals after every individual activity. This is to try & fill in the gaps as much as
possibie to ensure the issues are kept et 4 minimum

PURPOSE

With this evaluation, it is more of a summary assessment for all 4 management Pian workshop held.
Simple Questionnaire was designed to evaluate & assess the expected cutcome of the 4 Workshops
and to make improvements where possible.

METHODS

The methods undertaken for this Evaluation was using Questionnaires to get the participants views,
also from observation and side talk as well. Previous Management Plan reports were also used to
assess the expected outcome if fulfilled and to identify the iccpholes.

=== page 13 ===

A) Management Plan Reports assessment

With the four reports, it looks as though most of the expected outcome were being fulfilled beginning
with the introduction of the management plan concepts & guidelines in 2004 with conservationist
Philip Holden then in 2008, Jacinta Mimigari facilitated and the participants came up with the draft
Management Plan after identifying the environmental issues on the plateau. The third workshop was
a team effort of PWM team that went in to continue from where the (2° Workshop) stopped at and
the participants came up with the proposed Rules and penalties & CA Committee proposed
management implementation structure. They have also identified the stakeholders who will be in the
CA Committee as well. So with the forth MP workshop, it was also a follow up workshop in which the
rules and their penalties had to be looked at properly in order to finalize it into the documentation,
The roles & responsibilities of a CA committee had to be understood as well and the CAMC members
need to be confirmed too.

in summary, for the 5 boxes (i),(ii),(iii), (iv){v) the results show that majority (between 70 — 85%) of

in the long run.

While the few seem to state that they needed more information on (v)Bottom up planning process as
they feel it is very important in this regard with emphasis on follow up workshops or handouts for

(i), (iii) & (iv).

PARTICIPANTS B

For this cluster, it can be seen on the table that its results vary from bullet point (i), (ii),(iii) . Most of
the participants of this cluster although first timers followed through with the roles & responsibilities,
rules & penalties and the proposed Implementation structure while for (iv) & (v) most fell into this
category, aired their views that they need more time to understand especially the Bottom up planning
process at the loca! level. With (iv) point, since it was yet to be finalized, it looks as though they were
confused.

=== page 16 ===
Discussion

Based on the reports, Questionnaires and also observation, this results show very interesting facts
that can be pointed here. With this evaluation, there were challenges encountered during these
analysis, however, there is enough facts to guide this evaluation process.

Management Plan Workshop Reports

From the top, from al! the Workshop reports, the expected outcomes were gradually produced in
terms of drafting the Conservation Management Plan with contents of identifying their environmental
issues and countering it with Land use Plan that captures all activities regulated by the rules/laws
consisting of modern & traditional concepts combined together that is applicable up in the Managatas
Piateau. The participants were able to propose the CA implementation structure with the identified
key stakeholders who will make up the CA committee members. Even from the beginning, the
required participants to attend this workshops is particularily tne zone CBO managers (community
representation) and the Ward Councilors ( Government representative at the community local level)
as they will be acting as inter-phase of the impiementation process of actual the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Plan between all stakehoiders. Only in the 4 workshop, were most
of the agenda were on reviewing ali of the above especially the rules and its penaities, the prooosed
CA implementation structure and the committee members. The twc most important agendas within
this session was the CA Committees roles & responsibilities and Bottom up planning with emphasis
on the importance of involving the Ward & district clan that captures the conservation needs
especialiy to fund the Managaias Corservation Area Management when declared. A government
representative was there to stress on this point with regards to the protocols in place that enforces
the Management Pian to function.

Questionnaires

Now building on this, the questionnaires come into play in order to find out the practicality at each
zone level beginning with the participants’ consistency in attendance to the workshop as they were
follow up workshops. Some ciscoveries were made which looked at both facilitators and participants
as well so it will be interesting to discuss oa these.

Limitations

One of the challenges as the evaluator for this Vianagement Pian Workshops was te cesign a
simplified Questicnnaire that captures the realistic views of the participants that is in deptn to really
give an insight of their knowledge capacity and in terms of information dissemination to their
respective zone & ward levels. Because of the time factor, the questions were much in general,
however, as pointed above, those were the 2 most important objectives to assess from the feedback
given which wasn’t clarified at the top of the Questionnaire form. Other than that, observations
during the workshop did back up the evaluation process. There were only 40 copies made which in
fact were intended for the expected participants. So priority was given to the councilors and CBO
managers to answer the questions.

=== page 17 ===
Feedback assessment

When looking at the objectives of the Questionnaire, it was worked out that since the first question
was directed to the participants who attended the past workshops, they were the only ones required
to answer the first questions in terms of what they understood of the CA Management Plan after
attending all 4 workshops. From this also, the consistency of the participants were worked out to see
who were the regular attendees and as shown from table 1, only 10 were regulars while the rest were
all first time participants. Hence, from this result, it was later decided to cluster the participants into
two groups of one which is the regulars “PARTICIPANTS A” and first timers as “PARTICIPANTS B”

After assessing the feedback from PARTICIPANTS A, it can seen that the number of regular
participants seem to drop due to few reasons picked up along the way as they want results in terms of
declaration has taken awhile. The participants’ notion was that they wanted action to take place after
the concept was introduced and at the same time, to take them through the documentation of the
management plan. However, when the political hold up prolonged, it created loopholes for people to
lose interests and so they want some of the tangible benefits to eventuate. The longer it takes; people
tend to lose interests in the project all together so there needs to be applicable options to tighten the
loopholes

For the Participants B, although most of them are observers and the selected Rangers in each zone
which made up part of the increase of participants; it does give an overview of what people at each
zone level see this project. So from the results from table 3, it can be seen that majority had a fair idea
on the (i) roles & responsibilities, (ii) rules & penalties & (iii) CA implementation structure. The reason
being more time was spent on these three agendas with group discussions & activities that got
involved much of their participation. As for (iv) finalized CA Committees, they have their doubts on
who will truly represent their community in the Committee, hence, they were unsure and wanted
more time to be given for them to consensually decide in their respective zones who will represent
them. (v) Bottom up planning was stressed as a need for way forward to link the very marginalized to
the key service providers and so call for a separate workshop to go through it in detail.

Hence, looking at both groups, there are similarities however, for first timers, it's a new learning
experience for them and they are eager to learn more while the regular participants want visible
benefits that will motivate and practically apply their knowledge in their respective wards & zones.

=== page 18 ===
Action Plan

i.

The participants need to register and confirm their participation to PwM after a letter of invitation
is given out to attend a workshop. This will heip keep a record of the participants in terms of
follow up workshops.

In relation to the first point, to really monitor the participants in terms of information
dissemination to their respective zones, try to pay a visit to a zone after a workshop has been
carried out two weeks or three.

To tighten the loopholes; SLA’s must be strengthened to motivate them to take on conservation.
The SLA’s must be realistic that is applicable in that particular zone so that is sustainable.

Facilitation skills — it can be seen that one reason to keep the interest of the participants is looking
at it at the participants angie where facilitators need to assess their approach in facilitation and re-
adjust if one style does not work out. Some tips to consider;

i. Try paraphrase information in the handouts/sheets to be given with simplicity accompanied
with more visuals such as diagrams, charts, pictures etc... this is to jitustrate a point with
convincement

ii, It cam be very convincing if examples with visuals of similar situations to be used curing
worksnaps/trainings

iit. Try re-adjusting styie of aporoach of facilitation that does iess talking and more action in terms
of getting them involved from the heginning to the end such as doing 2 lot of activities.
This must be done by making them feel at ease to open up

iv. In between try to use energizer to keep them awake

v, Do a bit of practical by going outdoors & use their surrounding environment to illustrate a
point.

vi. Give opportunity to participants to share their experiences and learn from one & other and in
the event, point out the challenges they ‘ace and how they heve resoived them

vil. in terms of presentation, try to be brief, attractive and it covers the most important parts
resembling a ‘MIN! SKIRT’ as learnt from a facilitator in the Sub Regional Training.

vill. Always recap & stress a very important point as the workshop goes along such an example
was from observation was their fear of the rules & penalties with the land use plan seen as
permanent. However, it wes stressed during sessions that it is subject to review and can be
amended according to the outcome (5-3years}

This is long term recommendation; however, it’s brought forward as it is vita! in this regard. As we
know the challenge of breaking down science terminologies to the locals, it is best a simple
dictionary should be developed with descriptive definitions & illustrations.

=== page 19 ===
ry

It was a lesson learnt as the evaluator in terms of designing the Questionnaires.
i. The questionnaire must have a title, purpose and objectives in order to keep focus as guidelines

ii. The questionnaire must break down scientific terms into simple descriptive words in order for
the participants to give the answer you want.

It is very vital to include Evaluation at the end of every activity implemented.

Conclusion

This is an evaluation done by using a combination of techniques such as Previous Management
Workshop reports, Questionnaires and Observation during the 4'" Workshops. it has been seen
that it most effective to monitor and measure the success of an activity when an evaluation is
carried out at the end of an activity. It ensures to keep up with the pace and also to make
improvements if need be so it is a win win situation for both facilitators & the participants. Hence,
in future, it will best to include Evaluations in all work plan programs.

“ WARD NO. 4 - KAURA & AWARU VILLAGE
TITLE: WARD PROFILE ~ 2008 - 2013

Introduction
‘The Ward 4 is located at the Northeast direction of Afore District known as Kaura & Awaru community.
It is northwest of the main capital, Popondetta.

It takes about four (4) hours walk and 30 minutes by Transport from Afore Station to reach the ward 4
destination. It takes about 6 hours to travel from Popondetta Town to Afore along east coast road known

as Alex Highway.

‘The ward 4 consists of 458 adults and 408 children adding up to the total population of 866. The
topography is mostly tropical high land rainforest and grassland. The soil is organic which enables an
abundance of garden foods.

‘The main source of income for the local people is coffee and vanilla and other stuffs such as; peanuts
and betel nuts which they sell for basic necessities.

“ESE ESE?” is the unique reception meaning “Welcome” in the local ESE dialect.

Ward Profile
“The ward 4 has a total population of 866 which consists of 8 major clans of various age groups; 18 years
& above, male adults 255, female adults 203 and below 18 years; male children 228 and female children
180; which make up the community of ward 4.

Church Profile

Christian Revival Crusade and Renewal churches are the two (2) main religious groups in ward 4. CRC
has 118 congregation members with 2 pastors, 4 elders, 3 lady leaders, 26 ladies, 4 Sunday school
teachers, 50 Sunday school children, 4 young people leaders and 31 young people. Renewal Church has
150 congregation members, 1 pastor, 2 elders, 2 lady leaders, 2 Sunday school teachers, and 69 Sunday
school children.

Cash Crops

‘The ward’s major sources of income for the local people are Coffee and Vanilla; however, there is no
market for Vanilla at the moment. The people from the ward 4 area alone own a total of 205 coffee
gardens which grows 152,895 Arabica trees and produces 1,265 coffee bags of dried Arabica beans. An
annual earning cash income of K78, 000.00 for ward 4. Recently 54 coffee gardens of Arabica have
been destroyed by the recent disaster.

Vanilla is one of the major sources of cash crop well grown in ward 4 area and the plateau has a whole.
‘The Vanilla farmers have found that there is no market for Vanilla maybe due to lack of proper skill and
support from Government agency. The ward 4 has grown 1,523 vines in 31 Vanilla gardens. ‘Two
Vanilla gardens were destroyed by the recent disaster.
 usiness

Many people are interested in small scale business as we are aware, today we need money to buy goods
and services we need or want. Trade Store is the most common type of retail business people are
engaged. The ward 4 alone has nine trade stores and 14 peddles run privately by local people. Today
money has become important in people’s lives as people need cash for many reasons. They need cash to
pay basic necessities of life such as; food stuff, medicine, clothing and to pay children’s school fees.

El ita

Education plays an important role. The Ward 4 Kaura and Awaru Elementary School consists of 136
students of various grades.

Community Based Constable (CBC)

Concerning with Law and Order.
The Ward 4 Kaura & Awaru consists of four (4) community based Constables and four (4) Ward
Committees. They assist the Police at the village level in settling conflicts and disputes that arises in and
around the community.

‘Youths
‘Youths are mostly made up of a group of young people. Youths are the most concerned people in the
community. The Ward 4 is mostly made of youths. Youths in Ward 4 are keen in Sport activities such
as soccer, and volleyball. These are the two (2) main sports in which most youths in Ward 4 participate
in apart from other social activities. The Ward 4 consists of one (1) Soccer Club and Eight Volleyball
Clubs.

Housing
‘The Ward 4 is made up of 2 main communities Kaura and Awaru. The Ward 4 alone consists of 866
population, 153 houses, one (1) Elementary School and Two (2) Church groups.

Houses are built for people to; (1) _—_—Settle with their family
(2) Keep them warm and safe
 Kaura has 81 family houses, while has Awaru 72 houses adding to a total of 153 houses for Ward 4
alone.

Out off 153 houses, some houses are leaking now, due to no sago leaves to repair and maintain the
broken roof. In the recent disaster over 600 sago palm trees have been swept away by the floods and
landslides. It will take 20 to 30 years for the new plants to grow and replace the palm trees. Sago has
two main uses; one it is eaten as food, however, more importantly its leaves are used for housing roofs.

‘The local people need basic goods and services. We are need dire need of Government aid to assist the
Local people to repair the leaking roof. By assisting the local people with irom sheets to repair the
broken roofs while waiting for the new planted sago palms to be fully grown in the next 20 - 30 years
time.

ent
In the previous years the Ward 4 has been given 15 coffee pulpers (machine), 4 sewing machines and 54
iron sheets by the previous governments as a major need for the local people.
Private Assets
‘The local people have to strive for many years to meet their own needs. In their strive some have been

successful and others are not. The local people own 17 private coffee pulpers (machines) and sadly 26
have been washed away by the recent floods.

Climate Change Component have only two main activities with two others Monitoring and evaluation to check on the
progress of the Activity implementation. It was also the time to discuss the first Activity in April.

Purpose

Discussion

‘As this is a new component included for this year, It was the great opportunity to introduce this the Managalas Community
and the fact that this have been one of the cross-cutting issue that has been continuously raised in the Combine forum, the

Conclusion

‘The New Component was introduced and welcomed by the CBOs as it is long time coming for them. They anticipate the
information needed to develop the action plans that will protect them from further impacts of Climate Change. This year
illbe on data collection and Awareness will be needed for the appropriate measures.

2006 ANNUAL REPORT ——.
FOR mat wre Cure

RAINFOREST FOUNDATION NORWAY

Organisation: J —
Partners With Melanesians Inc

Managalas Conservation Area Support Project (MCASP)
Papua New Guinea’

National Capital District, Papua New Guinea

=== page 2 ===
'2

A. Introduction

1. Briefly state the goal/purpose of the project.

The protection of the natural cnvironment, biological diversity, sustainable livelihoods
and cultural heritage and values of the local Managalas society on the plateau and to
develop and strengthen these in a participatory and sustainable manner for the use of
present and future generations.

2. Give a brief summary of the development of the project from the start until
today, stressing the last year.

The project continued the past year (2006) with substantial amounts of time and money spent
on planning for both the organisations Five Years from 2007 to 2011, and an Exit Strategy
for Manugulus Development Foundation, the local partner. This caused a shortfall in our
budget for the year since these activities were unbudgetted for.

Under the Capacity Building Component, onlt the Gender workshop was conducted while all
other Outputs were postponed. However, continued capacity building of the Managalas
Development Foundation staff occurred throughout the year. including training in Planning,
Monitoring and Project Development.

Under the Conservation Component, a substantial amount of resources and time was put into
counterpart funding of coffee marketing and promotion, a third survey to map biodiversity
was completed and the continued sale of okari and fresh vegetables in Port Moresby.
Counterpart funding from IUCN enabled further charters for produce coming off the Plateau.

With the Consensus Building Component. after a reorganization of the component in 2005, work
commenced on the production of material and training of Literacy Co-ordinators and Facilttutors.
However, duc to our planning process. which took up most of our time, the Consensus building
process has now been deferred to start in early 2007 with the MDF AGM.

A new Project Officer for MCASP was recruited and bused on the Plateau tor a while. but due to
differences between the Project Officer and the MDF staff, he was recalled to Port Moresby and
worked from there.

Likewise, a series of excursions were carried out into three (3) possible sites for expansion in
Tetebedi. Musa and Enga. The trip to Enga was aborted due to transport dilficulties. Based on these
excursions, the organization will then decide which areas it should work in, in the future, as part of
our expansion program.

Furthermore, networking amongst the different NGO's, CBO's and community groups within Oro
Province, was another activily that took prominence during the year. Likewise,

3. How has the development on the national and local levels influenced the project
activities during the last year?

=== page 3 ===
‘we

The development in areas of politics and the national cconomy has not been helpful for the
implementation of the program. Powerful political and cconomical interest groups are now speeding
up the exploitation of the country’s natural resources in order to put the country’s economy back on
track. The recent government has declared tax breaks for companies interested in developing the oil
palm industry. Oil palm is now Papua New Guinea's largest agricultural foreign exchange carner,
ahead of coffee. International financial institutions and other funding agencics are now providing
funds for the Oil Palm companies. This model offers the companies a beter and more profitable
alternative [rom the conventional large-scale plantations owned by the company. Conversely, growers
do not own shares in the companies.

Time bas become critical as the logging companics are encroaching in buffer areas just to the
northeast and southwest of the plateau. Clan groups who have involved in the consensus building
process over the years, to date are vocal about ensuring sustainable development of the plateaus
according to locally defined guideline.

However, the majority of rural communities in PNG are by no means poor. With the exception of
areas degraded or polluted by large mines, logging. agriculture or fishery projects, the customary land
tenure system has enabled local communities to have free and casy access to land, clean water and the
abundance of natural resources for the decent quality of Tile.

The granting of oi! palm, logging and alluvial mining licenses to foreign developers in the province
will have tremendous impact on the rural communities. This is a set back for the program if these
projects impact on the natural environment on the Plateau. Government services such as roads,
schools and hospital are Jacking in most rural areas and development such as oil palm, logging and
alluvial mining will contribute to environmental and social impact on the rural communities.
Conversely, the local people do not own shares in the companies.

The project continues to face major transportation problems due to the state of the road linking
Popondetia to Afore thence to Itokama. While the road works were completed in 2005, a major
problem has been the bridge over Pongani River. which has collapsed. It is anticipated that as more
work is carried out in the area of eco-enterprise, there will be a major push by the communities on the
Plateau to have their roads fixed.

Likewise, the airlines that service the Plateau are unpredictable. We continue to Lace major setbacks
when the planes do not fly into the Plateau and while it is understandable [rom our point of view. the
local communities blame us for delaying activities and workshops.

Another positive for the MCASP has been the eventual involvement of both local level government
and provincial government in the activities of the project. We have likewise been fortunate to have
started a relationship with Conservation Melanesia and Dadacol. both have been points of contention
for many years. We have also been fortunate to have started a working with the Provincial AIDS
Commiltice who have supported us with transportation from Popondetta to the Managulas Plateau.

=== page 4 ===
B. Implementation of the project

I. Have the project activities been implemented as planned?

Unfortunately, duc to the pressing need for a Strategic Plan for the organisation, many of the pkinned
activilies Were not implemented and pushed back to 2007. A lot of time was spent working with stafl
and various stakeholders to draw up a strategic plan and an exit strategy for the MCASP as requested
by the Managalas Leaders during the previous years Leaders Summit.

The Consensus Building Programme was faced with delayed printing of material and this has also
been pushed back to this year 2007,

2. Have there been any changes in the implementation of the project? (Details to be
given in the work plan report)

A series of workshops were conducted which brought together stall and board members ol the
organisation as well as various stakcholders to discuss the work of the organisation and then develop a
Strategic Plan for the next five years. The workshops began with a Reflection Workshop at Motupore
Island: a Strategic Panning Workshop at Sivarai Namona, and a Staff Retreat at the Bluff Inn Motel.

This all culminated in the drafling of relevant documents. programmes and plans which will now be
used by PWM and MDF to implement various project activities within the next five years,

Towards the end of the year, a workshop was conducted under ODW Rainlorest Literacy to provide
training tor new CBO staff on the CB Process to prepare them for implementation this year. PWM has
now successfully merged the work of the ODW Rainforest Literacy with the CB Process utilising the
same personnel to carry oul both the Clan Group Discussions during the Literacy programmes in the
villages. This will then lead on to the Zone Forums and the Combined Forum towards the end of the

year.

While we had originally planned to visit two sites for the expansion of our project Lc. Musa and
Elem, we managed to visit Tetebedi as well which was a bonus. On the other hand, the visit to Elem
was abandoned when the Team could not get into the area after travelling half way there to Mt Hagen.
This trip was accomplished during December/ January by the Executive Director and the Project
Officer.

3. Have the changes, if any, resulted in any reallocations on the budget?

There was reallocation of funds with approval from RFN. with major reallocations occurring within
our programme budget to cater for the series of workshops that had not been budgeted for initially.
This necessitated a redirection of funds from planned program activities to cover a major part of this
expenditure, however, at the end of the year there was still a shortfall of over K60,000.00

4. To which extent have the expected results been achieved?

The past year has unfortunately been very slow for the organisation in terms of the implementation of
the planned activities. However, this was compensated for by the development of a Strategic Plan and
Exit Strategy which has now given us direction to move forward over the next five years. This has
been an ongoing issue of contention, in that there did not seem to be any guide or direction for the
organisation to follow until now. The Workplan and Budget for 2007 reflects this development.

=== page 5 ===
5. To which extent has the purpose of the project been fulfilled?

The program had been conducted widely through out the Managalas Plateau all year round. Ficld staff
have been carrying out regular fickd patrols to respective zones to assist management of each
community-based organisation with technical advice. Many of the communities involved have already
demonstrated considerable initiative in organising themselves to develop a sustainable development
plan for their areas.

These clan groups have had considerable experience collaborating with one another and with other
outside agencies and organisations on other local development initiative. The proceeding of

Training workshops to date make it clear that communities believe in their social and economic well
being is dependent on sound, long-term management of their resources. In effect, communities are
learning to build on existing social capital and to expand it for use with new eco-enterprise activities.

Communities are now becoming aware of the importance of managing their environment sustainably
and taking major roles to help themsclves as the result of the training and awareness. Every effort ts
being made to ensure that an opportunity to participate in eco-enterprise activity follows the initial to
provide greater awareness and participation with the communities. For instance, zone 10 is currently
under negotiation for Forest Management Area (FMA) to tie up deal with landowner for exploitation
of the rich forest resource. The negotiation is still continuing and this will depend on the landowner to
decide between conservation and development,

Individual CBO's and their Zones are now independently seeking technical and financial assistance
from other sources. Zones | and 2 have now basically become self-reliant in terms of project planning
and implementation.

Managalas Development Foundation, the local partner in this project, is now been given the tools to
develop to be independent and to work on their own as has been agreed Ww during the meclings and
workshops in 2006, MDF will have on board a Project Co-ordinator from outside of the area who will
assist them implement the Exit Strategy.

6. Please explain the deviations, if any, from the purpose and the expected results
according to the work pian.

A major deviation has been a relocation of funds towards the planning process. While many training
activities were not carried out due to this process, it is not a cause for worry as we now better
understand the situation and have planned relevant training activities to cater for this deviation,

Another change has been the need to move the Consensus Building Program over to the new year,
This has been an ongoing problem because of the printers and the studios that have been developing
the Rainforest Literacy material. We are now looking al other service providers who can produce on
lime.

7. How has the co-ordination of the project regarding local, national and
international co-operation, including field visits, functioned?

The program had been well accepted by the local communities so much so that people from the
acighbouring communities continuously ask for assistance to start something similar in their areas.
Interest continues to grow amongst CBO's, NGOs, government agencies and other interested parties
who have interest in both community development and environmental work,

=== page 6 ===
6

Local co-operation between MDF. CBO's and communities is quite good. They have shown keen
interest in participating and supporting the project. The project is working alongside other CBO's
programs because all of these organizations complement each other.

With complimentary funding from other donors, the work at the ficld level is proceeding with much
interest by the affected communities. the relevant government agencies and the MDF stall and Board,

A major problem faced by many NGO's including ours is the perception that we are the alternative
service delivery mechanism and therefore we should be catering for all the community needs. Local
staff continue to use their local knowledge and standing to make unreasonable demands on the
organisation. This should be addressed in the new year with the implementation of the Exit Strategy.

MOU’s have been drafied by our Lawyers to enable relationships between PWM and MDF. the LLG
and the Provincial Government for collaboration within the project area. This should be negotiated

and signed in the next year.

C. Other Considerations

I. Are there any specific internal or external conditions that have influenced the
implementation of the annual work plan?

a) There were a number of internal conditions that influenced the implementation of the anoual
workplan. These include staff reluctance to implement these program activities on specific
date as planned due to financial disagreements. Lack of major contribution and cqual
participation from all sectors of the communities. including in-kind contribution have had
serious and negative impact over the project due to the pervading cargo mentality, Although
this is a natural and common concern throughout rural areas in Papua New Guinea, the
Managalus people have taken advantage of the financial situation to demand almost
everything to be paid for before they will do anything.

There also continues to be a breakdown in effective teamwork between the Field and CBO stalf
on the onc hand, and PWM project and support staff on the other hand.

b) The major external condition, which affects the implementation of the project, is
communication and transportation difficulties given the remoteness of the project. Training
workshops and community meetings continue to be delayed due to poor weather and road
conditions, The road Jink from Afore to ttokama has been covered by bush and deteriorating
road condition has resulted in less and less produce transported to urban markets for sale.
Road and transportation difficulty has affected program implementation and can be very
trying for project staff who have to travel in these conditions to do their work. This is also
compounded by the lack of a reliable air transport system and rising cost of airfares.

2. Is it probable, after the fast year’s development, that the project will reach its
goals or is there a considerable chance for changes?

A lot of lessons have been learnt from the project over the years. The project has offered so many
good things such as awareness, trainings, exposure of national issues, exchange of ideas, and
collaboration of partners NGOs and government agencies, This last year has seen a number of events
which will have lasting impact on project implementation, especially with the recruitment of a [ull-
tcum ol staff in the Port Moresby PWM Office who are now able to plan, coordinate and implement
the programs based on the contract,

=== page 7 ===
This year will sce resurgence in community involvement and contribution due to he experiences of the
community with the MOCP’s contribution to their economic well-being. Likewise, the Consensus
Building Program which is now amalgamated into the main MCASP activities, will enter another
phase of involving children and schools in learning traditional knowledge and practices through our
traditional learning centres.

Training programs have been conducted to develop the capacity of field staff to carry out activities
with minimum supervision and also to transfer skills to other community members. It is also the aim
io maintain the staff base so that there are no gaps when technical project stall leave the organization.

A reorganisation of the MDF Board and recruitment of reliable and qualified MDF stall will see a
new and community oriented MDF in 2007, with the appointment by the PWM Board of a Project
Co-ordinator from outside the Managalas Plateau.

3. How has the last year’s development affected the probability of the project's
continuation after the professional and economic support from the REN has
been phased out?

It is anticipated that the project will attempt to seck funds exicrnally to continue, in the event that
funding from REFN is no longer available. This is in light of the fact that considerable amount of
resources and time have been invested in mobilizing the Plateau community to the extent they have
become a community that is ready to tackle issues affecting them. They have become an example of
organized communities in PNG that are now resourced to work together for their own well-heing,

At least for the foreseeable future, this is unlikely to happen. but steps are been taken to address this
eventuality. We anticipate with the MOCP coming on board and a push for diversification of MDF's
funding base, this will be a start of an independent organization to take over when PWM moves oul of
the Plateau

4. Please evaluate the project’s relevance and foundation according to national
plans and priorities during the last year.

The program is relevant at this stage during the economic hardships that are faced in rural
communities in Papua New Guinea. Current scenario is that investors are harvesting natural resource
at an alarming rate. In so doing. investors do not comply and failure to produce proper environmental
impact and reconstructive planning prior to government granting operational licenses. In the course of
harvesting the natural resources, socio-economic problems have risen to new heights; hence the only
option to prevent such rising issues is to encourage community development projects and actively
mobilizing communities to deal with issues for themselves,

The national government and international government donors have recognized the program as
significant. It is likely that after the end of project funding period, some of these organizations will
help in the funding of the project. This is because the program is also in line with poverty alleviation.
The program is in line with government priorities and public plans that encourage idea of “bottom-up
planning” for the Local Level and Provincial Government Reform System (PGRS) and the Education
Reform Sysiem (ERS) program in Papua New Guinea. The program equips rural communities with
wider thinking capacity and to produce well-framed plans for development.

D. Audit report

PWM’s account will be audited and the financial report will be sent to RFN by April 2006.

back to Ukarumpa while the 6 hives remained behind. But no one was taking
responsibility over them aad hater the bees died out. And the hive bodies were desirovesd
and nothing remained,

The second verbal information we reccived was in Afore and is described below.

Sometimes later, for some unknown reasons, the landowners chased out the (rer
bloke and he fled leaving everything behind. Among other things the bochive was left
untouched,

Later the bees gradually swarmed out in all directions and finally the hive was abscord
that nothing was left in the hive. The swarmed bees have found theit feral dests an
hollows of trees in the bush in all directions of Afore.

THE IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY

The first 3 weeks in August 2006, are engaged in the preparation of the bins anu
equipment. This will include purchase of the bees, the hive parts aud hive cauipnici!
which have been paid for by the Partners With Melanesiats.

In the last and final week of August 2006, we will make appropriate arian nienty fe
more the hives down to Managalas via Port Moresby.

On the 27" August 2006, Jonah Buka will fy down to Port Moresby. On ihe acct diay
28" August 2006, Enoch Asineha (Model Farmer) will be flying t@ Port Moresty 9 ith
the 6 colonies of bees. By then Jonah Buka will be standing by at the airport wr pick op
the hives on arrival.

The charter Might to tokama must be arranged well in advance se that the 2 Aue
2106 must fall due to take off from Port Moresby to Hokama to deliver the hives

On arrival in tokama a site location must be identified so that Jonah and bneckh wrt
Organise the hive stands. Then leave 3 hives in Hokamia and the other § hess be tikes
out to Koruwo.

location where the other 3 hives are to be placed.

=== page 11 ===
After a site location is identified, Jonah and Enoch will be allowed to construci a his c
stand, When the hive stand is completed, place the other 3 hives on the sand,

Popondetta to Port Moresby. On the 3° September 2006, Jonah and Enoch will fy oui o!
Port Moresby to Goroka.

THE HIVE MANAGEMENT SKILLS TRAINING

A beekeeping training will be conducted cither in ftokama or Koruwo, The tiiting will
be mainly on the basics of management skills. This training will take place on 9" in the
second week of October for a duration of one week (a training program will bo presented
separately on a later date with the costs involve).

Meanwhile, a representative from Partners With Melanesians to identify and nomiiai:
participants who will attend the hive management skills training in October. Tie
participants must be nominated one in cach zone.

The names of nominated course participants must be sent to us so that we Could orate
their certificates out here.

At the end of the training, a small gathering will be organised to witness the pres eniion
of certificates to the bee (raining participants. After certificate preseatitions the
participants will go back home and remain in their zones until beehives ave miroduced be
them respectively. Then they will take on from there and manage them.

RECOMMENDATIONS

E. There is high potential for beekeeping in Managalas Plateau ares. Theretore, it
the first 6 hives turn out successful, we would recommend that each zone muss be

4. Later if the bees in Manugalas are in full production we need to have established

6. The cost of tools and equipment for Managalas in relation to beekeeping will be
met by Partners With Melanesians in future.

SUMMARY

The Managalas Plateau has high potential for beekeeping activities. The environment
looks good and suitable. The climatic conditions are also favourable. The Managalas
Plateau lies at a right altitude for beekeeping purposes. There are many insects of the bee
family living in the area. There is no reason why the European honey bees | Apis
Mellifera should not be there.

The 6 hives of the European honey bee will soon be delivered into Manazelos. A couple
of months after the delivery of the hives — a farmer training will be organised. Pl

participants will received certificates after completing one week course.

3. Sustainability of Project/program results and effects

Sustainability of the project results and effects depends mainly with the time frame

In terms of the time frame it seems that there is a limited time frame to achieve the goals

The sustainability of the results and effects of the project could have progressed without

As PWM intends to exit from the current project site, the program and its activities are

title: Managalas Organic Coffee Project
snippet: Managalas Organic Coffee Project Meeting Minutes. Meeting 1 of 2006 Between: The Managalas Delegation Coffee Industry Cooperation Oro Provincial Administration Minutes by: Paul P Konia MOCP Manager 26" January 2006 The Managalas Delegation Meets with the Deputy Provincial Administrator, Oro Province
text:
Managalas Organic Coffee Project

Meeting Minutes.
Meeting 1 of 2006

Between:

The Managalas Delegation
Coffee Industry Cooperation
Oro Provincial Administration

Minutes by: Paul P Konia
MOCP Manager
 26" January 2006

The Managalas Delegation Meets with the Deputy Provincial
Administrator, Oro Province, Popondetta. PNG

Agenda:
Introduction of Managalas Organic Coffee Project (MOCP) and MOCP’s
interest in the Oro Coffee Mill, and associated infrastructural problems MOCP
that would directly affect its operations & other related issues to the Oro
provincial executives.

Introduction:

The purpose of the meeting was to discuss issues relating to the coffee project
that Partners with Melanesians Inc. had initiated for the people of Managalas.
The project, Managalas Organic Coffee Project (MOCP) will be in full
operation in late March 2006, thus Oro administration was given an insight
into the project.

‘The Managalas Delegation marketing the MOCP eventuated from a combine
foruny leadership summit that was held on 19" - 23" December 2005, under
the agenda of “MOCP and PWM Exit Strategy” the group was tasked with
certain responsibilities to ensure that MOCP took shape and got off ground
smoothly.

Alletter detailing the issues that will directly and indirectly affect the project
(MOCP) was highlighted by the Managalas Delegation and was presented to
the Deputy Administrator Mr. Kila Siboro, a copy of this letter is attached.

‘The meeting was schedule to start at 10.30am in the morning, as agreed to by
the Acting Oro Provincial Administrator, but he failed to address the
Managalas Delegation at the appointed time.

However, the Deputy Administrator, from his busy schedule, found time to
address the delegation.

At 10:45am Meeting Started.

Speaker | Designation [Issue/ Topic Of Discussion
Mr. Kenn | PWM- Executive | Thanked the ‘Deputy Administrator Mr. Siboro for
Mo!

| Director allocating his time to attend to the Managalas issues.
However, he expressed dissatisfaction at the
reception received from the acting Oro Provincial
Administrator who was absent even though he had
committed a time for the meeting. He stressed that I

the Managalas Delegation had travelled all the way

 down using their own funds to air their grievances
and views regarding issues affecting their district
and province.

He said if the Administrator was busy he should
have deferred the meeting or better still cancelled
it, he said, such behaviour should stop as rural and
isolated districts are suffering as a direct result of
neglect which leads to non existence of government
services.

However, he said he was happy that the Deputy
Administrator was there to meet with the Managalas
Delegation who was representing the 16,000 plus
people of the Managalas Plateau,

On that note he presented the letter entitled —-——-

—-—o the Oro Provincial Administration with a
st of questionnaires that the delegation identified
as issues which need answers to. He also gave a
brief highlight on PWM’s and MDF’s work on the
Plateau and a PWM brochure was given to the
Deputy Administrator for his reference.

He then introduced the 17 member delegation to
the Deputy Administrator.

Mir. Douglas
Garawa

MDF Chairman
(Former Provincial
Government Member
& Premier of Oro

| Province)

| of NGOs on the Managalas Plateau; the support

‘Thanked the Deputy Administrator for his time and |
expressed the same concern regarding the A/
Administrators failure to attend the meeting. |

He than explained to the D/ Administrator the work

communities had received from the NGOs to help
sustain their life’s. He said the people of Managalas
Plateau are organised and have been working in
groups as CBOs (Community Based Organisations)
which are functioning in isolation for so long, even
though Managalas Plateau has been branded as
“OVER ENGIONISED” (NGO) a term with no |
meaning as such the government may have

forgotten them but they have survived with the help
of NGOs for over 1Syears now.

He said they were there because the Managalas
people are going into coffee business and they

need the Oro Provincial Administration and the Oro
Provincial Government support to further their
coffee business, and that was the reason, why the |
Managalas Delegation were in the D/Administrators
office. Other issues that they felt will affect their
coffee business and the current problems they are
facing in the district are outlined in the letter that

they have presented to the D/ Administrator.

 He than proceeded to introduce MOCP. He said that
Managalas people have established a business that
| will be trading as the Managalas Organic Coffee
Project and the project has started as of October
2005. In order for the MOCP to operate and function
successfully the felt that infrastructural problems
such as roads, bridges and other government
services in the district that should be upgraded and
operational as well. Expensive PMV fares from
Popendetta to Afore and visa a versa. They would
also like a Managalas representative to be on the
provincial land transport board if there is such a
board in place. They are also interested in the Oro
Coffee mill.

Mr. Kila
| Siboro

Deputy Administrator

Greeted every one, and then introduced himself as
Kila Siboro and said that he was back from study at
an overseas university.

He said that he had just resumed duty but he is

aware of the issues and problems affecting the
people of Oro especially the rural population. With
the work of NGO he said that he is very supportive

as NGOs are partners in development and the
National Government's medium term development
strategy, NGO and the government can work
together to achieve the National Government
medium term development strategy. “With the aim
of alleviating poverty.” |

He further said that, the current National
Government is supporting conservation work when
our Prime Minister supported the carbon trade at
the world carbon trade meeting. As such he
explained that the people of Managalas will be
beneficiaries of the carbon trade because they are
organised and are currently doing conservation

| work. Carbon trade has a lot of money in it and it
doesn't need any work to be done, it is only the
fresh air that will be traded, he says that the NGO
representatives and organisation based at the
plateau can explain the carbon trade in detail

| further with the Managalas people.

He also admitted that the issues highlighted are
pressing issues and will be addressed when he

| replies to the letter that the Delegation presented to
him.

| ‘The current road condition of the Popondetta ~Afore

 | road was up- graded and only the bridges need
urgent maintenance, the worst being the Pongani
bridge which is yet to be maintained

He said that he is reliably informed by the
| Department of National Planning that aNGO based
in Oro Province is travelling to and from Goroka
visiting the CIC headquarters, coffee processors
and factories for the option of setting up a coffee
factory and doing coffee trading from Oro.

On the Coffee mill issue he said that the mill is
‘owned by the Oro provincial government, The

| current status is that it is going for tender, because

| there was a trip done in December 2005 by the
Minister for Agriculture and Live Stock (Hon.
Mathew Siune) and the Chief Executive of the
Coffee Industry Cooperation (Mr. Ricky Mitio) who
held a discussion with the Oro provincial executives
and have decided the mill be put on public tender

| and other interested people and individual can
apply to acquire the mill through the normal tender
process.

Mr. Kenn
Mondiai

PWM- Executive
Director

Replied that the NGO that is travelling to and from
Goroka is Partners with Melanesians, which the
delegation are part of. The trips are done as part of,
an ongoing research to establish the business plan
| for the MOCP and also to link up with coffee
factories and processors who can help in the coffee
business.

| The visite were dono also to the CIC headquarters in |
Goroka and Oro as well to acquire reievant
information to set up the MOCP.

| The coffee study done by PWM took three years for
ito come to this stage where MOC? started. PWM
has sought financial assistance from a partner NGO
in Holland to fund the MOCP, and they have agreed
and funding is now available. PWM provided
technical assistance to MDF who is the umbrella
organisation in the Managalas plateau who will be

| the direct beneficiaries of the MOCP.

‘The funding will end in three (3) years, as PWM
believes local capacity will be enhanced to master _|
the coffee trading and milling.

On the Oro coffee mill; he asked the Deputy
| Administrator to defer the tender, and call up a
meeting with the Managalas Delegation again to
deliberate on the option of acquiring the mill, he
further stated that the option should be done locally
first. He feared that the tender process maybe
abused and the mil! maybe be given to some

 individual or company who will monopolise the

coffee industry in Oro and pay less to the coffee

farmers as practise last year at Managalas, where

they were buying coffee at 10 toea per kilogram

when the coffee price in Goroka and Lae was at
K3.60 per kilogram.

MOGP is owned by the Managalas people and
MOCP is interested in the Oro coffee mill as MOCP
has coffee trees that can produce an annual
900,000kilograms plus and MOCP has finance
available to run the mill as well.

‘MOCP has linked- up with an overseas coffee
market in Europe and will be supplying its coffee to
Europe, thus the mill is vital for MOCP.

‘The Deputy administrator was asked to take it up
with the relevant government authorities to defer
the tendering of the Oro Coffee Mill?

Siboro

Mr. Kila”

Deputy Administrator

‘The Deputy Administrator agreed that priority
should be given first to the locals when the mill is
tendered.

He also said that he supported organised groups
such as the groups the Managalas people have, that
made work collaboration easier and wins donor
support. He said he was pleased but reminded the
delegation that their thoughts of Oro for Oro or
Managalas for Managalas should stop as it
discourages and hinders developments from taking
place. He says that we should all be thinking about
ourselves as Papua New Guineans and do things for
PNG that will allow true development to happen, he
said that PNG for PNG attitude will happen in the
next ten to fifteen years.

‘The Oro for Oro attitude must change, and Oro
people should get skilled people from outside to
come into the province to help them where ever
necessary for this province and the nation to

develop. He said the people for PNG have this kind |
of attitude and this kind of attitudes must change for |
the better of PNG. He said he believed that this,

kinds of attitude will surly change when mixed |
marriages that are practised and engaged is taking
place, (highlands & coastal, Papua & New Guinea,
Oro and Madang etc,) he said, out of this kinds of
cross cultural marriages will true PNG be borne.

Developed countries like Australia and America are
not thinking locally to them selves but are striving
for their national pride of which we should be doing
the same.

 Pp
i

MDF Vice Chairman

(Former Oro Provincial
Government Member-
OPG

Former Member of
PNG National
Parliament as Oro
Regional Member)

‘The 2006 Oro Provincial budget is being passed
and some of the issues as the upgrading of
Popendetta ~ Afore road has funds and Pongani
bridge is identified as well.

He said he will respond to the other issues in writing
later.

‘Thanked the Deputy Administrator for allowing his
time to address the delegation and said that Mr.
Siboro is a person that he trusted who can do things
better for the Oro province and he felt that with Mr.
Siboros support, MOCP will gain trust and
confidence from the Provincial Administration to
peruse its aim of acquiring the Oro mill. Thus the
tender of the Mill should be withheld pending a
meeting with the Provincial Government/
Administration and Managalas Delegation.

He also said that Oro can be competitive and rich as
Goroka, Mt. Hagen or Lae, because Oro has a lot to
offer in terms of agricultural produce and more. To
name a few, he said Oro has coffee, palm oil,
coconuts, copra, cocoa, vanilla and betel nuts, the
provincial authorities should now look at the
‘Managalas people and help them acquire the Oro
coffee mill.

He said even the location of the coffee mill is
unrealistic as it is no close to s coffee producing
area. He said, the coffee growers wanted the mill
and demand for a meeting with the relevant
authorities.

He believed the Deputy Administrator will support
the Managalas Delegation and put pressure on the
authorities to halt the tender.

Mr. Kila
Siboro

Deputy Administrator

He agreed that he will try and talk to the authorities
to defer the tender but said that a letter must come
from the Afore Local Level Government (ALLG)
stating that the tendering of the Oro Coffee Mill be
put on halt and a meeting between the Managalas
Delegation and the Mill Owners convene as soon as

possible.

He asked the ALLG President (Hon: Amos Jahevo)
| present in the meeting to take note and send aletter
outlining this issue and interest of the Managalas
people and said that ALLG has support for their

| project (OCP).

Mr. William
Suremo

Chairman of Nahara
Coffee Limited

‘The Chairman of Nahara Coffee, a small company
established by the people of Managalas as share

 holders to buy and trade coffee the Nahara coffee
holding is currently not functioning because of road

He also wanted to know from the Afore LLG council

for in the yearly provincial budgets.

Hon: Amos | Afore LLG President
Jahevo And current Member of
Oro Provincial
Government

Also Hon. Jahevo said that he supported the project
and will advice his Local Level Governments
members to put together a letter for the Oro
Provincial Government. He also said that funds for
infrastructure development were always late or
‘were never given. He said even though he tried his
best to get hold of his district funds, he is always

| unsuccessful as there is no support from the
provincial headquarters, thus with the Managalas
Delegation present, he said the Deputy
‘Administrator will now note that there are serious
problems regarding funds allocated for districts
such as Afore.

He also said that when the Minister for Agriculture
and Live Stock and the Chief Executive Officer of
CIC was in Oro Province to discuss the fate of the
Oro Mill he did mentioned to them that the Oro
Coffee Mill should be given to the People of Oro to
run.

He also said that funds allocated for the rural

whatever reasons he is unaware of. He said that

given for the last S years or so, even the councillor’s
development grants and salaries were not given on
time.

|
Mr, Paul P | Coordinator of MOCP
Konia |

4

‘The coordinator of MOCP said that if the Oro
Provincial Government is serious in generating the
internal revenue of the province it should consider
handing over the Oro Coffee Mill to MOCP to
manage.

 He also reiterated that if the MOCP failed in its bid
to secure the Oro coffee mill, he will ensure that all
coffee coming out of Afore district (Managalas

| Plateau) will be shipped out as parchment coffee to
Lae and Goroka for the coffee to be milled to green
bean.

He said the MOCP will begin its operations in late
| March 2006 and as such it is a matter of priority that
this matter is looked into urgently.

He also said that MOCP has an overseas market
where it is planning to export coffee directly to the
market there in Europe and it is in MOCP's plan to
package ground coffee as well.

He said if the bid fails MOCP will mill coffee outside
of the Oro Province until such time MOCP has

‘Thus, he asked the Deputy Administrator to alert the

Zone Briefing
17" February 2006
Naukenane Village, Zone 1

Three topics were chosen at the Leaders Summit held on 19 - 22 December 2005, as.
topics that should go through the 2006 zone forums. These issues will form the basis of
the end of the year combine forum. This brief is prepared to present these discussion
topics to the activity coordinators who will be leading and coordinating the clan and
group discussions. The topics are: 1) Council of Chiefs; 2) 2007 Council and National
Elections; 3) Traditional Leaning Centres. Each of the topics has questions that should
stir the discussions in the various groups. Each group will be required to note down
responses to each of the discussion questions and a general consensus reached on each of
the topics. The group’s consensus will be presented at the combine forum.

+ COUNCIL OF CHIEFS (COC)

a) _ Whatis the COC?
‘The idea of having a Council of Chiefs came from discussions during the Leader's
Summit held on 19% —22™ December 2005 at Serefuna Village.

b) Why having a COC?

‘This is an issue within the Managalas and especially in conjunction with MDF and the
issue of leadership between the Traditional and Contemporary Leaders- the Old and the
young educated leaders. It seems that the young educated people have displaced the
‘elders out of the new structure and they have become defunct and of no consequence to
the current developments, After a lot of discussion, the Summit agreed to have in place a
COC. Traditional elders are important members of the community and they need to be
more involved in the new developments that confront the plateau. They need to be
involved because they are important in more than one way.

Traditional leaders are important because:
© Have respect from their own clans.
Have traditional knowledge and wisdom.
Peace brokers
Settle disputes
Control the clan decision-making process,
‘Transfer knowledge and skills to the next generation.
Control over the land.
Control other issues in the village
Body to liaise with Goverment.

te eeceee

b) Who becomes a member of the COC?
 It was decided by the Leader’s Summit that each zone must have a representative at the
Council of Chiefs. The clan representatives from each village come together at the zone
level. The ONE representative representing a particular zone is elected at the zone level
and is represented in the Council of Chiefs.

©) Who does the COC represent?
Each member on the COC represents his zone. The whole COC body represents the
16,000 + people of Managalas.

d) What does the COC represent and what is their major function?
The COC is the highest decision making body on the plateau dealing with Traditional
Laws.

©) How much power does the COC have?
The extent at which COC is to exercise its powers will be vested in their constitution.

1) _Whatare their roles & responsibilities?
Some Specific Roles of Traditional leaders would be:

Deal with tribal conflict

Mediate on land matters

Oversee and provide advice to CBOs on cultural issues

Advice MDF on industrial and economic development and natural resources.
Lead and oversee on cultural, traditional, customary practices in Managalas.
Provide input on political agenda/issues on the plateau.

Liaise with MDF on consensus buil
Others to be included .

ecco eecee

h) Who are the COC answerable to?
They are answerable to the whole of the plateau (16,000 + people) and to each clan
member in their villages and zones of which they represent.

i) Can the community change the COC if they are not doing their job?
Yes. Only at the Zone Forum. Changes made at zone level wil] affect membership to
coc.

i) _Are women eligible to become COC?
Yes. If the woman has the customary right to be the chief of her clan.

k) If NOT, then why not?

Because chieftainship in most communities on Managalas are inherited from father to son
etc.

Dd How long can someone be on the COC?
As long as he/she is not voted out at the zone forum.

m) — Will the COC have a chair?
 Yes. The COC will have a chair elected by the COC to steer and guide the operations of
the COC in agreement and consent of the COC members.

©) _ Will the COC have a constitution?
Yes. The constitution will be written by CELCOR Lawyers with initial baseline data
compilation by the Community Learning Centres.

Pp) Will there be an MOU between MDF Board & COC?
Yes. The MOU will spell out the roles and responsibilities of the COC and how the COC
will complement the roles and responsibilities of the MDF Board.

n Will the COC have an AGM?
Yes. The AGM will be a part of the combine forum held at the end of each year.

8) What happens at the COC AGM?
This is when the COC reports back to the communities about what they have done during
the year including successes and failures. It is during the AGM when members of the
COC could be elected out of the COC. The election of new members of the COC will be
taken back to the zone level.
 ~& 2007 COUNCIL AND NATIONAL ELECTIONS

1. Why is PWM talking about this?

The Kjivitari Electorate is a big electorate that when it comes to choosing a candidate to
represent the people of Ijivitari in the National Parliament, people from the coast are the
ones voted in to Parliament by the people of Managalas and the Kjivitari electorate as a
whole. It has come to being that the Managalas area has long been forgotten. Government
infrastructures have deteriorated and services are worse than ever before.

PWM has been in the plateau for the past 16 years or so and have assisted the people in
small ways using donor support. But his cannot go on forever. PWM is implementing its
exit strategy beginning this year and will end in 2008.

If Managalas people continue to vote into Parliament someone from the coast, the
Managalas will be lost in time. Therefore, it is high time for the Managalas people to
speak with one voice and vote someone from Managalas into Parliament in the 2007
elections so that vital government infrastructure and services will come to Managalas for
the good of our children and their children’s children.

2. Where did this discussion start?
This discussion started from the Leaders Summit last December 2005. The Summit
appointed an election committee who will coordinate this on the Plateau.

 Executive Summary

From mere observation of its structure Managalas Development Foundation has
been unintentionally designed to function os a supra system consisting of various
sub-systems and systems of systems hence appropriating it to adapt a training
strategy that will enhance the various sub-systems to function independently yet
collaborate with each other to meet the overall goals of the community based not-
for-profit organization's capacity building needs. [Very similar to the Melanesian
circular system of governance in which service delivery, community mobilizing and
etc. is often led by influential individuals however the emphasis is placed on overall
community wellbeing. It involves active participation and interaction between
individual, groups of individual. and communities. Collaboration and
interdependency hos always been the norm].

The success of its various programs will heavily Gepend on the efficiency of the
individuals involved thus the training strategy is to produce learning individuals who
will tasked themselves to undertake various activities of MDF as personal action
learning projects. It is anticipated that by the end of an individual action leaming
project using “systems learning approach” the participant will have advanced
himself in his personal capacity whilst at the same time appreciating the overall
human resource capacity of MDF.

The ‘systems leaming’ approach is based on Kolbs experiential leaning cycle and
draws also Peter Checkland’s ‘soft systems methodology’. it emphasizes
participation and calls for open and active patterns of communication based on
interdependent relationships’, and necessitates action to develop it. This requires an
appreciation of stages in group development and how to facilitate group
processes. The key is to see things differently, if we are to act differently — and we
need processes that enable this.

Its application has been proven to be a success with MICAD in the Collingwood Bay,
and Dadakol in the Managalasi, where projects based on various activities of
different programs were undertaken by groups of individuals as personal action
learning projects hence meeting some of the overall objectives of their CBOs. The
Airara and Sinafa jetties, the Dadakol Canteen and Resource Center and Coffee
projects have been inspired by this program,

The personal action leaming projects generated through the MOF TNA workshop
basically encompasses the various actions that MDF otherwise would be expected
to deliver using traditional methods which evidently has not been successful thus the
emphasis now is for MDF to shift its activity funding to support this new approach.

Organization: Partners With Melanesiars Inc.

Annual plan for year: 2020

Have the 5-year results for the project changed? If YES, please explain.

No

Which at local and/or national may affect the and its results the upcoming year?

O'Neill Government from China, and the new Government has gone to China asking for re-financing that Loan with certain measures to service that Loan,
and that could have an effect on the general cost of living in PNG and the Goods and Services Tax could be increased in 2020.

How does the project aim to address security issues related to the planned activities? Are there any security issues of special concern?

No major security issues that will hinder the planned activities in the four project sites, However there are illegal loggers encroaching along the extemal
boundaries of Inaina Wildlife Management Area, Managalas Conservation Arca and the new proposed Collingwood Bay which loggers are still there but no
opcrations. On the Managalas, with recent Local Level Council Elections outcome, the Former President Douglas Garawa, who has been opposing the

detail. ’

Not meeting the targets because CBOs not taking ownership of the project and dependency on PWM is too high which sees that is still a conflict among
