Updated: 20.02.2020

How does the project promote the equal participation of men and women? Provide concrete examples in relation to the planned activitics.

in all planned activities for year 2620, men, women including youths and pcople living with disability are all part and partial of the project in order to
promote equal participation. Partners with Mclanesians have a new program called Gender Empowerment will promote equal participation of men, women,
youths and people living with disab‘iities.

The program has its specific piannec. activities to target equal participation for all men, women, youths and people living with disabilities. Recently, the
Managalas since being declared as a Offictally Government Gazetted Conservation, the Managalas Conservation Arca Management Committee has now
elected 4 representative of which 2 ere female representatives from Managalas and this is an example of equal participation and representation.

Are there any other relevant comments for considcration under this annual plan?
[ All PWM project sites are only accessivie by plane, boat and vehicics and most of ! time activitics are not implemented on time due to road and weather |
conditions. And also most of program activity funds are spent on transport anc fuei.

Collingwood Bay in 2020, PWM plens tc increase the Staff number by recruiting another Officer to bring the number to Three (3), since the Project is very
big with 650,000 hectares and in. addition to that, PWM plans to establish a Project Office and Transit Accommodation at Tufi outside of the Project Arca,
but at the Government Station. This is the only way for our 3 Officers to be fuily concentrating on delivering the CWB Project as planned.

As for Karimui, our plans for 2519, was for the Conservation Area application to be submitted to the Government in November 2019, but it is impossible as

one important component of the application which is the Landuse Pian for the District/L1G where the Conservation Area is located needs to be completed.
And so if the Landuse Planning documentation is completed in 2019, the process of documentation and making the submission to the Government will be
done in the 2nd or 3” Quarter of 2029.

=== page 3 ===
Updated: 20.02.2020

How will you work to ensure that decision makers listen to you to an even greater extent this year?

These questions try to address our reporting needs to Norad and it would be helpful to understand what you plan to do towards decision makers:
1. (How) Will you submit inputs to decision-making processes within the programme period?

- PWM at the community and project Icvel, we have a program called Community Empowerment and Decision Making Process which deals
directly with decision making process under the activity combine forum. In those forums, in all project sites, all issues are discussed and
solutions are reached through consensus where PWM facilitates the process.

- At the Local Level Government LLG in the Districts and at the Provincial Government Level in the Provinces, we have established very good
network with local political leaders and we are able to talk to them and brief them regularly via email, face to face and also via social media (
Facebook) on our Projects and issues. When we need the help and intervention of the Political or Administrative Leaders, we seck audience with
the leader and provide briefs and inform them of what we see and how we would like to see things happen and also provide possible advantages
and disadvantages and how thing will look in the long run, so bused on that brief and process of engagement; we expect political leaders to help
take action on our issues by them lobbying their colleagues or taking the issues to higher authorities for decisions that benefits us and the project
and the people.

- Atthe National Level, PWM Executive Director is a Member of the National Forest Board, and he has been previously on that Board, where
issues of poor governance and abuse of process exercised by the NFB led to legal challenge and so with his re appointment, we are hoping for a
better decisions to come out of the NFB, but due process and due diligence will be exercised.

2. Will there be field trips or mectings arranged by RFN's partners between regional or national authorities and local communities who practice rights~
based, sustainable rainforest management within the programme period?

- Yes there arc always field trips or meetings to project sites but between RFN’s partners on regional or national authorities and local communities
who practice rights-based, sustainable rainforest management within the program period will depend on the need basis. And when they plan to
come to PNG and for them to visit PWM Project sites. PWM will be more than happy to accept them and organise logistics for them to visit the
project sites and communities to meet them discuss and hear from them directly on how they are participating and benefiting as project owners.

3. Will there be publications produced within the programme period which document that rights-based, sustainable rainforest management does protect
forest?
- There will be newspaper publications, newsletters, radio and TV interviews and broadcast.

4. Will there be publications issued which document companies’ destruction of rainforest or human rights violations during the programme period?
- Yes

5. Plans to expose inadequate implementation of laws or corruption in the forestry sector to the authorities or campaigns within the programme period?
- Yes

6. Other?
PWM will collate all Reports on our investigations on Iliegal Logging activities at our Project sites and all correspondences and that we have sent to
the Authorities plus their responses to show how PWM is addressing the issues and problems of poor sustainable forest management and how
Authorities are responding; cither positively or negatively on our actions.

Dear Governor Hon. Gary Juffa,

© We have conducted the field inspection on the 8" August with your Team from Oro Administration. Acting PA
and Chairman of PFMC, Several Oro PEC and Sector Chairmen, your Staff Fred and Israel, Managalas
Conservation Foundation Staff and Director, Provincial Forest Officer Mr Sebastian Arthur King and 2 x Foresters,
Police Escort for 2 x Oro Police Officers, PWM Staff 2 x Patrick and myself, and other NGOs staff from Oro.

Onsite we had the Landowner’s Company Chairman and his people/supporters. During our visits, we saw no
Asian person.

© CEPA Officers (3 x named) were in Popondetta with us, decided not to accompany us on the field inspection
giving us excuses that, they are not in Popondetta for that, but to the Managalas Conservation Area
‘Management Committee meeting; saying they will come later. But using that trip to collect data and information
relating to the Ifane FCA etc.

‘* APNGFA Monitoring Officer (named) from POM HQ flew to Popondetta when we were there, but he was never
‘on site with us during the joint inspection, maybe he went there later alone with his PFO. We only saw him on
the plane back to POM at Girua.

In summary .... In 2017, we found them just inside CA boundary by 267 metres, now in 2019 we see they have
gone beyond the 267 meters and everywhere. Ifane FCA has 4 logging coupes, all 3 coupes are inside FCA
" undary, only one outside. ( 6 photos from Ifane)

Nee tien Ase, Patrick Vuet and I, are working on our Field Inspection Report which we will present to the Oro PFMC
and then Chairman OPFMC will then take it to Oro PEC for actions at the political level. We have given ourselves 2
weeks to get it done.

Thank you.

Kenn

‘Thanks Kenn, We totally endorse this request. In fact there are still instances if illegal logging taking place
in Oro despite our efforts to get National Government intervention. Ifane and Yema Gaipa are two
examples. Here logging companies are virtually plundering the forests with permits they obtained illegally.

What is being done about this?

“\n Wed, 31 Jul. 2019, 12:49 pm Kenn Mondiai, <kmondiai@pwmpng.org.pg> wrote:

Dear Mr Gunther Joku,

Thave attached here a self-explanatory letter with a photo of a map with GPS tracking to you copied to
many important people.

CEPA and PNGFA, Oro Provincial Forest Management Committee, Managalas Consezvation Foundation,
Partners With Melanesians and the Company Management (Oro Woods Ltd), we need to conduct a joint

' physical field inspection.

“lease can you liaise with your PNGFA Counterpart Mr Tunou Sabuin (MD) and his Area Manager
Southem (Mark Betuels), Field Services Acting Divisional Manager Mr Andrew Aopo and PFO Oro to get

organised for this joint inspection.

Itis two years since we raised the issue and now after 2 years, our people from the Managalas plateau
whose land extends down into the Girua and Lake Embi area are raising concerns about logging taking
place on their customary land which they have assigned to Conservation under the Managalas conservation
area, which was declared by Minister Hon. John Pundari and Governor Hon. Gary Juffa on the 29" of

November 2017.

This is serious and we want your Officer with PNGFA and Oro PFMC Officers to go on the ground with
you all to do a physical inspection of the extent of the logging within the IFANE FCA and also check on
the boundary of the Managalas Conservation Area.
 Please get back to me with your response for immediate actions after discussing with MD PNGFA.

Thank you.

Kenn.

1 undertook the 3“ trip to Managalas Plateau with the focus on Eco-tourism activities. The request
‘was submitted on a short notice but actually eventuated as planned. I flew out of Port Moresby on
the aforementioned date.

PURPOSE

28" September, 2019
LS

The main purposed of the trip was to deliver hardware materials to 3 different project sites who had
already ventured into eco-tourism activities through community initiative program. The request for
the hardware materials were done during the 2" trip, when visiting those sites with Patrick Vuet
from Bio Conservation & Community Mapping component and PWM Support Officer- Kovi Wara.
The locals from Ogan, Dareki & Yombu villages requested for various hardware materials through
their activity coordinators and zone managers during the visit alluded above. After seeing their
eagerness to venture into eco-tourism through community initiatives, I've decided to purchased and
re-visited these sites with few hardware materials to strengthened and support the ongoing eco-
tourism activities.

All materials were purchase on the 27" September, 2018 at Popondetta town after comparing prices
in 3 major hardware to cut down on costs. Hence, different materials were bought in different
hardware as per the receipts attached herewith.

 ‘The pictures above shows the hardware materials that were purchase at Popondetta town, loaded
and transported to eco-tourism project sites in Managalas Plateau.

DISCUSSION

_

‘Almost 90 percent of the requested materials were bought and delivered to the respective project
sites as per their requests. Locals were overwhelmingly exhilarated with astonishment when they
saw the truck load of needed materials at their project site during delivery. Due to lack of
communication as the mobile telephone network service has been off for the past few days, many
CBO officers and zone managers who were vocal in submitting requesting were unavailable on

eptember, 2018

/2
 sites during deliveries. Nevertheless, those on site showed gratitude, and excitement on behalf of
their CBOs & Zone Managers upon receiving the materials.

Below is the pictures of first delivery done at Yoivi village for the Yombu Community. The Yombu
community is further inside so closest location to drop the materials for locals to carry was at Yoivi
so I decided to drop the materials after getting assurance from the village chief to safeguard the
materials until the Yombu community comes for collection

Unlike Yoivi, the materials for Dareki were delivered late in the evening and therefore everyone
were there to receive the materials. ‘The village leaders, activity coordinator and CBO manager;
Conwell made complimentary remarks pertaining to PwM’s swift intervention in providing the
much needed hardware materials to enhance the ongoing eco-tourism activities. The entire village
people came and witnessed the delivery of materials to Conwell for the Darakol QABB Farming.

As highlighted above, the materials for Dareki were delivered in the night as shown in the pictures
above.

Material delivery at Ogan village for Darokol Lake
‘The materials for Ogan village were dropped off in MCF/PwM yard at Afore station. The activity
coordinator and the Zone Manager came in the morning to confirm the number of materials and

went back to inform the rest of the village people. An arrangement was made with the Health
Centre vehicle to drop the materials at the project site but the same vehicle was engaged by

AS
 Veronica Aure to transport the food rations and other materials required for Zone and Combine
forums to be held in Tahama and Kuorua villages in the coming weeks and came back very late in
the evening. Assuming that the vehicle would be back on time as scheduled, the locals at Ogan
prepared a big feast and dressed in traditional costume to receive the materials from PwM.
However, this never eventuated due to the late arrival of the vehicle and the materials are still at the
location specified above.

29 September, 2018
—_—=—————

Cecil and I together with Zone 2 activity coordinator and a local man decided to walk to Numba.
When we walked past Kavovoki village, some villagers met us and cautioned us not to continue on
to Numba. They reminded us that our presence at Numba would indubitably instigate locals to
assault Kingsford for the long deferred payment for building nursery and transplanting the seedlings
of orchids and other native plants. The entire village people involved in this activity after they were
assured by Kingsford for payment for the job. Consequently, we decided to tum back from
Kavovoki and walked back to Afore to avoid inconveniences. The designated polybags for Numba
was given to Ogan village to use them for nursery.

{30 September, 2018

Cecil and I walked to Niniuri village, just 1.5 kilometer away from Afore station to visit the
proposed reforestation Nursery site and a spring-water sprouting out from the earth, We took
pictures of both location and spent some time in the village before walking back to the station late
in the afternoon. Refer to the picture below

Afore Cave & Waterfall

The councilor for Afore LLG came and approached me at the guest house to advise that all the
landowners for the above distinctive sites have come to a consensus and thus agreed to allow PwM
officers to visit the scenes. During the last visit, Patrick, Kovi and I seek permission from the
councilor on the behalf of the customary landowners to visit the mysterious cave and the amazing
waterfall afer been briefed by Christopher- the Zone Manager. Consequently, we were forbade to
take shots and documenting the distinctive features due to existing in-house discrepancies among
legitimate customary landowners. However, after hearing the news of material deliveries to various

Jt
 ecotourism sites, the councilor came and approached me to inform that they have mutually reach
consensus the visitation is admissible henceforth.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

The locals at Ogan village which owns the mysterious Darokol Lake have already commenced with
the task of building the steps to the lake. The village leaders convened a public meeting on Sunday-
30% September, 2018 and allocated tasks as per their schedule; for the locals to load gravels and
other compulsory materials to start on the job. Even the women and the children were urged to
assist in any way possible to boost the manpower to complete the job before the end of this month,
‘Two guest houses had been completed and will be opened to the public and tourist in few weeks”
time. I advised them to build a nursery using 2 shed cloth rolls to plant native species of trees so
that they can be transplanted beside the lake for beautification and tourist attraction. The locals are
fervently devoted in undertaking designated responsibilities to convert the lake into a tourist
glittering destination in the entire Managalas Plateau.

visit.

RECOMMENDATION

Iam proposing to take a final trip to Managalas to visit those sites as well the new sites in Afore to
take pictures and collect data before 2018 ends.

INTRODUCTION

This was a planned activity, for the establishment and swearing in of the CA
committee members. The trip was planned for in collaboration with CEPA to jointly
fund the implementation of the activity. Letters were prepared by MCF Project
Director, Mr Damien Ase for the Representative from the Provincial, [jivitari District,
and Afore LLG.

Damien Ase and PWM Board Member Tom Huasi, went in advance to Afore for the
planning and MCF Board meeting. After the meeting, they travel down to Popondetta
with the four representatives from Managalas whom will represent the LOs in the CA
comnnittee.

There was a delay in the signing of the letters by CEPA MD, Mr Gunther Joku, thus
delaying the release and approval of their funds for the trip. This has also delayed
Rufus’ and myself travelling to Popondetta for the CA meeting.

PURPOSE

The purpose of the trip was to attend the first meeting for the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee, and swearing in of the CA management
committee members in Popondetta, Oro Province.

MCF PROJECT DIRECTOR'S 2019 FIRST QUARTER REPORT

1. INTRODUCTION

In 2018 many of the planned activities for the Managalas Conservation Area was not implemented
due to various reasons including the late approval and transfer of funds by the main donor of the
project Rainforest Foundation Norway (RFN) through Partners with Melanesia (PwM), the
holder of the project and implementing partner. The Conservation was gazetted and officially
declared in 2017 so there were a lot of expectation from the local communities/landowners
especially support for sustainable livelihood activities which is the main purpose for the funding
from RFN apart from the conservation objective. Also there were a lot of issues on this discussed
and decisions taken at the District Wide Combine Forum held in November at Yoivi village in
Zone 8. Therefore, the hope was some of these main planned activities will be undertaken in the
early part of the year because of the up-coming Local Level Government Elections in the second
quarter of the year. However, there was delays gain due to late transfer of funds by RFN because
of the delays with audit report. This report is record of activities in the first quarter of the year
which is from January to March 2019.

2. ACTIVITIES UNDERTAKEN IN THE QUARTER.

2.1 Follow-up on Financial Reports/Acquittals

Last year PwM transferred K59,000 to MCF account for its capacity building activities and
because the Finance Officer was new I worked with him to ensure that all acquittals of the funds
transferred were done to meet the audit requirements as stringent requirements were put in place
in the contract for this. Also the amount of K+1,000 was not transferred which affected payment
for services and MCF staff and CBO allowances and this remains major concern and issue where
staff wanted to boycott planned activities for the year. | also discussed the reporting requirements
and the financial management guidelines with the Finance Officer to ensure that he was well
versed with the financial reporting requirements

2.1. Follow-up Work on the Establishment of Managalas Conservation Area

Management Commiittee.
The District Wide Combine Forum held at Yoivi village in zone 8 last November approved the
landowner representatives on the Managalas Conservation Area Management Committee
(MCAMC) as required under the Conservation Areas Act. Therefore, armed with this decision, |
liased and worked with both PwM and Officers from the Sustainable Environment Protection
Division of the Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to formally establish the
MCAMC as required under Section 25 of the Conservation Areas Act as the committee plays an
important role in overseen the management of the conservation area including approving the
management plan, making rules/by-laws for the conservation area and supervising the work of

=== page 8 ===
rangers. These including writing letters. sending emails and holding one on one meetings with
relevant officers about establishment of the committee and funding for work of the committee.

2.2 Follow-up on Ministers Funding Commitment.

A lot of my time in the quarter was spent on following up on the commitment made by the Minister
for Environment & Conservation, Hon. John Pundari during launching of the Conservation Area at
Itokama on 29 November 2017. This was to assist the local communities/landowners with
sustainable livelihood alternatives especially marketing of coffee so I wanted to ensure that the
funding was released to MCF before the season proper starts for the coffee. Our plan was to give
the funds equally to each coffee growing zones accessible to markets to arrange for group
marketing of coffee from their zones organised by the partner Community Based Organisations
(CBOs). These including sending letters, follow-up emails and one on ne meetings with the CEPA
Managing Director and relevant Officers with CEPA's SEP Division. It was a frustrating effort as
this was continuing from 2019 after the submission of the necessary supporting documentation to
the CEPA Managing Director as requested by him.

2.3 Proposal and Budget to UNDP/CEPA GEF 5 Project for the
Managaias Conservation Area Buffer Zone Support Project.

Upon request by the GEF 5 Project Management Unit (PMU) housed within UNDP I developed a
proposal for the Managalas Conservation Area and Buffer Zone Support Project to cover costs for
establishing the MCAMC, selection and training of Rangers and support equipment and costs,
sustainable livelihood alternatives in line with the Protected Area Policy and education awareness
programme especially targeting schools in the area. They also asked me do develop a budget for the
MCAMC to cover its costs which I did and submitted to them and CEPA. The plan was to have the
proposal considered by the Project Board/Steering Committee at the planned Board meeting in
May, This was to meet some of the funding constraints for implementation of planned activities.

2.4 Meetings with Governor for Gro for Funding Assistance.

A number of meetings were held with the Governor for Oro, Hon. Garry Juffa including follow-up
letters and emails about the funding commitment by the Governor for activities in the conservation
area including establishment of the Council of Chiefs and the Community Leaders Summit. [ also
followed up with the Officers in the Governor's Office for this funding as these were also activities
agreed to at the District Wide Combine Forum in Zone 8 last November. The main issue according
to Governor Juffa is the late release of funds by the Finance Department so he told me to continue
with the follow-ups so that the funding committed can be released for the planned activities..

2.5 MCF Board Matters.

There has been problem with having the regular board meetings because of funding constraints and
also the board decisions have to be implemented so I have been in regular contact with the
Chairman who is in Popondetta due to his medical condition to update him on board matters. There
are important matters including funding, implementation of activities , staff matters and networking
with relevant Provincial and District Officers as well as management of the project vehicle that the
Chairman and other board members needed to be up-dated on so it is important for the regular
communication or one on one meetings when I am in the Province.

2

=== page 9 ===
2.6 Arrangement for Management of the Project Venicie.

The vehicle donated by New Britain Palm Oi! which was parked at the Oro Guest House for a
number of years was eventually serviced by the company mechanics and registered with MVIL last
year. This has assisted with easing some of the transport problems faced for implementation of
planned activities. However, because of the bad road condition it needed to managed and driven by
a reliable driver to serve its purpose. A committee of the board was established to manage the
vehicle including supervision of the driver as per board decision last November. This arrangement
was to be assessed to see if it was working out, if not to make changes to the arrangement.
Therefore, I was in constant communication with the Chairman and the MCF staff regarding the
management of the vehicle.

2.7. Other Administrative Matters

1 also developed reporting formats for MCF and CBO staff which will be presented at the planning
meeting before they can be finalised. I also ensured at that each MCF staff have proper
identification cards and that the MCF office in Popondetta is properly maintained by the Finance
and Admin. Officer.

3. PROBLEMS, ISSUES/CHALLENGES.

Some of the obvious problems and challenges have been funding constraints to implement planned
activities, communication problems, bad road condition and the main issue with commitment by
MCF staff because of the non-payment of allowances. The late release of funds earmarked for
capacity building activities by PwM has also contributed to some of these difficulties.

A lot of stakeholders including business groups, cooperatives, associations, women and youth
groups as well as schools are requesting for funding assistance for their own planned activities but
MCF being a small organisation with no funding base is unable to meet their request thus, creating
frustrations. There is for MCF to carry out awareness on its roles and functions as per its
constitution and the need to have the membership arrangement in place so that there is broad
representation on the board to assist with the work of the organisation.

4, FOLLOW-UP ACTIONS

There are number of urgent matters that need to be followed up including the funding commitment
by the Minister, the proposal to the UNDP/CEPA GEF 5 Project, establishment of the MCAMC
and funding commitment by the Oro Governor. The other activities are mainly administrative
matters including contracts for staff, organising the planning and board meetings and supervision of
the Finance and Admin. Officer to improve on the financial reports for MCF.

5. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, I can say that there are a lot of expectation of local communities/landowners and
stakeholders in the conservation area especially schools for funding and other support since the
declaration of the Conservation Area. MCF is unable to meet these expectations because of funding
constraints and other challenges including lack of support from stakeholders like the Afore LLG,
Oro Provincial and Ijivitari District Administration and line national agencies especially CEPA and
CCDA. Coupled with this is the problem of MCF staff not having the confidence to follow-up with
3

=== page 10 ===
Provincial Authorities to support the activities in the area. The main issue of MCF having its own
audit report needs to be addressed as this is affecting MCF’s ability to raise its own funding from
donors because the production of an external audit report is one major requirement by donors.

The need to have the MCAMC established and in place and properly funded to carry out its
functions provided for by law is a priority. CEPA Officer needs to constantly reminded of their
roles and the work of MCF as a local partner in implementing the Protected Area Policy and
relevant legislations especially the Conservation Areas Act. Also there is need to have MOU’'s
signed with Afore LLG, the Ijivitari District Administration and Oro Provincial Administration for
assistance with the implementation of planned activities and especially for aligning the
Conservation Area Management Plans with the plans of each of the various levels of government in
the province.

Respectfully Submitted,

Damien Ase
Project Director

Program and Project Reporting

INTRODUCTION
The Scriptwriting workshop is an on-going activity under the Education Awareness Program. It was

initially the Rainforest Literacy Program that works side by side with the Consensus Building
Program, now the Community Empowerment Program.

‘This Program adds value to PWM’s core program (Biodiversity, Conservation and Community
Mapping) because in order for communities to support and fully engage in this conservation
initiative, they need to be informed and we must ensure that they fully understand what we are
doing and so they can be able to make informed decisions.

So for this year (2019), the Scriptwriting workshop was held at Afore village, just at the edge of the
Afore government station.

‘There were two travel days both for participants, for me as Program Coordinator. i travelled on the
6" of July 2019 to Popondetta, spent a night there and travelled via PMV together with the two field
officers (Crispine Burawa - MCF) and Alking.Fufus - MKTG) to Afore on 7th July, 2019. The two
CBO Officers travelled a day from Afore to Popondetta just to assist me with logistics.

It was a week-long workshop organized jointly by PWM and MCF with Crispine Burava (MCF-
East Field Coordinator) as lead facilitator and co-fa ited by Alking.Fufus (MKTG-Director) and
PWM Program Officer.

‘The workshop started on Monday 8" July, 2019 and ended on 12" July, 2019. I was accompanied
by PWM’s Gender Officer. She was new and as part of her orientation and introduction to the
project area, she took advantage of this workshop to speak to the CBOs and gender reps.
highlighting this new Gender Program and also, picked up vital information during discussions that
are relevant to developing program activities for her program next year.

The workshop started very late the next day (08.07.19) because we had to wait for some
participants to arrive. They were the ones who received late notices for this workshop because they
are living in zones furthest from A fore stati
‘There were a total of 30 participants comprising of MKTG members, CBO reps, MCF Officers,
PWM and observers.

‘A good number of participants are females (see participants list attached). The females are both
mothers and young girls, a number of them are gender representatives from the 10 Zones of
Managalas Plateau.

 At the end of the discussion, it was decided and agreed by participants that this issue be discussed at
the management level and maybe an awareness workshop for a day or two planned out for PWM,
MCE, CBOs and other stakeholder representatives within Managalas to be invited to participate and
have this issues clarified out once and for all.

Gender Equality was the other issue of discussion that saw a lot of interest and because we have
PWM's new program coordinator present as part of her orientation and scoping and research
activity, she was able to grasp vital information/issues of need and contribute where she can.

‘The main issues that came out clearly is for Managalas women and girls to be empowered and be
able to participate in this project with no barriers especially cultural barriers which scem to be the
main cause of hindrance for women/girls to participate in developmental initiatives and in this case
the MCA Project activities.

There are other social issues surround this main issue that was discussed thoroughly and
emphasized like reviving the Afore Council of Women that was foreseen to boost to the women
folk in the Managalas plateau.

They also highlighted a number of necessary skills trainings that they need and further went on to
discuss issues like Violence again women that needs awareness in the community.

‘The gender empowerment coordinator took note of it all and will use them to develop activities for
2020 onwards.

‘The participants were then introduced to the issue on Climate Change and I asked by the
facilitators to define this big term ‘Climate Change’ and gave examples to clarify and further
highlighted that it is a global issue. I also explained that the main cause of CC which is human
activities and briefly highlighted the adaptation/mitigation efforts by governments and NGOs like
PWM. I then, further linked it up to PWM’s Climate Change and Reforestation Program (headed by
Cecil. Senive) as one of PWM's attempt to combating climate change in the plateau.

Trigger questions were asked to generate discussion around their own experiences on the effects of
climate change. In fact, through the discussions it was clear that they have unconsciously adapted to
some of these effects on a day to day basis. They also highlighted that they need awareness
throughout the plateau because some of these effects of climate change like low yield and airbome
discases are blamed on sorcery and other cultural beliefs. These has caused a lot of infighting and
dismantling of communities and within close family units.

A script was done and to be dramatized by the Theatre group.

Mismanagement was a heated issue that brought a lot of discussions all pin pointing PWM
management and MCF management. The discussion went off a little bit with name calling of
certain people in the management level and not so much on how best they would want to see this
issue resolved.

This discussion was not that very constructive and the facilitator did not steer the discussion
towards finding solutions and for participants to be able to do awareness. In the end it was put
forward to be discussed during the Leaders’ Summit.

Finally, it was the issue on Sustainable Livelihood Alternatives. It was an issue that became a
standalone issue and discussed separately because the whole of Managalas Plateau are so excited
about because everyone wanted to benefit from it.

CONCLUSION

‘The 5-day planned workshop ended well with 2 days allocated for travelling to workshop venue and
back.

So we travelled to Afore on the 8" of

=== page 22 ===
General Overview of Statistics

- While every effort has been put in obtaining the correct statistic, there are some reservations for
human errors and missed data that may contribute to the correctness. Therefore can be subject to

changes when necessary.
But generally from the data, the following information, can be deduced and can make general

conclusions.

Number of Trees.

The Managalas Plateau consist of Eastern and Western Zone. The date from the Eastern zone is
obtained mainly from five village with assistance of some CBO’s and other persons who cared to
assist. The other rest are from assumption as we could not be allowed under certain restrictions. It is
deduced that the Eastern zone has around 230,000 coffee trees. This includes newly planted and old
over grown trees. Newly planted coffee trees constitutes about 5%, and this amounts to about 11,500
trees in the Eastern Zone alone.

The Western zone of the plateau, from the statistics obtained, there is almost about the same around
230 thousand trees. This also includes newly planted trees, however newly planted contributes about
7%, which amounts to about 16 thousands trees.

Including the whole Eastern & Western zone, the Managalas plateau has about 460 thousands trees.

Area covered by coffee trees.

From the data collected all areas are measured in square metres. Within a one square metre area it
contains about 2to3 trees, and with that, it assists in acquiring these figures.

The Eastern zone has about 57.41 hectares of coffee growing area. While the Western zone has
about 55.96 hectares. And the total Managalas Plateau has about 113.37 hectares of coffee growing
area, This area consists of old and newly planted area. As these is not much planting, these are about
6 percent of the area consist of new trees which is about 6.8 hectares.

Number of Bags (Parchment) per Season.

The total number of bags recorded is based on information (figures) gathered in 2006 season. The
figures may vary more or less, and is depended entirely on farmer commitmenv/activity and other
various factors in a season.

There are certain main factors affecting production which are;

i Unavailability of pulping Machine

This has become the most significant impediment in the numbers of production. Most farmers share
on the average ration of 7 farmers is to one pulping machine or either resort to manual hand pulping,
thus is a tiring and time consuming process. And so almost about 30% of cherry volume is lost un
catered.

=== page 23 ===
a Road Transport condition and Market (price) factor.

There has been some uncertainty in the marketing factors that discourage farmers from not been
busy on coffee production. 2006 has been a year where M.O.C.P (Managalas Organic Coffee
Project) and other agents offering door step marketing system. This initiative has certainly refocused
their attention into coffee activity which would lead to increase in volume in year to follow.

Previously pricing has been a real concern. Farmers often receive 70 toea to 80 toea per parchment
kilo. Some do not even sell their bags due to no proper access road networking. At the moment the
state of road is in a dire straights , needing urgent repair and maintenance. Consensus effort from all
sector of community must be gauged, whether it be local level government, community groups or
any non government organizations in alleviating this problem. The only accessibility is through four
wheeled vehicle, and in raining season access in none at all. These factors contributes a lot to the
volume of production.

Through MOCPs introduction of competive price ie.K2.50t per kilo, and other agents competing in
the area, would certainly encourage farmers in rehabilitating their neglected trees as viable cash

crop.
Data’s shown are 2006 volume, they are;

Eastern zone about 2300 bags and Western zone is about 2000 bags. Totaling up to about 4300 bags
in kilogram its around 4300x 50 = 215000 kg’s which is about 215 tones.

Numbers of farmers and family involved.

From the data obtained, there are about 1200 farmers on the Plateau. On the average there are about
3 family members in each garden. This gives total to about 3600 people involve in coffee production
in the Managalas Plateau. This figures is sure to increase given competition incentives offered by
MOCP and may be other buying agents on the site, thus may encourage more farmer involvement.

Problems Encountered.

As in most ventures, the enumeration exercise has its own share of problems. Most viewed this
exercise from negative perspective, thinking its for personal benefits, for whom I myself could not
work out. The level of co-operation from the Eastern zone is almost none, and often times faces
verbal abuse and at few occasion near physical confrontation. This problems were often instigated
by ill informed local leaders especially councilors who may have no knowledge or rather ignorant on
the aspect for initiative taken by Partners with Melanesia in putting MOCP on the ground, with its
business plan for the betterment of MDF (Managalas Development Foundation) for financial self
sustenance in enhancing its various programmes in the Plateau in the long run. Despite this hurdles,
the statistics has been somewhat collected and compiled with some handful of individuals who have
rendered their invaluable assistance and support.

=== page 24 ===
Basic Maintenance Of Organic Coffee Quality Process.
The following steps are been emphasized in the coffee production steps in maintaining best quality.

Harvesting.

Only ripe cherries (fully red) are being encourage to be picked. Mixture of green cherries, half ripe
cherries and over ripened (brown in colour) does not give uniform out look, and often a problem in
sorting. It is bound to have effect in the final product ie. Tasted and quality as cach has their variable

quality at the end.
Pulping and Fermenting.

It is encourage that within 24 hours of harvesting, the cherries must be pulped. Prolonging will
certainly have effect on the beans, ie been getting brown coating, as a result of heat gencral in the
bags or containers. Once when beans are affected, it eventually lead to detriment of quality.

Pulped beans must be kept in cool locations for fermentation. Metal containers are discouraged as it
may coat rusting on the beans. Once when rusting in coated it affects the quality greatly.
Fermenting for 2 days is encouraged this is ample time for removeral of mucilage (greasy coating).
Plenty of clean water must be used for washing until clean.

Drying

Most drying must be done on beds above ground level which is a recommended method. In rainy
days solar drying ie, building canvas roofing above drying beds. This method absorbs heat and helps
drying effectively. The method has been in use in some parts of Managalas area like Silibu, Dea and

Numba.
Drying of beans should take about 3 good sunny day; to show that it has been amply dried, tooth
mark should not appear on the bean when bitten, a method by which most farmers should use for

testing ample dryness.
Storage.

All dried parchment should be stored in a house that is free from smoke (fire) and open to moisture
absorption. They must be stored in a house shed and covered with canvas to avoid exposure.

All coffee parchment should not exceed more than three month in a storage, the longer it is kept the
danger of quality deterioration is high. After 3 months efforts must be made to sell off stock to any

agent who is offering better competitive prices.

Pricing.
To get better price it is best to organize group marketing ie. Farmer co-operation and the co-

operation should gauge competitive buying agents or company for better prices at the current
markets or markets recommend by coffee industries co-operation (CIC).

text:
Compiled by Jacina Mimigari- Pariers with Melanesians (ly 2008)

Approach and Guide to creating Managalas Conservation Area
Management Plan

For the people of Managalas in their struggle in safe guarding their natural environment

This handbook is basically a guide to assist the Managalas People on how to go about in
creating their own Management Plan Guidelines and rules for the preservation and
enhancement of their Conservation Area. This will be used by the facilitator.

Getting a Conservation Area status is not as easy as you think it is. It is a continuous
commitment, where a Resource Management plan must be in placed to guide and preserve it.
Support must come from the rightful resource owners (Land owners), Local and provincial
level Government and the concern Government Department like the Department of
Environment and Conservation (DEC).

‘Acronyms:

CA- Conservation Area

DEC- Department of Environment and Conservation
NGO- Non- Government Organization

PwM- Partners with Melanesians

MDE- Managalas Development Foundation

What is Conservation NGO?

Conservation Agencies are non-governmental organizations that work in partnership with
government bodies such as DEC to help people improve their sustainable livelihood. They are
not part of the Government. There are many kinds of Non government organizations (NGO's).
The church is one kind of NGO that works to help people improve their spiritual lives. Other
NGO work on improving health (such as save the children fund), and others work on education
such as PNG Trust which works doing literacy training. Conservation NGO's (agencies) work
to help people look after their environment or their renewable natural resources. They provide
education on how to use and manage resources wisely.

Conservation Agencies are not a company or business that works to make money or profit.
They are not the same as trade store or a logging or mining company whose main work is to
make money. They are known as non-profit organizations, that ask other people or
organizations to give them money to do their work. Conservation Agency's main work is to
provide information and training to people on how best they can look after their resources.
Conservation Agency's’ work like schools. People don’t ask schools for money or other forms
of assistance that has nothing to do with education. The same is true for Conservation
‘Agencies. Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and its umbrella organization, the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF) are such agencies.

 Compiled by Jacinta Mimigart- Partmers with Melanesians (uly 2008)

‘What is 2 Conservation Area?

Comparing all the protected Areas in the country, Conservation Areas (CA) is a very promising
form of protection as customary land ownership can be retained. The general principle function
of the Conservation Areas act is to protect an area having a particular biological, topological,
historical, Scientific or social significance or other special value for the present community or
future generations. No conservation Area has yet to be established in the country (T. Pringel:

2007)

What is a Conservation Area Management Plan?

‘A Resource Management Plan or in our case Managaias Conservation Area Management
Plan is basically a directive plan on how to go about in maintaining the Protected area,
allowing it to still be intact or only littie damaged be done to the environment. Conservation
‘Area Management Plan is the next step after the area is granted the CA status but in light to
achieving the goal of a Conservation Area Status, 2 Management plan has to be drawn up to
ensure the sustainability of the project.

Session 1: Why do you create a Conservation Area?
(Why do you want to create a protected area and why other people create Protected Arca?)
(What is special about your Protected Area?)

Purpose: The purpose of this session is to:
1. Find out why people from Managalas think that they want to create a Conservation

Area
2. Explain why Landowners in other areas create Protected Areas; and
3. Clear up confusion about the benefits of creating a Conservation Area

Preparation and Materials: Posters of the “Only benefit you will receive”

Steps:

 Conpted by Jacinta Mimigar- Partners with Melanesians (uly 2008)

Step 1: Ask participants to discuss in small groups the reason that they want to declare their
‘area a Conservation Area and make list and a group member will present it to workshop

participants

Step 2: Do a big group comparison and discussion of all the presentation until a realis
picture is more obvious to all.

Step 3: The facilitator should explain why landowners in other areas of PNG have set up
protected Areas (CA or WMA)

In many places in PNG landowners have seen that some of their wildlife is becoming less
common from too much hunting, gardening or that, plants for building materials and other uses
are becoming scarce. They are worried that there will not be enough left for their children to
use in the future, because they are using too much now. So they set up a Protected Area, and
agree on rules to ensure that their resources are used wisely so that they will still have them in
the future.

In some other areas where landowners have most of their forest still intact, and there have not
been declines in resources landowners have also created protected areas. Why have they done
this? Mostly they do this because they do not want some ‘autsait lain’ coming in to destroy
their resources (animals, plants, etc). Sometimes this ‘autsait lai” might be another clan in the
area, or settlers from other places or big companies such as logging and mining companies
‘These landowners say “why do we want to sell our resources to some ‘autsait Jain’ that will
make plenty of money while we only make a little bit of money from it?” so they want to
tambuim this area to prevent outsiders coming in to destroy it.

Step 4: Explain that the real benefit from setting up a Conservation Area or protected Area is
that their resources will be used and managed wisely and that future generations will still have
these resources to use and sustainable development then can come in place.

Explain that if the community is setting up the protected area for the reasons other than these
that they will be very disappointed. Creating a protected area (CA) does not guarantee that the
landowner will gain some money benefit or that tourist or researchers will come to see the area,
Although it is true that tourists do visit protected areas in some places in PNG, creating a
protected area does not guarantee that they will come.

Note: The most important point to clear up before you get into further Protected Area Planning
is that there are no monetary benefits in setting up a Protected Area (CA). If landowners set up
a protected area for monetary motivations they are almost guaranteed to be disappointed and
the protected area is guaranteed to fail.

Purpose: To make sure that participants are familiar with rules that have been developed
elsewhere in PNG for protected areas

Preparation and materials:

Stationeries; Papers and pens, handouts- “Examples of rules from other CA or WMA-Pidgin

Steps:

Step 1: Explain that most of the areas in PNG are WMAs. Landowners must make and agree
to the rules because the WMA is on customary Land. In areas that have police they can assist
with enforcement of WMA rules. But in areas without police it is the landowners, through the
Conservation Area committee who must enforce the rules.

Step 2: Give participants the handout of examples of rules created in other protected areas in
PNG. Go through the examples with them. Some examples of rules are:

1) Banning the hunting of Birds of Paradise;

2) Banning the use of Shotguns

3) Completely closing certain areas from any hunting activities;

4) Charging entry fees for tourist

5) Banning Logging and minin

6) Preventing the clearing for

7) Banning littering

8) Restricting the type of Development that can occur in the area

9) Placing a fee or royalty payment for hunting

10) Restricting access by outsiders to culturally significant sites e.g. burial places or fambu
areas;

dens or burning of some or all vegetation;

However, rules can make provision for traditional hunting and collection.

Step 3: Explain that rules should be created to protect wildlife and natural resources that local
people believe that they are very important for their lives and their future. When rules are made
for other reasons, they usually collapse. The purpose of a protected area is not to make money.

 Compiled by Jacinta Mimigari- Partners with Melanesians (July 2008)

People may end up making money out of the protected Area, but that should never be the
reason why the protected area is set and the rules made.

Step 4: Explain that whatever rules are placed over the Conservation Area (PA) depend
entirely upon the iandowners. No Rules can be placed over the area without the landowners’
agreement. Rules will only if all landowners agree on them. The rules that are developed
during this workshop will only be a draft set of rules. They can be changed according to the
community wishes. There is a definite need to talk more about the rules in the community.

I, INTRODUCTION

The District Wide Combine Forum is the last activity of a cycle of activities under the
Consensus Building and the Rainforest Literacy Program. The two programs complement
each other and therefore their activities form a cycle.

The Managalas Plateau has a total of 150 major clan groups and the clans are further
divided into 10 zones.

The Combine Forum serves as an avenue where all 150 clan members come together and
discuss their issues and problems. Representatives from partner NGOs, government
departments and other statutory bodies are also invited and where necessary response to
the people’s issues. In a way, we try to help the people find solutions to the issues in
which they themselves are and will be the cause of development.

For this year’s forum, a representative each from the Media for Development Initiative
and Department of Community Development were able to make it to the forum. Other
partner NGOs and government department, and others send their apologies as they were
caught up with their schedules.

Program starts at 2 pm with welcome speeches by Forum Chairman Douglas Tumai;
Community Representative Zone 5; PWM Executive Director; MDI Representative;
Department of Community Development Representative; & MDF Board Chairman.

VI. WAY FORWARD WITH COMMUNITY PRIORITIES

The Combine Forum was actually last year’s forum brought forward and even though it
was, as commented by many as not following it usually procedure, it was a success. The
last Forum was in 1997 and there were a lot of issues hanging about from back then till
now and the 28 priorities were one of the issues that this forum had tried to address.

The 28 priorities were finally addressed and although there was no fair representation of
clan elders and clan members, there was a representative each from zone |, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8
& 9 (excluding zone 4 &10), CBOs, MDF and others who were there.

People by now afier the forum should have understood better why the 28 priorities have
not been achieved. The responsibility now is upon everyone to work together with

outside agencies like partner NGOs, government departments, business houses and
donors to make things happen. They have to take ownership of the projects and use their
local capacity and readily available resources instead of relying solely on outside agents.

The Consensus Building Process is the strength of MDF in terms of community
mobilizing and organizing and if revived and strengthen again, MCAP will serve as a

1.1 Development objectives of the program:
The development objective will be identical with that stated in the long-term plan,

1.1 The long term overall development objective is sustainable rainforest resource
management as well as informed community participation in sustainably developing their
natural resource base. The landowners must be empowered to play an active role in efforts to
protect the local environment, given its rich biodiversity. Additionally, landowners must be
involved in any decision-making related to planned development projects. Most donor funded
projects, whether they be in environmental protection or sustainable natural resource
management, have failed simply because the affected landowners did not have a well-
informed, active role in their design and development.

The government and other donor or development agencies both bilateral and multi-lateral
hhave realized the importance of ensuring well-informed landowner participation in such
projects and are now looking at mechanisms that enable that kind of participation.

1.2 Program objective:
The program objectives are identical with those stated in the long-term plan,
1.2 The program objective is to contain the expansion of food and cofiee gardens amongst

select groups beyond land currently dedicated to the fallow ground cycle and so maintain
existing levels of forested lands,

A related goal is to overcome the limitations of the current system of transferring critical
rainforest management knowledge by a) oral transfers through intermediaries with vested
interests and b) the distribution of ill-prepared print material to local clan groups.

In addition, the Rainforest Literacy Program will improve the low education levels common
among women and the least influential formalities of the targeted populations as a result of
the focused multi-channel learning strategies that will be used in the group learning sessions.

1.4 Describe briefly and simply the most important results of the cooperation with
ODW keeping in mind that information is to be communicated on to young people
between the ages of 13-19 years of age.

Write approximately half a page.

Papua New Guinea boasts in the diversity of its land and people. There are majestic
mountains, highland valleys, mighty rivers, vast marshes and swamplands, extensive coastal
plains with majestic rainforests, and many legendary islands scatter in abundance in the warm
seas.

Over 75 per cent of the land is covered with rich tropical rain forest. Plants and trees grow
rapidly and luxuriantly because of heavy rainfall and high temperatures. Many trees grow to a
height of 46 metres and more, their branches forming a canopy providing a rich environment
for unique animai and plant species.

The rainforests in which animals, plants and people depend on is becoming increasingly
threatened by commercial mining and logging interest, oil palm expansion and the current
cash crop and gardening practices of expanding local population.

Since 2003, the Rainforest Literacy program have provided critical background and
‘opportunity information to clan members including school children from elementary classes,
youths, women and girls and men who have a vested interest in ensuring their rainforest
resource base is sustainably managed.

 Critical opportunity information include skills related to resource maps and planning the use
of their land in terms of planting food gardens, expanding village space, planting and
expanding cash crop (especially coffee) gardens and other environmentally friendly
developments.

At the same time, Rainforest Literacy program also present modem conservation practices
where locals who are very familiar with local indigenous knowledge on preserving their plant
and animal species try to analyse the information and find a balance with their traditional laws
to conserve the resources on which they depend.

‘The Rainforest Literacy program uses the multi-channel learning system which includes
interactive radio instructions, elementary flyers, posters, newsletters, shell books and
facilitator guides to relate information translated in their local dialects to these various target
audiences in order to overcome the barrier to communication.

Production and circulation of this information are supported by the locally based community
eaming centres (CLC) and the community based organizations (CBO).

1.5 To what degree is the program objective achieved?

A. Since the program began in 2003, managing the use of the land has always been part
of the radio series every year. As part of the bigger conservation component of PWM,
clan members and landowning groups were taught how to manage their land in terms
of expanding community space, food and cash crop gardens, utilising forest resources
etc to cater for the expanding population. Rainforest Literacy provided them with
additional information to assist them in deciding how to use their land,

B. Rainforest Literacy has actually overcome the traditional barrier of limiting the flow
of information amongst local communities. Traditionally, information intended for
specific target population never actual reach their target groups when those
responsible for passing the information tend to limit its spread for various reasons.

‘The designing and presentation of the multi-channel learning systems in using the
audio as well as print in reaching the very under-privileged of society like the
disabled, less influential (women, girls and youths) and silent majority (Less important
members of society) has actually united different classes of people in reaching
‘consensus on issues concerning all members of the society.

‘Complemented by the Consensus Building Process, Rainforest Literacy provided the
different avenues where information is discussed at the various levels (family,
‘women’s groups, literacy classes, elementary classes, clan groups, youth & sports
‘group, church groups etc) and consensus is reached on issues before being presented at
the clan level, the tribal (zone) level and the District Wide Forum where important
stake holders are present to identify actions points and take responsibility in executing
the next course of action.

C. Over the years, number of women and less influential members of the community
participating in the Rainforest Literacy Program have actually increased. Internal
evaluation has shown that this was because the program has actually presented
information relevant to their specific need thus making them feel that they are just as
 important as any other member of the society. Additionally, the program provided the
avenue for them to meet and discuss issues at their own level where they are able to
fully express themselves without fear or favour. This has influenced their thinking
capacity and prompted them to becoming productive members of the community.

D. The multi-channel and interactive radio is fast becoming a model of community based
leaming where it reaches different members of the community at different times
suitable to their information needs. It allows all members of the community, regardless
of their literacy level, whether in school or out of the formal education system, and
even to those illiterate that do not understand the basic English language, to have
access to information that will not only increase their learning gain but to enable them
to become functionally literate with life skills that will enhance their livelihood.

E. Other Non-Government Organizations, Aid Agencies and Government Departments
have recognized PWM as the expert NGO with skills in multi-channel & interactive
learning. We were approached by the Department of Community Development and
the newly established Office of Climate Change to exchange ideas and show case how
we develop the multi-channel learning systems and help them package information to
be distributed to their target audiences on issues relevant to their work.

PWM participated in a media exchange program for the AusAID/PNG Government
Media for Development Initiative in 2007 where PWM produced one series of radio
program (4 programs) and print materials, show casing the on-going program on the
‘Managalas Conservation Area Project where PWM gained popularity amongst civil
society organizations who also participated in the media exchange program.

‘Additionally, the NGO sector in the country has recognized PWM as the expert NGO
in multi-channel and interactive learning and has referred queries relevant to multi-
channel and interactive learning to PWM since.

1.8 To what extent have girls and boys had equal opportunity to participate in the
program?

The program presentation and delivery includes all members of the community. In the radio
program, the drama segment involves characters that portray a typical local Managalas family
where the story line is built around factually events that happen in a family environment. The
segment gauges the attention of the boys and girls who easily identifies themselves with the
young character who by the way speaks in fluent Tok Pisin and uses English jargons and
expressions that excites and trills the audience. The elderly male character speaks in the local
dialect, which is repeated by the women character using simple English and Tok Pisin for the

‘The program also produces elementary flyers that directly feed the schools where girls and

TITLE: IMPACTS OF AGRICULTURE IN RELATION TO BIODIVERSITY

1.0 Introduction:
Tetebedi is located 170° North-cast of Popondetta, the provincial capital of Oro
Province. Tetebedi is at an altitude of about 3000 meters above sea level and has an
estimated population of 2,500 people. It has an annual rainfall of approximately
xxxxx milliliters. Tetebedi is only accessible by light aircraft as there are no roads
linking it to other parts of the country. The bulk of the population is Seventh Day

Adventists.

This compilation is an out come of an agriculture survey into the Impacts of
Agriculture In-Relation to Biodiversity. This is the fourth phase of the Biodiversity
Survey in Oro Province and was carried out at Mt. Guguavo, a conservation project
area reserved by the Managalas Development Foundation. The survey was carried out

on the 22/04/08 to the 03/05.08.

2.0 Objective
The primary purpose of this survey is to assess and establish facts on the impacts of

agriculture in relation to biodiversity

3.0 Topography
Tetebedi is on a sloppy and mountainous ridge with very fast flowing rivers at the

base of the ridge. The terrain is rugged and coupled with a few damp and swampy
spots.

The vegetation is mostly grassland at the village and gardening area while further
inland the entire area is covered with moss and pristine montane forest. The forest
floor is covered with thick leaf litter and is mostly damp and wet.

The type of soil found at Tetebedi is silty loam around the village and loamy from the
gardens into the forest.

4.0 Climate
Generally there is rain all year round at Tetebedi. The rainy season starts from late

November through December to January, while the dry season begins around June

and ends at September.
There is an average of XXXXX milliliters of rainfall daily and an average of five (5)
sunshine hours daily. That is the sun is fully visible at around 9:00 am every morning

and is covered by clouds by 2:00 pm everyday.

5.0 Mode of farming

Shifting cultivation is the preferred mode of farming at Tetebedi. Villagers often
cultivate one area at a time. After harvesting of food crops, the villagers leave it to
fallow for a period of fifteen (15) years and move on to the next area suitable for
cultivation.

In the event of making a garden, the women weed shrubs and other small weeds. The
men then cut down trees and other plants left behind by the women. After that
everything is burnt and the men will commence planting immediately thereafter.

“Fourth Phase Biodiversity Survey — Tetebedi, Popondetta, Oro Province, PNG.”
 Practically the gardens are made within easy reach from the vicinity of the village.
‘This has enabled the villagers not to disturb the existing flore and fauna found in the
forest.
In one gardening event a large area of land is cleared and is sub-divided into three
blocks. The first block will have only sweet potato (Jpomea batatas) cultivated while
the second block or plot will have yams (Dioscorea exaltata). The third and final
block of land will cater for assorted crops such as bananas, sugarcanes, pitpits,
cucumbers, pumpkins and a variety of vegetables.
Observations from the survey revealed that the forest is undisturbed from intrusion of
any sort and is intact.
The gardens are often cultivated on siopes and towards the river banks. Because of
the slopes, terraces will have to be made. Currently there are no contour terraces made
and as a result top soil which is fertile are washed off by surface run-offs when it
rains thus leaving the whole garden prone to erosion. Some soil nutrients are also lost
through leeching.
According to viliggers interviewed it is customary not to build contour terraces or
ridges. From an agricultural perspective contour terraces are very important as they
hold back or prevent soil from being washed away by rain and cause soil ero:
Contour terraces will also slow down the flow rate of surface run-off thus minimize
or prevent scil ercsion as well.
In order to prevent soil erosion the villagers have been informed to build contour
ridges on siopes where they are doing gardening. They can build temporary contour
ridges by using dead logs or permanent contour ridges.
Permanent contour ridges can be made with the introduction of the vertiva grass
Wertiva zenzaineades), The vertiva grass has many uses some of which are;

(a) Contour ridges

(b) The feaves can be used to thatch houses

(©) The roots are used as local pesticides (in developed countries the roots are

used in the pharmaceutical and confectionary industries)
(d) Used as a traditional herb in some Asian countries etc

The practice of ouildi
-asi0n, Soi nut

contour ridges will assist immensely in the prevention of soil

ent leeching and most importantly landslides.

6.0 Hunting

The villagers hunt animals to supplement their diets by setting traps to catch wild
pigs, cuscus, tree kangaroos, wallabies, bandicoots, etc. Apart from traps bows and
arrows are also used in hunting. Adult animals are only used for food while smaller
animals and birds are reieased in to the wild. This practice wili aid in the natural
increase of these species of fauna as the animals wil! mature and reproduce thus
keeping their population steady. Over hunting of these animals both mature and
immature and the using of sophisticated weapons such as guns will gradually reduce
their number and eventually lead to extinction.

7.0 Cash crop potential

 Tetebedi has the potential to raise cash crops such as coffee, vanilla, citrus, cabbages,
broccoli, lettuces, tomatoes, potatoes etc. The climate is favorable to cultivate the

above crops.
The dry season is suitable for coffee, citrus and vanilla as it will induce flowering

which leads to fruit formation after successful pollination by insects. Other wise the
other crops can generally be grown all year round.

Bees can also be kept to. generate honey and other by-products of honey such as

8.0 Ecosystems health
‘According to practical observations at the biosurveyed area, the river systems, plant
species, animal species and the environment itself is ecologically intact. Animal
species as well as human interactions have shown that they have been living a
symbiotic relationship.

Though trees and other plant species are used for buildings, food and for medicinal
purposes their use is minimal and can not warrant a threat to ecological damages or

loss.

9.0 Vertebrate composition
There is a vast diversity of vertebrates available at the biosurveyed area including
various species of amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles. The biosurvey team was
able to take a specimen of undocumented specie of the bird of paradise and a rodent
(rat). The team will have to confirm with other literatures available. Otherwise the
specimens will be a new specie found in Papua New Guinea.

A lot of vertebrates would have been caught and documented but bad weather at the
project area hampered the team’s progress and at the same time forced the animals to
hibernate.

For all animals documented, the list can be seen on the appendix.

‘The composition of plants is such that there are two plants in Im? of land. This is not

have dried up, fallen and rotten away because of old age.

There are many hard wood trees such as the oak and kwila available as well as
medicinal plants such as salat. From assessments and observations these plants are

well and fairly distributed.

12.0 Impediments

The main factor impeding cash crop establishment is transportation. Because of the
remoteness and isolation of Tetebedi roads and other infrastructures will be labor
intensive and very expensive to develop. Tetebedi is only accessible via light
chartered aircraft as all regular commercial flights to the area have been cancelled.
These aircrafts are often expensive to charter and even though cash crops can be
raised, the owners can not be able to meet the charter price in order to transport their
crops to markets for sale.

Some crops especially vegetables are perishable and because of transport impediment
mest local farmers have ceased growing vegetables on a larger scale for markets
Instead they have resorted to growing a substantial amount of vegetables enough for
their household needs. Perishability is also a factor hindering vegetable production.

14.0 Recommendations
It can be recommended from facts and findings from the survey that

(a) shifting cultivation must be the only practiced form of gardening. No
mechanical methods of farming must be encouraged

(b) all gardens on slopes must have permanent contour ridges. This can be made
possible via the introduction of vertiva grass (Vertiva zenzaineodes)

(0) all endangered species of flora and fauna identified must be preserved by the
community for future use in the field of medicine or research by the future
generations

(4)all landowners must ensure that the forest and everything it inhabits is
conserved from exploitation by outsiders (companies, individuals,
organizations etc)

(@) all gardens are to be made at certain specific, allocated and recommended
areas only and not anywhere

(®) any new species of flora and fauna found must be recorded, named, properly
identified, documented and be patented

(g) in preserving the biosurvey area all landowners must ensure that there are no
burning of bushes as bush buming is now a common practice and has become
a habit by today’s generation

(h) any young animals caught in traps must be released back into the wild so that
they can mature and reproduce

(i) no guns or firearms of any sort must be encouraged to be used in hunting

G) family planning methods must be introduced to curtail the current trend

(k) building materials obtained from the forests must be replanted with new ones

() when cutting down trees from the forest try to minimize environmental
damage as much as possible

15.0 Conelusion
It can be concluded that the Tetebedi conservation area has an enormous agriculture
potential in terms of cash crop development as well as a conservation reserve. In the
event of population increase, the number of fallow years will decrease with the
increasing need for food and as such will force people to cultivate the forest to grow
food.

The only impeding factor is transportation because of contributing factors such as
remoteness, terrain, local weather, topography and most importantly the cost involved
in building infrastructural developments such as roads and bridges.

‘The status of the biosurvey area is better left untouched as any new development into
the area will eventually lead to exploitation of endangered flora and fauna.

Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, Guguavo Ridge, Tetebedi,
Kokoda District, Oro Province

MAMMALS AND HERPETO FAUNA SURVEY OF THE PROPOSED
MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA
PHASE IV REPORT

April- May 2008

Report prepared for Partners With Malenesians, Inc., Port Moresby, Papua New
Guinea

Paulus Kei
Division of Biological Sciences,
University of Papua New Guinea

 Keip@upng.cc.pg

Abstract

From November ~ December 2004, phase one of the mammals and herpeto fauna survey was
‘conducted near Itokama and the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. Around the same
period in 2005 saw the second phase and again in 2006, was the third phase, which was the
extension of continuous assessment of the Proposed Managaias Conservation Area. The 4”
(last) phase of the survey was conducted at Tetebedi, which is further to the SW of Itokama
and the highest altitude range. The prime purpose of these surveys were to gather baseline
information on the mammals and herpeto fauna of the Proposed Managalas Conservation
Area. They were also conducted to assess and determine maminal diversity within the
proposed conservation area,

‘The mammals survey was carried out in two selected sites, on Guguavo ridge in a mid
montane primary forest, at an altitude of ~ 1400m asl. Each site had the same number and
types of traps used but different area sizes. Survey site 1 was 100x20m, subdivided into
smaller plots of 10x10m and a total area of 2000m" was surveyed for smaller mammals.

‘Twenty (20) Eilict trap and ten (10) Tamahawk wire cage traps were used in a total of 150
trapping nights, (which means that, a tota! of 30 traps X 5 nights, equals 150). Two (2)
different species of rodents were caught from the 1* site. Unfortunately no bats were caught

caught.
