areal hassle with no road rk and no regular flights. Locals rely heavily on walking. it is
found that, the, vertebrate faune of the surveyed site and the vicinity around itis diverse and
intact.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the people of Tetebedi, through
Managales Development Fund in coilaboration witis Partners With Melanesians be
strengthened arid mechanisms put in place to declare that area as Conservation Area.
 1.0 Introduction

‘The Managalas Plateau: Proposed Conservation Area is situated in the southeastern part of
Southern Papuan ecoregion in the Hjivitari District ~ Oro Province. The Proposed
Conservation Area covers an area of approximately 300,000 hectares. The Proposed
Conservation area is located on the Managalas Plateau. In the last three, (3) the Managalas
Plateau Proposed Conservation Azea has been a centre of biodiversity surveys on flora and
fauna conducted by scientists from UPNG and the, Department of Environment and
Conservation. This survey (phase IV) was the last of a series of surveys, which was
conducted on Guguavo Ridge, three and half-hours walk South east of Tetebedi village,
Kokoda District, Oso Province. This survey covered approximately one (1) hectare of area on
the ridge top. The mid montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley Renges, at
approximately 1400m asl. The composition of mammalian and herpetofauna of Tetebedi area
is relatively unknown with very little or no scientific investigations been conducted in the

past.

Aims and Objectives

‘© ‘The main purpose of this survey was to carry out a preliminary assessment or the status
‘of mammalian and herpetofauna of Tetebedi area, in the Managalas Plateau Proposed
Conservation Area as proposed by Partners With Melanesian.

© Provide hands on site technical scientific advice and experience to participating students
(ribution to manpower and capacity building at

higher education institutions in the coun
© Identify immediate threats to wild animals and other potential threats,
© Provide technical advises to the project coordinators and a preliminary report to

jandowners of the Proposed Conservation Area.

‘This report basically highlights the results and observations of the phase IV mammais and
herpeto fauna survey conducted within a period of 12 days.
 2.0 Methods

‘The investigation was carried using normal field equipment and from a general observation of
the survey site over a period of ten (10) working days

‘The field equipment used were:
1, Aluminium Elliot traps used for smaller ground mammals.
2. Tomahawk wire traps for larger ground mammals

3. Mist nets for bats and birds

Surveys of Frogs, Repliies and arborea! animals such as the marsupizis were done by chance
observations and from local informants.

Species listing of mammats were the results of actual trapping and also from loca! informants
using reference book(s). A total of 30 traps (20 Elliot traps and 10 Tomahawk traps) were set
at two 2) different trapping plots at different intervals.

Site one (1) 2 study plot of 100x2 metres quadrat approximately 150 metres from the camp
site was established at 10 metres intervals from the central baseline for five (5) trapping
nights per plot. Mist nets for bats and birds were erected adjacent to the plot. Traps were
baited with ripe bananas and than rebated with half bumt coconut flesh.

Site two (2) was estabiished approximately 500 metres from the camp site and 350 metres
from the first site along the same mountain ridge where ali the survey was conducted. Again 2
total of 30 traps were used for the same period of time, five trapping nights per plot. Mist nets
were erected paralie! to the trapping plot. The same type of baits were used for the traps in the
second study plot. Traps were observed for five (5) nights, rebaiting was done after every
second night. Mist nets were opened at eround 4.30 om.

Net observations were done every hour and closed at 10.00pm for bats. During this survey ¢
total of nine (9) nets were placed at different locations and observed for ten (10) working
days

3.0 Results

3.1. Mammals

A total of twelve (12) specimen of rats were collected after 300 trapping nights, that is 30
traps x 5 nighis per ploi x 2 plots. The specimens were coitected over ten (10) working days.
Out of the 12 rats trapped, 4 of the same species were released after collecting necessary data
/measurements taken and 8 are kept as specimens. Of those 3 species of rats, two (2) are
identified, while the third is in question mark. Could be e new discovery meaning new species
from that area.

Al specimens collected will be kept at the zoological section of the Natural Science Resource
Centre, division of biological sciences UPNG as reference collections.

(Table 2)

Although not many species of mammals were captured, their presence were evident, such as
the long-beaked echidna, Zaglossus bruijni and short-beaked echidna Tachyglossus
acculeatus. Fresh burrows in the ground were seen within the plot.

‘Though spot lighting in the night did not reveal much nocturnal activities from larger
mammals, especially marsupials, but there were signs of their presence in the area with
remains of claw marks on tree teunks.

Rodents (rats) were the abundant species of the mammals, which resulted in twelve been
caught during the 10 days of survey. (Table 1)

Wild boas (pigs) were no way close to be seen in the vicinity of the survey site. There were
totally no signs of its presence though it was evident closer to the village.

Wild dogs (Canis familiaris) are said to be present, though no signs of their presence. One
was heard calling in the night.

Other bigger mammals or marsupials, such zs the tree kangaroos, cuscus and wallabies were
hardly detected but are believed to be present according to local informants.

Domestic animals were seen in the villege, where they are kept as pets or in the case of a dog,
it is used for hurting. No domestic pigs (Sus scrofa Jere raised in the village because of their
religious status. Main religicus denomination in the area is Seven Day Adventist (SDA).

3.2 Amphibians

's survey was concentrated on mammais, however in just over 7 days, a good number of
frog specimens were collected. 15 frog specimens were collected and of those, 5 different
genus were identified, while the number of species are yet to be identified and confirmed.

It was observed that the frog species composition of the area is very high, Night observations
were also conducted with good results. Unfortunately there was no recording equipment to
record the calls during the night.

‘Of the 15 frog specimens collected, 13 are of the Microhylidae, | Ranidae and the other of the
Hylidae family. (Tabie 3)

3.3. Reptilia

Most efforts were concentrated on the mammals other than reptiles which includes, the frogs,
snakes and tizards

Lizards of the Emoia and Sphenomorphus spp were seen and also a forest gecko,
Hermidactylus sp was sighted within the surveyed sites.

‘A python, (Ziasis amethystinus) of approximately 2.5 metres long was recorded and released.
A water snake was caught at Tetebedi village recorded and was also released.
5
 4.0 Discussions:

The survey was conducted over a period of 10 working days that is from the 22" of April
through to 2™ of May 2008.

4.1 Rats

‘The results for the rats were quite good with 12 rats sampled in the period of ten (10) days of
trapping. Out of the 12 samples, one specie is in doubi, that it could be a new specie and a
new record for the area. This particular specie was common, that seven were captured from

both trapping sites.

‘The other species are commonly found in such vegetation. Non of the species caught is
arborea! Ai! ground dwelling species. frapping in both sites showed good results despite
drawbacks due to climate conditions. Both trap types, Tomahawk and Elliot were doing well,
capable of producing good resuits.

‘Considering the population size compared to the availability of food resources, indications are
that, the population matches the availability of food resources minimising competition rates.
With only few species captured in a particular aree, signifies the abundarice of resources
available and less competition,

This in turn gives a balance in the species composition of the area, As a result species that
cover wider territories can now share the habitat with other species. This could be the likely

case wheve competition for resources is low. The whole area surveyed was of the same

Spot lighting and night observations for nocturnal mammals were unsuccessful during the
survey. Since most of the higher mammals are seasonal species, for zhat reason the timing
wes inappropriate.

ing of bats was quite unexpected, with only 3 bat samples were collected with two
different species. This could have resuited from again time factor. It was not the right season
for the bat species that feeds on fruits { fruitivores) or nectars from flowers. Only 2 species of
bats were sampied over the 1C days period. This is a shocking result especially for

almost anywhere. It was shocking to see the decline in bat species in such an undisturbed
forests.

Observations were carried out in the evenings to determine bat activities but there were still
no signs. Time could be the main factor for these poor results.

 4.3 Marsupialia

‘Although there were evidences of their presence, such as claw marks on tree stumps or
trunks, hardly one was detected. Other species of marsupials including tree kangaroos,
bandicoots, cuscus were said to be present in the area by the locals. However non of them
were seen during the investigation. Most marsupials are rather hard to capture as they inhabit
tall trees and forage at night.

4.4 Amphibia (Frogs)

Sampling of frogs was done from chance observations and by searching the forest, under
leave litter and on shrub leaves. Frog species in the area is diverse according to the
assessment on the rate of calis. Generally it can be stressed that there are many more frog
species of interest to be found in the area.

Oftthe 15 frog specimens collected, three (3) different families, with five (5) genus and
couple of species yet to be identified.

4.5 Reptilia (Lizards and Snakes)

Snakes

‘A2.5 metres long python, Liasis amethestinus was caught recorded and released. Also a
water snake caught recorded and released. Although not evident it was pointed out by locals
that there other pythons like the Boelens python, Morelia boeleni (protected by flora and
fauna Act of PNG). Not much snakes were seen during the survey.

Lizerds

Lizards were not frequently encountered during the survey. Skinks of the Emoie ené
Sphenomorhus species wereseen, recorde and released. A forest gecko, Hermidactylus was
also spotted on a tree.

5.0 Previous Draft Repor:

‘The previous Draft Report on High Conservation Vatue Forest (HCVP) on the Managalas
Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) can be accepted on the basis of the value of the
lixerature content. It contains generalised information on the socio-environmental features,

that is; population informetion, location of the Proposed conservation Area, Geology, Climate
and the Physical features of the Managalas area and the types of forest that can accommodate
flora arid fauna of conservation significance within PNG and the Oceania region.

As stated in the report, whilst this survey report is prepared for the MPCA , the list of
mammals provided is based on fiterature information. Also the data presented in this report
does not include ail the mammals of that particular area surveyed, that surely occurs in that
region. Example, the rodents, marsupials, bandicoots, cuscuses, tree kangeroos and the
possibie presence of the echidnas (anteaters)

Many other information on the components such as, the herpeio fauna, insecto fauna (Beetles,
and many other insects) that make up the biodiversity of an area is not included in this report
 6.0 Recent Survey

‘The recent Biodiversity survey that was conducted on Guguavo Ridge near Tetebedi village,
indicates that there is a high rate of species diversity. High sampling rate in in less time, is a
00d indication of the diversity of the area.

6.1 Status of Mammals

At present there is no proper assessment of status of animal species composition for this
particular area. With the species listing and the collection (Appendixs1&2) further
determinations will be required to verify the correct specimens. However, itis a highly
possible that some of the specimens collected might be new species or records.

7.0 General Considerations

Some of the factors that are evident from this survey that supports the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people in close working relation with Partners With Melanesians.

‘The forest type and the distribution of animal species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmentai conditions. The vertebrate composition of i

and provides an opportunity for further sciemific investigetion/studies of the fauna in the
area.

@ The occurrence of certain species of frogs and mammals that are different will need

proper studies.

@ Due to lack proper infrastructure, the people of Tetebedi and the surrounding villages rely
ineavily on foxest resources for their basic needs. Desinuction of foresis will have very bad
effect on the vertebrate composition of the area.

© Local people should be told clearly on which animal species are on the protected list so
that they should be hunted.

8.0 Recommendations
Given the uniqueness of the vertebrate composition of the proposed conservation area on
Guguavo Ridge, itis highly recommended that the area be conserved. It is also recommended
thai more scientific surveys be conducted and other iong term studies are carried out in the
area, Permanent study plots should be established and consistently monitor the status of
vertebrate species.

Honorable Puka Temu MP
Deputy Prime Minister
Minister for Mining, Lands and Physical Planning
National Parliament, WAIGANI

Dear Honorable Minister.

SUB: OBJECTION TO GOLDMINEX LTD MINING EXPLORATION LICENSE No. 1547
MANAGALAS PLATEAU, AFORE SUB DISTRICT, ORO PROVINCE

On behalf of the 18.000 people of Managalas plateau in Afore sub district of Oro province, | am
bringing the above matter to your urgent attention because your Department (Mines) and the
Mineral Resource Authority (MRA) have already given issued or renewed a mineral expioration
license to Goldminex Ltd to do exploration in Afore sub district of Oro Province.

The area identified as ELA 1547 falls directly within the boundary of proposed Managalas
Conservation Area which covers approximately 360.000 hectares of land covered with forests from
altitude as low as 40 m to 2880 m above sea level. This area is the home of the {8,000+ people from
150 clan groups who have been living there for generations.

The area that | have described above is on the eastern side of the Owen Stanley ranges, which is
home to some of this country’s unique flora and fauna including the CITES, [UCN Red List and
PNG Protected Species under the Fauna (Protection and Contra!) Act 1966 but not limited to the
following:

The Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly ....te world’s largest butterfly

New Guinea Singing Dogs ...close relatives of the Australian Dingoes

7 species of the Birds of Paradise .... 2 believed to be new not vet described by science
3 new Species of Frogs ....not yet described or new to science

The Whistling Snake

Long-beaked Echidna

Numerous parrots and Cockatoos

The Doria’s Tree Kangaroo

BAIAwWi wise

Our organization, Partners with Melanesians (PwM). a national conservation and community
development NGO has been working with the locai communities since 1983 on a major
conservation and community development programme (see our profile). The Summer Institute of
Linguistic (SIL) has also been doing social and linguistic translation projects over the plateau since
1972. We have come so close to lodging our application to the Environment Council and here we
have this Mining Exploration License issued to Goldminex Limited. an Australian company.

=== page 2 ===
In the past the PNG Forest Authority demarcated the area as a logging concession called the Gora -
ltokama FMA. When it came to the notice of the Managalas community, the entire population
mobilized and lodged notices to refuse PNGFA because they oversighted the local landowners
rights over their forests and customary land. This was rejected outright thus the area was not
declared for forestry and logging and was excluded from the Provincial and National Forest Plans,
as the people opposed all forms of destructive developments, but opted for conservation and
sustainable development projects.

Currently. according to the community leaders on Managalas Plateau, only two or three people are
behind this mining activity and these three have signed the agreement by themselves without the
proper consultation and other due diligence processes with ail the indigenous landowners and
community members.

Our Organization has been involved with the Managalas people working on conservation and
community development activities for more than 20 years. we are fully aware of the negative
consequences of mining on the environment and the sociai status of the people who depend on the
environment for their livelihoods. We do not have te go far to see for ourselves the impact mining
have on the local people as there are evidence of environmental destruction and socio-economic
impacts such as situations confronted by the people of middie and lower Fly in the Western
Province, the Hungabungar River in Central and the Guava River in Bougainville. despite the
millions of kina coming from PNGSDP and Ok Tedi Mine Limited, Tolukuma Mine and
Bougainville Copper Limited. respectively. We definitely know that they will never fix the
probiems that were created upstream leaving huge ugly open cut landscapes that will continue to
have acid rock drainage and splits into the river system for thousands of years. There are scientific
evidences that the freshwater and riverine ecosystems such as those in the Fly River system will be
dead for almost 300 years after mine closure hence in the next 20-50 generations, the ecosystents
will never be restored quickly to its natural state.

From our predictions of the future of mining in Managalas. the most logical locations for any
mining waste dumping’tailings will be along the Musa or Barige River systems and obviously the
neyative consequences will be huge. Therefore. with the concerns of the Managalas people whom
we have been working with for many years. we strongly feel it is our responsibility to inform you of
our objection to the issuance of the mining exploration license of Goldminex Ltd over the western
sector of the Managalas plateau (ELA 1547). If mining is to occur we know for certain that the
entire ecosystem of Managaias Plateau including the Upper. Lower and Middle Musa valley will be
destroyed consequently affecting the people, the flora and fauna and the marine ard aquatic
ecosystems forever.

Managalas plateau is strategically linked to the proposed Kokoda World Heritage Site. which was
recently signed off by the Governments of Australia and PNG. with the Prime Minister Hon. Kevin
Rudd and Grand Chief Sir Michael Somare. The Managalas plateau lies directly east of the Kokoda
trail and so, the same consideration should be given to this areas as well as it has a historical and
biological significance. In World War Il. the Manayalas plateau was the path the American soldiers
followed to assist the Australian soldiers in the battles which were fought in the Kokoda area with
the Japanese. Therefore. it has a historical significance. plus cultural and biological importance for
the country.

Mining tor gold, nickel and other minerals for revenue and monetary benefits for PNG is a short
term development whereby the vast wealth generated fiom their industrial operations and
development will be transferred overseas by the mining companies and developer leaving behind
pittance for PNG. The entire area bold vast natural treasures worth far more then the gold and
minerals beneath the soil. and its best the minerals are left untouched and the natural treasures

=== page 3 ===
including the tropical rain forests on the surface are managed sustainably. In future when proper
management techniques are developed. the minerals can be allowed to be mined w hereby no andor
minimum environmental destruction and negative impacts from the mine occur that would affect
the natural environment including the local people.

Therefore. in view of all said above. we strongly object to the issuance of the Mineral Expleration
License Np. 1547 to Gokiminex Ltd over the land area known as ELA 1547 w Afore Sub-District

of Ore Province. Papua New Guinea.

The clan leaders of the 150 clans through their District Wide Combine Forum held at Ugunumo
village, from the 21-26 June 2008. have also experience dissatisfaction and anger at the manner this
ELA was awarded to Goldmine Ltd, and it will be interesting to see their letter that is on its way
trom the Managalas plateau down to Port Moresby.

Therefore, if you could kindly allow some of your busy time with us so that We can discuss this
issue with you. | would like to make an appointment for three of my staf¥ and | to meet vith you
and vour Departmental Secretary responsible for Mining anytime between the 22 - 26" of July

2008.

Thank you and jook forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,

 RFL Analysis of the efficient delivery, effectiveness and impact of RFN
funded literacy activities in Managalas Plateau.

Executive Summary:
The literacy participatory evaluation for rainforest literacy radio programs was conducted

by PWM under the Rainforest Norway funding.

‘The participatory evaluation was conducted in Managalas Plateau, from 04" to 09th
October 2008 to discuss the findings of the Rainforest literacy assessment and needs in
the base communities that are engaged in the literacy activities and foresee the Capacity
Building Training Conduct for CSO literacy facilitators, supervisors and managers.

Partners with Melanesians initially initiated these activities, with the funding support
form Rainforest Norway. In response to the issues of lack of government services
delivery and inequity for women and young girls, Civil Society Organizations (CSO)
have form to influence government policy and bring economic, education and health
services. Fundamental aspect was woman and underserved population has the high
illiteracy rate, which they could not compete with the changing social and economic
development.

In order to compete with the changing development people have to be educated,
rainforest literacy radio program has resulted in greater cooperation between women and
men at all levels, husbands and wives going together with their family and clan members.
The facilitators and adult learners who have gained increased confidence, which in turn
have resulted in increased leadership responsibility at the community level. The project
was aimed at developing small-scale business around conservation in Managalas Plateau
that in-still their capacity into more sustainable approach with the support of the
Managalas Development Foundation.

1. Rainforest literacy radio program in the Managalas Plateau

‘© Awareness raising within 10 zones in the conservation areas

© Hosting adult education forums between zones to enable sharing of
iessons learned and specialist skills through radio progra

© Facilitating the distribution of information on RFL activities and best
practices.
Clan and family group discussion.
Capacity Building training for facilitators and supervisors.

‘There are thus three main types of literacy learning programs in existence in the plateau.

- Critical literacy (reading and writing life)

- Technicist literacy (literacy and writing of print text without meaning)

- Functional literacy (listening to rainforest radio program ~ need for income

generation)

On the surface, all of these types of literacy learning programs claim help people to
become useful members of society, to help people to understand changes in their lives
and to participate in those changes. However through seven years of rainforest literacy in
the Managalas plateau, it has become clear that Technicist literacy is not real priority for
the people in the society has taken tremendous change in lifestyle. Critical literacy and
functional literacy are seen as appropriate tools to get back what they have lost and to
maintain what is with them and to build back their confidence in themselves.

In the process of radio series and understanding event that was affecting their daily lives,
people learn to associate and appreciate the nature of the program, making that living text
part of their lives. Critical literacy (in this sense) was already an integral part of peoples’
lives. Critical literacy literally means finding reasons for events and problems that are
occurring in ones life and ones community (critical reading), and then finding ways to
cope with these events and developing solutions to these problems on the basis of an
informed community-based decision-making process (which may be described as critical
writing).

Incentive to community, in contrast, was not critical literacy. Under such influence,
People began to accept cargo unquestioningly. Community participation deteriorate and
in the process repudiating their traditions culture.

text:
District Wide Combine Forum
Naukonane Village, Itokama
11" November 2008

Report:
The team of four including the PWM Program Manager, Communications Officer, an
Officer on attachment with PWM and a crew from the Nala Times Media left Port Moresby
for Itokama on Saturday 08" November 2008. The purpose of the advance party was to
ensure logistics and preparations for the combine forum are in order before the actual
forum began on Monday 10® November.

Upon arrival at Itokama, the team were told that the venue for the forum was moved
from Itokama to Naukonane because the community would not allow disturbances to the
grade eight students who were sitting for their examinations week 10” - 14" November.

Taking into account the time the plane will remain on the ground (45min) awaiting the
Minister for DEC and his delegation, the team was able to convince the community to
move back the venue for the launching of the application for the conservation area back
to Itokama. The Head teacher agreed and allowed deferral of exams until after the plane
takes off from Itokama, That was the alternative arrangement.

Meanwhile, communities in zone one (Itokama, Kwai, Naukonane and Mandokoro) were
exited and geared up to receive the Minister for Environment and Conservation Hon
Benny Allen at the official opening of the District Wide Forum and the launching of the
application for the Conservation Area Status.

‘On Monday 10 November, the feeling of excitement to receive the delegation from Port
Moresby was overwhelming. Singsing groups began dancing as early as 6:00 am in the
morning. A pig was slaughtered and food was roasted in the earth oven purposely for
the delegation.

The arrival time for the place to Itokama was schedule for 9:30 am but the plane was
delayed for about 3 hours and 15 minutes. If finally touched down at Itokama at 1:15
pm to an awaiting crowd of about 300 people singing and dancing excitedly to receive
the delegation:

Much to their dismay, the Minister for Environment and Conservation, Hon Benny Allan
was not on the plane. Nor was there a representative from the DEC Office or his Ministry
except for Mr Paulus Kulmoi, Principle Ecologist with DEC who was invited separately to
present the report of the Biodiversity Survey.

It was also disappointing for us because many of the stakeholders we invited were never
able to make it although they confirm their attendance. Only a handful was able to
attend the gathering at Itokama. This include; PWM Vice Chairman and Secretary
General, Uniting Churches of PNG Rev. Siulangi Kavora; PWM Board Member, Serah
Tsiamalili; MDI Executive Director, Mary Carlua; and George Baure, chairman Forest,
Mines and Lands, Provincial Executive Council, Oro Provincial Government.

Anyway, the community welcomed the small delegation to the grandstand and PWM Vice
Chairman and Secretary General, Uniting Churches of PNG Rev. Siulangi Kavora officially
declare the forum open. A community representative, Brian Kasira from Noukanane
 spoke on-behalf of the community and presented a petition to Mr George Baure,
chairman Forest, Mines and Lands, Provincial Executive Council, Oro Provincial
Government. The petition (a copy is attached to this report) basically called for the PEC
to meet and endorse the application for the Conservation Area Status so the completed
application will be presented to the Minister for DEC early next year. A traditional head
dress was presented to Mr Kulmoi to bring to the Minister for DEC. Pieces of pork meat
(lek pik) were presented to Rev. Siulangi Kavora and George Baure.

Mr Baure, upon receiving the petition, promised to push for the application for the CA to
be endorsed by the PEC at the next sitting.

The delegation left Itokama at 2:15 pm and forum participants were shown to their
sleeping quarters to rest and wait for the forum to begin. However, it was difficult
getting participants together again as they were spread throughout the four villagers so
the forum committee decided to call if off for the day and announced that the forum wi
begin the next day.

The forum committee (MDF/PWM) met in the afternoon and made final preparations for
the forum. There were six topics;

MDF and PWM Operations on the Plateau

MocP

Reconciliation rights

Kinship rights

Biodiversity Survey

Traditional Learning Centre

oy aune

Due to time factor, the committee decided that the forum will only deliberate on two
important topics, MDF/PWM Operations on the Plateau and MOCP. The others
(Reconciliation rights, kinship rights, traditional learning centre) were left to the clan
groups to discuss and come up with action plans as these topics were within their
control to effect changes. While MDF/PWM Operations on the Plateau and MOCP were
topics that concern PWM and MOF and needed to be discussed at the forum. The
committee asked Mr Kulmoi to make a presentation of the Biodiversity Surveys at the
forum as it was not really a topic for discussions as such.

That was the flow of the forum that proceeded the following day, 11° November. The
minutes basically explained who said what and what needs to be done. The forum was
divided into two parts, The issues were discussed, and prioritized; and options were
identified to work on the issue to bring about positive results.

Finally, the forum had a record turnout of 177 participants who represented zones 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, & 10. Zone 9 could not attend because the river flooded and they could
not cross over. A new inclusion was also present at the forum and attended as
observers. This was the Wawanga community identified as zone 11.

Assessment and Evaluation from the PWM team:

A lot of negative sentiments were said about PWM even from current and former PWM
Board Members and prominent Managalas leaders. That generally explained that the
‘communities no tonger appreciate what PWM is doing despite PWM working in the area
for over two decades and having made impacts in small ways that contributed to the
sustenance of the people's livelihood over time.

Capacity Building.
PWM is a national NGO and does not necessarily have to have board members
from the project areas as there is always a risk of project area representatives on
the board to miss-represent the organization because of conflict of interest. The
Board deals with highly confidential information that can either make or break
the organization. These local representatives should be the ones taking leading
roles in correctly informing the community about PWM, her mission, vision, aims,
goals, activities etc. but the opposite was happening with the Managalas
Conservation Area Project.

Aplanning meeting to be convened between PWM and MDF to deliberate on the

do with PWM/MDF administrative and program matters. Programs must be
designed to address some of their points and outcome must be presented to
them at the next forum together with points raised at the June forum.

 Introduction

The following document is in two parts. The first is the proceedings of a community development
strategy workshop held at Toma village from the 30" of November to the 4 of December 2009 and
the second part is the strategy for the Berefo Development Association as an output of the
workshop and an action plan to mobilise the Community Development Strategy.

‘The workshop was facilitated by Volunteers from OCEAN with the support from a staff member of
CELCOR with funding support from GGF.

Acknowledgements

We wish to acknowledge the financial support for this project from the Global Green Grants Fund
facilitated by Damien Ase through CELCOR, FoE PNG. Edrick Ninimiro for the submission to GGF,
Marjorie Warisaiho, for taking time out in the field to be part of the facilitating team and Bradley
Dabadaba from MDF for field support and Raymond Hekoroka and Philemon Balasi for local logistics
arrangements.

Back Ground

Berefo Community Development Association (BCDA) draws its membership from 8 villages in the
Afore LLG of the Ijivitari District in the Northern Province of PNG. It is a community based
organization focused on community development originally set up and registered by Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) in 1994 to work with to meet PwM’s Conservation project in the Managalas
Plateau.

Asa part of PWM's local partner MDF which is divided into 10 zones, BCDA is in zone 9 which also is
Census ward 15 in the Afore LLG.

It has an approximate population of 2,050 with just over 400 registered adults in the 2007 National
electoral roll. The bulk of the population are youth between the ages over 12 to 18 any only about
‘5% of them have ever been to a formal school. From physical observation social indicators are very
low. Based on reflection made by participants the mortality rate is very high more especially from
curable diseases and child birth. The strain on the population for just reaching basic services is very
high given the difficulty of the geography especially the Bareji river.

Over the years the people had felt neglected by the Government and their local partner MDF. They
turned to PWM with the hope that they would gain some social and economic benefits that the
government had failed to deliver however these dreams never materialised and the Berefo people
felt that they were an insignificant group of people for whom it was not in any body's be:
{fo risk their lives for. One can not miss the geographically difficult location that these very
humble people have decided to call home as we found out trying to get there.

Raymond Hekoroka and Philemon Balasi, however never gave up the hope that some day some
people crazy enough to risk their lives will come along and with them they will bring hope for a
better future for themselves and their future generation and their persistence finally paid off when
GGF came to their aid through CELCOR to pay costs for a community development strategic plan.
 Geography & Locality

In the hinterlands of the Musa river plains meeting the foothilis of the Owen Stanley range the very
simple, semi- primitive Berefo people go about their daily business of hunting and gardening. It is
made up of 8 villages with Toma, Gewoia and Biriri being the most populated villages. Set ina very
difficult geographic area cut of by fast flowing rivers and ravines these villages are amongst the least
advanced in today’s standards lacking government services as well as other service providers
including NGOs.

1. The Berefo Community Development Strategy. The strategy in its design is
focused on community development objectives which can be achieved through broad based
community participation. It had been identified in the planning workshop that outside
support in terms of skilled manpower lacked in their area, this was largely influenced by the
geography. Therefore the priority area is manpower capacity building and local initiatives
for small scale income generating options.

2. Action Plan. An action plan has also been developed as a catalyst to mobilise the
implementation of the Community Development Strategy. It is anticipated that the action
plan will form the core annual operational budget that can be implemented utilizing the
existing administrative structure. (refer to organizational structure, appendix 2)

The workshop initially began with general group discussions. Participants were given the
opportunity to introduce themselves and share with the group what their expectations were.

Expectations;

Having being isolated for so long from outside assistance, the general expectations, were that from
the workshop, participants wanted to clearly identify issues in which the Berefo communities were
facing and the best solutions to overcome these issues and to see change occurring in their
community that would improve their livelihoods.

Community Development;

Within the big group participants discussed in their opinion the definition of community and
development. From the discussion, the participants shared the view of community being defined as
either individuals or 2 group of people living in one place and sharing a common interest.

Their definition of development was planning and seeing changes occurring in the environment
around them. They also viewed development in the form of infrastructure such as aid posts and
schools, roads and bridges that wili enable them to have a better standard of living compared to the
current situations.

Partners With Melanesians

P.O. Box 1910, Port Moresby 121

National Capital District

Papua New Guinea

Email info@pwmpng.org pg or kmondiai@pwmpng.ore.pe

(Opposite PH Engineering Workshop)

Date: 2" March 2009

Ref: EIS-MPAgroforestry- 01/09
The Director of Environment
Department of Environment and Conservation
P.O. Box 6601
Boroko
National Capital District

Dear Director,

s FOR THE
MUSA PONGANI (BAREJI) AGRO FORESTRY PROJECT, SAFIA DISTRICT, ORO
PROVINCE

With reference to the above subject, which was sighted in the National Newspaper dated February
11" 2009; this is a letter of objection on certain issues relating to the Musa- Pongani Agro forestry
project Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) as prepared and presented by the Musa Century Lid
for the proposed Musa Pongani Agro forestry Project in Safia sub district in Oro province to the
Department of Environment and Conservation (DEC).

There are various points of objection to this submission that Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PwM)
have identified and would like to bring to your attention.

But briefly, PwM is a national conservation and community development organisation incorporated
under the Association Incorporated Act (1974) and has been operating in the Oro province in the
Musa, Pongani and Managalas plateau since 1985 and more recently with field projects in Enga
Province and Eastern Highlands Province.

PwM has been working with the people of Managalas (Afore sub district) and Musa (Safia sub
district) Pongani (Oro Bay LLG) areas with other NGO partners since 1985. The Managalas
Proposed Conservation area (MPCA) is our principal area of operation with the people and we are
getting near to the point where we intend to present to the Minister for Environment and
Conservation our application to have the area placed under the Conservation Area for the purposes
of flora and fauna conservation to have it declared as a Conservation Area after the normal

sereening process.

Now we find the Musa Pongani Agroforestry project some what an interference onto our proposed
area for conservation with the land boundaries and also the lack of proper consultation process,
where the legitimate landowners are not consulted and also the involvement of the local people on
the ground with DLPP Officer and Afore LLG Officer and Land Officer from OPG to do physical
land boundary survey of to be confirmed that the ownership of the land proposed for the project is
clear. This process is not done.

 However from the maps as presented in the EIS, it is clearly an indication that, there was no proper
consultation done on the ground with the very people from Zones 8, 9, 2, | and 4 from within the
Managalas plateau that consented to having their land area under Conservation Area.

The Managalas people who have signed up to be part of the Conservation area also have land on the
southern side of the Barije river that was used as the geographical boundary of the Agroforestry
project. They have not been consulted and their consent was not obtained through the proper
process without any field verification by the DepartmenvDivision of Lands and Physical Planning,
however their land has been included in the Agroforestry project and that is not right and proper.

PWM objects to the EIS and the Project on the following grounds:

1. Map of the area secured through the Department of Lands and Physical Planning (DLPP)
is lacking proper Managalas Landowners Consent and Consultation.

The first Objection is against the map projection of the Musa-Pongani Agro-forestry project
Area in Safia District Oro Province. The Resource Area for this Agro forestry project as stated
in the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), covers about 230,000 hectares of forest of which
over 215 000 have been identified as a net production forest while 161,000 hectares is
earmarked to be converted into integrated agricultural project over a period of over 20 years.
“The Reference Map No......on the submission for this Agro forestry project is not accurate as the
project area had been identified/marked out by the two rivers, the Bareji and Musa Rivers. The
head waters of Bareji starts from Awala (Zone 4) and flows North to Toma (Zone 9) and then
flows east through Marasi and Joivi (Zone 8) down to Gora (below Gewoia (Zone 8) and then
flows North out to sea emptying in the Dyke Auckland bay. The head waters of Musa also start
from Awala and further up around Tetebedi (Zone 4 and 11) and flows in a general direction of
South-east and North-Fast along the Musa valley and emptying out at sea, some kilometre cast
of the Barije. As shown this Map doesn’t have a proper key and scale (Refer to Appendix D
Project Area Map on the EIS Submission). As seen from the Map, the Boundaries overlap into
the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area, with which the communities in the area have
already signed up for Conservation Area. Also the process of Boundary identification is not
properly followed as there is no field verification on the ground and the people from the
following villages) Toma, Biriri, Tahama, Naukanane, Umwate, Aiari, Suari, Awala, Joivi,
Marasi, Bua, Orara) were not consulted nor were involved to do the field verification,

We have looked at the area as secured from the DLPP; it is obvious that, this plan was done in
the office based in Port Moresby by the Company, as the land boundary is clearly geographical
and following the Musa and Barije rivers. The people in the Upper Musa area and in the Central
Managalas whose land also lies East and South West of the Barije river have not been consulted
by the proponents of the Agroforestry Project and as such the land boundary is not proper.

Secondly the DLPP Officer who examined the proposed map have not done any field and
ground truthing to determine if the people who own the land have consented to being part of the
‘Agroforestry Project or have there any development ot conservation plans, it was done is a
hurry and so it is clearly and job done in a rush.

So in all, we object to the map that presented by the proponent which goes onto land that is out
of the Musa District and under the contro! of the Afore LLG.
 Thirdly, the issues of free prior informed consent was not done here and people who have
consented to conservation, and their land has been dragged into the proposed agro forestry
project as so ,we are not clearly sure if the DLPP have done their job properly.

2. No proper Documentations placed for Public viewing

a.

On this not, let us as members of the public state here very clearly that, on the 11/Feb
/09, when the advert was placed in the National Newspaper, the advertisement was very
small and many people who have land or have on going commitments with the Musa
Pongani area have not seen the advertisement has it was very small and did not get
people's attention.

Making the advert very small was deliberate to not get the attention of the general
public, we feel that both DEC and the Company have failed on their part to properly
ensure that standards are followed like the size of the advert, fonts size and font
characters etc. A case for comparison, is the advert placed in the Post Courier for a
similar EIS statement for Public viewing and there was another advertisement in the
Post Courier dated 27" February 2009...by InterOIL for the ELK/Antelope Gasfield
Project for the under the Environmental Act 2000 Sect 55 (2). For this advertisement,
the size is a full page and the fonts and character are very clear and it can clearly draw
the attention of any reader to it. This was not the case for the Musa Pongani
advertisement (attached for your clear reference) so there should be a standard
advertisement size.

In Popondetta, on the 25-26" February, we visited the Office of the Acting
‘Administrator (Mr. Thompson Manuda) and his staff and asked to have a look at the
EIS; and he had no idea about this document and said that we should provide a copy of
the advert. Which we provided and upon that he then instructed in officers to find out
who in the Provincial Administration and the copy.

‘As time was running out, and we did not have a copy to view we departed the next day
by plane and flew into Port Moresby and went to the DEC to look for the EIS.

However when we arrived at the DEC 5" Floor as stated in the notice, the office was
closed due to some renovation work and so, we enquired at the 6" Floor. We were then
directed down to the 3rd floor to see the Officer responsible where we have looked at the
documents. With no time, we requested if we can have a copy, but it was not allowed,
we asked if we can take the copy out and make photo copies, we were again denied that
request.

So we are making this submission based on the brief viewing process and we are not
going into any detail comments,

3. Afore LLG, not consulted

‘The Afore LLG and the Sub District administration have not been consulted on the proposed
iand boundary coming into the Afore LLG area, The people of Naukanane and Umwate,
(zone), Toma- Biriri, Gewoia, Orara (Zone 9) and Aiari Suari (Zone 4), Ondoro Joivi, Marasi,
Bua (Zone 8) are villages within the Afore Sub District and LLG, but have land that extends
towards the Barije river and also over the mountain into the Musa Valley. Based on the plan
submitted and enclosed into the EIS, we can clearly see that, our people have not been consulted

3
af
 and are not part of or party to this project. Our land has been included into the project without
our authorization or approval and we see this as a clear incidence of malpractice and we
unanimously object to this EIS and also to plan for the project until such time there is a clear
consultation on the ground. Note, before the submission of the Letter, we were in radio
communication with the Afore LLG President and Council Manager and they have informed us
that, they are aware of the project in Musa but the yare not aware of any land boundary work
and since it is a Musa LLG project, they have not been involved, but on our advise that the land
boundary has come into Afore LLG jurisdiction, the are worried that consultation was not
properly done. So may they will at a later date write in and inform of their concerns, but as time
is ticking away, at least we make your informed of their concerns, as the legitimate LLG for the
Managalas plateau and what they have informed us by HF radio.

Major Conservation Site - Tree Kangaroo Mountain
‘The site around Toma, Biriri and Orara are areas where PwM and MDF in our findings from the
Biological Survey have identified ad live population of Tree Kangaroos including the
Dendrologous Scotia, Dendrologous Dorianus Matsie have identified living on that mountain
and with the land boundary including g that area, we are very worried that all our plans and
work since 2003 for conducting the biosurveys will be a waste and more importantly is the fact
that, the Landowners were not consulted at ail in this process of the Agroforestry project.

Environmental Issues and Concerns

Although we have not had the time to look at the entire EIS documents, our main concer here
is that, this project is a political and project is done is a rush and we are very concems that, it
will be a total mess when it is implemented as the forest will be totally cleared and there has not
been a thorough assessment. Any plans for the flora and fauna will be haphazard done and
temporarily in nature just to secure approvals. and we know Asians generally have no concen
about the floras and fauna and the animals, insects and birds so forth, and more important our
culture. It still all be destroyed in the name of development, revenue and income to support the
national budget and the companies profits for its shareholders overseas and also for the people
to have access to development like roads, schools, hospitals and many our infrastructure and
goods. But at the end of the day, people of Musa and Pongani have rushed into this project
pushed by the political masters and bureaucrats in Port Moresby. Whatever the outcomes will
be at the mercy of the local people and the environment? As for the Managalas plateau, in the
future, we will be providing the source of strength and culture and many people from the Musa
and Pongani will become environmental refugees seeking refuge on the Managalas plateau.
‘That is our predictions and the Managalas people still maintain that the land boundary that
extends to the Bareji river be amended and pushed back to the Safia LLG land jurisdiction.

Results of Feasibility study (Make Reference to 3.4 Results of Feasibility Investigations
(pages 9,10,11)

We need to sce the forest survey plans and the striplines with coordinates and location- we are
very familiar with the Musa- Pongani valley area and looking at the Data in Table 3.2 on page

10-11, we have doubts as to the correctness and validity of the data used- due to the following:

i) Anisoptera thurifera (Mersawa) which has a standard density of 2.956 m’/ ha with a
percentage composition of 19.15 % is not correct based our professional view and
knowledge of the area.

) —— Mersawa composition with 19.15% is true for forest areas up from Kumusi to Morobe
Province, Within the Musa Pongani Project area, it is dominated by Pometia pinnata
(Taun) and Instia bijuga (Kwila), so obviously the data is taken from elsewhere around
Morobe and Oro border areas and used.

4

 Based on this we believe there was no proper forest inventory survey done and the Table
3.2 (is taken from another survey report and used here.

™ ‘The Musa- Pongani area simply has a high Instia bijuga (Kwila) and Pometia pinata
(Taun) Planchonella warbungii (Plancho) and so the data presented is in accurate and
misleading

7, Afore LLG and Oro PEC Endorsement of Managalas Conservation Area.

In the EIS, the Proponent has stated in Appendix :”H” that the Project is endorsed by the Oro
PEC by way of decision 20/2007 of Meeting 5/2007 held on the 7” of May 2007 (Ref Policy
Submission No. 19/2007)

From that decision, it is unclear as to the specific area. However the map used now in this EIS is
about an area much bigger then what was mentioned in the PEC decision.

Besides that, the Managalas Conservation Area also has Afore LLG Approval and Oro PEC
‘Approval and Endorsement and so very clearly the PEC decision over the area are in conflicting
and it seems that the Project proponent has used the ambiguity in the submission to extend the
area proposed for the project to encroach into areas in another LLG's jurisdiction (i.e. the Afore
LLG area.

Also the Oro PEC decision supporting the Managalas conservation area clearly stated and gave
their endorsement based on the maps for the area, and so it seems the Company has gone about
without properly consulting Landowners and also pushed for the DLPP to approve the Maps
without due care on the sensitive issues of Landownership and community consultation

The Afore LLG also endorsed the Submission made by PwM and MDF for the proposed
Conservation Area, in which it was used to get the endorsement of the Oro PEC, so very clearly
there are some manipulation of the geographical boundaries of the Project area in the Managalas
plateau and Afore LLG sub district and Council land areas.

‘Attached as Annex (2) is the Oro PEC endorsement of the PWM/MDF submission for the
Managalas Conservation Area.

Conclusions
Therefore in conclusion, we have the following to say:

1. The Project Area's geographical land boundary over laps with the proposed Conservation
Area Boundary of Managalas plateau where communities living in the following villages of
Toma, Biriri, Gewoia (Zone 9), Tahama, Kokoro (Zone 2), Naukanane, Umwate,
Mandokoro (Zone 1), Aiari, Suari (Zone 4) Joivi, Marasi, Bua, Ondoro (Zone 8) who have
agreed, signed and consented to the proposed Managalas Conservation Area and whose
customary land has been included in the Musa ~ Pongani Agroforestry Project.

2. This project has been included in the Afore Sub district, which is a different LLG altogether
from the Safia and we are sure the Afore LLG Council President and Council Members
from the villages named above are not aware of the project. This clearly signals of foul play
and lack of consultation and should be dismissed and not entertained as the Afore LLG’s
legal land boundary has been breached with no consultation

5
 3. This project was developed by a handful of people living in Port Moresby and Popondetta
who have motives of self interest and self wealth creation and forgetting the majority of the
people living in the Musa Valley. our CBO Partner from Musa Urua Yaura Association Inc.
has also expressed concern that this project is being pushed by a handful of people is ulterior
motives which is not in the best interest of the majority of the Musa people.

4. The majority of the people in the Musa Valley in fact are have not been consulted on this
project, it is a political project cooked up by Malaysia middle or agents based in PNG who
have a reputation of moving around the PNG country side and conning and bribing
Landowners and Government officials and using abusive processes to get Government
approval for natural resources development project is dubious ways and means just to sell
off at a higher bid to someone who will come is to do a quick job to recoup their monies.

5, We have very clear examples of such project already and we should not be blinded, for
example the Aitape Damasara Oil Palm project, the current Ili Wawas Oil Palm Project in
Pomio, ENBP, The now stopped, Kuinga Aiambak Road line Project.

6. Although, there was no time to fully view the EIS document, our main concerns are that,
this project will destroy the environment of the Musa Valley with its rich flora and fauna
through logging and then followed by mono-culture tree plantations. This is a clear sign that
the local people who have for generations depended on the natural resources from the
environment to sustain their lives will become flushed cash and also labour job sand they
will gradually over time spectator and employees on the own land.

On behalf of the people of Managalas Plateau in their fight to safeguard their natural Resources,
Partners with Melanesians would like to put forward this letter of Objection for the EIS submitted
by the Musa Century Limited for your consideration and action.

Yours Sincerely

wy

 Introduction:

Literacy is the base human need, which enable one to make informed decisions and to
control ones own affairs so as to achieve a better living standard with regard to economic,
social and other aspects, empowerment underserved population.

‘The Rainforest Literacy Program is meeting the development learning needs of largely
oral, marginally literate village populations in Papua New Guinea who are struggling to
conserve their forest resource base and meet food supply and income generation needs at
the same time, Deals between the national government and logging companies that
bypass the custodial relationships between indigenous peopie and their rainforests are
perhaps the biggest single threat to the expansive rainforest of Papua New Guinea. Local
populations need to understand issues and options related to maintaining their portion of
Papua New Guinea’s rainforests in order to be effective in doing their part. Partner With
Melanesians (PWM) is adopting a largely oral, multi-channel approach to helping women
groups, literacy groups and locai clan groups learn to monitor and though fully contain
the diminishing percentage of forested land in one of the world’s largest remaining
contiguous expanses of rainforest.

Objective:
© To act as an information centre for Provincial, District and community
base resources sharing and to cater to the needs of bibliographical
information of individuals, groups and institutions working in the field of
iteracy, adult and continuing education.

INTRODUCTION
The Managalas Reforestation Project is an activity (Activity 1.1.4) under the PWM and MDF

plateau have already been converted into grassland due to continuous gardening and burning of the
bushes. This had come about as a result of population increase. This report is an update on the
progress of the reforestation project on the plateau. Three clan groups are participating in this
project, in which two are now in the process of setting up their nursery shed and the other clan is
transplanting its seedlings. Nursery and transplanting equipments have been purchased and
distributed to assist the three clan groups with the reforestation work.

snippet: Partners With Melanesians 2 \ Nusienat Cupital District ‘Nail the Dance” Date: 7/9/2010 Report No: 02-2010 PROGRAM: Consensus Bui jing + Rainforest Literature ACTIVITY: Mock Combine Forum This report details my trip to the Managalas Plateau on the Ast of September 2010 to attend a mock combine forum
text:
Partners With Melanesians

2
\ Nusienat Cupital District

‘Nail the Dance”

Date: 7/9/2010
Report No: 02-2010

PROGRAM: Consensus Bui

jing + Rainforest Literature

ACTIVITY: Mock Combine Forum

This report details my trip to the Managalas Plateau on the Ast of September 2010 to attend a mock
combine forum staged in Noomba (Zone 6). | was accompanied by Kenn Mondiai (Executive Director),
Rufus Mahuru (Program Manager), Patrick Vuet (Conservation Support Officer) and Edrick Ninimiro. We
returned a week later on the 6th of September 2010.

The purpose of this trip was to witness and participate in the staging of a mock combine forum.

Schedule to precede the actual combine forum in early November, the purpose of this activity was
specifically used as a revisionary exercise to re-familiarise participants with the key processes and
procedures of the combine forum and to remind them on the guiding principles that govern the Combine
Forum process.

In addition, this trip was used to get updates on the status and progress of the Rainforest Literature
component and to get a rough idea as to the activities currently underway on the plateau.

From Girua Airport we left for Afore soon after only to find ourselves stuck at Pongani River due to
flooding. We opted to spend the night at a transit accommodation provided by the kind Pr Richmond of
Renewal Ministries at the Disaster Care Centre settlement.

Early next day we managed to make it across the Pongani and travelled up to Afore where the mechanic
and his supplies were dropped off. We then continued to Sila Junction, from whence we made it by foot all
the way to Noomba village by midday.

From there we dove right into the thick of things.

Using the facilities of the Ese Bible Institute, we went through the introduction and then began with the
main agenda — the mock combine forum.

 ‘The agenda

The list of agenda was as follows:

Opening Prayer ~ hosting zone

'* Welcome Speech — hosting zone

* Introductions

© The Forum Process
© Guiding principles
© Key procedures of the process
© Exercise - Climate Change

© Wrap Up

Topics

Once we were underway with the main agenda, the topics were listed as follows:
Guiding Principles:

1. Who should be invited to the forum

2. Setting the agenda

3. Seating arrangements

4, Roles of the facilitators, chairpersons, recorders and assistant co-ordinators of the forum

Key Processes

Managing patterns of Language
Posting participants’ contributions
Selection procedure

Setting action plans

Identifying next steps

Pen ae

The proceedings carried on into the first half of the next day as we could not continue into the night as
earlier planned. This was due to the fact that almost everyone one of us who travelled there was exhausted
from lack of proper rest.

After the first day, | sat down with Brian Kasira (MDF Consensus Building Coordinator) who briefed me on
progress of work, especially with regard to the zone group discussions. Discussed also were plans for the
actual combine forum in November 2010.

Education Awareness

After closing up the final day we broke for lunch and returned for a short awareness presentation where
Kenn Mondiai showed the participants a short video on climate change and reforestation.

| followed soon after with an awareness presentation on climate change, breaking down the basic facts into
laymen terms, starting with a brief description of the carbon cycle, going on into global warming and
eventually touched on climate change; as a direct negative effect of man’s impact on the natural
environment and the ecosystem.

Rainforest Literature Updates

also sat down with Bradley Dabadaba (RFL Coordinator — East) where he briefed me on the progress of
RFL activities on the plateau especially on the theatre productions/shows.

Sk
 Mock Combine Forum

The organisation of this event was fairly managed with support from most of the members of the
‘community in Noomba.

We were taken through the details of this process by Brian Kasira, the Consensus Building Coordinator of
MDF.

However, it was disappointing to see the absence of representatives from Zones 1, 3, 4 and 10. But the
most notable absence was that of the representatives from Zone 3. | had imagined them to put in an extra
effort to make themselves available at this forum given the fact that they would be hosting the actual
combine forum.

Brian said to conduct a supplementary mock combine forum. | advised him that PWM nor MDF (as |
understand) would cover any costs related to this activity as it was not budgeted for so participants
themselves would have to contribute to logistical requirements and other necessary costs.

MCF Test Topi

As we are all aware, Climate Change to most people is a relatively new issue to most people, even more so
for the simple grassroots and the illiterate people of our village. Similar to the facilitator training | had
attended in Umuate, there was deep interest from participants to know more about this topic and how
they can go about addressing it at the community and household level.

Climate Change

They therefore selected this topic as a test topic. This exercise resulted in a lively discussion giving us the
PWM personnel a preview of what was to be expected at the actual forum.

After the briefing by Brian, the test exercise seemed to follow the combine forum process to a tee.

‘Awareness on Climate Change

The video show by Kenn followed by my deliberation on climate change was even then, an eye opener for
the handful of participants at this meeting.

It has reinforced the understanding that more education and awareness is greatly needed in this particular
topic on the plateau. There is no doubt that this will again be raised at the actual combine forum come
November. PWM’s management personnel, Kenn Mondiai and Rufus Mahuru, were both at this event to
note it down for themselves.

RFL: Theatre Group

According to Bradley Dabadaba, at the time of the mock combine forum the theatre group wa
which is located in Zone 3.

Koruo

They have made good time in covering most of the zones on the plateau. At the time of this briefing they
had 1 more stop before then scheduled conclusion in Toma, Zone 9. This will take approximately 2 weeks to
complete, giving the participants or volunteers enough time to return to their various villages to prepare
for the combine forum.

/3
 Education & Awareness Outside of Project Site

During our forced stopover at the Care Centre area near the Pongani River, there were a few revelations
from the pastor on the great need for education and awareness on environment and conservation in the
Pongani area and along the coastal villages all the way to Bareji.

He pleaded with me to look into spreading our grounds outside of our project site. But even then, upon
closer inspection, the Bareji-Afore Junction is actually the entrance and hence, within the boundary of the
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area ~ our project site.

While travelling up the road the next day, it was visibly evident of a lot of extensive logging along the length
of the road from Pongani up to the Bareji-Afore Junction. Photographic evidence of this has been captured

on our return leg.

The legality of this logging work is quite suspicious and should be investigated by all means.

St
 Mock combine forum

This activity was a timely inclusion into our activity plan as it became apparent that participants in this
combine forum had lost their way in terms of sticking to the procedures of the combine forum process.

After this ‘revision’ exercise, we are of the belief that things will turn out better at the next combine forum
schedule for this November.

There is not much in terms of recommendation but if there's any then it would be to have some form of
penalty put in place for those zones that did not attend this event. By not attending, they are telling us and
everybody else that they know everything about this process.

Emergency Education & Awareness

Although it was only a test exercise, the topic of Climate Change featured prominently on the participants’
need to learn more about this hot topic.

As earlier stated in my earlier report dated 16" August 2010, there is need for more information on Climate
Change. Further to that, given the misunderstanding on the issue of Carbon Trade, it is imperative that
more effort should be put into educating and making people aware not only on climate change but also on
the related topic of Carbon Trade.

In addition to this, the population of people living along the coastline up towards Bareji should be educated
‘on environment and conservation and its importance — climate change notwithstanding. This is quite vital
and is a matter of EMERGENCY given the fact that a lot of logging has been carried out in that area as well
as the continuous detrimental practise of bush-burning along the road.

The Mock Combine Forum was a worthwhile and timely affair. By carrying out this exercise we can expect
to get a better result from the actual combine forum.

There were a few notable absences from some zone groups and it would be good to remind them on the
importance of this exercise as to the bearing on the outcome of the actual combine forum.

In addition, it was noted with interest that more work should be done in educating the people on the hot
issue of climate change.

Furthermore, we should look into including the people along the Pongani and Bareji area on our education
and awareness programmes as well on the importance of environment and conservation.

Due to most of the RFL activities happening on site, the Program Manager arranged for
me to visit the project site to learn how the activities were planned, who was involved in
executing and what other necessary arrangements that were set in place to achieve the
planned outcomes.

Rainforest Literacy is a project component of Partners With Melanesians (PWM).

The induction patrol, | perceived, was very educational and helped me so much in

are geographically assigned to work in the Plateau, how they communicate and what

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. DESCRIPTION OF THE ENTERPRISE

The Managalas Organic Coffee Marketing project is a joint undertaking between
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and the Managalas Development Foundation
(MDF), a Federation consisting of 16,000 highlanders organized in 10 cultural
zones living in a 360,000 hectares conservation area inside the Managalas
Plateau of Oro Province, Papua New Guinea.

The project will organize the marketing of organically grown Arabica coffee by
setting up a local company jointly owned by Partners with Melanesians (PWM)
and other local Non-Government Organization and the Coffee Farmers of
Managalas Plateau. Capitalization of the Company will be done on an equity
sharing basis with PWM investing K428,000 and the Farmers putting in shares
through their existing coffee trees and gardens.

Arabica coffee in the form of Parchment, green beans and ultimately an organic
certified blend produced by the Project will be sold both locally and exported to
outside markets. The development of these products will be done over a period
of 3-5 years time (CY 2006-2009).

The project objectives are:

a) To improve the capability of the Farmers to produce good quality
organically grown coffee by providing them adequate technical
extension services in coffee production and post harvest technologies;

b) Increase the Federations (MDF) capability to self manage their
organization and eventually the operations of the Project;

c) Provide a balance to conserving the ecosystem of the Managalas
Plateau and at the same time derive economic benefits from non-timber
forest products (NTFPs) found therein;

d) Provide an alternative trade system that can give the Managalas
Farmers fair prices and cost efficient services in marketing and
increasing value added to their coffee crops under a more equitable
profit sharing arrangement.

The Project will also have as a secondary objective of testing this model for other
coffee growing areas of PNG to replicate. The replication value of this mode! will
create a significant impact on the coffee industry of the country which is
dominated by small growers (80%). MOCP can also serve as a model eco-
enterprise system in developing other non-timber forest products (NTFPs) both in
Managalas and other conservation areas in PNG. NTFPs like buay (betel nut),

=== page 3 ===
vanilla, cocoa, rattan and other forest based and natural resources can be
developed for utilization using the MOCP model on coffee.

2. ORGANIZATIONAL AND MANAGEMENT PLAN

2.1 Form of Business

The Organization will be registered as a Corporation. In the case of a business
Corporation, this can be done by buying out a “shell company” or an existing
non-functional business corporation and replacing the Board of Directors,
Corporate Name and the Corporate Objectives.

The advantage of buying into a defunct business corporation is that it allows a
shorter period and lesser cost to establish a legal identity of the venture. Under a
corporate form, interference from government and political pressures can be
minimized, giving the project a wider leeway of movement and direction.

2.2 Management Plan

investing group (PWM and other NGO investors) and from representatives

to equity participation (Percentage of Share Holdings or Stocks per investor) of

2.3 Ownership Structure of MOCP

2.3.1 Capital Investors

Partners of the project that will invest assets and financial capital into the ventures
are called the Capital Investors. Capital investments can be in the form of cash,
equipment, vehicles, real estate and chattels (land and building for storage) and
other real assets that are dedicated for the use of the project. These capital
investments are valued and assigned stock certificates. Assignees to the stock
certificates will be represented in the Board of Directorship and hold voting rights
equivalent to their stock.

2.3.2 Farmer Shareholders

Partner Farmers of the project from the different cultural zones who will contract
their coffee gardens production to the project are called the Farmer
Shareholders. The investments of the farmer shareholders will be in the form of
coffee trees that they will enroll as their contribution to the project. Each stock
certificate shall represent 100 full bearing trees (defined as trees 3 years old and
above). As an example, a farmer who has five hundred trees who enrolls his
garden to the project will own 5 shares of stocks. The farmer shareholder
obligates himself to sell the coffee parchment from his trees exclusively to the
project as part of his responsibility as an owner to the project. A nominal value of
K 25/tree is assigned as the monetary equivalent to the holdings of a farmer
shareholder (the K 25 is an estimate of the total establishment cost of one tree
from planting up to year 3). A stock certificate of 100 trees equivalent therefore
will have a monetary value of K 2,500/stock.

2.3.3. Total Capitalization and Share Value of the Project

The total capital value of the project will be the sum of all capital from the capital
investors plus the stock value of the farmer shareholders.

Total stocks will be total capital value divided by the stock value.

2.4.3. Cost Recovery

3. Product Description
3.1 Product Description: Managalas Organic Coffee

Coffee grown within the Managalas Plateau is mostly of the Arabica variety

( Catemoor and Biue Mountain - Coffea Arabica). The rich voicanic soils of the
Plateau, an even rainfall distribution and cool climate (elevation: 900-1,000
MASL) allows a good coffee growing environment.

Farmers usually plant at distances between 1.5 x 2.0 meters to as close as 1m x
1m. Shade trees (Albizzia Falcataria. Leucaena Leucocepala and several
species of local pine trees - Casuarina) are used to moderate the sunlight
intensity to a desired level of 25 — 40% shade.

Among the cultural practices common to growers are quarterly weeding or under
brushing and pruning once every 2-3 years. Chemical fertilizers and pesticides
are unheard of among farmers; relying on the natural richness of the soils and a
balanced forest environment, Managalas coffee is as organically grown as can
ever be defined by any certification standards. The remoteness of the place.
difficulty in transport and high costs of chemical inputs pius the unfamiliar use (or
even knowledge of) of synthetic inputs are contributory factors to maintaining an
organic based production regimen among farmers in the Plateau.

Coffee cherries are ripened on the trees and handpicked when they reach cherry
red stage; the cherries are then depulped using a manual coffee depulper and
fermented for 6-12 hours. The fermented parchment coffee is washed
thoroughly and sun dried in elevated platforms or spread out in mats to dry for 5-
7 days. Parchment coffee is normally dried up to a level of 20-30% M.C. The
haif dried parchment coffee is then placed in jute sacks and sold to buyers, For
those areas where buyers are in frequent, the beans are further dried up to a
lower level of between 12% - 14% M.C. at which stage they can safely be stored
without undermining quality of the beans.

An average farmer in Managalas has around 500 trees in his garden. Yields can
vary between 1.5-2.0 kgs/tree of Parchment Coffee equivalent depending on the
amount of care he gives to the plants.

3.2 Sustainability of Maintaining an Organic Based Coffee Production and
the Environmental Impact of Coffee Production in Managalas
Coffee growing in Managalas or elsewhere in PNG enjoys popularity due to its

high economic returns and low production costs. The current world market and
prices for coffee is on the upward trend: particular to organically grown coffee,

13

=== page 15 ===
prices are very lucrative — reaching levels of $ 21 - $75/kg/of roasted beans in
specialty markets that cater to health and organic products.

The scenario that PWM/MOCP wants to create in Managalas is to balance the
ecological/biodiversity conservation of the plateau with the economic utilization of
NTFP’s within. This concept of ecoenterprise albeit new to Managalas has had
mixed results in other countries where it has been tested. Best practices and
lessons learned in the other experiences can be of much value to this project so
as not to repeat errors and maximize on good practices learned elsewhere.

The MOCP objectives of setting up a marketing support system to improve price
and market access among the Managalas farmers is a strategic economic
intervention but could create potential downsides that unless anticipated and
addressed could become a potential threat to the Plateau and the success of the
project itself.

Some of the possible scenarios that can impact on the conservation of
Managalas and the production of organic coffee:

1. Anticipate that with an efficient marketing system in place and good prices
given to farmers, there will be an increase in interests to expand areas to
coffee — this could mean opening new fields and cutting old growth forests.

2. In Migration. Previous experience in the Philippine setting (Kalabugao,
Impasugong, Bukidnon) witnessed the destruction of the Kalabugao Plains
ecological balance and the eventual loss of forest cover due to in migration
from people wanting to have a piece of the coffee trade. A similar thing
can happen in Managalas especially when road access is improved and
ingress is easy.

3. introduction of chemical inputs. In the belief that using synthetic fertilizers
and pesticides will increase productivity, people will begin to use them —
and lose the distinction of an organic marque; disturb faunal harmony and
potential water quality loss are possible side effects.

4. In road of more traders, buyers and new products. While competition is
always healthy for business, unrestricted and unqualified entry of new
players can create chaos to prices(Price war);pressure to farmers to
produce; “pole vaulting” or non compliance to contracts and agreements.
Introduction of new crops, products (alcoholic beverages for example) can
slowly erode a community's cohesiveness.

5. The development of a cash economy based on NTFP’s (coffee, buay.

vanilla and other products) in Managalas can create shifts in the needs and
wants among the community members. This shift from subsistence
