economy (home grown food and self sufficiency) to a cash economy for
over the counter items also creates changes in community relationships
and needs to be anticipated to counteract cultural degradation.

3.2.1 Recommendations and Insights:

PWM and the Partner Communities and Farmers have to formulate a joint policy
on a Forest Land Use Management Pian particularly on the matter of NTFP
utilization and agricultural development. The effects of open agriculture to the
biodiversity of Managalas have to be considered in the management plan of the
Plateau. Slopes, habitats, watershed areas and old growth seed trees have to
be protected. Growth cycles and allowable extraction rates of NTFPs and their
management practices need to be established before full utilization is
undertaken. An option that can be studied is to test crop combinations (multi-
cropping systems) that can optimize the use of current agricultural lands and
produce year round cash flows to farmers without (them) resorting to opening
new gardens. An example seen in the area is a combination of coffee-vanilla-
buay for cash crops and a multi-crop garden for sweet potato, plantain,
sugarcane, papaya and vegetables (squash, taro, yams and greens). The soil in
Managalas is very fertile and has a good carrying capacity for a multi-cropping
system.

As an example of the above scenario: If a househoid ts allowed 2.0 hectare for a
garden — one (1) hectare will be planted for food crops and another hectare
planted to a multi crop system of coffee-vanilia-buay for cash crops. The
hectarage that will be used for agriculture within the Plateau will only be 5,332
hectares (2,666 household population x 2.0 hectare each household). Out of a
total area of 360,000 hectares, this is only 1.5% of the total Conservation area.
This development to agriculture would be highly insignificant in affecting the
ecological balance of the whole plateau and in maintaining the sustainability of
the Plateaus productivity and maintaining ecological integrity; even with a 2.6%
annual population growth.

Another concern that has a big strategic value to the Managalas Plateau is its
road system. While currently in a sorry state of disrepair, this very status might
be contributory to people not going there. All these will change however when
economic development happens in Managalas. The increased productivity in
Managalas will eventually necessitate the building of a good road system. In
migration, entry of other players in the trade of coffee, farm and forestry products,
new ideas and tastes for new products will eventuaily change the cultural
environment of the villages as well as the surrounding physical environment.

The entry of chemical agricultural inputs in particular could undermine the very
reason of the project -- the production of organic products and conservation of
the Plateau. It is near impossible to prevent changes and development to
happen but in the present state of things, PWM, MDF, CM and other allied

developmental NGOs operating within the Plateau can exert efforts to direct the
kind of changes and type of development that can occur in Managalas by
planning its development in advance.

The role of the road system passing through Managalas from Afore to
Popondetta plays a very critical and strategic value to this directional planning for
the Plateau. It is the only road_system existing that allows entry and exit to the
area outside of using light planes.

PWM, MDF, CM and other groups operating in Managalas can present to
government (en banc) a proposal! to operate and manage this road system.
Build, operate, maintain and get exclusive transport franchise to the Managalas
roads in exchange to its conservation and management. Through some degree
of control to these road systems, the group can indirectly influence the
development of the conservation area.

Addressing the concerns on the cultural integrity of the communities can best be
done through an open communication and adequate information, education
campaign. Strengthening existing social and political structures within the
Plateau cements bonds of unity and creates a mechanism of solidarity capable of
answering issues, problems and concerns that will arise in the course of
development and change. 16,000 votes in the Plateau can aiso be a very
strategic political argument to use among the local and national bureaucracies, to
use as leverage for assistance for the Plateau.

4.0 Description of the Market

4.1 The Local Market (PNG)

There are 26 plantation processors and 40 processors listed in the CIC coffee
directory of PNG. All the processors buy parchment coffee and green bean and
also extend toll services by processing parchment coffee to green bean for a fee
(usually 0.25 toea — 0.30 toea/kg).

Interviews with five companies in Goroka showed very positive responses from
the owner/managers with regards to the plan of MOCP to market Managalas
coffee to them. Some of the feedbacks:

1. Most companies are operating at half capacity only — for lack of coffee or
the mills were over designed;

2. One company (Kongo Coffee) is paying a K 1.00/kg premium above
factory door prices just to get quality beans and is willing to extend that
premium to MOCP for quality beans;

3. All five interviewed offered to buy and/or process parchment coffee and
pay good prices for volume and quality;

4. One Company (Arabica’s Limited) wants to buy organic coffee beans and
offered to process MOCPs organic coffee and share market. Their main
problem for their organic coffee line is supply of organically grown beans
and the reliability of organic origin; An indicator that organic coffee
production enjoys premium prices is the fact that they (Arabicas limited)
still earn margins even with a very high cost of transporting coffee by small
plane from the interior highland areas. (K 2.60/kg).

5. All five were willing to cooperate in extending technical assistance to
MOCP to ensure good quality and prices;

6. Two processors (Yondu Coffee, Kongo Coffee) are doing private
extension services to coffee growing communities to promote good post
harvest drying and improve production. Both companies see the vaiue of
coffee as a means to developing village communities and want to
collaborate with efforts that go beyond just buying parchment coffee.

4.2 Export Market: Europe, Japan, US

Organically grown coffee enjoys lucrative markets in the developed countries in
Europe, U.S. and Asia, particularly Japan. To earn an organic marque however
needs the requirements of a certification body and standards. Each market has
a specific organic certification protocol and these have to be considered when
trying to enter into a specific market. Linkages with Fair trade groups and
ecoenterprise networks with the intended country markets can be of help in
facilitating product entry and distribution. A specific buyer in Holland — Travocca
has had initial discussions with PWM as potential buyer for organic coffee.

4.3. MARKETING PLAN

The Project will purchase from the Managalas farmers Parchment Coffee, then
process the parchment into green beans and sell the processed green beans to
local bean processors and roasters either in Lae, Goroka or Hagen through
auction.

Three stages of coffee marketing will be done over a period of three (3) years:

Year 1(CY2006)_—- MOCP will purchase parchment coffee from the 10
cultural zones and process them into green beans for
sale to processors and coffee roasters in Lae, Hagen
and Goroka by auction

Year 2(CY 2007) - Parchment coffee will be processed to green bean
and sold to local processors and roasters; 30% of
the processed green beans will be exported as
organic green beans

Year 3(CY 2008) - 50% of the processed Green bean will be sold to local
buyers, and 30% will be exported as organic green
bean; 20% will be processed into roasted ground
coffee and packaged as organic coffee under
MOCP's brand name for sale to end users (local and
export)

4.3.1 Location

The enterprise will be located in the Oro Province. Purchasing of the Parchment
Coffee will be done within the Managalas Plateau. Buying of parchment coffee
will be done through the 10 cultural zones; 6 Zones are selected for assembly
points: ltokama, Serefuma, Koruwo, Siribu or Ogonomo, Koino and Kawowoki. A
central assembly point of the product will be set up in the Afore Station where the
coordination of the coffee trading operations will be done. Through the station in
Afore, a communication system, purchasing and grading office and storage
facilities will be set up. Shipping and bulk storage will be done in Popondetta
through the wharf in Oro Bay. The Port of Oro Bay can ship the products to
either Lae and eventually to Goroka or Hagen. The Port in Lae is also the main
shipping point for export and export documentation.

The CIC Popondetta Coffee Plant:

There is an existing coffee processing plant in Popondetta that is non-
operational. The mill is owned by the Oro Province under the Department of
Agriculture. Most of the machineries and facilities are intact but needs repairs
and rehabilitation. Based on interview done with CIC, the original intent of the
plant was to service the needs of the coffee growers of Managalas. However.
since the plant was located in Popondetta (243 kms away) instead of within
Managalas, the plant became inaccessible to individual farmer growers and
eventually lost patronage with them. Buyers and traders also did not patronize
the use of the plant since it will just duplicate their work of processing the beans
which they can do by shipping the parchment to Lae, thus putting additional costs
to them.

The Coffee Plant is presently being offered for tender by the Department of
Agriculture. PWM can present a proposal to the Provincial Government with the
backing of the Managalas farmer Communities to take over the ownership and
management of the mill. A proposal to buy out the mill over a period of 5 years
and use it to process coffee from Managalas would have advantages to the
project. Costs can be reduced (instead of toll processing the parchment to other
mills) and quality of the beans can be better controlled. The need for a
warehouse and storage facilities prior to shipping to Lae is solved without
incurring costs for building. It can also serve as a central office for the project.

4.3.2 Main Customers (Target Clients)

The main customers targeted by the project will be the processors/roasters in the
major coffee growing areas — Western Highland Plateau, Eastern Highland
Plateau, Simbu, Morobe, Eastern Sepik, Enga and Southern Highland Plateau.
Coffee processing and buying however is mostly centered in Goroka and Hagen
with transshipments done through the port of Lae. There are 40 existing
processors in the Goroka-Hagen area with 5 companies that do roasting for local
and export markets.

The five (5) companies interviewed alone represents a market of 240,000 50 kg.
green beans/year. (Yondu — 60,000 bags; Airport coffee — 60 bags; Arabicas
coffee — 80,000 to 150,000 bags; 80 tons/year of Organic coffee; Kongo — 60
tons/year organic coffee; 70,000 — 100,000 bags green bean/year).

The volume of coffee needed from these five companies alone represents a
parchment equivalent of 320,000 bags or 16,000,000 kgs of dry parchment.

The 1997 data on coffee production from all the provinces of PNG recorded a
supply of 1,075,403 60 kg. bags of green beans. The data source was from

industry Affair Division — Coffee Report No. 42, March 1998)

The volume recorded by CIC can represent demand of processors for parchment

4.3.3 Total Demand and Market Share

Projecting the current production capacities of the Managalas coffee growers, the
latest survey by PWM shows that there are 700 farmers who grow more than
800,000 coffee trees that can produce about 8,000 bags or 360,000 kgs in 45 kg
bags of parchment.

Assuming the whole production of Managalas is marketed through the MOCP,
this volume represents a mere 0.4% of market share (4,500 bags green
bean/1,075,403 bags total demand). Comparing the markets demand versus the
volume of Managalas coffee production, it should not be a problem selling
Managalas coffee to processors since it represents only a very minor percentage
to their total demand (0.04%).

The key to Managalas getting a good share of the market ts by maintaining a
high standard of quality and this feedback was validated with interviews from the
processors themselves.

4.3.4 Selling Price

Selling price is a function of supply and demand for a particular period in time.
However, factors such as quality, reliability, volume and access to supply can
improve selling prices.

Three methods can be used to determine selling price “comparative method” -
by using benchmark buyers prices (example in Goroka or Hagen) or through a
“what the market will bear method” by way of an auction system. MOCP can use
whichever method suits it best and gives a better quote.

Coffee however is a traded commodity and usually buyers follow the index used

by the commodity market, so a similar system may have to be adopted by
MOCP

Introduction

The first Consensus Building Workshop for the year was conducted from 20" — 24”
February 2006 at Noukonane Village. It was attended by MDF, CBOs and active
stakeholders in the then Rainforest Literacy Program, now Consensus Building Program.

The workshop ran for five days. Day one was spent in a slow but heartwarming welcome
by the Noukonane Elementary School and an introduction of what was to happen during
the week. Day two was spent entirely on issues for the Managalas Conservation Areas
Support Project (MCASP) as a whole. Even before the workshop began, informal
discussions with participants indicated a community desperate for information on the
outcomes of the Managalas Leaders Summit held on 19° — 22" December 2005 at
Serefuna village, particularly, the three-year (2006 — 2008) Partners With Melanesians
Inc. Exit Strategy Plan. The Partners With Melanesians Inc. (PWM) Exit Strategy was
viewed as a ‘wake-up call’ by the Managalas community who are very much dependent
on PWM as the alternative service provider. The communities very much held the mis-
leading perception that PWM is a Managalas owned-organization and all funds should be
spent on the Plateau other then secing PWM as a National Non-Government
Organization, free to choose what they want to do in line with its (PWM’s) vision and

mission.

Thus the workshop accommodated for stakeholders to be engaged in this dialogue. This
perception was evident when a day was exhausted on reflecting on what worked well and
did not work well for the MCASP over the past 17 years since the project began in the
Managalas in 1987. Instead of leaving the people dissatisfied that nothing will be done on
issues that did not work well for MCASP, the afternoon session was constructive with
lively discussions, converting the disadvantages into positive outcomes which the
participants thought should be addressed in the MCASP program components and should
form parts of the PWM Exit Strategy Document. Some of the positive outcomes which
participants thought communities are able to do themselves as ‘community contribution
thru self-reliance’ were identified and marked out. Scriptwriting began on day three thru

=== page 4 ===
to day four, where participants were engaged in identifying and distributing the leaming
objectives on four main topics across the Multi-Channel Leaming Materials including the
four radio programs. At the end of the day, story lines and plots for the four drama
segments in the radio programs and a design guide was completed and ready to be
refurbished and finalized by the Senior Scriptwriter.

Zone briefing was conducted on the last day where a paper (brief) was presented to all the
CBO Activity Coordinators on the topics identified at the Leaders Summit as topics that
should go before the clan group discussions as a lead up to the zone forums and the
combine forum at the end of the vear. In addition, some of the issues discussed during the
week which participants thought needed more awareness and deliberation on were
identified as part of the zone briefing. The zone briefing was assisted by Roy Garawa,
Crispine Burava and Brian Kasira from the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF).

AGENDA # 2 - REFLECTION ON RAINFOREST LITERACY

2003 — 2005

MOU with CLC

PWM recognized the contributions of the Community Leaming Centers (CLC)
established by the Summer Institute of Linguistics in the early 60’s doing Bible
translations into the local Managalas dialects as well as conducting adult literacy.
Thm the then Rainforest Literacy Program, PWM has in place a Memorandum of
Understanding with the CLCs to undertake the compiling, printing and
distribution of the program’s newsletters in the local dialects in series I and Ill.
Prior to that the newsletters were produced by PWM. The MOU also specifies
how the CLC will work with PWM and their participation and contribution
towards formulating the work plan for the Rainforest Literacy Program since
2003 — 2005.

There were problems encountered during the implementation of the MOU, thus
the Consensus Building Program took this opportunity to reassess how best
situations could be improved for the good of the program. Amongst other topics
was the discussion on the production of the newsletters by the CLCs. It was noted
that MOUs did not work and CLCs were not producing the newsletters (one in the
beginning of the year and one at the end of the year) as required under the MOU.
These issues were weighed against the CLCs capacity to produce such a
newsletter and be able to distribute it widely across the plateau.

Participants felt that under the PWM Exit Strategy Plan, CLCs must be

introduction

This design guide describes how to design materials for the Consensus Building Multi-
Channel Learning Program. Materials to be developed using this Design Guide
include:

Overall Goal of the Program

The overall goal of the program is to create a multi-channel “system” of leaming that
enables women and less literate families to integrate conservation and development.

Target Audience

The target audience is women and less literate families on the Managalas Plateau.
The learning will take piace in many settings. However, the main forum for the radio
broadcasts will be clan groups, women’s groups, youth groups, sports groups and
elementary schools.

Learning as Dialogue

“Learning as dialogue” means that learning occurs through a dialogue process that
benefits all parties, both the facilitator and the participants. All parties bring their
knowledge and experience to the table and all parties learn from the dialogue process.
Learning as dialogue is a different educational model than the typical European
educational model. Learning as dialogue reflects traditional core values much more
than European core values, as shown in the table below.

In the Consensus Building Multi-channel Leaming Program, facilitators bring
information to the group, then put it on the table. Participants also bring their insights
and ideas to the discussion. Through that “mixing” action, plans are developed that
allow the group to move forward. Mistakenly, facilitators think they have something to
give to people who need it. Actually, the discussion is the heart of the learning.
Everyone learns together and everyone's ideas change in the process. The learning
materials must be designed to accommodate this type of learning.

=== page 25 ===
Multi-channel and Distributive Learning

Multi-Channel Learning

Multi-channel learning means that several media and several settings are used to get
the information to the learners. Following are examples from the Consensus Building
Program of multi-channel learning.

Multiple media used in the Consensus Building multi-channel learning:
Radio broadcasts

Newsletter :

Flip Charts with Symbol-coded posters

Literacy flyers

Facilitator guides

Multiple settings used in the Consensus Building multi-channel learning:
e Clan groups
Women's groups
Schools
Trade store walls and church and house walis, etc. (for the poster)
Literacy classes
Other settings where information is informally discussed (community space,
family homes, etc.)

There are two advantages to using multiple media and multiple settings:

1) Learners receive the same educational messages in several different formats
and places. Through repetition with fresh media and settings, they are more
likely to remember the messages and see how they relate to their lives.

2) Everyone has their own leaming style. For example, if you leam better by
reading, multi-channel learning provides reading materials. If you learn better
by looking at pictures, symbols and graphics are provided. If you learn better
by listening to people speak and/or talking about.the issues yourself, the
dialogue will be most powerful for you. In other words, multi-channel learning
anticipates the variety of learning styles that individuals possess.

Distributive Learning

Distributive learning is an instructional strategy that reinforces educational content by
distributing it in several locations repetitiously. This way, the learners are reminded of a
learning objective again and again so they are more likely to remember it. Also,
distributive learning works well with multi-channel learning because different media and
settings are used to reinforce specific learning objectives. This way, for example, the
learner can learn how important it is for women to participate in decision making from a
newsletter article, a radio broadcast interview, and a group discussion. Refer to
section, “Distribution of Learning Objectives” for distributive learning in Consensus
Building.

Interactive Radio

Interactive radio instruction (!RI) program consists of three kinds of participants:

1) Radio actors
2) Group facilitators (audience)
3) Group members (audience)

During IRI broadcasts, radio actors interact with the group members and the facilitator,
and the facilitator and group members interact with each other. Radio actors ask
questions, provide activity cues, and encourage the group members and group
facilitators to participate during the broadcast. Radio actors give instructions to the
group facilitator. The facilitator follows directions given by the radio actors, then
organizes discussion and other activities with the group after the broadcast. Group
members often respond to questions, respond with a familiar phrase, or do some other
activity such like hand claps as directed by the radio actors.

Active Learning

Active learning means the learners are active, not passive. !n other words, they
participate in activities with the teacher/facilitator and with each other. They do not sit
quietly in their seats for the information to be “dumped” into them. In active learning the
teacher will often pair students to work with each other, or conduct group activities.

This engages the students and makes them more interested in the activity. They will
tend to remember information better and look forward to the next learning session. It
also gives them some control in their leaming which helps them to improve
independent thinking and problem-solving skills.

Active learning is when leamers do something, as opposed to passively receive
information. Following are examples of active learning activities:

Zone Briefing
17” February 2006
Naukenane Village, Zone 1

Three topics were chosen at the Leaders Summit held on 19 - 22 December 2005, as
topics that should go through the 2006 zone forums. These issues will form the basis of
the end of the year combine forum. This brief is prepared to present these discussion
topics to the activity coordinators who will be leading and coordinating the clan and
group discussions. The topics are: 1) Council of Chiefs; 2) 2007 Council and National
Elections; 3) Traditional Leaming Centres. Each of the topics has questions that should
stir the discussions in the various groups. Each group will be required to note down
responses to each of the discussion questions and a general consensus reached on each of
the topics. The group’s consensus will be presented at the combine forum.

* COUNCIL OF CHIEFS (COC)

a) Whatis the COC?
The idea of having a Council of Chiefs came from discussions during the Leader’s

Summit held on 19" —22™ December 2005 at Serefuna Village.

b) Why having a COC?

This is an issue within the Managalas and especially in conjunction with MDF and the
issue of leadership between the Traditional and Contemporary Leaders- the Old and the
young educated leaders. It seems that the young educated people have displaced the
elders out of the new structure and they have become defunct and of no consequence to
the current developments. After a lot of discussion, the Summit agreed to have in place a
COC. Traditional elders are important members of the community and they need to be
more involved in the new developments that confront the plateau. They need to be
involved because they are important in more than one way.

Traditional leaders are important because:
* Have respect from their own clans.
Have traditional knowledge and wisdom.
Peace brokers
Settle disputes
Control the clan decision-making process.
Transfer knowledge and skills to the next generation.
Control over the land.
Contro] other issues in the village
Body to liaise with Government.

b) Who becomes a member of the COC?

=== page 56 ===
It was decided by the Leader's Summit that each zone must have a representative at the
Council of Chiefs. The clan representatives from each village come together at the zone
level. The ONE representative representing a particular zone ts elected at the zone ievel
and is represented in the Council of Chiefs.

c) Who does the COC represent?
Each member on the COC represents his zone. The whole COC body represents the
16,000 + people of Managalas.

d) What does the COC represent and what is their major function?
The COC is the highest decision making body on the plateau dealing with Traditional
Laws.

e) How much power does the COC have?
The extent at which COC is to exercise iis powers will be vested in their constitution.

f) What are their roles & responsibilities?

Some Specific Roles of Traditional leaders would be:

Deal with tribal conflict

Mediate on land matiers

Oversee and provide advice to CBOs on cultura! issues

Advice MDF on industrial and economic development and natural resources.
Lead and oversee on cultura, traditional, customary practices in Managalas.
Provide isput on political agenda/issues on the plateau.

Liaise with MDF on consensus building

Others to be included ..........

h) Who are the COC answerable to?
They are answerable to the whole of the plateau (16.000 + people) and to each clan
member tn their villages and zones of which they represent.

i) Can the community change the COC if they are not doing their job?

Yes. Only at the Zone Forum. Changes made at zone level will affect membership to
coc.

jp Are women eligible to become COC?
Yes. If the woman has the customary right to be the chief of her clan.

k) If NOT, then why not?
Because chieftainship in most communities on Managalas are inherited from father to son
etc.

} How long can someone be on the COC?
As long as he/she is not voted out at the zone forum.

m) Will the COC have a chair?

=== page 57 ===
Yes, The COC will have a chair elected by the COC to steer and guide the operations of
the COC in agreement and consent of the COC members.

0) Will the COC have a constitution?
Yes. The constitution will be written by CELCOR Lawyers with initial baseline data
compilation by the Community Learning Centres.

p) Will there be an MOU between MDF Board & COC?
Yes. The MOU will spell out the roles and responsibilities of the COC and how the COC
will complement the roles and responsibilities of the MDF Board.

r) Will the COC have an AGM?
Yes. The AGM will be a part of the combine forum held at the end of each year.

8) What happens at the COC AGM?

This is when the COC reports back to the communities about what they have done during
the year including successes and failures. It is during the AGM when members of the
COC could be elected out of the COC. The election of new members of the COC will be
taken back to the zone level.

=== page 58 ===
* 2007 COUNCIL AND NATIONAL ELECTIONS

1. Why is PWM talking about this?

The Ijivitari Electorate is a big electorate that when it comes to choosing a candidate to
represent the people of ljivitari in the National Parliament, people from the coast are the
ones voted in to Parliament by the people of Managalas and the ljivitari electorate as a
whole. It has come to being that the Managalas area has long been forgotten. Government
infrastructures have deteriorated and services are worse than ever before.

PWM has been in the plateau for the past 16 years or so and have assisted the people in
small ways using donor support. But his cannot go on forever. PWM is implementing its
exit strategy beginning this year and will end in 2008.

If Managalas people continue to vote into Parliament someone from the coast, the
Managalas will be lost in time. Therefore, it is high time for the Managalas people to
speak with one voice and vote someone from Managalas into Parliament in the 2007
elections so that vital government infrastructure and services will come to Managalas for
the good of our children and their children’s children

2. Where did this discussion start?
This discussion started from the Leaders Summit last December 2005. The Summit
appointed an election committee who will coordinate this on the Plateau.

3. What is PWM role?
PWM wiil play an advisory role to the election comnnmttce with Kenn Mondiai as the
Advisor.

1 INTRODUCTION

The submission for declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area (The Act) under the
Conservation Areas Act was submitted by community representatives from the plateau with the support by
Partners with Melanesians (PwM) to the Minister for Environment & Conservation Hon. John Pundari in the
presence of Oro Governor, Hon. Gary Juffa and Member for Sohe. Thereafter as required under the Act
advertised in the newspaper in early 2013. The 90 day period for objection lapsed lapsed on 18 May 2013.
An objection letter dated 18 March, 2013 was sent to the Minister for Environment & Conservation by the
President of Afore Local Level Government, Hon. Douglas Garawa MPA on behalf of the landowners in the 18
wards of the Afore LLG. The Department has not responded to the objection letter by the President of Afore
Loca! Level Government to the Minister for Environment & Conservation although a draft response letter was
prepared during the year. No satisfactory reasons have been provided by the Department for the long de __in
responding to the objection ietter. One year has lapsed after the submission for declaration of the
Conservation Area was given to the Minister for Environment & Conservation on 8 November, 2012. As a
result the President of Afore LLG has stopped al project activities on the plateau until he receives the
response from the Department. This has affected properiy planning and funding arrangement for project
activities especially activities leading up to the official declaration of the Conservation Area after its approval
by the Nationa! Executive Council and dectaration by the Governor General and subsequent gazettal as
requirec under the Conservation Areas Act.

In May 2013 | was engaged by PwM to hold was to hold consultative meetings in selected places with
stakeholders to verify the support for the objection to the declaration of the Managalas Conservation Area by
the Afore iG President. The trio was from 23 May-2°° june 20013 and a report was furnished to PwM with
eieven (11) recommendations to enable the stakeholders especiaily PwM to address the issues raised in the
objection letter oy the Afore Loca! Level Government President. Since then numerous correspondences have
been exchanged between PwM, MDF and the President of ALLG with regard to the issues raised in the
objection letter with a view to resolving them so that the declaration of the Conservation Area can proce.
after the NEC approves its declaration as required under the Conservation Areas Act but no agreement was
reached by the parties thus the need for a plateau/LLG wide Forum to discuss the issues raised by the
President in his objection with a view to resolving them. PwM decided that it was better for people from the
area who have the standing and respect from the community and who are well versed with the projects
objectives and programmes to facilitate at the Forum and guide the stakeholders to discuss and address the
issues raised in by the President of ALiG in his the objection letter to the Minister for Environment &
Conservation. This was main reason PwM engaged myself to facilitate at the forum with assistance from
Simon Savaiko, a member of the Board PwM. The forum was held at Ugunomo village from 16-20 December
2013. The forum was well attended by clan elders from all cultural zones on the plateau and community
leaders wherein they discussed the five (5) issues selected by the Facilitators in consultation with PwM and

2. BACKGROUND

“ A PEACEFUL AND SELF RELIANT COMMUNUAL SOCIETY LIVING IN HARMONY WITH NATURE”

This is the vision of Managalas people through their duly constitution entity , the Managalas Development
Foundation (MDF). Can we work together to achieve this vision was at the center of discussions at the
Ugunomo Forum.

The Managalas plateau in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora. And
more significantly the plateau is home to the Queen Alexendra Birdwing Butterfly, the world’s largest
birdwing butterfly which is listed on Appendix | of the CITES Convention and which is only endemic to Oro
Province of Papua New Guinea. The proposed Managalas Conservation Area covers 360,000 hectares of
pristine rainforest comprising lowland mountane forests and is also the water catchment area of the Popondetta
plains, The total population of the area is 18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari
District. The people live in 75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and speak four
(4) dialects.

The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale environmentally destructive
projects like logging, mining and oil palm plantations. Having being working with international and national
NGO partners since the early 1990’s the area is now in the process of being designated as a conservation area
under the Conservation Areas Act of 1978. The Managalas people submitted the Managalas Proposed
Conservation Area Appiication to the Minister for Environment and Conservation on 8" of November, 2012.
As required under the Act, the public advertisement was placed in the newspapers (Post Courier) for
stakeholders to view and file any objections if any. The advertisement appeared in the Post Courier on 18
February, March 4, March 18, April 1, April 29 and finally May 13 2013. The 90 day period expired on 18
May 2013. The President of Afore Local Level Government, Douglas Garawa filed an objection in a letter
dated 18 March 2013 wherein he raised a lot of issues why the Minister should not make the NEC submission
for it to approve the CA declaration and for the proposal to be shelved until such time the Managalas people are
able to manage the project themselves. The Department to date has not officially responded to the objection
letter by the President of Afore LLG and no reasons have been given for this long delay in responding to the
objection letter and no reasons have been given by the Department for this long delay in responding to the
President’s objection letter..

In May 2013 PwM carried out its own independent consultation to verify the support by the clan elders for the
objection filed by the President of Afore LLG engaging myself for this purpose. The consultation was
undetaken out and a report was furnished to PwM which among others recommended for all project activities
on the plateau to be put on hold until the issues raised in the objection letter by the President are addressed and

3

=== page 6 ===
resolved. It was found that that majority of the clan elders on the plateau did not sign the objection letter by the
President. Thereafter, PwM has been communicating with the President to trv and hoid meetings tc resoive the
issues he has raised in his objection letter but the President refused to attend such meetings saving he will need
to get an official response from DEC on his objection letter first. The President also stopped all project
activities saving he still stands by his objection. This affected the implementation of project activities by PwM
and its local partner Managalas Development Foundation (MDF).

3. Keys Issues Discussed at the Forum

There were five (5) main issues which were discussed at the forum. These issues were selected based on the
concerns and issues raised by the President of Afore Local Level Government in his objection letter to the
Minister for Environment & Conservation dated 18 March 2013 when the submission was made by PwM and
MDF to the Minister to nave the Managalas Plateau declared a Conservation Area under the Conservatior
Areas Act on 8 November 2012. These five (5) issues which was agreed to by the Facilitators and PwM
management and are as follows:

issue # 1, Future of the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area

“The Managalas people will not be pushed around and forced to accept this conservation
agenda by adamant, manipulative and self centered individuals using the NGO movement
to further their hidden agendas and secure employment for themselves in the name of
conservation”.

The above statement was made by the President of Afore Local Level Government (ALLG) in his objection
letter to the Minister for Environment and Conservation thus this was the main issue which needed to be
discussed and resolved at the Forum. if this issue was nct resolved then there was no need to proceed to the
other issues which were snecifically chosen to strengthen the work to have the area declared a conserva’
area which is the main objective of the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project (MCASP}. Theretore
considerable amount of time was consideration amcunt of time was scent on discussing this issue at the
forum, The question we posed for the forum was “do we all agree to have the plateau fenced so we can
keep outsiders out from intruding onto our lands or do we ieuve it open for outside intrusion’? This
question triggered a Iot of discussions on the issue arcund the reasons for the initiative, what went wrong
along the way and how we can collectively resolve the issues especially those raised by the President in his
objection letter to the Minister. There is stili confusion between conservation and land registration so many
questions were asked on this issue although we know that this was issue of discussions in the early years
leading up to the submission to the Minister. However, it did gc to show that there is need for on-going
awareness and public education on such important issues as a lot of young people are now getting educated
and so begin to get involved in issues at the community !eve! and are curious about such issues because of
4

=== page 7 ===
what they read or hear through the media or through other mediums of communication. it was also brought
to light that the influence of churches particularly the new charismatic movement on such issues raised
confusions in the minds of people especially the younger generation who were not involved in the initial
stages of the project.

issue # 2. Relationship, Collaboration and Partnership between Partners with
Melanesians (PwM), Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and
the Community Based Organisations (CBOs)

This issues was selected as a discussion issue at the forum not only because of the issues and concerns raised
by President of Afore LLG in his objection letter regarding management of the project by outsiders but also
because of the important role that MDF and the CBOs play in implementing project activities under the
MCASP and in light to PwMs plans to relinquish management responsibilities to MDF as part of its exit
strategy. MDF must be prepared to take on this huge responsibility of managing the Conservation Area after it
is officially declared by the government. Therefore, was need to discuss issues affecting MDF’ s work and
ways how it can improve and stand on its own two feet once PwM relinquishes the management
responsibility as per the exit strategy.

issue #3. Relationship and Partnership Between PwM, MDF and Afore Local Level
Government Council (ALLG)

This issue is very important because of the objection by the Afore LLG President to the CA submission. The
forum was organized with the aim to discuss and address the issues raised by the President in his objection
letter to the Minister for Environment & Conservation dated 18 March 2013. The conflict between PwM

clan level to have our land declared a Conservation Area so that we can make our own
decisions on how we use and manage our lands and resources for our use now and have
them replenished for the benefit of our future generations.

2 We have collectively agreed not to allow any large scale resource development projects
including logging and mining to be developed on our land because of the likely impacts
including environment, social, cultural and economical impacts as it is the case in other
parts of the country. This is because we are a subsistence community and we rely on our
land and resources for our livelihood so do not want to see it destroyed.

want on our land based on our culture and following our traditional decision making
process. We do not want any outsiders to make these decisions for us and we stand firm
to veto any development that takes place on our lands without our informed consent.

be part and partial of the development planning process at. the Ward, LLG and District
level so that our needs arel be included in such development plans. At this juncture, our
collective decision to have the Managalas Plateau declared a conservation area must be
included in such development plans.

LOCATION: Port Moresby and Managalas Plateau, Afore Local Level Government area,
Oro Province.

INTRODUCTION

The Managalas Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 — 2000 meters altitude
above the coastal plain of the Oro Province, Paupa New Guinea. It sits between the
Owen Stanley Ranges to the South and West, the Sibium Ranges to the south-east and
Mount Lamington and the Hydrographers to the north and east. The 360,000 hectares of
the Plateau encompass an extraordinary diversity of environment including alpine heath
at 3,800 meters, mountain and hill forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens.

Like many of the mountainous mid-altitudes valleys of PNG, the Plateau is an area of
high quality agricultural land and relatively dense populations. The surrounding
mountains, by contrast, are generally infertile and little populated. Over 20,000 people
from around !50 clan groups live in over 70 village communities on the Managlas
Plateau. These are largely subsistence farmers and depend almost exclusively on the
environment for their livelihood. Five dialects are found on the plateau that together
makes up five broad languages (Barai, Namiai, Samoi, Omie and Ese).

The Managalas Plateau is relatively isolated and remote from urban PNG. It is linked to
the Oro Provincial Capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality for-wheel drive road and by
two airstrips as well as by foot-tracks. This allows limited sale of coffee and other
produce during dry conditions but high freight costs and poor maintenance prevent
regular trade. Government services are restricted to a number of community schools, a
top up school, two aid posts and a station and Health Centre at Afore. The Summer
Institute of Linguistics (SIL) introduced an adult literacy programme to the Plateau in
the 1960's and this has provided an important foundation for many of the development
processes now taking place on the plateau.

Over the past decade, a number of proposals for timber extraction, oil palm and mining
development have been presented to the Managalas Plateau. While welcoming the
opportunity for development, Managalas communities are actively opposing many of
these projects due to poor consultation with resource owners and the failure to guarantee
benefits or environmental! protection.

=== page 46 ===
The Managalas piateau in Oro Province harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora and
isand more significant is that the plateau is home to the Queen Alexendra Birdwing
Butterily, the world’s largest birdwing butterfly which is listed cn Appendix } of the
CITES Convention and which is only endemic to Oro Province. The proposed
Managalas Conservation Area encompasses the foothills of the Sibium Ranges to the
South-East, the Owen Stanley Ranages to the South-West. Owalama Ranages to the
West and Guava Ranges to the North-east and stretches to the lower plains of Orobay.
The area is 360,000 hectares of pristine rainforest comprising lowland mountane forests
and is also the water catchment area of the Popondetta plains. The total population of the
area is 18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari District. The
people live in 75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and
speak four (4) dialects. The people are mainly subsistence farmers with main income
from organic Arabica coffee.

The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale
environmentally destructive projects like logging. mining and oilpalm plantations so
have been working with international and national NGO pariners since the early 1990's
to have the area designated a conscrvation arca under the Conservation Arcas Act of
1978. Their efforts have paid off when finaily on November 8 20!2. they presented a
submission together with the Governor for Ore, Mon. Gary Juffa to the Minister for
Environment & Conservation to have the area declared a conservation area (refer to
attached newspaper article). While there are few steps before the National Executive
Council approves the submission to get the Governor General to declare the area a
Conservation Area as required under the law, this is a significant break-through for the
people of Managalas Plateau.

ACTIVITIES

The following are the major activities envisaged under this legal intervention project to
get tne Department of Environment & Conservation to have the Managalas Plateau
declared a Conservation Area under the Conservation Areas Act.

FIRST QUARTER SUMMARY REPORT

Date: 20.06.14

Climate Change and Community Reforestation

INTRODUCTION

Climate Change and Community Reforestation as the 4" Key Component strategy of PwM
programs is well into its 2° year of existence since included in 2013. With the ideal of
linking the gap of Conservation efforts holistically in its entire project sites, all its activities
have taken on a one step at a time approach. The very first activity under this component
started last year in 2013 was prioritized on information dissemination alone mainly on
Awareness raising in all its 3 sites and only an exception of Managalas project site local
CBOs underwent a Community Basic Climate Change Awareness Workshop to assist in
conveying the correct information to their respective communities. However, there is
more to be done in terms of Awareness raising and so it continues to be implemented this
year. Much of the activities has been revised in terms of its implementation timeframe.
There are number of factors that limit this program component which will be highlighted
further in summary and what has been done so far and what is yet to be done.

needs more resources, effort and time. Based on past experience of many years of

activities identified must be rationally chronologic which explains the approach of
one step at a time.

one of the main challenge that is faced by many organization so as this is the first
for this component, Officer responsible is still in the process of researching and
collecting data within PwM library, internet and other resource books outside.

3. Establishing and strengthening Partnerships and Broaden Networks. This is very
important in this regard as in terms of collaborative effort through exchange of

information, co-financing and Technical expertise to address climate Change in all
project sites.

Conclusion

Nevertheless, all activities with its objectives in the 5 year master work plan still remains
however its timeframe is being revised accordingly. Hence, it needs support from other

relevant stakeholders to realistically specify the issues and link it with the compatible
Action plans in respective community's situation.

Project purpose: PWM have three project areas therefore the following are the three main project purposes as per their project area

situations:

A. Managalas Conservation Area Project
Traditional landowners are empowered to be involved in any decision making related to planned development projects as well as playing an active role
in efforts to protect and utilize their local environment and its natural resources.

B. Karimui Proposed Conservation Area Project
Communities are empowered to conserve and develop their natural resources sustainably so that present generations will not compromise the

livelihood of future generations as well as realizing and maintaining their traditional cultural practices.

C. Inaina Proposed Wildlife Management Area Project
The local communities are empowered to participate in the protection and utilization of their natural resources as well as in any decision making in

relation to the development of their natural resources.

Has any of the 5-year expected results (outputs) been changed? If yes, please explain.

There are no major changes to the 5-year expected results (outputs). However with the late inclusion of Managalas Conservation Area Project work
plan activities and budget, there will be changes to work plan activities within the expected 5-year activities. These new activities in Managalas
Conservation Area Project were developed from the clan group discussion and the District Wide Combine Forum in August and December respectively

last year 2013.

However these new activities have being slotted into each programme areas for year 2014 where the expected 5-year results (outputs) remain the
same as per all programme areas.

=== page 10 ===
What upcoming events both on national and local level may affect the project during the coming year?

As per the national Papua New Guinea Calendar, there are no national and local level events that will have impacts or affect the projects during the
coming year 2014. However, in Managalas and Karimui, the open members of Parliament are facing election petition matters which might end up in

| courts of disputed returns where there is high hopes of by-elections in these two area. As for Inaina, the disputed open member seat was nullified by
the court of disputed returns last year and the electorate in Kairuku-Hiri are having their by-election which ended on the last week of January 2014. A
winner of this seat will be declared in the month of February, 2014.

Other comments relevant to the annual planning?

The only comments that PWM can provide will be the Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP) issues and problems that needs to be dealt with |
before the area can be declared as a Conservation in Papua New Guinea. PWM had no problem in submitting the Managalas Conservation Area
Project Application to the Minister for Environment and Conservation Hon. John Pundari in November, 2012. There was only one objection to the
application by the Afore Local Level Government (ALLG) President Mr. Douglas Garawa during the 90 days public advertisement for the public to
object. However it has taken more than a year for the Department of Environment and Conservation to respond to the objection by the ALLG
President,

Due to the prolong respond to the ALLG president by the Department of Environment and Conservation, the remaining 2013 half year activities were
suspended but only two activities were conducted by the Managalas Development Foundation and two of Managalas leaders. The first was in August
2013 as The Clan Group Discussion on the East and West of Managalas Plateau. The second was in December 2013 The District Wide Combine Forum.
Out from these only two activities, the ALLG President decline to attend as he wanted to know his objection respond from the Department of
Environment and Conservation.

However from the above two activities, the Managa!as Clan and Community ieaders developed their own annual activities and wanted PWM to take
the activities seriously so that Managalas Conservation Area Project can be declared as a Conservation Area as per CA Act 1976 in Papua New Guinea,
Therefore all activities below are the relevant annua! planning activities derived from their Clan Group Discussions and the District Wide Combine
Forum. PWM have agreed to consider these activites and allocate funds after prioritizing them in our first annua! pianning.

Allin all, with the inclusion of Managalas Conservation Area Project work plan activities for the year 2014, the other two project areas Karimui and
Inaina remain same with their work plan activities with slight changes of activities.

File.

To The Programe Manager

Mr Rufus Mahuru

11" July 2014

Ref: Report for 5" Melanesians Arts & Cultural Festival
Dear, Mr Mahuru

Here is the report of the Managalas Cultural group and attached with the report is the pictures of
the articles with the pictures of activity done in each venue in Port Moresby
 Date: 10th July 2014

Introduction

The Managalas Cultural group is made up of members from the Managalas Kuafieaui theatre cultural
groups and the Faiama Cultural Group .The Faiama cultural Group has registered with the (NCC)
National cultural Commission in which the MKTG member have Joined to attend the S* Melanesians
Arts Festival in Port Moresby.

Method /Producers

‘The Managalas Cultural Group coming to Port Moresby for the 5" Melanesians Arts Cultural Festival
was initiated by PWM Program Manager Mr Rufus Mahuru for the group to participate and aio take
back home the message on the importance of Melanesian Art & Culture and why we need to
preserve or maintain them. Beside, a letter of endorsement was written to the Oro Administration
for approval but nothing has been done and no response to the letter was given to PWM office.

Purpose

The main purpose of the group's travel into Port Moresby for the Melanesians Arts and Culture
Festival is to promote their culture and tradition and as a way of strengthening the conservation
work which they are pursuing back at home (Managalas Plateau).

‘The Managalas cultural Group however with all their performance have relayed message to the
general public and the people of Papua New Guinea and pacific the importance of conserving land
Forest as well as the cultural identity like Legendry stories marks tattoos traditional costumes for
dancing ,etc.

Result and Findings

The Managalas Cultural Groups performed their traditional dances in all locations in Port Moresby
and also draw attention to the various species of fauna and flora they have in their forest such as the
diverse species of frogs found in Managalas plateau and the biggest birdwing Butterfly, the Queen
Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly found nowhere in the world but in Managalas plateau in Oro province.

The Managalas Cultural group after this festival has to take the lead to make awareness in all CBOs
in the newly remapped Propose CA areas. As the director of MKTG, the group has to play a vital role
in educating new members of CBOs to join the Theatre group with new skills of performing dramas
obtained through observations from other performing groups during the festival. This trip was an
eye opener, and by observing the performances from different cultural groups across Melanesia, the
MKTG cultural group has to change its performance to a broad standard and not the same style that
they use in the village.

Recommendation

With such activity like these in the near future, gender participation from CBOs should be taken into
consideration. MKTG should be responsible for the performances done under the rainforest Literacy
in the plateau. Also suitable person with good fair mind should be consulted for such programme
and also building of CLC in the plateau.

 Conclusion

On behalf of Managalas Cultural Groups | would like to acknowledge PWM Program Manager, Mr
Rufus Mahuru, and Mr Damien Ase for their time spent in taking the Cultural group to Port Moresby
and back to Managalas and also the staff of PWM who supported the group well in Port Moresby

Finally we acknowledge the donor /funder of this programme RFN through PWM for everything
provided and the Pari Women Development Association for the hospitality and accommodation.

ESE to youall

Reporting Officer

Mr Alkin Fufus
MKTG Director

snippet: 14) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978) gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB. 14)Despite four (4) bio …
text:
=== page 1 ===
14) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978)
gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to
CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB.

14)Despite four (4) biological surveys undertaken in the past by friends of the
Managalas plateau including the Department of Environment and
Conservation, the Science Faculty of the University of Papua New Guinea,
and Partners with Melanesia, there is a diverse array of fauna and flora of the
Managalas plateau that remain to be discovered and documented. Hence
having the area declared as a Conservation Area can allow further research
into the rich diverse ecosystems of the area.

Threats to Conservation & Sustainable Natural Resources use

15) The major threat on the environment and the forest ecosystems is from
agriculture; conversion of primary forests for both subsistence food production
and commercial cash cropping activities like growing coffee- undertaken by
the local communities to enhance human wellbeing.

16) There are potential threats from the private sector; especially companies who
are interested in industrial logging and mining in and around the proposed
conservation areas. Initially there was an intrusion and overlap with mining
Exploration Lease (EL 1547) but the boundary map has been adjusted
amicably between landowners, the Minerals Resources Authority, and the
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to allow mining
exploration activities to be undertaken outside the boundary of the proposed
conservation area.

17) Several industrial logging propositions have been made but landowners in
the conservation area have and are still objecting in preference over
conservation and small scale ecoforestry to meet local requirements including
housing, construction of schools and health centers.

Community Su apacity and Future Sustainabil

18) The Managalas communities were educated through a literacy program
through the University of Papua New Guinea since 1984 on the issues related
to the destruction of the natural forests and the biodiversity. As a result, all the
Managalas clan elders and chiefs agreed in at a public forum at zone 6
(Numba) in 1997 to have the entire Managalas plateau officially declared as a
conservation area to protect the habitat for the QABB and the forest for the
future generations.

19) The respective government agencies at the Provincial and Local level have
also given their support and endorsement on the declaration of Managalas
Conservation area; Oro Provincial Executive endorsement on 2” December
2008 followed by Afore Local Level Government endorsement on 8" June
2011.

20) At the invitation of the Managalas communities, the Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) a national Non- Governmental Organization (NGO) has
been working in the area since 1997 mainly in raising awareness and building
capacity with funding assistance from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway up

nF

=== page 2 ===

=== page 3 ===
to present with a total expenditure of some PGK10 million. PWM Focal
Programs in the past had been;

Education, training and awareness

Scientific research, data collection and analysis
Support for alternative income earning options
Facilitate conservation area declaration

21) Notable achievements include education and awareness of local
communities, conservation commitment of 360,000 hectares; establishment of
base line socioeconomic and biological data; and establishment of a
community based organization for the area; the Managalas Conservation
Foundation (MCF) with its Board, management and 5 -year organizational
strategic plan.

22)There are some level of alternative income earning opportunities that have
been supported over the years for sustainable livelihood purposes especially
Arabica coffee at small holder level: and as it is one of the few areas in the
Southern region, it has huge potential for increased production and marketing
at premium prices with eco labelling.

23) There is also opportunity for eco-tourism, there is an initial plan to develop an
eco-tourism industry on the plateau under the Conservation Area and besides
that tracking along the famous Black Cat/Ghost Trail from Abau up into the
Owen Stanley Ranges to upper Musa round Dorobosoro and into Aiari, Suari
and into the Managalas plateau (the path used by the American soldiers in aid
of the Australians) at Kokoda is now in the pipe line and it is predicted that it
will be receiving visitors so employment opportunity and other spin-off benefits
will be tremendous for the area along the lines of Kokoda Trail.

24) A geographical, socioeconomic and biological profile of the proposed
Managalas Conservation Area is annexed to this NEC submission as “Annex
A’ that includes information on the people, biodiversity, people's commitment
and support for conservation area declaration.

25) PwM and the MCF are working together under an existing collaborative
partnership Memorandum of Understanding on the mobilization and joint use
of both financial and technical resources for the conservation area program.

26) Through an exit strategy PwM developed between PwM and MCF, all
management responsibilities will be handed over to MCF to maintain and
manage the proposed Conservation Area once declared.

27) In line with the National Protected Area Policy which the NEC approved in
2014 (NEC Decision No. 5/2014) that provides for sustainable financing for
protected areas, the NEC consider and approve the amount of K8 Million to
cover initial costs for the management of the Managalas Conservation Area.
These includes costs for developing the Management Plan for the
conservation area including land use plans, establishment of the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee, training of local rangers and
funding of sustainable income generating projects for the local communities in
each zones in the project area.

=== page 4 ===
——Q ia ee we Jo Eo = —

=== page 5 ===
28) To provide for sustainable financing for the management of the conservation
area, the NEC consider an approve the amount of K4 Million to be set aside
as an Endowment Fund to be managed by representatives from CEPA,
Finance Department, National Planning and Monitoring, Oro Provincial
Administration, Ijivitari District Development Authority, Afore Level
Government. Partners with Melanesians and Managalas Conservation
Foundation under a trust deed.

29) An Endowment Fund is investment fund set up by an institution or
organisation in which regular withdrawals from the invested capital are used
for on-going operations or other specified purposes. Sustainable financing is
required to pay staff, purchase equipment, engage with local communities,
conduct natural resource monitoring and enforce rules for the protected area.
The interest generated by the resulting investments provides financial security
for protected areas. Local communities in the area will benefit in the form of
jobs, training, sustainable income generation and development projects. This
is important due to the fact that the land where the protected area is
established are owned and controlled by customary clan groups which is
recognised by the PNG Constitution and relevant laws in the country.

30) In line with the Governments Public Private Partnership and outsourcing
policy consistent with Pillar 6 objectives of PNG Vision 2050, field
conservation area management and sustainability issues including education,
awareness and capacity building functions will be outsourced to Partners With
Melanesians and Managalas Conservation Foundation by the Government
(CEPA) given their local knowledge and expertise in the area of conservation
and development enabled through the sustainable financing mechanism.

31) An organizational profile of Partners with Melanesians and Managalas
Conservation Foundation are included under Section Il] on Current
Management and Future Sustainability, pages 20 and 30 respectively of the
Managalas Conservation Area profile referred to as Annex A attached
herewith to this policy submission.

32) Employment opportunities will be created through the development and
implementation of the Managalas Conservation Area Management Plan
(CAMP) with input and guidance from Afore LLG, CEPA and other interested
stakeholders.

33) The track is called Ghost Mountain Track and it starts from Gabagaba to
Dorobisoro in Rigo District and goes over the ranges to Suari, Aijari, |tokama
to Gora (covers villages in zone 4, zone 1, zone 2, zone 3 and zone 10) in the
proposed conservation area. The Black Cat Track is another track that goes
from Kupiano/Abau over the ranges to Safia (Middle-Musa) to Embessa and
down to Foru (Lower Musa). So in our case we are looking at developing and
promoting the Ghost Mountain Track. A book was written by James Chalmers
about the track called " The Ghost Mountain Boys". He walked the track with
another Journalist from the USA in 2006.

34) There is considerable ongoing support and commitment by other
organizations within PNG and abroad who are interested in the biodiversity
conservation and sustainable use of the natural resources of the Managalas
plateau. These include Rainforest Foundation of Norway who has consistently

-5-

=== page 6 ===
—— £2 we ita fe __

Ll.

=== page 7 ===
supported since 1996 and Bishop Museum in the USA, the University of PNG,
and Department of Community Development, local NGOs and most
importantly the Oro Provincial Government and its people.

35) Managalas conservation area if declared will be the largest terrestrial
conservation area in the country with an increase by 0.9% bringing the total to
4.7% from the current 3.85% and hence contribute towards achieving the Achi
target of protecting 17% of the terrestrial biodiversity by 2020.

C. VIEWS OF THE PRIME MINISTER

36)Prime Minister has been briefed and he supports this submission.

D. VIEWS OF OTHER MINISTERS AFFECTED

37) Their views will be sought at NEC.

E. FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS

38) A one of PGK8 million will be required for initial establishment,
operationalization and community development support including
establishment of sustainable financing mechanism by Conservation Protection
Authority (CEPA) of PGK4 million; and Managalas Conservation Foundation
(MCF) K4.0 million will be required.

39) As not for profit organizations (NGOs) are involved in facilitating the
establishment of the Conservation Area and will take on the responsibility of
managing it and in recognition of the commitment by the landowners in the
conservation area to give massive parts of their land for the conservation
project, the NEC grants tax exemption status including Goods and Services
Tax, Interest Withholding tax and other relevant taxes application to the
project.

F. STAFFING IMPLICATIONS

40) The proposed one of funding assistance will enable both Conservation
Environment Protection Authority and Managalas Conservation Foundation to
mobilize manpower required for operationalization of the Managalas
Conservation Area programs including sustainable financing mechanism.

G. EMPLOYMENT IMPLICATIONS
41) This project will provide employment opportunities for both local and
appropriately skilled personnel in the area through Managalas Conservation
Foundation and other entities associated with the Conservation area and
other income generation and community development initiatives.
H. LEGISLATIVE IMPLICATIONS

42) Nil

=== page 8 ===

=== page 9 ===
MANAGALAS CONSERVATION FOUNDATION INC.
STRATEGIC PLANNING WORKSHOP

REPORT

KOKOPO

=== page 10 ===
Executive Summary:

The strategic plan workshop for Managalas Conservation Foundation was planned for the 2™ to 6”
of May 2016. The strategic plen was to coincide with the PWM fina! strategies program component
from 2013 to 2017. Before the actual strategic planning workshop which was held at Serefuna village
on the Managalas plateau, there were couple of meetings which | as the facilitator must undertake
under my ToR, firstly we had the combine staff and Board of PWM meeting, the second meeting was
with the Project officer of MCF, the third was with the Board Chairlady of PWM and finally a quick
meeting with the Chairman of MCF at Serefuna.

Apart from the five meetings that were held separately, there were some documents which | have to
do research into like the 2008 strategic plan for Managalas Development Foundation, the 2005
Leadership Summit Report -John Ericho, Managalas Conservation Area Support Project Combine
Forum Report —By ELS, Staff Policies and Procedures Manual by MDF, Conservation Application
Submission by Hon. Garry Jufa, Organisational Development Module 1 (Strategic Planning) and
Strategic Planning Manual by Frank Martinelli,7999 and lastly The constitution of MDF.

The summary of the meeting with PWM staff and Board is that;

i. They want MDE to have their own program activities in {ducation, Health and to do their
own fundraising fur their activities end that PWM will work with CBO’s on linking to the
Conservation program.

2. PWM strategic plan activities will finish on 2017 with RFN funding

3, The 2008 MDF strategic planning has the same vision, mission, core values, goals and
program activities has for PWM. It came like this as PWM saw it as beneficiazy to them to
implemen prograws et PWIA level with prozrem stafi working directly with MCF staff on
the Plateau implementing the same programs.

Key strategy 1: Conservation and Biodiversity

Purpose: To protect the forest and eco-systems from destructive land use practices

Key sicategy 2: Community Consensus Building

Purpose: Mobilise and empower communities through traditional decision making processes
Key strategy 3: Rainforest Literacy

Purpose: Infor conniuniy participation in sustainable evelopment options for the nature!
resource base

Key strategy 4: Community forestry and Climate change

Purpose: Mobilise communities in reforestation and mitigation and adaptation measures for socio

Background:

The Managalas Plateau is rich with untouched natural forest with pristine limestone streams, creeks,
and waterfall, rivers, watershed, rich in biodiversity including Flora and Fauna.

The Managalas Plateau is the home to the Barai, Namiai, Samoi, Berefo, Sofi, Oiko! and Omie
speaking tribe which are believed to be linked to the Koiari tribe.

The plateau is also home to the Queen Alexandra Bird Wing Butterfly and natural stance of the
Tamnalia well-known under its trade name as Okari. In 1984 a Feasibility Study was carried out on
the Managalas Plateau on the Okari tree and the Queen Alexandra Bird Wing Butterfly (QABB. The
QABB project was established in the Sofi speaking tribe area of the Managalas Plateau as a project.

Furthermore, the feasibility was initiated by Dr. Michael Olsson and students from the University of
Papua New Guinea.

3.0 LITERATURE REVIEW

3.1 General Background of Coffee Production
Coffee production in Papua New Guinea accounts for approximately 1% of the world production

according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). After oil palm,
coffee is Papua New Guinea’s second largest agricultural export, employing approximately 2.5
million people.

Coffee is the highest foreign exchange earner for Papua New Guinea, the majority of which is
grown in the Eastern Highlands Province, the Western Highlands Province and Chimbu. With the
industry not derived on a colonial plantation based system, production is largely by small farmers
with land holdings that grow as little as 20 trees per plot in coffee gardens alongside subsistence
crops. Predominantly in isolated places, the product is mostly certified as “organic coffee”.

Coffee production in the country dates back to 1926 and 1927 when the first Jamaican Blue
Mountain Coffee seeds were planted. However, the Coffee Research Institute claims that coffee
was introduced to British Papua in 1890, although it is widely accepted that commercial production

In 1950s, ihe infrastructure developed significantly in Papua New Guinea which facilitated a

The coffee industry in Papua New Guinea reached a peak in 1998 when it was responsible for some

3.4 Origin, Distribution and Uses

Coffee may have originated from Africa (Ethiopia esp. Arabica coffee) or South America. All species
are small trees (shrubs) and when left to grow, will reach a height of about 10m. Coffee is widely
cultivated and distributed throughout the humid tropics as a cash crop. Arabica coffee is important
in East Africa and is also cultivated in the highlands of Brazil as it prefers a cooler climate. Robusta
coffee is suited to production on lowland sites in the humid tropics and is extensively grown in
Brazil while Liberica coffee is grown in West Africa and Southeast Asia.

In PNG, only arabica coffee and robusta coffee are grown. Arabica is mostly grown in the highlands
and robusta is grown on the.coastal lowlands. P-oduction figures show that 95% of arabica and
only 5% of robusta are produced in PNG.

Like cocoa, coffee is used as a beverage. The relatively modern process is the preparation of
roasted coffee from the coffee seed. Other uses are masticatory (chewed as a stimulant) in Ethiopia
and can be fermented as an alcoholic drink.

3.5 The Coffee Industry in Papua New Guinea

3.3.1 A Brief History of Coffee in. Papua New Guinea
It is generally accepted that coffee was first introduced into the Pacific area in the late 18" century

by Dutch sailors. The first official record of its introduction to PNG is a note in the Annual Reports
of British New Guinea of coffee being planted in “a small botanical garden”. This same source
advised that by 1892 the crop was thriving in the Rigo district and that extensive plantings had
been established in the Sogeri area by 1898. Cartlege makes mention of the first research being
carried out by these pioneers. They were experimenting with direct planting of seed in the field.

Up to 70 hectares of coffee growing in the Papua area in 1908 with an export value of $915 in 1905
and 1908. Cartlege notes that the reports refer to at least three plantations in the Sogeri area and
that implementing of rubber with coffee was practiced. It is also reported that coffee was being
cultivated in Oro Province in the vicinity of Sangara with as much as 73 tons being produced in
1940.

The first plantings on New Guinea side were made by the New Guinea Department of Agriculture
close to Wau in 1928 and 1929. Coffee seed was first introduced into the highlands region by
Lutheran Missionaries in the pre-war years, this seed being taken from planting at the Dregerhafen
and established on their mission station at Asaroka in Eastern Highlands and Ogelbeng in Western
Highlands. it appears certain that coffee was established at Aiyura immediately after the station

8.0 DISCUSSION

The outcome of the activity was a success in marketing of the Managalas Organic Coffee from the East
zones (Kawowoki, Afore and Yoivi) all the way to Lae, Morobe Mountain Coffee Mill. It took almost 4
months to actually get results from the activity implemented. From the initial baseline information given by
Mr. Damien Ase, to the primary data collection at the plateau, to the actual implementation of the activity,
it was a very challenging task especially for a new employee of the organization.

The main idea was to help the farmers access a better market price other than the price they got from the
road buyers. The road buyers normally paid K1-K2 per kilo for the parchments and provide their own
container for shipment to the mills in Lae or as far as Goroka and Mt. Hagen, however, from the local
community's perspective, this wasn’t a fair price given to them. Hence Partners With Melanesians Inc. had
to take the initiative to help its local NGO on the plateau, The Managalas Conservation Foundation in
facilitating the process of the coffee marketing from the plateau all the way to the Morobe Mountain
Coffee mill in Lae.

A total of 286 organic coffee bags (brown bean) were collected from the three (3) zones weighing about
10854 kg. Zone 7A gave 86 bags, 78 gave 39 bags and Zone & gave 161 coffee bags, a total of 286 organic
coffee bags. The transport in the plateau was met by PWM in the hire costs as well as materials. After all
286 coffee bags were collected; the logistics in Oro Bay was arranged as mentioned in the methodology.

In Lae, the CBC representative and the SL¢ Officer both did arrangements fiom transport, logistics to the
dischargirg of the 20 foot coffee container at the Morobe Mountain Mill. The negotiations of the payments
were done by the CBO representative (Mr. Peter Sokane) and the Mill Manager vehich was agreed that
within 10 days the payments would be deposited into Partners account, however, it took 2months for the
payments to be done. This was;
