ACTIVITY: Managalas Conservation Area Onsite Official Declaration, 29% Tak

INTRODUCTION

‘This report entails activities starting from the preparation works up to the actual declaration
event. The event took place on the 29 of November 2017 at Itokama village. Stakeholder: f y
representatives from NGOs, TV &Print Media, Government and Donor Agencies were flown i) bl { t
on light planes from Port Moresby, some on the actual day while others two or a day earlier. Al

the logistics from Port Moresby to Itokama were arranged by PWM staff while most of ground

logistics were done by the MCF Officer responsible Mr Kingsford Nichoi and the CA Declaration

Committee that was set up purposely to take the lead on all the ground preparation work.

Prominent people and delegates that attended the event include Minister for Environment &
Conservation and Climate Change, Hon John Pundari, Oro Governor, Hon Garry Juffa, Member
for Sohe, Hon Henry Amuri, Deputy Head of Mission Ms Beate Gabrielsen from the Norwegian
Embassy Australia, Delegates from the Rainforest Foundation Norway, and UNDP Country
Director HE Mr Roy Trivedy,

It was a big event for the people of Managalas as the celebration marked $2 years of hard work
and perseverance to have their dream of protecting their land and rainforest from destructive
commercial development come true. The Managalas Plateau is now the second and largest
terrestrial Conservation Area in Papua New Guinea covering $60 000 Ha of forested land,
declared by the Minister for Environment & Conservation and Climate Change on the 29%
November 2017 at 12:51pm at Itokama village.

PURPOSE

This activity is the final step in the process of establishing a conservation area in PNG as per the
Conservation Areas Act 1978. The purpose is to officially declare to the whole country and the
international community that, the Managalas $60 000 Ha of land and forests is now a recognise
Protected Area in Papua New Guinea.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

Seven planes were chartered to airlift invited guests and delegates from Port Moresby and abroad,
as well as food stuff and other goods. The airline companies were, Air Saga, SIL and Air
Catalina/Helifix. The first flight into Itokama was on the 18 November 2017. Promotional
Materials, printed posters, banners, promotional printed shirts and caps and store food for the

Faeplas Cncivatn fova Declaration ~ 29° Uoreaber 2077
 event were airlifted on this charter including two PWM Officers (Patrick Vuet and Cecil Senive),
and PWM Board Member Tom Huasi. The three officers were on the ground in advance to ensure
ground preparations and logistic were going well and to give update on ground situations back to
the team in Port Moresby. The second charter was on the 27° November which airlifted mainly
media personnel’s from EM TV, NBC, FM 100 and Post Courier, accompanied by PWM Program
Manager Rufus Mahuru and PWM Board Member Mr Simon Savaiko. The rest of the delegates
and invited guests flew in on the 20%, Two charters manage to fiy back some guests after the
event while others were flown back to Port Moresby the next day because of bad weather in the
evening. Oro Governor Hon Gary Juffa and Minister for Environment & Conservation and
Climate Change flew in for the declaration event on a Chopper.

Cultural Day

‘The communities from the entire Managalas Plateau gathered at Itokama for the event. Itokama
village took the lead in preparing the venue, cleaning of the airstrip, school ground and oval, built
the stage and prepare accommodations for the people that came in from different parts of the
Managalas plateau and outside guests. A Conservation Area Declaration Committee (CADC) was
set up to oversee and took the lead in organising all ground logistics for the day. On the 28%
November, eve of the declaration Day, a Cultural Day organised by the CADC was held at
Navkonane village. Cultural Dancers from the 11 zones came and perform on this day with
speeches from invited guests Mr Manukayasi, Former PWM Executive Director and one of the
founders of the project, PWM Program Manager and other local leaders.

Prior to the charter trips to the plateau, 14x canvas (large), 2x tuffa toilet pots, assorted nails, and
other materials were sent on SIL plane to Sila airstrip Numba. MCF Conservation Officer
Kingsford Nichoi received them and hired youths to carry them to Itokama, as the road was in a
bad condition. Funds were also sent for airstrip clearance, road and bridge maintenance, and other
activities leading up to the declaration day. MCF staffs were assisting the CADC in the
preparation works toward the cultural day and the declaration day.

Community police officers were engaged to provide security on the day, as important people from
the government and other important people attended the declaration event. A local vehicle was
hired to move food from the zones starting from zone 8 all the way to zone 2 Tahama and shifted
them to Itokama village.

Collection of live animal species was done during the cultural Day show from all the CBOs that
took part in the event. The animals were collected and displayed near the grandstand on the
declaration day.

‘The event program was not adhered to by the two MPs resulting in them only spoke on that day
plus the welcome and opening remarks by Mr Malchus Kajia MCF BoD Chairman and Mr

 RECOMMENDATION

Observation from this event, in future similar events, funds must be controlled by the Officer in
charge at the project site. A committee can be formed to oversee the ground preparations but the
officer in charge must be the chairman or treasurer for the committee. The Officer in charge
knows very well financial situations and will control the use and spending accordingly, thus
minimize expectations.

Managalas Cultural Day Show should be celebrated annually on the 29" November at various
locations on the plateau.

CONCLUSION

Despite hiccups amongst CBOs and the Conservation Area Declaration Committee, the cultural
show and the declaration day went well and ended peacefully. There was no fair representation in
the committee, which cause some arguments and biasness especially on payment of some budgeted
activities. From the beginning of the year until the declaration, there was continuous emphasis for
community contribution toward the day. Some zones like zone + voluntarily contributed some
food and another clan contributed K1, 000.00 to the budget. There were also groups or clans and
individuals that contributed to the event. Cultural singsing groups came from almost all the zones

1. Give a short and to the point description of the project that you are applying for (max
0.5 pages)

A. Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project
Partners With Melanesians Inc. has been working with the people of the Managalas
Plateau, Ijivitari District, of the Oro Province for over two decades to protect the
360,000 hectares of rainforest, its habitants numbering over 20,000 and its natural
resources. Community mobilization and consensus building formed the cornerstone of
PWM’s mission in strengthening the traditional decision making processes, where the
communities voices are collectively echoed as one through the district wide combine
forums. The forums provided the platform to sortout miss-understandings, confusions,
conflicts and differences and to ensure peace, understanding, unity, stability and
cooperation is maintained amongst them as they continue to define their purpose.
The idea of protecting the Managalas Plateau was conceived much later, after
communities were organized, mobilized and made aware of the importance of several
important species of flora and fauna thought to be endemic to the area, one of which is
the Queen Alexandria Bird-wing Butterfly.

Additionally, due to the vastness and difficult terrain of the area, the 360,000 hectares of
landmass was divided into ten small clusters, made up of several clan groups, known as

=== page 2 ===
Multiple year application form:2018-2022

cultural zones, based on langauge grouping, kinship and family tics. Originally, those
clustered groups were convenicatly assembled for the purposes of building consensus
among clan groups, however, as it later turned out, these structures made management
of clan lands easily accessible for the participatory land use management planning in
Getermining the various uses of their land. Upon demacating the clan lands, sustainabic
livelihood alternative projects such as honcy bee farming, rice cultivation, subsistence
potato farming, organic coffee farming, amongst others, were encouraged on the
atlocated plots and proved to be sucessful, eventually providing alternative income for
the local communities.

The zones then formed community based-organizations (CBOs) and were formally
registered with the Investment Promotion Authority whose main purpose was to
management affairs of the cultural zones by raising income to support clan initiatives,
while sustainably managing the resources in the conservation area in the respective
zones, An umbrella organization, the Managaias Conservation Foundation, previousty
called Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) was set-up to coordinate and ensure
efficient performance and management of those CBO, after the arca becomes a
nationally declared conservation arca.

On the 8th of November 2012, PWM submitted an application to the Minister for
Environment and Conservation and CEPA for consideration uader the Conservation
Areas Act (1978) for processing for the next CA. After waiting for four years for all the

it finally went before the PNG National Execative Council (NEC) in 2016. On
the 15th of December 2016, NEC approved the PWM application by way of NEC
Decision No. 325/2016. The NEC decision will be effected for formality and legal status
through the National Gazcttal by the NEC Secretariat and CEPA after getting the
instruments drafted and sigace by the Head of State, HE Governor Genera! of PNG,
PWM is now awaiting that process and while waiting for the gazettal, PWM and the
loca! partacrs are preparing for the activities after gazcttal with the on-site declaration
to be on the Mamazaias plateau at Itckaimea,

For PWM, the challenge row is to cnsure that the Managalas Conservetion
Foundation’s (MCF) capacity is fully enbanced sand MCF made ready to take on the
huge task of managing the 360,000 hectares land, with 11 CBOs and over 20,000 peopie
in PNG’s second conservation. Additionally, the task beyong 2018 for PWM is to
consolidate the work with MCF in puttiug in place a Comservation Area Management
Committee to ensure the management and sustainability of the conservation area, and to
come up with a Conservation Area Management Plan and Strategies to guide tue
conservation efforts.

PWM will continue to facilitate and link MCF and its CBOs to other partners including
the respective government agencies who are able to support and ensure sustainable
development options are realised for the local communities as they continuc to conserve,
manage and utilise their natural resources for their livelihood for now and their future
generations.

3B. Inaina Wildlife Management Area Project
It began as an initiative of a visionary Clan Leader in opposing 2 scam SABL operation
for industrial large scale logging in the area and on their clan land measuring 9,712.20

=== page 3 ===
Multiple year application form:201 8-2022

hectares. The Fagagara clan from Inaina in the Kairuku Hiri District of Central
Province, approached DEC/CEPA and DCD for REDD+ projects and eventually, CEPA
invited PWM to be a partner in 2011 in what was a mere call for support in stopping the
logging operations. After successfully halting the logging operations, the success story
was an opportunity for concrete conservation efforts in protecting the arca from the
dangers of logging and other Industrial developments including Oil Palm. Guided by the
‘Flora and Fauna Protection Act’ PWM began the community consultation process,
mobilizing and creating awareness on environment protection and biodiversity
conservation as opposed to industrial, large-scale developments. In exactly five (5) years
of PWM’s involvement, Inaina was declared as a Wildlife Management Area (WMA) on
the 23° March 2017, after having passed all the requirements set by the government's
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) in accordance with the ‘Flora
and Fauna Protection Act’.

PWM is now working with the local communities to put in place a WMA Management
Plan and s WMA Management Committee to oversee the management of the WMA,
while at the same time, assisting to set up a focal body to coordinate conservation efforts

a) If you are applying for a continuation of a project please provide a bricf summary of the
project development and results until aow.

I. Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project:
The application for the conservation arca status was granted last year, on 15" December
by the National Executive Council and is now in the gazcttal process. Whilst this is
pending, PWM is working on the conservation areca managemcat plan in setting the
parameters of managing the conservation area once it is declared, PWM will work
closely with the Managatas Conservation Foundation (MCF), in setting up the
Conservation Aren Management Committec to oversee the management of the
conservation area. The local CBO (MCF) and the management committee will be
empowered to do fundraising and work closely with their local and provincial
government to assist the project in thcir annual budgets.

1 Proposed Karimaui Conservation Arca Project
PWM is currently putting together all mecessary documents and ensuring due processes
are completed for submitting the application for consideration of the conservation area
Status with Conseryation and Environmental Protection Authority (CEPA). The local
CBO known as Karimui Conservation and Resource Management Inc. (KCRMPI) have
already gone into fundraising and are working with their local and provincial
government to censure that project is recognized and included in their annual funding

budget.

Hil. Inaisa Wildlife Management Area Project:

Inaina was granted the Wildlife Management Arca status on 23 of March, 2017. PWM
is working closely with the local Community Based Crganization known as Fagegara
Development Foundation Inc. as the focal point of contact for the conservation initiative,
while at the same time, PWM is putting together 1a WMA Management Plan and
committee for the WMA. The local CBO will be also will be empowered te do
fundraising and work closely with their local and provincial government to assist the
project in their annual budgets. PwM is also approaching other stakcholders/donors for
an ecotourism hub to support the conservation efforts so far for sustainability.

IV. Proposed Collinwood Bay Conservation Area Project

This is a new Project and from our assessment so far, the communitics are disbaoded
and confused and it fs not very clear when actual activities will start despite a
stakcholder community consultation carried out in 2015, late 2016 and early 2017 to
gauge community consensus in establishing a fecal community group as point of contact
with PWM. in commencing work in the area.

b) How does the project relate to local, regional or national government plans and priorities?

All of PWM’s projects are guarded by the Fourth National Goal of PNG’s National
Constitution as the overarching goal: ‘Papua New Guinea’s natural resources and
environment to be conserved and used for the collective benefit of us all and are
replenished for the benefit of future generations’. PWM’s efforts are embedded in the
erabling legislations and policics in achieving the desired outcomes of the WMA (Inaina)
and the Conservation Arcas (Managa!as, Karimui and Collinwood Bay) sch include the
‘Environmental Act 2000’, and ‘Protect Area Policy 2014’. All in all, the PWM’s focus is

16

to achieve the National Strategy Framework as the Vision 2050 under the fifth Pillar
called ‘Environment Sustainability and Climate Change’.

c) How will the project you are applying for be monitored and evaluated? Please provide
information on the plans to monitor and evaluate the project, including how to monitor
indicators.

Monitoring and Evaluation tools were identified for cach of PWM’s nine (9) objectives
in its Strategic Plan. These tools will be developed and built into the project activities as
they happen. For example, a basic one-pager before and after sheet will be delivered in
an awareness workshop to measure the ‘learning gain’ in an issue. The same will apply
to all activities. Apart from that, measurable indicators like reports, documents, etc.,
(tangible products), number of participants in a training or capacity building workshop
will be used to indicate the total number of people attending trainings and workshops at

the end of the funding period or project cycle.

d) Outline the sustainability plan for the project beyond the application period (including
financial and managerial capacity to continue the project):

All four projects are community oriented and are from remote communities who very
much depend on the environment for their livelihood. The people will continue to utilize
their environment and its natural resources for sustenance. Hence, PWM is empowering
the people with environmental awareness, capacity building on effective leadership and
good governance, wealth creation, environment sustainability and natural resource
management etc. which they will utilize to conserve and manage their environment now
and in the future. In the meantime, the linkage, networking and partnership established
by PWM with outside sources will continue to support and benefit these communities,
even when PWM is no long present in these areas.

title: Report on the retreat at Dogarol site in the Managalas plateau Afore District Oro Province
snippet: Report on the retreat at Dogarol site in the Managalas plateau Afore District Oro province, on the 28June — 1° July 2019. Compiled by Simon Savaiko. (Vice Chairman of the PWM Board) Content: ¥ Acknowledgement. ¥ Day one purpose of the retre …
text:
=== page 1 ===
Report on the retreat at Dogarol site in the

Managalas plateau Afore District Oro province,
on the 28June — 1° July 2019.

Compiled by Simon Savaiko.

(Vice Chairman of the PWM Board)

=== page 2 ===
Content:

¥ Acknowledgement.

¥ Day one purpose of the retreat.

Y Day two: Brain storming for the challenges
Y Day three. Solutions for the challenges.

¥ Day four design future for MCF.

¥ BCF Board Meeting 1** July 2019

¥ Conclusion.

Introduction:

Tne symbolism of their welcome at the gate the splitting of plant was a sign of
harvesting a new garden. In all of Managalas plateau when people are harvesting new
garden this is a sign of showing families and relatives that the garden is now harvested.
Therefore it has a very significant symbc! shown from the beginning of the retreat as the
community welcomed us by splitting cf plant and second sign was the Bird Wing butter
fly breaking out of the piper during the retreat

The work that we have been doing in the plateau is very significant and simple
illustration of the above stories a reminding us of moving to another level in the work tht
we do for our people in the plateau. A new birth and a new beginning out from the pain
and suffering that we have been going through in the last thirty years So that boils
down to honesty and total commitment from all levels of leaders in this MCF unique
ministry that we are all called to serve.

The real actions of what we say and write must always been seen in the rea!
implementation of the work in the community. Transparency in our performance will
bring better transformation in the community where we serve as model for others to
learn.

=== page 3 ===
Acknowledgement: On behalf of the PVVM Board of management | thank the
Managalas Conservation Foundation Director Damien Ase and the MCF staff for the
invitation for Tom Huasi and | (Simon Savaiko) to attend the retreat and the MCF Board
meeting at Dogarol site in Afore, Oro Province on the 28” June — 1" July 2019. The
amazing clan group from Dogarol site who played very unique role to host the retreat at
their new site away from Afore main LLG station.

| also thank the clan groups from Dogaro! site who offered everything possible for the
four days retreat and to make sure everyone who are there enjoyed their time. That was
an exciting site where we experienced a real model for all the work we have been
fighting for many years in the Managalas plateau. Our going there was just only
beginning of all the many good things that we are going to do in the plateau. The big
lesson is to start with what we have in the plateau to show others what we have | the
plateau. | also want to thank all CBO’s who walked many hours by foot to get there for
this retreat. | believe their walking and time together was great beneficial because they
were able to put together new ideas to move MCF forward with their ideas in the
plateau.

And not forgetting to thank Tom Huasi PWM Board member who was able to come with
me to the retreat and was there for the whole week with the staff and the Board
members. His visit was an expression of his faith and love for the work in the
Managalas plateau. He was a motivator and good encourager to many of the old time
friends who journeyed the work in the plateau together early 1990s

Day one:

On Thursday morning Tom Huasi and Damien Ase, Obert and | (Simon Savaiko)
checked in 5am and travelled to Popondetta on the early morning flight. The MCF
Chairman Mr. Malcus kajia and the driver plus Ezekiel Garui met us at Girua airport
and drove us to town. After banking and shopping we than left met again at the MCF
Office.

=== page 4 ===
Then we left the town around 5.30¢m and travelled the high way to Afore. Damien and!
traveiled on MCF vehicle while Obert and Ezekiei travelled on hired vehicle and arrived
Afore at 11.30 pm. dropped off cargo and drove to the camp site at Dogarol at 12.30
midnight. We arrived very late so the clan group in Dogarol lake site did not welcome us
and we all went into our rooms and slept until next morning.

Day Two

Early in the morning after breakfast we all gathered at the main gate to the site. The
clan group performed a trad:tional weicome by singing composed songs and ied us te
the meeting house. The hosting clan weicomed us into the building at Dogarot site
where we conducted the retreat for four days.

The official opening began with welcome by the hosting clan leader Jarod and followed
by MCF Chairman Malcus kajia and the Director of MCF Mr. Damien Aseari. Then |
(Simon Savaiko} shared from the book of Acts 3:1-10 as an introduction before officiai
opening of the retreat: These were some of the challenges to us as people of the
Managaias pleateau.

e The cripple man for 40 years waiting to be healed = Managalas has been waiting
for 40year for change and development.

e Peter and John gave him not gold and silver but healed him in Jesus name for
eternity.= CBO’s MCF and PWM are like Peter and John to transform Managalas
with total commitment and trust in God for better transformation.

e Whatis the best gift that we can give to the people of Afore: Give the bst
dedication and commitment of honest service that we can offer to our people to
see God in our serve.

¢ Most importantly give them Jesus who is the source of management to manage
his resources (the garden forest) he has given tc us in the plateau.

=== page 5 ===
After sharing the challenges from the Scripture, on behalf of the PVVM Board
Management, | declared the retreat opened with a word of prayer.

Then all our meeting was conducted inside the same building for ail four days. After
official opening Damien Aseari the Director for MCF took the lead to share with us
the purpose and the objectives of the of what is a staff retreat. He outlined four
important reasons why retreats for any organizations are very important. Crispin
Burava and Dickson Darebo MCF staff members helped and did all writings on the
papers during the discussions. Every points were written and pined on the wall as
we all went through the discussion each day.

1. Team Bonding

2. Reflection and Evaluation
3. Creative drive

4. Design the future.

He elaborated more on the four key points the importance for retreat and went into
the following objectives of the retreat:

1. Old staff refreshed and refocused on the MCF and CBO’s work.

2. New staff oriented on MCF and CBO’s work

3. Obstacles and challenges addressed

4. MCF and CBO's old and new bonded as team to unity and work together to
move forward MCF work in the Managalas conservation area.

On the first day the CBO’s and the Board member with their MCF staff looked back to
all that they have done and struggles and experiences that they have gone through in
the past years within the Managalas Conservation work in the Afore district. They made
a list of 42 issues in the Managalas conservation area. Than before the end of the day
all participants were put into groupings and the issues were distributed to different
groupings to come up with some solution for the issues.

=== page 6 ===
Day Three:

On Saturday monring after the breakfast we met again in the same building the SLA
team to give report on the Coffee: But before Mr: Orbert reported on the plan for his first
shiftment of coffee in the plateau the chief of Dogarol called leaders to meet outside the
house. At the time of welcome Mr. Obert PWM staff arrived late and there was not
welcoome. So they called for a customary way to reconcil themselves with Obert before
continuing the meeting. The chief and the elders came with some vegies and had a
chicken with it and called Obert to shake hands to show their respect for the PW/M's
assistance to the development in the Dogarol site. After the shaking of hand Obert gave
a short appeciation talk and thank the leaders for the unexpected event that happened
durign the retreat which showed the great value of relationship.

~

a ~ eee 5 ic

Then we aii moved into the building again to continue the report from the cofffee team.
Mr. obert expiainea that the road is bad so he will plan to move the first 300 bags to
popondetta and traveii to Lae with Raynoid Asip to find the good buyers. They will talk
to them for good price before they wili continue to buy more coffee outside of Afore
area. The next station that the team will be based to shift all coffee will be at Kuaruwo
and that will begin as soon as they return from Lae depending of the weather.

Then Mr. Rayneld Asip gave his report on the trip to port Moreby for coffee awareness
in Port Moresby. He reported that already people from the plateau are taking other
companies and coming into the plateau to buy coffee and seiling to other people
overseas. The true organic coffee in the plateau is very rich and has a good price many
people are interested. We need to find only good buyers so the benefit of our good
organic coffee will come back to our growers in the plateau.

He continued to share about what makes the organic coffee very rich and some good
reasons why conservation is good for our coffee farmers in the Managalas plateau.
Then he showed a diagram that shows how coffee tree gets good food from the soil to
bear good fruits.

He explained clearly about how the soil becomes rich to provide good food for the
coffee tree to grow well. i felt that these are some important information that needed tc
be translated by young people in the village. So people who do not understand meaning

=== page 7 ===
in other languages can be able to read this in their own languages during adult classes
so they will look after their soil and land to grow good organic coffee.

He also explained, when is the best time to pick the right kind of coffee so when the
organic goes through the process and at th end the organic coffee will still taste organic.

As | listened | noticed that this is the very important information that the farmers in the
plateau needs to know in their langauge. So they can look after their coffee gardens
well and pick the right kind of coffee beans at the right time. These information /books
should be translated into languages for all farmers so they will read and understand this
information in their own languages, through their adult classes and clan group meetings.

Mr Raynold explained that the first lot of coffee and decide what he as was and each
groups were called to come out and present their solutions to the issues they were
entrusted to work on. Each groups presented their solutions and Cripsine Burava and
Dickson Darebo helped Damien Aseari and did all the recording of their solutions. That
was a great opportunity for all members to share their own thoughts and made
suggestions to looking back to their struggles and weaknesses in the organization.
Below are some of their issues as they did reflection and evaluation of their
achievement in the past.

Some of the challenges that they shared in the retreat were as listed beiow

1. Office space for MCF and equipment for the office are great need because no
office so all workers are scattered in the plateau.

2. MCF to have own donor and have separate financial accountabilbity to have
auditing for the organization.

3. MCF Board and the CBO's do not know their roles and responsiabilities in the
organization and so others are doubling their roles.

4. Lack of coorperation with in the staff and the CBO’s within the organization and
shows no respect for each other

=== page 8 ===
5. No equa! distributions to other zones with in the organization te encourage the
people in all zones in the plateau.

Introduction:

Planning is very vital for every organisation's and individual person to achieve their goals
or dreams. In order to achieve that goal and dream, you have to make plan to know how
much time and resources will be required to achieve it with given deadlines. Therefore
Partners with Melanesians is guided by its work plan to work towards achieving its goals,
purpose, vision & mission. Plans can be changed and revised as time goes by to allow for
improvement or alterations due to the surrounding circumstances along the way.

Partners with Melanesians annually has two planning workshop in February and June
respectively. This year 2019, we had the first planning workshop at PNG Bible Translation
Association, Waigani from the 8° — 12* of April 2019.

1:0: INTRODUCTION

Report writing workshop was conducted by PwM Project Officer and co-facilitated by
the Managalas Development Foundation at the Barai Non-formal Education
Association. (BNEA) from the 17 - 20" May 2004.

The workshop was purposely for the Community Based Organisations, Mothers
Groups, Community Learning Centres (CLCs) and any other interested observers.

A total number of thirty four (34) participants (appendix 1) attended the workshop.
The first day of the workshop was for the staff (MDF and PwM) to recap and
familiarized the topics prior to the workshop.

There were four (4) main components of the report writing workshop:
1. Field Trip Report Format;
2. Detail Work plan,
3. Activity Updates, and
4. Implementation Schedule.

This report will emphasis on the four (4) main components and will the exercises by
the participants as a result of this workshop.

1.1: OBJECTIVE:

The main objective of the workshop was to:
> To learn and understand the basic skills in report writing.
> For Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) to transfer the skills
to their Community Based Organisation.

1.2: BACKGROUND:

Most of the trainings conducted at the project site were conducted by outsiders
(facilitator/ trainer) and it was first of its kind that MDF took the lead to facilitate the

workshop.

The main idea behind this workshop was to put into practice what they (MDF) had
acquired since the beginning of the process since now. Much have been learnt,
however not much have been put into practice. This was one of the workshops that
will be seen as the stepping towards the theme “Kua flenmi” the self reliance society.

1.3: NORMS / VALUES:

Prior to the workshop, the participants came up with their norms and values as in
house rules for them to follow. The norms are;

i. No chewing/smoking inside
ii. Punctuality
iii. Disposal of rubbish in right place
iv. Use understandable language
v. Raise hands for questions
vi. Lost & found properties to owners
vii. Respect one another
viii. Use toilet properly.

Some of these norms and values were strictly observed and followed, however, some
of them didn't seems to be of that importance and they were changed during the
period of the session.

2.0: FIELD TRIP REPORT.

There are many methods to write a report and one of the simplest forms is the
“Field Trip Report”. The field trip report was a follow up of the report conducted
by Partners with Melanesians in 2003 at Serefuna village. The field trip report was
basically to build the capacity of the Community Based Organisations (CBO) to
report to Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) to monitor and evaluate the
activities implemented by the Community Based Organisations.

2.1. FIELD TRIP REPORT CONTENT.

A simple field trip report contains the following components:
a) Brief on the location of the visit, date of the visit and the officer

writing the report.

Village /Zone/ Place of visit,

Date of the visit,

Reported by, (name of the officer)

His/her position,

Date of the report.

i, ie a Vii

b) Purpose of the Field Trip.
The reason for the field trip carried out.

c) Description of the activities carried out.

a) List of activities that need to be followed up.
e) Other observations/comments by the officer.
f) Recommendation.

3.0: DETAIL WORK PLAN:

The Community Based Organisations (CBOs) have their monthly work plan, however
some of their activities clashed due to Managalas Development Foundation (MDF),
Partners with Melanesians (PwM) and the Community’s activities. The Community
Based Organizations were advised to get a copy of Partners with Melanesians and
Mananaglas Development Foundation’s work plan to avoid such inconvenienced,

Since it is a requirement to justify the Community Based Organizations (CBO) and
Community Learning Centres’ (CLC) advance and for MDF to monitor the CBOs’ are
actually implementing the planned activities, the CBOs are required at the end of
each month to submit their work plan for the next month at the end of the previous
month. However, most of the CBOs had doubts and cannot provide their work plan.

The CBOs were taught the basics about work plan during the workshop. The main
components for the Community Based Organizations to consider were the
followings:

Date ( day (s} week(s}, month(s} )

Detail activities to do,

Budget ( resources, funds, time)

Person/institute to coordinate the activity.

4.0: ACTIVITY UPDATE:

Activity update or monthly update indicates the activities that were planned for the
previous month were implemented. This update will indicate to Managalas
Development Foundation that the planned activities were implemented so that MDF
can request for their monthly allowance to compensate them.

Managalas Development Foundation then uses these reports to submit to Partners
with Melanesians whereas Partners with Melanesians categorise them into the major
components and report to the respective donors.

CONCLUSION:

* As aconcluding remark, the participants were told that the workshop was
conducted purposely for them by Managalas Development Foundation (MDF)

for these reasons:

* Easy Excess to information and assistance when they need help in terms of;
Report Writing,
Planning Detail Activity,
Activity Update, and
Implementation Schedule.
* The terms used can be translated in their own language(dialect)

* ‘To build the capacity of Managalas Development Foundation,

* Identify areas in which MDF can improve their skills.

The workshop was closed with a word of prayer and remarks from the participants
and observers, later added up with a break up lunch.

RECOMMENDATION:

1. MDF to attend trainings and transfer skills to the community,

2. MDF to monitor and evaluate CBOs activities and updates,

3. Want more of trainings conducted by locals.

text:
=== page 1 ===
Enumeration of trees and other vegetation at the Guguavo Ridge in the
Owen Stanley Range of Papua New Guinea.

Kasbeth Evei

Postgraduate Centre, University of Papua New Guinea P O Box 320 Uni PO, N.C.D

Introduction
This survey was basically done to establish the abundance and species diversity of trees
and other plants that occur in the primary forests of Tetebedi area. In Papua New Guinea
(PNG), Montane primary forests are home to many endemic plants and animals.
Likewise, the primary forests at Guguavo ridge is no exception since it contain some of
PNG’s endemic plants and animals.

The Guguavo Ridge upper montane primary rainforest has a sparse distribution of
trees and other forest fiour planis with a 20m visibility. The forest is made up of 80
species of trees ranging from 2m to more than 30m, several species of herbs and vines
(lianas), ferns, gingers, orchids, pandans, palms and bamboos which total up to more than
130 species of plants.

This study enabied us to establish tree density (per m2) and species distribution in
the survey area.

Methods

The survey plot is located on Guguave Ridge some !00km East of Port Moresby and
situated at 1600m above sea level in the Cwen Stanley Range. It is a three hours walk
away from the nearest airstrip of Tetebedi viliage in Cro province.

A 20m X 200m (0.4 ha) sample plot was randomly selected along the ridge. We
marked trees and saplings with the DBH (Diameter at Breast height) of 7cm and above.
We collected leaf voucher specimens for further identification. Cther forest flour plants
were noted as inhabitanis of the foresi area.

Tree height data analysis
Height of trees were categorized inte six height classes; dm-4m =1, Sm-9m =2, 10m-i4m
= 3, 15m-19m = 4, 20m-24m =5, 25m or more = 6.

Results
540 trees were sampled within the 0.4 ha plot. Just over half the trees were between !m

and Si, While nearly 40% were between 10m to iSm andi0% were above 20m. The
highest DBH of the trees was 150cm and the highest iree height was 32m (see
appendix1). There are more than 80 species of trees and another 70 to 80 other plant
species that make up the whole of Guguavo Ridge Rainforest area (see appendix 2).
There were about 2 trees/m2. Altogether, there were more than 130 species cf plants that
were observed. The dominant species of trees include, Cryptocarya, Litsea, Pouteria,
Evodia and Castenopsis.

Discussions

Tropical rainforests make up 7% of the world’s surface area (Swaine, 1965) and contain
more than half of the known terrestrial organisms but yet, the least understood of all the
major vegetation types (Collinson, 1975). Every effort must be made to protect all
sections of the tropica! rainforests of the world, including Papua New Guinea.

As such, the Guguavo Ridge montane rainforest is home to some of the Papua
New Guineas mest endangered and endemic species of plants (Trees and orchids} as well
as anime!s and fungi. Since the site occurs at the top of the mountains, it is vuineradis te
landslides, soil erosion and species loss shouid there be a slight disturbance in the forest
structure. This would then affect the distribution and dispersion strategies of several tree
species since not al! species of trees have the same dispersal mechanism. For example, in
this survey, the Evodia is randomly dispersed while Pouteria and Castenopsis are
dispersed regularly and the Cryptoceryas and Litseas have 2 clumped dispersion ia the
plot.

A good number of timber and non-timber forest products occur within the area
which means that a sustainable forest use practice be encouraged for the region. The
Forest in the long run, will act as a seed bank, sustain all life, retain and recycle nutrients
rapidly and will continue to so for thousands of years (Walter, 1985). Other benefits from
the forests includes poliution indications (esp. SO2) and standing forest biomass will act
as Carbon sinks (absorb carbon dioxide).

Recommendations
The people, especially the older men and woman of the Tetebedi area have an invaluable

ethno biolcgica! and natura! history knowledge of all the naiural resources that surrounds
them. it will be a bonus shouid there be some sort of documentation of these knowledge
in the future encounters.

i would push for a Wildlife Management Area to be established as soon as possible so as
to instill the concept of “public natural resource ownership” for sustainable resource use.
To continue to show up physically every now and then to oversee how things are being
conducted with the people, by the people with a little bit of outside intervention will be
rewarding for all stakeholders.

|. Introduction.

Two facilitators (John Ericho, Abane Haefa) were contracted to carry out the week long
meeting/workshop at Serefuna in the Managalas Plateau from the 19" — 25* December 2005. At the pre-
meetings with the Partners with Melanesians (PwM) the terms of reference was issued and a briefing was
given and questions were raised to ensure everyone was on the same wavelength. The two facilitators
met and presented a tentative outline of the programs to PwM staff to comment and improved the
program outline. The team was transported by hire transport to the Itokama over the Owen Stanley
Range. After about an hour and half walk the team arrived at our destination.

In this report a brief background is presented, followed by a brief description of TOR, a list of the team
members, a brief description of methods used, and the issues to be addressed. Then discussion points
are captured and presented followed by next steps and a summary at the end.

ll. Background.

Partners with Melanesians (PwM) are a national NGO established about 20 years to work closely with the
people of the Managalas Plateau. The Managalas Plateau is described below in the Terms of Reference
background information as follows.

Managelas Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 to 1000 meters of altitude above the coastal
plain of Oro Province and is situated south of Popondetta and North of Port Moresby. It stretches
between the Owen Stanley Ranges to the south and west, the Sibium Ranges and Mt. Lamington and
the Hydrogrphers to the north ands east. it encompasses 380 000 ha, comprising areas of alpine heights
of 3 800 meters, montane and hill forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens. The
countryside is very mountainous and ridges. rivers, and water falls make up the scenery. About 12-15000
people of approximately 150 clan groups are living in 40 village communities. Clusters of sub-clan
groups, around which most social and economical activity is organized today, effectively fall into ten
cultural zones.

People in Managalas are subsistence farmers and grow their own food of yam, taro, kaukau and other
garden produce. The Plateau also boasts cash crops which includes; coffee, vanilla and peanuts and
okari nut. Most of these have not been sold out due to lack of proper roads and air transport costs being
too high. While the opportunity exist to develop economically. Logging and oil palm development lurks
precariously in the background threatening menacingly to overtake the Plateau in the guise of economic
development. Thus the beginning and inception of the Managalas Program by PwM is to arrest that
threat. The Managalas Program includes three main programs. These include: the Consensus building,
the Capacity Building and the Conservation Program. The Consensus building program embarked on
mobilizing and organizing the Managalas communities into 10 cultural zones each zone incorporating a
community based organization (CBO). It was envisaged that the MDF will develop into a well trained and
organized organization to work with each of the CBOs to help realize the vision of developing, “A
peaceful and self reliant communal society living in harmony with nature’. This was the Exit Strategy
envisaged years ago. The Consensus building program has nearly completed this task. The Capacity
building project also worked hard to develop the capacity of the MDF and CBO Board and Management.
These two projects are ongoing and are nearing the completion stages. The Conservation project is
continuing with mapping and inventory work and this needs more emphasis and focus as it has the
possibility of being derailed by socioeconomic development requirements.

INTRODUCTION

Theatre is used to entertain as well as educate. Theatre has been a bridge between
entertainment and education and is used to share news, share history and or
educate communities. Jt is interactive where audiences discuss controversial and
sensitive issues in sexuality, H]V and or relaicd issues and other development
issues. Since HIV is linked to many sensitive and controversial issues, drama can
be seen as a powerful strategy to challenge certain attitudes and risky behaviours
and promote accurate information.

Theatre basically is to change the knowledge, attitudes, or behaviours of audience.
In this context, theatre will be used to educate people in the communities about
safer sex practices through drama performances, thus providing and enabling
environment for behaviour change.

Papua New Guinea, like many countries and cultures in the world, where more
than 75 per cent of the population are not too well educated, this media is very
familiar and popuiar and the skills are found in the community.

This manual will be used as a guide for facilitators of comnmunity based theatre
iainings. Representatives from district or community based Theatre Grouns will

be trained on the basics of theatre and the techniques which than could be used to
dramatise situations or issues affeciing ibe communities they come front.

1.3 Name games are many and varied. This is the most common, and involves
sitting in a circle and involves rhythmic beats.

The group establishes a simple four beat rhythm. Beat one is slapping the
thighs, beat two is clapping, beat three is clicking the fingers of the right hand,
and beat four is clicking the fingers of the left hand. When the rhythm has been
established (not too fast) the first player says their name on the third beat (as
they click their fingers on the right hand) and then says the name of another
player on the fourth beat (as they click their fingers on their left hand). The
new player continues the sequence and so on.

For example: Slap clap Ezekiel Lames, slap clap Hohora Sari, slap clap
Julieanne Gore, etc.

Players keep the beat constant. This is good fund and excellent for rhythm
development, The game relies on all players having pre-knowledge of each
other’s names.

SESSION 2: OVERVIEW OF THEATRE
Learning Outcomes:

e Be able to share and acknowledge the experiences of various district based

e Have a fair knowledge on the development of theatre from the Western to the
developing world.

Materials: |Manual, Butcher paper, paper, marker pens and pen
Duration: 45 minutes

Activity 1:
Sharing Experiences
i. Ask participants to get in to groups and share their experiences with the

different community groups they belong to.
E.g. what were some of the feedbacks they got from communities they
performed in, and or what are some of the impact in the community where
people have responded to the Response of HIV and AIDS after their
performances?

ii. After sharing within their small groups, ask each group to present one or two
experiences to the whole group.

Activity 2:

Give about 20 minutes to the participants to read notes on the development of
theatre, “Origins of Theatre” and “Popular Theatre” and do a general discussion on
the readings.

ORIGINS OF THEATRE

Theatre existed in the Civilization of the Western world for the lasi 3000 years.
Little information about the Origin of Theatre has survived. The information we do
have comes from wall paintings, decorations, artifacts, and picture writing system
that show the importance of successful hunts, seasonal changes, life cycles, and
stories of the gods. From these people have seen the necessity of passing along the
experience of the old to the young through art, storytelling and dramatising events.
Even today cultures that do not have written languages have developed some form of
drama to dramatise imagination and the spirituality of people.

Drama is part of most diverse societies’ cultural heritage and it mirrors daily
livelihoods. That is mainly because of its relationship to festivals and religious
practices. In most cultures, communities identify themselves in drama as
dramatization of specific issues reflect the cultures. Drama reflects reality and needs
an interpretation of it to which it has an effect on individuals. Drama provokes
reflection and in a way stimulates the analytic potential of individuals. And it creates
a mirror effect to which individuals look at themselves at a different perspective.

People are born with body languages which are the early steps of mankind, and
drama was very likely spontaneously embedded in those early steps. Theatre

emerged from myth, ritual, and ceremony. Early societies see connections between
14 Community Theatre Facilitator's Guide 2002

=== page 13 ===
certain actions performed by the group or the leaders in the group and the desired
results of the society. These actions moved from habit, to tradition, and then to
ceremony and ritual. Rituals have always being a way to communicate with gods and

spirits and are repeated every year, or every season, and relate very much to the
agricultural cycle.

Rituals evolve along two main avenues. Rituals are accompanied by myths and the
myths enter the story telling tradition, gaining a life beyond original rites. This new
life allows the myths to move towards entertainment and admirable and pleasant
appearance. The two main avenues which rituals evolve along include;
* rituals, where myths are central, evolve into full blown religious worship, and
e Rituals were performance was central, becomes artistic expressions such as
dance and theatre.
Although boundary between these trends sometimes seems narrow, the distinction is
valid for every culture, since the evolution has been similar.

Through these rituals. leaders, or actors of sorts, emerged. These acting or leadership
roles were often filled by elders and priests. In addition, the beginning of acting
spaces or auditoriums developed as a result of more elaborate rituals. The earliest
example of ceremony and ritual evolving towards theatre comes from ancient Egypt.
“Pyramid texts” dating from 2800 to 2460 B.C., contain dramas sending the dead
pharach off to the underworld. These dramas also the continuity of life and the
pharach’s power. There is also the Memphite Drama. recounting the story of the
death and resurrection of the god Osiris, and the coronation of his son Horus. The
most important Egyptian. drama, though, was the Abydos passion play. Like the
Memphite drama, the Abydos passion play concerns the story of Osiris. The
paramount Egyptian myth, this drama was enacied at the most sacred place in Egypt,
Abydos- the burial site of Osiris. Performed annually from 2566 to 550 B.C. and
full of spectacle, this passion play js the first of its kind ever recorded and is the first
exampic of theatre.

i is from these initial forms of representation that drama became a form of
entertainment. By studying the practices of abcriginal and the native people will
enable us tc understand what took place among our primitive ancestors. The sense of
play has been a part of drama since the beginning. Not only do aciors play but
midicnces do also play by enjoving the play and interacting with the actors. The
bridge between performers and the audience is build straight away and encoureges
Further artistic or creative creation.

Here in PNG, non-verbal communication is through the body movesment or dance as
the dance medium has been more dominant than drama. 4n example would be the
Dukduk dance from East New Britam Province. The Dukduk dancers represent the
unseen spirits of the ancestors.

15 Community Theatre Factinaror 's Guide 2003

=== page 14 ===
.

POPULAR THEATRE:

-In the Developing countries there are two types of Theatre: One is the Theatre which
takes place in a forma! context which is very much more European and is aimed at
smal] cultural elite in urban areas, and the other takes place in the open as an
instrument to communicate important messages for the community. There are many
encouraging experiences of popular theatre in some developing countries.

“Popular theatre is gaining increasing attention in the Third World as a tool for popular
education and community organizing. It finds expression in a number of forms including
drama, music dance, puppetry and poetry and is performed for — and aften by — ordinary
peasants and workers. Popular theatre is used as a means of bringing people together,
building confidence and solidarity, stimulating discussion, exploring alternative options for
action, and building a collective commitment to change: starting with people's urgent
concerns and issues, it encourages reflection on these issues and possible strategies for
change.

For three decades popular theatre has been used in processes of development
communication as part of adult education programmes. From these initiatives grew a
special type of popular theatre, called 'theatre for development.’ In workshops training
people in the use of popular theatre techniques an inventory of local problems is made for
later use in the plays. In each play one problem theme is explored by and for the local

community."
(By: Jaap R. Swart, Center for the Study of Education in Deveicping Countries/Radio Netherlands Training
Center, The Hague, The Netherlands)

The approach of popular or community theatre is that performances must be linked
to crucial analysis, organisation and struggle. The concept of community theatre
emphasizes the revolutionary value of art. Instead of being merely a pleasant and
gratifying spectacle, community theatre (and art) aims to distribute, to shake, to
move the society towards self and critical thinking and action.

Majority of the people in PNG are illiterate hence theatre has been identified as one
of the effective approaches in educating people especially in rural communities
about the HIV and AIDS and related issues , and about safe sex practices as wel! as
caring for people living with HIV. The objective of community theatre is to allow
values and behaviour to be discussed comfortably without directly challenging the
community or individual beliefs and values. And to generate further discussions in
communities on the issues of HIV and AIDS and the ways they can respond to
protect themselves and their children. The approach or the purpose of community
theatre is that communities use popular theatre as a medium to educate communities
on the basic HIV information. And since most of the Theatre Groups are district
based they are able to facilitate sustainability and local ownership.

Non — Verbal Communication:

Non-verbal communication is very important in acting. It is important in drama as
well as everyday life.

Non-verbal communication is an essential part of everyday life, 2/3s of all
communication is non-verbal. Non verbal communication includes, but is not limited
to: tone, mood, and posture, facial expressions, gestures, movement, clothing,
colors, distance, and touch, avoidance of touch, eye contact, pitch, rate, and volume.
Non-verbal communication can be used in addition to verbal communication,
because the definition of non-verbal communication is “Anything communicated
that is NOT the intellectual content of your words”.

There are four main types of gestures.

. The first one is Defining, it conveys a location. An example would be

pointing.

The second is Describing, such as texture, shape, or size.

Then there is Whole idea, this conveys an entire concept. such as twirling

your finger by your ear means crazy.

4. The last type of gesture is Emotional Tone, these display moods and are
illustrated with the Entire body.

The Circle and the cross: Participants stand in circle, apart from each other. Draw
an imaginary circle with their right arm. Tell them to draw an imaginary circle with

their right arm. Then, ask the group to draw _a cross with the left arm. Thirdly, the
trainer asks them to do both at the same time: right arm a circle, and left arm a cross.

Introduction:

Explain the main element of a script. Every play has to have a theme or a topic for
example ‘It Takes Two to Tango’, and a plot or story line (the incidence and events),
and the intention or message. Five or six scenes of 5 minutes each should be enough
for a 30 minute play.

A script should have different parts: First, an introduction to the topic which presents
the main characters and the story. The introduction in a play has to be such that it
captures the attention of the audience right away. Second, it has to present a conflict
that relates to the topic. Thirdly it has to_ build suspense so the audience will be
questioning the main issues. Fourthly, the tensions have to reach a climas which has
to be surprising and appealing to the audience. Finally, the script has to provide a
solution with which the audience will indentify. The concept of climax is very
important. There has to be a progress to reach the climax.

Before writing the script, it is important to create a simple story line or synopsis,
with a short description of each character and scene. Complete dialogues can be
written iater.

Group Activity:

Ask participants to get into three (3) groups and work separately on ideas for a story
line on any HIV related issues. The participants are to use a basic drama plot, with
only three or four characters; with a conflict and a solution to the conflict. The
groups should also decide which characters will deliver the main messages. The
initial plot should also have some allowance for comic situations, jokes, music, etc.

After the group work, ask the participants to present their story line. Retain the best
idea and note on the butcher paper. Then select a participant from each group to

Actor Space

in popular theatre the audience surrounds the performers while in classic theatre the
audience is facing the actors. However, it is important to divide the scenic space so
the actors can refer to their positions in a common language. There are various types
of acting stages. The most commonly used stages popular theatre are proscenium,
thrust, and in and around staging.

TYPES OF STAGING
1. Proscenium Staging

A Proscenium theater is a theatre space whose primary feature is a large archway
(the proscenium arch) at or near the front of the stage, through which the audience
views the play. The audience directly faces the stage, which is typically raised
several feet above front row audience level, The main stage is the space behind the
proscenium arch, often marked by a curtain which can be lowered or drawn closed.
The space in front of the curtain is called the "apron." The areas obscured or hidden
by the proscenium arch and any curtains serving the same purpose (often called /egs
or formentors) are called the wings. Any space not viewable to the audiences is
collectively referred to as offstage.

Above: an example of Proscenium staging - the interior of the Auditorium Building in
Chicago built in 1887. The arch around the stage is a proscenium.

3. In The Round Staging

Theatre-in-the-round or arena theatre is any theatre space in which the audience
surrounds the stage area.

Theatre-in-the-round concept requires no stage curtain, little scenery and allows the
audience to sit on three sides of the stage.

The stage itself in this arrangement is typically round, square, or triangular, with
actors entering and exiting through the audience from different directions or from
below the stage. Such a space is usually configured with the stage on an even level
with or lowered below the audience in a "pit" or “arena” formation. This
configuration lends itself to high-energy productions, and is especially favored by
producers of classical theatre.

Theatre-in-the-round presents problems since actors at all times have their back
facing some members of the audience. However, it also allows for interesting and
realistic staging. Special consideration needs to be taken in regard to the set design,
so as not to hide any audience member's view of the performance.

text:
=== page 1 ===
Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing
Butterfly (QABB) Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made
Threats to Habitat in Managalas Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New
Guinea.

T. MALA

CURATOR
ENTOMOLOGY
BIOLOGY DEPARTMENT,
UNIVERSITY OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA

For
Partners With Melanesia
25TH — 30TH MAY 2008

=== page 2 ===
Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing Butterfly (QABB)
Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made Threats to Habitat in Managalas
Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New Guinea Undertaken from 25" - 30th May 2008.

INTRODUCTION

The Queen Alexandra's Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) (Ornithoptera alexandrae) is
the world's largest butterfly with female wingspans up to and over 250 mm
(Parsons 1999). QABB are confined to primary and advanced secondary
rainforest from sea level up to 800 m in the Popondetta Plain, Cape Hunt Ward,
and Afore regions of the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea (PNG) (Fig.1)
(Parsons 1999, Mercer 1999). QABB is monophagous on Pararistolochia dielsiana
in the Aristolochiacea family, a plant family famous for it's potent toxic
compound aristolochic acid (Mercer 1999, Mebs and Schneider 2002, Jicki
2002). However, several forms or types of P. dielsiana are known to occur with
the range of QABB. These types are largely distinguished by their flower shape
and color (Fig.2). Local conservation biologists have noticed a disparate usage
of these P. dielsiana types by QABB but to date no studies have addressed why
and reportedly one vine form is thought to be harmful to the larvae (pers.
comm. E. Malaisia).

The tremendous size of QABB, its natural scarcity, and limited range of the
species has made it a species of concem for conservation biologist (Parsons
1984, Gimenze 1996}. In addition, in the 40 years increases in the oil palm and
timber industries in the Popondetta region have fragmented and destroyed
large tracts of suifable habitat for the QABB (Parson 1984, 1990). QABB is
currently protected by domestic, the Fauna and Flora Act, and international
law, the Conservation on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES). At
present it is listed as a CITES | species (highly endangered) and import/export
and collection is prohibited.

A number of research projects on the QABB have been carried out over the
past 40 years. The first was a study by Ray Staatman that helped to illuminate
the life cycle of the QABB and some of its basic habitat needs (Staatman 1971).
Throughout the 1980's and early 1990's a number of surveys and studies of QABB
and its host plant were completed by Michael Parsons (Parsons 1984, 1990,
1991). These surveys helped defined the present range of the QABB on the
Popondetta Plain and verified the importance of the Managalas Plateau
population in the Afore area (Parsons 1991). However, Parsons work on the hast
vine led to erroneous classification of host vines by splitting P. dielsiana into

species P. meridonaliana and P. alexandrae (Parsons 1996, Jebb 1993).

1

4!

=== page 3 ===
However, legitimate recognition of Parson's new Pararistolochia species by the
scientific community has been lacking (Mercer 1999). Until further research
reveals otherwise P. dielsiana is considered by the most as the legitimate host
plant of QABB. in 1992, Larry Orsack carried out surveys on the Popondetta Plain
and with a collaborative group of international and local researchers,
politicians, and wildlife biologists produced a five-year management action
plan (Orsack 1992). The plan provided an action in order to preserve the
species.

Later extensive surveys and monitoring efforts took place as part of Oro
Conservation Project, largely funded by AusAID, in the Afore region (Mercer
1999). However, surveys were completed in outlying regions to determine the
final extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and
another in the Musa River region (Mercer 1999). However, the Muse River
population was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the
region in 1997 (Mercer 1999). The Oro Conservation Project was finally
terminated in 1997. However, low level monitoring continued to take place in
the Afore region and Popondetta Plain region through the 21s' century overseen
by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Recently, a small two-week
study on the host vine and the QABB by a University of Papua New Guinea
honour’s student in the Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007).

In November 2007 Cyclone Guba struck the Oro Province dumping more than
72 cm of rain in less than 24 hours in some regions. The disaster greatly disrupted
the subsistence gardens of the local people and destroyed much of the
infrastructure in the region. Monitoring of QABB largely ceased and has only just
begun again in June/July of 2008.

While a number of research projects on the QABB have taken piace they have
not fulfilled the informational needs of local conservation agencies. Furthermore
the scientific rigor with which these studies were carried out is questionable and
what is currently known about QABB seems largely to be based on anecdotal
encounters and casual observation.

Evaluate Conservation and Survival Status of QABB.

Past efforts to conserve QABB have been hampered by a lack of understanding
of the fundamental life history traits of the butterfly and its host plant (Orsack
1992, Mercer 1999). In addition, incentives for landowners to maintain intact
forest are deficient. Proposed solutions to the dilemma have included eco-
tourism and butterfly ranging (Orsack 1992). The ability of PNG, Oro Province
and the butterfly to attract sufficient numbers of tourists to profitably sustain the
tourism industry is unlikely.

=== page 4 ===
Butterfly ranging is an attractive altemative and many within PNG have
experience in the insect trade. Indeed PNG is the only country in the world with
a government branch dedicated solely to trade and export of insects, the
Insect Farm and Trade Agency (iFTA) (Mercer and Clark 1989). However, there
are two hurdles that must be overcome for butterfly ranching of QABB to be
successful. First, the status of IFTA as a reliably operating agency must be
ascertained, as recently published literature suggests a breakdown of
functionality within IFTA (Small 2007). Second, the species must be down listing to
occur a formal recommendation must be made after or within the publication
of conservation management plan for the species. Due to the existence of a
number of data gaps the publication of a management plan at this point would
be irresponsible.

The objectives of this study is to fulfill these data gaps and provide those
involved in the conservation of QABB with quality information on the population
structure and life history of the QABB and its host plant, P. dielsiana. In order to
achieve this, the following specific priorities were observed:

e Evaluation of Conservation & Survival Status of QABB
Identification of threats of QABB

e Appraisal of Economical value of QABB, other bird-wing butterflies
and insects

e Provision of Appropriate Recommendations on QABB Habitat
Rehabilitation

=== page 5 ===
METHODOLOGY

Study Site:

There are essentially 3 WMAs around Popondetta town and within the study
area that support the QABB and other birdwing species. Numerous patches of
oil palm plots are interspersed between the WMAs, in addition to areas of high
human activity.

Sites visited in the target included Afore government station (S 09° 08.356’ and E
148° 23.369'}, Kawowoki (S 09 06.281' and E 148° 23.333), and Vanua (S 07
08.215’ and E 148° 23.783"). These areas are located at elevations of 751, 756
and 735 meters above sea level, respectively.

Figure 1. Map of Study site {Managalas Wildlife Management Area}

Data collection:

Data was collected using a number of approaches including; site-seeing
observations, insect netting trials for demonstrations on life-stage taxonomic
identification of QABB and other butterfly species, interviews with locals, and the
use of interactive pictorial conservations to draw information on the corect
identification of species of the birdwings buiterflies from QABB.

Pictorial tips of the methods applied in this study to aid in the observations
follows.

=== page 6 ===
Site Visits

Figure 2 & 3. One of the forest patches that is home to QABB and destruction
from recent flood disaster.

Visits were made to Kowoki and Vanua areas. Sightings and collections of
specimen were done together with surveillance for QABB and other birdwing
species in their different life-stages was caried out by foot patrolling between
the three areas.

insect Netting & Demonstrations

Figure 4 & 5. Insect netting demonstrations to Kawowoki. Vanua forest
demonstration

These demonstrations were performed to mainly collect delicately species for

correct species identifications of QABB from other birdwing butterflies.
Illustrations were briefly given for the correct identification of adult male and

5

=== page 7 ===
female QABB and their juvenile stages, making comparisons with those of other
birdwing butterflies.

Interview & Meetings

Figure 6. Afore guest house. Figure 7. Kawoki guest house. Demonstrating the
differences in species of life-stages. Gauging views during a meeting with locals.

Interactive approach was considered here to obtain technical information and
in return providing appropriate technical advice and solution to queries brought
forward.

Observation

Information collection during interviews and meeiings were viilized io make
direct observation of presence or absence of QABB and other species. A useful
marker for the study to determine presence and survival of QABB was the
availability, abundance and the distribution of host plant species in the study
area. Local information was helpful for independent but often referenced
observations. Although local knowledge can be worth noting, offen the lack of
reliability in quantitative precision has always existed.

=== page 8 ===
RESULTS
Survival Status of QABB

Monitoring activities in the area were up to 1997 by the Oro Conservation
Project under funding from AusAID in the Afore region (Mercer 1999}. These
surveys were however completed in the outlying regions to determine the final
extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and another
in the Musa River region. Mercer 1999, reports that the Muse River population
was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the region in
1997, where this project was put to rest in that same year. Monitoring at very
small scale continued to take place in the Afore region and Popondetta Plain
region by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Only recently, a two-
week study on the host vine and the QABB relationship was carried out by a
University of Papua New Guinea honour's student under my supervision, in the
Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007), looking especially at presence
of food vines {A. tagala, A. dielsiana and A. momanduil) and feeding
preferences.

The assessment of current survival status of QABB cannot quite clearly be stated
due largely to the limited timing of this study. Ample time is therefore required to
quantify the dynamics of their survival. Ongoing monitoring activities of the
QABB were disrupted by the disaster (Cyclone Guba) of November 2007, which
destroyed greatly much of the infrastructure and food gardens of the local
people.

There were a good number of sightings of GABB adults in the foot pairois taken.
However, comparably speaking, the frequency of these sightings was quite
lower than observations | made during my many years outings into the study
area (e.g. Parson 1991, Survey caried out for Conservation International) for
such and other entomological trips to Collinwood Bay, where O.meridionalis was
first ever found and collected by me. Locals interviewed and asked for sightings,
however indicated that the QABB population is sustaining but highlighted the
eminent threats from logging and human activities.

Threats (Natural & Man-made):

Obvious eminent threats were noted to exist that might have already affected
the QABB population. These among a host of other faciors included human
activities such as extension of oil palm fields, logging activities, and other
intensified human activities in response to population growth, and natural
disasters, all have a potential of destroying the QABB habitat.

=== page 9 ===
Extension of Oil Paim Fields

The recent extensions of oil palm field, both of private block-holder plots and the
Higaturu Oil palm have involved clearing of forest areas. A similar study such as
this was carried out in 1991 where | was part of, where we interviewed several
villagers from villages that are now gone. | have noticed that the expansions
have displaced several villages that were there in 1991. Such displacement
obviously increases social pressure to scavenge the surrounding forests thereby
increasing pressure on the forests habitat and QABB survival.

Population Growth

Pressure exerted on the local natural environment as a result of population
increase was apparent and observable and is deemed to be another important
factor that will influence the successful QABB population. Within the WMAs and
the study sites, increased human activities were noted that include extensive
subsistence gardening, regular combing of the woodlands for firewood, and the
general use of the forest products.

Logging

Logging activities are very common in the nearby regions of WMAs and has a
potential of expanding into the area. From the discussions and meetings held
with the locals, this was one other major potential QABB survival threats.

Reforestation

There are no plans curently in place to undertake rehabilitation of the
destroyed part of the habifat by reforestation. If this trend continues without
forward planning to reclaim wasted forest areas, then the ability to maintain
QABB population and other important species in the area over the next few
decades is dubious.

Natural Disaster/Floods

Disasters such as those of 1997 drought fuelled fires in parts of the area
especially Musa river (Mercer, 1999) that was affected, could occur at sites
where savannah or manmade grassland patches adjoin forest vegetation with
important food host species. Imesponsible clearing of forests (that is occurring)
and promotion of grassy and herbaceous vegetation will certainly encourage
bushfires in times of drought and dry season.

Experiences also from the 2007 Cyclone Guba disaster that devastated many
local communities in terms of infrastructure and food gardens can be seen as a

8

=== page 10 ===
potential risk for the survival of QABB. This can come about when feeding and
host plan species in the local area becomes destroyed by the disaster.

Butterflies & their host plants:

The essential component of the critical survival of QABB and other birdwing
species is and feeding ecology associated with their life-cycle, which include
how each individual species interact with host plant species at particularly
caterpillar and adult stages. This bulk of information is very important for the
local people, as they are the direct custodians and caretakers of the butterflies.
in order to ensure a sustained monitoring of the survival of the QABB population
in the WMA, locals need to correctly identify QABB at each life-stage and
equally identify the corresponding life-stage, from other birdwing butterflies.

This sort of information and the practical field training works may be required to
impart this very important piece of information. This is important because
interviews and communication with locals regarding taxonomical identifications,
often did misidentify, which indicated a need for practical training and
awareness in future.

Economical Value of QABB:

QABB is a protected species and cannot be harvested for any commercial
exploitation, whilst the other birdwing butterflies can be farmed, harvested and
sold commercially. Although QABB is not exploitable, the non-market value for a
pair (male and female) is at $US 10, 000 approxmately and is listed as a CITES |
species.

Other birdwings butterfly species are on CITES 2 which can be harvested for
export at market-value. It is noteworthy that direct harvesting from the wild is not
allowed and is not encouraged. It however can be farmed in order to maintain
a sustainable supply population from which harvesting can be made. The price
list of birdwing butterfly species is appended as Economical Group of Insect —
Lepidoptera (Butterflies & Moths) & Coleoptera (Beetles & Weevils) Please ref. to
Attached lists.

Outcomes of Meetings:

Meetings were held at different sites with locals in a bid to obtain information
related to the objectives of this study. Information related to the importance of
species to plant host relationships of QABB and other birdwing butterflies was
imparted as the need for it was apparent since the locals are the rightful
custodians of this rare creatures and their survival is in many ways connected to
their livelinood.

=== page 11 ===
During these meetings general impression was made by the locals for the need
to foster the concept of conservation from a rejuvenated paradigm. In this case
conservation which transpired mutual benefits was largely expressed. One
apparent examples of such mutuality in benefits was the need to venture into a
tangible insect farming project. It was also expressed that for over 20 years of
involvement with the Wild Life Management Area (WLMA}, there was a general
lack of tangible benefits. Venturing into Insect Farming would bring sustainable
monetary benefits to the locals, at the same time the maintaining of QABB and
other species diversity within the area.

An Insect Ranch and a guest house in the area have been constructed at their
own initiative. The establishment now requires Department of Environment &
Conservation (DEC) to give approval and also grant export license for their
insect specimens to be exported to overseas markets. This group of people from
what is known as DataCol WMA would like the establishment to serve equally as
WEI and IFTA. The reason being that, harvested and fixed marketable insect and
butterfly specimen often lose market value due to damages sustained while
transported to Wau for inspection. They also suggested that DEC would approve
of this proposal to help aspiring insect farmers in Oro and the Southern region as
