DISCUSSION

Potential threats to the survival of QABB and related species were identified and
highlighted providing specific details. Among these factors of influence
presented, logging activity in the area and oil palm has been seen as potential
risk factors. The monetary benefits associated with logging and oil palm were
seen to be more attractive to the local people who are the custodians of the
WMaAs who claim previously have not had adequately and tangibly benefited
since the establishment of the conservation areas. Influence of logging activities
and also the lucrative oil palm indusiry can however be suppressed by
encouraging incentive-based conservation practice in these areas.

Whilst observations made during this rather short visit has provided some basic
insights into the questions posed an extended time period in future can allow for
a full-scale species inventory. Anecdotal entry of such data is misleading
especially when information is required for management purposes.

Due to the general inadequacies in the monitoring and QABB management
skills of the local people, further workshops and practical field demonstrations
are encouraged. This is a way forward for responsible management of QABB
and other species by locals. This brings us to the idea brought forward by the
locals for an incentive-based conservation as has previously being discussed
extensively by Orsak (1999). This in fact is ‘gap’ identified. DECs approval for
Insect Ranching and issuance of a license would be a step in the right direction

VW

=== page 13 ===
when QABB conservation is priority of the government. in this concept of
incentive-based conservation rigorous training workshops on insect farming
techniques and related themes would urgently be taken as a prerequisite step.

RECOMMENDATIONS

From this desktop study there are essentially three (3) recommendations made
for an urgent consideration to pursue.

e Establishment & Approval of Managalas Insect Ranch

Since the people of DataCol & Nakoda, totaling approximately 3,000 plus
people, have initiated the establishment of an Insect Ranch, the DEC must
come in for the instrumentation of its approval.

e Import & Export License (Managalas Insect Ranch)

In line with the approval, the license for specimen inspection and mobility
(domestically and internationally) just as done at WEI and IFTA would be
required.

e Ongoing Workshops on Insect farming
Of the more urgent is the need for the local people to be able to attain the right
skills level in the management of insect farming, harvesting, postharvest storage,
and handling of valuabie but delicate insect specimen.

Please note that a proposal and itinerary of Insect Farming Workshops fo be
undertaken on an on-going basis is aftached.

Background

Environment and Conservation is a huge problem faced by our
community throughout the country in the global changes rapidly
happening; PWM is taking the lead in addressing the Conservation and
Land Use issues in the project site Managalas in the Afore District, with its
different partners. Each year, new concepts and strategies are spent on
community and institutional project to help people to understand the
basic function, roles and responsibilities of conservation and Land Use, to,
MAKE OUR ENVIRONMENT JUST, SAFE AND SECURE PLACE TO LIVE FOR
NOW AND FUTURE GENERATION.

There are several ways to devise different activities that could enhance
and create conservation issues to be easily understood by the community
members, by using Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication (
Theatre Arts Section). The most obvious one was in the area of Creative
Arts; however, to achieve solid results the workshop was conducted in
Poponedtta Town, Anglicare Training centre.

This workshop recognizes that one of the strategic way to create
awareness in the conservation Land Use issues is to involve the
community, particularly the youths and the senior members of the
community and expose their skills and abilities in different dimensions of
Art of Drama. This workshop illustrated the medium drama, exposed the
inner feeling of a person how they perceive Conservation and Land Use
issues in their community as evident in their drama session , the other
aspects of the arts will be addressed in due course time if similar
opportunity is given and please see the interview by the participants
after the closing ceremony DVD attached.

When we know why our community is not conserving and proper planning
for the usage of the land, then we can mitigate or hopefully stop
completely or strategize for a better community. The solution lies within
the community, the participants told us how they want to solve their own
problems by using the medium of Drama to create constructive and
creative environment for community discussion.

Artistic Product

The primary target for Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication
through the application of Community Sustainable Arts Education, in
using Drama helped different members of the communities in the target
locations within Managalas Development Foundation broaden the scope of
understanding. Towards the end of the workshop we achieved the
following results,

1, Basic Drama Skills
2. Different Techniques of Drama

=== page 6 ===
Written three scripts related to conservation and Land Use anid
finally performed for public at the Angiicare Training Centre

3. Produce the Photographs of the workshop from Day i- day 5

4. Video shoots of the workshop end its various sessions and
activities

5. Finally, the participants admitted that they are now very confident
to conduct awareness by using Drama

This project was coordinated and executed by the MIAC in partnership
with PWM under artistic cocrdination and direction of Mr. Motsy David,
Theater Arts Staff at the University of PNG as part of PWM Effective
Communication and Awareness Training. The Community Sustainable
Arts Education Strategy acted as the mirror of the society, decause it is
one of the most effective medium of communication and also empowering
the Members of the Managalas Development Foundation. The project
certainly make aware the peopie in the project area and other target
areas the consequences tc realize their abilities and creative skills so they
can meaningfully contribute to their own community and the country. The
Conservation and Land Use issues are of great concern for everyone,
drastic effects it nas on our country both economically and sociatiy. The
Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication through the workshoo
contributed artistically to minimize the environmental calamities and most
importantly through this treiring we will change the attitudes and the
behaviors of the people.

My concentration in this carticular workshop was to build a solid
foundation for sustainable and continuous promotion and preservation of
Conservation and Land Use by suing Drama. There are huge amount of
people in the target areas which are illiterate and ignorant of the
importance of PWM and MDF roles end it primary responsibilities must
consistentiy informed the community to various mediums of information
dissemination such as Dram.

1. Advocacy, Communication sna Social Mobilization activities for the
people in the target areas through the Community Sustainable Arts
Education program under Drama. It stimulated and created avenue for
community discussion on how best they can solve the issue of
Conservation and Land Use. This medium is very powerful tool to identify
some possible solution to the community problems. It is our firm believe
that through this exercise we have idenzfied and advice MDF and PWM
how best they can devise some possible strategies to overcome this
pressing issue of Conservation and Land Use issues.

The Community Theatre members are willing to work with Host
Institution MZAC ( Theatre Arts Section)and other stakeholders such as
Police Department, Community Policing, Establish Youth Association in
verious areas, Churches, Informal Sector Association and National
Cultural Commission for advice and possibie assistance for manpower

=== page 7 ===
and other relevant organization that we will be closely working with them
to improve their artistic skills.

2. To increase the awareness on the importance of Roles, Responsibilities
and its functions so the people must appreciate and respect the
significance of conservation and Land Use.

3. Development of a better understanding of the school children for the
future generation. Making use of all organization’s experiences in control,
share experiences, best practices and lessons learned for the benefit of
the children and the youths and communities in Afore.

Targets:

» Successfully, we inform target audiences on importance of
Conservation and Land Use and other social related issues, and
improve knowledge, attitudes and practices through the Workshop.

e Increase engagement and involvement of communities and
households at the Managalas and other relevant stakeholders in
analysis, planning and implementation of activities to protect and
respect , use it properly for the collective benefits in the

community

Increased quality assured, client oriented approach among service
providers to market the community must establish mutual respect for
others and themselves.

Goal:

Increase their knowledge and seeking behavior among communities, in
order to increase awareness about their own attitude and the
environment. Through Community Sustainable Arts Education, Drama
production and Exhibitions about the importance of the role of PWM and
MDF.

Objective:

To prevent the Community members and also to minimize its adverse
impact on Conservation and Land Use, among individuals, families and
communities and other social influences through the application of
Theatre Training

Inadequate political and societal commitment and poor levels of public
awareness on the importance of Role of Conservation and Land Use and
its function and other related issues contributed to diminishing of the
respect for goodness of the environment, properties and its ecological
contribution to the humanities. Advocacy, Communication and Social

=== page 8 ===
Mobilization through the workshop using Creative Skilis built stronger
political and societal commitment and enhance maximum use of
accessible, affordable and effective medium to produce an outcome that is
beneficial to the mass of the community by using Grama.

This workshop mobilize communities and individuais through a
participatory approach towards appreciating the value of the PWM & it’s
local partner -MDF contribution to the Afore Area and through this
workshop in the form of this Project seek behavior change, by increasing
knowledge and awareness among the members of the community. It also
contributed to successful awareness and reducing the potential of social
manipulation by the evil influences. The main targets are unemployed
youths, adults, schooi children, community leaders at ali levels, opinion
leaders, Youth Association, schools, community and faith based
organizations and households they all participated effectively. The
beneficiaries include the community at large. Sizeable number of peopie
in the community was addressed during the closing of the workshop and
reached by work through community volunteers and by targeted strategic
campaigns, using applied performances by way of participatory drarna
performance and community meetings and consuitation, community
orientated program and other medium of communication was utilized.

Service delivery area:

The workshooe cromoted and market PWM as well as educating people to
make our society a better place. Through the assistant of UPNG by
releasing me from teaching duty. We organized public participation by the
community leveis through situationa! analysis, pianning, intra and
intersectorai collaboration with different communities and relevant
agencies in the near future.

Activities

Estebiishment of this workshop, the artistic material in close collaboration
with experienced partner in the field of Drarna. Information schemes at
smaller scale mini-media was used in the during the workshop for the
purpose of preservation and appreciation of the project. This linked to
already existing efforts in communicating information and mobilizing
schools and community. The PWM under the supervision of Lillan Bago
provided logistics and materials for the workshop and UPNG support
artistically. To date, we have constantly established the dialogue with
them after the workshop.

1) Regulariy inform journalists and editors of the development, provide
them with fact sheets end requiar update by the production and
workshop on recent developments. See the attachment of the news
articles and other media listed.

=== page 9 ===
2) Developing strategies through different types of production and
dissemination/ distribution of materials (T- Shirt Printing, leaflets,
campaigns, events and radio Announcement etc) in close collaboration
with various schools and organizations that does the similar activities.

3) Ongoing assistance, support and supervision by the MIAC of the
School of Humanities & Social Sciences and PWM , focal point to all
levels for efficient and effective awareness strategy.

4) Evaluations carried out for population at the targeted area of the
Project must know that respect for the environment and proper use of
land is vital part of their life.

5) Increased the knowledge of the role of LISS over time, where by
people expressed accepting attitudes towards their own community as
very significant and economic generate activities.

Implementation

The project and Community consultation were implemented over a week
period by the community. The project facilitators encouraged to meet the
commitments make during the workshop to actively play their part in
implementing the project objective. The first step is to communicate the
strategy to all, Community and the general Public and the stakeholders
with the following Implementation approaches.

1) Have question & answer session after or before the workshop with
the students and the public

2) Distributed relevant information of the effects of Law & Order and
other matters to the audience, fine and the imprisonment duration.

3) Acknowledged the AusAID, USS & UPNG as the major sponsor
with its corporate logo on every publicity materials.

4) All public performance, Exhibitions and community consultation ,
video record and submitted back to the LISS for assessment and
further evaluation

5) Developed audience feedback assessment sheet about the work, for
the benefit of the PWM in summary it is captured in the
recommendations.

was excellent arnong the participants.

and video. See the copies attached for your records and information.

Staffing and Management

The workshop was managed and coordinated by Partners With
Melanesians in partnership with Melanesian Institute of Arts &
Communication, Schoo! of Humanities & Sociai Sciences and Managlas
Development Foundation. Namely,

1) Ms, Lillian Baggo - Workshop Technical supervisor

The level of support was very high as well as the artistic interest from the
participants (botn mate & female). MIAC through its Community
partnership program. We have experience of coordinating and managing
project and we produce the desire results and will meet the PWM
expectation in fuififing the objectives in the near future with the similar
workshop.

The marketing and the pubticity strategies of the workshop are as
follows,

1) Electronic Media

of securing the interview

2) Print Media —

National as weekender — Lillian Baggo will supply the news as
per my discussion with her after the workshop

The above publicity strategies carry the corporate logo of PWM, MDF and
UPNG , will be acknowledged before and after the performance and in all
media publication.

Consultation & Collaboration

The Theatre Arts Section worked with the established organization, such
as Monash Gallery of Art, National Museum of Australia, Sydney Gallery
House, and Queensland University of Technology through Life Drama
Project. Cairns Regional Gallery, National Aids Council, International
Education Agencies, theatre training Component, National Council
Commission, Hot Home Production and other relevant agencies, where
possible into the course of this project. We have sought their advice as
well as cooperatively working together to achieve better result. The MIAC
will constantly communicate with the PWM as well as seeking any further
assistance and advice in the near future.

Monitoring and evaluation

Theatre Arts, UPNG and PWM Theatre workshop on the Project will be
monitored and evaluated on three levels:

e Overall goal and thematic objectives
Key actions of the project activities in various sections of Drama
« Comments, views and suggestion from the PWM, MDF and the
general! Public will be accommodate where necessary.

At the level of the overall goal and the thematic objectives, the strategy’s
major indicator targets are linked to the performance goals and
Objectives. This is to assure that the Project thematic responses are
meeting the intended goals and objectives of the strategy as well as PWM
goals and targets. For example, an overall goal is to promote, preserve,
respect and protect environment and proper use of the land among the
community for a secure and safer society for the people and future
generation. And of course the use of this drama workshopt and other
medium to communicate message to the uninformed majority of our
people. The youths and adults of today must be responsible for the future
of our country. Final and most importantly is to empower the youth to

=== page 12 ===
realize their hidden abilities and skills to convert it into meaningful
activities for their survival.

Financial Assistance.

The workshop was make possibie by PWM funding through the
sponsorship of,

activities for the Managalas Theatre Group in close collaboration and
consultation with Partners With Melanesians,

* Register the Tneatre Group with NCC und NAC through IEA

> Put forwérd the expression of interest with the UPNG & QUT Life

with PWM

in partnership with MDF

e Facilitate other skills for recognition and acvancement for the
MANAGALAS Theatre Group

* Follow up training on technicality of Theatre

Sustainability of the theatre Training is paramount significant to us to

INTRODUCTION

Theatre is used to entertain as well as educate. Theatre has been a bridge between
entertainment and education and is used to share news, share history and or
educate communities. It is interactive where audiences discuss controversial and
sensitive issues in sexuality, HIV and or related issues and other development
issues. Since HIV is linked to many sensitive and controversial issues, drama can
be seen as a powerful strategy to challenge certain attitudes and risky behaviours
and promote accurate information.

Theatre basically is to change the knowledge, attitudes, or behaviours of audience.
In this context, theatre will be used to educate people in the communities about
safer sex practices through drama performances, thus providing and enabling
environment for behaviour change.

Papua New Guinea, like many countries and cultures in the world, where more
than 75 per cent of the population are not too well educated, this media is very
familiar and popular and the skills are found in the community.

This manual will be used as a guide for facilitators of community based theatre
rainings. Representatives from district or community based Theatre Groups wii!
be trained on the basics of theatre and the techniques which than could be used to
dramatise situations or issues affecting the communities they come from.

ORIGINS OF THEATRE
Theatre existed in the Civilization of the Western world for the last 3000 years.

Little information about the Origin of Theatre has survived. The information we do
have comes from wal! paintings, decorations, artifacts, and picture writing system
that show the importance of successful hunts, seasonal changes. life cycles, and
stories of the gods. From these peopie have seen the necessity of passing along the
experience of the old to the young through art, storytelling and dramatising events.
Even today cultures that do not have written languages have developed some form of
drama to dramatise imagination and the spirituality of people.

Drama is part of most diverse societies’ cultural heritage and it mirrors daily
livelihoods. That is mainly because of its relationship to festivals and religious
practices, In most cultures, communities identify themselves in drama as
dramatization of specific issues reflect the cultures. Drama reflects reality and needs
an interpretation of it to which it has an effect on individuals. Drama provokes
reflection and in a way stimulates the analytic potential of individuals. And it creates
a mirror effect to which individuals look at themselves at a different perspective.

People are bor with body languages which are the early steps of mankind, and
drama was very likely spontaneously embedded in those early steps. Theatre

emerged from myth, ritual, and ceremony. Early societies see connections between

POPULAR THEATRE:
In the Developing countries there are two types of Theatre: One is the Theatre which

takes place in a formal context which is very much more European and is aimed at
smal) cultural elite in urban areas, and the other takes place in the open as an
instrument to Communicate important messages for the community. There are many
encouraging experiences of popular theatre in some developing countries.

“Popular theatre is gaining increasing attention in the Third World as a tool for popular
education and community organizing. It finds expression in a number of forms including
drama, music dance, puppetry and poetry and is performed for — and often by — ordinary
peasants and workers, Popular theatre is used as a means of bringing people together,
building confidence and solidarity, stimulating discussion, exploring alternative options for
action, and building a collective commitment to change: starting with people's urgent
concerns and issues, it encourages reflection on these issues and possible strategies for
change.

For three decades popular theatre has been used in processes of development
communication as part of adult education programmes. From these initiatives grew a
special type of popular theatre, called ‘theatre for development.’ In workshops training
people in the use of popular theatre techniques an inventory of local problems is made for
later use in the plays. In each play one problem theme is explored by and for the local

community.”
(By: Jaap R. Swart, Center for the Study of Education in Deveioping Countries/Radio Netherlands Training
Center, The Hague, The Netherlands)

The approach of popular or community theatre is that performances must be linked
to crucial analysis, organisation and struggle. The concept of community theatre
emphasizes the revolutionary value of art. Instead of being merely a pleasant and
gratifying spectacle, community theatre (and art) aims to distribute, to shake. to
move the society towards self and critical thinking and action.

Majority of the people in PNG are illiterate hence theatre has been identified as one
of the effective approaches in educating people especially in rural communities
about the HIV and AIDS and related issues , and about safe sex practices as well as
caring for people living with HIV. The objective of community theatre is to allow
values and behaviour to be discussed comfortably without directly challenging the
community or individual beliefs and values. And to generate further discussions in
communities on the issues of HIV and AIDS and the ways they can respond to
protect themselves and their children. The approach or the purpose of community
theatre is that communities use popular theatre as a medium to educate communities
on the basic HIV information. And since most of the Theatre Groups are district
based they are able to facilitate sustainability and local ownership.

Introduction:

Explain the main element of a script. Every play has to have a theme or a topic for
example ‘It Takes Two to Tango’. and a plot or story line (the incidence and events),
and the intention or message. Five or six scenes of 5 minutes each should be enough
for a 30 minute play.

A script should have different parts: First, an introduction to the topic which presents
the main characters and the story. The introduction in a play has to be such that it
captures the attention of the audience right away. Second, it has to present a conflict
that relates to the topic. Thirdly it has to build suspense so the audience will be
questioning the main issues. Fourthly, the tensions have to reach a climax which has
to be surprising and appealing to the audience. Finallv, the script has to provide a
solution with which the audience will indentify. The concept of climax is very
important. There has to be a progress to reach the climax.

Before writing the script, it is important to create a simple story line or synopsis,
with a short description of each character and scene. Complete dialogues can be
written later.

Actor Space

in popular theatre the audience surrounds the performers while in classic theatre the
audience is facing the actors. However, it is important to divide the scenic space so
the actors can refer to their positions in 2 common Janguage. There are various types
of acting stages. The most commonly used stages popular theatre are proscenium.

TYPES OF STAGING
1. Proscenium Staging

A Proscenium theater is a theatre space whose primary feature is a large archway
(the proscenium arch) at or near the front of the stage, through which the audience
views the play. The audience directly faces the stage, which is typically raised
several feet above front row audience level. The main stage is the space behind the
proscenium arch, often marked by a curtain which can be lowered or drawn closed.
The space in front of the curtain is called the “apron.” The areas obscured or hidden
by the proscenium arch and any curtains serving the same purpose (often called legs
or, tormentors) are called the wings. Any space not viewable to the audiences is
collectively referred to as offstage.

3. In The Round Staging
Theatre-in-the-round or arena theatre is any theatre space in which the audience

surrounds the stage area.

Theatre-in-the-round concept requires no stage curtain, little scenery and allows the
audience to sit on three sides of the stage.

The stage itself in this arrangement is typicaliy round, square, or triangular, with
actors entering and exiting through the audience from different directions or from
below the stage. Such a space is usually configured with the stage on an even ievel
with or lowered below the audience in a “pit” or "arena" formation. This
configuration lends itself to high-energy productions, and is especially favored by
producers of classical] theatre.

Theatre-in-the-round presents problems since actors at all times have their back
facing some members of the audience. However. it also allows for interesting and
realistic staging. Special consideration needs to be taken in regard to the set design,
so as not to hide any audience member's view of the performance.

1 Background

In May 2011, Paul and | were invited by Partners with Melanesians inc (PWM) to talk to farmers and
inhabitants on the Managalas Piateau in Oro Province on the impact and coping strategies of extreme
weather patterns such as Drought. As project staff on the National Agricultural Research institute's PIP
project titled: ‘drought preparedness’. providing such information was a major project objective.
Confirmation of our participation eventuated in a visit being proposed and confirmed for August 2011. This
report outlines the activities and outcomes of our two day visit to the Managalas Plateau in the Afore
District of the Oro Province in Papua New Guinea in August 2011. L Kurika

My previous visit to Afore was to assess the after-effects of the 1997-98 drought with colleagues from the
Department of Agriculture and Livestock. | was eager to return to the Managalas Plateau fo educate people
in how they can prepare themselves and their communities if there is a drought. P Osilis

Google
4

1.1 Partners With Melanesians Inc.

Partners with Melanesians Inc (PWM) is a national, “not for profit’, non-government organization (NGO)
currently focused on conserving natural eco-systems and promoting community development in certain
locations in Papua New Guinea (PNG). The organization has worked with the Managalas Plateau
inhabitants for over 23 years and continually support and provide helpful information to assist the people in
conservation initiatives such as the recently started Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP).

1.2 The Managalas Plateau

The Managalas plateau is situated between 600-1,000m in the midst of the Owen Stanley Range (to the
south and west), with the Sibium Ranges to the south-east. Mount Lamington to the north and the
Hydrographers to the east. The plateau covers about 300,000 hectares of area and has an extremely
diverse environment, mooriands, mountains, hills, savannah, anthropogenic grassland and gardens.

=== page 7 ===
Awareness Trip Report L Kurika & P Osilis

The plateau is inhabited by about 15,000 people from about 150 clan groups who live in 70 village
communities. The people are mostly subsistence farmers who depend almost entirely on the environment
for their livelihood. Basic government services is restricted to a number of community schools, a top up
school, two aid posts, and a station and health centre at Afore. The Summer Institute of Linguistics
introduced an adult titeracy programme to the plateau in the 1960's which since then has helped paved the
way for more recent development initiatives on the Plateau. This relatively isolated and remote area Is
linked to the provincial capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality four-wheel drive road and foot tracks. There is
an airstrip at Afore station but it was overgrown with weeds and was not in use at the time of this visit.

The remoteness of the area, poor state of infrastructure like roads and airstrips and lack of markets pose
great challenges to cash income generating initiatives such as the production and sale of coffee. The
abundance of natural resources in the area and the high quality agricultural land has attracted in the past
decade a lot of interest from potential investors in timber extraction, oil palm plantations and mineral
mining. However the communities have actively opposed these interests due to the lack of consultations
with resource owners and the failure by interested developers to guarantee benefits and/or environmental
protection.

1.3. The Managalas Conservation Area Project

The Managaias Conservation Area Project (MCAP) is managed by PWM with support from various Donor
agencies; the main one being Rainforest Foundation Norway. The ultimate plan is for the Managalas area
to be declared a conservation area under the relevant conservation laws of PNG to enable the people of
Managalas to retain and transfer their inherited natural resources to future generations. The core
programmes under MCAP are: (i) consensus building, (ii) conservation and (iii) training and capacity
building. The overall objectives of the programmes are to promote conservation of natural eco-systems,
prevent unsustainable ways of resource exploitation and encourage smali-scale eco-enterprises to
generate revenue for the communities to meet their modest needs. The programmes are implemented
through a network of players that include: the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF), also an NGO,
and eleven smail community based organizations (CBO). For eco-enterprises and income generation,
PWM has been working closely with the local CBOs and community groups to promote the production and
marketing of organic coffee, village artifacts and handicrafts, okari nuts, peanuts, forest products,
vegetables and garden produce.

2 Workshop on Drought at Afore Station

The Managalas area like many rural locations in PNG received the full brunt of the negative impacts
caused by the 1997-98 drought. Both NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis visited Afore station on two
separate occasions in 1998. Kurika visited on an RAF flight that delivered relief food to the station while
Osilis was a member of the team that visited the area by road and conducted an appraisal of the food
security and water situation in Oro Bay and the Managalas area.

In the 1997-98 drought, the forest and grassland areas within the vicinity of Afore station were totally
ravaged by bush fires. There was a bad shortage of water and as a result people either left their villages to
resettle in places where they could access water or had to walk long distances to fetch water. Many food
gardens were destroyed and hence relief food was air-lifted to Afore station.

With the experiences of the 1997-98 drought still vividly fresh in people’s memories one can imagine the
sense of apprehension that can arise as a result of the recent news flashes in the media about a severe
drought looming to occur next year, 2012. To dispel any sense of apprehension amongst communities and
create awareness on drought, an awareness workshop on drought was conducted at Afore station.

=== page 8 ===
2.1 Workshop Purpose

The purpose of the workshop was to equip the CBO Managers and trainers with information on drought
and recommended drought coping strategies for them to disseminate to their respective communities to
prepare the communities to cope with the negative impacts of a severe and/or prolonged dry weather
period.

2.2 Sponsorship, Facilitators and Participants

The workshop was organized and sponsored by PWM and facilitated by Patrick Vuet, Conservation Officer
with PWM. The awareness on drought was conducted by Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis, staff from the
Drought Project with the National Agricultural Research Institute (NARI), based at NARI’s Southern
Regional Center at Laloki in the Central Province. There were a total of 38 participants who attended the
one day workshop. They included MOF Board Members, CBO Managers, Activity Coordinators, Gender
Officers and various community representatives from Afore District Zones 1-9 (Appendix 1. List of
Workshop Participants).

2.3 Workshop Terms of Reference

A Terms of Reference (ToR} was prepared for the workshop. The NARI Drought Project staff were
assigned the following workshop duties and responsibilities:

¢ Impart the basic ideas on the causes of drought and its impact on the lively hood of the
communities/people
Use case studies of other areas around the world that have been affected by droughts

e Basic ideas on the type of food that can withstand drought conditions

e Deliver posters or pamphlets containing information on drought. There are ten CBOs within the
Managalas Project areas.

e Deliver basic information on the concept of food security.

2.4 Workshop Programme

The workshop on drought awareness was conducted on Thursday 11” August 2011 at the MDF guest
house at Afore station. The workshop commenced with opening statements from Patrick Vuet and Luke
Mambe, Project Director for MDF on the purpose and the expected outcomes from the workshop. This was
followed by the core activity of the workshop which was the awareness on drought. The information
presented was put together in accordance with the five duties and responsibilities outlined in the agreed
ToR of the workshop between PWM and the two NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis. The awareness
campaign included the following:

e Poster Display
¢ Power Point presentation on climate change, 1997-78 Drought and its impacts on PNG and NARI
recommended drought coping strategies
e Session on preparing a Cropping Calendar
e Distribution of A4 portfolio posters and information leaflets on climate change and drought to
representatives of the ten Community based organizations
e Distribution of seeds: open-pollinated corn variety - Suwan and High Protein White corn varieties
to workshop participants
e An interactive session during which some important community perceived issues on climate
change, drought and food security were noted and discussed.
The workshop ended on the afternoon of Thursday 11” August 2011. On Friday 12” August 2011, all
facilitators returned to Popondetta and then returned via air travel to Port Moresby the next day; Saturday
13” August 2011.

=== page 9 ===
Awareness Trip Report L Kunka & P Osilis

3 Workshop Outcomes

The workshop was a success. It attracted a large number of participants despite its location; many of
whom had walked long distances to attend. Workshop facilitators were able to cover all workshop
requirements (as outlined in the workshop ToR). An overwheiming amount of information was provided and
open-pollinated com seeds were distributed so that farmers can use the seeds to replant, unlike hybrid
cor seeds. Participants were not only able to learn about drought impact and coping strategies but
understood the presentations and exercises well enough to raise questions and issues on related topics
such as insect pest management and the recording of traditional knowledge on famine and bush foods.

During the workshop we felt, first and foremost, that it was essential to clarify and dispel any sense of panic
or apprehension over the prediction that a drought with a severity equal to the 1997-98 PNG drought would
occur in 2012. We explained that the forecasting of an El Nino event that would cause a drought(s) was
quite complex and dependent on calculations from experts who are monitoring climatic developments at a
regional and global scale. We stressed that the primary importance at present is for communities to be
made aware of droughts and how to cope with their negative impacts.

3.1 Some Community Perceived Issues on Drought and Food Security from
the Workshop

3.1.1 Taro beetle, a problem in taro gardens
Taro beetle damage on taro cultivars was reported to be a problem in all nine Afore Sub-district zones.

Resolution(s): Taro beetle damage is a problem that NARI can immediately address through the
use of the two chemicals Bifenthrin and Mustang. The technology is available and NARI staff do
conduct training on taro beetle control upon request from various clients. A demonstration plot for
taro beetle control work can be established in collaboration with farmers at Afore station to
demonstrate how and when to apply the treatments and the effectiveness of the control method. It
may also be worth the effort to conduct some studies on taro beetle population in the gardens and
their breeding sites to see if the pest can be controlled using some form of cultural method. Other
reported insect pests e.g. cut worms and caterpillars can be controlled using Plant Derived
Pesticides (PDP) like chilli, derris plant and extract from the neem tree. This technology is
available with NARI whose Crop Protection Staff do conduct training on how to prepare and use
PDP to control insect pests.

3.1.2 Training on food processing and preservation e.g. how to make cassava flour
The need for practical demonstrations on the methods involved in making flour and jam was raised.

Resolution(s): The A4 portfolio posters supplied to each CBO Manager at Afore station contains a
number of recipes on how to process and preserve certain staple crops like cassava and bananas
in storable products like flour and chips. Food processing involving the processing of the
perishable staple crops to storable products is one of the important coping strategies for drought.
NARI does have experts in post harvest, processing and storage who can conduct training on food
processing and storage technologies; based at NARI's Momase Regional Research Center at
Bubia, in the Morobe Province.

=== page 10 ===
3.1.3 Documentation of traditional knowledge on the utilization of bush and famine foods

The recording of traditional knowledge on bush and famine foods for future utilization was realized and
understood to be a very important issue.

Resolution(s): Reports on experiences from the 1997-98 drought reveal that many rural
communities survived by eating bush and famine foods. There are quite a number of bush and
famine food plants that people have resorted to during times of food shortage. These include
banana corms (Musa sp.), Pueraria lobata, wild yam (Dioscorea sp.) and tulip (Gnetum gnemon).
The use of some is widespread while others are utilized only in certain places. However, the
knowledge on traditional recipes on how to prepare and utilize many of these bush and famine
foods often remains with the older generation and is in danger of being lost. NARI has documented
a number of these used by coastal and highland area communities in PNG. Each of the 30 A4 size
portfolio posters that were distributed to the CBO Managers at the workshop contains details on
foods and practices suitable for extreme weather patterns such as drought. There are however,
many more still out there that need to be documented and the knowledge passed on to the
younger generation. This has to be done on the Managalas Plateau as part of a strategy to
strengthen the community's ability to cope with droughts.

3.1.4 NARI Drought Project to utilize MDF base at Afore station as a Resource Centre

A query was raised for further NARI collaboration and participation by the PIP Drought Project at Afore;
continue drought awareness.

Resolution(s): The NARI Drought Project does not have the resources to separately undertake any
long-term programme activity at Managaias but it could collaborate with PWM and MDF to be
involved in certain specific activities that require NARI expertise and involving NARI released
technologies, especially in the area of food security. Some of the possible activities that NARI
could be involved in at Managalas are:

* Introduce drought tolerant and other useful crops and to encourage farmers to
maintain diversity of their food crops in gardens.

Introduce the rope and washer pump technology for accessing underground water
sources.

Conduct training on food processing and storage.

Conduct training on taro beetle control and use of plant derived pesticides.
Conduct training on seed and vegetable production.

Introduce small livestock like goats, ducks and chicken.

Establish fruit and nut orchards of both exotic and native species.

Conduct training on vegetative propagation method on certain fruit and nut species.
Rapid propagation of African yam and taro using mini-setts.

Rapid propagation of bananas using banana bits.

7.2 Appendix 2. Information delivered in relation to the Workshop ToR

7.2.1 Cause of droughts and its impacts

Droughts in Papua New Guinea are caused by the El Nino phenomena which is associated with the
unusually cold currents and high pressure systems that cause the air above the ocean to fall instead of
rising resulting in no condensation and little or no rain occurring. In addition, the high pressure areas push
clouds and air currents i.e. easterly winds downwards and away resulting in sunny cloudless weather.
Droughts occur when the cold currents stall the high pressure systems for long periods.

Predicting El Nino events is however a complex process because it involves analyzing and understanding
the relationships between multiple weather attributes and their patterns over time. There currently is no
certain indication from El Nino predicting models that a drought with the severity of the one experienced in
1997-98 is imminent and will occur next year in 2012. As illustrated in the PowerPoint presentation, the
prediction was based on historical data on the trend in occurrence of droughts in PNG since the 1950s. At
best, it only offers a clue on the possible time period of when to expect another severe drought in PNG.
What is important is that instead of delving on the debate on whether or not the drought will occur in 2012;
we should focus our attention on pro-actively creating greater awareness amongst communities on
drought, its impacts and relevant coping strategies to strengthen their ability to cope with the impacts ofa
severe drought.

Reports on the impacts of the 1997-98 drought in PNG indicate that an estimated 1.5 million villagers (40%
of the total rural population) suffered severe and life-threatening food shortages (Allen & Bourke 2000,
Bourke 2000, Haley 2000, Lemonnier 2000). There was an 80% reduction in production of garden food due
to depleted soil moisture. Over 400,000 people had grossly inadequate supply of drinking water, were
drinking water of questionable quality or were carrying water for long distances i.e. more than 30 minutes
walk. Certain institutions and community schools had to be closed due to lack of water while a number of

13

=== page 18 ===
small urban locations like Kerema, Kundiawa, Balimo, Rabaraba and Tambul experienced water supply
problems. There were anecdotal reports of an increased incidence of diarrhea, maiaria, typhoid, skin
diseases, respiratory ailments and dysentery. Extensive fires occurred in forests and grassland with
reports of large number of village houses burnt by bushfires with several accounts of people burnt in these
fires. Many airstrips were closed due to smoke and haze for as long as three weeks. The water volume in
the reservoirs of two major hydroelectric stations at Sirinumu (Central Province) and Yonki (Eastern
Highlands Province) dropped. At Sirinumu the water level fell to 20% water holding capacity disrupting
power supply in Port Moresby. The OK Tedi Mine did not operate from August 1997 to March 1998 and the
Government reported the drought as a contributing factor to the massive slide in the value of the PNG Kina
from PGK1 = US$0.72 in September 1997 to about PGK1 = US$0.40 by April 1998.

In rural areas, many crop varieties perished which resulted in a loss to the genetic diversity of staple crops
such as taro and sweet potato and there was a severe shortage in planting material to replant gardens. As
garden foods became scarce people were forced to rely heavily on eating bush and famine foods like pangi
(Pangium edule), marita (Pandanus conoideus), sago (Metroxyion sagu), tulip (Gnetum gnemon) and figs.
In some locations, even these were destroyed by bush fires. Fires also destroyed hunting grounds and
bush resources needed to build houses. As the food situation became desperate there was an increase in
stealing, more frequent disputes over land, crops and animals and a break-down in law and order. People
were forced to use their savings or cash from the sale of cash crops, livestock or from relatives to buy store
foods whose demand and price increased as other sources of food disappeared. The ‘wantok’ system
helped a lot of people and there was increased pressure on those formally employed to support their
relatives at home.

7.2.2 Case studies of other areas around the world

The catastrophic impacts of drought in other parts of the world are clearly evident in news flashes in the
internet nowadays indicating about some 12.4 million people in the horn of Africa including Somalia,
Kenya, Ethiopia and Djibouti being affected by the worst drought in 60 years. Scientists have attributed the
drought to the La Nina conditions that prevailed from June 2010 to May 2011 in the Pacific. There nas
been no rain in 2011 during the norma! wet period from late February to the end of March and if the
situation continues there will be no crop harvests in September. Indications are that the impacts of the
drought are made worse by the artificially high price for food and the civil conflict. There have also been
reports of food aid stolen and sold at markets in Somatlia. The worse affected communities are those in the
ethnically diverse and over-populated regions. The drought is affecting food security and putting millions of
people in urgent need of assistance. Tens of thousands of people have already died. In Southern Ethiopia,
malnourished children have been flocking into feeding centers and the country is teetering on the brink of a
food crisis. Suspected measles outbreak combined with acute malnutrition is thought to be the cause of
deaths. The United Nation’s Food Programme has been bringing 5,000 tons of food a month into
Mogadishu to help the famine hit Somalia where tens of thousands of people have been fleeing the country
to neighboring Ethiopia and Kenya.

7.2.3 Basic ideas on type of food that can withstand impacts of droughts

While the drought with the severity of the 1997-98 drought is capable of causing total devastation to food
gardens there are certain types of food crops that have a higher tolerance to dry conditions and minor
droughts i.e. with a less than six months duration. NARI after the 1997-98 drought through a World Bank
funded project on drought, evaluated and identified a number of drought tolerant varieties of sweet potato,
cassava and banana for the lowland and highland environments. Of these, both cassava and certain types
of triploid bananas like the kalapua, yawa and Cavendish bananas can tolerate minor drought conditions.
These types of bananas are big, robust and have huge and thick pseudostems that preserve moisture to
support plant growth during dry periods. Cassava has the ability to withstand moisture stress by closing its
stomata to reduce moisture loss and thrives well under direct sunlight. It however contains cyanogenic
glucoside (HCN) which is a toxic chemical that is harmful to humans. Most edible varieties are sweet (<100

The African yam (Dioscorea rotundata) is another crop that may prove useful because it can grow in
extreme climatic conditions. It is important therefore that we encourage farmers to increase planting of
these around their homes using best farming practices like mulching and composting.

rice (Oryza sativa), wae fan (Vigna radiate), corn (Zea mays) and peanut (Arachis hypogaea). They
have an advantage over the traditional staple crops because after harvest and drying they can be stored
for later use. These along with NARI released early maturing sweet potato varieties and other short-term
vegetable crops like pumpkins (Cucurbita moschata), aibika (Abelmoschus manihot), beans (Vigna
unguiculata), amaranthus (Amaranthus spp.) and karakap (Solanum americanum) are useful crops to plant
after droughts to quickly re-establish household food supply in the affected communities while they wait for
the more long duration staple crops to mature.

Food plants gathered from the wild like choko leaves (Sechium edule), sago, marita, tulip, swamp taro
(Cyrtosperma chamissonis) and many more that are extremely useful during droughts. Sago can be stored
but lack of water during a drought often affects processing. Some may survive under the protection of the
forest but can also be destroyed by bush fires. The coconut remains the most extremely useful nut during
dry periods, as a source of healthy and nutritious drinking water and a source of food.

Wild animals, fish and other marine foods from the sea and mangrove habitats are also an alternate food
source. Lastly, processed food from supermarkets and canteens such as rice, tinned meat, tinned fish,
dripping and flour contain protein and energy providing valuable supplements to diets of those who can
afford them during droughts.

7.2.5 Basic information on the concept of food security

According to Bourke (2000), food security is high if people have access to land and can grow most of their
food requirements and who also have access to cash income to buy food during periods of food shortage.
The most resilient production systems are the diversified systems where a wide range of food crops are
grown either on their own or integrated with cash crops, fruit and nut species, multi-purpose tree species
and even with livestock. A good example of a resilient production system is the one practiced by the Tolais
in East New Britain Province. There you find the hardier food crops like triploid bananas (ABB groups) and
singapo taro grown interspersed with various types of fruit and nut species and perennial greens under
coconut plantations. In addition to this, each family may have a block of cocoa and other food gardens
located in the foothills of the Baining Mountains in secondary and virgin rainforest. Here the tripioid
bananas, singapo taro and leafy greens like kalava (Ormocarpum orientale) and Valangur (Polyscias
verticillata) which are perennial, hardier and require less maintenance can withstand minor droughts and
act as a permanent source of reserve food. The other staple crops like sweet potato, cassava, taro are
planted in the main food gardens with vegetables. Some of these crops especially vegetables and peanuts
are grown for sale at markets. In this production system the peopie are not only able to produce food for
themselves but also produce and sell copra and cocoa to generate cash income which they can use to
purchase store food to supplement their dietary needs. Food and nutritional security can also be enhanced
if people are looking after livestock or able to extract food for consumption and sale from the environment
like choko leaves from the forest or mud crabs from the mangrove habitats. However, the harvesting of
such resources need to be properly monitored to prevent over harvesting. Lastly any food that can be
stored like sago, and rice and flour from the store would definitely boost the food security situation in
places where they are consumed.

1. Purpose:
The purpose of this submission is to inform the National Executive Council (NEC) on

the plans that the two NGOs (Managalas Development Foundation Inc (MDF) and
Partners With Melanesian Inc (PwM) have in place, and that is to apply for NEC
approval to declare the Managalas plateau as a Conservation Area in the, Afore Local
Level Government, Injivitary Electorate of Oro Province, under the Conservation
Areas Act 1978.

2. Background
Papua New Guinea (PNG), being a signatory to a number of International
Agreements, Instruments and Conventions such as the Conventions on Biological
Diversity (CBD) 1992 calls for:

i. The development of National strategically planned programs for

conservation, the sustainable use of biological diversity and the integration

to move this into sectoral plans, policies and programs (article 6) of the

National Government.

The identification of components of biological diversity important for its

conservation and sustainable use and monitor the components and identify

the activities which have the adverse impacts on conservation and

sustainable use of biological diversity and monitor their effects (article 7).

iii, The establishment of a network of protected areas and the development of
guidelines for selection, establishment and management of protected areas
where measures are

iv. needed to conserve biological diversity (article 8b and ¢).

v. The development of necessary legislation and other regulatory provisions
for protection of threatened species and populations and the promotion of
public education and awareness (article 8 (k) and article 13).

Page 1 of 66
 Other conventions include the Conservation of Nature in the South Pacific, Apia,
1976; the protection of Natural Resources and Environment of the South Pacific
Regions, Noumea, 1986; and the International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild
Fauna and Flora, Washington, 1973.

Furthermore, Papua New Guinea has undertaken its international obligations
approved in the CBD in 1992 by developing and adopting the National Biodiversity
Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2007. The NBSAP will be implemented to fulfil
not only its obligations under the CBD, but other international instruments such as the
Rio, and MDG (specifically goal 7), and other international environmental agreements
which PNG has obligations to perform. In addition, the Department of Environment
and Conservation has a new strategic direction which base around the Millenium
Development Goal # 7 (Promote Environmental Sustainability). Stipulated in this
strategy and action plan are its six (6) main goals;

Goal 1 To conserve, sustainably use, and manage the country’s biological
diversity

© Goal 2 To strengthen and promote institutional and human capacity building for
biodiversity conservation, management and sustainable use

© Goal 3 To strengthen partnership and promote coordination for conserving
biodiversity

© Goal 4 To strengthen existing protected areas and ensure that protected areas for
terrestrial species and marine species are increased to 10% by 2010 and 2012
respectively

© Goal 5 Ensure a fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of genetic and
ecosystem resources

© Goal 6 Promote and strengthen research of the country’s biological diversity and
the sustainable development of the country’s biological resources

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area is certain to have a range of measures
that act in accordance with the objectives and goals of the NBSAP and other
international conventions for Papua New Guinea. It promotes millennium
development goals (MDG); Goal 7: Promotes Environmental Sustainability, where
government seeks to and reverse the law of Environmental Resource, and address
pillar 5 of PNG’s Vission 2050 which focus on Environmental Sustainability and
Climate Change. Managalas Proposed Conservation Area if declared will increase
the percentage of protected areas in PNG by 0.9%, obviously contributing to achieve
Goal 4 of the PNGNBSAP (To strengthen existing protected areas and ensure that
protected areas for terrestrial species and marine species are increased to 10% by
2010 and 2012 respectively).

3. Facts and Considerations

Managalas Development Foundation Inc (MDF) and its facilitating partner, Partners
with Melanesians Inc. (PWM) are two “not for profit” organizations working as

Page 2 of 66

 partners with the people of Managalas Plateau since 1995 towards the goal of
establishing the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area, covering a land area of
360 000 hectares in the Afore LLG. The entire core program that is carried out in the
plateau is community based and the focus is on Conservation and Sustainable
development in the target community. The Afore LLG has 18 ward councils with a
population of over 18 000 people (2000 census), 152 clans and over a 100 villages.
Attachment - Appendix 2, details sociological information of the area and in
Appendix 4, is the Conservation Area Boundary Description and Map.

As detailed in this submission, the area under consideration has significant biological,
geographical, and cultural values to the local people of Managalas and the
International scientific community as a whole. The area is still in its proposed stage,
and foreigners are already enquiring to know more about the biodiversity of the area,
while some have visited the project site. One of the main animal species that is and
will be attracting the international community is the World’s largest butterfly (the
Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly) which is endemic to PNG particularly to the
Oro Province. This species have migrated from the Oro plains after it was deforested
for oil palm development. Managlas plateau provide the habitat for this endangered
and threatened species and if loss to improper management of commercial
developments, will result in the extinction of this unique butterfly species. Four (4)
biosurveys have been conducted in the area at various altitudes and locations and are
summarised in a separate document title; “The Biodiversity of Managalas Plateau”.
Specific advantages and facts of establishing the Managalas Conservation Area under
the Papua New Guinea Conservation Areas Act 1978 are as follows:

i. It would be the largest second recognized Conservation Area in Papua New
Guinea and would serve as a model for setting up conservation areas in other
provinces throughout the country.

2. 360 000 hectares of land area in the Managalas Plateau, Afore Sub district
would be inciuded to protect the endangered Queen Aiexandrea bird wing
butterfly, Doria’s Tree Kangaroo and other endangered and endemic wildlife
species.

3. It would extend from sea level to 2900+meters mountain rangers, spanning an
altitude and habitat range un-parallel among protected areas in PNG.

4. A Conservation Area Management Committee will be established to manage
this Conservation Area for the long term.

5. Given the uniqueness of the forests and the resources contained therein,
outside institutions, researchers and tourists would certainly want to visit the
area.

6. The Managalas Plateau presents good prospects to study past climatic changes
and their influences on the vegetation.

7. Through the Exit Strategy PwM developed between PwM and MDF, all
management responsibilities will be handed over to MDF to maintain and
manage the proposed Conservation Area once declared.

8. The Afore LLG as an important stakeholder and local authority will jointly
oversee the management of the Conservation Area along with other
stakeholders from the Managalas Plateau.

9. If declared will increase the percentage of protected areas in PNG by 0.9% to
4.1% from the current 3.2%. PNG is required to set aside 10% of its landmass

Page 3 of 66
 for bio-diversity conservation, as per its commitment to the Convention of
Biological Diversity (CBD).

10. Address pillar 5 in the Papua New Guinea Vission 2050, which focus on
Environmental! Sustainabillity and Climate Change.

‘The Conservation and Sustainable Forest Management Program carried out on the
Managalas Plateau has a community based approach and it is jointly implemented
with several other components which include: Consensus Building Programme, CBO
Capacity Building Program, Rainforest Literacy Program and Sustainable Livelihood
Alternative activities for the local population. The Managalas Proposed Conservation
‘Area Project (MPCAP) has developed its conservation approach in recognition of
PNG's unique land tenure ship laws and local needs. Because long term conservation
depends on the actions of the local people, the MPCAP is helping to provide the tools
and training necessary for making informed decisions and supporting the local
community. Partners with Melanesians have already established a locally owned NGO
= Managalas Development Foundation which will manage the Managalas
Conservation Area for the long term as stipulated in the Conservation Areas Act
(1978).

4. Views of the Provincial Governor:
Sought through the PEC endorsement

5. Views of other Ministers affected:
After the 90 days public viewing and negotiation with the NEC Secrateriat,
Department of Environment and Conservation will seck views of other vital
departments particularly, the Department of Mining and Petroleum, National Forest
Authority, Department of Agriculture and Livestock, Department of Community
Development and the Provincial and Local Level Government Affairs.

Five other major agencies nave given in their support through writing and these
include the Department of Community Development, Conservation Forum of PN
Bishop Museum, Oro Provincial Government, Afore Local Level Governement and
the Managalas Development Foundation (Refer Appendix $ for support letters).
Adversely views of other vital line agencies are yet to be sought; PNG National Forest
Auhtority, Department of Agriculture and Livestock, and Department of Mining and
Petroleum. Views of the three later Government Departments will be sought by DEC
during the 90 days public viewing.

6. Financial Imptications:

At this point in time no financial assistance is requested from the Provincial or
National Governments, but a longterm agreement with the Provincial Government is
to be arranged at a later date when the full submission is made for the endorsement of
the CA is an all stakeholder’s tasks. All funding required to facilitate the Managalas
Conservation Area Support Program is supporied by Norwegian Rainforest
Foundation (RFN), International Union of Conservation Networking (IUCN), the
World Bank, and other donors.

Page 4 of 66
 7. Staffing Impl

tions

‘The future management of the Managalas Conservation Area will be controlled by the
Managalas landowners themselves through the Managalas Development Foundation
and the Afore LLG and with assistance and technical support from the Partners with
Melanesians and eventually hand it over to the Managalas Development Foundation,
where a Management Committee will be appointed by all stakcholders in consultation
with the Department of Environment and Conservation.

8, Employment Implications:

Future employment opportunities will depend on the Conservation Area Management
Plan (CAMP) to be developed by the landowners with Afore LLG and with technical
support from PwM and its partners/donors. If the decision is made to develop some
areas of the land, itis assumed that these developments will be self sustaining.

For example, there is an initial plan to develop an eco-tourism industry on the plateau
under the Conservation Area and besides that tracking along the famous Black
Cat/Ghost Trail from Abau up into the Owen Stanley Ranges to upper Musa round
Dorobosoro and into Aiari, Suari and into the Managatas plateau the path used by the
‘American soldier in aid of the Australian at Kokoda, is now in the pipe line and it is
predicted that it will be relieving visitors. So employment opportunity along this track
will be a big income earner for the local people plus the Afore LLG through taxes and
this will create employment opportunities for the local people. The scale will be
similar to be near or bigger than the Kokoda Trail.

In light of the Conservation Area Plans, there is huge potential for the development of
a scientific research station within the area that will see the development of other
employment opportunities.

9. Legislative Implications

The Proposed Managalas Conservation Area submission proposal has been developed
ine with the Conservation Areas Act (1978). There are several steps followed as
stipulated in the Conservation Areas Act which culminates to two major phases 1)
declaration and gazettal of the Proposed Conservation Area by NEC and 2) approval
of the Conservation Area Management Plan and swearing in of the Conservation Area
Management Committee Members by the DEC Minister. The Managalas
communities, Managalas Development Foundation and Partners with Melanesia will
have completed phase | after this submission as the first requirement by the Act and
have began the preparatory work on the second phase which will also be submitted to
DEC for approval by NEC.

10. Constitution Implications

Papua New Guinea’s Fourth National Goal of its 1975 Constitution calls for the
conservation of PNG’s natural resources and environment for the collective benefit of
the current generation and should be replenished for future generations. The creation
and formal gazettal of the Propose Managalas Conservation Area directly
accomplishes this Constitutional goal. This is clearly stipulated in the Conservation
Areas Act, Subdivision IIL3.C (qualified rights) of the Constitution, namely—

Page 5 of 66
 (@ the freedom from arbitrary search and entry conferred by Section 44 of the
Constitution; and

(b) the right to privacy conferred by Section 49 of the Constitution,
is a law made for that purpose, taking into account the National Goals and the
Basic Social Obligations, particularly the fourth goal of the National Goals
and Directive Principles entitled "natural resources and environment”.

In addition, once declared and gazzetted will fulfil pillar 5 of Papua New Guinea

Vission 2050 which focuses on Environmetal Sustainability and Climate Change.

11. Political Implications:

‘The Oro Provincial Government and Afore Local Level Government support the cry
of the indigenous Managalas landowners’ to have their 360 000 ha of land and
pristine rainforests (Managalas Proposed Conservation Area) be declared the second
Conservation Area in PNG under the Conservation Areas Act (1978). The process has
followed a bottom-up approach and up to this level any unforeseen implications will
be of little significance. The Oro Provincial Executive Council formal endorsement on
the Propose Managalas Conservation Area was granted on the 02™ December 2008;
whilst Afore Local Level Government Ward Members endorsement was obtained on
the 08" of June 2011. These endorsements can be found in the Appendix 4.

12. Planning Implications:

All planning and development of the Managaias Conservation Area will be decided
upon by the entire Managalas community through their clan elders through the
Managalas Consensus Building Process which is a very unique process of
consultation and decision making where all the 152 landowning clans come together
to decide on the development priorities and options that are available to them, and
based on resource availability and by discussion and talking, consensus is reached.
The Afore LLG through the Ward Councillors will be fully involved so that the Afore
LLG has a major role in development planning which will also include the Oro
Provincial Government, the Department of Environment and Conservation (DEC) and
other major stakeholders.

41. Introduction

This manual is designed to assist the Board in the organizational management of the
Managalas Development Foundation (MDF). This initiative is supported by the Inter-church
Organization.

Since the formation of MDF there has been lack of direction and guidance in particular the
decision making on the Board’s front in governance, accountability and transparency relating to
decisions of MDF.

This manual includes the Board's general responsibilities, terms of reference for Board's
committees, general rules of procedure guiding the conduct of the Board's activities and other

Board's policies.
14. Ensure Mission, Purpose, vision and values Identified

The mission and vision of the organization should always be captured in striving to achieve the
vision of MDF in all its planned activities.

The Vision of a peaceful communal society living in Harmony with nature and a mission to
strengthen community participation & ownership through coordination of activity that promotes
self reliance, education & sustainable livelihood, while maintain cultural heritage & conserving
the natural resources.

The Board should at all times conduct activities in such a way as to uphold the mission and
vision of the Foundation.

1.2. Rational for a governing Body

Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) as an umbrella local NGO for the 10 CBOs
Managalas plateau that is expanding in terms of affiliations has seen that the board manual
should capture certain guidelines within which the Board should govern the affairs of MDF. The
mission and vision as enshrined in the Constitution of MDF.

a) To assist the Managalas plateau people in providing the medium through which they can
resolve issues of concern and conflicts amongst themselves and with groups or people.

b) To undertake education, training and awareness campaigns, and programs on
environmental issues, development, human rights, land and resource rights of the
Managalas Piateau peopie.

c) To assist the Managalas plateau people acquire resources and skills including

specialized training which could be used to advance their individual as well as collective
interests.

4) To promote the efficient management of customarily owned lands and sound economic
principles and to assist the Managalas Plateau people in establishing income generating
projects.
 © Managalas Development Foundation 2010

e) To regulate and monitor on behalf of the Managalas plateau people the sustainable
utilization of natural resources both on the land, in the land and rivers so as to ensure
that they receive maximum benefit from the development of these resources,

f) To receive, organize and administer funds, compensation payments, grants and gifts
from the nationals, Provincials and local-level government and other donor agencies in
Papua new Guinea or overseas in pursuance of its objectives

g) To plan and implement community based sustainable response management and other
community based projects in collaboration with other such Associations, Groups,
Cooperatives, Government agencies, Institutions and Non-Government Organizations
within Papua New Guinea or overseas whose aims and objectives are similar and lend
assistance and support to such other groups and organizations.

h) To collaborate and arrange for exchange programs with other like minded NGOs, CBOs
and institutions at the national and International level on issues relating to environment,
sustainable development and customary Landowners

Date: 08 September 2010

PROGRAM: Conservation

ACTIVITY: Community Reforestation /Mock Combine Forum/HCVF Dissemination

INTRODUCTION

This paper reports on our visit to the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area to attend to the
above activities. We spent almost a week at the project site and returned on the 6"” of September
2010.

PURPOSE

The purpose of the trip was to do a follow up on the progress of the community reforestation
project, deliver the summarised HCVF report to the Field Conservation Coordinator Mr Bradley
Dabadaba, and attend the mock combine forum which was held at Numba zone 6,

METHODS/PROCEDURES

Upon arrival at Girua airport Popondetta, we got on the hired vehicle and went back to town to
purchase parts for the damaged vehicie at the project site. There was a hold up at the Pogani
River. We could not cross as the river was tide due to heavy rain the previous night. We overnight
at the pastor’s house and cross over the next morning.

We dropped off the vehicle parts and the mechanic at Afore station and drove all the way to Sila
junction. We walked from there to Numba where the mock combine forum was held.

We were welcomed by the communities and the elders. i met with zone 7 manager (Ezekiel) and
Bevan Evare (the person heading the reforestation project in zone 6). Ezekiel updated me on the
progress of the reforestation work in zone 7 particularly the one in road 2; and Bevan showed me
his necessary shed where he is still filling his poly bags. There was a deceased in his family that
caused the delay of his work.

‘At the mock combine forum | played more of an observatory role. it was an eye opener for me so!
just observed and take note of the procedures that should be followed in a forum, but were not
followed in the past forums.

After the mock forum we walked back to Afore station. | met with the conservation coordinator at
the guest house and we briefly went through the simple version of the draft HCVF report. | was
told that the dissemination of this hcvf report will be done during the zone forums. This will also
 help prepare them for the actual combine forum asone if the issue to be discussed in the combine
forum is on land use planning

| personally visited the other nursery shed for the Sugokol Baru clan in zone 7. The nursery shed
has been built but the filling of the poly bags are yet to be completed. | was unfortunate to meet
Christopher (the person heading the reforestation work for the clan) as he was busy with the
theater arts performing groups doing the awareness on the western side of the plateau.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

Reforestation Project

The progress of the reforestation project is progressing well but not at a fast rate because the clan
members who are taking the lead in these work are also playing major parts in other programmes
such as the literacy and consensus building programs while others have personal problems. The
Narija clan in zone six and the Sugokol Baru clan in zone seven are currently still filling the poly
bags and collecting native tree species for their nurseries. The other group in zone ? (in road 2);
their nursery is ready for transplanting but the clan leader is continuously being sick thus the work
is delayed. From conversation with zone 7 CBO manager, | was told that, if the clan leader had
allowed him to take the lead in the reforestation work, the planting process would have been
done. However the conservation coordinator said that he will start off the transplanting in the
area now that he has free time as he was busy with preparations for the mock combine forum and
other activities under the RFL and CB programs.

Mock Combine Forum

One of the purposes of the trip was to attend the mock combine forum to see how it is conducted,
the procedures, and who the main participants in such gathering are. A full report of this mock
forum is compiled by the officer in charged Mr. Nickson Piakal (Education and Awareness Officer}
Delivery of the HCVF Report

Copies of a simple and summarised version of the draft HCVF report for the Managalas Proposed
Conservation Area was delivered to the field conservation coordinator for dissemination to the ten
zones on the plateau, This will be done during the zone forums that will be conducted before the
combine forum in November. The report is useful to provide information on various geographical
features such as; rainfall distribution, wind patterns, population distribution, threats, agricultural
activities, forest types, and the geology of the Managalas plateau. Being equipped with
information on these features will help the communities or clans to properly develop their land
use plans.

RECOMMENDATIONS

A contributing factor to some of these delays might be because there is no specialised
conservation officer that would concentrate on the conservation works and its other minor
programs. However, as we were about to depart the project site, | was advised by MDF Project
Director that he will employ a new conservation officer who will concentrate on the conservation
works.

It is important that the field conservation officer should have a digital camera to take pictures of
the work being done. Pictures are vital for reporting purposes. | am not sure whether this is the’
responsibility for MDF or PWM.

CONCLUSION

| found the trip to be fulfilling as it was the first time that | was involved in three activities at the
same time. | also learn new things from the mock combine forum that was conducted and to meet
new faces on that part of the plateau. Generally, the reforestation work is progressing well but it

/2
 will be better for a specialised officer that will work closely with the three participated clans so

that work will run smoothly and up to date.
