title: “ilaintaining the Lance”
snippet: “ilaintaining the Lance” Date: 28/6/2010 PROGRAM: Consensus Building ++ ACTIVITY: Education and Awareness INTRODUCTION This report details the awareness expedition | undertook under the banner of Hope Trek. Leaving on the 19th of May 2010, it took me and 9 youths from NCD one month through five (5)
text:
“ilaintaining the Lance”

Date: 28/6/2010
PROGRAM: Consensus Building ++
ACTIVITY: Education and Awareness

INTRODUCTION

This report details the awareness expedition | undertook under the banner of Hope Trek. Leaving on the
19th of May 2010, it took me and 9 youths from NCD one month through five (5) provinces to conclude this
awareness run in the Western Highlands Province.

Taking off from Ower’s Corner in Central Province, we took on the arduous Kokoda Trail and conducted
awareness and distributed posters every step of the way to Oro Province and onwards to Morobe, Eastern
and Western Highlands Provinces.

As put forward to you and PWM as an organization, this project is an initiative that takes a whole new
innovative approach into the idea of education and awareness on environment and conservation to include
people and places outside of PWM’s project sites without placing any extra financial burden on PWM’s
working budget. Furthermore, it was included in my initial work plan and was scheduled to coincide with
both my annual leave and the World Environment Day 2010, thus creating as little a dent in the overall
work plan of PWM and MDF and other stake hoiders.

But in so doing, | am of the strong belief that it has raised the profile of this organisation and helped shed
‘more light on our work and the whole idea of environmental and conservation awareness, notwithstanding
‘our commitment to the Managalas Plateau and our joint bid with the people there to attain its
Conservation Area status.

My push to engage the support of all media formats without any reservation has also seen more publicity
and increased support from interested people and organisations both within PNG and abroad.

PURPOSE

The purpose of this exercise was to reach not only PWM'’s project sites but beyond and outside their
confines to enlighten as many people as possible about the importance of the environment and what we as
Papua New Guineans and citizens of this world stand to gain or lose, in either the practise or non-practise
of conservation in our day to day living.

In topping of our run, we went and delivered donated library books to schools in Western Highlands
Province and Enga Province. This gesture was hoped to drive home into children and adults alike the
importance of books, as the most sure-fire way to help enlighten them and broaden their horizon. This in
time will help in addressing the challenges we face in educating our people and the future generation
about the importance of our natural environment because | believe that a literate society will be better
equipped to address not only conservation issues but the entire development of this country.

 METHODS/PROCEDURES

Awareness points

‘The key awareness points include the following:

1. Books and the importance of reading

2. Environment and conservation awareness

3. Climate Change

Looking into sustainable income generating ventures
Being responsible and self-reliant

Basic Hygiene & Cholera Awareness

oe

As appended to our list of awareness points above, the cholera outbreak was a hot issue (and still is) at the
time of our departure, so we made it as a last minute inclusion into our awareness points. Thus we also
made mention of this health crisis facing the country and explained its basic symptoms (information
gleaned from general knowledge) and pointed out its impact in the livelihood of their community in the
likelihood of a cholera case within their community. In closing, preventative measures by practising basic
hygiene in our day-to-day living was stressed and highlighted as the best possible way to keep our guard
against such a disease from reaching our door steps.

Methods of Awareness — Walking the Talk

‘As a demonstrative awareness exercise, we embarked with the silent motto of “walking the talk”. Hence a
total of six plastic shopping bags of litter ranging from empty containers and tin cans to candy wrappers
were collected, starting from Ower’s Corner all the way to Kokoda Station. The same was practised the
entire length of our travel up the Okuk Highway to WHP and back. Furthermore, we made certain to guard

against our litter as well.

Methods of Awareness — Outreach & Posters

‘On most occasions, all these points of order seemed new and foreign to them. As such, we used familiar
grounds to start with so we went back to relating the idea of conservation to traditional practises as well as
the Bible story of creation to drive home the message of conservation and environmental awareness.

In addition, our outreaches were structured to engage our audience in discussions through the idea of
having a Question & Answer session after every talk. Even in some instances ~ especially along the Track
route — some of the Hope Trek youths familiar with Motu stepped in to carry the discussion forward and
further helped to pave the way for the locals to step forward with queries and questions. This enabled us to

SD
 elaborate further on the discussed topics and to further gauge their views and get an overall understanding
of how they digested the underlying ideas of our talk.

The dissemination of information materials in the manner of posters also enabled them to better
understand concepts and the mechanics of what we were trying to get across to them. Furthermore, this
provided a way for them to be constantly reminded about our campaign, long after we were gone.

VIVE Nt
a \\

SS
 Leading up to and eventually coinciding with the World Environment Day, our awareness was aimed at
enlightening people to be more aware about the natural environment and to understand its significance in
‘our day to day living with an insight into the future as well. This was followed by the challenge put forward
to them to be more proactive in practising conservation in their day to day living by the mere act of
minding our litter, starting with the very mundane of actions of minding their cigarette stub, match stick
and bubble gum wrappers.

Target Audience
‘With our hope that these messages and ideas should be carried o1 (0 the future, our preferred target

audience were mainly school-aged children but not necessarily restricted to that. To further drive home
this message, our trekking awareness campaign was topped off with the delivery of library books which had
been sourced from Hope Worldwide (PNG) to schools in Western Highlands Province (Bukapena Primary
School) and Enga Province (Yambaitok Community School, formerly known as Saluk Community School as it
was earlier located in Saluk Village).

This awareness venture was void of any form of discrimination. In fact, whenever we came into contact
with any people, whether individuals or groups, we kept on with our outreach. And it did not stop there. |
carried on in the buses, on boats, on trucks, in schools, in villages, in urban settlements, in market places, at
bus stops, on local radio stations and even around the age-old fireplace. In short, | was simply on fire and
everybody else around me could fee! the heat and they were all burning and lapping up every single word
from this silver tongue. Whow!

Presentation of Facts & Figures
But it was not all verbal foreplay. We talked facts and figures while being mindful about the varied
background of our audience and made it as palatable as possible in their comprehension of key issues like
Global Warming and Climate Change — among others; by laying it down in the most laymen of terms as
possible, using local examples as illustrations whenever required.

‘As further illustrations of positive steps being taken by existing conservation organisations, we detailed the
work of PWM, especially with regard to our work on the Managalas Plateau and our bid to attain
Conservation Area status for Managalas. In addition, the work of the Eco-Forestry Forum and our partner
NGO's all over the country were highlighted to them.

We encouraged and promoted the idea of taking a more proactive approach by demonstrating that we can
start small by minding our litter, starting with the smallest of them like the match stick and bubble-gum
wrappers. Starting with this fundamental of idea, we appealed to our audience at the end of every such talk

/*
 sessions that there is the possibility of making a difference in looking after our natural ecosystem and in
being more mindful about our actions in relation to the bigger picture as to how our actions will impact our
natural environment. We further appealed to them to go on and pass on this message to their wantoks,
relatives, friends and neighbours about these issues.

PWM Project Site Visits

Managalas

In our itinerary, we made sure to include all the project sites of PWM. However, upon arriving
Popondetta, we bumped into Luke Mambe and Douglas Tumai who advised us that it would take us longer
than we were expecting. With our ship scheduled to leave in 2 days, | only followed up with the posters and
awareness materials that Bradley Dabadaba had taken with him the previous week.

Ona-Keta

After dropping off the rest of the Hope Trek team in Hagen, | came back to Goroka and caught up with
Patrick Jack, Richard Wapo and Nelson Duabane. The next morning | went over to Konningi Primary School
where we celebrated World Environment Day with the children and teachers there. It was interesting and
fulfilling to reach out to these eager children.

Lembena

Due to the situation on the ground at Lembena, | could not get into that area. Even if there were no
problems on the ground, | would have still had problems getting there due to financial constraints. But
because | initially got the library books for the school children of Lembena, | instead went and dropped off
a couple of boxes of books at the Baptist Union headquarters in Kimininga at Mt Hagen and advised people
responsible for the Lemebena area to take the books with them the next time they charter a plane to
Yamabitok.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

It was apparent that all the information presented was lacking in the communities we entered and passed
through. It was evident from their reception and feedback that they very much needed to hear about the
things we had to say. According to most people including village leaders, church leaders, women in the
‘community, and local youths alike, such vital information was lacking in their community and our messages
were an eye-opener for them.

As such they asked us to stop by again in future and ensured our safe passage as well as catering for our
refreshments.

Such gestures were very much encouraging and it further spurred us on with renewed energy in our
trekking campaign. it further gave us the reassurance that the spirit of giving in the traditional Melanesian
way was pretty much alive within most, if not all members of the community.

RECOMMENDATIONS.

It is therefore of my strong belief that the idea of environmental awareness and conservation is something
that needs to be shared with everybody in our country. From urban centres to rural isolated communities
alike. This is of vital importance because this notion has to be reiterated and ingrained into the psyche of all
members of our communities so that it can be transpired into ACTION at the individual level up to the
bigger community level. Only then can we make inroads into the communities in seeing the message of
conservation being spread and practised in our day to day lives.

Take for example the hot topic of Climate Change. We talk about trying to reverse this global crisis but the
fact remains that we cannot make even a dent in the outcome if this message is confined to only our
project sites. It has to reach out into all corners of this country if we want to truly drive home this message.
‘And we have seen time and time again that we cannot rely on the government and their various designated
 offices to further this cause. As such the onus is now on us as conservation organisations and individuals
within these organisations to spread the word.

In saying that | do not expect us to reallocate funds and realign our budget into such awareness exercises.
We can instead start small at the level of practising what we preach and look into supporting similar
initiative wholeheartedly instead of seeing it as a one man show.

Furthermore, programme activities aside, it is of my view that many a times those of us within the
conservation NGO network at often times only preach about such issues and that is about as far as we go.
Our actions often veer away from the path of our mouths. It is high time we reanalyse our very mundane of
actions. That brings me back to the point of littering. In saying that it takes me back to the very minute of
litter like cigarette stubs, match stick and bubble gum wrappers, buai spittle notwithstanding. In short, we
have to practise what we preach. Only by doing that will we be able to demonstrate to people that there is
a starting point where conservation can be practised.

CONCLUSION

All in all the Hope Trek expedition, as a demonstrative awareness exercise proved to be an eye opener
not only for me but for all who participated in this exercise, including the people who were the recipients of
the information (in our awareness outreach) and the donated books as well as the youths who trekked with
me.

We were all very well received in most areas we went to because the ideas being broached were all new to

the people and the children in the schools | attended. This is evident of the need for more similar initiatives
to be undertaken to promote our cause to garner more support from the wider PNG community at large.

INTRODUCTION

This report details my final visit to the project site for the year 2010. This trip was tied up together
with the trip for the District Wide Combine Forum which was held in Jorura in zone three (3). 1
took off on Wednesday 10" November to finalise conservation works with the field officer, and
then went on to join the participants from Port Moresby who went up for the Combine Forum
which began from the 16" to the 18” of November. We all return to Port Moresby on the 19" of
November 2010.

PURPOSE

‘The purpose of the trip was mainly to finalise with the field coordinator the remaining conservation
activities that were still pending. In addition, the trip was also meant to attend the District Wide
Combine Forum.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

On Wednesday 10" November, I flew over to Popondetta and got on a PMV to Afore.

I met Edrick Ninimiro, PWM Admin Officer and he updated that preparation work for the Combine
Forum on the ground need polishing up. Since Nickson was late for his flight and has to fly over the
following day, I took his place and together with Edrick, we went to Jorura to check for Brian
Kasira, the Consensus Building Officer on the ground, to polish up the preparation work.

In the afternoon of the same day we went back to Afore to meet with Nickson. The following day
(Friday), I met with Bradley and we finalised the remaining conservation works. On the same day, I
had the chance to meet with the Chairman for Afore Primary School where we had a walk down to
their school to see their nursery seedlings.

RESULTS/FINDINGS
From our discussion, Bradley is yet to carry out the CA Border Patrol in Zone 8 where the threat
from logging is slowly creeping into the CA Boundary. There are two clan groups that are pushing
for logging activities. What we have come up with from our discussion was to get CELCOR
officers, the field officer and myself to visit the zone and get their opinion whether we have to curve
them out from the CA Boundary or let their area remain as part of the CA. However, since we ate
winding up program activities for this year, this can be brought forward to next year’s work plan.
One of the primary reasons for the logging threat according to Bradley is that the deal between the
WMA and Dadakul has expired. The two clans here are Dokapol and Sarila.

 The reforestation work by Bewen in zone 6 is progressing well. Out of the 500 nursery bags given
to him for seedlings, he has transplanted 300 seedlings during the last rainy season. Now he’s
waiting for the next wet season to transplant the last 200 seedlings. The status of Christopher's
group in zone 7 is that they are still working on their nursery seedlings. According to the
conservation field officer, they are to relocate their nursery shed close to the area to be reforested
which is at Afore. Jerome and his clan has not settled the land disputes amongst them, so I have
advised Ezekiel who has prepared the seedlings for the grassland on Jerome’s land to transplant the
seedlings on the grassland areas around the Afore Primary School. Ezekiel is leading the students at
Afore Primary School to set up their nursery seedlings. The school is making use of the K200
which we have given to all the schools on the plateau during the World Environment Day this year,
to start up small reforestation projects for their schools.

A detail report for the entire District Wide Combine Forum is prepared by the officer in charged,
Mr Nickson Piakal. I'll just give a brief report as this was an eye opener for me. The participants
that flew over from Port Moresby are tabled below.

PEI AW EEN
 Introduction
‘This year’s scriptwriting workshop saw an increase in the number of women participants
and also an increase in the number of young participants compared to the previous
Scriptwriting workshops. This resulted in a better and more constructive discussion in the
course of the workshop.

By this, I don’t mean to say that the other participants are not contributing and sharing
ideas, they were very helpful because the new participants have learnt a lot from them
and vise-versa. This is where the heart of leaming is because each participant brings in
their ideas and views on what they know about each topics/issues. During the discussion
and sharing of ideas everybody learns in the process and at the same time learning
materials are developed.

In terms of producing learning materials, for this year we are going to include
Theatre/Drama instead of the usual radio programs that Rainforest Literacy produces.
‘The reasons are simple;
1. radio programs are too costly to produce
2. itis also (oo technical for MDF to take it on when PWM leaves full responsibility
to them to take it on.
3. the impact of RFL was at a very slow rate since the program began, so we decided
to try theatre instead

Review of 2009 Issues

The first part of the workshop was spent on reviewing last year’s topics and the topic that
‘most time was spent on was Land Use Plan. Through the discussion it showed that most
clan members in the plateau are realizing the importance of having a land use plan which
‘means that the program has had an impact by at a slower rate.

‘The participants identified main problem areas and discussed how they will solve these
problems. For example, members of Zone 8 have used their clan elders and chiefs to
solve any land related matters because the elders/chiefs have the upper hand in decision-
making. As for zone 10 they suggested that there is a need for awareness especially on
issues such as family planning as it leads to population increase and further to land
related problems. When people start to have more children, the population increased,
villages and gardens expand. This leads to all sorts of land related problems and disputes.
So they suggested that if they are better informed on the issue of family planning, this
would solve land related problems. Similar solutions were identified by the other Zones
while two zones (5 & 7) mentioned that there is no sign/indication at all on whether they
understand Land use plan or not.

As mentioned above, this was one of the reasons why we had to do a trial theater/drama
program instead of the usual radio program. We had to try something else because
different people have different learning styles e.g.; some learn better by seeing pictures
and illustrations while some learn better by listening and watching CD/DVDs.

‘The responses from the other issues/topics vary from zone to zone but the impact is
happening very slowly. We can’t really measure a person’s learning ability but in terms
of the impacts, there are visible impacts but then again it will take a while for the people
to really grasp the message and put it into action. This was one of the reasons why we

 had to take a different approach by trialing out Drama/Taeatre instead of the radio
programs.

The 2010 Issues & discussions

The second part of the workshop was spent on identifying and discussing the new
topics/issues for the year as per the 2009 clan group discussions and the Combine Forum
in November 2009.

Disaster Risk Management

Climate Change

Land Use Plan cross-cut with family planning

Conservation cross-cut with Social Problems

SeNE

These topics (above) are discussed by the participants and the discussion was based at
answering these 3 main questions;

1. what comes to your mind when you see or hear about these topics

2. how has it become an issue in your community (good/bad)

3. who are the main actors.

4. how do you solve them if they are a problem in your community

In the course of the discussion, it showed that participants have understood the topics on
land use plan and conservation better that Disaster Risk Management and Climate
Change.

They were able to comprehend and come up with good discussion points, views and ideas
for topics 1 & 2 than topics 3 & 4. They also needed more information and clarification
on the cross-cutting issues but they were able to connect them well with the two main
topics.

The interesting part is when participants get to develop trigger questions for each
topics/issues. The participants come up with very simple question (i.e. who, what, where,
when, why & how) for each of the topics.

Learning objectives are then formed out of the trigger questions while at the same time
they will be used (o stir up discussion during the clan group discussion sessions.

The learning objectives are then distributed to each of the learning materials (print &
theatre/drama). Using the learning objectives print materials will be developed and
produced soon while the story lines and scripts for the theatre/drama programs have
already been developed by the participants

There will be a basic theater/drama skills training which will be facilitated by the UPNG
‘Theater Arts Strand in a few weeks time. So the story lines and scripts that the
participants developed will be used during the training. It is only a trial program and we
don’t know yet what the training will be like but we are hoping that the training will be
made simple and the methods/skills will be user friendly to the participants and will suit
the Managalas setting.

Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report

Acknowledgement

The team members would like to thank the following zones; Zones 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10 for
their hospitality and making sure the Patrol was a success. Acknowledgement is also
extended to the management of both Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) for the logistical arrangement and approval. Special
thank you to all the patrol team members especially the Desert Storm and its Commander;
your jokes, encouragement and support all throughout the patrol was great.

May the spirit of oneness reign on Managalas Plateau, and let us continue the fight to
safeguard and protect our home which is also home to the endangered and unique species of
plants and animals.

Executive Summary

‘This is the combined report of the Conservation Area border Patrol (1) for targeted zones as
per the 2010 MDF/PWM Combine Conservation work plan. In light to the Conservation
area Application procedure, a complete Boundary map of Managalas Conservation Arca
(MCA) is required by the concerned Government Departments. Therefore the need for a
patrol to the disputed and threatened areas was planned. The targeted or affected zones are
zones 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10.

Two Patrols will be done as agreed upon by both PWM and MDF Staff during their
combine planning workshop that was done in January 2010. As MDF, PWM and the people
cof Managalas are gearing up and preparing to submit their Application to the Government in
June this year 2010, these patrols are vital to see that all requirements are in place. This first
patrol is to confirm boundary gaps in the disputed areas and find ways to solve that and also
to find out about the status of the threatened areas. The second Patrol will be done following
the recommendations from this report.

Se —$——_—
‘Authors: Jacinta Mimigari (PWM) and Bradley Dabadaba (MDF) 1
 Page 2
Managalas Conservation Area Border Patrol (1) Report

Introduction

‘The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) is found in the Afore Local level
Government in Oro Province and covers a land area of about 360, 000 hectares. A Boundary
Map of any proposed Conservation Area is one of the main requirements of the Department
of Environment and Conservation. There are 18 ward councils found within the MPCA area
and over 150 clan groups which are then divided into 10 zones. From these 10 zones, there
are 5 Zones (Zone, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10) with Boundary Dispute/ issues that had prevented the
mapping team to complete the Boundary of the Managalas Conservation Area, in 2005. To
tackle this, members of the patrol team were divided into two (Team | and team 2) and
visited the targeted zones.

Team I members are: Chrispine Burawa (Team leader), Edwin Noaka, Brian Kasira, and
Peter Sawari

Team 2 members are: Bradley Dabadaba (Team Leader), Jacinta Mimigari, Douglas Tumai,
and Malkus Kajia

Team 1 were assigned to Patrol areas on the Western flank of the Plateau, which are zones
(4, 10) while team 2 were assigned to the Eastern flanks of the plateau & 8 and 9)
excluding Gewoia, due to threats from that area. The teams departed on the 15" of February
2010 and returned back safely on the 25" of February at MDF base at Afore.

As PWM, MDF and the people of Managlas are in the process of submitting their
Conservation Area Application, such Boundary Patrols have to be done to see that all
requirements are met and that the communities are kept informed.

Found in this report also are recommendations, Action Plans and details of the Patrol.

Purposes

‘The main purpose of the Conservation Area Patrol was to identify disputed Areas/
boundaries and investigate and confirm threats in the suspected areas. MDF also see that
Patrol as an avenue to carry out some of their planned activities such as;

a) Awareness on reforestation projects

b) Reorganize clan groups

c) Explanations on importance of Land use plan

4d) Attend to CBO issues.

Results and Patrol Brief

‘A briefing was held on the 14" of February 2010, before both teams set off for the Patrol.
During the briefing, patrol teams were reminded and each encouraged themselves on how to
constructively attend to possible sensitive issues that could be raised during the Patrol. Each
teams’ schedules were drawn up, food rations, logistics and patrol equipments were
distributed during the briefing. (See full briefing minutes in Appendix 3).

At the end of the patrol a combined debrief was organized again by the Conservation Patrol
Coordinator, Mr. Dabadaba for 1 whole day to allow both teams to highlight issues/
challenges identified during the border patrol. The briefing found out that most issues or
challenges identified by both teams were similar but few new issues were discovered. These

were the findings;

a) Land disputes and Boundary mapping of the gaps
Clan leaders and elders explained about the nature of the disputes, and discuss
amongst themselves how they can tackle this so as to complete the CA Boundary. It
was also realized that communities themselves have their own internal issues, but the
Patrol members made it clear to them that this is their own problems/issues to
handle.

In zone 6, Kingsford. N, who once worked on the mapping project, gave a brief
background history of the mapping work and the problems faced that hindered the
completion of the project. From that Recommendations were down.

b) Awareness on Reforestation, Reorganize clan groups, Land use plan and attend to
CBO’s issues.
During the meetings communities were informed about the selection criteria for
potential reforestation project sites. And if communities/clans are interested then
they should inform their CBO’s about that. The importance of land use plans were
explained also. MDF also took notes of the CBO’s issues raised by the communities
and advised the communities to organize and re-elect new board members and CBO
Staffs to make the CBO function effectively. The power to create an effective CBO
lies in each community. CBOs were also told to reorganize clan groups and all the
sub clans must remain under the main clans. Communities were encouraged to work
closely with their CBOs. It was encouraging to see Ward 5 council member present
at the meeting in Numba and communities present saw the importance of both
Government and NGO’s working together.
‘The communities were also advised that the above mentioned activi are all in the
work plan for 2010, and these activities will mostly be carried out by the CBO’s
therefore the CBO staff, board and community members need to reorganize
themselves in order to execute these activities.

Partners With Melanesians

“Uinta

PROGRAM: Conservation Component

ACTIVITY: Afore LLG Resolution: Workshop conducted by PWM & CELCOR to explain to
the councillors the CA processes and the procedures, Conservation Areas Act and the
advantages and disadvantages of a Conservation Area.

During the 2010 Christmas Holiday a team consisting of officers from PWM and CELCOR, went
up to the Managalas platcau to meet with the Afore LLG President and his 18 ward councillors. The
purpose of the mecting was to get clarification from them as to why the assembly had adjourned the
signing of the Conservation Area (CA) resolution to the end of 2011. Unfortunately, only three (3)
councillors and the President attended. During our meeting with them, the President advice the team
that they (Afore LLG) have prepared a resolution and issues that they want PWM to address. One
main issue is for PWM and its Partners to conduct more awareness to the councillors as majority do
not understand /) the CA procedures, 2) the advantages and disadvantages of a CA, and explain the
3) Conservation Area Act. Therefore, this workshop was an action taken to address the main issue
that the President pointed out above.

The purpose of this trip or workshop was to make awareness to the councillors on the above
mentioned areas so that they can be in a better position to make decision. In fact a similar workshop
‘was also conducted in April 2010.

Officers that went up for the workshop were
Kenn Mondiai, Damien Ase and Patrick Vuet.
Damien was late for the flight so he flew over the
following day. Kenn and 1 flew on the 11" of
May 2011 and were supposed to go straight up to
the project site (Afore), however, a block road
occurred at Eroro Village where the villagers cut
down two coconut trees to block the road. We
couldn't passed through so we over night at Oro
Guest House with two councillors (Remingius
Juharo & Abraham Tarabu) and Edrick Ninimiro
(PWM SLA Officer).

 ‘We travelled up to Managalas on the 12" of May.

We arrived at around 11 am at Afore. We started the program for that first day after lunch and
ended at Spm. As per the two days program, Patrick went through the CA processes and
procedures, update on the current status of the Conservation Area, and the activities that PWM,
MDP, the LLG and the communities will do after the Managaias Proposed Conservation Arca is
declared a Conservation Area.

Afore Para- Legal Workshop

“This report covers the proceeding of the three days
paralegal workshop in Afore Sub-District, Oro Province
that took place from the 12th - 14th of October 2011

Sathieshar Lane (Legal Officer)
10/19/2011
 Contents

Introduction

Objective

Background

Proceeding of the Workshop
1. Para-Legal Workshop
2. Evaluation

3. MDF Constitution
Amendment Meeting

4. Members Code of Conduct
Conclusion

Recommendation

Page

3

 Introduction

‘The Para-legal Workshop was held on the 12 -14* of October 2011 at Afore Station, which was
about four hours drive form Popondetta Town, Oro Province. The Workshop was organized by
Partners with Melanesia (PwM) and facilitated by PNG Eco-Forestry Forum (PNG EFF) using,
the Para- Legal Manuel provided for by Center for Environment Law and Community Rights
Incorporation (CELCOR).

Objective
‘The main objectives of the workshop were:

i, Toconduct a para-legal training for the Managalas Conservation Area Project (MLAP)
stakeholders communities at Afore sub-district; and
ii, To conduct a Code of Conduct awareness to lobby support for its endorsement and
implementation by PNG EFF member organizations.

Background

‘The Afore Station is located on Managalas Plateau and is home to the Managalas Development
Foundation Incorporation (MDF) who is both a member of PwM and PNGEFF.

MDF is an umbrella organization that has eleven community based organization (CBOs) from
the local area affiliated to it. The organization was established in 2002 with the help and support
of PwM, The Managalas Plateau has been the focus for PwM for more than ten (10) years.

Currently, the Managalas area is under the process of being declared a Conservation Area
under the Conservation Act 1978. Over the year PwM has worked with the people and
communities in Managalas bringing them this far in almost achieving the biggest mile stone in

history.

This opportunity also gave PNG EFF the opportunity to bring the Code of Conduct (CoC)
awareness to our member's door steps in our effort to promote and lobby support from them to
have this policy endorsed and implemented effectively by the end of this year. The MDF is a
financial member of the Forum and as such as voting powers under the PNG EFF constitution.

In brief, the Code of Conduct contains the 10 Articles or Guidelines that govern the conduct of
the Forum and its members within and outside of the working environment.A CoC defines the
acceptable set of behaviors within a group/organization that guide behavior that guide the
decisions, procedures and systems of an organization in a way that contributes to the welfare of
its key stakeholders and respects the rights of all constituent affected by its operations

Proceeding of the Workshop

1) Para-Legal Workshop
 ‘The actual para-legal workshop ran for the first two days at the Council Chambers at Afore
Station. The workshop started at 9,30 am and concluded at 4.30 pm each day. The workshop
was also attended by forty participants from the Afore area from which eight were ward
councilors.

‘The program started with formal introductions of the facilitator and her assistants then
followed by the introduction of the workshop participants. This followed with the facilitator
outlining the purpose of the workshop before the para-legal topics were introduced for the day.
This process was followed the next day because some of the participants arrived after lunch or
early the next morning,

‘The workshop began with a review of the PNG Constitution which forms the basis of all law in
the country and its purpose and importance as a legal and political document. Further, the
facilitator took the participants through the PNG’s Constitutional Goal and Directive Principles
and Basic Rights and Obligations under the Constitution.

‘Then the discussions moved into looking at the three arms of government and their roles and
responsibility, the formal court systems in PNG and the special courts established under
different legislations and finally laws relating to the Use and Management of Natural Resources.
This session cover in brief the following laws; Forestry Act, Mining Act, Oil and Gas Act and
Land Act.

The program for the day ends with a question and answer session where the participants were
given the opportunity to ask questions regarding the laws that were discussed during the
session.

The second day began with recapping what was discussed in the first day of the workshop by
randomly selecting participants to contribute. This followed by the discussion on laws relating,
to the Conservation and Management of the Environment. This session covered the following laws
in brief; Environmental Act 2000, The Fauns (Protection and Control) Act, National Parks Act
and Conservation Areas Act.

The main emphasis of that session was for the participants to understand their rights and
responsibility as customary landowners under the Act and the steps involved in creating a
Conservation Area.

‘The second half of the day was spent looking at the laws relating to Landowner Groups and Land
Use Management. This session cover the following laws;Land Groups Incorporation Act, Land
Dispute Settlement Act, Land Titles Commission Act, Business Groups Incorporation Act ,
Business Names Act, Association Incorporation Act, Companies Act and Customs Recognition
Act.

Again the program for the day ends with a question and answer session where the participants
were given the opportunity to ask questions regarding the laws that were covered.

 2) Evaluation

At about 3.30 pm on the second day a general evaluation was carried out. The facilitator asked
the participants three main questions, firstly, what they have learnt from the workshop;
secondly, what they think about the Conservation Area because the Managalas area was
heading in that direction; and finally what do they want to recommend after the workshop?

The collective results of the evaluation are that
© Majority want a week of para-legal training conducted at Managalas;
«© Majority also are ant the Conservation Area Project to do ahead and have the area
declared as a Conservation Area; and
+ They have learnt so much in the workshop which was first of its kind and especially
about their rights and responsibility as landowners of a Conservation Area.

3) MDF Constitution Amendments Meeting.

On Friday the facilitator and Rufus from PwMmet with the Board Members of MDE, the MDF
Staff and CBO representatives to discuss the MDF constitutional changes. During the meeting,
apart from the MDF Board and staff, three CBO Managers and four zone managers were
present and the rest were absent even after they were served with notice from MDF to attend
this workshop and meeting.

‘The meeting began with Rufus highlighting the proposed changes and the implications that
would have on MDE. He had to draw up the MDF structure and make reference to the
constitution to illustrate to the listeners what changes were needed. He went on further to
explain the importance of AGM and Board Meetings for both CBO and MDF. MDF did not
have an AGM since 2002 which was contrary to their constitution.

From this meeting it was established by majority votes that the MDF constitution needed
amendments to reflect the objectives and purpose of the organization. Below are the proposed

changes to MDF constitution:
‘* CBO membership only to MDF and no individual membership.

+ Affiliation Fees for CBO must be determined by the MDF Board.

+ Affiliated members are the financial members who have the voting powers in during
AGM.

‘* Inco-operate penalties/fines for non-compliance

«Reflect facknowledge that CBO chairmen for the eleven zones automatically become the

MDF board members.

 + Reference is made to reflect the BOD Manuel and other important policies.

4) Members Code of Conduct.

After this, the facilitator made presentation on the CoC outlining its background, explaining the
ten articles of the COC and stressing its importance in terms of governance in any given
organization. It was agreed that it was a good initiative by PNGEFF and this policy must be
implemented soon. It was also agreed that MDF should also sign to the CoC when it is
implemented, however, this will be raised during the MDF Board meeting and decided on.

Conclusion

‘The workshop was very interactive and interesting for most of the participants who also
expressed their interest in having a full para-legal training that will go in depth on the study of
the different laws that were covered briefly during the workshop.

Many participants thanked PwM and PNGEFF to plan this activity to be carried out in Afore
were the people are preparing themselves for the establishment of the Conservation area which
is the whole area of Managalas Plateau, Afore Sub-District, Oro Province.

Recommendations
Below are the recommendations:

1. To have another Para-Legal Training at Managalas Plateau for a week and planned for it
carly next year.

2. Have the MDF constitution changed as agreed in the meeting on Friday and by way of
MDF Board resolution. These changes should be made before the end of this year and

lodged at IPA in Port Moresby.
3. Have the CBO constitutions amended to reflect the changes in the MDF constitution.

END.

Installation Report

a

 Background:

Aiari Village is in the upper-Musa area of the Ijivitari District in Oro Province. It saddles the
Managalas Plateau on i’s south flank and is one of the main villages in the head-waters of the Musa
River. The nearest airstrip is approximately 20 kilometers to the north at Itokama. It is also where there
is a Health Centre and School facil

Aiari village is the site for the establishment of a CBO office for one of the production zones in the
‘Managalas Sustainable Development Project. I was tasked by PWM-PNG to source and install this
CBO's HF Radio and Solar System. This report covers that exercise, which I have now completed

Please note that while my contract stipulated going in to Gora and installing their new battery, no staff
from that zone made themselves available at Itokama. This was further complicated by the rescheduling

 Acknowledgments

This training was initiated and hosted by Partners with Melanesia and the
Managalas Development Foundation Inc. for the teachers of the Managalas
Plateau.

All information and illustrations provided in this training guide were supplied by
Partners with Melanesia and the Research & Conservation Foundation of PNG.
Additional information was also sourced from Wikipedia, the Free Encyclopedia.
 Introduction

Papua New Guinea's (PNG) natural environment is very important to rural
communities as about 87 per cent of people living in these areas depend on it for
their livelihood. This dependence is illustrated by the fact that 97 per cent of
including almost all forest is owned by the local

the nation's total land mass,
people. Like other Melanesians, land ownership in PNG is owned by kinship groups
but used by individuals or households. These groups usually consist of clans to
which membership is recruited mainly by descent.

What makes PNG’s natural environment more important is the high biodiversity
it hosts. In fact PNG is thought to harbour more than 5% of the world's
biodiversity. As the largest and highest tropical island, PNG is a steward of
about 789 endemic species, 41% of which are threatened and 6% classified as
endangered. The existence of this biodiversity is mostly linked to the rich
ecosystems that it has. Papua New Guinea's rich ecosystems contain
considerable amount of biodiversity that supports the nation's primary resource-
based economy. The goods and services provided by the country's biodiversity
and the ecological stability that it helps to play a vital role in maintaining the
resilience of the biosphere.

With the current degradation rate, these natural environments are likely to
perish and require every effort from all citizens to protect them. In addition,
by protecting these natural environments PNG's diverse cultural heritage will
also be protected as culture and environment are very closely linked.

It is therefore the aim of this training to:
(i) enhanced teachers understanding of the environment.
(ii) enable teachers to integrate the knowledge and skills from this
training into their teaching.
(iii) enable teachers to develop a sound understanding of global, regional
and local environmental issues.
(iv) _ enable teachers to take action to promote biodiversity conservation.
 1. What is the Environment to You?

The environment refers to everything around us. This includes things which are
natural as well as built by men, things that are alive and not alive. The
environment consists of rivers, mountains, lakes, the sea, forest, mangroves,
wildlife and plants. The clouds, sun, moon, rain and wind are part of this
environment. Most important, humans belong to this environment too.

In the past, our ancestors, recognised this relationship and acknowledged that
humans are part of this interrelated system. Everything they obtained for their
survival was taken from the environment. Timber for construction, leaves and
grass for roofs, food and medicine were all taken from their environment. The
environment was their school, hospital, hardware store and supermarket.

They observed the rising and setting of the sun and moon and planned their
traditional voyages. The flowers of a particular tree spoke of the hunting season
ahead. The happy chirping of « special bird announced the season of the
favourite bush fruits. Life was simple. Our ancestors lived in harmony with
nature. They had their own rules that govern their existence. They took enough
for today and left some for tomorrow. They only hunted the cassowary when the
season was right. When they hunted the mother, they released the young ones
so that there would be some left for the next day.

This was the life of our ancestors; they recognized Mother Nature and its
providence. They took very good care of all that Mother Nature granted them
and made sure that there was always enough for the next season.

Thought Question
The above is a scenario from the past. What is it like today? How has this
changed?
 2. Environments of PNG

We learnt from the previous topic that our ancestors viewed the world as an
interdependent system and that each component was dependent on others for
their survival. Living things live in harmony with each other in their environment.
Different parts of the environment are home to different species. These places
provide all the survival needs for each of these species, Such places are called
habitats.

Types of environments in PNG

(a) Terrestrial environments
The diversity of the vegetation varies depending on factors as geographical
location, rainfall, soil, altitude and history of disturbance. Disturbances may be
naturally occurring or imposed by humans.

Key terrestrial environments include:
i) grassland

ii) swamps

iii) monsoon forest

iv) lowland tropical rainforest

v) montane forests

vi) sub alpine forest and grassland
vii) alpine forests

Terrestrial environments are highly vulnerable to exploitation due to increasing
human population in the region. With the economies driven by natural resources,
vast areas of terrestrial environments are bound for destruction. The
environments provide resources for personal as well as commercial benefits to
the people.

(6) Marine environments
PNG is one of the few blessed with a biologically rich, diverse and pristine
marine environments in the world.

Marine ecosystems encompass the following:
i) Mangroves

ii) Coral reefs and atolls

Rocky shoreline

Lagoons

Sea grass communities

Wetlands

vii) Sand and mud shoreline

 The marine resources in these ecosystems satisfy subsistence needs and
contribute to economic development.

Environments at risk

With the increase of destructive human activities such as logging and mining,
the Melanesian environments are greatly at risks.“Lack of strategies for
biodiversity conservation may result in widespread loss of endemic species of
fauna and flora.

Activity 2.1

1. List the different habitat types found in Tjivitari and describe two
special features of each of these habitats.

2. List the different habitats of Oro in the table below and give examples of
plants and animals found in each of these habitats.

t!

 One of the important habitats of Oro and Papua New Guinea is the rainforest.
Like other rainforests of the world, this habitat is scattered in discontinuous
bands along the equator, between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. This is
because the tropics offer an ideal environment for growth. Temperatures are
warm and stable and water is abundant. The warm wet conditions facilitate plant
growth. The presence of many different plants provide food and living spaces
for different kinds of animals. This results in high biodiversity.

Another reason for high biodiversity is the structure of the rainforests. There
‘are four main layers in the rainforests - forest floor, understory, canopy and
emergent layer. These layers cater for a variety of organisms from insects to
mammals to birds of prey such as the harpy eagle.

Activity 2.2
(i) Construct a rainforest mural.

 3. The Managalas Plateau

From the facts you already know of your local area and the information supplied
by PwM and MDF, let us discuss about Managalas Plateau and why it is special.

Managalas plateau has an area of 360,000 hectares of intact forest with an
altitude of 460m asl to 2900m asl, The area is classified as lowland tropical
rainforest with a fertile volcanic soil.

Let us discuss the following questions about the area.

1. What is the population like?

2. How many Wards are there in the Afore LLG?

3. How many languages do you speak?
4, What is the main religion?

5. What is the status of education and health on this area?

6. How do your people view their environment?

7. What do the people think about conservation?

8. List two special things about the area.

(Please refer to the copy of the power point presentation by PwM on the Managalas Plateau for
more discussions.)
 4. Environmental Threats

Environmental threats are possible activities that can cause damage or harm to
the environment. These can be classified into two broad categories, natural and

human-made threats.

a. Natural threats

Melanesian countries like PNG are at risk of biodiversity loss through natural
phenomena as well. With its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire, it is subjected
to severe seismic activities such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions which
often lead to habitat destruction. Landslips caused by heavy rainfall are also

another natural threat.

Even though natural threats contribute to biodiversity loss, it is less imperative
at this stage because humans have no control. However, human induced threats
are very crucial at this stage because only they can positively act to reduce the
‘amount of threats posed on biodiversity

b. Human-made

© Introduction of invasive species - this includes both plants animals
intentionally introduced into the region for various reasons. Principally the
introduction of new species may be for agricultural purposes, as pest
control, weed control, and soil erosion prevention or food source for
grazing.

* Habitat alteration and destruction- mainly influenced by commercial
activities such as /ogging, mining, agriculture, commercial fishing.

© Infrastructural development ~ also contribute to habitat destruction, by
clearing natural habitats for new roads, airstrips, wharfs, buildings etc..

* Pollution- When wastes of all states; solid, liquid and gaseous is not
disposed properly: they of course disturb the natural ecosystem of the
place where they are discharged resulting in loss of biodiversity

* Over hunting/harvesting - The combine effects of technology and
population growth represent a clear danger to wildlife especially near
populated area,

¢. Major Driving Forces

Threats to biodiversity in Melanesia and the world as a whole is basically
triggered by three major driving forces:

1. Population growth - number of people living an area

10
 2. Consumption - amount of resources consumed by individuals

3. Technology - how much space and resources are used and how much waste
is produced to meet each person's consumption demand.

d. Climate Change and Biodiversity

Climate change or global warming is probably the biggest threat to biodiversity
and humanity. Climate change is characterized by chdnges in temperature and
rainfall patterns, Climate affects all animals and plants that live in an area in
some way. It affects the ecological processes that are vital to life on Earth.

When the climate begins to change, all living things have to change their
lifestyles in order to survive. The entire ecosystems may change with global
warming. Since the development of ecosystems have been very slow processes
taking many thousands of years, many species will be likely to have problems
adapting to rapid climate change and may become extinct. Obvious impacts of
climate change on biodiversity may include changes in flowering time of native
plants, migration of animals like bird species, decline in trees. Some signs in our
environment may include disappearing wetlands, greater coastal erosion,
frequent landslips, flash floods, coral death due to bleaching, etc...

u
 5. Conservation Areas

A conservation area is an area set aside for the purpose of conservation under
the Conservation Area Act. Some preliminary stages in the creation of a CA are:

(i) Community Mobilization & Consensus
(ii) Submissions to LLG & PEC

(iii) Submission to Minister (DEC)

(iv) Deliberation by NCC

(v) 90 Days Public Consumption

(vi) Minister to NEC

(vii) NEC to Head of State (66)

(viii) Declaration of Conservation Area
(ix) Management & Development Plans
(x) Approval

(xi) Gazettal of Conservation Area
(xii) Launching & Celebrations

B. Conservation Area Act

This law applies to land under any form of ownership, and it requests
conservation along participatory and consensual lines. The basic approach is to
allow an area to be declared a Conservation Area, with its own Conservation Area
Management Committee. The committee prepares a management plan for the
Area, and this plan controls any development of this land.

There is a five member National Conservation Council, which is the expert body
to advise and ossist the Minister in fulfilling the Act. The Council establishes
criteria for Conservation Areas, and the Minister then recommends a
Conservation Area, This area must have “particular biological, topographical,
geological, historical, scientific or social significance’s or other special value for
the presently community or for future generation". This can be done on the
Minister's own initiative, or after receiving a request form a person, group or
‘authority. The recommendation must be made available for public inspection, and
must be publicly notified. There is then a 90 day period for people to share
their view by writing, after which the Minister must submit a final
recommendation and information to the National Executive Council (NEC).The
NEC will then decide to declare the Conservation Area or not. When an area is
declared, the Minister establishes a Conservation Area Management Committee.
This Committee must reflect the interest of the landowners and provincial and
local governments. The Committee will also prepare a management plan for the
Area, coordinate development,
 oversee rangers and generally manage the area. The Minister can make rules for
the Conservation Area, after consultation with the Management

Analysis

Failure to obey a rule of the CA attracts a penalty up to K500. Part (IV) of the
Act regulates development in Conservation Areas. In general, no person
(including @ landowner) may develop or alter the existing use of an Area except
if allowed by the management plan, or with the written approval of the Minister.
Section 32 to 34 outlines the process for applying for Ministerial approval. The
application must include supporting plans, consultation, and the Minister will
decide after due consideration. The State, too, is bound by this procedure.

However, if the development is by the State for a public purpose, the
landowners’ consent is not necessary. The minister must be very careful in
considering the environmental impact of public developments too, and can deny
the State's request if the environmental impact is too great. The penalty for
developing, or permitting the development of, land in a Conservation Area
contrary to the above restrictions is severe - attracting a fine of up to K40, 000
with K4, 000 default penalty for continuing of fences. The same high penalties
apply for developing land recommended for a Conservation Area, and the
penalties apply no matter how much the development damaged the environt
‘As a customary landowner, this Act gives you several rights and responsibi

nt.

You can request the declaration of a Conservation Area (S. 12 (2))
You can make representations on a proposed Conservation Area (S. 14)
> For a Conservation Area on your land, you have the right to be

represented on a Conservation Area Management Committee (S. 25 (3))
> You can veto any development contrary to a management pian (S. 32 (1))
> You are allowed to be appointed as rangers (S. 38)

 6. Natural Resource Management

Resource refers to stock or supply of materials which are used or aid in
producing other substances. ( Concise Oxford English Dictionary, 2004) For
example, gold, oil, trees, computers, rivers, rocks human etc..

(i) Human Made Resources

Human made resources are those aids of production which have been created by
humans to transform and utilize the gifts of nature as well as improve or
increase productivity. For example, equipment, machinery, buildings, technology,
legal bodies, institutions etc..

(ii) Natural Resources
Naturally occurring substances that are considered valuable in their relatively
unmodified form. For example, trees, crude oil, rivers etc. These are often
derived from the environment. Natural resources are categorised into renewable
and non renewable, Natural resource may also be categorised as:

(i) Biotic - are the ones obtained from living organisms

(ii) Abiotic - comprise of non -living things

(iii), Why must we manage resources?

¢ Human -made resources are available, because of the presence of natural
resources,

© Non renewable resources take millions of years to form, once depleted
cannot be replaced.

* Renewable resources can restock, but if the consumption rate exceeds
the natural rate of replacement, it will diminish in stock and eventually run
out.

We learnt in topic 1 that as indigenous people, our ancestors depended on
natural resources from their environment to sustain their livelihoods. This
dependence on the environment was passed down to the current generation so
we too are aware of the uses and importance of these natural resources. It is
therefore, our responsibility to ensure that the younger generation continues to
learn this useful knowledge and skills.

 7. Sustainable Management Practices

Sustainable development is a pattern of resource use that aims to meet human
needs while preserving the environment so that these needs can be met not only
in the present, but also for future generations. In short, it is development that
"meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future
generations to meet their own needs."

Sustainable development ties together the concern that earth as a finite system
has the ability to cater for a certain number. If humans go beyond this, there
may be tragic implications for life on earth

Environmental sustainability is the process of making sure current processes of
interaction with the environment are pursued with the idea of keeping the
environment as pristine as naturally possible, Sustainable management practices
are therefore encouraged to ensure that whatever activities humans are
involved in is in consideration of the current and future generations.

Sustainable Management Practices

These are practices that promote environmental sustainability such as
ecologically friendly forestry practices and alternate use of energy such as solar
instead of nuclear energy. Can you think of some more to add onto this list?

Tf people practice sustainable management practices in all their activities, just
imagine what the earth would be like.

snippet: MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA PROJECT IN-SERVICE TRAINING REPORT Managalas Teachers pose for a group picture with facilitators. Compiled by: Sangion Appice Tiu & Sheebah Mirisa Research & Conservation Foundation Introduction This is a brief report of the Managalas Plateau Conservation Area Teachers’ I
text:
MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA PROJECT
IN-SERVICE TRAINING REPORT

Managalas Teachers pose for a group picture with facilitators.

Compiled by: Sangion Appice Tiu & Sheebah Mirisa
Research & Conservation Foundation
 Introduction
This is a brief report of the Managalas Plateau Conservation Area Teachers’ In-service training

conducted for teachers in the proposed conservation area. The training was staged at Afore
Primary School from the 26" to 29" April 2011 and was organized by Partners with Melanesia
(PwM) and the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and financially supported by their
donors.

“The purpose of this training was to inform elementary and primary school teachers in the plateau
about the conservation efforts of PwM and MDF and how teachers can become the agents to
disseminate this message through the school system and further into their communities.

Attendance
A total of 36 teachers participated in the in-service training. These teachers were from the ten (10)

zones in the Managalas Plateau. There were eleven (11) primary and 25 elementary teachers.
Refer to attachment A for the list of teachers.

Day 1

An official opening ceremony was held at 8:30 am. Although, the program had intended for an
hour's opening, it ended at 10 am. The workshop was officially opened by PwM, MDF, the
chairman of Afore Primary School Board and the CBO chairman, The actual training started at
10:30 am.

‘Teachers were enlightened on the purpose and significance of this training in relation to the
Proposed Managalas Conservation Area, They were also asked (o write their expectations of the
training as an introductory activity. This was followed by an introduction of facilitators and
participants. The overview of the week’s schedule (see attachment B) followed next and
proceeded into the discussion on the importance of the environment. Questions were probed to
teachers to define environment and conservation which were then linked to the local people’s
view of the environment. Teachers had to identify the different types of environment in PNG, Oro
Province, [jivitari District and Afore LLG and discuss reasons why environments varied.

This provided the leeway to discuss the background of the proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area and Rufus Mahuru, PwM Project Manager took the opportunity to enlighten
participants on this. The reasons for establishing the proposed CA was aiso stated enabling the
facilitator to link the discussions to the area’s biodiversity, special species and rainforests.

The importance of the rainforest as a habitat was discussed in terms of the different layers and
how organisms prefer to live in cach of these layers. Species interdependence and adaptation were
also highlighted to enable participants to understand the wider picture of species survival and the
need for wider forage areas. An afternoon task was given to teachers to construct the rainforest
mural in three groups. The incomplete task was carried forward to Day 2.

In preparation for Day 2, a DVD documentary on ‘Since the Company Came’ was viewed by
teachers at 8 pm. Three quarters of the teachers did not turn up for this session.
 Comments/Issues

General discussions were held after cach topic presented and at the end of each day to wrap up.
Other comments are also noted below.

© General participation was very good throughout the day.

Teachers expectations were varied depending on how each person viewed the training.
‘Some saw this as an opportunity to broaden their skills and knowledge in environment and
conservation issues. Two participants saw this as an opportunity to get certificates that will
enable them to go to teachers college.

‘© There were a lot of questions raised after Rufuus Mahurw’s presentation on the background
of the proposed CA. Participants also wanted to know why the LLG president did not
endorse the proposed CA.

Facilitators. organizers and participants in the opening procession ‘An introductory session in progress.

Day 2

‘The second day began with morning devotion and then participants were asked to complete their
tasks on the Rainforest Mural activity which they did not complete the previous afternoon. A brief
discussion on the layers of the rainforest followed with teachers highlighting what they learnt
from doing the activity. There was also a discussion on the interrelationships that exists in natural
environments and how organisms are adapted to survive in these environments.

Participants were then introduced to the different environmental threats, both natural and human-
made to enhance their understanding of these threats. Each group was tasked with an
environmental threat - mining, industrial logging, bush fires, over population, shifting cultivation
and plantation (oil palm). After discussion, each group presented their responses. With the
facilitator’s guidance through probing questions, participants freely shared their personal
experiences on different environmental threats they have experienced. For example, one teacher
described the negative impacts of the Embogo River when the palm oil came into operation.
Another teacher shared the experiences from Orokaiva when their environment was seriously
affected by logging and stressed to other teachers about importance of preventing Managalas
plateau from such destructions. The third teacher commented that zone 8 and zone 10 peripheries
‘were exposed to potential development from commercial logging and mining industries and
something needed to be done immediately. The fourth teacher linked the significance of the work

 of PwM and MDF and encouraged them to make aggressive awareness to communities about the
potential threats of extractive and plantation industries.

‘The day ended with a drama presentation by teachers in their respective groups on environmental
issues.

‘Teachers performing their environmental dramas depicting various environmental issves they chose

Comments/Issues.

‘¢ General participation was very good throughout Day 2 as there were a lot of interactions
among the participants.

© Participants also freely expressed their views on the dramas performed and the
significance to real life situations.

Day3

‘The third day commenced with the recap of previous day’s topics. This was followed with
presentations by Rufus Mahuru and Patrick Vuet on the background of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area and the processes involved in the declaration of the conservation area, These
were then linked to why teachers have now become the target group to disseminate the message of
conservation to the children and as educators need to make the communities aware of the
significance of Conservation Areas.

‘The discussions that followed raised very sensitive issues which stirred up the participants. One
participant appealed to all teachers to relay issues regarding conservation work to their respective
communities so that people are not kept in the dark. Another participant stated that PwM and
MDF should make it clear to the people who will benefit from the Conservation Area in the
future. Also they should find a way to really convince the LLG President to endorse the CA. The
PwM and MDF need to find out why the LLG President has declined to sign.

‘After the break, teachers brainstormed on the different types of resources and discussed ways in
Which these natural resources can be managed in a sustainable way. This led on to the introduction
of sustainable management practices. ‘The discussion began with a couple of definitions on the
term sustainable, sustainable development and sustainable management, Teachers were put in
 different groups and then asked to identify and list traditional sustainable management practices
and modern management practices.

Patrick Vuet. PwM Conservation Officer and Nichson Piakal, PwM Education/Awareness Officer/Consensus Building Coordinator

Comments/Issues

© Again, like the previous two days, participation was very good with good feedback on the
topics discussed.

© Almost three quarters of the participants were local landowners from Managalas so their
views on the CA were very strong.

Day 4
A reflection on the topics and issues learnt in the past three (3) days was done. Teachers were then
asked to brainstorm on the upcoming commemoration of the World Environment Day in their

respective school clusters namely - Koruo/Dea, Afore, Sakarina and Itokama. The lists of
activities were compiled and given to Nichson Piakal, who is the Education Awareness Officer for

PwM.

fier the discussions, teachers got into the following groups - Elementary Prep, Elementary 1,
Elementary 2, Lower Primary Grade 3, Lower Primary Grade 4/5 and Upper Primary Grades 6, 7
& 8. In these groups, participants were challenged to link what they learnt during the week into
their existing school curriculum by identifying the theme and the corresponding activities. This
‘was then followed by discussions on curriculum integration and how teachers can integrate these
ideas, (Please refer to attachment C for a sample.)

Evaluations were done verbally as well as written on prepared evaluation forms. The participants
completed the feedback form. (see Attachment D for the summary.) Some verbal feedback noted

included the following:
 (i) Mr, Womo: commended PwM for organizing this training. He added that this training was
the first of its kind and a different approach that PwM has ventured into. The training
was beneficial to teachers who can further impart conservation knowledge to the
children. These children will then be well informed about the issues affecting the
environment.

(ii) Ms Piwen: teachers have learnt new concepts that they can try to master in their teaching.

(iii) Mr Joima: teachers especially the elementary, have appeated to the PWM to design more
conservation posters on plants and animals found in Managalas plateau so that these
can become teaching resources.

(iv)Mr Kasira: PWM need to pursue declaration of Managalas CA so that what was learnt here
doesn’t go to waste,

(v) Mr, Suari: We are great hunters of the Papuan King parrot but by going through this
training, I have realized the importance of conserving such species. I will go home and
create awareness about this bird.

(viyMr. Nanimai: I will carry out awareness to my people on behalf of the PwM and MDF
regardging issues facing the proposed Managalas CA. This training was a blessing for
those teachers who missed out on the training that was held with the inspector
regarding the integrated planning and programming, The teachers have learnt new
things and have gained new information about the environment. Thanks to PwM.

Grade 4 & 5 teachersin discussion. Integration exercise done by Grade 4/5 teachers.

Conclusion/Recommendations

‘The workshop was successfully implemented as anticipated with all planned activities completed.
Although certificates were not presented to teachers, it will be arranged later for teachers to pick
them up at MDF office.
 As the training was the first of its kind in the area, there were a lot of recommendations from the
participants. The details are captured in the feedback analysis however general suggestions
include the following:

‘* provide resource materials on animals and plants of Managalas Conservation Area that
teachers can be able to use. These include posters, brochures, and other materials.

© more awareness needs to be made to communities as not all of them understand the work
of PwM and MDF.

«more in-services to be held for teachers to empower them to effectively teach environment
and conservation issues in the CA.

¢ due consideratic
in the open haus ¥

must be given to logistics particularly for accommodation. Sleeping out
not acceptable especially when there is fear of sorcery.

# Give advance notice to teachers to attend such trainings so that they are organized and
prepared.

Some comments, recommendations and suggestions from the facilitators:

1. Open invitation is not an effective approach when dealing with teachers. Invite only 2
certain number of participants i.e. one or two from each school. This will assist you with
logistics. A total of 30 teachers can be adequately catered for in terms of classroom space,
accommodation and other logistics. These teachers should then be informed to carry out
in-services in their schools or clusters. This will ensure that more teachers are reached.
Off course a follow-up by project staff can ensure that this is implemented.

2. Have a confirmed list of participants before staging training as this assist with logistics as
mentioned above. This will also enable facilitators to prepare training materials with
consideration for costs and other expenses. Blank certificates can also be prepared in
advance.

3. A central location for trainings would also be a useful idea for consideration in future.
Otherwise, assist with some transportation from a ceniral location to the site of training.

4. ‘There is a definite need for additional in-service trainings. This particular training was
mostly focused on the work of PwM and MDF and the reasons for the CA. Tt would be
more appropriate to develop teachers’ background understanding of basic ecology before
linking their thoughts to the whole concept of conservation. This will ground in them a
better understanding of the whole issue of purpose of the work of PwM and MDF to
conserve the plateau.

text:
Ph: es Fay:
Email r Or
Location: Milan

“Maintaining the Dance” _ a

Date: 12" December, 2011

PROGRAM: Management trip to Popondetta

ACTIVITY: To deliver the Managalas Conservation Area Project Petition to Oro Governor
(Suckling Tamanabae) with Managalas elders in Popondetta and also to attend the MDF
Board meeting to discuss MDF misuse funds.

INTRODUCTION

This is a brief report on two activities that I attended in Popondetta basically to ensure that PWM is
facilitating the process and accomplishing its assistance to deliver the MCAP Petition to Oro
Governor. And also to sit in the MDF board meeting on behalf of PWM management and board to
discuss serious issues relating (o the misuse funds of MDF by its management and staff.

‘Therefore this report will highlight my trip to Popondetta for the two activities where the petition
was an action plan for PWM to take on board for before the end of the year 2011 and also will
feature the MDF board meeting with me as the Program Manager representing PWM management
and the board.

PURPOSE

‘The main purpose of this trip is to accompany Managalas elders to deliver the CA Application
petition as per the action plan in 2011 District Wide Combine Forum in November ang io sit in the
MDF Board meeting and discuss the MDF issues on misused funds by MDF management and staff.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

5" December, 2011 flew out of POM at 2.00pm and arrived at Girua airport, Popondetta at 2.40pm.
‘Went straight to Oro Guest House and prepared for all petition participants to arrive from
Managalas. At 5.00pm met with all of them at Oro Guest House and briefed them for the next
couple of day's activities. They were all taken to Anglican Guest House and they were all
accommodated there for the night.

‘Tuesday 6" December, 2011 at 8.00am, I met all of them at the Anglican Guest House and briefed
‘them what to do next. At 9.00am we all met at the Oro Provincial Headquarters to deliver the
petition but we were told to go back at 11.00am. So at 11.00am we were told that the governor is
not available so the provincial administrator will receive the petition on behalf of the governor on
Wednesday morning at 10,00am.

At 7.00pm, we had the MDF Board meeting at Oro Guest House which we discussed matters
relating to misuse funds, Kamilla and Rune’s email concerns and other MDF matters.

 Wednesday 7" December, 2011 at 10,00am the administrator advised that he will officially receive
the petition at 10.30am in which he did by receiving the petition from a little Managalas girl called
Esi in front of 24 Managalas Elders. In the afternoon I flew back to POM.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

The Governor, Suckling Tamanabae was not available to receive petition with reasons beyond our
control. The petition was received by the Oro Provincial Administrator on behalf of the Governor
(Suckling Tamanabae). The petition was delivered by a little called Esi in front of 24 Managalas
Elders. Upon receiving the petition, the administrator signed and was witnessed by the MDF Board
Chairman Mr. Malchus Kajia. MDF and PWM still waiting for the outcome.

During the MDF Board meeting, all MDF board were provided with all emails and other documents
regarding the misused funds by current staff and former staff. The MDF board realised that the
matter was Very serious and they need to act on it seriously. However no action was taken to get rid
of the Project Director (Luke Mambe and others implicated) but they have all agreed to fundraise to
recoup the misused funds. The strategy for them to fundraise is not yet known but they assured me
that they will discuss this at Afore and report to PWM as soon as possible. In addition tp their
fundraising strategy, the chairman also asked me on what is the status of their K20,000.00
contribution to the maintenance of the former MOCP vehicle. They all said that since time is short,
they can use that to repay the misused funds and all implicated current staff and former staff with
their families and all Board members can fundraise next year 2012 to repay that MOCP money for
MDF since MOCP also owe farmers.

RECOMMENDATIONS

* To follow up with the petition by MDF and PWM. Never give up as this is part of our effort
to ensure that the governor must submit the CA Application to the Minister for Environment
and Conservation.

MDF Board and staff to strategize on how they will fundraise to recoup the misused funds
especially by current MDF staff implicated in the K 13,900.00 and also by former staff
Douglas Tumai and Brian Kasira.

No refund with misused funds, dissolve MDF and bring in a care taker until constitution is
amended to suit their local situation and those implicated should be arrested and locked
away to show other Managalas that this is a professional project and no one should take
advantage of donor’s fund as their own.

CONCLUSION

Allin all, the trip is an important part of what was discussed in the District Wide Combine Forum
as PWM and MDF are taking the lead role to deliver the petition to the Oro Governor.

‘The MDF board meeting has paved the way for them to open their eyes that the matter is very

serious and needs to be addressed by both management and board. Therefore the MDF Board and
its staff need to put their heads together and refund the donor funds.
