OBJECTION TO THE MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA SUBMISSON

AREPORT TO PARTNERS WITH MELANESIANS INC ON THE COMMUNITY
CONSULTATION TRIP

JUNE 2013
 Executive Summary

‘The proposed Managalas Conservation Area in Afore Local Level Government of the ljivitari
District of Oro Province is a cumulative effort of over 25 years of planning by various
stakeholders including local landowners, community based organizations, national and
international NGOs and Government agencies. The dream is now closed to be realised when
the submission for the Conservation Area was submitted by community representatives
support by Partners with Melanesians (PwM) to the Minister for Environment & Conservation
Hon. John Pundari in the presence of Governor Gary Juffa and Hon. Delilah Gore in Parliament
House on November 8, 2012. This will be the second Conservation Area to be de declared
under the Conservation Areas Act and the largest protected area in the country with 360,000
hectares if the National Executive Council (NEC) goes ahead and approves its declaration . The
first Conservation Area to be declared under the Act was the YUS Conservation Area in Morobe
Province with 75,000 hectares. However, after the submission for the proposed Conservation
Area was first advertised in the Post Courier on February 18, 2013 as required under the Act
an objection letter dated 18 March, 2013 was sent to the Minister for Environment &
Conservation by the President of Afore Local Level Government, Hon. Douglas Garawa on
behalf of the landowners in the 18 wards of the Afore LLG. The 90 day objection period lapsed
on 18 May 2013. There have been numerous threats issued to PwM and local MDF staff
involved with the project including the assault on PwM Executive Director, Kenn Mondiai on 26
March 2013 at the Afore Station market place. Thus, the reason for the trip to the plateau was
to hold consultative meetings in selected places with stakenolders to verify support for the
objection to the declaration of the Managalas Conservation Area by the Afore LLG President.
The trip was from 23 May-2™ June 20013 and provided below is an outline of the views of
various stakeholders with regards to the objection. Based on this, a number of
recommendations have been made to enable the stakeholders especially PwM to address the
issues raised in the objection letter by the Afore Local Level Government President.

1 Introduction

The Managalas plateau in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea harbours a diverse array of fauna
and flora, And more significantly the plateau is home to the Queen Alexendra Birdwing
Butterfly, the world’s largest birdwing butterfly which is listed on Appendix | of the CITES
Convention and which is only endemic to Oro Province of Papua New Guinea. The proposed
‘Managalas Conservation Area covers 360,000 hectares of pristine rainforest comprising lowland
montane forests and is also the water catchment area of the Popondetta plains. The total

2
 population of the area is 18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari District.
‘The people live in 75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and speak
four (4) dialects.

‘The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale
environmentally destructive projects like logging, mining and oil palm plantations. Having being
working with international and national NGO partners since the early 1990’s the area is now in
the process of being designated as a conservation area under the Conservation Areas Act of
1978. The Managalas people submitted the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area Application
to the Minister for Environment and Conservation on 8" of November, 2012. As required under
the Act, the public advertisement was placed in the newspapers (Post Courier) for stakeholders
to view and file any objections if any. The advertisement appeared in the Post Courier on 18
February, March 4, March 18, April 1, April 29 and finally May 13 2013. The 90 day period
expired on 18 May 2013. The President of Afore Local Level Government, Douglas Garawa
filed an objection in a letter dated 18 March 2013 wherein he raised a lot of issues why the
Minister should not make the NEC submission for it to approve the CA declaration and for the
proposal to be shelved until such time the Managalas people are able to manage the project
themselves. The objection was submitted through the office of the Minister for Environment &
Conservation and Partners with Melanesians (PM) was given a copy of the object by DEC after
the expiry of the notice period as it has now become a public document, While PwM is working
on the response to the objection by the President of Afore LLG, it wanted to gather more
information on the objection submission thus my engagement to verify and gather the
information for skakcholders on the plateau (Refer to Appendix “A” for the TOR ).

“Another major threat to the CA proposal which arose at the same time was the exploration
licence for mineral exploration by Australian mineral exploration company, Goldminex
Resources Limited. The company has a current exploration licence ( EL 1547) which covers
villages in Kokoda Local Level Government including Upper Kumusi and over the Guava
Ranges to villages in West Managalas which is part of the proposed Managalas Conservation
Area. The exploration licence will expired on June 30 2013 and as required under the Mining
Act, the Chief Mining conducted the public hearing at Afore station on 24 May 2013 to get
views from landowners for extension of the exploration licence for a further two years. The
notice for the public hearing was placed in the Post Courier on April 4, 2013 but not notices were
sent to the Afore LLG and the Afore Sub-district Administration, thus the landowners in the
exploration licence area were not adequately informed about the public hearing. PwM had on
behalf of the people of Managalas n, submitted an objection to the Registrar of Tenements at the
Mineral Resourees Authority 29 April 2013 which was covered in the front page of the Post
Courier on 1 May 2013. As mentioned, this is a major threat to the CA proposal and so PwM

 together with the landowners and community based organized need to push for the exploration
activities to be stopped.

2. — Objection Letter to the Minister for Environment and Conservation by
Afore Local Level Government President.

The President of Afore Local Level Government, Hon. Douglas submitted the objection letter
dated 18 March to the Minister for Environment & Conservation Hon. John Pundari on behalf of
people in the 18 Council Wards in the Afore Local Level Government of the ljivitari District. The
PwM management has received and read the objection submission but for ease of reference
issues and reasons for the objection are contained in the objection submission which attached
hereto as “Appendix B”.

3. Community Meetings

While on the plateau, !held meetings at number of villages as per the Terms of Reference as
well as other villages because of the importance of the issue at hand. These included Itokama,
Serefuna, Umbuara, Tahama, Koruwo and Afore. There were request from community leaders
in other villages on the plateau for meetings but | could not manage more meetings because of
the bad road condition and time factor. Below, | have attempted to capture the views from
people especially community leaders and clan elders in the villages where the consultation
meetings were held during the trip.

3.1 Meeting at Itokama Village

The meeting at Itokama village was held on Sunday 26 May from 3-6pm. It was attended by
clan elders and community leaders from itokama, Naokanene and Kuai villages. This is where
the initial plan to have the Managalas Plateau declared a conservation area was formulated so
it was good to have the first meeting there to gauge the views of the clan elders and
community leaders on the objection to the CA Submission by the Afore LLG President. |
introduced the two main issues for the consultation, which is the objection to the CA
‘Submission and the Mining Warden hearing for extension of EL 1547 to gauge their views and
positions on these two issues.

Acommunity leader from Kuai village that the people in zones 1 and 2 spearheaded the project
from its initial start-up and the clan elders in these two zones have signed up in support of the
CA submission and declaration. Many of the names of the clan elders that signed the objection
letter we included in the list without their consent. They did not sign themselves and in some

4

 case two clan elders we put down for one clan where one in signing in support and the other is
signing against the CA submission. He said this is not right and proper investigation should be
carried out to determine the signatures of the clan elders.

Aclan elder from Kuai said and | qoute , ” the people in zones 1 and 2 initiated the CA project
with advice and support from Dr. Mike Olsson and our educated people like Damien, yourself
and so we support the CA submission and declaration. We do not understand why other the
people are now going against the CA declaration at the last minute”.

‘Another community leader from Itokama who is more aligned to President Garawa though
marriage stated and | quote, “it appears that majority of the many are against the CA
submission and declaration so the plan should be shelved while there is further consultation
and awareness at the village level on the pros and cons of conservation”. He said the issue is @
big issue and needs to be addressed properly as it may result in conflicts like the confrontation
some youths had with the Partners Executive Director at Afore station.

Another community leader from Itokama village said we need to look at the reason why
President Garawa has objected to the CA submission and declaration. There may be other
hidden reasons for him to do this as the majority of the people especially clan elders signed for
the area to be declared a CA.

One CBO Manager this CA project idea started in Zones 1 and 2, the Birarie and Namiai
tribe and we wanted the area to be declared a CA because of experiences in other areas where
the land and rivers are destroyed by large scale development projects like logging and mining.
He said people from others zones in the plateau joined in later so may have other motives. He
said and | quote “the President is objecting to the CA submission and declaration because of his
‘own interest, he is just one man. We cannot shelve the plan for the area to be declared a as CA
we have worked almost 30 years on the project to have the area declared a CA. We must go
ahead with the CA declaration”.

‘An elderly man from Naokanene village commented and | quote “why is there division amongst
the educated people from the area. You should all work together and assist us to bring services.
You should help guard our interests and resources”.

‘The later part of the discussions at the meeting focused around the two organizations working
on the project, I,e, PWM and MDF. One question asked was, can MDF operate as a separate
and independent entity? This is was one of the issues President Garawa raised in his objection

5
 against the CA submission. One community leader stated that that some confidential
information were leaked because of the problems between PwM and MDF. There are no MDF
staff now as all have been removed by Partners. He said MDF must be re-established so it can
operate again to avoid such problems in the future.

Another community leader stated that the project started in West Managalas and the Project
Field Office and MOF office was established here at Itokama and later it was moved to Afore
and the people were not informed of the rationale for this. He said the project office as well as
MDF office must be re-established in Itokama to start the work again.

‘Another clan elder commented that the problem is with the MOF board and Partners in moving
the project office to Afore station. This is why there is division from people in East and West
Managalas. He said the people in West Managalas started the CA initiative and so the project
office should be based here in Itokama and not at Afore.

‘One former MDF staff commented that there are now threats issues against form MDF and
PwM staff and people who are support the CA submission and declaration He stated and |
quote, “we are now threatened because of our involvement in the project with MDF and PwM.
We cannot travel to Afore and Popndetta because of these threats.” He said tThis has divided
the community and many are now going against the declaration of the area as CA because of
these threats by some sector of the community. The problem is with the removal of former
MOF and PwM field staff which is now creating this problem.

There are personal reasons here between individuals including the LLG President and PwM
Executive Director which is creating this division in the community and many are objecting to
the CA declaration. There is overall view that the PwM be replaced because of problems with
management of the project and bad working relationship with community leaders including
mandated leaders like the LLG President.

Overall what | gathered at this meeting which was the first during the consultation was that all
clan elders and the majority of the people support the CA submission and declaration. Most of
them signed for the area to be declared a CA.

‘The meeting finished at 6.30pm and after dinner with the community leaders, | walked back to
Serefuna village (my village) to spend the night there.
 3.2. Meeting at Serefuna Village

The meeting at Serefuna village was conducted at the request of clan elders and community
leaders from Serefuna, Kokoro and Anatua villages after they heard about the purpose of my
trip to the plateau. The meeting was held on Monday May 27 from 9-12pm.

informed the meeting that | am here to gather information and views from the community on
two main issues which the objection to the CA submission by President Garawa and the Mining
Warded hearing for extension of Exploration number 1547 held by Goldminex Resources Ltd
which expires on June 30, 2013.

There is conflict between the mining exploration and conservation area. How do we deal with
these issues was one of the questions asked at the meeting by a community leader.

‘A community leader said there was no proper notice given to landowners to attend the Mining
Warded hearing t Afore station so none of us attended the hearing. There was no proper
awareness on the mining exploration renewal application. As landowners who have rights by
law, we must be consulted by the government and companies before such activities take place
on our land. What MRA has done is not right and so we must do a petition against the renewal
of the exploration licence.

A clan elder said the CA objection was done by the LLG President. He said were not consulted
and did not give our informed position. The President is from here, Namiai tribe so he should
come and sit down with us and talk about such issues openly so we can make informed
decisions. The President did not do this like you are doing now which we very much appreciate
‘as you have provided good background information on the two big issues in our own language
and we now fully understand them.

Another community leader said one main point is about the funding for the project. The funds
earmarked for projects or activities at the community level is not reaching the people. They are
blocking opportunities for services to the reach the people. This is not right and must be
addressed by all concerned especially, PwM, MDF and the LLG President.

A church leader said the issues raised in the objection to the CA submission by the LLG
President are very big issues and concerns us all. Some are genuine issues and must be
addressed immediately. There is need for a meeting or forum to get together and resolve the

7
 issues the LUG President has raised in the objection. The LLG President is also a landowner and
so he has right to speak about the issues especially to do with land and resources. The problem
| see is personal problem between the PwM Executive Director and the LLG President so one
‘option is to replace the PwM Executive Director and get someone from the area to manage the
project. We need to hold a big stakeholders meeting to address and resolve the issues raised in
the LLG President objection letter.

Another community leader stated that land is big issue so the issues raised in the objection
letter by the LLG President need to be addressed properly as some part of the community are
concerned that their land will be taken away from them when the CAis declared by the
government. The landowners are not always made aware of such issues that will affect them so
these issues that the President has raised must be addressed properly. One main concern is
that the CA covers a large area so needs to be looked at again.

‘Another community leader commented that some threats have been issued against clan
elders, CBO staff and MOF staff so it can develop into a big conflict if the issues raised are not
resolved properly by those concerned. He said and | quote “ Land is a big issue and it is our life
50 it is important to address and resolve the issues raised in the objection letter by the LLG
President properly and in a peaceful manner. The last thing we want to see is conflicts and
divisions in the community, which we are now seen in the Namiai tribe because of the CA
submission and the objection by the LLG President. If the issues and problems are addressed
though conflicts and fighting they will still remain and continue”.

One clan elder stated that the other issue is about the registration of ILG or land. The people
have been asked to contribute K5 each for registration of ILG/land and so far K6000 has been
raised for this purpose. The purpose of the contribution is for the advertisement for the
objection but need to collect more information.

Finally, a community leader stated that work of MOF is another important issue that needs to
be addressed quickly. MOF is an independent group estabiished as a result of the clan group
discussions and combine forums so it is what the people decided as their voice. A lot of MOF
staff have left as a result of control by PwM. MDF needs to have its own board, staff and
funding to carry out its own programmes at the community level. This is one reason that
resulted in the objection to the CA submission by the LLG President. There is urgent need for
stakeholder consultation forum or meeting to organized to discuss and address the issues
raised in the objection letter by the LLG President.

 Generally, the people in zone 2 are supportive of the CA declaration and they are against any
logging and mining in the area. They want a meeting to be organized to address and resolve the
issues raised by the LLG President in his objection letter as they are of say some of these issues
are genuine issues concerning the management of the projects and benefits to the people
amongst other issues.

3.3. Meeting at Umbuara Village

After the meeting at Serefuna village which was attended by clan elders and community leaders
from Serefuna, Anatua, Kokoro and Kuai villages, ! walked to Umbuara village at 1.00pm for the
community consultation/meeting after sending word people going to the village. | arrived
there and waited for the elders and community leaders to arrive as most have left for their
gardens in the morning. The meeting started at 2.30pm which was attended by clan elders,
community leaders and some local church representatives.

This is praise item and on behalf of the PWM Board I take this
opportunity to thank PWM Admin and the MDF interim Board for
arranging this forum at Kokoro village. This is another opportunity to
bring people together around the plateau and also bring people from the
media to come out to the village and see For themselves and get report
to present to the print media for the leaders in the country to see and
help the concerns for the people in the Managalasi plateau.

Thank you Crispin Burava and Bradley for job well done to accommodate
people and toorganize people to Feed them during the forum. Thank you
all members of the Kokoro and Serefuna community who worked
together to look after people who came to the Forum.

A big thank you to the media team who took time out From their busy
schedule and willing to come to the remote villages in Barai. Especially
the representative from DEC Mr David Kau who was happy to be with us
out there in the village to respond to peoples questions.

Then Finally the MDF Chairman Mr Malcus Kajia who lead the staff of MDF
and the community From Namiai dialect to host this forum for Four
days. Once again thank you for every bit of work done to make this
forum a successful forum.
 Logistics work

The people began arriving at Kokoro village on the 2" November 2014 where
they were accommodated by the community members from Kokoro and Serefuna
villages. Arrangement was for people to eat in their houses and eat together only
for lunch and dinner in the central place in the community.

The facilitators Crispin Burava from the West and Bradley from the East worked
together with the community members to get people there in time for the forum.
There were would have been a big traditional welcome in Kokoro community how
ever there were two deaths in Kokoro village just few weeks before the forum. So
the welcome was only arranged by Elementary school children to bring people
into the community. Thank you Kokoro Elementary school teachers and the
children for participating in this forum.

There were groups set aside that helped and did all the logistics work in the
community. The officers from Port Moresby were placed in homes where people
cared for them. We ate our breakfast in homes where we stayed but ate lunch
and dinner together in the one place. The clan groups and participants for the
forum did the same and ate lunch and dinner together separately from the officers
from PWM and the DEC and media from Port Moresby.

Thank you facilitators for involving the church leaders to share Word to encourage
people about the importance of conservation. The challenge was to manage
Gods creation and know him better and seek his wisdom to manage his creation.
 Day 1

The forum on the first day began at 9.30 am with a word of prayer and devotion
was led by George Isurufa from Kokoro village.

Devotion

The reading was taken from Prov: 3:1-6 to encourage the people of the plateau to
be good managers of the God’s resources in the world as well as the blessings in
the Managalasi plateau.

He also quoted from the Gospel John:10:10 to challenged the members of all
clan leaders and the people of Managalsi plateau that thieves comes to steal and
Destroy but Jesus came to give life in full.

We are to have him in our lives to give us the wisdom and guidance through his
Spirit to manage his resources.

The facilitator Crispin Burava continued and welcomed every one for coming to
the forum. He then explained to the clan leaders and the participants the purpose
of the forum.

1. This forum is a follow up of the last forum hosted by the Ugunomo
community last year November 2013.
a. Managalasi plateau to be conserved as a conservational area in the
Afore district Oro province.
b. Then discussion of the new remapped area for Managalasi Plateau

This was the first kind of forum that the facilitators allowed leaders from the church
to share the Word that was related to conservation. The passages shared were
all about the creation and the work delegated to us to manage them.
 Apologies

Then Remenge’s the clan leader and the councillor from Kawowoki apologised
the forum on behalf of that the people in the west near Sakarina. The people may
not attend the forum because they are attending another meeting for the newly
opened high school at Sakarina. They all knew that the topics for this forum are
the same discussed in the last forum at Ugonomo in November last year 2013.

The ward councillor from Kavovoki said the people in Sakarina area sent their
apology that they will not attend the forum at Kokoro because they are attending
the a High School meeting in Sakarina. They sent their apology but they are all in
favour for the whote Managalasi area to be conserved. He aiso said, what ever
decision the forum make to set date and venue for declaration, they will agreed
and work forward to the date for declaration.

He also said the High School for the district is one of the big needs so they are
attending the meeting to discuss and distribute work load for churches and people
in the communities to participant and complete work in the short time frame give.
This is one of the development in the district and so conservation for the
Managalasi plateau is a urgent need in plateau.

Alban Varure and Emmanuel Garava were there from Popondetta representing
the LLG President to observe in the forum. So Alban apologise the forum that the
LLG President Hon: Douglas Garava will not be in the forum because of the issue
related to the Oro Governor Hon: Mr. Garry Juffa in Popondetta.
 First topic For the forum.
Crispin Burava then introduced the first topic for the forum:
Agenda 1: CA for Managalasi plateau for more discussion again.

The five councillors who attended the forum spoke strongly that and supported by
the clan leaders that we do not want to our area or district be divided again
because of the conservation. We want to call ourselves Afuruve people meaning
that we are people who live and work together as one people and so conservation
the Managalasi area will hold us together as one people.

Hon: Mr Brian Kasira who is the ward councillor for ward 14 and the founder of the
MDF project in the Managalasi plateau spoke strongly that, We the Managalasi
people do agreed that the Managalasi area be conserved. There should not be
any more forum on conservation because we all agreed in our first forum in Tama
that our 360 hectors of our Managalasi area must be conserved. We do not want
any outsiders to influence us and take our land for their own benefit by logging or
mining in the plateau.

He said that the work that he started must bring benefit to the people of
Managalasi. But why is one person making it difficult for us to make our 360
hectors of our land to be conserved. This is unfair for one person to stop the
change that the majority want it to take place in the plateau.
 The people were sent out again to their clan groups discussion on the same topic
reported back to the forum that they all were happy to see their area be
conserved. The discussion on the CA took us to the end of the day

The facilitator told the forum to go and talk more and come back with fresh mind
next morning and give their last comments before moving into other agendas.
Then he dismissed and closed the forum for the day at 3.30 pm.

Day 2 continues the First days topic on CA.

On the second day the question was raised about the ILG because the council
president Mr .Garava wants to see ILG done first before going into the CA.

iin

After few comments of ILG and the CA Mr. George Tumai one of the founder of
MDF told that forum that we have come iong way seeking CA deciaration so in
this forum date should be set for us coming together for celebration. Then he
strongly supported Hon: Brian that there should not be any more forum for this
same agenda CA. Then he referred question to PWM and DEC to explain where
is the hold up in the process.

Alban Varure and Emmanuel Garava were sent by the LLG President to observe
the forum. So they travelled by road on his vehicle and arrived there on Tuesday
morning and attended the discussions for Tuesday. Alpban mentioned that this is
‘one of his priority for the people in the Managalasi plateau before CA.
 Tom from the PWM Board was very helpful to explain the different between ILG
and the CA. Tom explained that the ILG is not yet because we need to get the
whole area conserved first and come down to the clan and family groups to talk
about ILG. That is the next lot of work that we need to do and we are not to jump
over the first step. The Afore LLG President needs to know that CA must take
place first. If we give the priority to the ILG then the whole area will not be
conserved and that is not safe. ILG is all about small clan groups and family trees
to really see where you belong and do the ILG. So that will come about later when
the CA is done.

Then David from DEC explained the steps that people go through to get their
areas ready before conserved. All the decisions are made from the community
and clan groups level and not from the National Government of Department of
Environment and conservation. People are the owners of land and the
Government will not make any decision with the land owners.

There are several areas that we will need to go through to get our area conserved.
The Department of Environment and Conservation can not give okay for
declaration. But he can work with the people concern like the LLG president and
the provincial level Government to Government to get this area conserved.

After the long talk he said he heard their concern and he will take it from there to
the Government level to see that the people cry can be heard by the leaders at
different level in the LLG level and in the provincial level.

In this forum the main people who spoke strongly and wanted to see the area
conserved were the councillors and the Former Regional member for National
Parliament Mr .Benson Garui.

Agenda 2: Topic was on Remapping.

After the morning break the second agenda was introduced in the forum. Crispin
Burava the facilitator from the west showed the copied of the remapped area and
told the forum to their clan groups and discuss the on this agenda and report to
the forum. He then dismissed the forum again into their groupings to discuss and

Not much was discussed on this agenda because many of the clan leaders
disagree on this remapping agenda. The name Afore in about working together
and sharing together and this map is a bad sign to divide our people in the district.
We are people working and deciding and listening together and that is what Afore
really means in the language . If one man is making a decision to divide our
people then that is not the decision from the people in the plateaus. The motto
for Kuaefienami will be destroyed by one single person because he want s to
bring division.

The five Ward Councillors who were there in the forum totally agreed and spoke

people in the Managalasi plateau. We do not want to tell them something that they

 Benson added that this forum is not about the remapping but it is about deciding
date to declare the Managalasi area as a conserved area. We are not here to talk

Good leaders are for people to work together and see there is unity and peace in

The women representatives also gave their views to support the discussion for CA

| (Simon Savaiko) added that CA is not just for the land but the people and

I, Simon Savaiko took this as a big issue for the churches and the

text:
DRAFT

The District Wide Forum Report 12" November 2014

Managalas plateau in the Afore district is the last sanctuary for the largest butterfly in the
world, the Queen Alexandra Birdwing butterfly. Along the foot of the ower Stanley range so
called developments in the form oil palm plantations clear large amount of virgin rainforest
to plant small amount of trees. A seedling needs a space of 10cubic square meter so in a 100
hectare plot a mere 100 trees are planted which is too much space for less production
unlike the cocoa and coffee trees. And so as the plantation slowly eats up the jungle slope
50 too did these unique species endemic to this region eventually head up high to settle in
the cooler plains of this beautiful valley.

Unlike the people living along the main highway, here the people of the Afore LLG have a
different mindset. They want their rugged vegetation only to be used by them and their
generation. But in a corporate world where global economy fights to take over everything,
the simple people wage a losing battle. There only hope of salvation is through
internationally recognized nationally declared conservation area projects. Only then can
their efforts be protected from outside manipulation.

Over twenty years ago PwM an NGO who with the support and financial assistance of
international donors such as from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway (RFN) have pushed
and prodded, slaved and paved their way through sometimes hostile environment to
promote conservation and sustainable development awareness to the Afore people
including facilitating the eight CA steps in the process. Until now the Managalas
Conservation Area Project (MCAP) application is in the gazettal stage to be validated by the
Department of environment and Conservation (DEC).

Introduction

My name is Talitha Kove and | am a freelance writer. | was engaged by PWM to cover the
annual District wide forum of the people of the Managalas plateau in the Afore LLG of oro
province. The event was held from the 3 to the 7" of November 2014 in Kokoro village of
the ijvitari electorate. The forum is that time of the year where community leaders of the
different zones along with their ward councilors gather to appraise and evaluate the years
end progress of their respective areas. Addressing issues and discussing ways to best go
about in help solving them. The two main issues this year were;

1. Department of environment and conservation (DEC) and Afore Local Level
Government (ALLG) to respond to the status of the Conservation Area (CA)
 2. Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and Community Based Organizations
(C80) work programs to resume.

‘The forum was a success; the most important agenda on top of the list was the people's
vehement demand for the declaration of the CA. The three days of open discussion saw
some women and youth reps present who also contributed to the group talk times. On the

PURPOSE

When an application for a proposed CA is in its gazettal stage awaiting validation, a 90 day
window period is allowed for any matter pertaining to the project site can be raised within
this timeframe. Any concerns, any loopholes and any grievances this is the time they will be
considered. In November 2012 the governor of Oro Province Garry Juffa on behalf of the
majority of the Managalas people presented the CA application to the DEC Minister.
Unbeknownst to them, a small faction of the east side community was also compiling their
objection letter to stay the project. This group of clan elders along with the LLG president
claim that the purported CA application may have the majority’s support but does not
represent the whole community's view on the proposed 360 000 hectares. Thus the CA has
come to a halt. The last remaining years has been dedicated to consultation processes.
Trying to find loopholes and how best to address this issue of the objection letter. My task in
this forum was to

‘The forum then asked an LLG rep for the president to tell the people of his view. The
representative- Alban said he is only here to observe and deliver the president's message via
a phone text stating that CA is non-negotiable and only the ILG can be discussed within Clan

purpose was to deliver the message and nothing more.

This caused confusion among the participants as ILG or incorporated Land Group was a new

 MANAGALAS people demand for Conservation. by Talitha Kove

Papua New Guinea is one of the last remaining countries in the twenty first
century whose people still own and live off the land. Its landmass is covered
with thick impenetrable rainforest and wild rugged terrains, its biodiversity
flourishing right to the treetops with a wide variety of fauna and flora. It is a
scientist wonderland where the discovery of new species are inevitable and
most often its endemic uniqueness a certainty.

One such place is the Managalas plateau situated high up between the dividing
ranges of the central and oro provinces. The Plateau is home to about 20000
people under the Afore Local Level Government (LLG) in the ijivitari electorate.
This high plain has become the last sanctuary for the largest butterfly in the
World, the Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly (QABB), which is also the

provincial emblem endemic only to Oro.

However, along the foot of the Owen Stanley Range developments such as oil
palm plantations have slowly eaten up the jungle slope destroying their homes
causing this beautiful insects to flee upwards into the plateau. Unlike those
living along the highway people the Managalas people have a different
mindset. They want their virgin vegetation only to be used by them and their
generation. But in a corporate world where global economy fights to take over
everything, the simple people wage a losing battle. Their only hope of salvation
is through internationally recognized nationally declared conservation area
projects. Only then can their efforts be protected from outside manipulation.

Over twenty years ago Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PwM) an NGO who with
support and financial assistance of international donors such as the Rainforest
Foundation of Norway (RFN) have pushed and prodded, slaved and paved their
way through sometimes hostile environment to promote conservation and
sustainable development awareness to the Afore people including facilitating
the eight Conservation Area (CA) steps in the process. In 2012 their efforts for
the Managalas plateau to be conserved paid off when the Governor of Oro on
behalf of his people presented the CA application to the Minister of the
Department of Environment and Conservation.
 Unbeknownst to them a small faction of the east side community led by the
president of the Afore LLG raised an objection letter staying the project. They
claim that the purported CA application may have the majority's support but it
did not represent the whole community’s view on the 360 000 hectares
proposed. A week long district wide forum held at Kokoro village on the 3° to
the 7" of November 2014 saw the people discuss ways on how to best address
this issue.

Everyone who attended the forum vehemently demanded the Managalas
Conservation Area Project (MCAP) to be declared. They stressed that twenty
eight years is a long time to be waiting for the declaration. There are other
projects that they would like to pursue but wanted to be assured that the
conserved area can be protected from outside manipulation.

Tom Huasi a member of PWM board of directors and one of the surviving
project initiators paid tribute to those who had passed on and hopes that
before the rest go they would love to see their project (MCAP) fulfilled. “You
must take ownership. It is for your future generation.” He said.

Newton kasiri a local leader supported Mr.Huasi, by giving an example where
some parts of Africa humans share the same waterhole with the animals.
“Don’t let others take away your rights. You must fight for your rights now
otherwise we will lose our land and become like these Africans.” He said.

The Afore LLG president has refused to comment. He has not responded to the
two letters of invitation sent to him by the forum requesting his presence. The
forum has asked if Department of environment and Conservation can help
liaise with the Afore LLG on their behalf and set aside a date.

 Barai women in Literacy workshop report
27" -29" Dec 2017.
Summary.

This is the kind of workshop that the Barai ladies have been struggling to attend to get
help for their fluency classes. It came to the right time where this workshop was conducted
in Itokama village in the Barai tribe to encourage the women in literacy in the Barai
language. That is where all thirty three (33) Barai ladies representing two tribes in the
Barai speaking area who attended the workshop. For them this is just the beginning of
many workshops yet to happen in the Managalasi plateau to encourage women in the
area of Life Long Learning for women in that has been neglected for years.

This workshop brought vibration in the lives of ladies in the two tribes to see beyond
women’s future. Women in the plateau are always seen as house wives and cargo
carriers and this workshop highlighted their minds and hearts to see beyond opportunity
ahead of them. The workshop opened their minds to have vision beyond grade six (6) or
grade eight (8) in the Primary schools. There is great opportunity for women in the Life
Long Learning in the village level They need to start from their own language to be fluent
before learning outside ideas and ways to make right decisions for their communities in
the plateau. The name literacy now called as Life Long Learning will help them to accept
what is good for better transformed communities in the tribe.

| take this opportunity to thank Managalasi Conservation Foundation (MCF) who
authorized PWM to release Literacy Fund for us to conduct this four days workshop for the
women in literacy in BNEA training centre at Itokama village. This is just the beginning of
many more good materials production workshop for the Barai adult fluency classes to
have more books to read about conservation and other helpful information from outside.

In this workshop the production of materials began with a book on conservation of land
and the garden food that the women plant. Then the book also quoted related scriptures
from Genesis where the students learned about what the Scripture says about
management of ail that God created. These stories brought excitement for more of this
workshop to produce more books to encourage women to study about creation. They also
were encouraged to do more to see some can be good writers of stories of the forest in
their plateau in their own languages.

Managalsi ladies are hard working ladies but they are always neglected and do not get
them involve in workshops and leadership like Life Long Learning. This kind of workshops
motivated women to have voice and to play leadership role in the village starting from
literacy classes. It was amazing to see the number of women who turned out for this
workshop and how they show their interest in the workshop.

In their the officials closing, Mrs, Ritha Bania expressed her concern on behalf of the
jadies and urged the fathers and husbands to help their wives and mothers to be involve
in Life Long learning to qualify them to play leadership role in the tribe. Women have
 supported men for many years and men has dropped some of these opportunities. So this
‘is an opportunity for men to give the women chance to start with Life Long learning. Thank
you for the support to send women to the course and may you continue to encourage
__ them to apply what they have learnt in the workshop. That will help them to start playing
their leadership role in a small way in the village level.

~ The workshop
The women met next day, on Tuesday after our arrival on Monday to have closing
ceremony for the Women in literacy for the year 2016. Then before they went home they
agreed to meet again for the workshop straight after Christmas Day 27" Dec 2017 at
Itokama in BNEA classroom. Then they all went home on after the closing of the work for
> the year.
Then on Tuesday 27" after Christmas all women met for the literacy workshop at BNEA.
The workshop was officially declared opened with few remarks by the MCF Manager
Dickson Darebo. The literacy workshop lusted for only four days at BNEA classroom.

~The workshop started with thirty three women all Barai the two different dialect the Birare
and Namiai tribes. The four day teachers in service workshop was conduct in BNEA
centre. Most women from outside of Itokama village stayed with families in Itokama village
for the workshop. It was a busy time but the women really made commitment to stay away
from families for four days to attend the workshop. Many of them were all women leaders

eo

from all villages in Barai speaking area.

a ee
The workshop was planned for only fifteen women leaders to do teachers in service
however there were many other women who were interested to take teachers training
course. So | extended the schedule to fit the request made by all participants by adding
materials production with teachers training. That is why we started with materials
production and finished with teachers training with materials related to conservation.

 Each one of those women trainers from seven villages were already conducting Adult
fluency classes at home. Five of the villages who were conducting classes came to stop

during the planting season while Tama and Itokama continued to the end of the year. In

the workshop they reported their concern and needs of materials and support from the

men.

Material production:

In the workshop women listed all their issues in the communities and put them into
priorities. Amongst the many very high priority (25) issues they decided to take
conservation. The women were divided into five different groups to develop stories on kind
of food they grow in their gardens. That is to help them with easy stories where they knew
the best and can handle well before going into harder stories. The women developed thirty
three short stories in their own Barai language about food they grow. Many of them plant
all these vegetables in gardens but when it came to writing stories it was amazing to see
how they struggled to put into words. Many of them struggled to write in the same way as

_ they speak about kinds of food they grow in their gardens in Barai area. The translators
George and Dunston Unini helped them to edit their stories. Time could not allow us for
printing all three books so taken to Moresby for printing.

Practice teaching:

Then we printed 120 copies of book prepare in Port Moresby for the workshop on what
Bible says about conservation in Genesis the teachers guide. Then we used the book for
practice teaching adult fluency classes in Barai. On the third day after the demonstration
in the afternoon all women got into their groups again and started practice teaching using
the book on conservation.

There were three levels of needs that the women brought to the workshop. The beginner's
need that related to children and even adults while others have needs for adult fluency.
~The fluency was a big priority because they need fluency in understanding and reading
and writing. Amazing to see how women can read fast and if were were giving 100% for
students in the class, almost 75% of women in the class can read well and fast. But for
fluency in understanding is almost 35% of women in the class could understand well what
they read. But the great needy part was the fluency in writing could almost be 10-15% of
participants in the class would creatively write well. So there is a great need for literacy or
 long life learning in the Managalasi plateau. We need a good literacy survey to see the
real literacy need in the Managalasi plateau to help RFN to see why their support is

) All women showed great interest and took seriously to learn the best ways to teach
classes in their own villages to encourage women. This training has encouraged many
women to see beyond 2017 to see that many of those ministries in the Barai area are to
be led by women. That is because many times men lead and they do not manage well and
many of the projects in the Barai area come to stop. Women in literacy is the way to raise
women up to another level because people see them as house wives and also men’s
PMV's to carry heavy cargo to the houses.

53 Endangered Echidna (Zaglossus bartoni) sighted

‘Sometimes known as the spiny Anteater, an Echidna the egg-laying mammal was sighted on the 16"
of July during the usual Saturday morning market at Afore station. Research has found that under
three genus, there are eight different species of Echidnas and their population is declining at an
alarming rate. Sadly, humans are the main factors in diminishing population of echidnas,

Being part of the Biodiversity survey team that carried out the survey in various altitudes/elevations
on the Managalas plateau, it stunned me to see this particular specie of Echidna, the eastern long
beaked echidna (Zaglossus barton!) at the market place that day. This specie is rare, even the records
of the past biodiversity survey carried out on the plateau did not show its sighting only the specie
Zaglossus brujjni the short beaked echidna. Under the IUCN Cites listing species conservation status,
the Eastern Long beaked Echidna (Zaglossus bartom)) is threatened and considered to be critically
endangered

The echidna was caught using traditional trap by a local hunter from Toma village and sold for K150.
It was bought and released back into the wild after carrying out a brief awareness to the small crowd
gathered there, making special mention on the current conservation status of this particular critically
‘endangered species of echidna. They appreciated the awareness and felt sorry for the poor animal

ABSTRACT

A preliminary survey was conducted in ltokama and surrounding villages of Kuai. and
Nibaiba within the Managalas Plateau, fjivitari District, Northern Province. The aim of
the survey was to gather baseline information on vegetation types, determine the siruciure

and assess the piant diversity.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three randomly selected sites, 2 to 4km apart;
Jarefa forest 3km west from Itokama, Kadiakala forest 2.5km northwest from ltokama
and Barije 4km northwest from ltokama. Within each site strip transects of 5 x 50m were
laid out and trees greater or equal (o Scm dbh were measured and height recorded.

To get a picture of species number as a function of increasing area, two 20 x 20m plots
were established at Jarefa and Barije forests. Within each ptot all species were assessed in
5 x Sm plots and new ones not encountered in 5 x 5m plots were added in subsequent
larger plots of 10x 1Gm and 20 x 20m.

Apart from forest sampling general botanical collection was conducted over the entire
area. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid proper identification of
specimens. -
Samplings and general observations indicate that e number of forest formations occur in
the area; mixed lowland forest. mixed Castexopyis forest. mixed upland foresi and
secondary regrowth. The result from the transects show that high proportion of trees have

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
upland and montane forests. These forests are intersected by many crecks and rivers that
form the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. Coarse scale analysis of land-
use threats, specics concentration and endemism, catchment pollution, forest
defragmentation and habitat lost places whole plateau ecosystem as High Conservation
Value Forest (Partners with Melancsia (PwM). 2004). Through conservation awareness
programs initiated and run by PwM within the plateau, the villagers have decided to
conserve their forests. The villagers have formed a core group: the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF), that will work in partnership with PwM to develop
conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua New
Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. Samplings (plants and
animals) were conducted over 14 days (11 effective sampling days) in forests around
Itokama Government Station. General observations on biodiversity were conducted
around villages of liokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highlights the vegetation survey. Note samplings were concentrated in one
area representing only a small fraction of the whole proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area.

2.0 Managalas Piateau — Environment Settings

The proposed Managalas Conservation Arca constitutes an area of approximately
300.000ha and is located on the Managalas Plateau in the Isivitari District of Oro
Province.

The Managalas Plateau is located within the Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests ecoregion.
This lowland and montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley Range and
surrounding lowland and coastal areas in southeastern PNG (Figure 1.0).

2.2 Geology

The geology of the proposed Managalas Platcau Conservation Area is largely influenced by the
surface geology of the Central Cordillera. of which the Owen Stanleys are an extension. Much of

and Quaternary his as and pyroclastics (Bleeker. 1483),

The Manuagalas Plateau itself is a volcanic areca predominantly composed of rocks derived from
deposits of volcanic orgins. The rock types found in the arca and surrounding areas are shown in
Figure 3.0.

A high degree of endemism has been found to de associated with Ultrabasic deposits (Bleeker.
1983) and in Papua New Guinea these are likely places to find species that have never been
scientifically described.

2.3 Vegetation

Most of the Managalas Plateau is composed of tropical wet evergreen forest. with a
significant percentage of tropical montane evergreen forest. Smaller percemages of upper
montane und freshwater swamp fores! are alsa found.

Lowland forest up to 1.400 m on the north side of the Owen Stanileys is made up of
Pometia, Terminaiia, Celtis. aad Elaecearpus. aww itand forest is made ap of both alluvial
and fill types (Paipmans, 19763. Lowland alluvial forest has a canopy that is multitiered
and irregular. with many emergents. The understory contains 2 shrub-and-herb layer
with 2 variety of climbers. epiphytes, and ferns. The dominant canopy trees include
species of Pometia. Canarium, Anispoptera, Crypiocarya, Terminalia. Syzygium, Ficus,
Celtis. Dysoxvhun. and Buchanania. Other species such as Koompassia, Dillenia,
Eucalpiopsis, Vatica, and Hopea are locally abundant. Dense stands of Araucaria the
tallest tropical trees in the world, are present in scattered locations (Paijmans. 1976).

The Managalas Piateau is predorminantly composed of four major forest types: low
altitude forest on uplands. iower montane forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans,
and savanna. The MPCA js largely covered by low altitude forest on uplands below

=== page 7 ===
1000m, and lower montane forest on high lands above 1000 m. Also, small scattered
forests of low altitude forest on plains and fans which were found to be predominant
below 1000 m.

The vegetation types of the proposed Managalas CA are fragile forests and of biodiversity
importance comprised the low altitude forest on plains and fans, the lower montane
forest, and savanna. The dominant forest types are the forest on plains and fans, and the
lower montane forest which cover more than 75 percent of the MPCA. The lowland
forest and Jower montane forests are predominant and extend to areas where rainfall
exceed 1800 mm per annum, and at higher altitudes with decreasing temperature
respectively (Bleeker, 1983). The lowland forest is structurally and floristically the richest
and typically contains numerous palms, vines and climbers on well drained alluvial
plains. However, in very poorly drained to swampy conditions, sago and pandanus are
found in the understorey.

3.0 Study Site

Because of time limitations, study on vegetation was conducted in forested areas within
the vicinity of Itokama Government Station and the surrounding villages of Kuali. and
Nibaiba situated approximately at latitude 9° 12.02" S and longitude 148” 15.91°E. The
elevation range from 670m to 900m asi (Figure 4.0). The area is rather flat with
undulating terrain and rolling hills.

Figure 4.0. Study site within vicinity of tokama.

than 1000m asl. This is a typical lowland rainforest formation with canopy heights
reaching 40m. Canopy is discontinuous with many gaps (Figure 5.0) created over time by
various factors including senescence. Major canopy tee species include Castanopsis
accuminatissima, Syzygium spp.. Cryptocarve spp., Elaeocarpus spp., Sloanea spp., and
Weinmannia sp.

Three sites were selected randomly; Jarefa, Kadiakala and Barije forests. [In each site strip

To get an overall picture of the plant biodiversity of the area, 2 plots of 20 x 20m were

General botanical collections were also conducted over the survey period and plants

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic.
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets.of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation appears
irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest observation on
surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are influenced by

topography.

Certain features, characteristic to lower montane formation become obvious at around
700m asl. The presence of Castanopsis accuminatissina and even Lithocarpus and
Dacrydium in the forests at Jarefa and towards the villages of Nibaiba and Kuai indicate
low montane elements. Large woody lianas. plants with compound leaves, cauliflorous
plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and lowland hill
forests (Whitmore 1975) become scarce at Jarefa.

By comparison, forest adjacent to Barije River represents typical lowland forest with
abundant plants possessing compound leaves. cauliflory and large lianas. Common
lowland species of Elmerriilia, Aglaia. Dysoxvium, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia. Cryptocarva,
and Terminalia are abundant.

Based on this observation the upland foresis surrounding [tokama can be further classified
into the following types: mixed Castanopsis forest. mixed upland forest and lowland.

6.1.1 Mixed upland forest

On rather flat {eztains mixed forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. The (orest
is vertically multilayered. Dominant canopy tree species include Cryptocarya, Sloanea,
Castanopsts, Syzygium, Weinmania and Elavocarpus. The ground layer is dense and
largely composed at shrabs of various species.

6.3.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tall.
The forest is two-layered: the canopy and the ground layers. Castanupyis acctuininatissima
is the dominant canopy species in this forest pe. Other coexisting canopy species

6.1.3 Mixed lowland forest

Predominant on flat areas near rivers. The forest is multilayered with the main canopy
Stretching up to 40m (Figure 8.0). Dominant canopy species include Cryptocarya.
Syzygium, Elaeocarpus, Slonea, Artocarpus and strangler Ficus. Lower canopy trees
include species of Garcinia, Gironniera, Barringionia and Dysoxylum. The ground floor
is sparse with abundant seedlings. This forest type is probably the dominant type below
700m asl and extend throughout the proposed Managalas Plateau Conservation Area.

6.1.4 Secondary Regrowth

Disturbed forests also form major formations within the area and are represented by early
regrowth, secondary and advanced secondary forests. Overall height range from 15 to
20m. The formation depends on the intensity and frequency of disturbance. Common
secondary plant species that dominate the canopy include Macaranga, Homolantius,
Ficus, Glochidion and Gastonia. The ground layer is densely vegetated by Imperata
cylindrical, Alpinia, Hornstedtia sp., Nephrolepis and various spinny creepers.

7.0 FOREST USE

The local people depend heavily on planis and forest resources for their livelihood. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
constiucuon, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants, germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
Services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for
instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and raflers of houses.
Stems of palm tees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

8.0 GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the survey thal support the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people.

* The forest types. and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. !n effect this means that the vegetatina is quite
unique and presents window's of opportuaiies for long teym scientific siudies on this
forest ecosystems. ;

* The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees 10 larger size classes requires
proper studies.

The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an
intriguing fuctor and further research would help tc explain its effect and impact on
biogiversiiy.

Due to the lack of proper infrastructure. the people of Managalas rely heavily on
planis and other forest resources for their basic necds. Destruction of these forests
Would reduce ihe resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

The Araucaria hunsteinii trees represent a historical time seate. Dendroclimatology
Siudies in New Zealand have established time periods of similar sott wood species

=== page 17 ===
ry

dating several thousand years back into the past. The remnant trees within the
Managalas Plateau present good prospects to study past climatic changes and their
influences on vegetation.

* Standing forests act as carbon sinks. With respect to global warming, it would be
interesting to know the carbon sequestration potential of these forests by carrying out
appropriate studies.

* Given the uniqueness of the forests and the resources contained therein, outside
institutions, researchers, and tourists would certainly want to visit the area. To prepare
for such influx, the landowners through PwM can draw up sets of conditions and
guidelines that would protect the pristine forest and at the same time generate income
for the forest owners.

9.0 RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, we highly recommend
that the forest be conserved. The followings are offered for guidance.

* Proper tramping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting
sites be identified then design to allow minimal disturbance.

* The pine is a tree of scientific and historical significance. Scattered Stands of these
species should be identified and mapped out. both. within and outside the proposed
conservation area and these areas be protected.

¢ The mixed Castunopsis forest is very sensitive to human disturbances. Conversion of
this forest type io grassland is already a common feature in the Highlands of Papua
New Guinea. ft is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

¢ Proper records of plant animal uses be established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and riwals to be able to readily access traditional
knowledge.

¢ Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally assess the ecology
of the area. This should also encompass u full botanical reconnaissance survey of the
area. Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored.

* Establish research collaboration with known research organizations like FRI, Wau
Ecological Institute. Unitech and UPNG. so that research can be conducted in the area
to generate more knowledge on the ecology of the forest communities.

PLANTS, BIRDS, MAMMAL AND HERPETOFAUNA SURVEYS OF
THE MANAGALAS PLATEAU PROPOSED CONSERVATION

AREA, NORTHERN PROVINCE

Prepared for Partners with Melanesia (PwM)
Pius Piskaut

Rose Singadan

Paulus Kulmoi

=== page 2 ===
SUMMARY REPORT

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
hill and montane forests. The forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form
the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. A rich diversity of fauna and flora are
supported by these forest types. Oil Palm development, and subsistence agriculture are
posing great threats to these pristine forests. The villagers within the plateau have decided
lo conserve their forests and are seeking assistance from Partners with Melanesia (PwM)
to develop their conservation initiatives. The villagers have formed a core group; the
Managalas Deveiopment Foundation (MDF). that wil! work in partnership with PwM to
develop the conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004. preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists. Samplings (piants and animals)
were conducted over i4 days (11 days effective sampiing periods) in uphill forests of
Jarifa near Kam creek. General observations on biodiversity were conducted around
villages of Itokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highlights the summary of the survey. A more detailed repori of the survey

will be provided after thorough synthesis of the data. Note samplings were concentrated
in one area representing only a small fraction of the whole proposed Managaias Plateau
Sonservation Area.

2.0 Plant species diversity

The forests surrownding Janis is a typical uphill forest type situated at an elevation of
approximately 700 to 800m as]. This forest type comprises different cohorts or stands that
are in part influenced by the different landscape formations. On rather flat areas mixed
forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. Dominant tree species include
Criptocarva, Sioanea, Casianopsis, Svzygiuni, Weinmania and Llaeocarpus. On ridges
mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tali. Castanopsis
accuminatissima is the dorainant tree species in this forest type. Disturbed forests also
form minor formations within the area and are represented by early regrowth, secondary
and advanced secondary forests. The frequently disturbed riverine forest forms a narrow
strip along the rivers.

have diameter <30cm (Figure 1). This indicates that the forests are relatively young
consequently there is limited recruitments into the higher size classes.

3.0 Bird diversity.

Summary report to be provided by Paulus Kuimei, Department of Environment and
Conservation. At least 100 species of birds were observed within the viliages of Itokama,
Kuai, Nidaida and the Jarifa forest.

=== page 7 ===
4.0 Mammals and Herpetofauna

Fifty five specimens of rats and bats were collected after 440 net and trapping nights over
11 working nights. In total twenty-three (23) specimens of rodents were captured and
thirty two (32) specimens of bats were collected. After measurements were taken
seventeen (17) bats, all Syconycteris australis were released. Of those, eight (8) species of
rodents were trapped and 3 species of bats were netted. A colony of 5 of the large Forbes
tree mouse were captured when the villagers chopped down the tree they were living in.
The colony of 5 rodents are now kept alive at the Museum of the University of Papua
New Guinea. Details are all given in Table 2.

Although, our netting and trapping nights did not produce any marsupials we observed
three (3) species of marsupials at different times of the survey. That included a juvenile
southern brown cuscus that was kept as a pet after the mother was killed for consumption,
Dorias tree Kangaroo was also kept as a pet by a family after the mother was also
captured and consumed. During the period of the survey, villagers captured three (3)
forest wallabies, which were later consumed (refer to Table 2).

4.1 Wild dog (Canis Familiaris dingo):

The presence of the wild dog was confirmed when a half-crunched bird was left hanging
in the lower shelve of the mistnet in the undercroft of Pandanus trees. Villagers insisted
that this could not have been left behind by domestic dogs but wild dogs.

4.2 Reptilia:

Most of our efforts were concentrated on mammals and not on reptiles and frogs.
However, over the 11 working days our chance - collection and observations resulted in
thirteen (11) specimens of reptiles and frogs. Of those thirteen specimens, three (3)
species of reptiles (2 pythons and a keelbacked snake) were seen. The two species of
pythons were captured by villagers and eaten, while the Keel-backed snake was seen at
the Camp site. The other eleven (11) species (4 frogs & 8 reptiles) were collected with the
help of the villagers and taken as specimens. The frogs comprise of two ground frogs of
the same species, one hylid and one ranid (refer to Table 2).

4.3 Domesticated animals:

Domestic animals were seen in the villages. Of the three, domestic dog, pussy cat and
chicken, dogs and cats can have an influence on the presence of wildlife. Both dogs and
cats are kept as pets but villagers seemed to keep dogs especially for hunting. From our
investigation, it seemed that dogs were kept for hunting more than as pets.

Wild animals were also captured and kept as pets to be sold later of for consumption. A
Doria's Tree kangaroo was kept as a pet after the mother was killed several years ago. In
another house, a juvenile southern brown cuscus was also kept as a pet but later escaped.

5.0 FOREST USE

The local people depend heavily on plants and forest resources for their livelihood. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
construction, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants, germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for

instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and rafters of houses.

Stems of palm trees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

6. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the survey that support the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people.

e The forest types, and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. In effect this means that the vegetation is quite
unique and presents windows of opportunities for long term scientific studies on this
forest ecosystems.

e The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees to larger size classes requires
proper studies.

e The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an
intriguing factor and further research would help to explain its effect and impact on
biodiversity.

¢ Due to the lack of proper infrastructure, the people of Managalas rely heavily on
plants and other forest resources for their basic needs. Destruction of these forests
would reduce the resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

e The Araucaria hunsteinii trees represent a historical time scale. Dendroclimatology
studies in New Zealand have established time periods of similar soft wood species
dating several thousand years back into the past. The remnant trees within the

influences on vegetation.

Given the umueness of the forests and the resources contained therein, outside

7. RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, we highly recommend
that the forest be conserved. The followings are offered for guidance.

Proper tramping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting
sites be identified then design to allow minimal disturbance.

The pine is a tree of scientific and historical significance. Scattered stands of these
species should be identified and mapped out, both, within and outside the proposed
conservation area and these areas be protected.

The mixed Castanopsis forest is very sensitive to human disturbances. Conversion of
this forest type to grassland is already a common feature in the Highlands of Papua

Proper records of plant animal uses be established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able to readily access traditional
knowledge.

Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally assess the ecology
of the area. This should also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey of the
area, Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored.

Establish research collaboration with known research organizations like FRI, CRI,

Wau Ecological Institute, and UPNG, so that research can be conducted in the area to

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation appears
irregular. Although the forest type resembies tropical lowland forest observation on
surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are influenced by

topography.

Certain features, characteristic to lower montane formation become obvious at around
700m asl. The presence of Castanopsis accuminatissima and even Lithocarpus and
Dacrydium in the forests at Jarefa and towards the villages of Nibaiba and Kuai indicate
low montane elements. Large woody lianas. plants with compound leaves, cauliflorous
planis, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and lowland hill
forests (Whitmore 1975) become scarce at Jarefa.

By comparison, forest adjacent to Barije River represents typical lowland forest with
abundant plants possessing compound Icaves, cauliflory and large lianas. Common
lowland species of Elmerrillia, Aglaia, Dysoxylum, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia, Cryptocarya,
and Terminalia are abundant.

Based on this observation the upland forests surrounding Itokama can be further classified
into the following types; mixed Castanopsis forest, mixed upland forest and lowland.

6.1.1 Mixed upland forest

On rather flat terrains mixed forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. The forest
is vertically multilayered. Dominant canopy tree species include Cryptocarya, Sloanea,
Castanopsis, Syzygium, Weinmania and Elaeocarpus. The ground layer is dense and
largely composed of shrubs of various species.

6.1.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tall.
The forest is two-layered; the canopy and the ground layers. Castanopsis accuminatissima
is the dominant canopy species in this forest type. Other coexisting canopy species
include Canarium. Ternstroemia, Cryptocarya. Terminalia and several species of

Syzygium. The ground layer is sparsely vegetated by Pandanus spp., ferns and creepers
(Figure 7.0).

respectively (Bleeker, 1983), The lowland forest is structurally and floristically the richest
and typically contains numerous palms. vines and climbers on well drained alluvial
plains. However, in very poorly drained to swampy conditions, sago and pandanus are
found in the understorey.

2.3 Vegetation

Mosi of the Managalas Piateau is composed of tropical wei evergreen forest, with a
significant percentage of tropical montane evergreen forest. Smaller percentages of upper
montane and freshwater swamp forest are also found.

Lowland forest up to 1,400 m on the north side of the Owen Stanleys is made up of
Pometia, Terminalia, Celtis, and Elaeocarpus. Lowland forest is made up of both alluvial
and hill types (Paijmans, 1976). Lowland alluvial forest has a canopy that is multitiered
and irrreguiar, with many emergents. The understory contains a shrub-and-herb layer
with a variety of climbers, epiphytes, and ferns. The dominant canopy trees include
species of Pometia, Canarium, Anispoptera, Cryptocarya, Terminalia, Syzygium, Ficus,
Celtis, Dysoxylum, and Buchanania. Other species such as Koompassia, Dillenia,
Eucalptopsis, Vatica, and Hopea are locally abundant. Dense stands of Araucaria the
tallest tropical trees in the world, are present in scattered locations (Paijmans, 1976).

The Managalas Plateau is predorminantly composed of four major forest types; low
altitude forest on uplands, lower montane forest, Jow altitude forest on plains and fans,
and savanna. The MPCA is largely covered by low altitude forest on uplands below

2.1 Climate

The climate of the Managalas Plateau is tropical wet, which is characteristic of this part of
Melanesia, located in the western Pacific Ocean north of Australia.

The proposed Managalas Plateau Conservation Area itself has a relatively high annual
rainfall and range from 2000mm to 3500mm., The eastern most part of the conservation
area is slightly drier compare to the eastern part (Figure 2.0). Overall the weighted
average (according to PNGRIS mapping unit averages) annual rainfall is 2,725mm.

Rainfall distribution is associated with the two major seasonal wind patterns of the
region: the northwest monsoons occurring in the months of November to April and the
southeast trade winds occurring in May to October. The northwest monsoon is the wettest
while the southeast trade winds is drier resulting in pronounced dry season (PwM, 2004).

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
upland and montane forests. These foresis are intersected by many crecks and rivers that
form the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers, Coarse scale analysis of land-
use thicais, species conceatration and endemism, caichmeni potiuiion, forest
defragmentation and habitat lost places whele plateau ecosystem as High Conservation
Value Forest (Partners with Melanesia (PwM), 2004). Through conservation awareness
programs initiated and run by PwM within the plateau, the villagers have decided to
conserve their forests. The villagers have formed a core group: the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF). that will work in partnership with PwM to develop
conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2(4}4, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua New
Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. Samplings (plants and
animals) were conducted over 14 days (11 effective sampling days} in forests around
ltokama Government Station. General observations on biodiversity were conducted
around villages of ttokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highiights the vegetation survey. Note samptings were concentrated in one
area representing only a smal! fraction of the whole proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area.

The Managalas Plateau is located within the Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests ecoregion.
