5.2 Social impacts
5.2.1 Hunting Practices

Hunting is still one of the activities that the villagers take part in from time to time. During the
period of survey, a female bandicoot with two young joeys was captured and eaten. Onit the
lower mandibie was retrieved for collected.

Food is abundant. Peopie are well nourished with surplus garden food resources. Wild foods
for human consumption is also abundant except for protein supplements. Therefore hunting for
wild meat seemed to occur on a regular basis. People have pigs, dogs, chickens and cats in
the villages. However, domestic pigs and chicken are only consumed during important cultural
occasions, while dogs are kept for hunting and cats as pets to keep house rats away.

People in the area of survey lack protein supplements. Therefore, they will continue to hunt for
wild meat until they can be able to afford protein supplements that are sold in village trade
stores.

5.2.2 Gardening/Subsistence

People in the MPCA are gardeners. Each family has several gardens and food is surplus.
There are so many varieties of food crops, which can cater for their daily supplements.
However, the slash and burn method of gardening and shifting cultivation that they practice
tend to make way for large areas fo be left exposed to the disadvantage of smaller ground
animals. Many trees around new gardens are chopped down indiscriminately and left to rot
That was seen in many villages where we walked.

According to the villagers, people are currently making gardens in forested areas, which were
never touched in the last two (2) decades. Gardening in previously untouched forests at higher
will continue as population increases. Currently with the slash and burn method that these

=== page 46 ===
peopie use, there will be more open areas, which will affect smaller animais that utilise forest
cover for survival and allow invasive species of piants to colonise these areas which may result
in permanent grass patches.

5.2.3 Outlook on People’s lifestyle

The overall outlook on the lifestyle of the peopie is generally like those of other people in rural
areas of PNG. The basic resources for human sustenance are available, food, fresh and clean
water, clean air. firewocd and other resources for human survival. Generally the people are
healthy and enjoy a good village lifestyle.

The project area has an airstrip, which is serviced by PNG Airlines, Health Center, A
Community Top-Up School, pius various churches (Anglican, SDA, and United Pentecostal
Church) and other agencies that act on behalf of the government.

5.2.4 Logging and Mining Activities

Managalas Proposed Conservation Area is Resource rich. The area is abundant with food
resources. which are sufficient for the people. Natural (wild) resources are also abundant that
is; wild animals, forest products etc which people utilise. There are other viable resources
(Coffee, Vanilia, Garden foods, Bete! nuts etc) that people can sel! for extra income but
currently these are consumed at the village level and therefore they are not economically
viable.

However, if this trend continues and the pressures of external economic activities are inviting,
people may redirect their attention to alternative sources of generating economic activites that
are beneficial to sustain their immediate needs (eq.. Children’s Education, Schoo! fees. Medical
fees, Family commitments. Travel/Entertainment requirements and basic numan needs).

Very common examples and experiences gained from other parts of the country show that
mechanised clear-fell logging and mining activites are often inviting. They bring in cash
incomes although short-term and very destructive for peogie in rural settings whe have been
basically left neglected by their respective governments for too long. Therefore, a main road is
what the Managalas people need quickiy.

A proper road network linking all the main villages to each other, to Afore Sub District
Station and to Popondetta, main town center for Oro Province is what the people need
most. It is a major setback for all the people who live in the Proposed Conservation
Area.

Until this problem is resolved in the next 5 to 10 years, Conservation Efforts, deliverance
of Basic Rural Services and Developmental activities will continue to progress at a very
slow pace in Manaala in comparison to other areas in Papua New Guinea.

Discussions
(a) possible threats to bird lives of the conservation area.

In references to sites covered from phase 2 bird biodiversity surveys, there were no major threats
encountered to justify possible threats to bird lives of the area. Commercially involved activities were
discouraged by the loca] landowners of the conservation area, except for mini projects, like the growing of
coffee trees that generate little cash income and subsistence cash cropping. The small coffee gardens
already established at each villages sites may have little impact of the available bird species, but clearing
for new garden sites may have some effects to some species having their habitats permanently destroyed,
displacing them seeking possible refuge in the nearby vegetation’s. Magagals Plateau has a very rich soi!
profile and if the local people can clear secondary vegetation’s for new gardens, much of the rainforest will
continue to remain good biological grounds for not only the birds, but all the fauna species in the area.
Much of the higher elevations ranging from 1000 meters above sea level and beyond remain naturally, a
biological habitats for many species, and these encourages high species diversity.

It was good to know that local people from the sites visited, have been practicing traditional methods of
catching birds. The idea of conservation within the plateau have developed high feelings between the local
landowners and Partners With Melanesia. This trend have continue without having the conservation area
concepts declining and having the area ceveloped for other commercial activities. Bird species density will
decline when landowners are not too happy with the conservation concepts, which will lead to more natural
habitats destroyed for cash cropping and other activities. Close participation’s of conservation programs
must be regular and informative to avoid any possibles threats.

(b) Site discussions of Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveys.

When comparations were made from the two phases of biodiversity surveys, many bird species recorded
were similar except for few species that were confined be a different altitudinal ievels. This depends very
much on food types and adaptations to habitat types required. It is so important to note list of the bird
species to avoid possible destruction’s to habitat types and the loose of species.

Recommendations

Managalas Conservation Area may be recognized one of the first type of conservation area in Papua New
Guinea if declared at a later stage. It’s rich biodiversity have encouraged local landowners who have deep
thoughts of conservation for their available valued natural resources as a tool for themselves and their

area may remain having it’s valued natural resources without major destruction’s from developments,
Small agro-forestry projects may be viable and be encouraged to sites where there will be less destruction’s
with no valued fauna and flora species. To maintain the valued richness of biodiversity of this conservation
area, I would recommend for these few ideas be exercise.

1. Management and planning of each individual, clan and village lands for smal! agro-forestry projects, to
avoid loose of any important species in the area.

2. Where possible, all identified important species at each zones of villages be made known to them for
protective measures. Not only that information’s, but other biological information's that the villagers
have to know.

3. Rehabilitation programs of three species planting in grasslands, secondary vegetation’s and other man
made clearings to maintain species diversity, which includes the host plant for Queen Alexandra’s

4. Some important fauna species were recorded through interviews with the local people to be available
in high mountainous areas, that the use of helicopter wil] be more appropriate in future biodiversity

5. The two phases of bird results, so far covering zones 1,2 and 7 in November 2004 and November

ABSTRACT

In November, 2004, a rapid vegetation assessment was conducted near Itokama and
the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. In November, 2005, a phase 2 survey
was conducted as an extension of that survey. The overall aim of the survey was to
gather baseline information on vegetation types, determine the structure and assess the
plant diversity within the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three selected sites, Kierim lower montane
forest, Tahama forest and Pongani forest near the coast. Within cach site plots of
50x50m were demarcated. Within the plot, strip lines of 5 x 50m were marked out at
10m interval. The strip line was subdivided into 5x10m subplots and trees 25cm dbh
were measured and heights recorded.

To account for shrubs, herbs and saplings, at least 5 quadrats of 5 x 5m were randomly
placed within the demarcated plot and all species enumerated.

Apart from forest sampling general botanical collection was conducted within the
vicinity of each site. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid
proper identification of specimens.

Samplings and general observations indicate that a number of forest formations occur
in the proposed conservation area; lower montane forest comprising of mixed
Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans, monsoonal or dry evergreen
forest and patches of savanna grassland towards the coast. The results from diameter
measurements in all plots showed that high proportion of trees have dbh <30cm
suggesting that the current forest types are quite young. However, there are indications
that there was a period of suppressed growth that has some bearing on the current
forest structure.

The Shannon Diversity Index average score is 1.50. This is higher than the first survey
at Itokama. Species area curve also show increasing species number as area increases
from mountain to the coast. All in ali the Managalas Conservation Area has a very

high species diversity.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the Managalas Development
Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia be strengthen and instrument
put in place to declare the Managalas Plateau as Conservation Area.

1.0 Introduction

In November 2004, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals
and herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua
New Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. In November
2005, phase 2 study of the survey was conducted. The survey covered larger forest
areas ranging from lower montane forest to ficod plain forest near the coast. The
overall aims of the survey are 2 fold:

1. to assess the general plant diversity of the Managalas Proposed Conservation

Area (MPCA).
2. assess the diversity of vegetation types and their formation occurring within
the MPCA area,

This report highlights the results and observations of the phase II vegetation survey
conducted over a period of 20 days.

2.0 Managalas Plateau

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area constitutes an area of approximately
300,000ha and is located on the Managalas Plateau in the Isivitari District of Oro
Province.

The Managalas Plateau is located within the Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests
ecoregion. This lowland and montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley
Range and surrounding lowland and coastal areas in southeastern PNG (Figure 1.0).

A detail description of the cnvironment settings of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area is given in Partners with Melanesia Report (2004) and summarized
in Piskaut (2004).

surveyed is located at S° 8° 47.2" § and 148° 12° 44.5”, at an elevation of 1200m as
and siope inclination of . approximaiely 45°. The forest formation is largely iower
montane with Castancpsis accuminatissima and Lithocarpus sp. being the dominant
canopy tree.

3.2 Tahamea forest

fahama forests is situated at 9° 11° 41.8°S and 148° 19° 37.2”E, at an altitude of
600m asi. The topography is represented by gently undulating rolling hills. The
general forest formation is a typicai !ow altitude forest with species of Anisoptera,
Hopea. Pometia, Pangium and Elaeocarpus dominating the canopy.

3.3 Pongani

Pongani is situated near the coast at 9° 04’ 18.9"S and 148° 31’ 31.0” E, at an
elevation of 53m asl. The area surveyed is adjacent to the Pongani River just at the
foot of the chain of hills that rise toward Afore. The major vegetation types in this area
include flood plain forest, savanna and monsoonal forests.

4.0 Methods

The methodology employed here slightly differ from previous survey where strip
transects were taken randomly. Here plot of 50m x50m was demarcated in each site.
In each plot, belt transects of 5 x 50m were laid out systematically at 10m interval. To
get an overall picture of the plant biodiversity of the area, the strip transects were
subdivided into quadrats of of 5 x 10m (50m’*). In each quadrat all trees 25cm dbh
were enumerated. Parameters measured include diameter at breast height (dbh), height
and identification of species at least to genus level. Diameter and height were
measured to elucidate the structure and dynamic of the forest.

Note strip transects only account for tree species. To assess the species density within
the 50 x 50m plot, further 5 x Sm quadrats were laid randomly and all herbs, shrubs,
creepers, climbers and saplings enumerated. At least 5 quadrats were laid out.

General botanical collections were also conducted over the survey period and plants
samples pressed and transported to the UPNG Herbarium for further identification,
and storage.

were catergorised into one of 10 size classes; 1=5-10em; 2=10.1-1 Sem; 3=15.1-20em;

(Table 1.0). Species area curve was drawn base on all plots pooled together.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation
appears irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest
observation on surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are

influenced by topography (Piskaut, 2004).

At Anatua there appeared to be some distinct zonation. The lowland forest gradually
grades into montane forest above 1000m asl. However, certain features characteristic
to lower montane formation become obvious at around 700m asl. This is similar to the
vegetation pattern observed at Jarefa and the surround hills. The presence of
Castanopsis accuminatissima, Lithocarpus, Podocarpus and Dacrydium in the forests
indicate low montane elements. Large woody lianas, plants with compound leaves,
cauliflorous plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and
lowland hill forests (Whitmore 1975) become rare or scarce above 1000m.

The forests at Tahama represent typical lowland forest with abundant plants
possessing compound leaves, cauliflory and large lianas. Common lowland species of
Elmerrillia, Aglaia, Dysoxylum, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia, Cryptocarya, Anisoptera,
Hopea and Terminalia are abundant.

At Pongani, a diversity of vegetation types coexists. These include flood plain forest.
lowland hill forest, monsoon forests and savanna grasslands.

In general the vegetation within the sites surveyed so far can be classified into the
following types; mixed Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest, savanna and monsoon
forest.

6.1.1 Low altitude forest

Predominant on flat terrain and near rivers. The forest is multilayered with the main
canopy stretching up to 40m. Dominant canopy species include Cryptocarya,
Syzygium, Elaeocarpus, Slonea, Pometia pinnata, Artocarpus and strangler Ficus.
Lower canopy trees include species of Garcinia, Gironniera, Barringtonia and
Dysoxylum, The ground floor is sparse with abundant seedlings. This is the dominant
vegetation type on the Platcau and include the mixed upland forests.

Canopy species dominance varies locally. For instance, at Jarefa. the forest comprises
of mixed canopy tree species. At Tahame and toward Afore and even to Pongani. the
forest is dominated by dipterocarps (4nisoptera and Hopea).

6.1.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges and mountains mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy
reaching up to 35m tall. The forest is two-lavered; the canopy and the ground lavers.
Casianopsis accuminatissima and Lithecarpus are the dominant canopy species in this
forest type. Other coexisiing canopy species include Cararium, Jernsiroemia,
Cryptocarya, Terminalia and severa! species of Syzygium. The ground layer is
sparseiy vegetated by Pandanus spp., ferns and creepers.

6.1.3 Savanna grassiané

This vegetation occurs in patches from the flat coastal area to the foothills. The
dominant tree is Eucalyptus confertiflora that forms the main canopy. The ground
cover is dominated by /mperata cylindrical (Kunai grass). Patchy occurrences of
savanna indicate that the area from Pongani towards Afore were once dominated by
grassland. In the absence of fire the vegetation has reverted to forest.

6.1.4 Monsoon forest or dry evergreen forest

Monsoon forest occurs at Pongani. This vegetation type is very similar to the
monsoonal forest along the southern part of New Guinea and is an indication of
pronounced dry and wet seasons. The overall canopy height is reduced and range from
10 to 15m. Common plant species that dominate the canopy include species of

layer is densely vegetated by seedlings, saplings and various thorny creepers and

6.2 Forest structure

The forest structures are similar in all sites as indicated by the diameter class
distributions (Figure 3.0). That is the current forests are younger. There is lack of
recruitment into the higher size classes. However, the proportion of trees >50cm
further indicate that the original forest was impacted upon by natural disturbance
events in the recent past. According to the locals the drought period of 1997/98 did
affect the forest on the plateau.

6.3 Plant species diversity

The species diversities of the areas surveyed appeared similar with slight variations
that could be attributable to the sampling error. Overall, a total of |.22ha was sampled
with 289 species enumerated. This number excludes other species not present in the
plots. This is suggestive of very high species diversity. The overall species diversity
score for all sites is 2 with the Tahama forests having the highest diversity. This figure
is quite high considering the small area sampled. It is envisaged that this figure will
increase if a permanent tha plot is established in each site.

6.4 Status of Plants.

Currently there are no proper assessments on the status of plant species in Papua New
Guinea. The only plants that have received much attention and included in the CITES
list are members of the Orchid family. Although oniy few orchid specimens were
collected, both epiphytic and ground orchids were abundant especially at the Jarefa
forest.

With the collection (Appendix |) further determination is needed to verify the correct
specimens. However, there is a high probably some of the specimens collected might
be new records or new species.

7.0 GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the 2004 and this survey (2005) that support the
conservation initiatives undertaken by the local people.

¢ The forest types, and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by
the prevailing environmenta! conditions, In effect this means that the vegetation is
quite unique and presents windows of opportunities for long term scientific studies
on this forest ecosystems.

* The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees to larger size classes
requires proper studies.

¢ The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is
an intriguing factor and further research would help fo expiain its effect and
impact on biodiversity.

® Due to the lack of proper infrastructure, the people of Managalas rely heavily on
plants and other forest resources for their basic needs. Destruction of these forests
would reduce the resource base of these plants and their products and may affect
the local inhabitants.

* Standing forests act as carbon sinks. With respect to global warming, it would be
interesting t know the carbon sequestration potential of these forests by carrying
Out appropriate studies.

8.0 RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, it is highly
recommended that the forest be conserved. Jt is also recommended that more surveys
and other iong term studies be conducted to optimally assess the ecology of the area.
This shoulé also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey of the area.
Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored within the four
comers of the Managaias Plateau.

Introduction:

I was tasked by Partners With Melanesians Inc. and Managalas Development Foundation
to conduct a research and provide to the two (2) organizations some Non Timber Forest
Products (NTFP) that are found on the Managalas plateau in order for the organizations
to utilize them to serve the people of the Managalas plateau who have given their land for
the purpose of conservation and have opted against destructive logging, mining and large
scale agricultural plantations and farms.

The main purpose of this survey was to identify the commercial potential of Non-Timber
Forest Products of the Managalas Plateau.

This rapid assessment included seven days of field visits and interview with locals form
the area in identifying the species and documenting them. Each species was assessed for
its commercial potential and recommendations were given for development and further
work. A further 14 days was taken in compiling this report using data collected from the
field.

Despite being assigned to note down only five NTFPs that are economically viable for
the Plateau, I have produced ten priority NTFPs because some NTFPs were not found to
occur in some areas which left other areas having their own priority NIFP.A total of 44
NTFPs are also listed for PWM to consider.

It is recommended that further detailed information, botanical and NTFP specimen and
plant species including quantitative and qualitative work be carried out on these as a
matter of priority.

Although economic overheads in the Managalas plateau are considerable (in particular
the lack of and cost of transport and poor communications), it may still be profitable to
commercially develop some NTFPs with careful species and product selection and a
marketing strategy that emphasises the links between their production and biodiversity
conservation in the area.

=== page 6 ===
Paul Kontal NTFP/ Managalari- survey 2005/07

Geographical Location:

Managalas Plateau is located at approximately 9 degrees longitude north and
approximately 148. 2 degrees latitude south of the equator. The district head quarter is
called Afore District and it is administered at the township of Popendetta. The province
was formally called Northern Province but was later changed to Oro province where
Managalas Plateau is located.

The total population of Oro province is about 120,000 people according to the 2000
census of which the Managalas people makes up 5% of the total population which is
almost 16000 (15,000 accordingly to the National Census in 2000).

Managalas Plateau is located at the most remote part of the Oro Province and almost
isolated from the rest of Papua New Guinea. The total land area is approximately 360,000
hectares. Thus life at Managalas Plateau for an outsider can be very challenging due to
the fact that walking is difficult on the rugged terrain while basic and essential
government services are very minimum or non existent at very isolated locations through
out the plateau.

Access to the Managalas Plateau is either by foot, a four-wheel-drive to Afore or a twin-
Otto aeroplane serviced by the third level airline, Airlines PNG. There are five (5)
airstrips on the Plateau which are at Afore, Itokama, Sakarina, Sila and Gora. However,
Itokama airstrip is the only one commercially serviced by Airlines PNG while the others
have been closed because people were not using it regularly or they have not met the

Access to Markets:

Access to market is now made easier since the Popendetta — Afore road is upgraded and
trucks are moving up and down in less than three hours. The indication is that this route is
the best route to the markets for zones in the Eastern part of the Plateau because this route

Oro Bay- Afore Road:

Since road was chosen as the best alternative route to transport crops from the plateau for
selling at other markets, [ will give my assessment on the current condition of the Oro
Bay-Afore Road.

The Oro Bay-A fore road was built and declared in the carly 1970s as a national highway
for the province. However, over the years there were no maintenance work done to the
road and the road has since deteriorated from bad to worse and non serviceable by
vehicles until late last year when the provincial government decided to upgrade the old
road. When this report was written, the road was still under construction. Trucks,
especially 4WD (4 wheel drives) can now travel to Afore in less than 3 hours and is
accessible through Numba, Koino, Basabe, Tabuane and Dea. The traveling time from
Popendetta to Afore in the 1980’s- 2004 and early 2005 used to be 11- 12 hours one way
up by a 4 wheel drive. Today it can be done under 3 hours one way up and under 2 hours
down to the coast, at the port of Popendetta.

The existing road was re- constructed by a coffee buyer, who constructed the road so that
he can ferry his coffee bags to a coffee mill at Popondetta. Thus the particular coffee
buyer did the clearing, filled the pot holes and scraped the soil just to allow for his trucks
to travel during the dry coffee season. In my view, the road will deteriorate at a very fast
rate as soon as the rain falls as there was no drainage. The road base gravel and stones
were placed and gravelling was done. For the moment, it is a much needed service
rendered to these forgotten people after 30 years of the country’s independence.

The coffee buyer is an investor from Australia. He has been hailed a hero and a redeemer
for the people of Managalas plateau and was also featured in one of the two daily
newspapers in the country, the Post Courier’s front page picture of one of its July 2005
edition, In my opinion his good deeds are yet to be assessed and for how long will this
investor continue to service this road is a question we will all have to ponder.

Way Forward - 2005 and Beyond:

PWM has been working in the Managalas Plateau since 1997. Over the years, emphasis
has been placed on the three main components (Conservation, Capacity Building and

with activities derived from these components. Other support projects were also
implemented during the course of the project including Community Land Use Planning
linked to the Community Boundary Mapping, Rainforest Literacy and the Natural
Livelihood Resources and Poverty Alleviation Project.

Thirty years after Independence and there is nothing tangible from the government to this
forgotten part of the country. Major infrastructures are not in place including roads and
bridges, although there are minor maintenance and upgrading done to the Oro Bay- Afore
road, Government services are restricted to basic health (aid post) and Education
(primary/community/elementary).

In this area where there is limited government support, Non-Government Organizations
(NGOs) are perceived to be the alternative source of providing much of what the
government is not able to offer in terms of government services.

In light of the current global economic trend, communities are pressed with hard
economic times when deciding to meet basic household needs including school fees,
medical expenses, clothing, supplementary food requirements, etc. Now, more than ever,
communities feel the pressure to utilize available forest resources to meet their needs in
an area that is designated to be declared a conservation area.

When communities are discouraged to exert more pressure on their forest, land and water
in order to conserve their environment and its habitats, it is only appropriate to provide
alternatives to bring in revenue to sustain their needs.

The way forward for the MSCAP is two-folds: (1) Forest protection and, (2) Using forest
resources sustainably to alleviate poverty [poverty in PNG as defined by the World
Health Organization means the absence of health, education and other basic services).

This could be achieved through the Natural Livelihood Resources and Poverty
Alleviation Project whose main objective is to maintain a sustainable forest resource base
for a sustainable livelihood by utilizing and maintaining the environment which has the
potential to alleviate poverty.

Appendix I
Common Name: Okari (English, Tok Pisin)
Local Dialect: Makam/ Fandav

Scientific Name: Terminalia kaernbachii (Combretaceae):

Traditional use:

The fresh fruits are cut open with a bush knife and the kernel eaten fresh. The shell is also
burnt and ashes collect to make traditional salt. The kernel is also grated and cooked with
vegetables in bamboo tubes and also baked in earth ovens (mumu) which is very
delicious to the mouth. It substitutes for any meat or protein supplement.

Potential as a NTFP:

Largely depends upon processing and access to markets. In particular on-farm handling
and storage of kernels and reliable cost effective transport to domestic markets (see route
proposed on transport). The major technical processing problem is the kernel’s instability
at ambient temperatures and humidity’s and its tendency to fall apart when handled.
Ideally the fruits (and kemels) should be treated as a fresh vegetable, but refrigeration and
freezing are either feasible or appropriate in most places of the Managalas. The
alternative is to dry kernels using either traditional techniques (such as kitchen fires) or
appropriate village-based thermal dryers such as those used for copra. Solar drying is not
appropriate or feasible in the plateau which experiences cloud cover and associated rain
most days, Okari nuts are not traditionally stored in the area, so this is also unlikely to be
feasible. It should not prove too technically difficult to introduce appropriate thermal
dryers in to the area -a number of designs are supported by PNG based organizations- but
experience elsewhere has shown that unless their introduction is accompanied by
comprehensive management training (in particular quality control) they are unlikely to
be successful. Even if kernels can be successfully dried, there is currently no standardized
media and system for packaging and storage (Evans 1996b).

Unfortunately, any effort to develop okari nuts in the plateau is unlikely to enjoy many

spin offs from any efforts in the plateau because —should it go ahead- it is recommended
that processing there would be based upon refrigerated storage of fruits and kernels.

Paul Konia! NTFP/ Manugalasi- survey 2005/07

However, an example of a project to develop okari nuts under similar socio, economic
and environmental circumstances does exist in PNG.

The Partners with Melanesians-supported Barai Okari Estates project in the Managalas
Plateau of Oro Province has been marketing okari nuts sporadically since 1993

(Ase 1996). The project is run by a community-based cooperative of producer groups
who organize purchasing through a network of village-based buying points, transport by
plane to Port Moresby and sold to informal and formal markets (Olsson 1996). In 1994,
two shipments of 600 kg of kernels were purchased from producers at village buying
points for K1.50/kg (USD1.70/kg)' and then sold to Steamships in Port Moresby for
K4.50/kg (USD5.23/kg) who retailed them for K7.80/kg (USD9.10). The quality of the
kernels was reasonable, but problems were experienced with kernels falling apart,
pilferage at Steamships and organizing supply lines (Houghton 1996). Since 1995 the
project has been hampered by intermittent donor support, continuity of supply and
quality control. A small amount of nuts continue to be sold at informal markets in Port
Moresby (Ase, D. pers. comm. Aug. 1998).

It is concluded, therefore, that given the experience of Barai Okari Estates and the (even
greater) remoteness, poor communications and low level of infrastructure at the plateau,
it is unlikely that efforts to develop okari nuts there will meet with any more success. The
situation can be re-assessed if okari nuts are successfully developed. In particular, drying
and packaging.

Background:

Around the birth of Jesus Christ, coffee was reportedly first discovered growing in
Ethiopia by a sheepherder named Khaldi. Whenever he moved his sheep into one
particular pasture, the sheep would start acting extremely lively and erratic after cating
the “red cherries” on a particular bush found in that pasture. Tentatively, Khaldi tried
eating a few of the beans himself and experienced the same reaction. The local area
monks heard about Khaldi and this “devil’s fruit” but soon they too were eagerly
sampling it so they could stay awake for their prayers. Arab traders, during a trading
expedition, decided to bring back some beans to their homeland and began to plant and
grow their own beans. Soon they began to boil the beans and produced a drink called
“qahwa” (meaning “unable to sleep”). The drink gained popularity until around 1453
when the Ottoman Turks introduced the beans to Constantinople and in 1475 the world’s
first coffee shop; “Kiva Han” was opened in the city. The “coffee craze” developed to a
point where women could even divorce their husbands if they failed to provide the
women with a daily ration of coffee. The mere existence of the plant was a closely
guarded secret in the Moslem countries when an Arab named Baba Budan started the
actual spread of this delicacy to the outside world illegally. Baba Budan smuggled some

In 1600, Italian traders brought some of the beans to Pope Clement VIII who was urged
to ban the drink as “unholy” because it came from Moslems that were “Non Christians”
but he surprised them by “baptizing” it instead. Now “coffee” was an acceptable
beverage for Christians. A few years later, Dutch traders smuggled out a coffee plant
from the port of Espresso to the island of Ceylon and to their East Indian colony of Java,
source of coffee’s nickname today. In 1713, the Dutch unwittingly gave a coffee bush to
Louis XTV of France that, from which, in 1723, a French naval officer, Gabriel Mathicu
do Clieu, stole a seedling and took it to Martinique. Eventually, 90 percent of the world’s
coffee spread from this one plant.

Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee (the variety found at Managalas):

In 1728 Sir Nicholas Lawes, then Governor of Jamaica and owner of Temple Hall Estate,
brought the first coffee plants to Jamaica. First, cultivation started in the foothills of St.
Andrew but soon plantations extended deeper into the fertile Blue Mountains. The coffee
industry has experienced many ups and downs from those early days until today.

From 1800 to 1840, Jamaica produced 70,000 tons per year making her the largest
producer in the world. Then, in 1838, came the abolition of slavery. This spelled the end
to many coffee plantations, as newly freed farmers began planting and clearing all the
available hillsides to eam a living and to have land to live on. By 1891, the coffee
industry was in general disarray so legislation was passed to provide “instruction in the
art of cultivation and curing by sending certain districts, competent instructors.”

The effort to increase quality was largely unsuccessful as the largest buyer in those days
was the Canadian market and thcy resisted it as being unacceptable. Finally, in 1944 the
Jamaican government established a Central Coffee Clearing House where all coffee for
export had to be processed. This cleaning and grading process was a giant step in the
improvement in the quality of the Jamaican coffee being exported.

Following the devastating hurricane of 1951, there were only three Coffee Processing
Plants (called “pulperies”) remaining in operation in the Blue Mountains. In an attempt to
regulate the growth that was sure to follow, the Coffee Industry Board was formed to
establish guidelines in quality, cultivation and processing. The Coffee Industry Board is
still an active force today and garners some of the credit for the resurgence of Jamaican
coffee. In 1973, the three coffee processing plants at Mavis Bank, Silver Hill and Moy
Hall along with a new comer, Wallenford, registered the name “Blue Mountain Coffee”.
A few years ago, the Twyman family’s Old Tavern Estate Coffee won the legal right
through the Jamaican courts to also sell its superior product under the “Blue Mountain”
name.

Jamaica is famous for producing some of the finest coffee found anywhere in the world.
What makes this little island such a prime spot for growing a world-class coffee? As in

real estate, it’s “Location, Location, Location” and in this case, that location is the Blue
Mountains. Coffee plants need to be well watered, well drained and experience periodic
coolness during some stages of development. To be called “Blue Mountain Coffee”, it

Plant Description: The coffee plant is a woody perennial evergreen dicotyledon that
belongs to the Rubiaceae family. It has a main vertical trunk (orthotropic) and primary,
secondary, and tertiary horizontal branches (plagiotropic). Two main species of coffee
are cultivated today. Coffea arabica known as Arabica coffee accounts for 75-80% of the
world's production. Coffea canephora, known as Robusta coffee, is more robust than the
Arabica plants, but produces an inferior tasting beverage with a higher caffeine content.
The coffee plant can grow to heights of 10 meters if not pruned, but producing countries
will maintain the coffee at a height reasonable for easy harvesting.

A common tended, planted or cultivated medium-large tree with distinctive lateral

branches, deciduous green to red leaves and fruits with hard corky pink/ purple shell that
is cut open in to equal halves.

Plant Development: Three to four years after the coffee is planted, sweet smelling
flowers grow in clusters in the axils of the leaves. Fruit is produced only in the new
tissue. The Arabica species is self-pollinating, whereas the Robusta species depends on
cross pollination. About 6-8 weeks after the flowers are fertilized, cell division occurs
and the fruit remains as a pin head for a period that is dependent upon the climate. The
ovaries will then develop into drupes in a rapid growth period that takes about 15 weeks
after flowering. During this time the integument takes on the shape of the final bean.
After the rapid growth period the integument and parchment are fully grown and will not
increase in size. The endosperm remains small until about 12 weeks after flowering. At
this time it will suppress, consume, and replace the integument. The remnants of the
integument are what make up the silverskin. The endosperm will have completely filled
the cavity made by the integument nineteen weeks after flowing. The endosperm is now
white and moist, but will gain dry matter during the next several months. During this
time the endosperm attracts more than seventy percent of the total photosynthesis
produced by the tree. The mesocarps will expand to form the sweet pulp that surrounds
the bean. The cherry will change color from green to red about thirty to thirty-five weeks
after flowing.

Root System: The root system can extend 20-25 km in total length and the absorbing
surface of a tree ranges from 400 to 500 m’. There are main vertical roots, tap roots, and
lateral roots which grow parallel to the ground. The tap roots extend no further than 30-
45 cm below the soil surface. Four to cight axial roots may be encountered which often
originate horizontally but point downward. The lateral roots can extend 2 m from the
trunk. About 80-90% of the feeder root is in the first 20 cm of soil and is 60-90 cm away
from the trunk of the tree (Mavolta, 195-196). However, the greatest root concentration
is in the 30 to 60 cm depth. The roots systems are heavily affected by the type of soil and
the mineral content of the soil. To be thick and strong the root system needs an extensive
supply of nitrogen, calcium and magnesium. During planting the main vertical roots are
often clipped to promote growth of the horizontal roots, which then have better access to
water and added nutrients in the top soil.

Leaves: The elliptical leaves of the coffee tree are shiny, dark green, and waxy. The leaf
area index is between 7 and 8 for a high-yielding coffee. The coffee plant has become a
major source of oxygen in much of the world. Each hectare of coffee produces 86 Ibs of
oxygen per day, which is about half the production of the same area in a rain forest
(source: Anacafe).

Harvesting: Each year coffee is harvested during the dry season when the coffee cherries
are bright red, glossy, and firm. Ripe cherries are either picked by hand, stripped from
the tree with both unripe and overripe beans, or all the beans are collected using a
harvesting machine. These processes are called selective picking, stripping, and
mechanical harvesting, respectively.

To maximize the amount of ripe coffee harvested it is necessary to selectively pick the

ripe beans from the tree by hand and leave behind unripe, green beans to be harvested at a
later time. In Brazil, harvesting the same tree several times is more cost prohibitive than

Paul Konia! NTFP/ Menugalast- survey 2005/07

separating and discarding the unripe or overtripe cherries. Therefore, Brazil typically
harvests using the stripping method when 75% of the crop is perfectly ripe. Stripping is
feasible and cost effective in Brazil due to the uniform maturation of Brazilian coffees.
In stripping the beans are pulled from the tree and fall to the ground where they are
caught by sheets. The beans are removed from tree debris by tossing the coffee im the air
allowing the wind to carry away sticks and leaves. The coffee is then put in 60 L green
baskets, which is the measuring tool used by coffee producers to determine wages. Some
estates, such as Fazenda Monte Alegre in Sul de Minas Brazil, have a computerized
system to determine wages, which accounts for the amount of coffee collected from each
person, the difficulty of the harvesting conditions, and the production of the region being
harvested. About 12-20 kg of export ready coffee will be produced from every 100 kg of
coffee cherries harvested.

Processing:

Irrespective of the harvesting method, green coffee beans and overripe coffee cherries
inevitably end up mixed with the perfectly ripe cherries and must be separated. Over ripe
coffee cherries, undeveloped coffee cherries, sticks and leaves float in water. Ripe coffee
beans and green coffee cherries are dense and sink. Therefore, the first separation step
takes place by separating the floaters from the sinkers. The floaters are usually sent
directly to the patio to be dried and are then slated for internal consumption. The ripe and
green cherries can be sent to the patios to be dried using the natural (dry) process or can
be sent to the pulping machines.

The first stage of pulping is used to remove the green cherries from the ripe cherries. In
the pulpmg machine the internal pressure is monitored to push the coffee against a screen
with holes only large enough for a coffee bean (not cherry) to pass through. Since the
tipe cherries are soft they break and the seed is released through the screen.

The green cherries are hard and cannot be pulped. Instead of passing through the screen,
the green beans pass to the end of the barrel system and are separated from the ripe
beans. The pressure inside the barrel controls how many cherries will be pulped. A very
high pressure will cause all of the cherries including the green beans to be pulped. It is
necessary to continuously monitor the pressure so that about 3% of ripe cherries are not
pulped and are removed with the green cherries. This margin of error ensures that no
green cherries are mistakenly pulped. The pulp and beans are then separated by
centrifugal force and a barrel screen system.

The beans covered in the slippery mucilage can be sent to the patios to dry as pulped
natural coffees or can be sent to fermentation tanks. The fermenting tanks are used to
remove the mucilage before drying. The pulped beans are put into cement tanks with
water and are allowed to ferment for 16-36 hours. On the way to the fermentation tanks
another density separation can occur. The highest quality coffees are the most dense and
should be separated and fermented in a different tank.

The fermentation time depends on a number of factors including the amount of coffee

fermenting, water temperature, and humidity. The mucilage is made up of pectin
materials including protopectin (33%), reducing sugars including glucose and fructose

25

=== page 27 ===
Pun! Konia! NTFP/ Manugalaté survey 2005/07

(30%), non-reducing sugars such as sucrose (20%), and cellulose and ash (17%)
Protopectin is not water soluble and will hydrolyze to pectinic acid in the fermentation
tanks. Hydrolysis of the protopectin and degradation of the pectin by enzymes is the
process that occurs to remove the mucilage during fermentation (Wrigley, 455).
Currently, the best way of determining the end of fermentation is to feel the beans to
determine if the beans are still encased in mucilage. If the beans are fermented for 36-72
hours stinker beans develop. Lactic, acetic, and propionic acids are produced in this
process and are believed to prevent the traditional fermentation taste by inhibiting mold
growth that regularly occurs during drying on a patio in humid conditions.

From the fermentation tanks the beans are moved to drying patios and dried to 11-12%
moisture content. A small portion of the lot is hulled and milled by a mini-huller. Three
hundred grams of coffee is classified for defects (100 grams is often used), and the
percentage of cach screen size is determined. Then, 200-300 grams of coffee is roasted in
a sample roaster and cupped to determine quality. Ideally no lots will be mixed until the
coffee has been classified and cupped. The coffee remains in pergamino until shipment
time to help protect the flavor and aroma of the coffee.

Before shipment coffee must be dried from approximately 60% moisture content to 11-
12% moisture content. Coffee is typically dried on large patios made of asphalt or cement
and then transferred to mechanical dryers. The coffee on the drying patios is shifted every
30-40 minutes and is shaped into long rows of no more than 5 cm in height. Next to each
row is open ground, which is warmed and dried by the sun. The coffee is then shifted
onto the dry portion of the patio, and the section where it was previously is now allowed
to dry in the sun. This helps accelerate the drying process and prevents fermentation and
moldy beans from developing. This method is widely used in Brazil, but less widely used
in Guatemala or Costa Rica where the coffee is more often piled perpendicularly to the
old piles. To dry coffee solely by patio drying it takes 6-7 days for washed coffees, 8-9
days for pulped naturals (semi-washed), and 12-14 days for natural (dry-processed)
coffees. This is why coffees are typically dried on a patio until they reach a moisture
content of 15% and are then transferred to mechanical dryers. Once the coffee reaches
25% moisture or less it can be piled at night and covered with cotton cloths to allow the
coffee to breath. If it rains these piles can also be covered with plastic. Coffee should not
be covered with burlap sacks since this will impart a distinct burlap flavor and aroma to
the coffee.

In a study done in Kenya, the report highlights that there are six stages to drying coffee.
1) Skin drying. Moisture 55-45%.

2) White Stage drying. Moisture 44-33%.

3) Soft Black stage. Moisture 32-22%.

4) Medium Black Stage. Moisture 21-16%

5) Hard Black Stage. Moisture 15-12%

6) Fully dry coffee and conditioning. 11-10%.

In this study it was discovered that sun drying for stage three is mandatory for coffee
quality. It also reported that as long as the temperature was between 40-50°C--which
means a bean temp of 35°C--then the coffee quality will not be seriously compromised
during the other stages.

Paul Konia! NTFP/ Managalart survey 2005/07

The final two stages (15-11% moisture) in just six hours at 40°C in a mechanical dryer.
There are several dryer systems available. Many older dryers are converted grain dryers
that are not as efficient as the new horizontal barrel dryers. The new dryers are designed
to mix the coffee evenly to ensure uniform drying. Drying by using mechanical dryers
accelerates the slowest part of the drying process (15-11%) and helps prevent
fermentation. In some environments that have a high humidity the entire drying process
must take place in mechanical dryers. Mechanical drycrs should never be set higher than
40-45°C and this question should be asked before buying any coffees that have been
mechanically dried. At higher temperatures the germ is killed and the flavor potential of
the coffee is ruined. At extreme temperature the bean crystallizes and when smashed with
a hammer will break like glass.

The best, but least utilized method of drying coffee is by using drying tables. In this
method the pulped and fermented coffee is spread thinly on raised beds, which allows the
air to pass on all sides of the coffee. The coffee is mixed by hand and the drying that
takes place is more uniform and fermentation is less likely. Most coffee from the
Managalas Plateau is dried in this manner and it is the commonly used drying method
used widely in Papua New Guinea. It is sometimes known as Solar Drying. Solar Dryer is
good during rains and at nights. A drying bed is built with a shelter over it with plastic
sheet. The sides and ends of the bed are properly covered and coffee parchments are
spread on the bed to dry. Parchments are turn regularly for sun to dry all sides. It takes
about 3 — 4 weeks for the parchment to dry properly.

Diseases

Coffee Leaf Rust:

Coffee leaf rust first destroyed Brazils crop in 1970. Since then, it has spread to every
coffee growing country in the world. The disease was first observed in Sri Lanka in the
1860's. Many countries, including Sri Lanka and Ethiopia, replaced much of their arabica
coffee with disease resistant robusta coffee. The disease is spread from spores from
lesions on the underside of the plant by wind and rain. Rust is prevented by spraying with
copper-based fungicides at 3-5 kg/ha at 4-6 week intervals during the rainy season. In
PNG, this disease was discovered in the 1980's. Efforts by the Coffee Industry
Corporation have successfully curbed this disease.

Coffee Berry Disease:

Coffee berry disease was first discovered in Kenya in 1920 and is caused by the virulent
strain of Colletotrichum coffeanum the fungus lives in the bark of the coffee tree and
produces spores which attack the coffee cherries. Spraying has been determined to be the
best way to avoid the coffee berry disease. Captafol and copper-based fungicides have
been effective. The Kenyan coffee hybrid Ruiru 11 is resistant to both coffee berry
disease and leaf rust.

Bacterial Blight:

Bacterial Blight (Pseudomanas syringae py. garcae) is a disease that occurs where wet
and cold conditions prevail.

The leaf miner (Perileucoptera cofeella) occurs mainly in Brazil. Coffea stenophyila is

Description:

Yam is the common name applied to plants of about 500 species of the genus Dioscorea
of the Dioscoreaceae family. Other terms for yam are true yams, greater yams and
tropical yams. True yam plants are climbing perennial vines with heart-shaped leaves.
Underground tubers vary in size and shape, averaging 3-8 pounds but sometimes reaching
60 pounds or more. Aerial tubers may develop in the axils of the leaves, especially when
vines run on the ground. The species occur rather abundantly in tropical and subtropical
regions of the world.

Use:

The cultivated species bear edible starchy tubers that resemble the potato in food value.
In some areas, the sweet potato (Kaukau) is popularly called "yam," which is a misnomer.
Although resembling each other in many other respects, the true yam and sweet potato
(Kaukau) are not related botanically. Many species of Dioscorea contain sapogenin, a
compound having medicinal value. Species have been collected from all parts of the
world and evaluated for steroidal sapogenins. It has been reported that many wild species
contain the poisonous principle dioscorine which makes them inedible. For this reason
aerial and underground tubers of the wild plants should not be eaten.

In addition to having food and medicinal value, some species have strikingly variegated
leaves and are of interest as ornamentals. Some of the edible species and varicties follow.
Culture: Portions of tubers or whole small tubers are used for seed pieces. Each seed
piece should weigh 4-5kg. They can be planted 2-3 inches deep in 42 inch rows with
plants spaced 18 inches apart, or in hill plantings 3 feet apart. Yams do well when planted
in a hill filled with compost. In Managalas, tubers should be planted in July, August,
September and October and harvested 6 months later. Best results are obtained if the
vines are supported with some sort of trellis. Stakes can be used, or yams can be planted
along the fence for support.

Those who know the tropical yam, however, will not mistake it with kaukau (sweet
potato). Yam is a tuber crop that is well known throughout the humid tropics: in Tropical
America, the Caribbean, Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Yam is an important carbohydrate
food that is relatively easy to grow. Yams have a very specific life cycle. Unlike the
Kaukau (sweet potato), which can be planted by vine cuttings almost all year-round, yam
is planted once-a-year, when the tuber begins sprouting. As the tuber breaks dormancy,
the energy is transferred from the tuber into stem and leaf growth. This vegetative stage,
lasting 6 to 8 months, occurs during the warm and humid months. A new root system and
tuber develops with most of the tuber development occurring toward the end of the rainy
season and into dry season. When the vine dies back, the tuber is ready for harvest. At
Managalas it happens in June, July and August.

Yams do well in sun or partial shade and prosper with ample rainfall. They require good
drainage, and therefore, are often planted on mounds or ridges. They are most commonly
staked but can be planted on a trellis or at the base of a sufficiently strong tree. At
Managalas it has worked weil to stake them with sticks, not more than Scm in diameter as
the vines have some difficulty twining up the large stick exterior. Growth is lush and
very vigorous once the rains begin. Remember the vines dic back in the dry season.

They then get a number of leaf diseases and look sickly; however, this has little effect on
the tuber. When harvesting, be careful as the tuber skin is thin and easily damaged. The
tubers are often large, several kilograms a piece, but as great as }5kg or more. The yam
is used similar to a potato - peeled (peel away any discolored areas), then boiled or
baked, They reportedly make a good French fry and chip. The storage life is long,
averaging between four to six months, due to the high moisture content. One
recommendation is to harvest them as needed when they are in the dormant stage. If
unused, the tuber will begin to sprout after 6-8 months. The yam sprouts first at the top,
which is the most desirable planting piece next to a whole ‘seed’ tuber. Cut off a section
about the size of an adult's fist and cure it a few days in the shade before planting. Yam is
a wonderful food and is generally an easy, dependable crop to grow.

Traditional use:

The fresh tubers are cooked and eaten. The tuber is cooked in many different ways. It can
be roasted over the fire, boiled, baked in earth ovens (mumu) and cooked in bamboo
tubes. The flesh is also grated and cooked with vegetables in bamboo tubes and baked in
earth ovens (mumu) which is very delicious. The yams play a very important role in the
daily lives of the Managalas culture, because yam is considered a valuable asset and it is
used as a monetary unit to solve disputes and pay for bride price and compensation

payments etc.

Background:
The true origin of Bananas, world's most popular fruit, is found in the region of Malaysia.

By way of curious visitors, bananas traveled from there to India where they are
mentioned in the Buddhist Pali writings dating back to the 6th century BCE. In his
campaign in India in 327 BCE, Alexander the Great relished his first taste of the banana,
an unusual fruit he saw growing on tall trees. He is even credited with bringing the
banana from India to the Western world. According to Chinese historian Yang Fu, China
was tending plantations of bananas in 200 CE. These bananas grew only in the southern

38

=== page 40 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/ Monagalate survey 2005/07

region of China and were considered exotic, rare fruits that never became popular with
the Chinese masses until the 20th century.

Eventually, this tropical fruit reached Madagascar, an island off the southeastern coast of
Africa. Beginning in 650 CE Islamic warriors traveled into Africa and were actively
engaged in the slave trade. Along with the thriving business in slave trading, the Arabs
were successful in trading ivory along with abundant crops of bananas. Through their
numerous travels westward via the slave trade, bananas eventually reached Guinea, a
small area along the West Coast of Africa. By 1402 Portuguese sailors discovered the
luscious tropical fruit in their travels to the African continent and populated the Canary
Islands with their first banana plantations. Continuing the banana's travel westward, the
rootstocks were packed onto a ship under the charge of Tomas de Berlanga, a Portuguese
Franciscan monk who brought them to the Caribbean island of Santo Domingo from the
Canary Islands in the year 1516. It wasn't long before the banana became popular
throughout the Caribbean as well as Central America. Arabian slave traders are credited
with giving the banana its popular name. The bananas that were growing in Africa as well
as Southeast Asia were not the eight-to-twelve-inch giants that have become familiar in
the U.S. supermarkets today. They were small, about as long as a man's finger. Ergo the
name banan, Arabic for finger. The Spaniards, who saw a similarity to the plane tree that
grows in Spain, gave the plantain its Spanish name, platano.

It was almost three hundred and fifty years later that Americans tasted the first bananas to
arrive in theit country, Wrapped in tin foil, bananas were sold for 10 cents each at a
celebration held in Pennsylvania in 1876 to commemorate the hundredth anniversary of
the Declaration of Independence. Instructions on how to eat a banana appeared in the
Domestic Encyclopedia of Practical Information and read as follows: Bananas are eaten
raw, either alone or cut in slices with sugar and cream, or wine and orange juice. They
are also roasted, fried or boiled, and are made into fritters, preserves, and marmalades."

Description:

There are two main varieties of bananas, the fruit or sweet banana and the plantain. The
fruit banana is eaten raw out of hand when it turns yellow and develops a succulent
sweetness with a soft, smooth, creamy, yet firm pulp. The plantain, a cooking banana, is
also referred to as the meal, vegetable or horse banana. Plantains have lower water
content, making them drier and starchier than fruit bananas. Though the banana plant has
the appearance of a sort of palm tree, and is often called a banana palm, it is actually
considered a perennial herb. It dies back after cach fruiting and produces new growth for
the next generation of fruit. Bananas do not grow simply from seed. Man intervened long
ago and crossed two varieties of African wild bananas, the Musa acuminata and the Musa
baalbisiana, got rid of the many seeds that were an unpleasant presence, and improved the
flavor and texture from hard and unappetizing to its present soft and irresistibly sweet
flavor.

Today bananas must be propagated from large rootstocks or rhizomes that are carefully

transplanted in a suitable climate, namely the hot tropics, where the average temperature
is a humid 80 degrees Fahrenheit (27 degrees Celsius), and a minimum of 3 1/2 inches

39

=== page 41 ===
Paul Konial NTFP! Mantaguiati- survey 206507

(75 mm) of rainfall a month. The soil must have excellent drainage or the rootstocks will
rot. The plants grow new shoots, often called suckers, pups, or ratoons, from the shallow
rootstocks or rhizomes, and continue to produce new plants generation after generation
for several decades. In about nine months the plants reach their mature height of about 15
to 30 feet. Some varieties will grow to a height of 40 fect. From the stems, that are about
12 inches thick, flower shoots begin to produce bananas. If you have never seen bananas
growing, you might be puzzied that they appear to be growing upside-down with their
stems connected to the bunch at the bottom and the tips pointing upward.

Bananas possess a unique scientific phenomenon called “negative geotropism.” As the
little bananas start to develop, they grow downward--as gravity would dictate. Little by
little, several "hands" or double rows develop vertically and form a partial spiral around
the stem. As they take in more and more sunlight, their natural growth hormones bring
about a most puzzling phenomenon, and they begin to turn and grow upward. As the
plant becomes heavier with maturing fruit, it must be supported with poles. The stems are
made of layers and layers of leaves that are wrapped around each other. Though quite
large and thick, the stems are not strong and woody like most fruit trees and can break
under the weight of many bunches of bananas.

Though there are approximately 300 species of bananas, only 20 varieties are
commercially cultivated. Local populations and visitors who experience the regional
cuisines when they travel enjoy the many non-commercial varieties. Members of the
Musaceae family, the banana plant belongs to the monocotyledons, a group that includes
palms, grasses, and orchids. Bananas are mature about three months from the time of
flowering, with each bunch producing about 15 "hands" or rows. Each hand has about 20
bananas while each bunch will yield about 200 "fingers" or bananas. An average bunch of
bananas can weigh between 80 and 125 pounds (35 to 50 kilograms). Though bananas
can be left to ripen on the plant, they would perish too quickly. It is important that they
are harvested in the green state at just the right time. If harvested too early, they would
develop a floury pulp instead of a delightfully sweet flavor.

Bananas begin the ripening process as soon as they are harvested, when laboratory tests
have shown that they contain 20% starch and 1% sugar. When the bananas turn yellow
with some brown spots, they are fully ripened, and these figures are completely reversed.
The sugar content breaks down as follows: 66% sucrose, 14% fructose, and 20% glucose.
After the bananas have been harvested, the giant stems are cut down to provide rich
humus for the next crop that has already begun to sprout new shoots. Those that are poor
quality are sold in local markets or pureed and used as animal feed. The next step is to cut
the bananas into individual hands and wash them in a water bath to stop "bleeding" their
natural latex or rubber substance that tends to stain the bananas as well as clothing.

Though there are many countries where bananas are grown, not all grow them for export.
Brazil, China, India, and Thailand grow them as a local food source and export very few.
The major exporters include Ecuador, Costa Rica, Colombia, Honduras, the Philippines,
Panama, and Guatemala. Surprisingly, 80% of the bananas grown throughout the world

are of the plantain or cooking variety. To many tropical cultures, plantains are an
important part of the daily diet and are prepared in as many ways as other cultures have
devised for potatoes. Plantains may be more familiar to you as banana chips that are first
dried, and then fried. These cooking bananas are even employed in the brewing of beer in
some areas of East Africa. Brazil and Kenya grow a unique fruit banana called Apple
Banana whose flavor reminds one of an apple. This special variety is only three to four
inches in length. Another special variety is the Lady's Finger, an especially small banana
with a sweet, creamy texture that grows in Thailand, Malaysia, and Colombia. You can
recognize the Red Banana by its reddish brown skin. The flesh inside also has a reddish
tinge, and the flavor is sweet with a satin-like texture. These grow in most regions where
bananas thrive.

Medical Use of Banana:

Because of their impressive potassium content, bananas are highly recommended by
doctors for patients whose potassium is low. One large banana, about 9 inches in length,
packs 602 mg of potassium and only carries 140 calories. That same large banana even
has 2 grams of protein and 4 grams of fiber. No wonder the banana was considered an
important food to boost the health of malnourished children! Those reducing sodium in
their diets can't go wrong with a banana with its mere 2 mgs of sodium. For the
carbohydrate counters there are 36 grams of carbs in a large banana.

Vitamins and minerals are abundant in the banana, offering 123 1.U. of vitamin A for the
large size. A full range of B vitamins are present with .07 mg of Thiamine, .15 mg of
Riboflavin, .82 mg Niacin, .88 mg vitamin B6, and 29 mcg of Folic Acid. There are even
13.8 mg of vitamin C. On the mineral scale Calcium counts in at 9.2 mg, Magnesium
44.1 mg, with trace amounts of iron and zinc.

Putting all of the nutritional figures together clearly shows the banana is among the
healthiest of fruits. The plantain, when cooked, rates slightly higher on the nutritional
scale in vitamins and minerals but similar to the banana in protein and fiber content.

Common Name: Kaukau (tok pisin)

Common English Name: Sweet Potato

Local Dialect: Kirota (Birare)

Scientific name: Pomoea Batatas - CONVOLVULACEAE, Morning Glory

Family

Background:

Commonly known as: Sweet potato, kumara, uwi, ubi, or U.S. yam. Batatas, an Arawak
name, which is called sweet potatoes, were used during pre-Columbian times in Central
and lowland South America, as well as in the West Indies.

It is thought that /pomoea batatas originated from an unremarkable trailing climber
(vine) on the mainland, probably in Central America. Workers have looked at species
with similar lobed leaves and growth habits, such as /. trifida or I. tiliacea, or possibly
from some hybridization event involving these species. Wild species lack swollen below-
ground structures, whereas the cultivated species, which is a perennial herb, produces
"root tubers" on adventitious roots, which arise from the nodes of the trailing stems. The
cultivated sweet potato is a hexaploid (= 90 chromosomes) and must be propagated from
stem cuttings or the root tubers, because the plants seldom produce fruits or seeds.

Sweet potato was already an important crop on Pacific islands when Europeans landed on
the islands: Easter Island (Roggeveen, 1722), New Zealand (Cook, 1769), and the
Hawaiian Islands (Cook, 1778). Sweet potato, known as kumar (kaukau in PNG), was a
staple in the diet of the Maoris of New Zealand; interestingly, the name kumar is used for
this plant in Peru! Rongo ma-Tane, a Maori god, protects this plant; a buried tuber is
powerful enough to cause enemy to go mad and run away.

Given that the species does not generally reproduce from seed, the spread of this plant
must have been by the transport of the root tubers. Therefore, the pre-Columbian
occurrence of sweet potato in southern and eastern Polynesia, as well as in New Zealand,
needs an explanation. Certainly the plant originated in the Americas and was carried
westward into areas where Asian root crops had not yet arrived. Two equally plausible

=== page 48 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/ Managalasi- survey 2005/07

hypotheses have been proposed: (1) Polynesians raided the Peruvian coastline and took
sweet potatoes back with them; or (2) early Peruvians, who used balsa rafts, transported
sweet potatoes to Polynesia on their oceanic forays (as tested by Thor Heyerdah!'s Kon-
Tiki experiment in 1947). Long-distance dispersal by ocean currents has been ruled out,
because the tubers spoil in seawater. Experts agree that Polynesians carried sweet
potatoes eastward from the Society Islands to the Hawaiian Islands, along with other
economic plants, such as the root crop taro (Colocasia esculenta, for poi), the candlenut
tree (Aleurites; for torches, oily fruits), and the ti plant (Cordyline terminalis, for grass
skirts and luau materials). Spaniards introduced sweet potato into the Philippines and at
an early date into Spain, From Spain, sweet potatoes were carried eastward through the
Mediterranean region to the Far East, where the sweet potato became a vital starchy food
crop. In Japan and Taiwan, this food has been dried and stored as "typhoon insurance."
Sweet potato has many cultivated forms, but in the United States two forms are common:
(1) the dry, mealy, yellow sweet potato, and (2) the watery, orange "yam," which is not,
of course, a true yam (Dioscorea). Yellow and orange pigments are carotenoids, and
therefore sweet potato is a rich source of vitamin A. The root tubers also have fairly high
concentrations of calcium and iron but little protein. Over one-fourth of the tuber is
carbohydrate, mostly starch; but the sweetness of the tuber tells us that glucose is also
present, especially in the watery yams, in which 3-6% by weight is glucose. In sweet
potato there are 50% more calories per unit weight than in Irish potato (Solanum
tuberosum) but less protein.

Japan leads in production of sweet potatoes, and throughout the Orient this tuber is a
common table vegetable. This root crop is generally eaten fresh, but it can be canned,
desiccated, and made into flour or syrup, and the carbohydrate can also be converted into
alcohol via fermentation. The green foliage is used for livestock fodder, along with the
below-ground parts.

Background:

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is a very important spice plant from tropical Asia,
specifically from the East Indies. This species is also called Jamaican ginger where much
of it is commercially used. History has it that this spice was brought to the West Indies in
the early 1500s when the Spanish first occupied the Caribbean islands. During the Middle
Ages in Europe, ginger had become an important and expensive spice from the east, and
the Spaniards fed that interest in the 1500s from their ginger plantations in Jamaica.

This spice plant is a monocotyledon having shoots less than a meter in height with
alternate leaves that occur along two vertical rows, 180 degrees apart (distichous), so the
plant is fairly easy to identify. The shade-loving plant is a perennial with green shoots
that live less than a year. Below-ground are knobby, branched, horizontal rhizomes with
adventitious roots. These rhizomes, when cleaned and leaf bases are removed, are golden-
brown in color, and they are the ones sold fresh in our markets. Occasionally you will
notice the whitish-green growing tip. If fresh, you should be able to grow these, but
remember that they need tropical to subtropical temperatures so must be protected from
freezing.

The flesh (parenchyma or ground tissue) of the aromatic ginger rhizome contains resin
and volatile oils (terpineol, linalol, methyleugenol, and others), which provide the
pungent spice of commerce. In addition to being used in powdered form, candied, and
fresh, ginger also fills an important role in drinks, such as ginger ale, and perfumes,
Ginger snaps and many bakery products contain ginger. Don't forget the gingerbread
man, supposedly first introduced or popularized by Queen Elizabeth I of England. Fresh
ginger is used widely in stir-fried dishes, especially with fish or meat, and has a much
different flavor than do powdered preparations.

Ginger has a very long history of use in folk and herbal medicine, especially in ancient

treatment for nausea. In eastern Asia ginger consumption has long been recognized as a
way to eliminate or guard against intestinal parasites, and ginger was widely used also by
Romans for that purpose. Some antibacterial properties of Z. officinale are in the

curative properties of ginger have been promoted in books, popular articles, and on the
