Common Name: Peanut

Other names: Groundnut, earthnut, cachuate, mani
Local Name: Finate

Scientific name: FABACEAE, Legume Family

Background:

The peanut plant (Arachis hypogaea) hides tts fruit in the ground - for what reason
nobody seems to know - and therefore has been given names that refer to this strange
event, Groundnut is a widely used common name, and the Aztecs- American Indians
called this plant dalcacahuatl or "ground cacao." Linnaeus named this species hypogaea,
which means "under earth.” Surprisingly, there is another cultivated legume that forms
fruits below-ground; but the Bambara groundnut (Voandzeia subterranea), a native of
tropical West Africa, has largely been replaced in Africa by the peanut.

Natives in Africa have stated categorically that the peanut originated in Africa, where this
crop plant is deeply integrated into their diets and cultures. Likewise, some have
supposed that peanut occurred in the Orient and India in ancient times, because these
fruits are in common use, ¢.g., in many characteristic foods of Indo-China and Indonesia
(peanut sauces). The truth of the matter is that Arachis is a genus endemic (restricted) to
South America, and the homeland appears to have been the Andean foothills in Bolivia.
From Bolivia, this odd diploid plant (2 = 40) spread to coastal Peru, to southern and then
coastal Brazil, and to tropical northern Brazil. Cari O. Sauer, a famous ethnobotanist,
suspected that peanut was part of the manioc (cassava) cultivation complex in the New
World. Earliest archaeological records of peanut come from fossilized fruits in Peruvian
tombs (3000-2800 B.C.) and images on ancient pottery and textiles. The peanut also
occurred in the Valley of Tehuacan in Puebla, Mexico before 100 A.D. and was
widespread in tropical America before Columbus arrived.

Ethno botanists once thought that hump-backed peanuts were present in southern China
before Columbus, but this idea has not been authenticated. Instead, peanuts probably

51

=== page 53 ===
Paul Kania/ NTFP/ Manugalasi- survey 2005/07

circumnavigated the globe with Portuguese sailors. For example, on his second voyage to
the New World, Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon, Portugal to Brazil to the Cape of
Good Hope to Goa, India. Several years later the Portuguese reached Canton, China
(1516) and soon established the colony of Macao south of Hong Kong. During the 16th
century, peanuts became a staple in African diets, especially within the Portuguese
colonies, and African slaves took them to Virginia--back to the New World.

Today peanuts are cultivated throughout the tropical and subtropical world and even
grow at 45 degrees N in Asia and Canada, where the summers are hot. The leading
producers of this crop are China, India, the United States, Nigeria, and Senegal, and
peanut production (over 20 million metric tons annually) ranks in the top 25th among
world food crops. In the United States, most peanuts are grown in Georgia (remember
Jimmy Carter!), North Carolina, Alabama, Texas, and Virginia.

Peanut plants can only grow where there are no freezing temperatures; they do not
tolerate frost. Moreover, this crop is generally cultivated where the annual precipitation is
100-120 centimeters but where about half of that rainfall occurs during the growing
season. The British government ignored these facts when in 1946 they proposed to plant
three million acres of peanuts in East African colonies; that peanut project was
abandoned in 1951, because rainfall was unreliable (also other problems). Peanuts must
also be grown in light, sandy, well-drained, slightly acid soil (pH 5.5-6.5) that is rich in
calcium and has moderate amounts of organic matter but no salt (NaCI). Light soil not
only permits rapid root penetration (peanut has some very deep roots) and good water
percolation, but also is crucial for fruit development. The crop may also need substantial
fertilizer application.

The plant is a trailing, bushy annual 20 to 30 centimeters tall with (usually) quadrifoliate
leaves, large stipules, and runners (stolons). The flowers, usually yellow, are small and
tend to be self-pollinated. About a weck after fertilization takes place in the ovary, a
meristem at the base of the ovary is activated. This meristem forms a stalk beneath the
ovary, called a carpophore or, simply, a "peg." The stalk is positively geotropic (grows
downward) and pushes the ovary toward the ground (pegging); the ovary tip hardens and
is pushed into the sandy soil 3 to 10 centimeters. Belowground the ovary develops into
the fibrous, tannish, indehiscent pod, a legume. The small Valencia cultivars have up to
five seeds per pod, but conventional forms have one to four seeds. Each seed, also called
a kernel, has two large cotyledons--the two halves of a peanut--and a small embryo axis
but no endosperm, and is covered by a papery seed coat. The corky fruit wall (pericarp),
the shell of a peanut, is slightly constricted between the seeds. Peanuts are propagated
from fresh (raw and untreated) seeds with intact seed coats and are removed from the
shell to prevent rotting.

On peasant farms in Third World Countries including Papua New Guinea, peanuts are
frequently planted and harvest by hand. Plants must be dug just beneath the fruits, and
then plants are stocked by hand to dry before threshing, drying, and storing.
Mechanical harvesting digs plants and may even strip off the pods. Fresh pod moisture
(30-40%) must be reduced for storage (to 8-10%) to avoid mold growth. One serious

52

=== page 54 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/ Manugaleti- survey 2005/07

disease is aflatoxin, a fungus-produced human toxin (Aspergillus flavus). Typical time for
the process from planted seed to dried pods is about five months.

Seeds are important sources of vegetable oil and protein. The triglycerides (oil) are high
in oleic acid and moderately high in linoleic acid but low in others; it is a nondrying oil,
i.e., it remains liquid and does not form a surface film when exposed to air. Seeds contain
36-50% oil and usually 25-30% (to 40%) protein. Oil can be expressed simply by
crushing or with hot or cold treatments. This product is widely used as cooking oil and as
a lubricant. In India peanut oil is hydrogenated to make ghee, a semi-fluid, clarified
butter. The oil is also used to manufacture items ranging from shaving cream and soap to
plastics. Seedcake had been used for livestock feed and fertilizer, and shells have been
used as filler for wallboard and insulation. George Washington Carver was a great
promoter of multiple uses for the peanut.

Of course, seeds can be consumed after being salted or roasted. In the United States more
than 50% of all peanuts are used to make peanut butter, with the recent trend of lower fat
products. Peanut butter was invented in 1890 by a St. Louis physician and was
popularized in 1893 by Dr. John Harvey Kellogg, a health food faddist and creator of
breakfast cereals, for patients with poor teeth! Peanuts are also used to fatten hogs.
Peanut cultivation still holds an honored place in modern agriculture, even though it is
not the centerpiece of any dict. These seeds are an excellent protein source and are
valuable for the malnourished peoples in Africa and Asia.

In the southeastern United States the peanut helped to save plantations when cotton was
hit with boll weevils. Many Americans weekly, if not daily, eat peanuts or peanut-
containing products (e.g., Snickers and Baby Ruth candies), which use mostly Virginia or
smaller Spanish peanut cultivars. Farmers plant peanuts because in slightly acid soils they
are nitrogen fixers; the plant is used therefore in crop rotation. Southeastern farmers use
seeds that have been inoculated with rhizobium bacteria, so that they do not have to add
nitrogen fertilizer. Well inoculated peanut plants are also resistant to drought. Most
peanuts are rain grown, and do not need irrigation. The U.S. harvest is almost two metric
tons of fruits per acre.

In tropical regions such as ours (PNG), peanuts grow well in soils that are not heavy; they
also tolerate levels of aluminum in the soil that are toxic to most crops, and their roots
can penetrate soil layers (horizons) that stop the root growth of most tropical crops.
Finally, peanuts are an important cash crop for poor tropical countries - something they
can sell and export - but this is often done at the expense of not growing the conventional
crops needed to feed their hungry people.

In Managalas, peanut is cultivated and grown in abundance. When harvested, it is mostly

eaten fresh. The shell is split with the thumbs and the pointer fingers pressed together
with the shell in between, leaving the nut exposed once the shell is split open.

Species cultivated: Vanilla tahitiensis & Vanilla planifolia
Genus: Vanilla

Background:

Commercial vanilla is the fruit (capsule) obtained from several different species of
Orchidaceae, namely, Vanilla pompona Schiede (West Indian vanilla), Vanilla tahitiensis
J. M. Moore (Tahiti vanilla) and Vanilla planifolia Jackson (Mexican vanilla). The most
important is Vanilla planifolia Jackson, from which almost all vanilla fruits come from
(Ferrio, 1993).

The genus Vanilla has about 100 species, and the Orchidaceae family is one of the largest
in the Plant Kingdom, with more or less 20,000 species. Etymologically. the word vanilla
came from the Spanish vainilla, which means a small pod, due to the great similarity
between this fruit and a true pod (Ferrao, 1992; Mabberley, 1993).

Floriculture is the field that we immediately recall when we think of orchid plants.
However, the genus Vanilla is the only one of the family that is of direct economic
interest.

57

=== page 59 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/ Mearagratari- survey 2005/07

Some rural societies in Turkey and Greece still use sa/ep, staple flour made from the
tubers of certain orchids, especially those included in the genus Orchis. Although the use
of orchids for this purpose is rather localised, it is bringing some species of this genus to
the edge of extinction (Baumann, 1996).

The vanilla plant is a vine, native from the tropical forests of Central America and some
areas of South America. In its natural habitat, it may reach a length of 25 meters,
climbing with the help of adventitious roots. The stems are thick and fleshy green; the
leaves are alternate, long elliptical, sessile and bright green. The flowers, in clusters,
appear in the leaf axils. They live only 8 hours and die if fertilization fails to occur. The
plant blooms three years after the cuttings are planted and the yellow greenish fruits
many have up to 90,000 seeds, taking five to seven months to mature. ‘The fruit is
scentless when harvested; it has a length between 10 to 25 cm and a weight of 5 to 30g
(Ferrao, 1993).

Vanilla was brought to Europe by the Spanish conquerors of the New World. They found
it in Mexico, when Montezuma, the last Aztec Emperor, offered them a drink made of
chocolate, vanilla, red pepper and honey. Local aristocracy used it to flavor chocolate, a
custom still practised today (Brosse et al. 1989).

The Dutch introduced vanilla in Java (Indonesia), a former European colony in East
Indies, at the beginning of the nineteenth century and the French did the same in the
Reunicn Island, Mauritius and Madagascar, all located in the Southwest Indian Ocean.
All plants grown in these areas were fruitless, but no one knew exactly why. Later,
people realized that this was due to the absence of pollination, because there were no
insects or hummingbirds to do it rightfully. The only region where the plants could give
fruits was in their native habitat (Boisvert et Hubert, 1998; Brosse et al., 1989).

In 1841 a black slave named Edmond Albius, from Reunion Island, invented an easy
method to pollinate and cultivation became widespread (Ferrao, 1993).

In the fields, harvesting is always scheduled according to the stage of maturity of the
fruits (Ferrio, 1993).

Commercial vanilla is obtained after special processing of the fruits. First they are put in
hot water and then dried to allow fermentation to occur. In Madagascar, the world's
largest producer of vanilla, the fruits are sun-dried and wrapped in blankets at night to
remain warm. This is a long process that takes months and increases the cost of the
product. This spice is one of the most expensive, second only to saffron (Crocus sativus
L.) (Ferrao, 1992).

The commercial fruit has a black/brown colour and a soft and flexible touch, due to
several oxidations that take place inside it, If they are harvested before the proper time
they are poor in aromatic compounds and if the harvesting is made too late, they will
initiate the dehiscence process, with a great loss in market prices. Usually, 6 kg of green
fruits produce | kg of commercial vanilla, The fruit must not have a water content above
25% and should always be kept in a very tight box to avoid the loss of aroma (Boisvert ct
Hubert, 1998; Ferrao, 1993).

58

=== page 60 ===
Poul Konial NTFP/ Managatasi- survey 2005/07

After all these long lasting processes, small crystals of vanillin, the most valuable
compound of the fruit, naturally cover the fruit. The final contents of vanillin are up to
3.5%. Vanillin was isolated in 1858 and its artificial synthesis was made in 1874, from
eugenol extracted from clove. In the fruits there are many more aromatic compounds,
besides vanillin, that make the natural flavor unique. Nowadays, the synthetic vanillin is
obtained from lignin, a by-product from paper pulp industries (Bruncton, 1995).

Sugar with vanilla flavor is made by putting a vanilla fruit inside a tightly closed
container with sugar. The product so obtained can last for years. Chocolates, liquors,
cakes and the famous ice cream are some of the delicacies made with this fragrant and
delicious spice (Grieve, 1981; Norman, 1990).

Formerly, vanilla was used in medicine as a mild sedative and to aid digestion, but
nowadays it's no longer used for these purposes. Vanillism is a disease that appears in
sensitive workers who deal with huge amounts of vanilla daily. It is characterized by
headaches, lassitude and allergic skin reactions of the face, neck and hands (Bown, 1995;
Touissaint-Samat, 1994). The perfume industrics also use vanilla as a basic or middle
note because of its rich, sweet and balsamic scent (Williams, 1997).

In the nineteenth century, Mexico was the largest vanilla producer, but since the First
World War some islands in the Indian Ocean have become the world's largest centre of
production. Today the largest exporters are Madagascar, Comores Islands, Reunion
Island, China and Indonesia. The big consumers are the western countries: the USA,
Canada, EEC countries, Japan and Australia (Ferro, 1993). Although the advances in
chemical synthesis are great, natural vanilla will always be one of those delightful spices
that take our mind and senses to exotic places and wild dreams.

Vanilla in PNG:

Vanilla boom began in Papua New Guinea in the early 1990s especially in the East and
West Sepik provinces and along the Mommas region. And in the mid 1990s and towards
2000 the major vanilla producing country Madagascar had a natural disaster that affected
all its cash crops, that was when the world market demand for vanilla rose higher and the
vanilla buying price tripled.

In PNG, banks ran out of cash in the Momase region when the vanilla fever had hit them.
More cash was seen like never before. People had cold-hard-cash of up to K1000 when a
sale was made.

From then on vanilla was nick-named the green gold! It took farmers in PNG head on,
and farmers began farming the two species of vanilla, the tahitiensis and the planifolia.
Farmers were not taught the techniques of cultivating, curing and handling this newly
introduced crop. Despite this, the crop earned them much needed cash as the world
market demand that time determined the price.

Now that the Madagascar market has recovered from the draught, prices have dropped,
leaving the farmers with whatever is offered to them. This situation has called for

59

=== page 61 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/ Monagalurt- curvey 2005407

trainings to be conducted on correct cultivating, curing and handling techniques to meet
the required world market standards.

There is almost ‘4 a million vanilla farmers in PNG now. But as little as 10 000 framers
knows the cultivation, curing and handling processes. About 6 000 farmers practice land
use management, that is by inter cropping the vanilla with other cash crops so that they
do not use up more land reserved for other purposes or future use.

By this estimates one could say that we need to learn more about vanilla before farming
it, Vanilla farming is a fulltime work! The plant needs constant attention from cultivation
through to harvesting and curing. It takes almost 1&1/2 —2 years of labor, thus the job
starts at 5.00am and ends at 6.30pm in the evening once the crop starts to flower.

People were rushing to cultivate vanilla and they were not aware that Madagascar would
recover in 2 years and the vanilla buying price would fall. It did fall in late 2002. PNG
farmers were caught napping and were discouraged that their time and efforts were
wasted when the focus was on the market price at that time when they were enjoying
huge returns during the Madagascar crisis. Farmers were grieving that their labor was
unaccounted for. Many gave up before harvesting when that happened. Some quit when
they found out the work involved was too much. However, others continued hoping that
another natural disaster hits Madagascar again. The price has now dropped too
dramatically from approximately K8.00 per kilo to approximately K 1.00 per kilo.

At Managalas Plateau there are many people cultivating vanilla. A head-count is yet to be
conducted to know exactly how many farmers are growing this crop. From known
farmers growing this crop, each farmer is growing 150- 300 vanilla vines which means.
Some Managalasi started vanilla farming as early as 1999 and 2000. The vines were
bought from Kokoda, Popendetta, Port Moresby and Afore markets at K4.00 per vine
cutting that was a meter in length. Others bought it from the first buyers who grew them
again for the same price or less.

Most farmers at the plateau lack general knowledge of the crop on cultivation,
pollination, curing and marketing. They farmed from “hear say” from other people. Some
have seen people cashing in on vanilla sales and have taken up the business. They lack
land use skills and intercropping techniques.

Recommendation:

PWM and MDF must identify vanilla experts to educate the people on the impacts of
vanilla farming, the work/ labor involved, land management and land use, the species of
vanilla that is suitable for the Managalas climate, intercropping, the current buying price
and where to sell their vanilla etc.

text:
=== page 1 ===
Paul Konia! NTFP/Managatasi- survey 2005/07

By: Paul P Konia.

Recommendations & Assumptions:

Common Name: Kopi/Kofi (Tok Pisin)

English: Coffee

Local Dialect: Kofuke

Scientific Name: Coffea Arabica- Family: Rubiaceae

Background:

Around the birth of Jesus Christ, coffee was reportedly first discovered growing in
Ethiopia by a sheepherder named Khaldi. Whenever he moved his sheep into one
particular pasture, the sheep would start acting extremely lively and erratic after
eating the “red cherries” on a particular bush found in that pasture. Tentatively,
Khaldi tried eating a few of the beans himself and experienced the same reaction.
The local area monks heard about Khaldi and this “devil’s fruit” but soon they too
were eagerly sampling it so they could stay awake for their prayers. Arab traders,
during a trading expedition, decided to bring back some beans to their homeland
and began to plant and grow their own beans. Soon they began to boil the beans and
produced a drink called “qahwa” (meaning “unable to sleep”). The drink gained
popularity until around 1453 when the Ottoman Turks introduced the beans to
Constantinople and in 1475 the world’s first coffee shop; “Kiva Han” was opened in
the city. The “coffee craze” developed to a point where women could even divorce
their husbands if they failed to provide the women with a daily ration of coffee. The
mere existence of the plant was a closely guarded secret in the Moslem countries

=== page 2 ===
when an Arab named Baba Budan started the actual spread of this delicacy to the
outside world illegally. Baba Budan smuggled some beans to Mysore, India where
descendants of these first smuggled plants can be found to this day.

In 1600, Italian traders brought some of the beans to Pope Clement VIII who was
urged to ban the drink as “unholy” because it came from Moslems that were “Non
Christians” but he surprised them by “baptizing” it instead. Now “coffee” was an
acceptable beverage for Christians. A few years later, Dutch traders smuggled out a
coffee plant from the port of Espresso to the island of Ceylon and to their East
Indian colony of Java, source of coffee’s nickname today. In 1713, the Dutch
unwittingly gave a coffee bush to Louis XIV of France that, from which, in 1723, a
French naval officer, Gabriel Mathicu do Clieu, stole a seedling and took it to
Martinique. Eventually, 90 percent of the world’s coffee spread from this one plant.

Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee:
In 1728 Sir Nicholas Lawes, then Governor of Jamaica and owner of Temple Hall

Estate, brought the first coffee plants to Jamaica. First, cultivation started in the
foothills of St. Andrew but soon plantations extended deeper into the fertile Blue
Mountains. The coffee industry has experienced many ups and downs from those
early days until today.

From 1800 to 1840, Jamaica produced 70,000 tons per year making her the largest
producer in the world. Then, in 1838, came the abolition of slavery. This spelled the
end to many coffee plantations, as newly freed farmers began planting and clearing
all the available hillsides to earn a living and to have land to live on. By 1891, the
coffee industry was in general disarray so legislation was passed to provide
“instruction in the art of cultivation and curing by sending certain districts,
competent instructors.”

The effort to increase quality was largely unsuccessful as the largest buyer in those
days was the Canadian market and they resisted it as being unacceptable. Finally, in
1944 the Jamaican government established a Central Coffee Clearing House where
all coffee for export had to be processed. This cleaning and grading process was a
giant step in the improvement in the quality of the Jamaican coffee being exported.

Following the devastating hurricane of 1951, there were only three Coffee
Processing Plants (called “pulperies”) remaining in operation in the Blue
Mountains. In an attempt to regulate the growth that was sure to follow, the Coffee
Industry Board was formed to establish guidelines in quality, cultivation and
processing. The Coffee Industry Board is still an active force today and garners
some of the credit for the resurgence of Jamaican coffee. In 1973, the three coffee
processing plants at Mavis Bank, Silver Hill and Moy Hall along with a new comer,
Wallenford, registered the name “Blue Mountain Coffee”.

A few years ago, the Twyman family’s Old Tavern Estate Coffee won the legal right
through the Jamaican courts to also sell its superior product under the “Blue
Mountain” name.

=== page 3 ===
Jamaica is famous for producing some of the finest coffee found anywhere in the
world. What makes this little island such a prime spot for growing a world-class
coffee? As in real estate, it’s “Location, Location, Location” and in this case, that
location is the Blue Mountains. Coffee plants need to be well watered, well drained
and experience periodic coolness during some stages of development. To be called
“Blue Mountain Coffee”, it must be grown at altitudes between 2,000 and 5,000 feet
in the Parishes of Portland, St. Andrew and St. Thomas and, most importantly, be
grown on the estates of; Mavis Bank, Silver Hill, Moy Hall or Wallenford. Coffee
grown elsewhere in the Blue Mountains or anywhere else in Jamaica cannot be
called “Blue Mountain Coffee. Blue Mountain coffee is exclusively made from the
Arabica Bean. The Arabica bean is more fragile to grow but is considered more
flavorful and has less caffeine than the Robusta Bean grown in many parts of the
world.

Small growers like James Dennis in the District of Section are finding success in
selling their production directly to discriminating tourists as most of the “official”
Blue Mountain Coffee is currently exported to Japan. First they must harvest their
beans and then sun dry them on bamboo racks before roasting them over a smoky
wood fire. They weigh and package the beans in plastic bags for sale to passing
tourists and locals. Want your coffee ground? They will pour the roasted beans into
an old hollowed-out log and have someone pound and pulverize the beans using a
stout, tapered hardwood branch with a flat surface on the end.

More small growers, like James Dennis, along with the officially recognized and
established “Blue Mountain Coffee” growers known as JABLUM (Jamaica Blue
Mountain) are growing and producing what is regarded as the “Best Coffee in the
Caribbean” and quite possibly the “Best Coffee in the World”.

Coffee was introduced to Papua New Guinea in the late 1940s thus in the late 1960s
it was taken up to Afore and the Managalas plateau by the colonel administration to
be grown as a cash crop.

The Managalas plateau has almost over 700 farmers who grow more than 800 000
coffee trees that can produce about 8000 bags annually at an average weight of 360
000 (45kg per bag) kilograms. In monetary terms, the current coffee buying price at
the plateau is K2.00 which means that the revenue going in annually will be about
K720 000.00. Moreover, if coffee is sold at factory door price in Goroka which
stands at K4.50 per kilogram, then farmers of Managalas plateau would have
collected K1, 62000.00 annually.

Plant Description: The coffee plant is a woody perennial evergreen dicotyledon that
belongs to the Rubiaceae family. It has a main vertical trunk (orthotropic) and
primary, secondary, and tertiary horizontal branches (plagiotropic). Two main
species of coffee are cultivated today. Coffea arabica known as Arabica coffee
accounts for 75-80% of the world's production. Coffea canephora, known as
Robusta coffee, is more robust than the Arabica plants, but produces an inferior
tasting beverage with a higher caffeine content. The coffee plant can grow to

=== page 4 ===
heights of 10 meters if not pruned, but producing countries will maintain the coffce
at a height reasonable for easy harvesting.

A common tended, planted or cultivated medium-large tree with distinctive lateral
branches, deciduous green to red leaves and fruits with hard corky pink/ purple
shell that is cut open in to equal halves.

Plant Development: Three to four years after the coffee is planted, sweet smelling
flowers grow in clusters in the axils of the leaves. Fruit is produced only in the new
tissue. The Arabica species is self-pollinating, whereas the Robusta species depends
on cross pollination. About 6-8 weeks after the flowers are fertilized, cell division
occurs and the fruit remains as a pin head for a period that is dependent upon the
climate. The ovaries will then develop into drupes in a rapid growth period that
takes about 15 weeks after flowering. During this time the integument takes on the
shape of the final bean. After the rapid growth period the integument and
parchment are fully grown and will not increase in size. The endosperm remains
small until about 12 weeks after flowering. At this time it will suppress, consume,
and replace the integument. The remnants of the integument are what make up the
silverskin. The endosperm will have completely filled the cavity made by the
integument nineteen weeks after flowing. The endosperm is now white and moist,
but will gain dry matter during the next several months. During this time the
endosperm attracts more than seventy percent of the total photosynthesis produced
by the tree. The mesocarps will expand to form the sweet pulp that surrounds the
bean. The cherry will change color from green to red about thirty to thirty-five
weeks after flowing.

Root System: The root system can extend 20-25 km in total length and the absorbing
surface of a tree ranges from 400 to 500 m*. There are main vertical roots, tap
roots, and lateral roots which grow parallel to the ground. The tap roots extend no
further than 30-45 cm below the soil surface. Four to eight axial roots may be
encountered which often originate horizontally but point downward. The lateral
roots can extend 2 m from the trunk. About 80-90% of the feeder root is in the first
20 cm of soil and is 60-90 cm away from the trunk of the tree (Mavolta, 195-196).
However, the greatest root concentration is in the 30 to 60 cm depth. The roots
systems are heavily affected by the type of soil and the mineral content of the soil.
To be thick and strong the root system needs an extensive supply of nitrogen,
calcium and magnesium. During planting the main vertical roots are often clipped
to promote growth of the horizontal roots, which then have better access to water
and added nutrients in the top soil.

Leaves: The elliptical leaves of the coffee tree are shiny, dark green, and waxy. The
leaf area index is between 7 and 8 for a high-yielding coffee. The coffee plant has
become a major source of oxygen in much of the world. Each hectare of coffee
produces 86 Ibs of oxygen per day, which is about half the production of the same
area in a rain forest (source: Anacafe).

Harvesting: Each year coffee is harvested during the dry season when the coffee
cherries are bright red, glossy, and firm. Ripe cherries are either picked by hand,

=== page 5 ===
stripped from the tree with both unripe and overripe beans, or all the beans are
collected using a harvesting machine. These processes are called selective picking,
stripping, and mechanical harvesting, respectively.

To maximize the amount of ripe coffee harvested it is necessary to selectively pick
the ripe beans from the tree by hand and leave behind unripe, green beans to be
harvested at a later time. In Brazil, harvesting the same tree several times is more
cost prohibitive than separating and discarding the unripe or overripe cherries.
Therefore, Brazil typically harvests using the stripping method when 75% of the
crop is perfectly ripe. Stripping is feasible and cost effective in Brazil due to the
uniform maturation of Brazilian coffees. In stripping the beans are pulled from the
tree and fall to the ground where they are caught by sheets. The beans are removed
from tree debris by tossing the coffee in the air allowing the wind to carry away
sticks and leaves. The coffce is then put in 60 L green baskets, which is the
measuring tool used by coffee producers to determine wages. Some estates, such as
Fazenda Monte Alegre in Sul de Minas Brazil, have a computerized system to
determine wages, which accounts for the amount of coffee collected from each
person, the difficulty of the harvesting conditions, and the production of the region
being harvested. About 12-20 kg of export ready coffee will be produced from every
100 kg of coffee cherries harvested.

Processing: Irrespective of the harvesting method, green coffee beans and overripe
coffee cherries inevitably end up mixed with the perfectly ripe cherries and must be
separated. Over ripe coffee cherries, undeveloped coffee cherries, sticks and leaves
float in water. Ripe coffee beans and green coffee cherries are dense and sink.
Therefore, the first separation step takes place by separating the floaters from the
sinkers. The floaters are usually sent directly to the patio to be dried and are then
slated for internal consumption. The ripe and green cherries can be sent to the
patios to be dried using the natural (dry) process or can be sent to the pulping
machines.

The first stage of pulping is used to remove the green cherries from the ripe
cherries. In the pulping machine the internal pressure is monitored to push the
coffee against a screen with holes only large enough for a coffee bean (not cherry) to
pass through. Since the ripe cherries are soft they break and the seed is released
fitrowgbethelnesries.arc hard and cannot be pulped. Instead of passing through the
screen, the green beans pass to the end of the barrel system and are separated from
the ripe beans. The pressure inside the barrel controls how many cherries will be
pulped. A very high pressure will cause all of the cherries including the green beans
to be pulped. It is necessary to continuously monitor the pressure so that about 3%
of ripe cherries are not pulped and are removed with the green cherries. This
margin of error ensures that no green cherries are mistakenly pulped. The pulp
and beans are then separated by centrifugal force and a barrel screen system.

The beans covered in the slippery mucilage can be sent to the patios to dry as
pulped natural coffees or can be sent to fermentation tanks. The fermenting tanks
are used to remove the mucilage before drying. The pulped beans are put into
cement tanks with water and are allowed to ferment for 16-36 hours. On the way to

=== page 6 ===
the fermentation tanks another density separation can occur. The highest quality
coffees are the most dense and should be separated and fermented in a different tank.

The fermentation time depends on a number of factors including the amount of
coffee fermenting, water temperature, and humidity. The mucilage is made up of
pectin materials including protopectin (33%), reducing sugars including glucose
and fructose (30%), non-reducing sugars such as sucrose (20%), and cellulose and
ash (17%) Protopectin is not water soluble and will hydrolyze to pectinic acid in the
fermentation tanks. Hydrolysis of the protopectin and degradation of the pectin by
enzymes is the process that occurs to remove the mucilage during fermentation
(Wrigley, 455). Currently, the best way of determining the end of fermentation is to
feel the beans to determine if the beans are still encased in mucilage. If the beans
are fermented for 36-72 hours stinker beans develop. Lactic, acetic, and propionic
acids are produced in this process and are believed to prevent the traditional
fermentation taste by inhibiting mold growth that regularly occurs during drying on
i wratidlin formichcavidmianks the beans are moved to drying patios and dried to 1 1-
12% moisture content. A small portion of the lot is hulled and milled by a mini-
huller. Three hundred grams of coffee is classified for defects (100 grams is often
used), and the percentage of each screen size is determined. Then, 200-300 grams of
coffee is roasted in a sample roaster and cupped to determine quality. Ideaily no
lots will be mixed until the coffee has been classified and cupped. The coffee
remains in pergamino until shipment time to help protect the flavor and aroma of
the coffee.

Before shipment coffee must be dried from approximately 60% moisture content to
11-12% moisture content. Coffee is typically dried on large patios made of asphalt
or cement and then transferred to mechanical dryers. The coffee on the drying
patios is shifted every 30-40 minutes and is shaped into long rows of no more than 5
cm in height. Next to cach row is open ground, which is warmed and dried by the
sun, The coffee is then shifted onto the dry portion of the patio, and the section
where it was previously is now allowed to dry in the sun. This helps accelerate the
drying process and prevents fermentation and moldy beans from developing. This
method is widely used in Brazil, but less widely used in Guatemala or Costa Rica
where the coffee is more often piled perpendicularly to the old piles. To dry coffee
solely by patio drying it takes 6-7 days for washed coffees, 8-9 days for pulped
naturals (semi-washed), and 12-14 days for natural (dry-processed) coffees. This is
why coffees are typically dried on a patio until they reach a moisture content of 15%
and are then transferred to mechanical dryers. Once the coffee reaches 25%
moisture or less it can be piled at night and covered with cotton cloths to allow the
coffee to breath. If it rains these piles can also be covered with plastic. Coffee should
not be covered with burlap sacks since this will impart a distinct burlap flavor and
aroma to the coffee.

In a study done in Kenya, the report highlights that there are six stages to drying

¢o fin drying. Moisture 55-45%.

2) White Stage drying. Moisture 44-33%.

3) Soft Black stage. Moisture 32-22%.

4) Medium Black Stage. Moisture 21-16%

=== page 7 ===
5) Hard Black Stage. Moisture 15-12%

6) Fully dry coffee and conditioning. 11-10%.

In this study it was discovered that sun drying for stage three is mandatory for
coffee quality. It also reported that as long as the temperature was between 40-
50°C--which means a bean temp of 35°C--then the coffee quality will not be
seriously compromised during the other stages.

The final two stages (15-11% moisture) in just six hours at 40°C in a mechanical
dryer. There are several dryer systems available. Many older dryers are converted
grain dryers that are not as efficient as the new horizontal barrel dryers. The new
dryers are designed to mix the coffee evenly to ensure uniform drying. Drying by
using mechanical dryers accelerates the slowest part of the drying process (15-11%)
and helps prevent fermentation. In some environments that have a high humidity
the entire drying process must take place in mechanical dryers. Mechanical dryers
should never be set higher than 40-45°C and this question should be asked before
buying any coffees that have been mechanically dried. At higher temperatures the
germ is killed and the flavor potential of the coffee is ruined. At extreme
temperature the bean crystallizes and when smashed with a hammer will break like
glass.

The best, but least utilized method of drying coffee is by using drying tables. In this
method the pulped and fermented coffee is spread thinly on raised beds, which
allows the air to pass on all sides of the coffee. The coffee is mixed by hand and the
drying that takes place is more uniform and fermentation is less likely. Most coffee
from the Managalas Plateau is dried in this manner and it is the commonly used
drying method used widely in Papua New Guinea. It is sometimes known as Solar
Drying. Solar Dryer is good during rains and at nights. A drying bed is built with a
shelter over it with plastic sheet. The sides and ends of the bed are properly covered
and coffee parchments are spread on the bed to dry. Parchments are turn regularly
for sun to dry all sides. It takes about 3 — 4 weeks for the parchment to dry properly.

Diseases

Coffee Leaf Rust:

Coffee leaf rust first destroyed Brazils crop in 1970. Since then, it has spread to
every coffee growing country in the world. The disease was first observed in Sri
Lanka in the 1860's. Many countries, including Sri Lanka and Ethiopia, replaced
much of their arabica coffee with disease resistant robusta coffee. The disease is
spread from spores from lesions on the underside of the plant by wind and rain.
Rust is prevented by spraying with copper-based fungicides at 3-5 kg/ha at 4-6 week
intervals during the rainy season. In PNG, this disease was discovered in the 1980's.
Efforts by the Coffee Industry Corporation have successfully curbed this disease.

Coffee Berry Disease:
Coffee berry disease was first discovered in Kenya in 1920 and is caused by the

virulent strain of Colletotrichum coffeanum the fungus lives in the bark of the coffee
tree and produces spores which attack the coffee cherries. Spraying has been
determined to be the best way to avoid the coffee berry disease. Captafol and

=== page 8 ===
copper-based fungicides have been effective. The Kenyan coffee hybrid Ruiru 11 is
resistant to both coffee berry disease and leaf rust.

Bacterial Blight:
Bacterial Blight (Pseudomanas syringae py. garcae) is a disease that occurs where wet

and cold conditions prevail.

Nematodes:
Meloidogyne exigua, M. incognita, M. coffeicola, Pratylenchus brachyurus, and P.
coffeae are the most common species of root-knot nematodes. All arabica cultivars

are susceptible to nematodes.

Leaf Miner:
The leaf miner (Perileucoptera cofeella) occurs mainly in Brazil. Coffea stenophylila is

the only coffee cultivar resistant to the leaf miner

Traditional use:
There are no traditional uses of coffee recorded on the plateau because this crop was

introduced.

Potential as a NTFP:

Largely depends upon processing and access to markets. In particular, handling and
storage of beans and reliable cost effective transport to domestic markets (sce route
proposed on transport). The major technical processing problem is the beans
instability at ambient temperatures and humidity and its tendency to either rot or
over dried, eventually loosing it correct moisture when tested at the laboratory.

Coffee is feasible to store in most places on the plateau. The best alternative is to dry
the beans using the common technique of solar drying or sun dry. Solar drying is
appropriate because of the plateau’s climatic conditions of cloud cover and
associated rain most days. It should not prove too technically difficult to introduce
appropriate thermal dryers in to the area for down stream processing (making
green beans) — a number of designs are there and supported by the PNG Coffee
Industry Corporation and other local based organizations. However, experience
elsewhere has shown that unless their introduction must be accompanied by
comprehensive management training (in particular quality control) they are
unlikely to be successful. There is currently a standardized system for packaging
and storage in Goroka, the country’s leading coffee producing province.

Recommendation:

1.

PWM must seck more information on establishing a coffee roaster/ factory to
produce green beans at the plateau, preferably at Afore, and conduct a

Irene, you have a very clear idea of the problems with coffee on the Managalas plateau in the way you
have presented our case.

The main cause of our problems here is Market Inaccessibility, poor road conditions in the zones to Afore
where it leads to the coast. Because of the poor road condition in the zones, there is no truck coming in to
pick up the coffee from the farmers. Added to that is the very low price paid to the farmers at the road
side (point of sales — normally in the villages). We don’t think it is poor processing methods, but it has
something to do with storing the coffee over long period of time due to no buyers coming into the villages
as the road is poor. As the coffee beans are stored over time, the beans get mouldy from the cool tropical
humidity and the coffee beans go bad.

On another note, PWM feels very reluctant to introduce into the plateau community a new cash crop, as it
might have other negative impacts that may lead to added problems, so PwM feels, that we should utilise
what cash crop that is already there (coffee) where the people are knowledgeable about it.

Results (or problem):

Decreasing coffee retums has led to the abandonment of the coffee plots and to the trend that locals turn
to less sustainable manners in order to gain a new income (such as logging, oil palm plantations and
mining)This in turn leads to risking the anticipated conservation effects of the Managalas Community
Conservation Area Project. [See map of threats)

To tackle these problems, PwM wishes to strengthen the marketing opportunities of certified coffee
beans, by establishing links between the local producers and (inter) national certified coffee buyers and

Executive Summary

Partners With Melanesians in pursuit for the Proposed Managalas Community Conservation Area
Project has been working with the Communities on the Managalas Plateau for the last 15 years
and has assisted the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and successfully established the
ten (10) Community Based Organisations (CBOs) on the Managalas Plateau to enhance its
programme activities and to mobilize community collaboration and participation through as
sustainable approach to development options and encourage a self-reliance community economic
base.

The role of PWM is facilitating the core-programme activities and assist in eco-enterprising
activities for the local communities. The current eco-enterprise activities are Okari nut (Tropical
Almonds) Marketing Research and Sales, Vegetable Sales and Researching on Coffee and other
potential non-timber forest products, PWM also charters Third Level Airlines to transport market

produce to Port Moresby for marketing.

The soil and the climatic conditions of the Managalas Plateau have proved to be very conducive
for Arabica Coffee. The area is known for its coffee and for the last ten years there has been
drastic setbacks due to very poor road conditions that alienated the area from possible markets
and other basic government services. According to a survey carried out in December 7" — 15th,
more than 300 tonnes of coffee are destroyed every year due to market inaccessibility. That has
put the local communities under immense economic pressure,
as the economy of this nation has been in the doldrums for more than a decade.

This is a threat to the proposed Managalas Community Conservation Area Project as the
communities might succumb to the options provided by big industrial development especially,
mining, logging and Oil Palm due to the economic pressure mounting as a result of the
Government’s User Pay Policy whereby the essential government services are now payed for
and money is a big player in the game.

PWM after a thorough assessment of the whole situation identified that coffee is one of the best
eco-enterprise options for the Managalas People. Even though the domestic prices are not good,
yet compared to other local products, coffee is the winner, yet it is losing because of some of the
issues this proposal aims to address.

Brief Report on the Proposed Managalas Organic Coffee Project

The idea of starting Managalas Organic Coffee Project (MCOP) was established under the PwM eco-
enterprise drive for alternative development options for the Managalas communities. Coffee was there
long before the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project was established and the local people of the
Managalas Plateau are well acquainted with it and they often refer to it as “Coffee em Bun blong of

Managalas"

Last year when the NC-IUCN’s funding for the NLRPA program come in, the Management decided that
PwM will concentrate the Marketing Budget Line for coffee marketing research because PwM saw Coffee
to be a more viable produce from the plateau and given the worst economic conditions, coffee still comes
out the winner in comparison to other potential alternative produce from the plateau.

Whilst pursuing Coffee Marketing research which includes sample testing and grading done last year and
this year with our assessment of the fluctuations of the domestic pricing and local buying rates on the
plateau by interested parties, quality control, organic certification, rehabilitation programmes, and the
location of the Oro Coffee mill PwM also saw the need for a separate and specific funding for the MOCP so
that these issues can be addressed to enable the success of the project and the benefits reaching the local
communities.

On that note, I sent an enquiry email to Erick Wakka of DOEN Foundation asking him if PwM could submit
a proposal for Managalas Organic Coffee Project. It was on Erick’s invitation that I developed a proposal
for the MCOP that was initially submitted last year August. However, DOEN Foundation wanted more
information about the Managalas annual production which we initially stated on the proposal as 60 tons
based on Jacob Ramoi’s Report. DOEN responded that, 60 tons annual production is too low for PwM and
MDF to export and requires between 250-300 tons annual production to be viable for exports. Therefore
around late November 2004, Edwin and I conducted a survey, which we established our findings in our
report to be extremely higher (around 950-1500 tons annual Managalas Production). I furnished an
updated report and send it together with a re-submission of our proposal to DOEN.

A further delay was caused again early this year when Kenn indicated to Irene who is the DOEN advisor to
our proposal to include the cost of a specialist (consultant) from the Philippines to draft or develop the
MCOP Business plan and marketing strategy. Crissy from the Non-Timber Forest Product Exchange
Program in Philippines was our contact that introduced the specialist in community business plans and
marketing strategies to PWM and produced the Terms of Reference, which was sent to me last month. I
incorporated the TOR and revised the MOCP proposal budget and re-submitted it again to DOEN on the
last week of last month. We were advised accordingly that the MOCP proposal will be deliberated on the
1* of August DOEN Foundation sitting.

I sent an email to Eric Wakka on Monday and he response that our proposal was accepted for processing
and the final status will known by September 2005, not far from now.

Introduction

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses about 360 000 hectares of pristine
rainforest in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari District, Oro Province. The area is bordered by the
Owen Stanley Range to the southwest and the Sibium Range to the southeast. Popondetta town
and the famous Kokoda Trail are situated north of the proposed conservation area.

Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, but at
the moment is poorly documented. Biologists from the University of PNG have carried out two
previous surveys but the truc biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. This is evident
from the diverse frog fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs are a good indicator of a
rich and a vibrant environment.

There are about 250 frogs recognised from NG. This number increases at a fast rate because new
species are discovered and described every year, some remain undescribed in museum
collections throughout the world (e.g. American Museum of Natural History, British Museum of
Natural History, Bishop Museum, South Australian Museum). More than 50% of NG frogs
comprising the one family Microhylidae reproduce out of the water. Therefore the wet and
humid environmental condition of the whole Managalas Plateau provides an abundance of habits
for these frogs. However, no previous attempts have been made to quantitatively document this
rich component of the plateau before the previous two surveys by members of this team.

This report summarises the results of the herpetological survey conducted during Phase III of the
Managalas Plateau from 20" May 2006 to 5" June 2006.

Methods

Frogs were detected at night by locating calling males and by visual encounters. Efforts were
equally distributed along rivers and streams for aquatic frogs, and away from water bodies for
non-aquatic frogs.

Some frogs were identified in the field, and voucher specimens were also collected for further
confirmation and storage at the UPNG Natural Science Resource Centre.

Snakes and lizards encountered were also captured and specimens collected for preservation.
Three snakes Furina tristis, Stegonotus modestus and Tropidonophis statisticus were brought to us by
local people.

Survey sites

Numbumare, Aiare village along Musa River.
Altitudinal range: 547-600m.

GPS location: 09° 19° 50°* S, 148° 13° 50” E

Dakara, Umwate village
Altitudinal range: 778-800m
GPS location: 9° 16’ 27°° S, 148° 14° 50" E

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp. palms
and Calamus spp.

Results

A total of 15 species of frogs from three families were recorded. Of these 47% of the species are
of the family Microhylidae, a normal observation for other parts of NG where microhylid frogs

usually dominate. The other families, Ranidae and Hylidae constitute 26.5% of the total species

each. Six species of snakes and three species of lizards were also documented during the survey,
although less time was diverted for snakes and lizards (Table 1).

Local information mentions the presence of Green Tree Python (Morelia viridis), Death Adder
(Acanthophis sp) or probably NG Ground Boa (Candoia) because the later two snakes
superficially resemble each other. Local informant also mentions the presence of large green
frog, which could be Litoria infrafrenata. These animals were not encountered so are not
included in the species accounts.

Discussion

Frogs are secretive animals and hide during the day but come out during the night to feed, mate
and carryout their other essential biological functions. Daytime encounters are usually
accidental, or when one actively looks for them in likely hiding places. Therefore sampling has
to be done during their active periods so that maximum encounters can be made. Heavy rains
also trigger higher frog activity but some species of the subfamily Asterophryninae may call
during the day.

Diversity Patterns

Diversity at generic and specific levels is high for microhylid frogs in the Managalas Plateau
(Figure 1). This is expected because elsewhere in NG. microhylid frogs usually dominate the
Anuran fauna. For example, Richards (2002) recorded 30 microhylid frogs, 19 hylid frogs and 5
ranid frogs from the Kikori Basin. Richard’s survey was conducted for three years covering

=== page 14 ===

=== page 15 ===
altitudinal range of 40-1300m. It is expected that the number of frog species in the Managalas
Plateau will increase as more surveys are conducted covering all altitudinal ranges of the plateau.

Some species documented at Nabumare were not recorded from Dakara and vice versa, but this
is an artefact of environmental conditions and sampling period. Dakara was much dryer than
Nabumare, so the number of species encountered at Nabumare was higher than for Dakara
(Table 1). At the moment this comparison does not mean anything at all, because a long term
sampling with a lot of rainy periods will reveal the truc diversity of frogs from the two sites. But,
there is some similarity between the two sites, with the presence of four ranid species,
Hylophorbus sp and Mantophryne lateralis at both sites. The three Nyctymystes species collected
along the Musa River were not encountered along smaller creeks, suggesting these species
preferred larger fast flowing rivers compared to smaller creeks.

The six snakes and the skink lizards documented during this survey should be indicative of a
more diverse component of the Managalas fauna. Additional efforts directed towards these
components of the fauna should be prioritised during future surveys.

New Species

A sizable frog fauna (47%) of the surveyed sites are undescribed, including a small skink lizard,
suggestive of many new species yet to be documented. As the survey moves higher to over
1000m new species, especially hylid frogs that prefer fast flowing mountain streams would
undoubtly be discovered. The three Nyctymystes frogs, a genus endemic to NG appears to be new
to science, but further analysis will be done to confirm this.

Environment and Conservation Considerations

Frogs are sensitive to environmental change and are a good indicator of the status of an
environment. In a pristine environment free of pollution, the diversity of frogs at the family,
generic and species levels are usually high. Most of the environment of NG is still under pristine
conditions, except probably around the vicinity of large mining/industrial areas and cities. By
comparing past frog diversity to future diversity should large scale environmental degradation
activities occur, the status of the environment could be determined by assessing the decline in
diversity of frogs.

The environment in the Managalas Plateau still remains intact providing numerous microhabitats
for many animals to utilize. The consequences of clearing forests for large scale agricultural
activities, logging or mining operations would be loss of habitat for many of the rich biota. These
include the Bird-wing Butterfly, Tree Kangaroos, Cuscus, Bandicoots, and a host of many new
species of frogs yet unknown to science.

All these rich biota are the traditional rights and heritage of the Managalas people. Everywhere
in PNG, people are close to their forests and depend on it more than 90% of the time and would
not sustain a good living should the forests go, especially in rural areas where government
services are lacking. A comprehensive list of forest products depended upon by the Managalas
people is out of the scope of this report, but suffice is to say that, wood, food, building material,
Okari nut, bamboo, rattan, Pandanus are some of the things that come to mind. If NEC approves
the Managalas conservation area, the forest will continue to provide for the current generation
and those to come in the future.

Recommendations

The following recommendations are drawn after sampling at lower altitudes (547 — 785m) i in the
Proposed Managalas Conservation Project Area, Afore District, Oro Province from 20" May to
5™ June 2006.

a) Several more surveys should be carried out at 2 or 3 higher altitude localities, Uwolome
Range (2800m) and Sibium Range (1800m). I suggest one survey each close to or at the
summit of these ranges, and a further down at around 1200 — 1500m. These will provide
a comprehensive preliminary fauna and flora checklist covering all altitudes for decision

making.

b) Frog survey should be prioritised for higher altitudes to document species in these areas
so that future environmental decisions can be made by comparing present results with
future results. As mentioned above, frogs respond to environmental change quicker than
other animals, and the changes in diversity can be utilized to determine the status of the
Managalas environment in the future.

c) On future surveys, include people exclusively for the survey of snakes, lizards, insects
(and other arthropods) and fresh water fauna. These are also an integral component of the
environment and play their role in the Managalas ecosystems.

The conservation area remains un-exploited for major developments, except for mini
sustainable projects enhancing human well-being. The 350,000 hectare area were
categorized into 10 zones for proper and equal dissemination of conservation related
programs for all to be aware and understand. Small projects encouraged by Partners with
Melanesia were introduced in different zones to help generate small cash income for the
local landowners. The projects are so small that they have little biological effects, which
can change the ecosystems of the living organisms and plants, but it may not be that
threatened to many fauna and flora species of the area. The area is virtually high in
biological diversity naturally valued in their own ecological characteristics establishing
high profiles that makes this conservation area a place encourageable for future
generations and education.

Both the plants and bird species remain widely distributed and were common for any
traditional purposes to people. Species depletion occur only when major destruction's
takes place, reducing population density. After the third biodiversity surveys, bird
species were more widely distributed than the mammals, reptiles, amphibians, except for
the insect population that inhabit all vegetation types at all levels of different elevations.
Main objectives Partners With Melanesia would like to have in place for the
conservation area, were the biological information's which are not readily available at the
moment. The unique and the important species have to be identified for a better
recognition of the area that can attract tourist, researchers, scientist and the public at
large. For that, such requirement were important to identify with the yearly biodiversity
surveys to provide:

The existing fauna and flora species lists.

The protected species of the area.

The endemic species of the area.

The traditionally important species of the area.

Map-out the exact locations of the important species, as a guide to
promote tourism and other educational purposes.

3. Birdlife of the conservation area.

As explained in the Humate site description, many bird species, though were confine to
their own territorial ranges, travel far distances in seek for feed. This happen so with

the canopy birds then the under-canopy. It was observed that most bird species were the
same in the lowland rainforest and the secondary vegetation's. Mid-montane to higher
montane mossy forest, may have few species that are different, or are only confined. Rest
of the species remain the same, either in montane forest, lowland rainforest, or the
secondary vegetation's.

(species lists provided in reports 1,2 & 3, Paulus Kulmoi, will show where cach species
adaptations). It is possible other unrecorded bird species maybe available, but this
depends on future studies at areas un-surveyed.

Bird species diversity is very high, because most parts of the conservation area remain
undisturbed, that many species can be easily observed confined to a habitat type or to
the suitable feeding zones. Species become difficult to observe when their sources of
living is not readily available, or have been destructed by man in any form of

4, Methods used in the surveys

Methods of surveys were still the same as of the first and the second surveys, that was
the use of mist nets to catch bird species during the day for identifications and specimen
collections. For this particular surveys, random sampling was applied in-order to cover
larger areas at each sampling sites. Also random sampling was done because of the
different vegetation types at each sampling sites.

Site one (1) have been identified to have four different vegetation types, the mid-
montane forest, secondary vegetation's, riverine forest, and the grassland. Site two
(2) have identified four (4) different vegetation types, the mid-montane forest,
secondary vegetation's, riverine forest and the old garden sites.

Site descriptions of the two study sites.

1. Nabumare survey site, Aiari village, zone 4, Musa area.

As it was categorized by Partners With Melanesia, Aiari, Suari and Jaure villages are in
zone 4 of Managalas Conservation Area. The villages lay far north-west of Itokama at
the foothill ranges of Owalama bordering Central and Oro Provinces. The cool breezes
and the presence of dominant oak vegetation's describes the elevational level of the
villages. From this elevation, we described the forest zone as mid-montane within the
conservation area. The presence of dominant oak tree species, Castanopsis
accuminatissima and Lithocarpus sp, were common in this vegetation type than any
other tree species.

The biodiversity studies were conducted in the surroundings of Aiari village, which was
about 4-5 km east of the village, at an altitude of 537m.a.s.| in a depression, though there
were presence's of hills and mountains that have higher elevations. The site was a coarse-
way plains of the Musa River systems, having it's vegetation's disturbed through
flooding and old garden sites. Although it was the tributaries of the Musa River, species
composition of both plants and animals were still high, due to it's lower human
population at Aiari village.

Many bird species recorded in the area were same, except for a new record of Bird of
Paradise species, Drepanornis albertisi (a Buff Tailed Sicklebill Bird of Paradise). Being
in the mid-montane forest, we believed there could be other two or even more other bird
species that have not being recorded in our previous survey lists. Other Birds of Paradise
species recorded at this site includes; Magnificent Rifle Bird of Paradise (Ptiloris
magnificus), and the Magnificent Bird of Paradise, (Cicinnurus magnificus).

2. _Dakara survey site, Humate village, zone 1.

Dakara was the second survey site, Humate village, last of the villages in zone one. The
site is also categorized to be in the mid-montane forest with the presence of dominant
aok tree species, Lithocarpus & Castanopsis spp. Bird species of both crown and under-
canopy were frequent and were common indicators, except for few that only inhabit this
level of the habitats. Traditionally, people of Humate have their rights to go as far as they
can on their land to make gardens, hunting and gathering resources for their needs. Much

6. Discussions

it is most interesting to note from each biodiversity surveys conducted, the bird species
listings inchudes at least one or two new names of species. The results shows that bird
species diversity is very rich in species distrubution, that as we explore the untouched
areas of the conservation area, the unrecorded species names becomes a record. Good
examples were in survey two, Papuan King Parrot (Alisterus chloropterus), was
recorded in the mountains of Anatua village. and the Suff Tailed Sicklebill Bird of
Paradise, (Drepanornis alhertisi), was recorded at the mountains of Aiari village in the
third survey. Bird population and species richness remains high, though after several
years the conservation area being at it’s propasai siages, the conservation concepts with
the local Jandowners of the area remains a value to own for their future generations.

By far, there is no immediate threats to fauna species, being that no major deveicpment
were inline to take place within the conservation area. Maybe there are plans for such
projects that Partners With Melanesia might have for the conservation area, in which I
am not aware, but currently there are no major activities that can threaten fauna species.
except for smail coffee plantations and forest clearings by local landowners for
subsistence cash cropping. It have been realized that species compositions remain the
same at the lower altitudes, but species profile changes as we go up the higher altitudes.
This have been evident enough due to the fact that, higher altitudes have less
interference’s with people fer hunting and gathering of other resources for their needs.

1.0 INTRODUCTION

This report presents the findings from the third Managalas Biodiversity Survey, which was conducted
from 20" May 2006 — 05° June 2006. The Managalas plateau is proposed for conservation, which if
approved by the National Executive Council (NEC) will become a Wild Life Management Area
(WMA) in Papua New Guinea (PNG). A team of biologists from the University of Papua New Guinea,
and Department Environment Conservation were involved in this survey. The survey covered both
flora and fauna diversity. Fauna survey included mammals, frogs, reptiles, snakes, birds and bats while
flora compiled plants data.

In this survey, two areas were sampled, one at a lower altitude while another at a higher altitude. The
rationale was to determine the species composition of a typical coastal lowland vegetation and a typical
coasta! mid montane forest. The main focus of the survey was to determine the species composition of
the area surveyed which would indicate various important species in the area.

The first survey site was Nabumare of the Aiari area, which is surrounded by lower montane forest.
The soil type is mainly black loamy volcanic and is rich in debris from leaf litter on the forest floor.
This site has an altitude of about 547m above sea level (as!). The people in the area are very friendly
and their population is about 200 from the 2002 national census although they live in a very large land
area. This population excludes the children who were born after the census. At the moment there is no
functional goverment services in the area although they have an Aid Post and a Community School.
There are no stuff to serve the people, as the geography is so rugged and mountainous that no body
from outside is willing to go. “Even if they went, they would retum after a couple of weeks” was a
remark made by the councillor of Aiari village. The people have initiated an airstrip and is completed
but they have no funding to obtain the necessary equipment to get the airstrip registered and
functioning to be able to have small planes landing. An important service to the people and will
certainly have an enormous impact in the lives of the local people.

The second survey site was Dakara, which is located within the vicinity of the Umuate village. The site
has an altitude of about 778 m asl and is mostly surrounded by a typical mid montane forest. The
vegetation is a bit similar compared to the first site except that it is at a higher altitude. The soil is
mostly black loamy volcanic with lots of plant debris. Umuate village is situated between Itokama
airstrip and Aiari village (first survey site). The people in Umuate go to Itokama for various services
such as medical treatment as well as sending their children to attend primary school there. The
population in the village is estimated to be between 100 and 200 excluding infants.

1.1 GENERAL BACKGROUND OF MANAGALAS PLATEAU

The Managalas area is in the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea. It is quite remote and is isolated
from other parts of the Oro Province as well as PNG at large. It is situated between Owen Stanley
Ranges to the southwest and Sibium Ranges to the southeast. The pleateau is mostly rich in volcanic
soil from the famous Mt. Lamington’s eruption in the 1940's, which is located to the northeast.
Managalas has an altitudinal range of 500m -- 1800m asi and encompasses an area of 300,000 hectares.
It bas an extreme rich flora and fauna biodiversity, which has not been documented yet. There are
about 150 clan groups, which are divided into ten zones, which make up the bulk population of more
than 15, 000 people.

2.0 METHODOLOGY
2.1 SURVEY SITE

This survey was conducted in two different sites within the Managalas Plateau in the Oro Province.
Managalas Plateau encompasses a total area of 300,000 hectares and is situated between the Owen
Stanley Range to the southwest and the Sibium Range to the southeast while Mt Lamington and the
Hydrographers to the north and east. It has an altitudinal range of 500m to 1800m as}.

The first survey site was located at Nabumare in the Aiari area at 09° 19’ 51.4” S and 148° 13'50.1" E
and ranges from 547m to 600m elevation. Nabumare is a half to one-day walk from Itokama airstrip
and passes through another village called Umuate. The survey site is surrounded mostly by lower

2.2 POPULATION AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE OF THE AIARI AND UMUATE PEOPLE

At these sites the local people have a special relationship with their environment. Their forest is intact
and contains large amount of unexploited flora and fauna biodiversity not known to the rest of the
world. The people were exposed to the outside world in the 1960's when the Summer Institute of
Linguistics (SIL) was introduced into the Itokama area. This implies that their understanding of the
world around, pattern of social structure, leadership and their interactions with the environment is
unique,

Aiari and Umuate villages are in Zone 4 and zone | respectively of the 10 zones in the Managalas
Plateau, ljvitari District. The local people in these areas have a number of bases in the form of houses.
The permanent houses are built in the main village while temporary garden huts are built in the forest
near the garden for shelter. Moving around has become part of their lives ever since and is considered
to be very important in both the social organization and the subsistence of the local people. The local
people inter marry, usually from other groups in the other villages. Most married couples live on the
husbands land. Their real social life is centred around hunting, gardening, house construction and
gathering wild nuts during its season.

The Aiari and Umuate areas are both not densely populated as in Aiari there are about 200 people
while Umuate has about 100 — 200 people.

2.3 PLANT SAMPLING TECHNIQUES

A 50m x 50m plot (total area of 2500m’*) at compass bearings was set up and a peg with coloured
flagging tapes were placed at each comer to demarcate the four comers of the plot. A 50m transect was
run through the centre of the plot and pegs were placed at 10m intervals along the transect. All trees
with DBH of Scm and or more Im away from transect line on both sides were identified and recorded.
Each tree species with DBH recorded had its estimated height recorded as well. Voucher specimens
were collected for taxonomic identification and deposited at the UPNG Herbarium.

Five quadrats (Sm x 5m) were placed within the established 50m x 50m piot at random compass
bearings and random number of steps. Ali plants (herbs, shrubs, palms, pandanus, lianas, trees and
grass) of 0.5m or above within the quadrats were enumerated. Voucher specimens were also collected
for taxonomic identification.

A general collection was also done from both survey sites to determine the type of plants that comprise
these areas.

3.0 DATA ANALYSES TECHNIQUES

Analyses include descriptive graphical representation of morpho plant groups in each survey site.
Descriptive analyses will also be done to see which DBH size classes were common in the survey sites.
Other statistical tests were not done due to not all plants were identified.

5.0 DISCUSSION

5.1 People and their relationship with plant biodiversity

Papua New Guinea’s forests are among the richest in the world and its biodiversity plays a major role
in the lives of many rural Papua New Guineans. Most people (85%) in PNG depend on forest resources
to sustain their livelihoods.

The Aiari and Umuate people have a special relationship with their forests. The forests have become
part of their lives from which they extract various natural plant resources for their needs. They depend
on the forest plants for food (wild fruits and nuts), medicines, raw materials to make tools and
weapons, to build houses and fences, for rituals and magic, for arts and crafts and many more. Thus,
plant biodiversity has enhanced the people's general understanding in the uses and their status in the
community. This has led the people to believe that they have respect for the forest they dwell in and the
resources they extract for their use. This relationship has mutually and equally benefited the people as
well as the environment they live in.

5.2 Plant Biodiversity and Conservation

The proposed area is very rich in plant biodiversity with little disturbance. The forest is intact and has a
greater potential to offer to the people of Managalas and PNG many various products. However, the
forests are also vulnerable to treats from logging, mining, growing population etc. Many PNG forests
have already been exploited by logging and mining companies and have left the forest owners no forest
to dwell in freely, or no long term benefits to the resource owners.

This may happen to the Managalas forest if it is not protected from exploitation of such nature in the
future. Therefore, the proposed idea of conserving Managalas for future generation is important and is
crucial for all stakeholders (landowners, conservation NGO's, Government) to cooperate and work
together to protect Managalas proposed area. Conservation will bring in various benefits to the local
people both directly and indirectly. For instance, tourists will be attracted to come into the area to see
Bird Wing Butterflies of Oro. Bird wing butterflies will disappear if the host plants are destroyed in the
forest. There is also potential for drug discovery in this forest because drug discovery program has now
increased in Papua New Guinea and such forest has a potential to offer for drug discovery.

5.3 Vegetation and species of concern

The vegetation in the Managalas area ranges from a lower coastal forest to mid montane forest to a
higher altitude forest and there are some transitional forests in between which comprise species of both
vegetation types. This implies that a good representation of species of both lower and higher altitude
occurs there. In this survey and the gencra! observations that were made, species such as Gyrinops
(eaglewood), Castanopsis (strong wood for house construction), orchids (ornamentals), Terminalia
(okari nut trees) and Aristolochia (host plant of Bird wing butterflies) are found in the area. These are
important species of concern which if not conserved will disappear and the future generation of Oro
and PNG at large will not sce for instance Birdwing butterflies and will not have okari nuts to eat and
enjoy.

6.0 SUMMARY

This survey shows that both survey sites are extremely rich in plant biodiversity. However, first survey
site comprises more species than the second site. These sites were only a small portion of the proposed
Managalas Conservation Area. In both sites only a few different species occurred in each otherwise the
Species composition was quite similar (refer to appendix 3). The various new species found in each site
were subjected to preference of the altitudinal range. There is a greater family diversity in Nabumare
than in Dakara which results in the more diverse plant groups in Nabumare. A complete species list of
the area is important and is desired to assess the important species that occur there. After taxonomic
identification of the voucher specimens a complete florai list will be provided for the area.
