Introduction

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) covers an area of over 360 000 hectares.
It is situated in the south eastern part of the Southern Papuan Ecoregion in the ljivitari District,
Oro Province. It lies between the Owen Stanley Range to the southwest, the Sibium Range to
the southeast and Mt Lamington to the northeast. The area is comprised of 40 villages with
approximately 16 000 people scattered throughout the plateau. The approximate population size
within the study sites is around 100 individuals. The area is abundant in forest resources and vast
areas of the MPCA are covered in a variety of vegetation types from secondary regrowth,
montane forest to open grasslands. Higher altitude forests exist beyond 2000m.

Partners with Melanesia (PwM), is a national NGO which focuses its work on the Managalas
Plateau. PwM in its conservation programme aims at protecting the undisturbed environment by
carrying out awareness and in the process of establishing a conservation area.

From May 20" to June 4” 2006, PwM engaged UPNG scientists to carry out the third phase of
an on going biodiversity survey in the Managalas Plateau. The main objective of UPNG Post
Graduate student being part of this survey was to gain experience in field techniques and to
render assistance to the experienced field scientists. The information compiled on the flora and
fauna will be used toward the establishment of the Managalas Wildlife Conservation Area.

Methodology

Different sampling techniques are used for plants and animals in the field. A one hectare plot or
a line transect may be used for plant sampling. Mammals are usually trapped or spotted by spot-
lighting using visual encounters at night, while other vertebrates such as frogs, snakes and lizards
are captured during the animals’ active periods. Birds and bats are usually enumerated with the
aid of mist nets. and some times by visual encounters using binoculars. Local information is
some times useful and may be utilized. The sampling methods used in this survey are detailed
below.

Study Site Description.

Two sites were surveyed during this trip. The first site was at Nabumare, located at 09° 19°50”
S, 148° 13°50” E at an altitudinal range between 547-600m. It is in the lower Musa area towards
Aiare village. The second site was at Dakara, located at 09°16°27°°S, 148°14°50°°E at an
altitudinal range between 778-800m. 11 is about half an hour walk from Umwate village.

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Flora Sampling

A 50m x 50m plot was established using compass bearing. At the 25m mark. a line transect was
placed across the plot for enumerating all plant species. Trees with a diameter at Breast Height
(DBH) equal to or greater than Sem were recorded within Im on either side of the line transect.
Tentative identification and height of each tree were all recorded. Five quadrates measuring 5m x
5m were also marked out randomly within the 50 x 50m plot and plant species contained in each
quadrate were enumerated. Voucher specimens of all plants within the plot were collected for

Managalas Plateau, particularly within the surveyed sites.

Fauna Sampling

1. Mammals

Mammals were sampled using Tomahawk and Elliot traps, while mist nets were used for bats.
The Elliot and Tomahawk traps were alternatively placed every 10m interval in a 50m x 50m
plot previously marked out. At site 2 Tomahawk traps were placed along Kuman and Pingi creek
for water rats. Baits used included roasted coconut with peanut, ripe banana and tinned fish.
Species caught were later skinned and dried for preservation at the Natural Science Resource
Center, UPNG.

2. Birds

Birds were sampled using mist nets erected at about 30cm above ground level to 10/15 meters.
Visual identifications were done for birds too high for nets. Bird identifications follow Beehler er
al (1986) and Coates (1990). Local informants were also utilized for birds not encountered but
were known to exist in the survey areas. Calls were used to identify nocturnal birds,

3. Herpetofauna

Frogs were captured with naked hands as they are harmless. The frogs were found close to
streams, rivers and further inland - terrestrial frogs. Frogs collected were either hiding on/under
leaf litter, exposed on vegetation while others burrowed into the topsoil 10-15cm deep and they
had to be dug out. Frog capture was maximized after rainy periods. During the periods where no
rainfal] occurred, few species were calling higher up in the canopy layers. Hence, the favorable
times or periods of collecting frogs are usually during wet weather conditions.

Although less time was spent on sampling snakes and lizards, some specimen were also
collected. The local people brought others in.

Results

Appendix 2 (Tables 1-4) provides a full list of plants and animals found within the two survey
sites, Figures |-4 are pictures of some of the animals sampled at the two localities surveyed.

Mammals

Twenty species of mammals from seven families were sampled from the two sites (Table 2). The
families Muradie and Chiroptera had more species than the other families (Figure 1). Figure 1
depicts species distribution in each family and Figure 2 shows the species count from the two
sites, Nabumare and Dakara. All the mammal species found in Nabumare also occurred at
Dakara, including 30% more species that were not encountered at Nabumare. This could explain
species prevalence and endemism at higher altitudes.

Discussion

The preliminary results from the two sites were rich in the diversity of plant and animal species
sampled (Appendix 2), The Managalas Plateau encompasses a vast area and the number of
species documented so far may double with further surveys. There was a slight difference
observed in the general make up of the biota of the two sites sampled. Nabumare had more
species of animals than Dakara. The different species distribution is influence by factors such as
the altitudes, climatic conditions, vegetation types and the production time of the forest. Dakara
was at an altitudinal range of 778-800m, which is higher than Nabumare, at 547-600m. The
vegetation of both sites were typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs were well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Apart from our experience in participating in a biodiversity survey, we gained first hand
experience on various field methods that were used to sample the animals and plants. These
included trapping methods, transects for plant sampling and mist netting for assessing birds /
bats. Frogs sampling requires a lot of patience and effective hearing ability. We saw that it was
normally during the rainy period that the catch rate was maximized.

From this trip we were able to experience some unexpected problems that may arise in a
biological survey .We learnt that to collect good results one had to be patient at times, be open-
minded in any discussions and good public relations with the local people. These would avoid
problems such as loss of sampling time, loss of specimens due to domesticated dogs, and the
general lack of understanding from the local people.

Recommendation

The following recommendations have been done after the survey.

1) Study sites should be confirmed and everyone in the area be informed of the survey
team’s arrival. No last minute decision for survey site location.

2) More awareness is required in the potential survey sites. There has to be prior ground
work done so there is ample discussion with the people and they are aware of all that is to
happen in there in advance.

3) Campsites should be restricted to survey team and field guides (or cooks) only,

4) Experienced personnel from PwM should always accompany trainees out in the field.

5) PwM should continue to engage students in such training because it helps in the capacity
building of our country’s up and coming young scientist.

Conclusion

We can say that this has been an exciting and very educational trip for us as we were able to see
what actually happens in the field and develop some skills that may be helpful to use in whatever
field we may be employed in. The training provided in the field was complementary to what we
learnt in school whilst also giving us much needed practical hands on experience in biological
field surveying. To PwM we say keep up the good work and we hope student engagement in
such surveys will continue.

Bird-life of the Conservation Area.

The avian species within the Managalas Conservation Area represent a wide variety of species from
Passerines to Non-Passerines. It has a very high species diversity and good distribution of bird species in
the mountain and the Jowland rainforest where few of the birds of paradise can be heard or sighted. The
disturbed natural vegetation have species composition of the common indicator species like the friar birds,
parrot species, starlings, fly-catchers and the Raggiana bird of Paradise. The lowland vegetation also have
a wide variety of species distribution, which includes some good number of important and protected bird
species that can be found available in this vegetation type. Species identified common indicator species at
crown canopy levels under canopy levels, shrub layers, and the forest floor, where species including, the
pigeons (Ducula spp) the fruit doves (Ptilinopus spp), the hornbill (Aceros plicatus), The cockatoos
(Cacatua galerita and Probosciger aterrimus), the parrots of different species, the fly-catchers, the honey-
eaters, the robins, King bird of Paradise (Cicinnurus regius), the magnificent rifle-bird of Paradise (Ptiloris
magnifeus), scrub fowl, brush turkey, followed by less indicator bird species.

The high mountain bird species confines themselves due to habitat types and the sources of feed available,
depending on tree and other plant species. These group of species have their own territorial zones in flights
and feeding. Of these species group, birds includes the brown or the black sicklebill bird of paradise (spp
have yet to be identified), and the Papuan king parrot, (Alisterus chloropterus), can only be observed
availabie in their range of adaptations. Other bird species can also be found in this habitat type but have a
wider territorial zones in flights and in searches for desired fruiting trees in the nearby vegetation type like
the lowland rainforest.

ABSTRACT

In November. 2004, a rapid vegetation assessment was conducted near ltokama and
the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. In November, 2005, a phase 2 survey
was conducted as an extension of that survey. The overall aim of the survey was to
gather baseline information on vegetation types. determine the structure and assess the
plant diversity within the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three selected sites, Kierim lower montane
forest, Tahama forest and Pongani forest near the coast. Within each site plots of
50x50m were demarcated. Within the plot, strip lines of 5 x 50m were marked out at
10m interval. The strip line was subdivided into 5x10m subplots and trees 25cm dbh
were measured and heights recorded.

To account for shrubs, herbs and saplings, at least 5 quadrats of 5 x 5m were randomly
placed within the demarcated plot and all species enumerated.

Apart from forest sampling genera! botanical collection was conducted within the
vicinity of each site. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid
proper identification of specimens,

Samplings and general observations indicate that a number of forest formations occur
in the proposed conservation area; Jower montane forest comprising of mixed
Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans, monsoonal or dry evergreen
forest and patches of savanna grassland towards the coast. The results from diameter
measurements in all plots showed that high proportion of trees have dbh <30cm
suggesting that the current forest types are quite young. However, there are indications
that there was a period of suppressed growth that has some bearing on the current
forest structure.

The Shannon Diversity Index average score is 1.50. This is higher than the first survey
at ltokama. Species area curve also show increasing species number as area increases
from mountain to the coast. All in all the Managalas Conservation Area has a very

high species diversity.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the Managalas Development
Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia be strengthen and instrument
put in place to declare the Managalas Plateau as Conservation Area.

4.0 Methods

The methodology employed here slightly differ from previous survey where strip
transects were taken randomly. Here plot of 50m x50m was demarcated in each site.
In each plot, belt transects of 5 x 50m were laid out systematically at 10m interval. To
get an overall picture of the plant biodiversity of the area, the strip transects were
subdivided into quadrats of of 5 x 10m (50m‘*). In each quadrat all trees 25cm dbh
were enumerated. Parameters measured include diameter at breast height (dbh), height
and identification of species at least to genus level. Diameter and height were
measured to elucidate the structure and dynamic of the forest.

Note strip transects only account for tree species. To assess the species density within
the 50 x 50m plot, further 5 x Sm quadrats were laid randomly and all herbs, shrubs,
creepers, climbers and saplings enumerated. At least 5 quadrats were laid out.

General botanical coliections were also conducted over the survey period and plants
samples pressed and transported to the UPNG Herbarium for further identification,
and storage.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation
appears irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest
observation on surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are

influenced by topography (Piskaut, 2004).

At Anatua there appeared to be some distinct zonation. The lowland forest gradually
grades into montane forest above 1000m as]. However, certain features characteristic
to lower montane formation become obvious at around 700m as!. This is similar to the
vegetation pattem observed at Jarefa and the surround hills. The presence of
Castanopsis accuminatissima, Lithocarpus, Podocarpus and Dacrydium in the forests
indicate low montane elements. Large woody lianas, plants with compound leaves,
cauliflorous plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and
towland hill forests (Whitmore 1975) become rare or scarce above 1000m.

6.2 Forest structure

The forest structures are similar in all sites as indicated by the diameter class
distributions (Figure 3.0). That is the current forests are younger. There is lack of
recruitment into the higher size classes. However, the proportion of trees >50cm
further indicate that the original forest was impacted upon by natural disturbance
events in the recent past. According to the locals the drought period of 1997/98 did
affect the forest on the plateau.

6.3 Plant species diversity

The species diversities of the areas surveyed appeared similar with slight variations
that could be attributable to the sampling error. Overall, a total of |.22ha was sampled
with 289 species enumerated. This number excludes other species not present in the
plots. This is suggestive of very high species diversity. The overail species diversity
score for all sites is 2 with the Tahama forests having the highest diversity. This figure
is quite high considering the small area sampled. It is envisaged that this figure will
increase if a permanent Jha plot is established in each site.

4.0 BIODIVERSITY INVENTORY (DISCUSSIONS)

The survey was conducted over twenty working days and nights. A total of 820 trap and 120
net nights and days were utilised in all the three sites. Although maximum effort was put into
the survey in November 2005 the results were quite unsatisfactory.

At site one, only two species of mammals, Paramelomys mollis, a rat and Syconycteris
australis, the common blossom bat, were captured at 1240m asl. We had anticipated more
than five (5) different species of both rodents and bats. The same number was expected of
smailer marsupials and one or two of the larger animals. The reptile composition was aiso
unsatisfactory. No other species was seen except for the very common Emoia lizards.

Putei, which is site two of the survey also yield the same results. After a total of five nights of
sampling none of rats and marsupials except for a bandicoot was caught by locals, five
species of bats and five of reptiles were captured. This is very unsatisfactory because of the
high number of species which are expected to be present in a lowiand rainforest.

The same unsatisfactory results were seen at Pongani. We expected more but caught two (2)
species of rats (Rattus exulans, Melomys rufescans), and four (4) bats (Syconycteris
australis, Pranyctimene raptor, Nyctimene albiventer, Macroglossus minimus) from the
nets. Apart from the white bandicoot (possibly Peroryctes broadbenti) that we saw and some
rats (possibly Uromys caudimaculatus, Mottled Tailed Giant rat) that the survey team saw
scavenging amongst the leaf litter in the forest, there were no captures either from the people
or from children as is often seen in other villagers.

Although actual captures were not what we had anticipated, ethnographic information and also
from our observations, we can say that other factors could have contributed to the poor turn-
over of sampling.

5.2 Social impacts
5.2.1 Hunting Practices

Hunting is still one of the activities that the villagers take part in from time to time. During the
period of survey, a female bandicoot with two young joeys was captured and eaten. Onit the
lower mandible was retrieved for collected.

Food is abundant. People are well nourished with surplus garden food resources. Wild foods
for human consumption is aiso abundant except for protein supplements. Therefore hunting for
wild meat seemed to occur on a regular basis. People have pigs, dogs, chickens and cats in
the villages. However, domestic pigs and chicken are only consumed during important cultura!
occasions, while dogs are kept for hunting and cats as pets to keep house rats away.

People in the area of survey lack protein supplements. Therefore, they will continue to hunt for
wild meat until they can be able to afford protein supplements that are sold in village trade
stores.

5.2.2 Gardening/Subsistence

People in the MPCA are gardeners. Each family has several gardens and food is surplus.
There are so many varieties of food crops, which can cater for their daily supplements.

tend to make way for large areas to be left exposed to the disadvantage of smaller ground
animals. Many trees around new gardens are chopped down indiscriminately and left to rot.
That was seen in many villages where we walked.

According to the villagers, people are currently making gardens in forested areas. which were
never touched in the last hve (2} decades. Gardening in previously untouched forests at higher

INTRODUCTION

The Island of New Guinea fauna consists largely of frogs. According to Richards (2002), the 250
frog species were documented from New Guinea, more diverse compare to other countries. This
is because New Guinea has a constant warm and wet environment that provides humid habitats
and cool temperature at widely different elevations (0-3600m asl) (Richards 2002).

Frogs and other amphibian make up the important component of New Guinea ecosystem and
occur at high densities. They provide important source of food to other organisms and for many
local people (Allison, Bickford et al. 1998).

One aspect of identifying diversity of plants and animals species is to understand and make
broader ecological assessment of biodiversity (Richards 2003). For example Orsak, Easen et al.
(2001), illustrated Lepidoptera, especially moths were chosen because it was used as a general
biodiversity indicators.

This study was intended to document frogs of Managalas Plateau, within approx. 3600 hectares
of virgin forest. Papua New Guinea has difficult mountain terrain which is inadequate to conduct
studies in many interior areas.

Frogs collected at Managalas will contribute to our knowledge of frog fauna in Papua New
Guinea.

The main objectives of Herpetofauna biological survey were to:
1. Document the number of frog species found at 3 elevations at each sites.
2. Identify species abundance and diversity, enable proper management and promote
conservation in sustainable way.

METHODS

A month biological survey was conducted at Managalas plateau, Oro Province from g* ~~ 2°
November. I conducted frog survey at night by search and visual encounter survey. I detected
frogs by their advertisement calls and recorded their calls using a tape recorder. | also did
thorough search on the forest floors, turning over logs and going along streams and search
rugged mountain and steep hill slopes.

At daytime I took photographed of all new frog species in life. I took several body measurements
of frogs and fixed the specimens in 10% formalin and later store them in 70% ethanol. | also
took tissues for future DNA study.

For the purpose of this report, I identify and named frog species according to their morphological
characters. Proper identification of specimens will be given with scientific names and the
specimens will be stored at Natural Science Resource Centre (NSRC) at University of Papua
New Guinea.

CONCLUSION
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) has extremely high diversity of frog fauna.

There was a significance differences in frog species collected at 3 sites. Some species of frogs
collected live and are found only at certain elevation and habitats, (e.g. A/bericus sp) was found
in montane forest. other species do well in high and low elevation, ¢.g. Oreophryne (arboreal sp).
Some species lived only in low elevation (¢.g. Platymantis papuensis).

The data showed high species diversity in family Microhylidae at site | and site 2. The other
family Hylidae, Ranidae may likely show increase diversity. In addition different frog species
forage different habitats. For example, Hylidae are tree frogs and are common along streams,
rivers and live above ground on trees.

SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION

1) Actively carry out awareness program to educate resource owners the importance of
research and conservation.

2) Clearing large areas for gardening increase temperature within surrounding environment,
this practice in future provide good habitat for other introduce animals, ¢.g. Bufo marinus
(introduced toad), easily finds its way in hot temperature. Many frog species become
disadvantage when their habitats and environment change and will from the heat.

3) Develop long term monitoring and research into special plants and animal species. Such
long term monitoring guide good forest management and promote sustainable
development and is vital for decision makers in future.

8. CONCLUSION

Allin all the training was very successful where the trainer demonstrated very useful skills for the rice
farmers. The farmers are now well trained to look after their rice farms and have a very good
knowledge of rice farming.

Therefore such a training is very useful because it provides an option for the locals to use their
resources instead of engaging in industrial activities like logging, mining and oil palm. So such a
training can provide an alternative where the farmers can consume the finish products and also give
them opportunity to sell some of the products in markets.

Rice Survey Report
Date of Survey: 23-27 August 2006
Location: East of Managalas

Survey Done by: Mack Kumoro- PwM Project Officer

Introduction:

As part of PwM’s attempt to alleviate poverty and to improve local livelihood in the
Managalas Conservation Area, under the [UCN funding, this survey was carried out.

Survey location:

The rice survey was carried out in almost all parts of the Managalas Plateau. The survey area
as was divided into two parts. The Eastern part which covers villages and zones starting from
zone 5, at Siribu, Ugunomo, through the zone 6 (Dea, Tabuane, koino, Numba, Kaira, Sila,
Kavoki and A fore was carried out by myself.

hh
Starting from Koruvo (Zone 4) up to Kaitavna, Tahamo thrpugh to Serepuna, Kokoro,
Buamfu, Anatua, koe, Itokama and Nokunane Villages was carried out by PwM’s Eco-
Enterprise Coordinator (Doradora Sogaye).

Farmer Information:
Managalas people have not yet gone seriously into rice forming. The survey indicated that
only few farmers have actually tried out planting, but on a very small scale.

During the course of this survey, the list of interested farmers names was collected.

We also noticed there was lack of knowledge on farming methods. From few rite plots
observed, it became obvious that we found the following:

a) None of the farmers had attended any formal training on rice farming

b) Harvested rice (from few farmers) had not been properly consumed- no proper
milling equipment and all harvested grains got spoilt

c) Current farmers admitted they got their rice seeds from friends and trukai rice
Industries at Popondetta.

snippet: BOOK KEEPING WORKSHOP Afore Council Chambers Afore — Ijivitari District | 24% — 26 May 2004 Report Compiled by: Jacob Ramoi - PwM Project Officer June 2004 1.0: Introduction The book keeping workshop was facilitated by the Managalas Develop …
text:
=== page 1 ===
BOOK KEEPING WORKSHOP

Afore Council Chambers

Afore — Ijivitari District

| 24% — 26 May 2004

Report Compiled by: Jacob Ramoi - PwM Project Officer
June 2004

=== page 2 ===
1.0: Introduction

The book keeping workshop was facilitated by the Managalas Development
Foundation (MDF) Bookkeeper - Luke Mambe and co-facilitated by Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) Project Officer —- Jacob Ramoi from the 24" - 26" May 2004.

The workshop was conducted at Afore Council Chambers for three (3) days. Only
four (4) basic topics were covered because of the experience and the level of
understanding of the Community Based Organisations (CBO).

The topics were:
1. Basic Principles of Bookkeeping,
2. Record keeping and acquittal of funds,
3. Information about Cashbox and Bank Account,
4. Using a manual cashbook.

Thirty four (34) participants and observers attended the workshop. They set up
their own norms & values and their expectation for the bookkeeping workshop.

This report will briefly summarised the four main topics and the
Sub- topics for the workshop. The four topics have their own aims and objectives
for the participants,

1.1. NORMS & RULES

The participants set up their own nine (9) norms and values as house keeping rules
for them to follow during the workshop.

Ask if you want to borrow something
All question are good

Punctuality

Respect one another

Raise hands to talk

No vandalism

No smoking inside

Unnecessary movement

Equal Participants

1.2. PARTICIPANTS EXPECTATIONS

OM NAM SEP

The five expectations of the participants are;
Financia! Report for board of directors
Assist him in his books (bookkeeping)
Specified Roles & Responsibilities
Learn Basic Methods of book keeping
Transfer to skills.

Nal Ba

2.0: PRINCIPLES OF BOOKKEEPING

The main aims and objectives of this topic are:
> To apply the basic book keeping rules
> Identify the responsible of Treasure & book keeper & Committees

=== page 3 ===
2.1: BASIC PRINCIPLES OF BOOK KEEPING

2.1.1. What is book keeping?

1, Financial records correct (accurate recording)
2. Total amount of money received
- membership
grants
office rents
Bookkeeping is a process of accurately recording income, all money received or going
in and accurately recording expenses (all money paid out) of a group. Simple book
keeping is a CASH BOOK.

2.2.2. Why is Bookkeeping Important?

{a}: Group moncy belong to the member of the groups, the moncy,
the group has does not belong to the treasurer or committee. It
belongs to all members together.

(b): -Know what happen to the money
-Know how much money the group has and how it is used.

(c): Help to use money according to plan
Know how much money is left to spent or already spend
Know how much to spend on other things

(d): Show that a group can take care of money (keep good record)

2.2.3. PARTS OF BOOK KEEPING (8 important parts)

(a) Treasurer/ bookkeeper - looks after money
(b) Finance Committee:
a group that help the bookkeeper /treasurer look after the money.
{c) Cash book — safe
(d) Bank account — Bank keeps money
{e} Cash book — Book where you record Incomes & Expense
() Receipts - Book showing money moved from onc person to another.
(g) Monthly Report - Income and Expense record for one month.

(h) Procedure — good way to do book keeping.

2.2.4. TREASURERS & FINANCE COMMITTEE

A Treasurer and Finance Committee are people who look after group's money.

The Treasure or Finance Officer (Roles & Responsibility)

(a) A treasure is an Individual man or woman who looks after money.

(b) He or she should know how to read, write and work with numbers (add,
subtract, multiply and divide)

(c) Treasurer keeps the Cash box, cash book, receipt and receipt book, he/she holds
the bank documents (if they have a bank account.

{d) He/She records down Income & Expenses

(e} Only treasurer takes money out or puts money in the Cash box.

(} Treasurer has the power to take money out of this account.

(g) Finance Committee gives permission to the treasurers to buy some items (they
set limit).

(h) Treasurer submits monthly report.

(i) Treasurer teachers one or two people to do book keeping.

=== page 4 ===
2.2.5. FINANCE COMMITTEE

(a) Smal! group of people who helps the treasure look after the moncy.
(b) They decide what the treasurer can do and can not do.
(c) They decide how much can be used within the budget.
(a) They ask the treasurer to report to them
Correct Records — Easy to prepare
Incorrect records — Hand to prepare & present.

2.2.6. ADVICE TO TREASURER

(a) Open bank Account

(b) Pay expenses by Cheque is possible

(c}) Withdraw funds from Bank Account for cash box expenses
(d) Issue receipts, keep carbon copy

{ec} Obtain receipts for all money paid

(} No. of receipts in order of payment

(g) Reduce details in the cash book

(h) Pay outstanding / invoice promptly.

(i) Keep cash book with analysis on both side.
(j) Asset register

(k) Keep record of money paid and received

(l) Cash in the Cash Box everyday.

3.0: RECORD KEEPING & ACQUITAL OF FUNDS

Aims and objectives for topic 2 are:
> Appreciate the importance of record keeping and acquittals of funds.
> Understanding and prepare different types of source document
> Understanding the process of acquitting funds.

3.1. FINANCIAL RECORDS.

Record keeping are.
* Records of financial transaction (receipts & invoicc)
* Records of financial for goods & equipment (stocks)
* Records of financial of important documents (contact, agreement)
Financial records means to write down organisations money received and paid out.

Record Keeping helps in these ways:
(1) Control] Cash
(2) Performance of the Organisation
(3) Show other Organisation your performance
(4) Records are also needed for performance

3.2. GOOD RECORDS KEEPING SYSTEM

3.2.1. Elements of Good record system
a) Cheque Accounts

b) Petty cash for small expenses

c) Deposit receipts often

d) Support your entries

=== page 5 ===
3.2.2. BASIC RULES OF PROPER RECORD KEEPING

a) Neat & tidy

b) Written clearly

c) Correction fluid not allowed

d) Proper document to be presented at anytime.

3.2.3. SOURCE DOCUMENTS

a) Receipt
is a document which usually shows the money on organisations receives?

5.1. WHAT IS A CASH BOOK?
A cash book is a book in which cash receipts and payments are recorded.

Cash book namely have a column for:

* Money coming in

* Money going out (paid out)

* Moncy which is left in cash book/ bank account

* Date & description of money

Every time money is recorded on paid out it must be recorded and balance
calculated, this cnable us to know how much moncy is in our cash box or account

at anytime.

1. Introduction

In pursuit for the proposed Managalas Community Conservation .\rca, Partners With Melanesians through its
eco-enterprising program and sustainable alternative approach to development to provide a more viable
covironmentally sound development in contrary to large scale destructive development opnons has devised
several alternatives, and Manayalas Organic Coffee tops the list as one of the best possible alternatives for a
sustainable rural livelihoods of the local communities ot Managalas Plateau.

PWM sent a proposal to DOLEN Foundation secking possible funding tor Managalas Organic Cottee Project
and the fecdback actually resulted in this survey to answer certain quarries in the proposal for re-submisston on
the $” of January 2005.

2. Coverage of the Survey

PWM officers conducted a rapid survey covering cach zones from village to village. Only the farmers who
were present at the Hime the survey team visited their villages were interviewed.

3. Objective

‘The purpose of this survey is to obtain an updated baseline data for Manayalas Organic Coffee to back the
proposal to DOEN Foundation to answer specific queries from the previous proposal furnish PW'M's
Manayalas Organic Coffee Project Proposal for Resubmission by January 8" 2005 as per their request.

4. Methodology
A questionnaire was developed with specific questions, which was used by the team carrying out the survey that
traveled from village 10 village interviewing cach farmer who was present at the time of the survey. Who ever

not present was not interviewed. ‘The server team also mspected storage facilities and other capital assets that
might be useful for the MOC?

6, Result Analysis

Reliability: Only those farmers who were present on the time the survey team visited their village were
interviewed. An estimated of 1/3 of the farmers interviewed because they were not aware of the teams visit and
2/3 of the farmers were attending school breakups and graduations some miles away from their villages oF
went hunting or attending their gardens, ‘The timing for the survey was not a good time, however the urgency
of the bascline information gave us no option but to go through with whoever was there. Despite the fact that
2/3 of the farmers were no interviewed, the result from the 1/3 exceeded the previously 60 Tonnes mark with a
massive increase (© 315.99 ‘Tonnes annual production volume. A tough cstmation for the Managalas Plateau
would be between 850-950 ‘Tones annual production level.

For storage facilities where farmers use a spare room to store coffee bags is good for a short ame, however
longer periods will encourage build up of moisture given the tropical humid climatic conditions on the Plateau.
‘The use of wind house for storage purposes is not a good option since the rain can be swept by the wind inte
the wind house thus geuing the coffee bags wet.

‘The production will increase dramutically if there ts proper and constant market accessibility and rcasonable
buying rate. And that would also encourage people to rebabiliiate their abandoned coftce plots and possible
new plantings. ‘There should be a bit of caution because MOCP might encourage more forest to be cleared for
new plantings and this might compromise the purpose of Managalts Community Conservation Area Project.

‘The quality of the coffee is not only affected by the wpe and period of storage but by the type of cherry
harvested and the method and penud of drying as well. ‘The survey questionnaire did not include method of
drying and it will be difficult co verity the ype of beans picked.

‘The questionnaire alse did not include whether the fanners use chemical application to control weeds or ther
weed them manually. ‘This requires specialist information whether heebicides and pesticide application affects
organic status and quality of coftec.

7. Recommendations
We recommend the following:

> Supplementary Survey to be carried out by exch CBO's to cover the 2/3 of the farmers left out in the
first survey as the baseline data is important for MOCP use by PWM and MDI in future.

> Awareness on proper storage, drying method and picking to be carried out to educate all the farmers on
the plateau for quality control.

> ‘There should be proper training on rehabilitation proyranunes and all skills required to produce quality
Manayalas Organic (Cottce.

PWM to start developing a controlled system for MOCP from local growers right through to the

PARTNERS WITH MELANESIANS’ RAINFOREST LITERACY PROGRAM

Scriptwriters’ Series II Design Workshop

(15 ~ 19 March 2004 and follow-up planning 22-25 March)

Summary:

The overriding objective of the Series II Workshop was to provide the Senior Scriptwriter
with a simpler, more streamlined plan for executing the second series of radio
broadcasts and interactive community group discussions. With that in mind, back-up
strategies were developed for keeping progress on target, whether or not difficulties
‘emerged in terms of getting people to and from the Plateau or in terms of people
‘communication over the radio as planned. The production, distribution, and use of the
newsletter (to be completed by the CLCs) was separated from the production,
distribution, and use of the remaining materials (radio programs, flip charts, and
booklets) which will be completed according to schedule in Port Moresby with the help of
Managalas families in POM even if timely checking on the Plateau becomes a problem.
In another move to make things simpler, instructions for helping the facilitators will be
printed on the back of the flip charts.

Finally, the cascade system for training facilitators which called for training events in
each zone following the East/West training of Activity Coordinators has also been
simplified. This year the Activity Coordinators will attend the Master Training Workshop
along with Simon Savaiko, PWM and MDF staff involved in rainforest literacy activities
Then, all the participating group facilitators will attend either the East or West facilitator
training workshops that follow. Zone level activity coordinators will offer additional
coaching to weak facilitators during the four weeks of broadcast but no zone level
trainings as such will be held.

These changes plus technical changes arising from the formative evaluation feedback
are expected to keep the production and implementation of the Series Il broadcasts on
target in terms of meeting broadcast goals and help make the overall program easier for
the limited staff at PWM to manage.

workshop and the first part of the following week where follow-up activity was carried out

Report title: SEWING WORKSHOP

Compiled by Tina Beata — Sewing Workshop Facilitator

1.0: INTRODUCTION:

‘The Sewing workshop was conducted from the 19" ~ 23° of April 2004. This workshop was to
help the mothers to know the basics of sewing and how to sew various type of clothing so they
don't have to spent money on buying expensive cloths. Also to help the women on the plateau
to generate income to help improve their living standard. The sewing workshop was conducted
in Itokama village, Zone one (1) which lasted for five days (one week}.

‘There were 24 women participants participated in the workshop. Six participants each from
zones 1, 2, & 3 and two and four from zones 4 & 10 from the Westerns side of Managalas
attended the workshop. Ten (10) groups of women were formed of three participants each and
were allocated a machine in each group. The participants represent their zones to attend the
workshop so they can go back to their respective zones and teach the mothers. Some
participants came with their husbands who were willing to observe what the mothers were
doing and help get some notes for them. They stayed all through out the workshop till it was
closed on Friday

Generally the workshop was conducted well, not much inconvenience was caused but the
mothers were really happy for such a workshop to be conducted in the plateau because that
was what the mothers were desperately in need to know. This workshop was first of its kind to
be conducted up in the Western side of the plateau.

1.1: AIMS:

‘The main aim of the sewing workshop was to teach the women basic sewing skills so that they
can sew their own clothes and to know how to use the machine. Also to get to know each and
share what they have in common.

1.2: OBJECTIVE:

The main objective of the workshop

+ Teach the women the basic skills of sewing,

+ Teach them how to handle and fix the machines.

+ Participants to go back and transfer the knowledge /ideas/skills to the women in their
respective zones.

1.3: PARTICIPANTS EXPECTATIONS:

Learn how to show various patterns
Generate income from sewing and selling
Learn how to fix machine parts

Know basic skills on sewing
Transferring of skills.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY.

‘The Managalas Development Foundation Strategic Planning workshop was tainted
with external forces. These forces had a great impact firstly on my Terms of

‘There was the management direction to stop the MDF strategic planning workshop,
the unconfirmed tickets to go to Managalas which forced

representative did not come due to the break down in communication. The planning
workshop started on Tuesday and had to be stopped on Wednesday for parents to
attend school breakups. In between there were things like, breakfast
was not provided on time and there was no accommodation arranged for the first
couple of days.

‘The Strategic Planning Workshop would look at a new Strategic Direction for
MDF and help members to self-appraise themselves. The participants were
facilitated and use participatory approaches tools and methods and processes,
to identify an d decide on the following ;

‘The participants were briefly introduced to PNG Pre- history timeline and the
changing societies that PNG is going through. Participatory participation was
explained through an “House Building” exercise. The participants were then
taken to look at what is not Development and what is Development. Introducing
the participants 0 CARGO DEVELOPMENT and the true development, the
Integral Human Development.

The participants used SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunities & Threats) analysis
to identify the Strengths and Weaknesses from within the MDF and then they went
‘on to do a scan of the trends (SWOT- Opportunities and Threats) that are coming
from the outside and affecting MDF as an organization and upon its individual
membership. By looking at the challenges obstacles and/or issues faced by the
Managalas communities internally as an organization and individual membership,
family, clan and the plateau overall. These exercises led the participants to identify
and discuss fully the MDF Needs. The Trends Scan and the Community Need
Analysis helped the participants identify issues that created tensions within
themselves as individuals, the community at large, the 10 zones, MDF and CBOs and
MDF and PWM.

Furthermore, the participants together discussed in smaller groups what is currently
happening and what needs to happen to address these trends and community
needs/issues/challenges/obstacle. The Internal scan, the Trend scan and the MDF
community need analysis including the comments and discussions raised during recap
and group presentations helped the participants to come up with organizational
program components/strategies. Using SMART (being Specific, Measurable
Achievable, Relevant and Time bound) exercise the participants in smaller groups
formulate objectives then identify major activities, then minor activities and
performance indicators to achieve these objectives.

Finally the group defined and have in place a new Strategic Direction and plan, This
plan must be implemented. This executive summary must be read together with the
whole strategic plan if one is not familiar with the concept and approaches in
Participatory Strategic Planning

Background

The socio- economic impact of the Okari nut project on the Managalas plateau
became apparent that communities became organized around it. The establishment of
Partners with Melanesia tasked to organized the Managalas communities around their
cultural and natural resources and further carry out research into Okari nut as a viable
non forest product. There were already threats of large scale logging moving into the
plateau. PWM facilitated communities to be organized into zones created structures
like the Combined Forum Steering Committee Meetings zone boards, clan
committees, zone office and admin support staff and program staff. There are ten
zones established on the plateau. There were few zones that were suspended along the
way, while the most organized zones got incorporated as recognized Legal entity with
IPA. The most notable ones are zone 1, zone 2, and the umbrella body on the plateau,
Managalas Development Foundation.

In 2001, seven after the overall Managalas Conservation Area Support Project
(MCASP) PWM held its first Strategic Planning Workshop at Naukanane. The focus
areas identified were, Consensus Building, Training, Gender and Eco- enterprising
became the main focus component of all the programs carried out on the plateau. As
identified in the strategic plan where there were low interest in eco- enterprising
consensus building stopped. The literacy program in the non formal sector was
established prior to the MCASP and strengthened through the formation and
incorporation of the Barai Non-formal Education Association (BNEA). There were
many activities that were not implemented in Gender and the Training component.

‘The new Strategic direction for MDF identified the need to further up skill staff
program officers and volunteers and provide gender equality in MCASP on the
plateau.

THE NEW DIRECTION FOR MDF

Introduction

‘This report is written and submitted to the Bourd of MDF, PWM and Donor and the
CBOs of Managalas plateau. It will highlight what strategies and recommendations
the one week Strategic Planning workshop identified to enable board members of
MDF to improve its governance within it’s organizational and program
implementations. Most importantly this report contains the Vision/ Mission Statement
Core Values and Beliefs, Goals and Culture of MDE.
The objectives of this workshop are;
1. To develop knowledge, skills and experiences in conducting Strategic
Planning exercises
2. To identify and analyze the needs, issues affecting the work of MDF
3. To develop a shared vision to guide the work of MDF
4, To involved and complete a draft Strategic Plan with Goals, Objectives,
Activities and Performance Indicators for MDF.
5. That this Strategic Planning workshop re-visit PWM Strategic Plan

‘Then outline in general the issues as identified when the strengths and weaknesses of
MDF, through a SWOT analyses exercises as carried out during the workshop.

As results of the participatory exercises prioritized strategies were arrived at for MDF.
The key activities were identified together with their Performance indications. The
issues affecting the Board and Management relationship, policies at the board level
were highlighted as critiqued in the participatory group exercises.

A Plan of Action was documented as an end result of this participatory strategic
planning workshop.

Finally some recommendations for the MDF board and PWM to consider urgently.

The Managalas Development Foundation was incorporated in with IPA in 2001 as an
entity of it’s own.

MDF is committed to coordinating and supporting the work of its stakeholders
towards a fuller realization of a community that is rich in resources, fresh clean water
and abundance in forest, life, land and people, where it’s people respect each other,
live harmoniously now and in the future.

CORE VALUES SUMMARY
The workshop participants MDF core values are summarized as follows:

HOLISTIC and INTEGRATED

MDF believes that for the whole community to benefit , the developmental process

must take into account the Physical, Mental, Emotional and Spiritual development
aspects of an individual, the family, the community and the country.

PEOPLE PARTICIPATION
MDE believes that stakeholders and all people must be active participants in any
transformation processes or programs intended to develop their resources and in order
to improve their lives, through what they have within in order to live and upon which
their well being depends.

EQUALITY AND SOCIAL JUSTICE
MDF believes in the equal participation of all stakeholders within the whole
population of community elders, adults (women and men), youths and children of all
back grounds and abilities, allow equal spread of resources and access to services.
The Managalas plateau has its own ethnic groups with indigenous cultures in addition
to ethnic groups that have migrated and settled in the area permanently. As there are
differing cultures, there are different religious groups that are to participate equally
and should not be over looked.

PROGRAMME GOALS, OBJECTIVES AND ACTIVITIES

The Strategic Planning Workshop emphasized a need for a strategic plan and areas of
focus in program implementations. The main emphasis of this direction will be the
intertelationships between the MDF and PWM, the decentralization of which
programme activities to the MDF to be implemented at community levels through
strengthening of the community based organizations (CBOs) and a closer and clearer
coordinated working relationship with the MDF, and other agencies including the
government through trainings, networking, gender, awareness and resource inventory.

All programs will be coordinated from a central office based at Itokama. However,
there is a need to clarify the roles and responsibilities of PWM and MDF and to
inform the CBOs and the plateau communities of their functions.

For the MDF programmed activities to be implemented successfully, CBCs and PWM.
will have to go through a process of consensus building, community organizing and
participation that enables them not only to work with euch other but also be able to
work with the other partners and agencies that are carrying out similar activities.

cording participant contributions can be
part of the circle if arranged so

. Its best if the room has a blank or nearly
blank wall that can be seen from most posi-
tions within the circle. Ideas coming from
the group should be taped to the wall

22
 Posting Participant
Contributions

Posting Individual participants contributions fos-
ters respects and leads to greater sharing of per-
sonal knowledge and experience

As the set of ideas on the wall gets bigger, the
» group begins to see which ones go together and
which ones don’t really fit with the others

“It is best to record and post contributions in the
2 most dominant languages

If you have to move the ideas on the front wall.
.. Do when participants are present and can see --- |
what happened to their ideas

=

23
 Keeping the discussion
moving

Support staff must work quickly or group dis-
cussion will slow down

+ Care must be taken not to allow the writing and
posting of issues or options to slow down the
discussion

The recorder needs to be writing a short version
of the idea being contributed while the facilitator
in managing the group discussion

. If the flip chart is large, the recorder can divide it
into 4 parts and record 4 ideas on one sheet be-
fore passing it to his assistant to separate and
put on the wall

. The person posting the ideas helps the recorder
by quickly removing completed contributions
and putting them on the wall while the recorder
moves on to what the next person has to say

“ 24
 Selection Procedures

Some groups prefer secret ballots and ask par- _.| -
ticipants to vote by ballot for the three ideas they
feel are the most important

Many traditional groups oppose voting because
it creates winners and losers. They may prefer to
talk things through until a general consensus is

reached

A good compromise for mixed group is to pro-
..vide participants with 4 or 5 small stickers and

ask them to walk to the wall and place their

stickers on the ideas they support the most

The consensus of the group becomes obvious
as some ideas receive far more stickers than the
others and there are no suspicions of what vote
counters may have been doing

25

 Managing patterns of
language use

- Opinions are better expressed and under-
stood if they are given in the language the
Participant finds it easy to use

. Use interpreters for a second dominant lan-
guage to improve understanding and to en-
courage speakers of that language to con-
tribute

. Cluster 3rd or 4th minority language speak-
ers and allow bilingual interpreter to whis-
per key pieces of the larger dialogue

Write down the ideas given by the group in
at least 2 languages so more people under-
stand better

26

 | Setting action plan
priorities

. Participants look at the ideas on the wall to see

which ideas are really parts of the same idea
rather than a separate idea

. Facilitator asks group how many would put them
together and how many would separate them.
Similar items are combined into one group

. Facilitator then asks group if any of the items or
groups need to be implemented before any of
the others

. Facilitator picks out two ideas at a time and asks
group if one of them needs to be done ahead of
the other

. The end result of this step is a prioritize list of
actions that becomes the action plan endorsed

by the group

27

 Identifying next steps

. Facilitator has participants review the
high priority ideas in their plan and
asks them what steps can be taken now
to begin moving those options forward

. Next steps suggested by the partici-
pants are written on the flip chart and
then taped to the wall

. Facilitator then asks participants who
wants to volunteer take responsibility
for the next steps identified

. Participants write their name on a card
and then attach it to the step they are
willing to take responsibility for

28

 Wrap up Options zal at

Think of a closing activity that brings clo-
sure to the forum and lets them celebrate

all they have accomplished

Construct a trigger question that creates an
opportunity for participants to express what
they thought was best about participating in
the workshop

Distribute evaluation forms to assess the
strengths of the process and how best to

improve it

Close the event with a cultural ceremony
respected by the majority of the partici-
pants

 2 Reflection on project progress

Briefly reflect on overall project progress by answering the following questions:
* Are you satisfied with project progress and management so far?
Progress is satisfactory.

* Can lack of progress as planned be explained by risks or assumptions as defined in project proposal? If yes, possibly adjust work
plan or project as a whole,
Work plan 2007 was revised according to the revised business plan and the operation of 2006.

* Do you think the project will end at expected end time? If not, provide adjusted work plan.
It depends on the annual outcome of project implementation, however | don’t think it will end at the expected end time as we seem
to run into unexpected hick-ups such as late release of funds in 2006, PNG National & Local Level Government election that will
be conducted in 2007 (May- July) and least we forget mother nature has its own fury such as rain that causes the road to
deteriorate which is always impassable all the time, During the dry season the roads are quite ok but very rough as a saw tooth
which impacts the springs of the MOCP vehicle and it snaps regularly. The road to the West may be impassable any time when
there is a land slide/ slip between Afore and Sakarina, There is only about 2.Smetres of road passable between two land slip that
slipped from both sides at almost 300metres down. When the land there (2.5m) slip that will be the end of the road to Managalas.
‘This may halt the project for quite a long time because to build a new road it will take 2-3 years to complete around a land slip.

* Do you want to suggest other changes to the work plan? If yes, provide adjusted work plan.
Yearly work plans will be developed depending on the outcome of project implementation for each year.

* Is the budget sufficient? If no, suggest changes and provide revised budget.
2006 budget is sufficient, however, the initial costs of setting up the project was not taken into account at the beginning of the
project. Thus the management systems, central MOCP base, shed and fencing etc cost more as we in reality needed a base and a
proper set up which is safe and secure. As a result, the budget was expended to cater for these items.

In order to achieve quality coffee we needed an expert coffee grader to produce quality coffee. To achieve organic certifi
needed an expert coffee extension officer and to ensure that our vehicle is constantly running we needed a driver/ mechanic not
just a driver, Our operation in 2006 went smoothly as planned and we had achieved results when we milled 14400kg of parchment

Page 15 of 17
 coffee to acquire 11000kg of green bean which brought K66, 000 to MOCP, this was not reflected in the initial Proposal but as we
saw what was needed to achieve results we had to adjust the initial proposal to suit the current setting of MOCP focus and
operation. MOCP needed technical expert staff to acquire results. Those technical officers impart hands on training to locals
during the course of the project. Thus substantial amount was spent to hire technical staff at a reduced rate which included routine
travel to and from the project site and accommodation costs.

* Do you need adjustments to project management? If yes, give concrete suggestions.
Itis realistic to make some sound judgment from the project management as the failure rate of this project is as high as the success of
the project, these is due to the fact that and or if these measures are immediately under taken to rectify the following;

1. The business plan we does not include a fall back/ back-up plan if the prices of coffee at the external cofive markets! mills
drops. In the event that during the course of our operation, the prices of parchment coffee falls bellow K2.00 per kg, MOCP
Will just stop its operation and wait for the external market prices to improve.

‘Thus. in order to beef up its coffers and to have in place a price buffer at such times, | suggest that we should immediately start a
model coffee plantation’ farm using the savannah grassland of Afore or Itokama whilst we have the technical expertise. These
would act as our investment at the time of external market price cuts and the plantation/ farm would greatly help in bringing in
extra cash and not to exert pressure on stafi/ farmers to work over time and also to minimize the use of forested areas
(environment) as new coffee plots to meet set targets. This may only lead to frustration in remote locations like the plateau. Thus
to ease such pressures, it is most appropriate to consider these factor. Further, | am suggesting that we invest our cash income from
coffee sale in other businesses such as trade store, wholesale or other cash income generating businesses so that the funds can be
used to boost the coffee project and make it a self sustainable project. My view is that the prices of cofive are not controlled
locally and that we can adjust prices according to local markets. But as it is determined by the world market pricing we have no
choice but to have in place a buffer system to beat the price cuts, t
2. In the business plan we have also missed out on the issue of the security of our assets, cash and human recourse. In the course
of our operation we had implemented some strategy that worked well in ensuring that our funds, assets and staff were
protected. From past experiences and from our encounters with criminals in and out of the plateau, we had acquired a firearm
as a means of protection against rascals. This had also got us into trouble with the police due to jealousy from our competitors
and other people who were against NGO work on the plateau,

Page 16 of 17
 However, when the government authorities saw that we were genuine in our course to acquire a firearm as security measure for the
protection our kind of business and personnel, the District Court in Popondetta decided in our favor and asked us to obtain the
firearm license ASAP.

Popondetta is well known in PNG as the cowboy town, so cash and lives there are always at the mercy of the thugs/ rascals. As a
result MOCP needed a fire arm for the protection of its assets. From MOCP’s experiences we had K3000 stolen from our CBO
buyer at Koino village on the plateau by thugs, we narrowly escaped unhurt twice on a road block set up by thugs between
Popondetta and Afore. We were held- up at gun point at Barola after coffee sales in Goroka and we were assaulted by locals three
times. Our MOCP vehicle was stoned at least three times last year so we decided to acquire the firearm, which will remain the
property of MOCP.

Previously we were remitting cash by plane straight to the plateau but this practice has ceased as there are no longer routine
service flights done by the third level airline MBA into Itokama anymore. We are moving and will be moving more cash in 2007
by the 280km stretch of rough and rugged road from Popondetta through to Itokama. Thus is very risky task, and we believe
having a firearm as security would guarantee our safety and only to scare away threats from rascals/thugs.

3. Insurance cover is now required for the staff and assets of MOCP. As experienced last year we had no insurance cover and lives
and properties of MOCP were constantly placed at great risks. So J strongly recommend that we take out insurance cover as a
matter of priority,

Page 17 of 17

Managalas Proposed Conservation Area
ORO Province

Students Report on the 3™ phase of the Biodiversity Survey
in the Managalas Plateau. .

June 2006

Report Prepared for the Partners With Melanesian Inc., Port Moresby, Papua
New Guinea. =

Compiled by

Jason Alonk y
Florence Jicki
Jacinta Mimigari

=== page 2 ===
Acknowledgement

We would like to convey our sincere gratitude to the following people for granting us the
opportunity to participate in this survey.

Mr, Ken Mondiai, Executive Director of Partners with Melanesians, Mr. Vincent Manukayasi,
Program Manager, Miss. Danga Mark, Research Assistant and the rest of the staff at PwM. We
are also indebted to Mr. Roy Garawa, the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) West
Field Coordinator and Mr. Dickson Darebo, the Mapping Coordinator, for their assistance during
the trip. Much gratitude also to Mr. Walter (the Aiare village councilor) and the people of Aiare
village for their hospitability stay there. Also thanks to Mr. Samuel (the Umwate village Chief)
and the people of Umwate village for their hospitality. To Douglas Tumai (MDF Chairman) and
family for their selfless giving and hospitality, for their patience and kindness, we say thank you.

We owe our utmost thanks and gratitude to our three team leaders, Ms. Rose Singadan, Ms Janet
Gagul (UPNG) and Mr. Paulus Kulmoi (DEC). We also thank Jones Hiaso (UPNG) for teaching
us how to catch frogs. It was a wonderful experience. Thank you all for the knowledge imparted,
the Jaughs and for making our training a memorable experience.

Thank you!

J. Alonk, F. Jicki

=== page 3 ===
Introduction

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) covers an area of over 360 000 hectares.
It is situated in the south eastern part of the Southern Papuan Ecoregion in the Ijivitari District,
Oro Province. It lies between the Owen Stanley Range to the southwest, the Sibium Range to
the southeast and Mt Lamington to the northeast. The area is comprised of 40 villages with
approximately 16 000 people scattered throughout the plateau. The approximate population size
within the study sites is around 100 individuals. The area is abundant in forest resources and vast
areas of the MPCA are covered in a variety of vegetation types from secondary regrowth,
montane forest to open grasslands. Higher altitude forests exist beyond 2000m.

Partners with Melanesia (PwM), is a national NGO which focuses its work on the Managalas
Plateau. PwM in its conservation programme aims at protecting the undisturbed environment by
carrying out awareness and in the process of establishing a conservation area.

From May 20" to June 4" 2006, PwM engaged UPNG scientists to carry out the third phase of
an on going biodiversity survey in the Managalas Plateau. The main objective of UPNG Post
Graduate student being part of this survey was to gain experience in field techniques and to
render assistance to the experienced field scientists. The information compiled on the flora and
fauna will be used toward the establishment of the Managalas Wildlife Conservation Area.

Methodology

Different sampling techniques are used for plants and animals in the field. A one hectare plot or
a line transect may be used for plant sampling. Mammals are usually trapped or spotted by spot-
lighting using visual encounters at night, while other vertebrates such as frogs, snakes and lizards
are captured during the animals’ active periods. Birds and bats are usually enumerated with the
aid of mist nets, and some times by visual encounters using binoculars. Local information is
some times useful and may be utilized. The sampling methods used in this survey are detailed

below.

Study Site Description.

Two sites were surveyed during this trip. The first site was at Nabumare, located at 09° 19°50"
S, 148° 13°50” E at an altitudinal range between 547-600m. It is in the lower Musa area towards
Aiare village. The second site was at Dakara, located at 09°16°27"’S, 148°14°50°°E at an
altitudinal range between 778-800m. It is about half an hour walk from Umwate village.

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Flora Sampling

A 50m x 50m plot was established using compass bearing. At the 25m mark, a line transect was
placed across the plot for enumerating all plant species. Trees with a diameter at Breast Height
(DBH) equal to or greater than Scm were recorded within 1m on either side of the line transect.
Tentative identification and height of each tree were all recorded. Five quadrates measuring 5m x
5m were also marked out randomly within the 50 x 50m plot and plant species contained in each
quadrate were enumerated. Voucher specimens of all plants within the plot were collected for

=== page 4 ===
preservation at the UPNG Herbarium. This serves as a record of all plant species in the
Managalas Plateau, particularly within the surveyed sites.

Fauna Sampling

1. Mammals

Mammals were sampled using Tomahawk and Elliot traps, while mist nets were used for bats.
The Elliot and Tomahawk traps were alternatively placed every 10m interval in a 50m x 50m
plot previously marked out. At site 2 Tomahawk traps were placed along Kuman and Pingi creek
for water rats. Baits used included roasted coconut with peanut, ripe banana and tinned fish.
Species caught were later skinned and dried for preservation at the Natural Science Resource

Center, UPNG.

2. Birds

Birds were sampled using mist nets erected at about 30cm above ground level to 10/15 meters.
Visual identifications were done for birds too high for nets. Bird identifications follow Beehler et
al (1986) and Coates (1990). Local informants were also utilized for birds not encountered but
were known to exist in the survey areas. Calls were used to identify nocturnal birds.

3. Herpetofauna

Frogs were captured with naked hands as they are harmless. The frogs were found close to
streams, rivers and further inland - terrestrial frogs. Frogs collected were either hiding on/under
leaf litter, exposed on vegetation while others burrowed into the topsoil 10-15cm deep and they
had to be dug out. Frog capture was maximized after rainy periods. During the periods where no
rainfall occurred, few species were calling higher up in the canopy layers. Hence, the favorable
times or periods of collecting frogs are usually during wet weather conditions.

Although less time was spent on sampling snakes and lizards, some specimen were also
collected. The local people brought others in.

Results

Appendix 2 (Tables 1-4) provides a full list of plants and animals found within the two survey
sites. Figures 1-4 are pictures of some of the animals sampled at the two localities surveyed.

Mammals

Twenty species of mammals from seven families were sampled from the two sites (Table 2). The
families Muradie and Chiroptera had more species than the other families (Figure 1). Figure 1
depicts species distribution in each family and Figure 2 shows the species count from the two
sites, Nabumare and Dakara. All the mammal species found in Nabumare also occurred at
Dakara, including 30% more species that were not encountered at Nabumare. This could explain
species prevalence and endemism at higher altitudes.

Discussion

The preliminary results from the two sites were rich in the diversity of plant and animal species
sampled (Appendix 2). The Managalas Plateau encompasses a vast area and the number of
species documented so far may double with further surveys. There was a slight difference
observed in the general make up of the biota of the two sites sampled. Nabumare had more
species of animals than Dakara. The different species distribution is influence by factors such as
the altitudes, climatic conditions, vegetation types and the production time of the forest. Dakara
was at an altitudinal range of 778-800m, which is higher than Nabumare, at 547-600m. The
vegetation of both sites were typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs were well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Apart from our experience in participating in a biodiversity survey, we gained first hand
experience on various field methods that were used to sample the animals and plants. These
included trapping methods, transects for plant sampling and mist netting for assessing birds /
bats. Frogs sampling requires a lot of patience and effective hearing ability. We saw that it was
normally during the rainy period that the catch rate was maximized.

From this trip we were able to experience some unexpected problems that may arise in a
biological survey .We learnt that to collect good results one had to be patient at times, be open-
minded in any discussions and good public relations with the local people. These would avoid
problems such as loss of sampling time, loss of specimens due to domesticated dogs, and the
general lack of understanding from the local people.

=== page 7 ===
Recommendation
The following recommendations have been done after the survey.

1) Study sites should be confirmed and everyone in the area be informed of the survey
team’s arrival. No last minute decision for survey site location.

2) More awareness is required in the potential survey sites. There has to be prior ground
work done so there is ample discussion with the people and they are aware of all that is to
happen in there in advance.

3) Campsites should be restricted to survey team and field guides (or cooks) only.

4) Experienced personnel from PwM should always accompany trainees out in the field.

5) PwM should continue to engage students in such training because it helps in the capacity
building of our country’s up and coming young scientist.

Conclusion

We can say that this has been an exciting and very educational trip for us as we were able to see
what actually happens in the field and develop some skills that may be helpful to use in whatever
field we may be employed in. The training provided in the field was complementary to what we
learnt in school whilst also giving us much needed practical hands on experience in biological
field surveying. To PwM we say keep up the good work and we hope student engagement in
such surveys will continue.

2. Executive Summary

The following Report provides a Summary of the four phase preliminary Biodiversity Survey done
on the Managalas Plateau, in November 2004, November 2005, May 2006 and April 2008 basically
to identify the Biodiversity Significance of the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

Very high diversity of species inhabits the mountains of the Proposed Conservation Area that may
play a major role in diverse species distributions that can be so attractive to the tourist, scientists,
researchers and the public at large. The Managalas Conservation Area is in its proposal stage,
required biological information’s to be recognized diverse and unique in its natural resources,
especially the important species, endemic, protected, rare and threatened. The information’s were
much required by Partners with Melanesians (PWM), that it funded the four Biodiversity surveys.
After all the biodiversity surveys, the managalas community through PwM is now furnished with the
needed biological information’s of the area. Should that be sufficient biological information’s,
Department of Environment and Conservation be convinced that the area be declare a Conservation
Area.

Habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation are the most critical challenges to maintaining
biodiversity globally. Like most areas of New Guinea, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse
array of fauna and flora, but at the moment is poorly documented. Biodiversity surveys have been
carried out but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. Ones the area has gained its
Conservation Area status then further survey and research will be done to investigate the
biodiversity of the area.

3. Objectives of the Biodiversity Survey

The conservation Area remains un-exploited by major developments, except for mini sustainabie
projects enhancing human well-being. The 360 000 hectare area were categorized into ten zones for
proper and equa! dissemination of conservation related programs for all to be aware and understand.
Small projects encouraged by Partners with Melanesians were introduced in different zones to help
to generate small cash income for the local landowners. The projects are so small that they have little
biological effects, which can change the ecosystems of the living organisms and plants, but it may
not be that threatened to many fauna and flora species of the area. The area is virtually high profiles
that make this conservation area a place encouragable for future generations and education,

Both the plants and bird species remain widely distributed and were common for any traditional
purposes to people. Species depletion occurs only when major destruction’s takes place, reducing
population density. After the third biodiversity surveys, bird species were more widely distributed
than the mammals, reptiles, amphibians, except for the insect population that inhabit all vegetation
types at all levels of different elevations.

Main objectives Partners with Melanesians would like to have in place for the conservation area,
were the biological information’s. The unique and the important species have to be identified for a
better recognition of the area that can attract tourist, researchers, scientist and the public at large. For
that, such requirements were important to identify with the yearly biodiversity surveys to provide:

The main purpose of this investigation was to carry out a preliminary assessment of mammals, birds
and herpetofauna that are present in the Managalas proposed conservation area. This investigation
was done to:

(A) Assess the Conservation status of protected species

(B) Identify immediate threats to those animals and other potential threats.

(C) Provide a checklist of both fauna and flora that to our knowledge protected by
CITES, protected by our acts of Parliament.

4, Introduction

Managalas Plateau, for it's conservation area, stretches from the Foothill Mountains of Sibium in the
south-east, Owen Stanley Ranges in the south-west, Owalama Ranges at west, and Guava Ranges in
the north-west with it's high diversity, stretching to the lower altitude plains towards Oro Bay. Much
of the lower plains of the conservation area is disturbed vegetation's, due to high number of villages
that much of the area have been cultivated for subsistence cash cropping, which includes small
plantations of coffee, vanilla, and coconut. The upper mountain and hills remains very high in it's
natural resources, may deplete through careless management's and other major developments. The
area has been divided into 10 zones for equal dissemination of conservation related activities and
viable projects that can generate cash income to the local people of the area.

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses about 360 000 hectares of the pristine
rainforest compromising of the lowland hill and Montane forests in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari
District, Oro province. The forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form the main
catchments for the Bariji and Musa River. The area is bordered by the Owen Stanley range, to the
Southwest and the Sibium range to the Southwest. Popondetta town and the famous Kokoda Trail
are situated north of the Proposed Conservation Area.

Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, which is
poorly documented. Hence having the area declared a Conservation Area, this can allow further
research into the rich diverse forest. Biologist from the University of Papua New Guinea and officers
the Department of Environment and Conservation have so far carried out three Biodiversity Surveys
but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. This is evident from the diverse frog
fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs habitats were good indicators of a rich and vibrant
environment.
