5. Methods of the Survey

To have a very good biological data of Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, various biological
field methods were deployed by each field scientist's to capture different biological information.

All sites of surveys were investigated to find different vegetation types to apply applicable methods
for the data collections.

5.1 Fauna

Birds

Bird species have larger ranges than other animal groups. They also are inhabitants to different
stories of the forest. Species lists involve applying different methods. Managalas area is very large
and has different altitudes, that different species can be observed. Bird surveys of this proposed
conservation area involves few different methods for species identifications.

e A transect-line was established for approximately Ikm and plots were set, in which mists
nets, and mammal traps were layed out to capture birds, mammals’ insects and reptiles.
Specimens were capture and identified. Only unique pecimens were collected to represent
the area. Many species were common indicator, and release after catch.

e A visual observation was done during the day and night of species that were hard to catch in
mist nets. These observation can be done using the established transect-lines, or generally
within the site of surveys.

e Hire of local hunters using traditional methods, (spears, bows and arrows, traditional traps,
and village dogs.

e Conducting biological resource utilization surveys. This method is done to have local
knowledge’s of fauna species being experienced in the area.

Mammals
Mammal species can also be observed at different stories of the forest, that a site survey involves

different methods similar to that of the bird surveys. As stated in the bird surveys, except that
mammal traps were used to catch species within the site.

Herpeto-fauna
Frogs were detected at night by locating calling males and by visual encounters. Efforts were equally
distributed along rivers and streams for aquatic frogs, and away from water bodies for non-aquatic

frogs.
Some frogs were identified in the field, and voucher specimens were also collected for further
confirmation and storage at the UPNG Natural Science Resource Centre.

Snakes and lizards encountered were also captured and specimens collected for preservation.

Insects
The insect sampling was done alongside with other fauna and flora surveys, not very much in detail,
but in observations and collections to available important, protected or endemic species within the

Managalas Plateau.

Others
Other species samplings include, freshwater fishes, eels, prawns, were also an observations and

collections as records of the plateau.

Flora

A 50m x 50m plot (total area of 2500m?) at compass bearings was set up and a peg with coloured
flagging tapes were placed at each corner to demarcate the four corners of the plot. A 50m transect
was run through the centre of the plot and pegs were placed at 10m intervals along the transect. All
trees with DBH of Scm and or more Im away from transect line on both sides were identified and
recorded. Each tree species with DBH recorded had its estimated height recorded as well. Voucher
specimens were collected for taxonomic identification and deposited at the UPNG Herbarium.

Five quadrats (5m x 5m) were placed within the established 50m x 50m plot at random compass
bearings and random number of steps. All plants (herbs, shrubs, palms, pandanus, lianas, trees and
grass) of 0.5m or above within the quadrats were enumerated. Voucher specimens were also
collected for taxonomic identification.

A general collection was also done from the survey sites to determine the type of plants that
comprise the areas.

5.2 Site Sampling

Site sampling is based on where the selected site for biological data will be collected. In_ the first
instant, the formation of the site have to be observed so that the samplers have some basic
knowledge’s of the topography, terrains, the slopes, mountains, the vegetation types, and with
experiences, what records can be expected from species distribution of fauna and flora.

Different methods involve, different biological data collections are then applied to have in place
collected information's of a site.

5.3 Diurnal and Nocturnal Sampling

At every site selected, day and night methods are applied in sampling of the area. Specics
distributions are also distinguished at the same time. The method is very convenient especially with
the findings of the nocturnal fauna species.

All sites from 2004-2008 biodiversity surveys, both day and night samplings were very effective in
recording fauna species. In year 2005 surveys, new records of frog species were recorded in the
mountains of Anatua village, a magnificient bird of paradise was recorded at Aiari village, and
vultrine parrot and sickle billed bird of paradise was recorded at Tetebedi in 2008 surveys.

5.4 Ethno ecological interview with locals

This applicational method is very effective and informative as local knowledge’s provides good
biological data of a sampling site.

6. Survey Sites Descriptions

6.1. 2004 (Phase I) Survey Sites (Altitude Range 672m - 783m asl)

Area of Study: Itokama, Kuwai, Nibaiba, Jarefa and Kadiakala at aprox. 783m asl.

The first biodiversity assessment surveys in 2004 were established at Nibaiba, Kuwai, and Itokama
villages. Seven different vegetation types were identified from the three villages Surveyed, lower
montane forest, lowland rainforest, secondary vegetation, garden sites, (old & new), village sites,
and rivers and creek vegetations.

The main camping area and site for study was at 672 m ASL and located at 9, /2” 35'S; 1480 14”
26'E of Itokama, the nearest airstrip and main village center for any government and cultural
activities. Nibaiba the nearest village is approximately Skm Southwest from where we sampled.
There were 2 sites that were chosen to investigate the composition of the mammalian and
herpetofauna of the area. Both, Jarefa and Kadiakala were within 15 minutes of each other.

Jarefa was the first site of sampling. It is located at the south castern-most tip of the the Yuanga
Range, which continues up into the Owen Stanley Mountains in a northerly direction. The site is
dominated by tall trees of about 20 to 30 m with loads of epiphytes especially those of orchids, moss
and ferns. The understory of the forest was observed to be dominated by fallen trees that were cither
decomposing or had recently fallen due to old age or from other natural causes eg., lightening.
Lianas and vines from the Calamus family seemed to dominate in the undergrowth with loads of
young saplings regenerating areas where the fallen trees had creating gaps for saplings to grow.

7. Results of the Surveys

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area covers a land area of approximately 360,000 hectares.
It is a plateau situated within and around the Owen Stanley Range to the South and West, the Sibium
range to the South East and Mt. Lamington to the North and East. The Managalas Plateau
encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from alpine forest at an altitude of 3800 metres to
tropical rainforest to the mountains and hills as well as savannah grassland and anthropogenic
garden areas. The Plateau is isolated from most of the urban centres within the Oro Province as a
result of poor road conditions.

The plateau has very high biodiversity, with different fauna and flora species, common to rare and
protected. Being a large area, ranges of each fauna species depends entirely on how far each species
can travel. Some are only confined to their required habitats and the food sources in each vegetation

types.

people within the Managalas Plateau have decided to conserve their forest. The information

4. Endemic species
Out of the four-biodiversity surveys conducted in the area, only Queen
Alexandria Bird- wing Butterfly was recorded endemic within the Proposed
Conservation area. The findings from these biodiversity surveys are not final.
Therefore, it is hoped that future surveys might discover species of endemism or
new discoveries to both fauna and flora.

12. Sacred Traditional Areas
The four biodiversity surveys have not encountered any traditionally sacred areas, except for the

cemeteries to all the villages within the proposed Managalas Conservation Area. The biodiversity
surveys have not fully covered the entire land mass of the plateau to finalize sites that were regarded
as sacred traditional areas. It is believed there are certain areas at few sites that were sacred to the
local people at their own village boundaries.

13. Recommendations
Given the uniqueness of the forest within the conservation area, we highly recommend that the forest

be conserved. The following are offered for guidance.

- Proper trapping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting sites are
identified to allow minimal disturbance.

- The pine is a tree of scientific an historical significance. Scattered stand of these species can
be identified and mapped out, both within and outside of the proposed conservation areas and
these areas must be protected.

- The mixed castanopsis forest is very sensitive to Human disturbance. Conversion of these
forest types to grassland is already a common feature in the highlands of Papua New Guinea.
It is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

- Proper record of plant animal uses is established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able te readily access traditional knowledge.

- Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally access the ecology of the
area. This should also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey. Permanent study
plots are established and consistently monitored.

14. Conclusions

The biodiversity surveys of Managalas Proposed Conservation Area have covered zone |, zone 2,
parts of zone 4, and parts of zone 7. There are ten zones within the proposed conservation area, of
which, 6 were initially not covered in the biodiversity surveys. Reasons for not covering the whole
area, is because of the fact that, the four surveys have in general covered the lower, mid and the
higher altitudes of the plateau. However, after the area is declared, detail biosurveys and reaearch of
the entire proposed conservation will be carried out.

The out-come of the biological findings from the four surveys are quite encouraging to have the area
recognized to be declared a conservation area. Many fauna species of importance were recorded
with the avi-fauna and the mammalian communities. No new findings were encountered with the
birds and mammal species of the area, but it is believed that new discoveries were done to the
herpetho-fauna community, especially the frog species of the areas, Murayane mossy mid montane,
inland of Anatua village and Dakara, Humate village.

iwrmooucTion ffl

‘The Managalas Conservation Area is now moving into its phase 2 program activities. There
are several activities under the conservation program that will be implemented that will
collectively form the management plan for the conservation area.

The first and foremost activity that will pave way for the activities to be implemented is the
establishment of the conservation area management committee. Thus this trip was to meet
with the MCF BoD and Staff, CBOs, to make them aware of the Roles and Responsibilities of
the CA Committee and the composition of the committee.

As part of this trip, I was able to attend the MCF 2019 planning workshop held at Oro Guest
House, Popondetta before heading to Afore. Several other visits to community initiative
project sites were done during the trip at the project site.

PURPOSE

‘The main purpose of this field trip were,

Be part of the MCF planning workshop in Popondetta

Workshop on the CA Committee Roles and Responsibilities at Afore
Follow up with Kingsford Nichoi on the zone mapping activity

Visit project sites at the zones level on eastern side of the plateau

METHODS/PROCEDURES

23/08/2018 (Thursday)

PWM team depart Jackson's airport for Girua Airport Popondetta at 2pm. We landed at Girua
after 20minutes at 2:20pm. Oro Guest House vehicle picked us up at Girua to Oro Guest House
where we joined the MCF planning meeting.

At the planning meeting we introduced ourselves and state reasons for the trip.
We overnight at Oro Guest House and depart for Afore the next day with the MCF BoD, MCF
Staff and CBO Managers.

 MCF Planning Meeting at Oro Guest House

24/08/2018 (Friday)

‘Three vehicles were hired for the MCF Board and Staff, CBOs and PWM Officers. Food stuffs
and other items were bought from town and we travel up the whole day. Recent road blocks
along the Afore highway caused fear thus vehicles convoy whenever they travel in this,
highway. Road condition to Afore is bad, thus travel time is 4 to 5 hours, and we arrived at

night.

Arriving at Afore Station from Popondetta

25/08/2018 (Saturday)
Hobert, Kovi, Zone 7B activity Coordinator Nathaniel, and I walked to Numba to deliver green
shed cloth for the reforestation project at Numba.

We arrived at night in Numba and spend a night with the community at Joruba’s House.

 26/08/2018 (Sunday)

The team paid a visit to the reforestation nursery shed. Kovi Wara is doing a separate write up
on the reforestation project. Kingsford Nichoi joined us for the visit to the shed. Apart from
that the community took us around to see their, coffee, and vanilla gardens. They also showed
us bags of rice that are yet to be milled. Their request to SLA Officer was for a rice mill.

Before we left, Kingsford updated me on the issue that he has with his families. He said some
of the stories reported to PWM office are not true, so he is waiting for his broken arm to heal
then he will take the issue to court. I advise him that a PWM BoD Member is leading the
investigation on the money that was released under the Biodiversity Conservation and
Community Mapping to him for zone mapping and for the site inspection of the illegal
encroachment of the logging company. It is now up to MCF BoD and PWM BoD to make a
decision.

The team left Numba early on Sunday morning. We went to zone 7B to visit a community
project initiative and tourist attractive sites.

Reforestation Nursery at Numba Village

Bags of unmilled rice

 Dogarol Lake - Ogan village, Zone 7B, The lake is inside a crater, surrounded by cliffs and thick jungles.

 27/08/2018 (Monday)
Workshop program started on this date. Veronica’s workshop on community empowerment
and Awareness started on this date. The team was part of this workshop. Chrispine and
Veronica Aure have a separate report for this activity.

Participants in the couuunity Empowerment and Awareness Program

28/08/2018 (Tuesday)

Morning session on this day, was schedule for the Biodiversity Conservation and Community
Mapping activity “CA Committee Roles and Responsibilities’. | went thru the roles and
responsibilities for the CA Committee as stipulated under the Conservation Areas Act 1978 to
the participants. The composition of the CA Committee was also outlined. Four (4)
representatives from the Managalas who will be representing the LOs in the CA Committee
will be selected by the communities from the eastern plateau (2x) and western plateau (2x) at
their own time and will be announced during the leaders’ summit in September and then

submitted to CEPA via MCF or PWM. MCF staffs have come up with a selection criteria
guideline for the selection of representatives.

Participants in day 2 of the workshop

 29/08/2018(Wednesday)
‘The team went and visited zone 7B bird watching site and location for a proposed guest house
for the clan. The zone is also embarking on QABB project. They have started planting vines.

Team prepare for site visit to zone 7A community projects sites.

Vines planted for the QABB

 30/08/2018(Thursday)
We left Afore for Dareki in zone 7A. We walked the whole day. On our way we paid a visit to a

proposed reforestation nursery site for MCF Board Member Reynold and his clan. We were
Wwelcomed by the village chief and served with refreshments upon arrival, In the evening we
paid a visit to the QABB site led by zone manager Conwel Nukara.

Welcome by the Chief at Dareki village.

 Female QABB - Caterpillar stage

 30/09/2018 (Friday)

We left Dareki in the morning to Yombu village in zone 8, ward 1. On our way we took some
shots of the boikiki water fall. This is one of the amazing attractive sites for tourists. At Yombu
a sing sing group welcome us. We had a little briefing in the morning and move on to see the
QABB project site and a team of boys from the village was sent with camera to get shots of a
war relics site.

Boikiki Waterfall

 »  Yombu Guest House, Zone 8,
Ward 1

Welcome by a sing sing group at
Tombu Village

 Presented with Gifts from the community

We travelled down to Popondetta the in the evening overnight in Popondetta and travel back

to Port Moresby.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

> Workshop on the roles and responsibilities of the CA Committee was delivered. The
MCF Chairman was not present as he was away in Popondetta and also three other
Board Members from the west. Board members from the east were present.

» Four representatives that will represent land owners in the CA Committee will be
appointed and names announced during the leaders’ summit this month September
and submitted to CEPA via MCF and PWM. Most of activities under the Conservation
Biodiversity and community Mapping Program will be lead by the CA Committee.

> CBOs on the eastern part of the plateau are showing great interest to pursue
community initiative projects, as part of SLA activities. That is evident in the project
sites that the team visited in this trip. Some communities have already engaged with
other stakeholders to support their community initiative projects. An example is the
clan in Zone 7B who are working with Officers from Fisheries to establish a fish farm.

 > Conwell Nukara is assisting other zones conducting surreys to establish QABB farming.
He has done it for zone 8. The CBO in zone 8 are seeking assistance for green cloth to
establish their QABB cage.

> The zones that we visited are now looking forward for phase 2 activities with the focus
‘on SLA. The SLA Coordinator Hobert emphasize that the focus will be on Coffee. He
also stated how work will be carried out next year 2019. Implementers will be MCF
and CBOs while PWM will only facilitate and oversee.

RECOMMENDATION

¥ A few other zones will not fully participate in the coffee work next year, thus t is vital
that community initiative projects that the community have embarked on be taken into
consideration for support as part of SLA activities next year.

Y Zone 8 is seeking assistance for a roll of green cloth to establish their QABB cage.
Conwell Nukara has done a survey on the site and ground works by the community has
started. A roll of green shed cloth in Popondetta costs K500.00 only, so that has to be
done before year end.

¥ Some communities raised frustration that they want to see the fruit of the
conservation work on the plateau. Mr Hobert assured them that SLA will be the focus
program for phase2. Most have recommended the door to door coffee buying.

Y Bishop Ehove have also asked for the work on the signboard at Lamington Park.
Permission has to be granted first for the one that will be erected at Girua Airport. A
letter to NAC Director in Port Moresby needs to be drafted and delivered. In addition,
content of the signboard has to go to CEPA so it can be laid out in the standard layout
template used for all protected areas in PNG.

Y A-community at Buna is interested in the work that PWM is doing. Thus, in the next
trip a day scoping will be taken to see the place and its surrounding.

Y What I gathered from Kingsford regarding the his issue and funds for zone mapping
and illegal logging site inspection, is that he will be taking the matter to court after his
broken arm gets heal. Some of the stories reported to PWM and MCF are not true so he
will take the persons involved to court. However, he was told that PWM Board Member
was on the ground to investigate on the issue, so it will be PWM and MCF Board who
will deal with the issue.

CONCLUSION

The trip went well as it was also an orientation for the Support Program Officer to the project
site. Mr Hobert will be doing a separate report on his program while Mr Kovi will write up for
the Reforestation work.

text:
Video Documentary Report

Numba village (Zone 6)
Managalas Conservation and Sustainable Initiatives project

Community Reforestation and Climate Change program
 1. Executive Summary

This trip report covers the shooting of the documentary of climate Stories in Managalas project site.
Due to the vastness of the plateau, the plan was to start in the eastern side, to at least cover 3
villages of zone 7A (Kawowoki), 76 (Afore) and Zone 6 (Numba).

The team was made up of Climate Change and Reforestation Coordinator Mr. Cecil Senive and
Rainforest Literacy Coordinator Miss Evengelyn Kove and the two Media Consultants.

The Documentary was to cover at least two stories; (1) to capture the stories of local people's
experiences of the impacts of climate change on their livelihood and how they are dealing with it on
a day to day basis.

(2) The Endemic Queen Alexandrae Birdwing Butterfly Conservation as the indicator species
threatened of extinction in the face of climate change.

PwM engaged 2 media freelancers as consultants on a short term contract to produce the
documentary within the given period of time from April through to May 2017.

It was a four days trip from 18” April to 21* April with 2 days planned for travel and 2 days for
shooting interviews on location. However, due to flight delay, Transport delay coupled with weather
conditions the team was quick to revise the plan to shoot in one location. As a result, Numba was
chosen as the ideal site to cover its stories. With the assistance from MCF staff and zone 6 CBO staff,
the video shooting was completed with 5 maximum interviews, audio recordings and cut aways.
Apart from that, primary data collection on Numba profiling were collected including information on
Literacy work, Women and main income generating activities.

2. Introduction
2.1 Background

Managalas plateau lies between 600-1,000 m altitudes above the coastal plains of Oro Province in
Papua New Guinea. It is located between the Owen Stanley Range to the South and West and the
Sibium Range to the South- East not far from Mount Lamington.

The Plateau consists of 360 000 hectares of extremely diverse environment that includes heat at
3,800 meters, mountains and hills, savannah, anthropogenic grassland and gardens. The forest type
{check with Cecil) The plateau is inhabited by over 18,000 plus people from 152 clan groups who live
in over 70 villages. Many of the villages are either located on the foot of the hills, on the ridges or in
between valleys. The people are mostly subsistence farmers who depend almost entirely on the
environment for their livelihood, The Managalas Plateau is relatively isolated and is linked to the Oro
Provincial Capital, Popondetta by a poor quality four wheel drive road and foot tracks. There are 2
airstrips within the plateau, one on the Eastern side of the plateau in Sila and the other on the
western side of the Plateau in Itokama. The remoteness, poor state of infrastructure and lack of
markets pose great challenges toward efforts to improve the livelihoods of the communities
especially in cash income generating initiatives such as production and sale of coffee and other
produce out of the plateau.

Basic government services is restricted to a number of schools, a top up and two aid posts and a
station and health centre at Afore. The University of Papua New Guinea in partnership with The
‘Summer Institute of Linguistics introduced adult literacy classes in the 1960s which has paved the
way for recent development initiatives on the plateau.
 The Plateau with its vast natural resources and high quality agricultural land has over the past
decade attracted interests from potential investors on timber extraction, Oil palm ana mining,
However, the communities have been actively opposing these due to lack of consultations with the
resource owners and the failure by interested developers to guarantee benefits or environmental
protection

2.2. Managalas Conservation and Community Sustainable Initiative project

‘The Managalas Conservation Area project is managed by PWM working in partnership with local
partners the Managalas Conservation Foundation with its 11 zone CBOs on the ground funded by
Rainforest Foundation Norway (REN). The Conservation Area has been approved by NEC on the 16"
of December 2016 for gazettal stipulated under Conservation Areas Act 1978 and the Protected Area
Policy. Currently awaiting gazettal notice from Conservation and Environmental Authority.

The supplementary programs includes Education and Awareness, Consensus Building, Capacity
Building and Sustainable Livelihood Alternatives. The overall objectives of the programs are to
promote conservation of natural eco-systems including endemic and endangered species and
encourage Small scale iatives to generate cash income for the communities to meet their basic
needs. The program activities are implemented through the organizational structure or network that
includes Managalas Conservation Foundation and the eleven Community Based Organisation (CBO).
For SLA, PWM has been working closely with the local CBO and community groups to promote
production and marketing of the following;

© Organic Coffee
© Village Artefacts and Handicrafts

‘© Okari Nuts, peanuts and other forest products
‘© Vegetables and garden produce
 ‘The Managalas Conservation Area Project, Afore LLG, ljivitari Electorate, Oro Province

As this phase of establishment of Protected Area ends at the end of this year of 2017, the next phase
will be looking at strengthening Management Plan and its Committee that integrates community
sustainable livelihood alternatives.

The challenges still remains with the disparity within the mainstream systems in terms of planning
and designing, implementation and monitoring and evaluation of project development and
management. This hinders the progress of achieving the desired outcomes. One of the challenges
that cross-cuts all sectors is Climate Change.
 2.3. Climate Change in Managalas

Climate Change only became an issue in Managalas after two major climatic events occurrence 10
years apart with the Drought in 1997-1998 and the cyclone Guba in 2007 that altered their way of
life since then. The after effects of this natural disasters have caused many locals to question the
changes which were at that time new and unfamiliar to them. They perceived this as a major threat
to their future and sprung up to action by raising it at their District Wide Combine Forum in 2010.

As a result, In 2011 NARI was engaged and conducted an awareness Workshop on Drought impact
and coping strategies held at Afore Station. The participants consisted of 11 Zone CBO staff and MCF
formerly known as MDF. The participants were given information package, a few drought resistant
crop seedling (mammy yam, cassava) to carry out awareness and distribute in their respective zones
through their consensus building process afterwards.

Due to immense pressure to continue with programs related to climate change, it gave rise to
climate change and reforestation intervention under the ongoing Conservation and Community
sustainable development project in 2013 funded by Rainforest Foundation Norway (REN)

2.4.Climate Change and Reforestation Program

For this first five year period, Climate Change was focused on Education and Awareness and trying to
link it to reforestation initiatives as a way to offset conservation efforts. The program tried to look at
identifying the knowledge gaps of the communities in order to bridge the gaps between local and
scientific knowledge. The intention is to assist the locals in comprehending the meaning of Climate
change as lead up to the next phase, the program looked at how best to plan and design best
practices compatible to specific site needs.

From the results, many of the locals are aware of the signs of the climate change, however in terms
of adaptation, it would need creativity and innovation as the way forward. Many locals without
realizing have been using traditional Knowledge at their level, however it is not enough to withstand
the onslaught of the impacts hence, scientific knowledge with user-friendly technology can capitalize
on this knowledge to bring about change in the long run. It is when identifying gaps and innovate
strategies that strengthen and build new concepts promoting best practices.

With that in mind, the idea is to empower communities through initiatives that can positively
influences people's consciousness or their behaviour to adapt to changes happening around them.

One of the very influential area in this era of Information intelligence is the use of Media. In the past,
information were stored in the library, in schools and with experts which most times were
inaccessible. Now more than ever, information is accessible and shared faster through different
platforms using available mediums.

Therefore, this Initiative of documenting the stories of the locals is one way of showcasing diverse
stories where platforms are created for dialogue. Different People can relate to one another and
share experiences and learn from each other for best adaptation practices.
 3. Purpose

Climate Stories project
The primary purpose is to capture captivating stories of the locals on how they are coping with the

changes with the objective of creating a positive imagery on embracing climate change whereby
locals take initiatives to address climate change on a daily basis.

Literature Review

Using the power of Media to tell the stories of people who are affected and to change the outlook of
the issue of climate change. Everyone takes action and engage in ways that will improve the concept
of taking ownership of climate change. Mediums such as film making (documentary), audio
recording, photographs.

“Climate Change is a story or rather billions of interlinked personal stories. For the most part,
however, we distance ourselves from Climate Change through the buffers of scientific data’s or
political battles. As a result, mony people relate to Climate Change on paper. In order to change
public attitudes, we need to tell the stories of people around the world for which Climate Change is
present reality”

Unknown, Climate Stories Project

Story telling is the timeless, universal language that ties all together as human kind. It helps to make
sense of each and every individual's lives and the world around. It can illuminate the human spirit
and not only delight and entertain but enlighten, engage and inspire change for a better world.

Story has the infinite power to connect people across time and space and frame the human
narrative by transcending borders, cultures, boundaries and barriers. It gives voice and meaning
especially to those who may have been silenced or where no voice existed before.

Story can have an extraordinary force for good; for transformation for positive social change,
influence and impact. And at this critical moment in human history, there is a need more than ever
before for a new diverse humanistic voices to be heard and for new stories to be told and delivered
over a multitude of platforms that digital technology has democratized and made available to
everyone.

Story cuts across everything we do. Scientist, engineers, business leaders and doctors are now
looking at the power of story to help them communicate their ideas and research more effectively to
both their peers and a broader public audience

“A powerful medium of cultural preservation in a country of mythologies, film making may become
the only solution to an already threatened cultural autonomy in PNG. Feature films such as Marabe,
Tukana and Walkabout belong tonten are stories of different protagonists amid their own conflicts,
however, from these films, one may learn of the lifestyle, history in the pre-independence, their
attitude and reaction to the changing times. On the other hand, documentary films such as First
Contact, Kama Wosi and Gogodala as well as several others, depict culture in the art of cerving,
dancing, music and customary rites.”

Shirley Komogi, Freelance Writer, The National Weekender og 4, 16/06/17
 On April 13-15 of April 2017, Rising Voices brought together Indigenous and Western Sciences in
addrassing Climate Change Adaptation and mitigation. Over 14C participants from around the globe
convened for dialogue and strategies for action. The theme for Rising Voices workshop was
“Pathways from Science to Action. Its objective was to diversify Climate Science and solutions to
weather and climate extremes that includes indigenous science.

“Indigenous people have drawn on Indigenous Knowledge and science for millennia to understand
‘and respond to change and environmental change they faced. This knowledge is deeply embedded in
‘our worldviews and relationships with the natural world in our cultural practices. What is different
and challenging today is the rate of climate change occurring made by man and our ability to
respond to it. We must correct the path we are walking on and return to the special relationships, the
teachings, the knowledge ond the practices that maintains respect, honour and relationships in the
natural World”

Suzanne Benally, Cultural Survival Executive Director.

The need to capture the historical events whether it’s oral histories or written histories using such
mediums is crucial at this rapid changing times. It provides an opportunity to see the transition of the
people and their relationship with nature to sustain each other up until today. This videos and
recordings can be showcased at different platforms locally, provincially or nationally to start dislogues
and conversations on current issues such as Climate change with the objective to challenge and
engage every stakeholder to be part of the solution only through innovation.

 Feature Stories

“Benefits of CA/Outcome of Establishment of Managalas Conservation Area
1. Education and Awareness
2. Training
3. Community Mobilization
4. Facilities
5. Mapping
“Short term and long term

INTRODUCTION

‘The Combine Forum for this year is different from the last 33 years because it is the start of the new
era for the Managalas Conservation Area and is now the second phase after Conservation Area
(CA) declaration last November.

‘The declaration is followed by the signing of an MOU between PWM and MCF during MCF’s
planning meeting just few months back (September). The MOU clearly spells out roles and
responsibilities of PWM and MCF.

MCF will now take on more roles with the implementation of activities while PWM will only be
here to facilitate.

‘The Combine Forum is part of the Consensus Building Process where the process starts from the
lowest Family unit, up to the clans, then onto the Zone levels and finally to the District Wide
Forum. issues discussed within the family units, clans and zones are then presented and discussed
in the District Wide Forum.

PWM and other stakeholders assist where they can in terms of providing guidance and available
options so communities can decide and agree on the way forward.

Hence, this Consensus Building Process/Rainforest Literacy Program has now evolved to
Community Empowerment and Education Awareness with an objective to facilitate, mobilize and
empower communities through traditional decision making processes and aiso inform, encourage
community participation and networking in sustainable management and development and
development options for the natural resource base.

As stated above, this new approach has left out the other parts of this process and still maintaining
the Scriptwriting workshop, Zone Forums and the Combine Forum.

‘The Combine Forum was jointly implemented by Managalas Conservation Foundation (MCF) and
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and it was held in Yombu village, Zone 8 on October 29" —
November 12018. The participants from around the plateau were warmly welcomed by a sing sing
group with the sound of the kundu drums and a variety of local fresh produce straight from their
gardens.

Despite logistical problems and other minor shortfalls during the 3 days forum, there was a good
turn-out of people, plus we had two (2) very resourceful people from the Oro Provincial
government representing Fisheries and Dept of Agriculture and Livestock.
 MCE Literacy Field Coordinator, Crispine Burawa is the lead facilitator, while PWM supervised
the process.

PWM’s Program Manager Rufus Mahuru and Staff (Veronica, Hobert, Patrick) also attended the
District Wide Combine Forum.

PURPOSE

The purpose of the Combine Forum for this year as discussed above is basically for;

~ the Managalas people to come together, discuss pressing issues brought forward from the
Zone forums

- Collectively identify the way forward for each of the issues.

- Identify specific plans to bring forward in terms of sustainably managing the CA

- Give the Managalas people are sense of direction and for further clarification regarding life
after CA.

- PWM and other stakeholders to guide the discussions, ensure the activity happened as
planned and reports/acquittals are in place.

The Combine forum took place on 29" October ~ 1° November, 2018 at Joivi village, Zone eight
(8).

‘The three days’ forum saw a good number of turn out by both male and female from around the
plateau, While there was no representation from Zone 10 presumably because of the distance to the
Forum Venue and late confirmations of the Forum venues/dates, the issues discussed seem to fairly
include them to some extent. There were two GoPNG reps at the provincial level; one from
Fisheries and the other from Department of Agriculture and Livestock.

To get a clear picture of the representation/participation, see the attendance list attached with the
MCF Forum report.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

‘As per my observation;

1. The logistics on ground was not as expected, participants were accommodated outside of the
forum area. It was raining in the mornings and participants had to take shelter until the rain
stops. They were late for the morning sessions. Access to river/creek was a problem to
participants because it was distance away from where they were accommodated.

2. The Forum Process was not followed resulting in discussions going off track/diverted from the
main issues of concern.

/8
 3. Network/link was created with the Provincial Fisheries and DAL office and this is an
opportunity for the CBOs to make use of this opportunity especially with SLA activities in their
respective CBOs.

4, The roles and responsibilities of MCF/PWM have now been spelt out clearly during this forum
with reference to the MOU signed recently which means this year in, year out issue on “ROLES
and RESPONSIBILITIES” will no longer be an issue.

5. During the combine forum a lot of issues were not discussed in depth because they were not
clearly understood. This showed that CBO’s on the ground are not creating enough awareness in
their respective zones regarding the issues.

6. When organizing such forums in the near future, first and foremost, we must always look at
accessibility to clean and safe drinking water and road. A lot of participants walked a distance to
access the above which resulted in their late attendance at the forum.

7. More networking must be established between responsible authorities of the government so that
they can also have their say in the sustainable management of the plateau by working alongside
with MCF/CBO’s in the CA.

CONCLUSION

‘The Combine Forum is a great avenue for the people of Managalas to come together come end of
each year to discuss and identify way forward for the benefit of all. Hence this avenue must be
maintained and taken seriously if the Managalas people want progress and development in the
Plateau.

RECOMMENDATION

My recommendations are on areas that I feel strongly towards as per my working experiences in
local communities including the Managalas Plateau.

1

Community Empowerment and Education Awareness Program

‘This program is vital and its activities must be revisited/redesigned and aligned with its
Purpose/objective since it has shifted away from Rainforest Literacy and a part of the
consensus building process left out. Theatre activities must be included because it is the
only medium currently being used for awareness and information dissemination purposes
around the plateau.

Also, this scriptwriting workshop be changed to content development workshop or
something along that line (only a suggestion) because as it is, we are no longer developing
radio scripts for the radio programs and learning objectives for the print materials like it
used to be.

The lessons Jeamt from this Program especially in Managalas must be taken into careful
consideration and NOT repeated in the new Project areas.

Also have a Neutral Forum Facilitator

It is always essential to have a facilitator who is neutral and will not take sides. Having a
fair and balanced discussion is fundamental for an effective consensus building process.
Therefore, facilitation of any forum in the near future must always have a neutral facilitator
and also a co-facilitator to take on the facilitators responsibility if need be.

There is a Need to Identify Proper Program Activities
In addition to recommendation #1, there is a need to revisit the Consensus Building
Process/Rainforest Literacy and clarify certain changes. We should be careful NOT to

/6
 repeat the Managalas experience in other project areas because obviously their social
structure and fabric of society is completely different. Therefore, we must seriously look at
how best the overall program will suit individual areas.

Executive Summary

From mere observation of its structure Managalas Development Foundation has
been unintentionally designed to function as a supra system consisting of various
sub-systems and systems of systems hence appropriating it to adapt oa training
strategy that will enhance the various sub-systems to function independently yet
collaborate with each other to meet the overall goals of the community based not-
for-profit organization's capacity building needs. [Very similar to the Melanesian
circular system of governance in which service delivery, community mobilizing and
etc. is often led by influential individuals however the emphasis is placed on overall
community welibeing. It involves active participation and interaction between
individual, groups of individual and communities. Collaboration and
interdependency has always been the norm].

The success of its various programs wili heavily Gepend on the efficiency of the
individuals involved thus the training strategy is to produce learning individuals who
will tasked themselves to undertake various activities of MDF as personal action
learning projects. It is anticipated that by the end of an individual action learning
project using “systems learning approach” the participant will have advanced
himself in his personal capacity whilst at the same time appreciating the overall
human resource capacity of MDF.

The ‘systems learning’ approach is based on Kolb.s experiential leaming cycle and
draws also Peter Checkland’s ‘soft systems methodology’. it emphasizes
participation and calls for open and active pctterns of communication based on
interdependent relationships’, and necessitates action to develop it. This requires an
appreciation of stages in group development and how to facilitate group
processes. The key is to see things differently, if we are to act differently - and we
need processes that enable this.

Its application has been proven to be a success with MICAD in the Collingwood Bay,
and Dadakol in the Managalasi, where projects based on various activities of
different programs were undertaken by groups of individuals as personal action
learning projects hence meeting some of the overall objectives of their CBOs. The
Airara and Sinafa jetties, the Dadakol Canteen and Resource Center and Coffee
projects have been inspired by this program.

The personal action leaming projects generated through the MOF TNA workshop
basically encompasses the various actions that MDF otherwise wovid be expected
to deliver using traditional methods which evidently has not been successful thus the
emphasis now is for MDF to shift its activity funding to support this new approacn.

PURPOSE

The main purpose or the aim of this workshop was to grow temperate vegetables like cabbage,
carrot, Chinese cabbage, lettuce, capsicum, parchoi etc. Due to the fertility of the existing soil,
which is considered as volcanic soil in Managalas Plateau, through the initiative and invitation of
Managalas Fresh Produce Limited, PNGFPDA was invited to train the local farmers on how to sow,
transplant and grow aforementioned temperate vegetables to meet the market demand which is
evident in Port Moresby. However, before the practical, 2 days of comprehensive theory sessions
were held from 2™ to 3" July to ensure all participants understood the procedures involving in
preparing the soil for sowing; how and when to sow and the allowable distance between each seeds
in enabling them to germinate. On 4" July, first morning session was spent on theory until lunch.

‘Afer the lunch break, participants were sent out in groups to the nearest rainforest to collect trees
and other local building materials required for building nursery and the green house. Late in the
afternoon, the men folk started building green house until it was satisfactorily completed.

The programs were diligently executed as planned in the activity plan, Through the mutual

novices’ methodologies which is essentially expedient for the locals to ensure every participants
understands disseminated information thereafter.

Afier completion of the green house and sowing of seeds, we inspected the model farm and were
contented with the availability and the preparation of landmass, the clearance and the drainage
structures, especially the well-constructed access water outlets that can be disastrous for the plants
during continuous rain.

Notwithstanding the above, no major problems identified during the training. Hence, all went in
well according to the plan.

‘As per the call received from the local SLA officer, Ezekiel Garui- all seedlings transplanted and

sowed seeds which are still in the nursery germinating. They are anticipating to the sell their first
produce of the first transplants this month.

CONCLUSION
‘The hosting of the week long training for the locals to grow temperate vegetables was a success as
the result of reciprocal participation through cohesive cooperation convened by the local
participants, the Tahama village people and the onlookers.

PWM to support the locals living through liaising with Managalas Fresh Produce Development

arrived at six o’clock morning. Dickson Darem¥o, MCF Project Officer was at Popondetta waiting

We went to Oro Guest House and made a quick plan for the trip and he was out on the road looking
for a hire car to take us to Afore. He finally came back with an Open Back Land Cruiser after an
hour and we were on our way to the main shopping mall to buy the rations, We started our journey

We spent a night there and was planning to take a long hike along the Managalas Plateau to

On the 28" June, I walked to Tahama village with local SLA officer. Spent a night there and when

produce. Therefore, 1 went there with farmers’ payment to buy okari nuts from the farmers living

However, the envisioned intention of my trip was not accomplished due to charter delay, The

INTRODUCTION

A trip was organised and taken by Cecil Senive who is Coordinator for Community Reforestation and
Climate Change Program (CRCC) from the 27" August to 02 October 2018 to Managalas Conservation
Area. It was an assessment trip taken to evaluate the situation on the ground relating to halt of work in the
forest nursery in Numba, Managalas Plateau as a result of misleading information being fed to the local
people and also the mismanagement of Conservation Biodiversity & Mapping funds for the Managalas
Plateau or CA.

Accompanying me to the site and also for SLA (sustainable livelihood alternative) activity errand is Hobert
Poria (SLA Coordinator). Hobert was on site with Patrick Vuet (Conservation Biodiversity & Mapping
Coordinator) and Kovi Wara (Program Assistant Officer) that time when the issues were raised. The trip
however did not achieve its intended purpose.

This report entails the details of the trip and also why the trip was not made to Numba for the evaluation. The
diversion made hence is also discussed in this report.

PURPOSE

‘The ultimate purpose of this trip was to evaluate the situation on site given the issues that halted the work at
the Numba Nursery in the Managalas Plateau and to assess the seedlings in the shed as they are well passed
the transplant time.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

Information received from the site prior to actual visit was that Kingsford Nichoi who is the Officer for MCF
(Managalas Conservation Foundation), a local CBO in Managalas Conservation Area Project has caused
some problems or misunderstanding which eventually halted the work in the nursery in Numba in Zone 6,
Managalas CA. It was reported that he initially advised the locals that payment will be made to them under
reforestation program for their service rendered when he clearly knows that such is not catered for under
PWM program budgets. Since it is a community conservation project, the locals know that programs
implemented are to help them in their endeavor to sustain their natural environment whilst they look
elsewhere to sustain themselves. Instead, he raised expectation that led to queries and threats.

This problem surfaced after he deliberately misused the funds for boundary remapping and investigation on
suspected logging infringement around Managalas CA. That triggered a misunderstanding amongst the
locals that had them think that part of the money that was misused was for their nursery compensation.

 Hence, the locals stopped work and threatened to vandalize nursery shed and all seedlings within. They also
threatened to beat Kingsford if he confirms that the allegation against him was true.

Besides, Hobert, Veronica, Lillian and Cecil all arrived in Afore on the 28" of August. The following
morning, Cecil confirmed the information through the youths who went to Numba for theatre performance
the week before. They also advised that the situation is tense out there and that there are no proper talks
between Kingsford and the people and if Cecil as the program coordinator for reforestation was to go up to
refute the arrangement {o pay locals as misinformed, they would fight against Kingsford and his family
members. The issue has escalated since then and to this date has become a village or family matter. Upon the
advice given, Cecil opted not to take the journey to Numba. Even though an attempt by Hobert and Cecil
was made to walk up to Numba on the 30" of August together with some youths, villagers along the way
stopped them and echoed the same story hence the trip was not taken.

Given the unsuccessful tum of events, Cecil made the decision to divert food rations and the 5,000 polybags
to Nathaniel and the youths at Darekol Lake in Afore to put up a mini nursery whilst working on the SLA
Eco-tourism Project at the lake. In fact, it was there interest as part of their beautification program.
Otherwise, the polybags brought up to Numba would do nothing but await outcome of the issues and in the
process might be misplaced.

During the same time, Hobert also presented materials bought under SLA program to Dadakol QABB farm
in Deriki where Zone Forum was conducted by Veronica and Lillian, and some more materials to youths at

Darekol Lake respectively.

DISCUSSION

As highlighted in the findings, the issue with the nursery has gone up a notch, involving family members of
Kingsford, people in Numba and neighboring clans that have worked in the nursery. This has now caused
disharmony and so the coordinator responsible decided to let MCF to deal with Kingsford on this issues.
Mean time, locals were advised to be rational in dealing with issues and not to go to the extent of destroying
the nursery where the seedlings are all matured and are ready for transplant.

A formal letter will be written and addressed to Kingsford by Cecil and Patrick regarding respective issues.
MCF through their director Mr. Damien Ase has also advised that the work in Numba will be on hold until
the maiter is sorted out in the best possible manner that will not affect PWM and MCF work in Managalas.

‘On the other hand, the diversion of polybags and food rations to Dadakol Lake in Afore was scen fit as
nursery scedlings will complement their beautification program in their endeavor to create an eco-tourism
site for tourist and other outdoor enthusiasts that come to visit. Cecil will continue to monitor the progress of
that nursery and will assist where appropriate under the community reforestation and climate change

program.

CONCLUSION

As far as the issues are concemed, the bark is on MCF and Kingsford to resort the issue. PWM will only
come in as far its (CRCC and BC&M) programs are concemed.

Reforestation program will still continue after the matter is sorted out. Reforestation training will be
conducted followed by transplanting of seedlings as well with the appointment of the reforestation

‘management commitice to oversee the management of the nursery. This committee is on voluntary and the
committees are free to leave and be replaced by any one member who will be willing to take up a position.

RECOMMENDATION

Recommendations are:
= MCF to fast track the investigation and resolution processes for programs to continue;
= PWM to only intervene when it concerns program activities or its assets; and
= No reforestation work in Numba until there is certainty that the issues are settled accordingly.

in the last 3 days. However, the only concern raised was for such training to be conducted twice in

S6

=== page 7 ===
the plateau as many farmers are concurrently into vanilla cultivation. When each participant was
asked to disclose the number of vanilla tress in their gardens, I was amazed to discover that almost
80% of the participants exceeded 100 plus trees. Hence, vanilla would inevitably be another major
cash crops apart from coffee. Subsequently, it is foreseen that if the local farmers produce quality
beans by following all standardized procedures disseminated by the trainer, vanilla will
undoubtedly supersede coffee by becoming the major cash crop for substantial income generation
due to its exceptional global price per kg.

No major hindrances or problems encountered during the training. The only notable problem was
the capacity of the training venue unable to sustain the number of participants. Nevertheless, this
didn’t hinder interested and unregistered participants from listening and taking notes during the
training from the outside of the hut.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

I cannot summarize on the result and the finding at this time. Therefore, | need to take another trip
March 2019 to Managalas purposely to visit vanilla gardens in the plateau and to see if there were
new gardens made after the training and to see the final produce ready for market. As per Mark
Gozapao, a requirement for a bean to be graded as A grade are:

U 1Scm( +) in length

(ii) Black in colour

(iii) Produces strong vanilla odour

(iv) All beans straight and not curvature

Having the above rudiments as prerequisite for assessment, it'll be more convenient for me to visit
the gardens and the beans harvested and are ready for sell. After undertaking the filed visit, I will
compile a comprehensive summary for all to glance through and comment should deemed
necessary as part of the conclusion of this reporting.

CONCLUSION

Vanilla is an expensive commodity and hence its price per kilogram has already enthused a lot of
farmers to venture into vanilla cultivation. Affirmatively, in the next few months, | am anticipating
a lot of new vanilla gardens to emerge in the plateau inevitably.

During the training, the local farmers realised that coffee requires a lot of odd jobs but the
remuneration package after selling doesn’t value the amount of job entailed during the processing.
Likewise, the cost involves in transporting this commodity to the nearby market is also excruciating
for low and average income earners. Despite vanilla warrants skills, placidity, commitment and
concentration to produce prudent outcomes, when evaluating its transportation cost with the coffee,
vanilla isn’t troublesome. Hence, is another advantageous attribute that will induce the farmers to
venture into it,

The training was well conducted and all participants were satisfied. However, most of them
proposed for MCF/PWM to arrange for another training for those farmers who missed out on this

one.
Highlands Vanilla Project also assures farmers of buying their product using the current price

henceforth.

=== page 8 ===
RECOMMENDATION

Highlands Vanilla Project to conduct another training somewhere in Koruwo Ugunomo, or Koeno
in 2019 as per the farmers’ demand. During this proposed training, those farmers who ventured into
vanilla farming will also bring their beans to the trainer for grading and buying during the training.
Since Highlands Vanilla Project also involves in buying the beans, it is undoubtedly advantageous
for the vanilla farmers in Managalas Plateau because the trainer will also became their buyer

simultaneously.

MONTHY REPORT — SEPTEMBER 2015

1 INTRODUCTION
‘

This is the repgrt for the month of September 215. The report covers the activities
undertaken in the moth. Much of the work has been around working with PwM in
coordinating the assessment on the draught affecting communities on the plateau and
continuing liason with CEPA. staff for the gazettal process for the Managalas
Conservation Area. There has been good coverage by media of the drought on the
plateau and together with assessment by MCF and CBO staff should get the
government to act in providing relief assistance to affected communities. As for the CA
gazettal process, we finally had the CEPA field Officer in Popondetta to meet with the

2 COORDINATION FOR DROUGHT ASSESSMENT

As mentioned in the last report the drought (El Nino) on the plateau like other parts of
the country started at the end of April and after almost four months the peéple are
feeling the effect of and all leaving their villages and going igo the forest iti search of
food, water ete, This is affecting implementation of field activities and MCF staff have
reported that the food gardens are drying up as well as rivers and streams. The drought
is also affecting schools in the area and they are sending children home 12pm. PwM
management responded promptly to the request for, ititial assessment of the drought
and planning meetings were held to develop plan on iow to assist the affected
communities not only on Managalas Plateau but otligt,PwM's project sites as they are
also affected by the drought. ,

Together with PwM staff, arrangements vere madg for medidiegreaentatives were

evel to update them on the situation and gather information on the action by the

 for disaster response and management. This off-course will dependent on approval being

the drought affected communities.

LIASON WITH CEPA FOR GAZETTAL OF MANAGALAS CONSERVATION
AREA.

‘This particular activity is an on-going activity as it is important and to meet our overall
objective to have the plateau designated a Conservation Area (CA) under the

work together with CEPA staff to move the process forward. One of the main challenges

ARRANGEMENT FOR CEPA OFFICERS MEETING WITH AFORE LLG

text:

EL NINO ASSESSMENT & BASIC
PREPAREDNESS AWARENESS
SUMMARY REPORT

MANAGALAS CONSERVATION
PRJECT SITE

AFORE, ORO PROVINCE........
 1. Introduction

El Nino effects of drought are being felt everywhere in PNG with evidence all over the media
concerning food &, Water shortages causing health issues for people particularly the local people
who are directly depended on their land to sustain themselves. During this time, Weather Office
has warned the public that it might continue for longer period & the effects are much worse
‘comparing it to the 1997 Drought impacts. This was a major concern for PwM project sites as it
has affected the ongoing activities of conservation and community development initiatives. For
this reason, PwM has re-strategized and have taken up the task of collecting information on the
status of the communities in its project sites as a lead up activity to present to Department
Responsible to respond accordingly. This is a summary report of the activities implemented in
Managalas whereas for Inaina and Karimui reports have been submitted by Noel Gisawo &
Steven Poya respectively.

2. Purpose/Objectives
The primary purpose of this trip was to send out two patrol teams on the ground to the Eastern
and Western sides of the plateau respectively to inform the community the basic measures to take
during this El Nino drought period & to collect information of its impacts of Drought on the local
communities
Y Objective 1: Communities to take on basic measures while waiting for responsible
agencies to respond
Y Objective 2: Collate report & provide to Mainstream Media
Y Objective 3: to provide this information to PwM to assess & provide reports to
Responsible departments to take further action (Disaster, NARI etc.)

3. Method

3.1 Patrol teams
1. Eastern Team
= MCF staff
- Zone CBOs 5,6,7A,7B, 8 & 9
Westem team
- MCF staff
= Zone CBOs 1,234

 3.2 Information Collection

The team was set out to collect general information through observation & intervi

& other stakeholders in each community on the effects of Drought.

Table 1: The 5 Categories defining the Status of Drought impact areas

Categories

Description

‘One

Virtually dry but no major food supply or drinking water problems

Two

TThere will be some inconvenience such as staple food is reduced & other food
| crop available, people may walk further distances to get water which is basically
satisfactory

Three

Conditions are difficult with food reduced & some famine food being eaten which
means that they are dried up. Water is only available at a long distance or some
cannot walk far to_get water and there is a little bit of risk as it involves life

Four

There is no food in the gardens. There is famine and water supply is in short
supply or there is no water, it is possibly polluted & may increase sickness & also
life of children & the old even the animals may die because of no food & water so
this is a very sever situation

Five

This is an extreme situation where food is going to be very short, there is no water
& people will be sick, small children or old people will be at high risk or even
death

structures

and cash income, and remittances

3.4 Materials for Patrol

Stationeries (Writing pads, Pencils, Camera, Biros)
Awareness Materials (Pamphlets & Brochures & videos)
 4. Results

Using table 1, the findings indicated that Managalas community fell under category Three (3)
however, in the event that drought prolongs, quantity of food stored will run out coupled with
poor water quality which will have detrimental effects on Health & Hygiene of the people.

4.1 Direct Impacts
a) Bush Fires
Bush Fires are a threat since there is lack of rain & almost all the vegetation are dry
enough to start a fire. Fires in this case are commonly started by locals who tend to forget
to put off the fires after clearing bushes for new gardens, cooking in open fire place while
in the garden or hunting.
b) Food
Lack of rainfall & reduced water table have caused garden food to dry up & even burnt to
the core due to intense heat. Staple foods like banana, native yam & taro have been
reduced & are being substituted with African yam, mammy yam & sago
¢) Water
The water cycle has been affected particularly the lack of rainfall well over 2 months &
still continuing have compromised the supply of fresh water into streams, creeks and
rivers. As a result, many of this streams & creeks have dried up forcing people to walk
long distances to get to mainstream rivers. There are some areas on the plateau that
heavily depend on rainwater harvesting such as Government & mission stations which
most of them have now ran out of water supply and have joined the rest of the villagers to
take refuge near mainstream rivers. With many people including livestock using the
mainstream rivers, it poses the threat of water contamination coupled with poor water
quality causing it not safe for consumption.
d) Health
The basic human requirements for an individual is to have access to safe drinking water,
sufficient food, secure shelter & good conditions, however in this situation, these
s have been compromised & have given way to waterborne
malnutrition, There have already been reported cases on dysentery, malnutrition &
typhoid in some areas on the plateau.

e) Schools & Other Service providers
Many of the schools that are being worst hit such as Afore Primary School & those that
are located up in remote areas have closed down including Health Centres & District
office to search for avenues to survive.

1) Cash Cropping
Market supply in terms of agriculture especially those that are engaged in selling of
garden food have been reduced as well as cash cropping such as Coffee, coconut and
Vanilla as well. There are no surpluses produced to supply the market.

2) Other Community Projects
There are some community projects such as Conservation Area & Queen Alexandra
Birdwing Butterfly Rehabilitation projects that are being affected & halted at the moment
for this period.
 4.2 Indirect Impacts
Because of these direct
survive such as:
© Families are looking out for each other only and unable to provide for additional people.
© People sought other means of survival such as stealing from others garden, livestock & in
some cases using violence to take from the others.
‘© Public servants have stopped working particularly the health & Education sectors
particularly the areas that are worst hit.
Much of the economic activities have stopped in terms of agriculture & livestock
Prices of goods & services have increased
‘Community Initiatives have halted as well.

pacts, the consequences are that people are doing what they can to

4.3The Vulnerability Status
Using table 2,
a. Natural
Much of Managalas Forests are intact comprising of lowland hill to montane Forests with

presence of grassland in between. Many creeks and rivers form the main catchments of the
Bareji and Musa rivers that intersect the forests. The local people utilize the lower area for
subsistence agriculture, coffee, coconut and vanilla plantations therefore constitutes disturbed
vegetation and secondary re-growths.

Strength

i. Intact Forested Areas with Main river catchment are able to withstand the onslaught of
drought to a certain degree; however, Bush Fires will only be threat. Fact is if it’s
naturally instigated then it will be able to rejuvenate over time.

Challenge

ji, Areas of Disturbed Vegetation are currently victims to the impacts of Drought
particularly with communities living in & around these areas it further puts pressure on
the ecosystem services. As a result, there is occurrence of poor soil quality due to lack of
moisture present causing crops to dry or even die out. Water body of creeks, streams and
rivers are reduced and water quality has dropped as well.

b. Social
Strength

On the plateau, The Zone CBOs have been actively working closely with MCF staff to
coordinate much of the Awareness and the assessment of the situation on the ground using
their Consensus Building Process-a traditional decision making structure to reach out plateau
wide.
 e. Financial

Most communities on the plateau are subsistence farmers, a few in each communities are
engaged in other cash crops like Coffee & cocoa and so with this drought situation, the
market supply has decreased due to low crop yield causing farmers with their families to
lose income and are unable to afford goods and services on a daily basis solely depending
on organic enough to keep them going

Public servants and business persons are able to afford the goods and services however
are spending more to keep up with the demand.

5. Recommendation

Basically the active stakeholders are the CBOs and the MCF on the ground, with the help of
PwM are mobilizing the communities and are currently networking with other stakeholders to
take further action, Emphasis is that only through partnership initiatives can help reduce the
vulnerable sectors particularly the loss of lives & properties.

Immediate action has to be relieving the communities to cope with the impacts however it comes
with a cost which is short term particularly food and clean water supply. Looking long term
would call for actions like Capacity building of locals through Education and Awareness.
Develop long term Disaster risk plans that ties all relevant stakeholders through an MOU etc. It
is important to note that every stakeholder involved have specific roles to play and that needs to
be clarified right from the start which basically means that they all complement each other. For
Instance, PWM plays the role of enabling communities to know the processes/concepts in order
to participate & benefit meaningfully. It also plays the role of networking the communities with
service providers. Thus, immediate action would be;

I. Dialogue with NARI, Disaster and Fire Service on how they can assist by providing
this report.
Il. Engage NARI, Disaster and Fire Service to carry out a plateau wide Awareness &
Workshop on Drought Preparedness for the long run
TIL. Review Climate Change program activities to accommodate the frequent extreme
events phenomenon to offset conservation efforts.

6. Conclusion

The assessment was carried out with the two patrol teams for Eastern & Western side. The
impacts are directly felt by the locals on the plateau which water & food supply are gradually
reduced and will continue to do so if the drought persists. This calls for further assessment and
provide assistance to locals during this harsh times.

NB: Attached are detailed compiled Reports from the two Patrols team i.e. East and West.
 PwM has assisted to mobilize the CBOs to update information. Media was engaged to tell
the plight of the Managalas people in order for relevant agencies to take further action. PwM
continues to provide that medium for relevant stakeholders to respond accordingly.

Challenges

Communities are spread across the plateau and are far from each other which are quite a
challenge when it comes to effective means of communication particularly getting messages
across to one community to another. There is obviously missing link between stakeholders
onsite 10 co-share the responsibility of partnership initiatives in terms of resource
mobilization to facilitate the drought situation. For Instance, The CBOs & MCF staff have
worked alone to carry out awareness & collect information on the ground plateau wide for
communities to be on the lookout. The Local level Government was unable to carry out any
emergency exercise as there is lack of plans and enforcements particularly in the areas of
Disaster response, Health & Sanitation & Education causing all to stop function on an
indefinite period leaving many communities to survive off whatever they have or can at the
moment.

¢. Human
Strength

For the locals particularly, traditional knowledge is the only salvage at the moment
particularly in terms of food and water storage such as the yam house or garden house and
the bamboo for water storage.

Challenges

However, it won't be long until they run out as they are unable to make new gardens. This
will affect the health and hygiene of the people causing many sicknesses and even death at
the extreme. Malnutrition and other water-borne diseases are prevalent during these times

4. Physical

Managalas have been missing out at receiving vital services such as Education & Health in
terms of inadequate facilities to fully function. There is only one effective
Telecommunication the famous Digicel network on the plateau however, its costly to
maintain communication. There is no major water supply but water tanks are supplied to
Education, Health and mission stations only usable when there is rain. Otherwise everyone
else uses the natural fresh water catchments for their consumption.

NAME

The Association shall be known as Managalas Development Foundation Incorporated.

OBJECTS AND PURPOSES.

The objects of purposes of the Association are :

a) To assist the Managalas Plateau people in providing a medium through which they can
resolve issues of concern and conflicts amongst themselves and with other groups of
people.

b) To undertake education, training and awareness campaigns and programs on environmental
issues, development, human rights, land and resource rights of the Managalas Plateau

people.

) Toassist the Managalas Plateau people to acquire resources and skills including specialized
training, which could be used to advance their individual as well as collective interests.

d) To promote the efficient management of customarily owned land and resources in
accordance with local customary laws and sound economic principles and to assist the
Managelas Plateau people in establishing income generating projects.

) To regulate and monitor on behalf of the Managelas Plateau people the sustainable
utilization of natural resources both on the land, in the land and rivers so as to ensure that
they receive maximum benefit from the development of these resources.

f) Toreceive, organize and administer funds, compensation payments, grants and gifts from
the Nationals, Provincials, District and Local Level Governments and other donor agencies in
Papua New Guinea and Overseas in pursuance of its objectives.

8) Toplan and implement community based sustainable resource management and other
commut projects in collaboration with such other Associations, Groups, Cooperatives,
Government Agencies, Institutions and Non-Government Organizations within Papua New
Guinea or Overseas whose aims and objectives are similar and lend assistance and support
to such other groups and organizations.

h) To collaborate and arrange for exchange programs with other like-minded NGOs, CBOs and
institutions at the national and international level on issues relating to environment,
