1.0 Background

Partners With Melanesians (PMW) is a Non-Government Organization (NGO) currently
aimed at conserving the rainforest at certain locations of Papua New Guinea (PNG). But
applying policies in order to conserve the forest can have major implication on rural areas
where development is of great importance. PMW has managed to collaborate with some
of the natives of Oro (Northern) Province to conserve their forests, but faced with another
challenge of how to bring income into the region without destroying the forests.

The solution was to establish projects on Non-Timber Forest Product (NTFP). These
projects enabled the production of organic coffee & okari nuts to be exported to other
centers of Papua New Guinea (PNG). However these main cash crops both were exported
only during the months between June to August and the rest of the year there was very
little income from alternative NTFP. So a new NTEP project was proposed to grow

vegetables and spices for export to supplement the main cash crops at present.

In the Managalas plateau of Oro Province in the Ijivitari district, the livelihood of all the
locals is based on shifting cultivation and on the use of natural resources of the forest.
However the need for development in a region where oil palm production flourishes,
logging looming around the comer and petroleum exploration licenses granted by the

Government stress is mounting up on forest conservation organizations.

Although the region has a wide range of agricultural activities the problem is reaching the
market. The area is so remote and fed by a rough dirt track for vehicles from the Oro Bay

and several, almost extinct, airstrips. Because of these deteriorating transport problems
 markets are hard to reach and even if reached the produce loose its viability and the cost
of transport, freight, and essentials are too costly that there isn’t any financial savings.

Hence, given the existing needs in the Managalas plateau, PWM has been working with
the people and identifying NFP projects. PWM has also successfully established
Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) in which is administered and owned by the
locals for the locals. MDF with the support of PWM have worked on several other
projects and unlike coffee and okari, which is well established, there are still more
projects in progress for altemative NTFP. One of the projects proposed was the
production of vegetables and spices for an alternative source of income apart from the

main cash crops.

1.1 Aims and Objectives

PWM is committed to establishing and promoting conservation, community development

and eco-enterprise initiatives through education, consensus-building programs that
encourage equal participation and self-reliance. Eco-enterprise involves the assessing of
zone project ideas with community-based organizations and conducting a market research
committed to ensuring that local communities are engage in alternative sources of

income.

My objective for PWM was to observe, interview and possibly run tests in the target area
for the production of vegetables and spices. Recommendations emanating from this
survey will contribute to improved production of vegetables and spices and subsequent

market access and increased household cash income in the targeted area.

2.0 The Study Site

Managalas plateau is located in the Ijivitari district of Oro Province in PNG. The plateau
is located between the Owen Stanley Range due south and west, Sibium Range due
south-east, and Mt Lamington due north. The plateau lies on a raised valley at on altitude
 ranging from 600 to 1000 meters above sea level. The plateau occupies an approximate

area of 360,000 hectares. The plateau is accessible via road or by airstrips.

The plateau is divided into 10 zones with 5 zones in the western end (zones 1, 2, 3, 4, &
10) and the other 5 zones in the eastern end (zones 5, 6, 7, 8, & 9). The 10 zones are clan
based which were divided by MDF with 10 Community Based Organizations (CBO):
Itokama (zone 1), Serefuna (zone 2), Koruwo (zone 3), laure (zone 4), Ugunumo (zone
5), Numba (zone 6), Kawowoki (zone 7), Koivi (zone 8), Bariji (zone 9), and Gora (zone
10). The plateau has 150 clan groups that live there and over 70 villages with a
population of approximately 16 000 people with just over 7000 eligible voters. The two
main native dialects that are spoken are Barai (western end) and Ese (eastern end) but
apart from those two Pidgin and Police Motu are also spoken with a minority speaking

English.

3.0 Process and Result

‘The study was conducted by observing and interviewing (Appendix A) villagers between
Afore station and Itokama station. The observation involved visually surveying the
various crops grown, factors affecting the normal physiological function of these crops,
the environmental conditions and health status of locals in the plateau with regard to their
nutritional daily intake. The interviews conducted were to gather information verbally
from locals about the crops grown, what affects the crops, and their personal views and
experience with vegetable and spice. Besides observing and interviewing, literatures in
relation to this study was used for reference.

Some general constraints affecting development of agriculture in the Managalas plateau
include; lack of access to good sced materials, lack of crop husbandry skills, lack of

information, and limited market access.

Landform and soil distribution: The plateau generally has a black-sandy or reddish-
brown clay soil, which shapes the plateau into various landforms. These include low

mountainous ridges and ash blanketed hills. The soil distribution is generally volcanic ash
 soil and is more evident on used land unlike the brown forest soil and red clay soils at

various locations between Itokama and Koruo.

Climate and vegetation: The plateau has an average annual rainfall of 3000mm with
marked seasonal rainy periods usually from late August to February. The temperature
ranges from between 26 to 16 degrees Celsius depending on the altitude. Vegetation
ranges from well-developed lowland hill forest and alluvial plain forest, to grassy plains.
These vegetations include various agricultural crops that can be classed as beverage crops
(coffee & cocoa), starch crops (yam, taro, sweet potato...), fruits (papaya, pineapple...)
grain (rice), spices (chili, cardamom...), salads (lettuce, cabbage...), and tobacco.

Land use: Besides residential areas, cash crops are grown on the flat plains of the plateau
while gardens are done on short slopes within the plateau. Livestock production isn’t

practiced on the plateau.

Cultivation method: The shifting cultivation is used in the Managalas plateau besides
sedentary cultivation for coffee. Shifting cultivation involves land clearing, land
preparation, and cultivation of crops for several seasons before moving onto anther plot
of land. Land clearing is done by slash and burning the area to be cultivated but not all
the area is cleared leaving a few trees here and there. The land is than prepared by
digging drains and preparing the bed for planting of crops. After several seasons a new

plot of land is than cleared and the process continues.

Sedentary cultivation is only done for coffee where land clearing and land preparation,
similar to shifting cultivation, is done. Sedentary cultivation is only done on one plot (i.e.
it doesn’t shift) of land, Coffee, cocoa and vanilla are cultivated using this form of

cultivation.
Vegetables and spices: On either side of the plateau the vegetables (Table 3.1) and spices

(Table 3.2) grown are the same but vary due to access to the market and preference. The
vegetables that are grown are shallot, aibika, Chinese cabbage, cabbage, snake bean, egg

“J -
 plant, tomato, and carrot. The spices that are grown are ginger, turmeric, capsicum, chilli,

and vanilla.

snake beans are usually grown because of the access to markets via road. Unlike the

and market access.

as a concem, however on the eastern side, insect damages were common on both Chinese
and English cabbages. However, in general, incidences of insect and disease damages in

the area were very low.

Both Tables 3.3 and 3.4 indicate that pests and diseases pressures were very low or
negligent in the region except for caterpillar damages on cabbages. This could also be
attributed to the isolation of the plateau from the rest of the country and production
practices in the area. The pests on cabbages may be attributed to Diamondback moth
(Plutella xylostella) or cabbage cluster caterpillar (Crocidolomia binotalis). Both of these
insect pests can cause severe damages on the coast but are kept in check by cool climate
and natural enemies. The Fruit fly (Bactrocera bryoniae) is a major pest on chili and

myrids on cardamom.

Nutrition and health: The plateau itself is rich in natural resources and can sustain a
diversity of crops but malnutrition still prevails and is evident in children. This could be
due to unbalanced diets. The vegetables and spices that are grown on the plateau do not
contain sufficient nutrients to maintain the day to day physiological demands of children

and active adults (Appendix B).

Most rural people do not recognize the nutritive values of locally available food crops
such as avocado, amaranths, beans, peanuts and aibika, Crops which are grown in other
parts of PNG and were not observed on the plateau, but should be considered for
introduction are soybean, mungbeans and pigeon peas. All of these crops are rich in
protein, vitamins and minerals essential for good health. There is a need to address
malnutrition through awareness on improved household nutrition, food security and
healthy living.

Marketing: Market access is one of the main constraints identified in this survey.
Marketing in the plateau is mostly limited to the eastern end of the plateau due to access

-10-
 to markets via road. The western end only concentrates on marketing coffee and okari
because of the services provided by MDF with the support of PWM. Vegetables are not
marketed in the western end unless there is a charted flight.

In the eastern end the markets are accessible via the road. The vegetables (i.c. shallot,
Chinese cabbage, cabbage, and snake bean) spices (ginger) are either sold at local road

side markets or to urban supermarkets in Popondetta.

text:
Managalas Mapping Project

Field Mappers Training Report

31% May — 11" June 1999

“Maintaining the Dance”
 Brief

Partners With Melanesians undertook a 2 week training exercise during the above period. This was
carried out to prepare and familiarise field mappers from the Managalas with skills necessary to map
the outer boundary of the Managalas Sustainable Development Program's Conservation Area.
While this has been a widely supported priority, till now it has remained a difficult one to address due

to funding restrictions.

Prior to this, field mappers (Mapping Team) were identified to carry out preliminary awareness with
the outer boundary clans, and to sketch the outer boundary (and scope of work) from elders in those
‘communities. In the process, areas of difficulty (land disputes with non-Managalas clans) were also
identified and other questions were also raised. This preliminary work was brought out during the
training as issues to be dealt with by the Mapping Team, as well as a focus for training and practice.

Background:

‘The protection of Managalas lands and resources has been a long held and widely supported priority
across all sections of the Managalas society. Within the context of a Conservation Area and the
protection given under the relevant (existing) legislative framework, it is felt that the people of
Managalas can better achieve their vision for Sustainable Development. This would entail cooperation
between the Managalas people and their local, provincial and national government representatives and
their relevant institutions. While this is challenging enough, it is more daunting that the establishment
of Conservation Areas in PNG has never been done. It is, nevertheless what the Managalas people
have chosen, duc to a number of key considerations:

(2) The Managalas people want to define and nurture development in their own way, recognising
their strengths, their weaknesses and their vision for long-term sustainability.

(6) The maintenance of their cultural values and political systems is an important part of carrying
out this process of grass-roots based development and ensuring it remains rooted in
Managalas society.

(©) That these and other considerations, must be recognised by and requires the cooperation of all
levels of government and private industry.

(4) Inrelation to government, the Managalas people see the relationship as a mutually respectful
and cooperative arrangement, formalised by instruments established under the exi
relevant legistative framework. In other words, they see their government as an a:
productive participant in their vision, within terms agreed to by both part

(©) The support and consensus building with non-Managalas clans on the perimeter of their land
must be maintained and improved to give strength to the perimeter of Managalas lands and
the locally defined principles for sustainable development.

and

These considerations are an important part of the Mapping Project and thus, for the Mapping Team in
that their work will provide much of the base information that is required to establish the various
instruments and documents for a Conservation Area. This training aims to clarify each necessary step
required of the Mapping Team in building the base data, Fundamentally, this data needs to be accurate
and agreed to by all concerned, and therefore, indisputable. This requires a combination of basic
mapping skills (technical skills) but more critically, communication and negotiating techniques that
may be unprecedented in this country. Mapping what is territorially “yours” in many instances
PNG leads to disputes with bordering clans as it can be interpreted as a provocative act. More
specifically, mapping what is NOT yours (eg. For land registration, Logging, Mining, etc..) or where
ong standing disputes exist, can and does lead to confrontation and violence. The Mapping Team
must and is taking into consideration the traditional ties and affiliations (and the lack of them or
existence of animosity) in negotiating and building consensus on where the perimeter lies.
intended to be a confrontational exercise with neighbouring clans but perhaps can be interpreted as an
aggressive move against insensitive and non-consultative development plans for the area, that are and
will continue to be pursued by institutions and individuals outside of the Managalas society.

 In this context, their technical skills are not as important as communication and negotiation skills and
they (technical skills) will only be employed once there is definitive consensus between all parties
concerned. Achieving consensus also minimises the technical work-load of mapping since it
simpler to plot a line that passes through agreed points, as opposed to a line that passes through points
somewhere out there, and for which there is no consensus.

The Participants:

‘The Mapping Team is made of Field Mappers from 4 of the active zones, 2 of which are acting as
team leaders and who coordinate the various mapping activities on the plateau. A material production
trainer observed the training with the view that a basic training guide needs to be put together for
reference when needed in the field. My role as a technical assistant was to learn from the training
conducted by Russel Collier and follow up with the Mapping Team after the training. This includes
fine tuning mapping skills, helping with GPS use, and collating all data from the field for processing
on the GIS system in the PWM office.

Russel Collier has been involved with a mapping project in his country with parallels to our own. His
knowledge of the field skills, GIS and GPS implementation and the requirements under law, provided
the participants with a wholistic approach to mapping the Conservation Area. In addition to this, his
wolvement in dealing with bordering clans in his own country, gave important insight into problems
encountered in getting consensus and negotiation skills employed to get support from those clans.

Zone/Village Capacity

Russel Collier CANADA-Gixsan Mapping Specialist-Trainer

‘Two meetings where held with clan elders and community facilitators. One in Numba and the other in
Serefuna. Both were half-day meetings in which the team was introduced as well as the concepts and
skills that were being imparted to them during the training. It was also used as an opportunity to
introduce Russel to talk about the Gixsan experience and how it related to what he had seen so far in
PNG.. particularly the Managalas. Overall, the meetings reinforced the message of close and careful
cooperation between the elders, facilitators and the Mapping Team, in negotiating the outer boundary
of Managalas territory.

‘The Training:

The training focussed on different aspects of mapping skills, GPS use and recording data. The
relationship between these and the need for accuracy and consensus as required by law, was also
discussed in general terms.’ The need for accuracy was stressed by recent developments in relation to
a secretive transfer of much of Maisin customary land to the State. Every aspect of negotiation,
interpretation, consensus and measurement, needs to be done in such a way that it cannot be disputed
by government or corporate lawyers. In relation to this, part of the training involved how
measurements should NOT be taken, Also much discussion took place around how to approach clans

1 These requirements under law, need further elaboration by lawyers so the mapping team is conscious of what
they need to achieve.
 in areas of dispute.. it was felt that in such instances, both mappers and elders would need to facilitate
consensus with outer clans, using a process that avoided antagonising existing disputes. Kingsford had
several experiences already where he found an approach which involved clan elders on both sides,
resulted in demarcations that were agreed on both sides, or at least in areas where land was shared for
certain functions only. His approach also involved clarifying the project objectives and the reasons for
and functions of a Conservation Area.

Project Management

Russel also took us through the various aspects of Project Management in relation to the
implementation of GIS/GPS mapping systems. We used the experienced gained during one field trip
to demonstrate and understand this process, which is basically a cyclic process that involves planning,
implementation, evaluation and the feeding of results from the evaluation into further planning and
implementation.

‘The main components of such a report which are important for project management are: Who was
involved, What was the task, when it happened/how long did it take, where did it take place, what was
achieved/observations and conclusions/recommendations.

 ‘The recommendations in that report are relevant to this report in that they are real considerations for
farther implementation in this project. That is, they form the basis for further planning which must
take place before any further mapping can take place.

In this sense, the combination of both technical and project management skills, has been an eye-
opener for further implementation of the mapping project. It has exposed our weaknesses and helped
us identify approaches to dealing with these problems through further training, awareness and
reinforcement.

Recommen

The task of the mappers is quite complex. Considering the implications of the Conservation Area
and all the requirements of law which they are expected to uphold in mapping the boundaries of, not
only are they expected to achieve this. They are expected to understand, respect and map [aspects of]
the different cultural relations between bordering clans and communities. On top of this they have
obligations to their zone management, families and communities.

‘A meeting of the mapping team must be held to plan the next stage and deal with some of the
problems ident 1g the training. The most important problem is the fact that various members
of the team are already involved in other aspects of the project, in different capacities. Their
utilisation of time will be extremely difficult considering the scope of the work involved in the
mapping project. Much time will be required in the field and this will have to be balanced with their
other responsibilities, project related or domestic... It is suggested that the timing of various mapping
activities, be considered in the context of existing priorities, unless the mapping team members can be
relieved (in part or totally) of their other responsibilities. This, therefore, has to be done in the context
of a much broader planning. In any case, monthly meetings need be held to collate data, exchange
experiences and plan for further tasks.

Improved mapping equipment needs to be purchased for the team (sce attachment).
tools for mapping as well as trekking and camping equipment. ‘They cannot be expected to carry out
an enormous task unless they are adequately equipped for the circumstances. It would be demoral

to start them on a task which they might be ill-prepared for, only to face major problems that could
have been dealt with through adequate equipment. From my point of view, they are now equipped
with the basic skill to carry out the task and are motivated to carry it out. They are well aware of the
complex problems that lie ahead but are nevertheless prepared to face and deal with them. The
facilitation of planning and support will greatly improve their ability to complete the task.

Remedial Training will be required at the early stages as problems in data collection are identified.
This can be done with the entire team or with the team members having difficulties. It would probably
be better to do it with the entire group as a means of reinforcing everyone’s skills. The first
opportunity for this will be the first planning meeting that is recommended above.

There is no reason why the objectives for the team in the mapping project cannot be met. If finances
are not sufficient, they should be improved. At this stage, the office has gone ahead and made
purchases to improve mapping equipment. Some furniture for the mapping desk has been purchased
for the office. Trekking equipment is the next priority, while waiting for the planning meeting.

MANAGALAS PLATEAU LAND TENURE AND BOUNDARY DELINEATION
PROJECT. FINAL REPORT.

41. SUMMARY OF ACTIVITIES AND FINDINGS.

The Project was aimed at providing legal and technical support to the people of
Managalas Plateau in the preparation and development of a proposal to the
government for establishing an innovative partnership agreement between the
people of the Managalas plateau and the government of Papua New Guinea that is
based on locally established sustainable development guidelines

The idea of this component of the Managalas Plateau Conservation Area Project
came from the clan groups on the plateau through their clan group discussions as
part of their efforts to protect the area from ground logging and other large-scale
commercial projects that have enormous impact on their livelihood. They also want
to be involved in sustainable development projects that allows them to make
decisions for themselves and share benefits derived equitably using established
customary mechanisms of sharing benefits. The Project partners and the Field
Assistants have in fact received considerable support from the clan groups and
community leaders on the plateau in implementing the project. Therefore, it is truly a
local initiative, which was supported by project partners and other stakeholders and
certainly it is an initiative which may become a model for customary landowners in
Papua New Guinea and indigenous peoples elsewhere.

It was also found that land is a valuable asset for the clan groups as it is elsewhere
in PNG because people depend on it for their livelihood. The Managalas clans use
only fertile land which they leave to fallow for a_ number of years to plant yams which
is the main staple food and culturally an important food crop on the plateau which
are used for payment of bride price and yam exchanges and for other important
cultural events. The yam exchange feasts are an important part of the people's
lives on the plateau and there are a lot of rituals that go with yam planting and yam
exchanges for which ingredients are derived from the forests. People whe de not
contribute to these cultural activities are considered to be outsiders and are highly
regarded in the community because it brings shame to the clan if he is not
contributing in his clans efforts to beat their rivals in terms of the amount of yams
given. It is for this reason that land on the plateau is a very valuable asset to the clan
groups.

It was also found that customary landownership promotes conservation and allows
for land use planning of which decisions are made collectively by the clan members.
There are also traditional conservation practices which are used by the local people
which if given the force of law can be the best model of conservation because is not
something that is introduced but something that the people are used to and have
been practicing it. The shifting cultivation is an important and widely used traditional
conservation practice. The recognition of traditional decision making by clan elders
relating to clan land coupled with traditional conservation practices is found to be an
effective way to control use of land dispute settlement. This practice can be clearly
seen especially in the use of clan land for growing of cash crops like coffee and other
indigenous nuts like okari nuts and bettlenut. The latter two because of their cultural
values but now have some commercial value but not at a larger scale.
 It was also found that the clan groups on the plateau have well defined land
boundaries and the olan lands have names, which are different from other clan
groups land. Physical features like rivers, stones, mountains or large trees that can
be identified by names, can divide the clan boundaries. There are also well
established ways of traditional dispute settlement mechanisms including land
disputes although the systems seems to be eroding in favour of the introduced court
system but only for major disputes. Some of these traditional mechanisms are
recognized under the formal law including the Land Dispute Settlement Act and the
Village Court Act where village elders are appointed land mediators and Village
Court Magistrates to mediate and settle disputes at the community level applying
local prevailing customary laws. However, there seem to be some land disputes
between neighboring clans and tribes of which the reasons have not been
established but they seem to be land, which are far away from the villages especially
hunting grounds. These may have been brought about by some promised
commercial activity including mining and logging as well for Numpa the Repeater
station for communication signals set up by Telekom PNG.

It was also found that boundaries of land clans belonging to clan groups on the
plateau extends down to the coast close to Eroro, Anakiro and Pongani as well as
across the mountains to Tetebedi, Jaure, Ajjari and Toma. For this reason the clan
groups on the plateau are inclined to include all of their land in the boundary map.
Also clan groups from outside of the plateau and sharing land boundaries have
requested that their land be included in the boundary map and be part of the project.
This is not possible because of funding constraints and lack of dedicated institutional
support. The clan groups from outside of the plateau will also need to follow the
three-tier consensus building process used on the plateau in order to participate in
the project. This in itself is an enormous task and will require adequate funding
institutional support to extend the Managalas project model to these areas and
elsewhere in PNG.

The other important findings of the project are that of various land disputes between
clan groups on the plateau and neighboring tribes or peoples. These land disputes
were never settled or brought before the formal court system because of the costs
involved and more importantly lack of knowledge of the procedural requirements
under the laws. As a result they have brought their disputes to the project team to
assist settle them but this was to part of the aims of the project nor does the team
have authority to do that. But this is an important area that needs to be looked at
especially if the boundary mapping and the Managalas project are to be successfully
completed. The land mediators and other community elders need to be trained and
empowered to deal with these disputes and settle them at the community level.

Finally there was lack of institutional support from PNG NGO's especially ICRAF and
Partners with Melanesians because of lack of capacity and resources. ICRAF was a
party to the project agreement but had their in-house problems, which did not allow
them to participate although funds were allocated to them to assist in implementing
the project. Therefore there is a need to establish in PNG a legal NGO dedicated to
promoting public interest law to assist clan groups and other stakeholders in such
efforts. To be successful such projects need dedicated legal and technical support
and advice so this needs to be ratified by identifying appropriate institutional
arrangement.
 2.BACKGROUND

In Papua New Guinea (PNG) 97 percent of the total land of approximately 45 million
hectares is owned and controlled by customary landowners and only 3 percent is
held by the state and other private freehold although the Governments title to land
acquired so long ago is still contested by customary owners. The vesting of the of
the ownership of mineral resources on the state by law is even contested by the
people and to address this issue the government as devised a system to share
benefits derived from the development of these resources with the customary
landowners on whose land the project is developed, These includes equity
participation, compensation payments, sharing of royalty payments and provision of
services by the developer through Tax credit schemes. To outside developers, this
cultural fact which has the protection of the PNG Constitution and relevant laws is
seen as a threat over-shadowing any investment in PNG. Projects operate under
constant fear of landowner disruption, the most notorious one is the forced closure of
the giant Panguna mine on Bougainville in i989 by armed landowners. It is now
realized that it is a mistake to treat customary tenure as an impediment to orderly
development in PNG. Custom is installed by the constitution as one of the primary
source of the country’s legal system and it supports the very fabric of PNG society.
For this reason people who want to have access to customary land in PNG must
deal with customary landowners. There is one basic principle that one should keep in
mind when dealing with customary landowners in PNG, “build on custom, do not by-
pass or deny it’, This may not be true in logging projects where the resource is
‘owned by the landowners and so having access to extracting them is easy. This has
contributed to deforestation in PNG.

This issue coupled with that of social and other problems has prompted the clans on
the Managalas plateau to find ways to secure their land from outside influence and
control, thus the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project.

2. LAND TENURE ON THE MANAGALAS PLATEAU

The Managalas plateau is a partlineal society which means that land is inherited
from the father side including rights relating to the use of the land. The land on the
plateau is owned by clan groups rather than by individuals. The concept of private
individual ownership of the land does not exist on the Managalas Plateau.

4. LEGAL OPTIONS AVAILLABLE FOR PROTECTING THE MANAGALAS
PLATEAU

As part of the project and to allow the clan groups on the plateau to make informed
decision on what legal option is best suited to be used for protecting the plateau from
unsustainable activities different options were presented to the clan groups. These
included discussions relating to the advantages and disadvantages of the available
legal options. This aspect was done successfully with invaluable assistance from
CIEL Intern Anastasia Telestesky and PWM's’ Flint Hobart through artistics
illustrations and which were translated into the local language by local translators.
 3.1 Conservation Areas Act.

The Conservation Areas Act provides for an area to be declared a “Conservation
Area" with its own Conservation Area Management Committee which prepares a
management plan for the area and then to restrict any development of land in the
area except in accordance with that management plan.

The Act provides for a five member National Conservation Council, as the expert
body to advise an assist the Minister in the administration of the Act. It is now twenty
years since the enactment of the Act in 1978 but the Council is yet to be established
and as a result no Conservation Areas have been established in Papua New Guinea
The first step in declaring a conservation area is for the minister based on criteria
established by the Council, to recommend that an area having particular biological ,
topographical, geological, historical, scientific or social significance or other present
value for present community or for future generations. This can by done by the
Ministers own initiative or after receiving request from a person, group or authority.
The recommendation has to be available for public inspection and must be publicly
notified. Then there is a period of 90 days within which written representations
needed to be received after which the Minister must submit must submit a final
recommendation and associated papers to the National Executive Council (NEC) for
its decision on whether to declare the Conservation Area or not.

When the area is declared a Conservation Area by the Head of State acting on
advice of the NEC , THE Minister establishes the Conservation Area Management
Committee , reflecting the interests if the landowners, Provincial Government; Local
Level Government , which body is responsible for preparing a management plan for
the area coordinating development and directing work the work of rangers. The
Minister can make tules applying to the Conservation Area, after consultation with
the Management Committee, the National Conservation Council and landowners
Failure to comply with a rule attracts a penalty of up to K500.

The Act also regulates development in a Conservation Area. No person including
landowners may develop or alter the existing use of a Conservation Area except in
accordance with the terms of the management plan. Or with the written approval of
the Minister. The Act also provides for the process for seeking such approval
including an application an application with supporting plans, consultation and
decision. The State too is bound by the procedure. The result of this is that
development in a Conservation Area can only proceed, if allowed under the
management plan or if the landowners agree to the development and the Minister
after due consideration approves it.To this there is and exception if the development
is by the State for public: purpose. In this case landowners consent is not necessary
but the Minister must still consult and exercise his discretion in deciding whether,
considering the environmental impact, the State's application to develop the land
should be approved.

The penalty for developing, or permitting the development of land in a Conservation
Area contrary to the above restrictions is severe, a fine of up to K40; 000, with K 4
000 default penalty for a continuing offender. The same high penalty apply for
 developing land recommended for a Conservation Area, and it is no defence in either
case to claim that the development did not adversely affect the environment.

3.2 Steps Involved in Establishing a Conservation Area

Step 1. (optional) : written request to the Minister that a area be declared a
Conservation Area. Sec. 12 (2)

Step 2: recommendation by Minister that a CA be declared - sec 12(1)

Step 3: notification to public of recommendation which is made available for
inspection - sec.12(4) & 13.
Step 4: representation to the Minister_sec 14

Step 5: submission by Minister to NEC - sec 15

Step 6: decision by NEC - Sec 16,

Step 7: Declaration of CA by Head Of State - sec 17

Step 8: Minister appoints Management Committee for the CA - sec.15

Step 9: Management committee prepares management plan for CA - sec 27
Step 10: Minister approves management plan — sec.12

Step 11: Consultation by Minister on rules of CA — sec. 28 (1).

Step 12: Rules for Management of CA made by the Minister — sec. 28(1).

3.3 Fauna (Protection And Control Act)

The Act was one of the laws in operation before independence and , and it provides
in conventional manner from strong State intervention to protect specified animals,
by a range of measures, beginning with a vesting of protected fauna in the State.
The Minister declares a protected fauna. It is an offence to take or kill any protected
fauna including disturbing or injuring them and to posses a protected fauna. It is an
aggravated offence with a higher penalty to kill a protected fauna with a firearm.

The Conservator of fauna can issue permits to approved scientific organizations to
take protected fauna and exemptions from the Acts prohibition may be granted by
the Minister. The automatic citizens of PNG have been exempted from above
restrictions, provided that mis-nets, guns and explosives are not used and that
animals are only taken for use in traditional ceremonies from land over which the
person has a traditional right to hunt.

Apart from declaring protected animals the other main protective devices under the
Act related to according special status to particular areas as sanctuaries’ protected
areas or wildlife management areas. The difference between the three catergories
are not great . Sanctuaries, protected areas and wildlife management areas can all
 be established on customary land. Their great advantage would seem to be that the
people become involved in the conservation of their own wildlife, it is not something
that is being forced on them from outside. Their effectiveness would would very
much depend on how comprehensive the regulations are for each areas and how
well they are enforced.

However, as it stands now the Act is outdated and may not be effective in the current
circumstances. The areas established under the Act also face conflicting land use
options and planning. There are instances where mining and logging concessions
have been granted by the government to companies to operate within a wildlife
management area. Added to this there is lack of government support and
coordination and the tasks seem to be taken on by outside conservation NGOs’ with
little input from landowners and the government. The Act only provides for the
protection of fauna without realizing that the fauna depend on the flora to survive.
There is therefore need to also include conservation of biodiversity in the same area.

4. CLAN GROUPS ON THE MANAGALAS PLATEAU.

There is no register of customary land and landowners in PNG including the
Managalas plateau. This does not mean that things are chaotic and unmanageable.
PNG has thousands of years of settled agriculture and traditional and community
land management systems. People basically knew who owned what land and who
belongs to which clan group or tribe. This does not mean that there are no dispute
over land ownership. In Managalas as well as elsewhere in PNG land were acquired
and boundaries established in different ways including the use of force. The land are
owned and controlled by tiny communities better known as clans. A landowning
group or clan is that group of people empowered by custom to make fundamental
decisions about their land without reference to any other group.

For the Managalas Conservation Area Project in order to have a plateau wide
support for the sustainable development guidelines developed by the clans and the
partnership agreement between the PNG Government and the people of the
Managalas plateau. For this reason part of the project teams effort was to record
each clan group names and the clan elders by consulting the clan groups concerned
in each village. Below is the list of the clan groups and names of the clan elders in
each cultural zones.

‘Ad hoc decision-making arrangements have emerged in many parts of the country largely
in response to growing awareness regarding natural resource management opportunities in
which local landowners can have an important stake. The process for holding the dialogue
and for identifying which stakeholders will participate is frequently the result of ill-
planned circumstances rather than systematic consensus building among the population
affected. ‘This being the casé, the authority of the conclusions reached often become the
basis of continuing disputes.

‘The primary purpose of this pilot activity was to expand fill stakeholder participation in
the consensus building process established earlier to players in adjacent culture zones
who are also interested in sustainable development activities on the Plateau, so that
participants may a) build .on set of sustainable development

guidelines, b) collaborate together on a set ‘of next steps for a forward action plan, and c)
reinforce enduring core cultural values in the process. Significant progress was achieve
around these objectives. A tentative set of sustainable development guidelines has been

1.0 Remobilizing Project Support

Because little project activity took place during 1995, it was important to begin these
pilot activities under a new funder with an awareness campaign to explain the nature of
the activity and the intentions of the new funder. This initial set of public awareness
meetings across the Plateau was followed by a consensus building forum between Culture
Zones #1 and #2, and commencement of facilitator and materials development training in
preparation for a six week series of clan group discussions.

‘A vehicle was arranged through the Department of Works in Popondetta to make it
possible for the Consultant, the project's Legal Advisor, and the management of Nacoda
and Okari Ecoenterprises to move project leaders and advisors between a series of open
‘community-based meetings designed to explain how these activities relate to the previous
activities funded through WWF and to other project activities on the plateau (viz., local
Government sponsored projects and the Queen Alexandrae Birdwing Butterfly project
funded through Australian bilateral aid).

A full-day open meeting was held for Itokama, Naokanane, Umvwuate and Kuae and
surrounding hamlets at Naokanane on Friday, Feb 8. Another meeting was held at
Serefuna on Saturday, Feb 9 for Kokoro, Serefuna, Anatua, Tahama, Uisoro, Ubuvara and
surrounding hamlets. And a similar meeting was held for the eastern end of the Plateau.
involving DUST (Dea, Uganumu, Siribu, and Tambane) and the dense cluster of villages
around Numpa on Sunday, February 10.

In each case, the meetings were attended by a broad cross-section of the community who
traveled from a number of neighboring villages in the immediate area. The questions

raised, in each instance, were similar. Is the World Bank seriously interested in becoming
involved in development on the Plateau over the long term? Is the World Bank interested
in becoming involved in the widerlying problems inhibiting sustainable development on
the Plateau? Had the PNG Government endorsed this activity and the link between the
consultant, EDC, and the local community groups involved? Was there any link between
this activity and the 666 movement thought by a small group on the Plateau to involve
the World Bank and to be responsible for bringing about the end of the World?

‘The questions were answered in a collaborative manner by the consultant, the legal
advisor, or by the managers or board chairmen of the participating local NGOs. The
result of these meetings was that the project was endorsed with solid support from the
majority in ¢ach instance with many keen to get further information on the sequence of
specific events that are expected to take place.

2.0 Emerging Consensus

The consensus building process used during the project period on the Managales Plareaw
proved to be an effective mechanism for pooling together informed opinion from all the
cultural units living in that eco-system about both development objectives and project ~
priorities. At the final combined forum in July, a visiting lawyer from the Lake Kutubu
region who has been involved in all kinds of landowner planning and disputes, said this
was the first time in his experience that he had seen such a broad range of clan groups
reach consensus on sustainable development objectives without disruptive confrontation,
_In both the local zone fora and the combined forum, each groups’ contributions were
| honored, written down and placed onthe wall, holding any questions until each speaker's
| perspective was fully understood and appreciated. Questions were then asked at a later
"point, but only to either clarify the speaker's intent or to decide whether it was
essentially the same or different from a similar contribution. At a still later stage,
participants selected from the full set of contributions those they felt to he the most
important. The result was that suggestions that many people felt strongly about rose to
.the bighest priority positions While those with less support filtered do
anyone having to openly condemn them. In so doing, very sensitive issues
between traditional enemies were dealt with without open confrontation.

The sustainable development guidelines and the prioritized project activities that emerged

Ywere the result of a three-tiered process of participation. Relevant issues and options
were first discussed in village or sub-clan units of 70-100 people, with leadership from a
clan elder assisted by trained group facilitators selected for their reading and waiting skills.
Opinion arising from sets of these groups was amalgamated at a forum within cach
established Culture Zone. The objective of the larger combined forum was then to
consolidate the conclusions reached in the smaller zone forums.

3.0 Sustainable Development Guidelines

Figure 1 captures the consensus reached through this three-stage process on specific
guidelines that are locally held to be important to directing all development that emerges

onthe Plateau. These guidelines were then prioritized by the participants according to
which were felt to be the most critical to the development process.

‘The guideline with the highest priority underscores the strong feeling across the Plateau
that it is their common agreement around how to develop the Plateau that will keep out
unscrupulous resource grabbers, control the more greedy of their own people, and ensure
long-term sustainable development on the Plateau. The guideline prohibiting ground
logging and strip mining outranked all the others. Clearly the large majority fear that such
development is not in their long-term interest even though a few individuals are known to
meet behind closed doors with outside interests to explore such options. It also became
abundantly clear that the population at large does not want the rich cultural and spa
traditions of the Plateau to be threatened by any new forms of development coming in " }

from the outside.

4.0 Project Priorities

Figure 2 above captures optiotis for potential projects that the participants felt to be
important and worth pursuing. These also occur in the order of priority assigned by the
participants.

Like many rural areas of Papua New Guinea, transportation and communication scored
‘extremely high as the most critical development priorities for the area. In this case,
however, the local communities are not asking for major new infrastructure development

but smaller initiatives such as maintaining just the worst spots so that existing roads can
be reopened or nearly completed airstrips could be finished and opened.

Ithas also become clear from the time and expense wasted on air charters that did not
arrive on time that some kind of electronic communication system between the zones will
be essential before collaborative economic efforts can really become profitable. The rural
telephone service established in two of the zones during the course of these pilots is going
to make a huge difference but the other eight zones will need to be in regular contact as
; well. A mobile radio service complementing two or three rural phones may then be the
Uoest sotution.

Making coffee more profitable and linking it to other sustainable development initiatives
is clearly seen by many as the easiest way to increase the per capita income on the
Plateau and some way of getting enough power on the Plateau for the Managalas to
process their own coffee fram parchment to green bean is widely seen to be the best way

to go about it.
5.0 Expanding Eastward

These pilots sought to expand the formal network of discussion groups that has been
strongest in the two Western cultural zones (Zones #1 and #2) to two additional zones in
the East (Zones #5 and #6). See Figure 3 below. The Wester zones were happy to
share what they had learned to assist the two emerging zones in the East to establish their
‘own local development agencies through which they too could play a greater role in their
future development. The level of collaboration that emerged between groups with strong
differences in the past was quite phenomenal. Many traveled considerable distances
under adverse conditions to be part of the deliberations throughout the six-month period
of the pilots. Strong delegations from all areas of the plateau turned up in force for the
final combined forum in July in particular.

Standards had to be set for limiting the aumber of people who could participate in that
combined forum simply because of the limited space in the community centre at Itokama.
“This was unfortunate because facilitators and clan elders representing a very large nurnber
of both formally and informally organized clan groups traveled to the forum in hopes of
being able to sit in on the deliberations even if they were not among the seven
spokespersons to be selected for their particular culture zone.

 PART I: MISSION REPORT

Summary of findings

‘The mission was confined to Managalas Plateau in Oro Province, Papua New Guinea, a
‘mountainous region within a tropical rain forest with high annual rainfall (see figures 3 and 5).
First-hand evaluation was made on the economic and related activities in the Plateau, as well as
on the availability of renewable energy resources such as small-scale hydraulic and solar energy
(thermal and photovoltaic) to meet the energy needs in the plateau.

‘The bulk of economic activities in the area is concerned with agriculture; high quality,
organic, arabica coffee is grown, as are okari nuts (terminalia kabernachii), bananas, oranges,
yams and different types of vegetables. The method of drying fruits, nuts or coffee is still crude
(see figure 6). The area is almost completely isolated from the rest of the country; transportation
and communication infrastructures are poor or nonexistent. The one road that connects the area
to Popondetta, the provincial headquarters, is in poor shape. Consequently, in order to reach
outside markets, the produce from the plateau has to be airlifted, at a high cost, thus rendering
them almost uneconomical.

‘The team visited four villages: Dust, Itokama/Naekonane, Numba, and Serafuna and
surveyed their respective surrounding areas. There are a number of streams in the Managalas
Plateau, some of which are in the vicinity of respective villages. Many of the streams are
tributaries of larger rivers with sources outside the plateau; they have (according to the local
habitants) steady, year-round flows; and a number of them have sites with high heads and
adequate flow rates, thus rendering them suitable for small-scale hydroelectricity development.

“The team was able to see a few of the sites. However, there are many more sites within
the area, some small, some large, that are yet to be visited and thereby evaluated to determine
their suitability for harnessing. Each site visited is within one, two, maybe three kilometres from
the nearest village. Most of the sites are known only to the villagers living near them, and have
yet to be reflected in the resource map of the country.

There already is a small p.v. station at Nackonane, adjacent to Itokama. This is used mainly for
telephone communications and minimal lighting, “Within Itokama, at a school, a solar array,
complete with an inverter for small alternating current loads, has been installed for audio-video
production for education and awareness generation. There is also a health centre, a non-formal
education office, a comnmmnity retail store, and other community facilities. There are a project
office, a school, and a health centre at Dea in Dust.

Mm,
 Introduction

Purpose and Scope of the Mission

The purpose of the mission was to have a first hand, on the spot, a preliminary appraisal of
socioeconomic and related activities in Managalas Plateau and associated energy requirements; to
identify small-scale hydroelectricity sites that could meet the envisaged demand for electricity to
dry and process agricultural produce, and thus enhance their value before transport to markets
outside the plateau; to ascertain the potential for using photovoltaic systems for communications
(radio and telephone), education, lighting, and preservation of medicines in local clinics; to
ascertain the potential for solar energy for drying of nuts, fruits and vegetables.

‘The scope of work included the following: discussions with officials of Partners with
Melanesians (PWM) about the nature of the mission and issues to be addressed; discussions with
the different communities and their leaders in Managalas Plateau about their economic activities
and energy requirements as well as the kind of assistance that the United Nations could provide to
the area; a one week field tip to different villages to identify and obtain first hand information of
(small-scale) a hydroelectric site for possible hamessing to meet energy needs of the area.

‘A team consisting of myself, Ms Fiona Delaney of Partners with Melanesians (consultant),

and other members of PwM visited the Managalas Plateau from 4 to 10 July 1998. While in the
Plateau, the team visited various villages - Dea, Itokama/ Naokanane, Numba and Serafima - and
held discussions with the commninities and their leaders on their development objectives and
plans, associated energy requirements, and how best to meet these. Tinformed them about the
nature of the United Nations involvement in technical cooperation in energy and in the procedures
involved in providing assistance to projects such as those envisaged in this particular mission.

‘The team, guided by local habitants, visited a number of potential sites for small-scale
hydroelectric development near each village and ascertained their suitability for more a detailed
appraisal. The team also visited PV sites at Naekonane, Itokama and Numba and held discussions
with the communities and their leaders about the potential of using PV’s for education,
communications, and preservation of medicine at the respective clinics; the team also held
discussions with the communities and their leaders about the feasibility of introducing solar dryer
systems for drying fruits, vegetables and nuts, incuding the need for training local people in the
design, production and quality control.

In Port Moresby the team had meetings with the UNDP office, during which the purpose
of the mission was elaborated; substantive discussions ensued, which touched on the possibilities
of extra (GEF) funding, especially for the expansion and installation of new photovoltaic systems
for communications, lighting, education, and preservation of medicines in the clinics Managalas
Plateau.

‘The team also had meetings with officials of the Ministry of Water Resources and
Environment of Papua New Guinea, to inform them of the nature and scope of the mission, and to
survey ways and means in which the Ministry, in particular, and the Government, in general, could
cooperate with and thereby enhance the activities of the PwM, and more important, facilitate the
technical assistance process envisaged by the United Nations.

During the stay in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea, I had discussions with officials and
members of PwM about the nature of their involvement in the Managalas Plateau, their objectives,
and the kind of assistance that the United Nations could provide in helping the communities meet
their developmental objectives. A final meeting was held with the officials of PwM during which
the next steps were suggested and discussed at length. A list of the meetings is given in Annex I.

PwM is to be commended for the initiative, effort and unabated enthusiasm which it has
displayed over the years in helping communities in Managalas Plateau. It is my sincere hope that
this initiative will bear fruit and that this and other related projects will succeed. I wish also to
express my appreciation to PwM for the arrangements and logistics that allowed for the mission
to proceed smoothly. My special also thanks go to the communities in Managalas Plateau, for
their hospitality, belief in themselves, their optimism about the development of the area, and for
open and serious discussions about their economic and social development situation as well as
concerns occasioned by the lack of energy and transport services. I wish also to thank the United
Nations Trust Fund for providing the fimds for the mission to Papua New Guinea, the UNDP
office in Papua New Guinea, as well as the officials of the Ministry of Water and Environment, for
their valuable and fruitful discussions. And last, but not least, I wish to express my sincere
appreciation to the Permanent Mission of Papua New Guinea to the United Nations for its
assistance in connection with my mission to Papua New Guinea. I wish, in particular, to thank Mr.
Adam V. Delaney for the keen interest he has shown in the project and for the usefial information
he has provided on the issues and problems facing the communities in Managalas Plateau.

Background

Papua New Guinea is one of the largest nations in the South Pacific region, with a total
area of 460,000 km2 consisting of a mainland - the eastern half of the island of New Guinea (85%
of the country’s land mass)- and some 600 other islands, including New Britain, New Ireland,
Bougainvillea and Manes (see figure 1). The country is characterized by extensive geographical
diversity, comprising mountainous regions, rain forests and low-lying swamps. It is rich in
resources and exports gold, copper, oil and timber. More than 80 per cent of its population -
estimated at 4.3 million - live in rural areas, a number of which are inaccessible. Large numbers of
people do not have access to modern energy sources, clean water, nor modem health services.
‘Managalas Plateau is a case in point.

Being geographically diverse and spread out, Papua New Guinea's onerous challenge is
with regard to developing an adequate infrastructure, The road network is scanty, and for more
 5

emote areas, nonexistent. Air transport has thus taken on special significance. In some areas,

for example, Managalas Plateau air transport offers a lifeline and provides the only effective link
with other parts of the country.

Managalas Plateau is situated in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea; the area of interest
measures about 400-500 square kilometres (see fig.2). There are 10 villages, of which eight are
actively involved as community-based organizations; four of the latter were visited (see figure 4).
‘No accurate figures are available on the total population in the plateau; the number of habitants of
the respective villages visited ranged between 700-1500. Numba is by far the largest. Overall the
area is marked by the lack of a basic infrastructure such as roads, electricity communications and

‘water supply systems.

‘The project exemplifies concrete steps in the implementation of Agenda 21, especially in
the light of the decisions of 19th Special Session of the General Assembly (Ga S-19-2:
Porgramme for the further implementation of Agenda21) relating to energy. It also underscores
the important role that energy plays toward achieving the objectives of sustainable development.
To this end, the Global Conference on the Sustainable Development of Small Island Developing
States, held in Barbados in 1994, adopted the Declaration of Barbados and the Programme of
Action for Sustainable Development of Small Island Developing States, which includes a chapter
on energy; the chapter identifies issues, problems and constraints facing small island developing
States and recommends ways and means for ensuring adequate, environmentally sound energy
supplies for meeting their social and economic development objectives in the most efficient
manner.
‘As part of the implementation of both Agenda 21 and the Barbados programme of Action,
many initiatives have been undertaken by Major Groups, including Non-Governmental
Organizations, in pursuit of sustainable development at the community level. Such collaboration
of national NGO’s, governmental authorities and Community - Based Organizations (CBO’s) has
proven to be a successful model.

‘The project was initiated by Partners with Melanesians a national NGO currently involved
in supporting local communities in Papua New Guinea in maintaining their environment while
developing socioeconomic benefits from the entire community. It demonstrates the commitment
of the national partners and the shared responsibilities that the international community can offer
in the implementation of universally accepted Plans of Action.

Main findings and Conclusions

The economic activities in the Managalas Plateau are quite substantial, involving as they
do the growing of coffee, collection of okari nuts and production of fruits and vegetables. These
activities would be significantly enhanced through the introduction of energy supplies, for
example those from small-scale hydroelectric plants, of which there are many suitable sites in the
area or from solar energy. Each village has a school, and many have health centres that provide
rudimentary social and health social services and whose effectiveness could be further improved
by the provision of electricity.

‘The communities in Managalas Plateau are hardworking and dedicated to their economic
activities; their efforts could bear fruit was it not for the exorbitant costs they have to incur in
transporting by air their goods to outside markets. They have formed into well functioning CBO’s

,
 8

with clearly-defined development objectives, and are keen to receive assistance to help them meet
their objectives. The consensus-building process involves these CBO’s in developing guidelines
for sustainable development, including the setting of priorities. The processes are interactive and
involve women in decision-making. The communities hope that the United Nations will lend a
much needed hand. To further develop the socioeconomic activities of the plateau, there is an
urgent need to develop energy resources and energy services.

While Managalas Plateau receives a significant amount of rainfall, being as it is within a tropical
rain forest belt, no accurate rainfall figures are available, especially near the rivers or streams of
interest for small-scale hydroelectric development.

render them suitable for small-scale hydroelectric developments (see figures 10 and 12). Many of
these sites are within one to two kilometres of the villages visited. Further work is however

and social activities including coffee growing, collection of okari nuts and other produce.
Potential users of electricity include a local vernacular teacher training facility, a project office and
a church. Nearby at Sila Mission are a health centre, and a school. There are three potential sites
at Numba which require further attention (see figure 11). Site 1 on the Pongani river, situated 2.5
km from the village, has a low to medium head (10- 15m); see figure 12. Site 2 on the Pongani
river has a low head; while site 3 has the smallest volume; site 3 is the main source of drinking
water for the village and at one point it has a head of 70m.

‘communications (radio and telephones), and lighting and preservation of medicines at the
respective villages. There is also scope for the development and application solar thermal systems
for drying fruits, nuts and vegetables; the use of driers would-reduce weight and add value to
produce from the area.

title: Zone 6 Nursery Progressive Report, Numba — Managalas Community Reforestation & Climate Change (PWM, 2018)
snippet: Partners With Melanesians — Managalas Conservation Area — Community Reforestation & Climate Change program — Nursery extension Zone 6, Numba Village. PROGRESSIVE REPORT, Zone 6 Nursery – Numba, 23 Aug - 2 Sept 2018. Date 20 June 2018. BACKGROUND: The initial scoping for the nursery at Numba was cond
text:
Partners With Melanesians — Managalas Conservation Area — Community Reforestation & Climate Change program — Nursery extension Zone 6, Numba Village. PROGRESSIVE REPORT, Zone 6 Nursery – Numba, 23 Aug - 2 Sept 2018. Date 20 June 2018.

BACKGROUND: The initial scoping for the nursery at Numba was conducted in 2017 by the Community Reforestation and Climate Change officer (CRCCO) Cecil Senive to identify the need for reforestation for the surrounding forest and logistics such as local labour, accessibility and funds. First nursery construction began in Numba mid-September to completion late October 2017. The need for reforestation was necessary due to destruction brought by the 2007 Cyclone Guba that damaged households, took lives and destroyed surrounding forest habitat. The interior rows of the nursery shed are divided into 12 sections each given to the 12 tribal clans at Numba to locate endemic orchids and tree species needing immediate reforestation.

PURPOSE: Trip conducted by Program Support Officer Kovi Wara in place of Cecil Senive (facilitating a nursery training at proposed Mt Karimui CA). Objectives: transport materials to local CBO at Numba for nursery extension; follow up current status of nursery success, needs and issues; help coordinate construction with local CBO and activity coordinator; provide report back to PWM.

Itinerary 23/08/2018–02/09/2018: Popondetta, Afore, Numba nursery site, Dogarol crater lake, Organ village, Theatre and Script writing workshop on SLA issues, Afore village bird watch site, Masave proposed nursery site, Dariki, Misiu QABB site, Yombu ward 1 QABB site, back to Port Moresby.

DISCUSSION: Nursery current status — much progress since establishment; most seedlings ready to transplant awaiting PWM officer to tally; nursery structure built using bamboo shafts and veins, still solid. Issues and concerns — CBO manager Zone 6 Jiroba Sarari; MCF officer Kinsford made commitments to youths for local labour payment not delivered; community aware Kinsford misused money allocated for project activities; advised traditional conflict resolution; PWM board investigating. Youths initiated own small projects (rice, coffee, vanilla). MOU signed in Popondetta between PWM and MCF on 23 August 2018 giving MCF financial independence to manage funds for people of Managalas CA. Proposed wildlife display area to complement nursery suggested by Kinsford. Tally of seedlings to be counted before transplanting when Cecil facilitates nursery training.

FINDINGS: Progress towards program purpose — mobilise communities in reforestation and appropriate mitigation and adaptation measures for socio-economic and ecological purposes. Community at Numba well organised. CRCC officer confirmed a nursery training workshop for next activity. Progress towards project outcomes — conservation area status granted and communities empowered to sustainably manage the conservation area. MOU signed 23 August 2018 between PWM and Managalas Conservation Foundation (MCF); starting 2019 MCF spearheads core management functions of Managalas CA with PWM oversight.

CONCLUSION: Visit brought to light opportunities aligned with sustainable community development; individuals from Numba have cocoa and cash crop establishments seeking assistance; advised to develop proper reports for submission to MCF and PWM. Reporting Officer: Kovi Wara (Program Support Officer), date of reporting 10/09/2018.

OKARI ECOENTERPRISES PROJECT

SEMI-ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

D

During the course of Year I (YRI), a strong commitment to conservation principles has emerged in the central zones of the project. The sphere of influence continues to expand as awareness, research, and ecoenterprise activities get going in adjacent zones. Considerable requisite social and economic change has been accommodated in the course of a single year. Biological research activities were initiated with a high level of community participation and local ownership of the process. Longterm support for the development of related legal support mechanism has emerged as well.

A formal business institution was established and a product was successfully gathered, packaged, transported to a central location, sorted and repackaged, air freighted to a consumer center, again transported to temporary storage and distributed to sellers, sold and profits recouped and redistributed back in the community. The community succeeded in creating an enduring demand in the urban marketplaces for their product as the largest and tastiest of all the terminalia nuts. Claiborne/Ortenberg funding was leveraged to strengthen and expand the project into a regional one aimed at establishing sustainable forest management guidelines across the Managalas Plateau utilizing PNG's new conservation area legislation.

At the same time, the project faces a number of critical challenges in maintaining the momentum gained over YRI. Experienced in-country administration and coordination remains the greatest single obstacle to increasing project effectiveness. The biological research component requires closer professional guidance and oversight. Tighter financial accounting and cross-checking must be initiated to ensure sound management of increasing cash flows at the community level. The sourcing of new information and the development of multi-media awareness materials lacks is not keeping pace with the demand being created through the clan group meetings.

Other economic alternatives, in addition to the okari nuts, must be developed soon in order to ensure that the logging option is kept at bay. Eco-timber alternatives should be monitored in the event that a sustainable model viable for conditions on the plateau does emerge. Creative means for achieving greater participation and involvement among provincial and national bureaucrats and politicians are urgently needed as well.

1.0 Review of Project Objectives:

The objectives of the Okari Ecoenterprise project as stated in the original proposal of August 1992 are:

a)

b)

d)

e)

f)

to develop a model of conservation and development among clan groups living and working in PNG forests that combines participatory conservation research and community-based issue management with ecoenterprise development,

to develop the model in a way that incorporates training of regional and national NGOS to replicate the process elsewhere in PNG;

to empower rural communities to play a greater role in their own development through active participation in establishing and maintaining local commercially viable micro-enterprises

to incorporate the Barai Okari Estates project, previously approved under DAL's 1984 SRDP program, into a larger, regional okari micro-enterprises development project

to develop a viable value-added nonwood forest product in a manner that balances land used for cash cropping with subsistence gardening and tropical forest conservation; and...

to build partnerships that promote genuinely reciprocal learning around the issues of conservation and development.

The Foundation, in its response letter of October 5, 1992, expressed particular interest in:

\* development of "culturally viable patterns of issue management and decision-

making" in order to ensure participating clans a full proprietary interest in the project

\* implementation of a fully participative research program to elucidate the biology,

ecology as well as traditional knowledge of the okari nut, and to monitor the impact of harvesting on forest ecology, an okari nut populations and on the economy and culture of the participating clans

The Foundation also expressed an interest in their funding becoming a means of leveraging additional funding for an expansion of such conservation and development initiatives to other groups in Papua New Guinea.
