SEMI-ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT

2.0 Progress on the Development of a Culturally Viable Issue Management and

Decision-Making Process

The key to the long-term viability of both the conservation and the development components of the project lies in the degree to which the local clan groups feel a sense of ownership for the programs. Clearly, that ownership cannot be achieved simply by organizing meetings, producing materials, or teaching concepts for unloading propaganda.

At the same time, however, given the strength of group identity and group processes on the plateau, open dialogue coming from a variety of points of view, reacting to new materials, and responding to new information, when put together, provide a powerful context for ideas to gel, for new convictions to develop, and for reaching the kind of consensus that does create a strong sense of community ownership.

An important link between conservation principles and development patterns lies deep within the core of the traditional cultural values among the clan groups of the plateau. Unfortunately, it is more the pattern of development accompanying the outsiders moving into the area that has been in conflict with these traditional values. Along with that, and most importantly, the dominant influence in the planning and decision-making processes that precede development activities has excluded the kind of consensus building that gives the local community a serious role in decision-making.

Rather, development activities are typically designed outside the community. The setting basically is a foreign one where other languages and other meeting styles dominate. Frequently, isolated "representative(s)" from the community are asked to endorse a program in the presence of influential outsiders. These may be people with whom they need to do business, who may want to help, and who really do not understand the power of consensus building in creating the kind of local ownership that will give a program deep roots at the community level. The result is a polite "yes" from the community representatives but one that does not stick during implementation because it has not fully incorporated the position of all elements of the community.

Culturally-sensitive decision-making is much slower but the results are enduring. It is particularly attractive for integrated conservation and development programs of this type because

page 5

OKARI ECOENTERPRISES PROJECT

SEMI-ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT

culturally acceptable behavior - a sense of right and wrong that is built into the fabric of everyday life falls directly in line with carefully looking after the environment while sustaining development. Numerous social sanctions, woven into the culture, perform just that function.

The critical element that has been missing here and in many parts of the "developing world" is a mechanism that can bring shared cultural sanctions to bear on the planning and decision-making processes... one where it would be totally and completely embarrassing to face ones peers or even dare to support a program that would violate those sanctions, one that takes place on local turf where local patterns are the dominant, acceptable ones and where it is outside stakeholders who feel a need to fit in. Such social sanctions... such cultural values... are still strong on the plateau, largely because of the short colonial history in the area, creating an excellent opportunity to create the kind of processes we have been developing through YR\!1.

By way of example, the discussion around topic five at the last forum demonstrates how core traditional values can become a positive force in shaping contemporary development decisions. 93 clan leaders from all across the plateau were building consensus around acceptable practices regarding access to land and trees. The entire audience impulsively responded with a resounding "yes" when there was consensus with the speaker; and alternatively, with a resounding "no", when there was not. Those practices were then recorded as candidates for the emerging forest management guidelines for the region.

The strongest guarantee of such links between the biological component and the enterprise component of the project lies with the planning and decision-making process, the degree to which it genuinely steers the project, and the extent to which the consensus reached gains credibility within the modern legal framework.

Progress with consensus building during YRI led to the self- definition of administrative "culture zones" (see map below), to the

1 The attached article covering the Conservation and Development Issue Management

Process as it has developed over YRI has been produced to facilitate wider distribution.

page 6

OKARI ECOENTERPRISES PROJECT

SEMI-ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT

establishment of an Okari Ecoenterprises Board of Directors, to a revision of the Board of the Directors for Partners with Melanesians to reflect more input from the communities affected, to the formal registration of Okari Ecoenterprises Inc., and to the training of facilitators for each participating clan, creating an even stronger foundation for on-going decision-making.

The discussion around the role of women in the project triggered several protracted discussions about cultural values, cultural change, the introduction of innovations, and the level of harmony in the homes where women do take leading roles in planning and decision-making activities. The results of those discussion have led to reserving one position of the Okari Ecoenterprises Board of Directors for a woman, placing a woman in charge of the development and production of awareness materials, and encouragement for women to participate as clan group facilitators as just woman is doing at the moment. Facilitator training will also include strategies for encouraging the active participation of women in the clan group discussion meetings.

Management conflicts that cannot be resolved internally will be referred to the Community Relations Council who will hear both sides of the dispute and facilitate its resolution in much the same manner as they facilitate with other disputes. At the same time, the need to produce more and more effective public relations material as a means of forestalling misunderstandings has been stressed and added to the materials production entry of the budget.

Another lesson learned during the planning stage is that monitoring and evaluation tend to take a back seat to the pressing day-to-day problems of implementing a comprehensive program of this kind that touches almost every aspect of community life. At the same time, it is critical that such monitoring and evaluation is largely in the hands of those affected and that it reflects the pressures and realities of the inside situation. Experience has demonstrated that the more contrastive the cultures and value systems, the less likely evaluators from a dominant society will be able to fully "read" the social dynamics of the development program.

The alternative here, then, is to dedicate manpower to facilitate the monitoring and evaluation rather than trying to build it into the responsibilities of each staff person and his or her activity. This will introduce a stakeholder into the project program who will focus

page 7

OKARI ECOENTERPRISES PROJECT

SEMI-ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT

solely on monitoring and evaluation. The first objective of this monitoring and evaluation process will be a modest one but still a worthy one given the scope of the project and the critical need to deliver some record of its successes and failures. That objective is simply to maintain a running collection of records covering all meetings, forums, workshops, and data gathering exercises.

Easily a thousand pages of material was generated during the 6 month planning stage from each step of the forum process, from records of the clan group meetings, from the development of the resource maps, from the baseline data surveys and from the recording of local land use/tree access practices. However, all of that material is in various stages of processing at the moment and different pieces of it are different hands. Report prepared for Partners with Melanesia, Inc., Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. Author: Pius Piskaut, Division o
text:
VEGETATION AND PLANT SURVEY OF THE PROPOSED MANAGALAS PLATEAU CONSERVATION AREA: PHASE II REPORT. November 2005. Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, Ijivitari District, ORO Province. Report prepared for Partners with Melanesia, Inc., Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. Author: Pius Piskaut, Division of Biological Sciences, University of Papua New Guinea.

ABSTRACT: In November 2004 a rapid vegetation assessment was conducted near Itokama and surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. In November 2005 a phase 2 survey extended that work to gather baseline information on vegetation types, structure and plant diversity within the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area. Survey carried out at three sites: Kierim lower montane forest, Tahama forest, and Pongani forest near the coast. Plots of 50x50m demarcated; strip lines 5x50m at 10m intervals; trees >=5cm dbh measured; 5x5m quadrats for shrubs/herbs/saplings. Forest formations found: lower montane mixed Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans, monsoonal/dry evergreen forest, patches of savanna grassland toward coast. High proportion of trees dbh <30cm indicating young forest. Shannon Diversity Index average 1.50, higher than first Itokama survey. Very high species diversity. Recommends strengthening conservation initiatives by Managalas Development Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia and declaring the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area.

Managalas Plateau ~300,000 ha on the Managalas Plateau, Isivitari District, Oro Province, within Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests ecoregion (Owen Stanley Range). Study sites: Kierim Mountain (1200m, lower montane, Castanopsis accuminatissima and Lithocarpus dominant); Tahama forest (600m, low altitude, Anisoptera, Hopea, Pometia, Pangium, Elaeocarpus); Pongani (53m near coast, flood plain forest, savanna and monsoonal forests). Methods: 50x50m plots, 5x50m belt transects, diameter at breast height, height, species identification, Shannon diversity index, species-area curve. Total 289 species enumerated over 1.22 ha sampled. Vegetation types: low altitude forest, mixed Castanopsis forest, savanna grassland (Eucalyptus confertiflora, Imperata cylindrica kunai grass), monsoon/dry evergreen forest. Discussion of forest structure (young forests, suppressed growth, 1997/98 drought impact), plant species diversity, status of plants (orchids CITES-listed). Recommendations: conserve the forest, conduct further long-term studies, establish permanent study plots. References include Partners with Melanesia (2004) Coarse Scale Analysis of HCV1-6 of Managalas Plateau Conservation Area Project; Piskaut (2004). Appendix 1: full checklist of plant species (Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms — Fagaceae Castanopsis, Podocarpaceae, Araucariaceae, Arecaceae palms, Orchidaceae, Dipterocarpaceae Anisoptera/Hopea, Myrtaceae Syzygium, Lauraceae Cryptocarya, Meliaceae, Moraceae Ficus, Euphorbiaceae Macaranga, and many more). Appendix 2: photographic plates of flowering plants from 2004 and 2005 surveys.

text:
Partners With Melanesians Inc. — ANNUAL PROGRESS REPORT 2019. A National Not For Profit Conservation and Community Development Non-Government Organization operating in rural communities in PNG for over 30 years. Highlights from programs and project activities in four project sites, measured against the Partners With Melanesians strategy and five year logframe.

Contents: 1. PWM Vision Mission & Strategic Plan; 2. Program, Purpose and Results; 3. Project Sites and Activities; 4. Major Activities implemented in 2019; 5. Project Challenges; 6. Lessons Learnt; 7. Other Activities.

PWM is a national non-profit NGO involved in conservation and eco-friendly community development in Papua New Guinea, founded 1984 from a literacy project by academics and students at the University of Papua New Guinea to assist education initiatives in the Managalas Plateau of Oro Province.

Vision: Melanesian societies living in peace and harmony with nature and the environment. Mission: facilitate, formulate and strengthen conservation and sustainable community initiatives through education and consensus building with networking and partnerships. Strategic Plan 2018-2022. Core values: environmental stewardship, indigenous peoples, community empowerment, partnerships and networking, transparency and accountability. Policies: Environment Act 2000, Protected Areas Policies, Conservation Areas Management Act, Flora and Fauna Wildlife Management Act.

Eight key strategies/outputs: 1. Biodiversity Conservation and Community Mapping; 2. Community Empowerment and Decision Making; 3. Education and Awareness; 4. Community Forestry and Climate Change; 5. Sustainable Livelihood Alternative; 6. Gender Empowerment; 7. Appropriate Technology; 8. Capacity Building. Outputs targets 2018-2022 across four declared protected areas.

Four project sites: 1. Proposed Managalas and Mt. Karimui Conservation Areas — Managalas Conservation Area status granted, communities empowered to sustainably manage; Mt. Karimui status pending, Conservation Area Application to CEPA in 2020 with Karimui Conservation and Resource Management Program Inc. 2. Inaina WMA (Wildlife Management Area) sustainably managed. 3. Proposed Collingwood Bay Conservation Area — all 9 main tribes agreed to conservation, Collingwood Bay Conservation Foundation CBO, 5 zone system in 11 council wards, 650,000+ hectares.

Major 2019 activities: Annual Mt. Karimui Conservation, Agriculture & Culture Show (theme 'Life on Land: Our Livelihood', UN 17 SDGs), launch of Mt. Karimui Farmer's Cooperative Society, funded by RFN; sales of Managalas Organic Coffee in Lae, Morobe Province; Inaina WMA first Annual Village Combine Forum and stopping logging encroachment; Collingwood Bay scoping and research.

Risk Management: internal risks of threats to PWM officers by local CBO officers, high demand on project funds, incapable CBO leadership in Managalas; external risk of logging encroachment into Managalas Conservation Area zone 8 (eastern side) reported to PNG Forest Authority and exposed at Legal Forest Resource Week in Washington DC; Mt. Karimui CBO Project Director ownership disputes; Inaina WMA staff physically abused, awareness with University of Goroka interns; Collingwood Bay illegal logging FCA in lower Musa area, working with CELCOR and Oro Provincial head.

Lessons Learnt: time management and prioritization; addressing community and leadership issues including threats; addressing illegal logging with the right authorities. Organisational assessment: new finance officer; need for a Collingwood Bay project support officer. Unintended effects: PNG Provincial Local Level Government Elections July–September 2019 put activities on hold. Learning, partnership and capacity development with RFN.

Other Activities: Participatory 3 Dimensional Model (P3DM) — mapping method extracting topographic information and constructing a physical model to locate peoples' spatial memory of their land; a planning tool for resource owners and stakeholders; used for infrastructure, disaster management, health and education surveys, forest resource utilization, population survey, eco-tourism. PWM also supports World Environment Day and World Wildlife Day with schools in project sites.

snippet: 📊 Presentation. The Mammalian Fauna Composition of the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, Afore Subdistrict; Oro Province, Papua New Guinea A Condensed Presentation to the Board of Directors of Managalas Development Foundation and Partners With Melanesia Inc, Port Moresby.
text:
The Mammalian Fauna Composition of the 
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, Afore 
Subdistrict; Oro Province, Papua New Guinea 
A Condensed Presentation to the Board of Directors of 
Managalas Development Foundation and Partners With 
Melanesia Inc, Port Moresby.
Rose Kualke Singadan,
Division of Biological Sciences, University of PNG
Waigani Campus.

 
 
Fig 1. Map of the Managalas 
Proposed Conservation Area, Oro 
Province, PNG.

 
 
Contents
•
1.
Introduction
•
1.1. Sites of the survey – 2004, 2005, 2006
•
1.2
Aims and objectives
•
2.
Survey Methodology
•
2.1
Site Sampling
•
2.2
Diurnal and Nocturnal Sampling
•
2.3
Ethno Ecological interviews with locals
•
2.4  Cross referencing with previous records in 
Museum collections or Scientific publications
•
2.5 Other methods: - 1) Village markets  2) villagers looking 
after animals as pets.

 
 
Apologies.
• Mr. P Piskaut – University of PNG
Mr. P Kulmoi – Department of 
Environment and Conservation – Waigani
Both send their sincere apologies 
and warm wishes to everyone present.
 

 
 
Mammalian Composition and 
Diversity  
• Introduction:-
• 3 Biodiversity Inventories since 2004
2004 . Jarefa and Kadiakala – 674m asl
2005. Murayane at 890m asl – 1200m asl
Putei at 624m asl
Pongani at 100m asl
2006. Nambumare, Aiari at 563m asl
and Dakara, Umwate at 785m asl 

 
 
Survey Methods
• 1.
Site Sampling
• 2.
Diurnal and Nocturnal observations
• 3.
Ethno Ecological  interviews with Local 
people
• 4.
Cross referencing with previous 
records in 
Museum collections or with individual 
researchers
• 5.
Other methods:-
By chance at village markets or villagers 
keeping wild animal pets

 
 
Sampling methods
• 1. 
Site Sampling. 
• a. Rat traps (Elliot, Tomahawk traps or 
native traps)
b. Mist nets:- These are used for 
catching bats at night and 
birds 
during the daytime. 
• c. Hunting:- People set traps to catch 
animals eg., cuscus

 
 
2. Diurnal and Nocturnal 
sampling
• A. 
Walking, seeing or listening to sounds 
or 
calls in the bush / scents 
•
1.
Movements in the bush eg., scratches 
• 2.
Sneezing by animals 
• 3.
Scents of animals left behind when 
marking their 
territories
• 4.
Leaving behind ‘kitchen wastes.’ That is 
left over 
food & fecal materials eg., half eaten 
nuts, land snails, fruits and cherries
5. 
Sound of wing beats (bats/birds) 

 
 
3. Ethno Ecological interviews 
with locals
• Traditional knowledge of  local people
• Interviews with people by asking them to 
identify animals that are already in the books.
• Those that are caught are usually identified by 
the locals
• e.g., Phalanger intercastellanus
–
‘Nagiko’ &/or ‘ Ladia’

 
 
4. Cross referencing with known 
records in Museums
• a 
Cross reference with museum collections 
often happens when specimens are taken back 
to the Museums. In PNG there are two certified 
institutions:- The PNG National Museum, 
Waigani and University of PNG NSRC 
Collections.
• b.
Records kept by individual Researchers 
(Nationals or Expatriates) or kept at 
Department of Environment, Waigani.

 
 
5. Other methods
• 1. By chance at village markets eg., a new 
species of Tree Kangaroo found by Dr. 
Flannery in Wamena, West Papua – Indonesia.
• 2.
Villagers keeping animals as their pets
• E.g Cuscuses (Spotted Cuscus), Tree 
Kangaroos (Doria’s Tree Kangaroo)
• Dendrolagus sp
“Dingiso”

 
 
Results:- Biodiversity Inventory 
• Phase I – 2004 (11th – 27th November) 
• Itokama, Kwai,Nibaiba Jarefa and Kadiakala
approx 783m asl
• Phase II –  2005 (7th to 28th November 2005) 
• Murayane > 800m asl
• Putei  approx 630m asl
• Pongani approx 100m asl
• Phase III – 2006 (20th to 4th June 2006) 
Numbumare, Aiari at 537 masl
• Dakara, Umwate at 785m asl

 
 
Plate 1. Representative example of 
an Anteater.
The Long-beaked Echidna

 
 
Plate 2A. Representatives of 
Marsupials 
A.  Tree Kangaroos and Cuscuses. 

 
 
Plate 2. B.  Carnivoroues Marsupials
Dasyuridea – e.g., New Guinea Wild 
Pussycat

 
 
Plate 2. C. Bandicoots and Wallabies

 
 
Plate 3 : Representative examples of 
Rodents
A. Arboreal Rats (those that live in 
trees)

 
 
Plate 3. Representative examples of 
Bats
A. Flying Foxes

 
 
Plate 4. Insectivorous Bats

 
 
Plate 5. Nectarivorous Bats

 
 
Plate 6. Other interesting Bats

 
 
Plate 7. “The New Guinea Singing Dog”
Canis familiaris dingo (Cannis halstromi or 
Canis familiaris halstromi)
• Distributed across Island 
of New Guinea.
• Not recognised as a 
species yet
• Found at > 800masl
• Very aggressive and 
evasive behaviour
• Very territorial

 
 
4. Conservation Implications.
A. Species of Conservation value
• 1.
Protected Species – PNG
• 2 species of Tree Kangaroos, D. dorianus, D. 
goodfellowi
• Long-Beaked Echidna, Zaglossus bruijni
• 2. Others that require some conservation 
attention
•
All Cuscuses 
•
Mountain wallabies
•
Carnivorous Marsupials
•
Rare insectivorous and nectivorous bats 
•
The Water Rats of New Guinea
•
The New Guinea Singing Dog

 
 
5. Summary:- General Comments 
Managalas Proposed Conservation 
Area
•
A:- Very high diversity of mammals across the Plateau – 
Total of 26 species of mammals
•
8 Marsupials, 8 Rats, 6 Bats, 3 Domestic animals, 1 
Canine – still under species controversy
•
B:- There are still many more species to be sampled
•
C:- 2 species – Tree Kangaroos are already protected. 
Others data deficient to propose protection
•
D:- Gardening methods (slash & burn) creating gaps in 
forested areas for small mammals
•
E:- People still hunting wildlife indiscriminately BUT
•
F:- Abundant food resources for both humans and 
animals
•
G:- Basically People are self sufÏcient but lack extra 
cash income generating activities due to lack of proper 
road network.

 
 
6. Final Comments
•
I must say that people are very conscious of the 
environmental and Social issues that PWM Inc and 
MDF are trying to promote and facilitate. They  
understand because protection of the environment 
is about themselves (People), their children’s future 
and their Land.
•
The major issue now is infrastructure establishment. 
Proper Road and Bridge network into rural areas 
where the majority of the population in this country 
live AND where protected areas are concentrated 
and proposed.
•
I see that in Managalas and elsewhere throughout 
the country where I have been to. 
•
IF ONLY THERE ARE GOOD ROADS AND BRIDGES 
PEOPLE MIGHT LEAVE THE ANIMALS AND BUSH 
ALONE TO CONCENTRATE ON CASH CROPS AND 
OTHER SOURCES OF PROTEIN.

Introduction
The Managalas Plateau has a diverse frog, snake and lizard fauna not yet 
fully documented.
This is also true for other animals and plants including, orchids, insects and 
animals that live in many of the rivers and streams in the plateau.

Frogs
In NG there are about 250 different types of frogs known 
to science. This number increases every year as new 
species are discovered and described. Yet some frogs 
remain unknown in museum collections throughout the 
world.
The potential this holds for Managalas in terms of 
discovering new species that may strengthen the 
proposal for a conservation area is enormous.

 
 
Types of Frogs or Families documented
Four different families of frogs in NG. All represented in the Managalas 
Plateau. Cane Toads of the Bufonidae family is an introduced family.
Microhylidae
Asterophryneae

Myobatrachidae
Large to tinny. Do not breed in water, no tadpoles, give birth 
directly to froglets. Contains over 50% of frogs known from NG. 
Diverse group, lives underground, ground surface, tree tops and 
some spent some time in water.
Tree frogs, Litoria & Nyctymystes. Live close to rivers, streams, 
other water bodies. Greatest diversity in high altitude torrential 
streams. Usually beautiful colouration. Nyctymystes endemic to 
NG.
Large to medium sized, dark brown with bands on thighs. Live 
close to or along rivers, streams or pools. Sharp nosed, long 
jumpers.
Medium sized frogs. Easy to tell, have angular jaws. Live mostly

text:
Partners With Melanesians Inc. — ANNUAL REPORT 2020. A National Not For Profit Conservation and Community Development Non-Government Organization operating in PNG for over 30 years with support of the Rainforest Foundation of Norway. "Maintaining the Dance".

Chairlady's message (Laeko Bala, representing PNG National Council of Women): 2020 was a year full of challenges — financial setbacks and COVID-19 restrictions/lockdown prevented PWM Board, management and staff from implementing planned 2020 program activities.

Executive Director's message (Kenn Mondiai, Senior Forestry Officer): First AGM since incorporation as an NGO in 1998; PWM began on the Managalas Plateau of Oro Province in 1983-84 out of the UPNG Students' Project in Language and Literature. Over 36 years PWM moved from literacy and adult education into conservation (from 2000). Key achievements: 2017 double declaration of the Managalas Plateau as PNG's 2nd Conservation Area under the Conservation Area Act 1978 (360,000 hectares, Oro Province) and the Inaina Wildlife Management Area (9,700 hectares, Doa, Kairuku, Central Province). New projects: Collingwood Bay (CWB) in Tufi, Oro Province (650,000+ hectares, 9 tribal groups, SABL and illegal logging challenges) and proposed Karimui Conservation Project in Simbu (27 wards, KCRMPI local CBO). 2020 marks the 25th year of partnership with the Norwegian Rainforest Foundation (RFN). Staff numbers grew to 14 (then 19).

Brief history, Vision ("Melanesian Societies living in peace and harmony with nature and environment"), Mission, Core Values (Environmental Stewardship, Indigenous Peoples, Community Empowerment, Partnerships and Networking, Transparency and Accountability). Strategic Direction 2001-2022 across four strategic planning documents (2002-2006, 2007-2011, 2013-2017, 2018-2022) aligned with Government Vision 2050 Pillar 5 Environmental Sustainability and Climate Change. Key Strategies/Programs: 1 Biodiversity Conservation and Community Mapping; 2 Community Empowerment and Decision Making; 3 Education and Awareness; 4 Community Forestry and Climate Change; 5 Sustainable Livelihood Alternative; 6 Gender Empowerment; 7 Appropriate Technology/Special Projects; 8 Capacity Building; 9 Finance and Administration.

Board Members and Staff (2020, 19 staff): Kenn Mondiai (Executive Director/Senior Forestry Officer), Patrick Vuet (Acting Program Manager/Biodiversity & Community Mapping), Jacinta Gure (Finance & Admin Manager), Kovi Wara, Hobert Poria, Lillian Bago, Rozabelle Horta, Cecil Senive; Board Chairlady Laeko Bala; Simon Savaiko; Tom Huasi; Ps Albert Rovi; Kelly Kalit (The Nature Conservancy); project officers Bradley Dabadaba (Collingwood Bay), John Songi and Peter Noimbano (Karimui), Chris Jaimie (Fundraising and M&E).

Four project sites: Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP, 360,000 ha, Ijivitari District Oro, declared 27 November 2017 by Minister for CEPA & Climate Change Hon. John Pundari, now managed by Managalas Conservation Foundation MCF via MOU); Inaina Wildlife Management Area (IWMA, 9,712.2 ha, Fagagara Clan, Kairuku Hiri District Central Province, gazetted 23 March 2017); Proposed Karimui Conservation Area Project (PKCAP, Mt Karimui 14,000 ha, Chimbu/Simbu Province, KCRMPI); Proposed Collingwood Bay Conservation Area Project (PCWBCAP, Tufi LLG Ijivitari District Oro, 650,000+ ha).

2020 program progress (all affected by COVID-19): biodiversity/mapping; community empowerment (Karimui combine ward forum held October before Karimui Show); education and awareness; community reforestation (nurseries at Inaina WMA and Karimui, ~4000 seedlings); sustainable livelihood (Karimui cooperative society, IRC certificate, 150+ members); gender empowerment (gender-based violence awareness workshops); capacity building (Training Needs Assessment TNA). Budget decreased by K780,000 due to depleted back-donor funding to RFN; 2019 audit issues; new donor Earthworm Foundation Inc via Forest Conservation Fund (FCF) 2020-2025 for Inaina WMA ranger program.

Risk assessment: COVID-19 State of Emergency restrictions; logging encroachment into Managalas Conservation Area zone 8 (reported to PNG Forest Authority, exposed at Legal Forest Resource Week Washington DC); Karimui CBO leadership disputes; Inaina WMA tensions and officer abuse; Collingwood Bay illegal logging FCA lower Musa (with CELCOR, Oro Provincial head). Lessons learnt: time management, addressing leadership issues/threats, addressing illegal logging. Recognised by the Asian Ecotourism Network (AEN); Chairman Masaru Takayama visited Inaina WMA. 2020 Karimui Conservation, Agriculture & Cultural Show (3rd, 18-20 November). Participatory 3 Dimensional Model (P3DM) mapping with Tree Kangaroo Conservation Program at YUS LLG, Kabwum District, Morobe Province. World Environment Day and World Wildlife Day school programs.

text:
DECLARATION OF THE MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA, 29th NOVEMBER 2017 — Post-Courier newspaper feature (Wednesday, November 29, 2017). Official declaration at Itokama, Afore sub-district, Ijivitari District, Oro Province. Theme: Kuaefienamp. "ESE ESE ESE... Welcome to Managalas Conservation."

The Managalas Conservation Area was officially declared by representatives from the Ministry of Environment and Conservation and Climate Change (CEPA) and the Department of the Prime Minister and NEC. Partners With Melanesians (PWM) worked on the Managalas Plateau for over three decades to protect 360,000 hectares of rainforest, its 22,000 inhabitants and natural resources through community mobilization and consensus building.

The Managalas Plateau rises from 60 to 2,888 metres above sea level in the Owen Stanley ranges, covered with pristine tropical rainforest and anthropogenic grassland. Home to the rare Queen Alexandra's Birdwing Butterfly (Ornithoptera alexandrae, the world's biggest butterfly), several species of Birds of Paradise, insects, frogs, snakes, New Guinea Singing Dogs, Tree Kangaroos, and the Managalas people of 5 dialect groups: Barai, Namiai, Samoi, Omie and Eise. One of the few remaining areas of Oro Province untouched by logging and oil palm development — the second biggest Conservation Area in PNG.

On 8 November 2012 the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area application was submitted by the Managalas people led by Governor Hon. Gary Juffa MP to Hon. John Pundari, Minister for Environment and Conservation and CEPA, under the Conservation Areas Act 1978. Approved 15 December 2016 by NEC Decision No. 325/2016, signed by Governor General Sir Bob Dadae, published in the National Gazette 22 March 2017.

PWM eco-enterprise activities based on local produce (Okari nuts, vegetables, coffee) faced challenges of transport, weather, communication and markets. With the declaration, PWM works with local partner Managalas Conservation Foundation (MCF) and its eleven (11) CBOs, building human resource capacity to independently manage the conservation area and pursue sustainable livelihood activities. Financial support mainly from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway (RFN), partnership since 1996. Community consensus building process began when tribal and clan elders came together at Dea village in 1992. Unlike YUS Conservation Area (Huon Peninsula), the Managalas Plateau is an area where humans co-exist with the natural environment. Biodiversity surveys conducted 2004-2008 by PWM with partners UPNG, CEPA and others.

MANAGALAS PLATEAU COMMUNITY CONSERVATION AREA
REPORT ON THE FIRST MANAGEMENT PLAN WORKSHOP

1. INTRODUCTION

This report is presented in partial fulfillment of my terms of reference but itis also hoped that it
will make a constructive contribution to the work of all parties in the project area in achieving the
primary objectives of having the Managalas Plateau declared a conservation area, managing it as
such, and facilitating the type of development that is sustainable over the long term, socially
‘equitable, and not destructive to the unique environment and culture of the area. This is important
not only for the well-being of present and future generations of its inhabitants, but also for
conservation in PNG in the hope that it may present a viable, alternative mode! for development in
the country.

In line with my terms of reference I have included observations about the way the project seems to
bbe proceeding and some recommendations that may improve the project's activities. This report
obviously cannot be and is not intended to be a comprehensive project evaluation. I have only
been in PNG a short time and have had very limited exposure to the project area, the community,
and the PwM and MDF staff on the ground. However, that said, my insight is based on years of
‘experience in similar types of initiatives and community conservation work and will hopefully
prove to be useful.

MANAGEMENT PLAN WORKSHOP.

2.1 Pre-planning for the Werkshop

‘A short meeting was held with the PwM staff in Port Moresby 4s to the typical contents of a
‘management plae: and it was agreed that it would be useful for me to sitare my expertise with the
project whilst in PNG and assist in the initial devetopment of a such. It was suggested that I visit
the project area and hold two (east and west) two-day workshops with the community, firstly to
introduce the concept and secondly to facilitate discussion around issues that need to be addressed
by the management plan. This information would then inform the management plan framework
and my suggestions on how to proceed with the further development of the plan. Whilst it was the
only option open to us given time constraints, | think it would have been more constructive if we
had had time for more detailed preparatory discussions with the Project Officer and MDF staff.

‘A detailed workshop programme was prepared, together with a list of participants to be invited to
the workshop, and this was handed over to the PwM Admin Officer to circulate and send out
invitations, Unfortunately it scems that neither the Project Officer in Afore nor the MDF staff
received this programme and so they were Jeft in the dark as to the details of what the workshop
‘would be about, as were the community.

Not having first hand experience of the project and the level of understanding around the issues
proposed for discussion it was also very difficult for me to know at what level the workshop
 should be pitched, and the guidance of project staff was crucial in this respect. Stephen Sukot was
also in a disadvantaged position as this was his first visit to the project area.

22 Workshop at okama

We arrived in Itokama on Sunday afternoon and were greeted by Robert Kubin and George
Tumai, The afternoon was spent in general discussion with them about the area and they offered
various insights into project activities and conservation issues. Monday had been put aside for
planning the workshops together with the Project Officer and MDF staff (west). Unfortunately
Jacob was unable to join us for the first planning session and workshop and also felt that it was
more important that he stay in Afore and organize things for the second workshop, making sure
that as many people as possible attend. An agenda was proposed by myself and discussed with
Stephen Sukot and the MDF staff (Dagi, Luke, Roy and Alberta) and it was agreed who would
Jead which discussions.

‘The workshop was to start on Tuesday at 08400 as MDF suggested, but few people were there by
even 09H30, including the MDF staff. Eventually the workshop commenced at about !0H00, still
without Dagi, who was supposed to do the welcome and introductions and get the workshop going
but who was busy on the radio. George Tumai stepped in and played this role and then Steven
‘Sukot took over and facilitated from then on. Alberta who was supposed to have being taking the
minutes arrived late and was clearly not happy. When I asked her what the problem was she said
that Luke had threatened her with a knife in the office the day before.

‘The following points can be made about the first workshop:

‘* Itsoon became clear that the agenda that had been set was very ambitious and with ongoing
problems with punctuality the time for discussion was also cut short.

‘+ There seemed to be a lack of awareness about the purpose of the workshop and indecd the
subject of the management plan. The perception seemed to be that it was a course and that
there should be handouts, rather than it being a workshop designed to gather information and
ideas from the participants. This may have been the first wo:kshop of this nature and if so,
people will probably be better prepared and know what to expect for the next one.

‘© Representation and attendance were relatively poor (register attached), with no elders, women
‘or youths from any of the zones present, and no general community observers. It is not clear if
this was due to a lack of awareness about the importance of the workshop, short notice being
given to participants, or if it was due (o it being an important time of the year for gardens - the
reason given for the elders’ absence. Furthermore, there were only two local government
councilors present on the first day and only one on the second day. Neither provincial nor
national government representatives attended

© Some of the MDF staff chose not to attend and participate in the full workshop proceedings
and this sent out a bad message to the participants. George Tumai and Robert Kubini attended
both days and provided useful guidance, both as board members and as elders.

‘* Apparently there were problems with the budgeting for the workshop, which caused tension
between PwM and MDF. Unfortunately this was allowed to spill over and affect workshop
proceedings. This may perhaps have been further exacerbated by some of the MDF staff
feeling they were not in control of proceedings?
 ‘Translations between English and Pigine took place as and when required. It would obviously
have been betier had we not faced this constraint, however, it scems that the understanding
between myself and the participants was reasonable.

CELCOR was unable to send a Lawyer and thus the presentation on the Conservation Areas
‘Act was based on CELCOR's pare-legal training manual and our lay knowledge of the Act
However, this seems to have been sufficient for the purpose of the workshop (presuming
Steven Sukot and myself have interpreted the Act correctly). There was a heated discussion
around whether or not a move should be made requesting the retevant minister to recommend
that the area be declared CCA. The argument against doing so was that the boundary
‘mapping and the biodiversity survey are not complete. Eventually it was agreed that there are
already more than sufficient grounds for making the motivation and that the onus is on the
Minister and the NEC to request further information should they require it. There were also
strong fears voiced that any further delays could be disastrous as threats to the area grow and a
number of people voiced frustfation over slow progress being made with certain activities,
particularly the boundary mapping.

Once the opening and background presentations (purpose of the workshop and review of
activities to date and what's needed in the future, review of Conservation Areas Act and
introduction to what a management plan is and what information it contains) were complete
‘we moved onto the more interactive discussions around natural resource management and land
use planning. Participation in these sessions was better as people were able to relate to the
discussion and draw on their knowledge and experience. Once we broke into groups, people
seemed to be enthusiastic and they worked well to develop management guidelines and plan
Jand uses. The report backs indicated that they were thinking about things but there was an
obvious lack of exposure to many of the more technical issues and to this way of planning,
One of the groups presented a method or plan of action for developing the management
guidelines, rather than starting on the guidelines themselves, and there was some debate about
Which was more appropriate. It was again pointed out that the workshop was simply a first
step or starting point and that it would not eliminate the need for further broad-based
discussions and consensus. However, it was disturbing in that one presumes that as
community clected representatives the participants should have felt sufficiently empowered to
speak on behalf of their communities and it again begs the question as to the level of
understanding and acceptance of the project within the community.

‘The presentation and discussions around Sustainable Development Options was cut short due
to a lack of time but a further observation from this session is that there is a strong need for
training and skills development with respect to small business and economic activities. People
also require further exposure to sustainable development options, particularly tourism, as itis
clearly (and understandably) not something that most of them have had exposure to. Without
such exposure it is very difficult for them to imagine what potential tourism might hold for the
area,

‘The workshop was closed with the participants drafting a statement for submission to
CELCOR for legal drafting, requesting that the area be declared @ CCA. This was an
important and empowering step and renewed people’s sense of purpose ~ rather than just
talking about it and preparing for it they were finally doing it!! It was made very clear that the
statement was drafted by the workshop participants and that once put into legal terms it would
have to be brought back to the communities for complete clarification and consensus before
signing by all landowners and submission to the Minister.

‘The following way forward was agreed on. (1) Workshop summary to be written up,
translated into Pigine and then distributed to all the CBO’s. People agreed that it would be
 useful if this included some points for further discussion amongst the community and that this
‘would also form part of the preparation for the second workshop. (2) Second management
plan workshop to be held before the end of the year. (3) Ensure the involvement of other
stakeholders, particularly government, and efforts are to be made by PwM and MDF in this
regard. (4) CBO members and all workshop participants to increase their efforts at building
awareness in their communities and talk about what they learnt and did at the workshop and
the need for conservation. (5) CELLCOR to draft a statement and return this to the community
for discussion, consensus, finalization and signing as soon as possible.

‘The participant's comments (attached) on the workshop were very positive in that most of them
felt that they had learnt 2 lot, which empowered them. They thought that the topics under
discussion were of importance to their communities and ensuring the conservation of the arca.
‘There were frustrations with the short duration of the workshop and most people seemed to think
that it needed to be much longer. The pace could then be stowed down, giving people the chance
to come to grips with the new things they were being asked to think about and participate more
fully. In this respect there were also requests that the presenters/facilitators get concepts across
more simply. Many people asked that further workshops of this tature be held though one
frustrated person noted ‘what upsets me is workshop after workshop but no changes?” A lot of
people felt that the absence of notebooks and handouts was a problem, even though they were
encouraged to participate rather than take notes and were assured that the summary of proceedings
would be sent to them (possibly duc to past failures to keep this promise?). There were also
requests that attention be paid to ensuring the involvement of other stakeholders (women, elders,
government, etc) and disappointment at the lack of participation of senior PwM staff and MDF
staff,

2.3 Workshop at Afore

Afier a very beautiful (if wet) walk across the plateau we arrived in Afore and were met by Jacob.
As the second workshop was to start the next day we met that evening and discussed how things
had gone with the first workshop and how we needed to adapt the programme in the light of
‘comments received from workshop participants. Having conducted one workshop already we
were able to simplify and streamline the programme, leaving more time for discussion and
allowing us to go at a slower pace. Jacob was also very helpful in this respect, giving us guidance
‘on what to expect and making some useful suggestions on how to adapt the programme,

‘The following points can be made:

© The workshop got off to a punctual start the next day at 091100 and was well attended by
CBOs and general observers with elders, women and some youths also present. Rules were
suggested and agreed on and Jacob facilitated proceedings in an efficient manner, ensuring
full understanding and encouraging participation by everyone present.

* After the welcome and introductions, the morning was spent reviewing project activities and
what needs to happen from here on, and in this regard the purpose of the workshop was
clarified. The Conservation Areas Act and what a management plan is and what information
it contains. People were very interactive and asked a lot of questions, generating some
insightful discussion. This also served as a good basis for the rest of the workshop.

. After lunch the workshop focused on resource use and management, and threats to those
resources. People broke up into groups and continued into the carly evening working on
their presentations for the next day. The presentations were well done but again it became
evident that there were different levels of understanding amongst the participants. People
 were able to identify the various threats and problems they were facing, but were not always
clear on the root causes of these problems. Nor were they sure about what management
actions could be taken to address these.

+ The rest of the day included a session on tanduse planning, a presentation on sustainable
development options, including tourism and the drafting ef statement for CELCOR. ‘The
way forward was agreed on and the workshop was closed.

‘The participant’s comments (attached) were again very positive. They felt that they learnt a lot
and there were a number of requests for more workshops of this nature. It was also requested that
workshops be more widespread and that they be held in different zones so that more people
participate in and benefit from them. A few people noted that a longer workshop would be useful

2.4 General Comments on Workshops

‘The workshop at Afore went off better than the workshop at Itokama. Things were better
organized, there were more participants (and observers) and they were also better informed as to
the purpose of the workshop, there was better representation by elders and women (though it is a
very strongly recommended that far more effort be put into ensuring the involvement of women in
all levels of project activity) and there was more open and active participation in proceedings. The
facilitators were also better prepared for the second workshop having been able to gauge the level
of understanding from the first workshop and were abie to present the material in a more
streamlined fashion, focusing on fewer issues and leaving more time for discussion and
understanding around those.

3. OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

3.1 Community Awareness

Whilst it is difficult to assess how far things have come in terms of building awareness amongst
the community around environmental issues, i is possible to comment on what seems to be needed
into the future. Participants at both workshops were aware of the critical importance of
conservation and protecting their environment, some more strongly or more vocally than othc:s,
and with the most focus on extemal threats and the least focus on dwindling forest resources.
However, they seemed less able to translate this into practical action. This may simply have been
an artifact of the way the workshop and subject material was presented, but it seemed also to stem
from a lack of exposure to critical thinking about resource use, planning and management.

‘A further example of this that also raises the question of how well people are able to communicate
issues that they discuss and Jearn about in workshops to their communities happened when 1
visited the village of one of the participants in the evening, at the end of two long days talking
about conservation, dwindling animal populations, the potential of birds for eco-tourism, etc.
Whilst gathered around chatting to villagers there was sudden excitement and then one of the
young men in the group dashed to one side and shot a stone up into the trees with his catapult.
When I asked what they were shooting at J was told it was an owl. When I asked why and if they
were going to eat it I was told no, just for fun. The workshop participant showed no sign of being
bothered by this and made no move to discuss the issue with the group. When I asked him why
not and I talked to the people about the need to look after the animals and trees carefully and
 ‘mentioned that that is why tourists will pay to visit the area, they thanked me and he looked very
embarrassed. Perhaps coming from me it carried more weight or perhaps he would have said
something if | had not been there? Either way the message needs to get out to many people as
possible and it needs to be certain that this is in fact happening through ongoing monitoring and
evaluation of the effectiveness of awareness and educational efforts. Cause for concem was also
raised a participant at the first workshop said that many people from his zone (10— new?) were
‘wary of conservation and the negative impacts it might have on their lives, though it was
mentioned that these were mostly elders and it is possible that they feel threatened by changes to
their lives that they feel unable to control,

People were obviously stronger when it came to land tenure and agricultural issues, but in
discussions about depleted forest resources were less able to articulate the causes of problems and
articulate possible solutions. There were also seemingly few traditional and customary
‘management practices that could be applied to the situation, though these may come out in time
with further workshopping and more widespread discussion.

It became apparent that people need to be prepared for the impacts of “westem style” development
and ‘western’ goods, for example, there were a number of alarming discussions around the use of
houschold, industrial and agro-chemicals with people displaying a very limited understanding of
the proper use and the negative impacts of these. At both workshops there was limited
understanding displayed of business and economic issues and it is recommended that some sort of
training and skills development in this regard be organized. An in situ small business centre that is
